there was a discussion of welcoming Qín and resisting Xiāng—
this is the fifth;
failing to plan the defense of Yān and surrendering instead—
this is the sixth;
disregarding great righteousness,
serving the Jīn—
this is the seventh;
confiscating the wealth of Yān,
seeking to please the Jīn—
this is the eighth;
causing the people of Yān to migrate and lose their livelihoods—
this is the ninth;
instructing the Jīn people to dispatch troops to first conquer Píngzhōu—
this is the tenth.
You have ten crimes,
for which you cannot be spared execution."
Zuǒ Qǐgōng and the others had no reply,
and were all strangled to death.
They still proclaimed the third year of Bǎodà,
painted the likeness of Tiānzuò,
paid respects morning and evening,
ensuring that matters were reported before being carried out,
and used the official ranks of Liáo.
In the sixth month,
a proclamation was posted instructing the people of Yān to resume their livelihoods.
Permanent property that had been occupied by the Chángshèng Army
was entirely returned.
Once the people of Yān were able to return,
they were greatly delighted.
Hanlin Academician Lǐ Shí changed his name to Ānbì,
and together with the former Commissioner of Finance Gāo Dǎng, went to Yānshān.
They advised the Sòng leader Wáng Ānzhōng, saying:
"Píngzhōu has over ten thousand armed troops,
and Jué possesses civil and martial talents.
He can be used as a bulwark;
otherwise,
he will become a threat close at hand."
Ānzhōng highly approved of this,
and ordered Ānbì and Dǎng to proceed to Sòng.
The Sòng ruler commanded the commanders Wáng Ānzhōng and Zhān Dù to provide generous pacification,
and granted an exemption from regular taxes for three years.
Jué heard of this,
and considered his plan successful.
In the seventh month of autumn,
the Jīn people were stationed at Láizhōu.
Shé Mǔ heard that Píngzhōu had allied with Sòng,
and, with two thousand cavalry, marched to punish them,
first entering Yíngzhōu.
Jué used ten thousand elite cavalry to defeat them.
Sòng established Píngzhōu as the Tàiníng Military Command,
making Jué the Jiedushi (Military Governor).
Ānbì and Dǎng were made Huīyóugé Dàizhì,
and the Pacification Commission was ordered to disburse tens of thousands in silver and silk for rewards.
Jué was delighted,
and traveled far to meet them.
The Jīn scouts learned this,
raised troops and came to attack.
Jué was unable to return,
and fled to Yān.
The Jīn people conquered the three prefectures,
and began to demand Jué.
Wáng Ānzhōng concealed his whereabouts.
As the demand became urgent,
he executed one person who looked similar and sent the body away.
The Jīn people said,
"This is not Jué,"
and came to seize him with troops.
Ānzhōng had no choice but to
kill Jué,
enclose his head in a box, and send it to the Jīn.
Tiānzuò had already regained the troops led by Chief Minister Yēlǜ Dàshí,
and also gained the forces of Mógěshī of the Yīnshān Shìwěi.
He considered himself to have heavenly assistance,
and plotted once more to launch troops
and recover Yān and Yún.
Chief Minister Dàshí strongly advised, saying:
"When the Jīn people first captured Chángchūn and Liáoyáng,
the Imperial Carriage retreated to Guǎngpíngdiàn,
and made Zhōngjīng the capital;
when they captured Shàngjīng,
Yānshān was made the capital;
when they captured Zhōngjīng,
the court moved to Yúnzhōng;
and from Yúnzhōng, it was exiled to Jiāshān.
Previously, with intact armies, we failed to plan for war preparations,
allowing the entire nation's Hàn territory to fall into the hands of the Jīn.
When the state's power has reached this point,
to still seek battle
is not a wise plan.
We should build up our forces, await the right moment, and then act;
we must not make rash moves."
The advice was not followed.
Dàshí then killed Yǐ Xuē and Pōlǐ Kuò,
established northern and southern official departments,
declared himself king,
and led his subordinates westward.
The Emperor then led all the armies out of Jiāshān,
descended Yúyánglǐng,
and captured Tiāndé, Dōngshèng, Níngbiān, Yúnnèi, and other prefectures.
He proceeded south to Wǔzhōu,
encountered the Jīn people,
and fought at Yǎn’èxiàshuǐ.
He was defeated again,
and headed directly for Shānyīn.
In the eighth month,
the Imperial Maternal Uncle Xiāngwěn Xiāo Tàbùyě and the Palace Attendant Cà Lā surrendered to the Jīn.
In this month,
the Jīn ruler Āgǔdǎ died.
In the ninth month,
Jiànzhōu surrendered to the Jīn.
In the tenth month of winter,
Āngě, the wife of É Gē of the Tūlǚbù tribe, was accepted.
É Gē was made the Jiedushi (Military Governor) of his tribe.
Zhāo Gǔyá led his multitude to surrender to the Jīn.
The Jīn attacked Xīngzhōng Prefecture
and captured it.
In the eleventh month,
those who followed the Emperor raised a rebellion.
The Northern Guard Grand Tutor Shùzhě and Shèlì Xiāngwěn Yábùlǐ, among others, defeated them.
In the twelfth month,
two Commanderies-in-Chief were established.
Basic Annals Thirty: Emperor Tiānzuò IV
In the fifth year, spring, the first month, on the *xīnsì* day,
Xiǎohúlù (小斛祿) of the Dǎngxiàng (黨項) sent men requesting [His Majesty] to approach their territory.
On the *wùzǐ* day,
[He] hurried toward Tiāndé (天德).
While crossing the desert,
Jīn (金) soldiers suddenly arrived.
The Emperor (Shàng) fled on foot.
A close attendant offered a pearl cap,
but [He] refused it.
Riding the horse of Zhāng Rén’guì (張仁貴), [He] managed to escape
and reached Tiāndé (天德).
On the *jǐchǒu* day,
[They] encountered snow.
Lacking gear to ward off the cold,
Zhúzhě (朮者) presented a sable fur coat and cap.
When food ran out along the way,
Zhúzhě (朮者) presented dates to eat.
When [He] wished to rest,
Zhúzhě (朮者) immediately knelt down,
allowing [Him] to lean upon him and feign sleep.
Zhúzhě (朮者) and his company only chewed ice and snow to relieve their hunger.
They passed Tiāndé (天德).
When night fell,
intending to lodge in a commoner's house,
[They] falsely claimed to be scouting cavalry.
The family knew [the truth],
then struck the horse’s head,
knelt, and wept bitterly.
[The Emperor] secretly lodged at their house.
After staying several days,
[The Emperor] commended their loyalty,
and remotely granted them the title of *Jiédùshǐ* (節度使).
Subsequently, [He] hurried toward Dǎngxiàng (黨項).
Xiǎohúlù (小斛祿) was appointed Commissioner of Pacification of the Southwest Sector (*Xīnánmiàn Zhāotǎoshǐ*),
overseeing all military affairs,
and furthermore, his son and various officers were given titles and rewards according to their rank.
In the second month,
when [He] reached a spot sixty *lǐ* east of Xīnchéng (新城) in Yìngzhōu (應州),
[He] was captured by the Jīn (金) people, including Wányán Lóushì (完顏婁室).
In the eighth month, on the *guǐmǎo* day,
[He] arrived at Jīn (金).
On the *bǐngwǔ* day,
[He] was demoted and enfeoffed as the Prince of Hǎibīn (Hǎibīn Wáng).
[He] died of illness,
at the age of fifty-four.
He had reigned for twenty-four years.
In the second month of the first year of Huángtǒng (皇統) of Jīn (金),
[He] was posthumously re-enfeoffed as the Prince of Yù (Yù Wáng).
In the fifth year,
[He] was buried next to Qiánlíng (乾陵) in Lǘyáng County (Lǘyáng Xiàn), Guǎngníng Prefecture (Guǎngníng Fǔ).
As for Yēlǜ Chún (耶律淳),
his era is historically known as Běiliáo (北遼) [Northern Liáo].
Chún’s (淳) nickname (small name) was Nièlǐ (涅里).
He was the fourth grandson of Emperor Xīngzōng (興宗),
and the son of Hélǔwò (和魯斡), the Grand Protector of Nánjīng (Nánjīng Liúshǒu) and Prince Sòng Wèi (Sòng Wèi Wáng).
In the beginning of Qīngníng (清寧),
the Empress Dowager raised him.
Once grown,
he deeply enjoyed literature and scholarship.
When the Crown Prince Zhāohuái (昭懷) committed an offense,
the Emperor (Shàng) wished to make Chún (淳) the heir.
The Emperor (Shàng) was angry at Yēlǜ Báisībù (耶律白斯不).
Knowing that Báisībù was close to Chún (淳),
[the Emperor] sent Chún (淳) out to serve as *Jiédùshǐ* (節度使) of the Zhāngshèng Army (Zhāngshèng Jūn) and others.
When Tiānzuò (天祚) ascended the throne,
[Chún] was advanced to Prince of Zhèng (Zhèng Wáng).
In the second year of Qiántǒng (乾統),
he was further granted the title Prince of Yuè (Yuè Wáng).
In the sixth year,
he was appointed Chancellor of the Southern Administration (*Nánfǔ Zǎixiàng*).
He was the first to propose establishing ritual procedures for the two administrations (Liǎng Fǔ).
The Emperor (Shàng) was pleased,
and moved [Chún] to the title Prince of Wèi (Wèi Wáng).
When his father Hélǔwò (和魯斡) died,
Chún (淳) immediately inherited his father’s post as Grand Protector of Nánjīng (Nánjīng).
He attended court in winter and summer,
and his favor surpassed all other princes.
In the fifth year of Tiānqìng (天慶),
during the Eastern Campaign,
the Metropolitan Supervisor Zhāngnú (章奴) crossed the Yāzǐ River (Yāzǐ Hé).
He and Chún’s (淳) son Āsā (阿撒), along with over three hundred others, fled and returned.
They first sent Dīlǐ (敵里) and others to inform Chún (淳) of their plot to depose [the Emperor] and establish a successor.
Chún (淳) cut off Dīlǐ’s (敵里) head and presented it [to the Emperor].
[Chún] was advanced to the title King of Qínjìn State (Qínjìn Guówáng),
appointed Commander-in-Chief (*Dū Yuánshuài*),
granted a golden certificate,
exempted from the Hàn (漢) style of kneeling rituals,
and addressed without his personal name.
He was permitted to select his own generals and officers.
Thereupon, he recruited elite soldiers from Yān (燕) and Yún (雲).
Traveling east to Jǐnzhōu (錦州),
Squad Leader Wǔ Cháoyàn (武朝彥) raised a rebellion
and kidnapped Chún (淳).
Chún (淳) hid and escaped capture.
[He] captured Cháoyàn (朝彥) and executed him.
At this juncture, Jīn (金) troops arrived.
[He] gathered troops and fought at Ālǐzhěndǒu (阿里軫斗),
but suffered defeat.
[He] rallied several thousand surviving soldiers to resist them.
Chún (淳) went to court;
[the Emperor] pardoned his offense,
and decreed that a stone tablet be carved in Nánjīng (南京) to commemorate his achievement.
In the second year of Bǎodà (保大),
when Tiānzuò (天祚) entered Jiāshān (夾山),
Huílíbǎo (回離保), King of the Xī (奚), Yēlǜ Dàshí (耶律大石), *Línyá* (林牙), and others invoked the precedent of Língwǔ (靈武) during the Táng (唐) dynasty,
and discussed establishing Chún (淳) as emperor.
Chún (淳) initially refused.
His officials and subordinates urged him to ascend the throne, saying:
"The sovereign (Zhǔshàng) is in distress,
and the Central Plains (*Zhōngyuán*) is in turmoil.
If the Prince is not established,
where will the people turn?
You should consider this carefully."
Consequently, [Chún] ascended the throne.
The officials presented him with the title Emperor Tiānxī (Tiānxī Huángdì).
The second year of Bǎodà (保大) was changed to the first year of Jiànfú (建福),
and a general amnesty was granted.
Nineteen people, including the *Jìnshì* (進士) Lǐ Bǎoxìn (李寶信), were released.
Tiānzuò (天祚) was remotely demoted to Prince of Xiāngyīn (Xiāngyīn Wáng).
The six circuits of Yān (燕), Yún (雲), Píng (平), Shàngjīng (上京), Zhōngjīng (中京), and Liáoxī (遼西)
were administered by Chún (淳);
while the area north of the desert, the two Pacification Commanderies (*Dū Zhāotǎofǔ*) of the Northern and Southern routes, and all various dependent tribes
remained subordinate to Tiānzuò (天祚).
From this point, the Liáo (遼) state was divided.
He enfeoffed his wife, Pǔxiánnǚ (普賢女), as Virtuous Consort (Défēi).
Huílíbǎo (回離保) was appointed to oversee the affairs of the Northern Chancellery (*Běiyuàn Shūmìshǐ*).
All military affairs were entirely entrusted to Dàshí (大石).
Furthermore, he sent an envoy to report to Sòng (宋),
requesting exemption from annual tribute,
and seeking to establish good relations.
The Sòng (宋) people dispatched troops to question [his legitimacy] and punish [him],
but [Chún's forces] defeated them.
Soon after, [Chún] sent an envoy to present a memorial to Jīn (金),
begging to become their vassal state.
Before the matter was resolved,
Chún (淳) died of illness,
at the age of sixty.
The officials posthumously gave him the false title Emperor Xiàozhāng (Xiàozhāng Huángdì).
His temple name was Xuānzōng (宣宗).
He was buried at Yǒng’ānlíng (永安陵) in Xīangshān (香山), west of Yān (燕).
His dying command was to remotely establish Qín Wáng Dìng (秦王定) to preserve the state,
and that the Virtuous Consort (Défēi) should become Empress Dowager (Huáng Tàihòu),
and assume regency.
The era name Jiànfú (建福) was changed to Dédéxīng (德興) first year.
One hundred and eight people, including the *Jìnshì* (進士) Lǐ Qiú (李球), were released.
At that time, Sòng (宋) troops came to attack.
[The Liáo forces] defeated them in battle.
Due to this, the morale of the people was greatly boosted,
and the military power strengthened daily.
Chancellor Lǐ Chún (李純) and others secretly admitted Sòng (宋) troops.
Residents inside the city provided internal assistance,
and many of those guarding the passes were killed.
The next day,
[the Sòng troops] attacked the inner east gate.
The guards fought fiercely,
and the Sòng (宋) army suffered a major defeat.
They climbed over the wall and fled;
the dead lay piled upon one another.
[The regency] sent five memorials to Jīn (金),
requesting the establishment of the Prince of Qín (Qín Wáng),
but [Jīn] did not comply.
When the Jīn (金) army arrived in force,
the Virtuous Consort (Défēi) fled to the Tiāndé Army (Tiāndé Jūn),
and met Tiānzuò (天祚).
Tiānzuò (天祚) was enraged.
He executed the Virtuous Consort (Défēi),
posthumously demoted Chún (淳) to commoner,
and removed him from the imperial genealogy.
As for Yēlǜ Yǎlǐ (耶律雅里),
he was the second son of Emperor Tiānzuò (Tiānzuò Huángdì).
His courtesy name (*zì*) was Sāluán (撒鸞).
At seven years old,
[Tiānzuò] wished to establish him as Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ).
Separate forbidden guards were established for him,
and he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Liáng (Liáng Wáng).
In the third year of Bǎodà (保大),
when the Jīn (金) forces besieged Qīngzhǒng Fort (Qīngzhǒng Zhài),
Yǎlǐ (雅里) was among the troops.
Grand Tutor Tèmǔgē (特母哥) took him and fled,
traveling along minor roads until they reached Yīnshān (陰山).
Hearing that Tiānzuò (天祚) had suffered a defeat and was hurrying toward Yúnnèi (雲內),
Yǎlǐ (雅里) rushed to meet him.
At that time, those attending him numbered over a thousand men,
which was more than those attending Tiānzuò (天祚).
Tiānzuò (天祚) feared that Tèmǔgē (特母哥) might instigate a rebellion
and wished to execute him.
[Tiānzuò] rebuked him for failing to rescue all the princes entirely
and was about to interrogate him.
Holding a sword, [Tiānzuò] summoned Yǎlǐ (雅里) and asked:
"What did Tèmǔgē (特母哥) instruct you to do?"
Yǎlǐ (雅里) replied:
"There were no other instructions."
Thereupon, [Tiānzuò] released him.
Tiānzuò crossed the river and fled to Xià.
The detachment commander, Yēlǜ Díliè, and others kidnapped Yǎlǐ and fled north.
Upon reaching Shā Lǐng,
they saw a snake crossing the path,
which observers took as an ominous sign.
Three days later,
all the officials together established Yǎlǐ as their ruler.
Yǎlǐ then ascended the throne,
changed the reign title to Shénlì,
and ordered officials and commoners to submit proposals for expediency.
Yǎlǐ was generous and broad-minded by nature,
and hated executions.
When he captured runaways,
he merely flogged them.
If someone surrendered voluntarily,
he immediately granted them an official position.
He then said to his attendants:
"If you wish to follow me, then come;
if you do not wish to follow, then leave.
Why must there be coercion?"
He often took the *Zhēnguān Zhèngyào* of Táng and the poem on governing the state written by the *Línyá* Zīzhōng,
and ordered his attendants to read them.

Jiūzhé, the Military Governor (Jiédùshǐ) of the Wūgǔ tribe; Tàbùyě, the Commander-in-chief (Tǒngjūn) of the Diéliè tribe; and Dūlǐbù, the Supervisor (Dūjiān), along with others, each led their respective followers to join him.
From this time onward, various tribes arrived successively.
However, Yǎlǐ gradually became negligent and decadent,
and enjoyed playing polo (jī jū).
Tèmǔgē offered earnest remonstrance,
and thereafter he stopped going out.
He appointed Yēlǜ Díliè as Commissioner of Military Affairs (Shūmìshǐ),
with Tèmǔgē as his deputy.
Díliè impeached Xiāo Jiūlǐ, the Commissioner for Pacification (Zhāotǎoshǐ) of the Northwest Circuit, for misleading the public
and harboring disloyal intentions.
He executed him and his son, Má Niè.
He appointed Yáoshè as Commissioner for Pacification.
He fought several battles against the various tribes,
and was repeatedly defeated.
He was punished with a flogging and dismissed from office.
If those accompanying him were weary and distressed,
he would always provide them relief and supplies.
Bǎodé, the Palace Attendant (Zhícháng), remonstrated, saying:
"The state treasury is now empty,
if you grant gifts like this,
how shall we provide for each other?"
Yǎlǐ replied angrily:
"Previously, when hunting at Fú Shān,
you falsely accused the hunting officials,
and now you speak like this again.
If I do not have the various tribes,
what shall I possess?"
He refused to accept the advice.
Initially,
he ordered the herd administrators (Qúnmù) to transport grain from the Yánluò granary,
but the common people stole it.
There was a discussion to compile a register to make them compensate.
Yǎlǐ then personally set the standard: For every cart of grain [stolen],
one sheep must be repaid;
three carts, one ox;
five carts, one horse;
eight carts, one camel.
His attendants said:
"Currently, one cannot even obtain two *dòu* of grain for one sheep,
yet you require one cart of grain to be repaid!"
Yǎlǐ said:
"What the people possess, I possess.
If I make them repay it completely,
how can the people endure it?"
Later, while hunting at Chálà Shān,
he shot forty yellow sheep
and twenty-one wolves in one day.
Consequently, he fell ill
and died,
at the age of thirty.
Yēlǜ Dàshí
is historically known as the Western Liáo.
Dàshí’s courtesy name (zì) was Zhòngdé.
He was the eighth-generation descendant of Tàizǔ.
He was proficient in the Liáo and Hàn scripts,
was skilled in archery and horsemanship,
passed the *Jìnshì* examination in the fifth year of Tiānqìng
and was promoted to Attendant in the Hànlín Academy (Hànlín Yìngfèng),
and soon thereafter was promoted to Compiler (Chéngzhǐ).
Since the Liáo referred to the Hànlín academician as a *Línyá*,
Dàshí was thus known as Dàshí Línyá.
He successively served as Prefect (Cìshǐ) of Tàizhōu and Xiángzhōu,
and Military Governor (Jiédùshǐ) of the Liáoxīng Army.
In the second year of Bǎodà,
as the Jīn army pressed closer daily,
Tiānzuò fled.
He and various high officials established Qínjìn Wáng Chún as emperor.
When Chún died,
they established his wife, Xiāo Défēi, as Empress Dowager (Tàihòu),
to guard Yān.
When the Jīn army arrived,
Xiāo Défēi submitted to Tiānzuò.
Tiānzuò, enraged, executed Défēi and rebuked Dàshí, saying:
"While I was alive,
how dare you establish Chún?"
Dàshí replied:
"Your Majesty, possessing the resources of the entire nation,
was unable to repel the enemy even once,
abandoned the state and fled far away,
causing the common people to suffer terribly.
Even if ten Chúns were established,
since they are all descendants of Tàizǔ,
is this not better than begging for survival from outsiders?"
The Emperor had no reply,
so he granted him wine and food
and pardoned his crime.
Dàshí felt insecure,
so he killed Xiāo Yǐxuē and Pōlǐkuò,
established himself as king,
and led two hundred iron cavalry to flee overnight.
After traveling north for three days,
he crossed the Hēishuǐ (Black River),
and met the Xiángwěn Chuánggǔ'ér of the White Dádá.
Chuánggǔ'ér offered four hundred horses,
twenty camels,
and a certain number of sheep.
Traveling west, he reached Kědūn Chéng,
and stationed his troops at the Protectorate General of Běitíng.

He assembled the seven prefectures of Wēiwǔ, Chóngdé, Huìfān, Xīn, Dàlín, Zǐhé, and Tuó, along with the royal masses of the eighteen tribes: Dàhuáng Shìwéi, Dílà, Wángjìlà, Cháchìlà, Yěxǐ, Bí gǔdé, Nílà, Dálàguāi, Dámìlǐ, Mì'ěrjǐ, Hézhǔ, Wūgǔlǐ, Zǔbǔ, Pǔsùwán, Tánggǔ, Hūmǔsī, Xīdì, and Jiū'érbì.
He instructed them, saying:
"Our ancestors endured hardship to establish the foundation of our state,
passing through nine rulers across successive generations,
lasting for two hundred years.
Jīn, though subjects,
aggressed against our country,
slaughtered our common people,
destroyed our prefectures and towns,
and forced our Emperor Tiānzuò to suffer exile abroad,
causing us heartache and grief day and night.
I now rely on righteousness and proceed west.
I seek to borrow strength from the various foreign tribes,
to destroy our enemies,
and restore our territory.
Are there among you who also sympathize with our state,
worry for our altars of soil and grain,
and intend to help save the ruler and father,
and rescue the living people from disaster?"
Consequently, he obtained over ten thousand elite soldiers.
He established officials,
organized the ranks (pái jiǎ),
and prepared weaponry.
In the second month, *jiǎwǔ* day, of the following year,
he offered sacrifices of a black ox and a white horse to Heaven, Earth, and the Ancestors,
and organized his army to move west.
He first sent a letter to the Huíhú king Bìlègē, saying:
"In the past, when our Emperor Tàizǔ marched north,
he passed Bǔgǔhǎn Chéng,
and immediately dispatched an envoy to Gānzhōu,
issuing an imperial decree to your ancestor Wūmǔzhǔ, saying: 'If you remember your former state,
We shall restore it for you immediately;
if you cannot return,
We shall claim it.
Its existence under Us
is the same as its existence under you.'
Your ancestor immediately submitted a memorial expressing gratitude,
stating that since the country had been moved here
for more than ten generations,
the military and common people were accustomed to the land and reluctant to move again,
and thus could not return.
Therefore, the friendship between [our dynasty] and your state is not merely recent.
Now I am proceeding west to Dàshí.
I request passage through your territory;
do not harbor any suspicion."
When Bìlègē received the letter,
he immediately welcomed Dàshí to his residence
and held a great feast for three days.
When Dàshí was about to leave,
Bìlègē presented six hundred horses,
one hundred camels,
and three thousand sheep,
and requested to pledge his sons and grandsons as hostages to become a dependent state.
He escorted Dàshí outside the border.
Wherever he passed,
he defeated those who opposed him
and pacified those who surrendered.
The army marched ten thousand *lǐ*.
Several states submitted,
and the camels, horses, cattle, sheep, and wealth acquired
were beyond counting.
The military strength grew daily,
and their fighting spirit doubled day by day.
Xúnsī-gān,
the various states of the Western Regions raised an army of 100,000,
calling themselves Hū'ér-shān,
and came to resist the battle.
The two armies faced each other, about two *lǐ* apart.
He instructed his officers and soldiers, saying:
"Although their army is numerous, it lacks strategy.
If we attack them,
their front and rear will be unable to assist each other,
and our army will surely win."
He dispatched Xiāo Wòlǐlà, Great King of the Six Bureaus Administration, and Yēlǜ Sōngshān, Vice Commissioner for Pacification, leading 2,500 troops to attack their right flank;
Xiāo Là'ābù, Vice Commissioner of Military Affairs,
and Yēlǜ Zhúxuē, Commissioner for Pacification, leading 2,500 troops to attack their left flank;
he himself led the troops to attack their center.
The three armies advanced simultaneously,
Hū'ér-shān suffered a great defeat,
with corpses lying stiff for dozens of *lǐ*.
The army was stationed at Xúnsī-gān for a total of ninety days.
The King of the Huíhuí state came to surrender,
presenting local tribute.
Traveling further west to Qǐ'ér-màn,
the civil and military officials enthroned Dàshí as Emperor.
He ascended the throne on the fifth day of the second month of the *Jiǎchén* year,
aged thirty-eight,
and was titled Gě'ér-hǎn.
He restored the Chinese honorific title Tiānyòu Huángdì (Heavenly Blessed Emperor),
and changed the reign era to Yánqìng.
He posthumously titled his grandfather as Sìyuán Huángdì,
and his grandmother as Xuānyì Huánghòu.
He designated his primary consort, Consort Xiāo, as Zhāodé Huánghòu.
Thereupon, he addressed the officials, saying:
"We, along with you gentlemen, have traveled thirty thousand *lǐ*,
trudging through deserts,
toiling hard morning and night.
Relying on the blessings of the ancestors
and the efforts of you gentlemen,
We have dared to ascend the great position.
Your ancestors and fathers should appropriately be granted special compassionate treatment,
sharing in the honor and glory."
Beginning with the ancestors and fathers of Xiāo Wòlǐlà and forty-nine others,
they were granted peerages and titles according to their rank.
In the third year of Yánqìng,
the army was ordered to return eastward.
After twenty days of travel by horse,
they found a favorable location,
and consequently built a capital city,
naming it Hǔsīwò'ěrqiáng.
He changed Yánqìng to the first year of Kāngguó.
In the third month,
Xiāo Wòlǐlà, Great King of the Six Bureaus Administration, was made Grand Marshal of Horse and Foot Forces.
Xiāo Chálà'ābù, former Deputy Administrator of the Bureau of Military Affairs from the Dílà tribe, served as his deputy.
Tūlǔ Yēlǜ Yānshān of the Cháchìlà tribe was made Chief Commander,
and Yēlǜ Tiěgē, the bodyguard, was made Chief Supervisor,
leading seventy thousand cavalry on an eastern expedition.
They sacrificed a blue ox and a white horse to Heaven,
erected banners, and swore an oath to the masses, saying:
"Our Great Liáo, since Tàizǔ and Tàizōng, established the imperial enterprise through hardship.
Subsequent rulers indulged in pleasure without satiety,
paid no heed to state affairs,
bandits and thieves rose up fiercely,
and the empire disintegrated.
We led you masses,
far into the northern desert,
aiming to restore the great enterprise
and illuminate the revival.
This is not the land where We and you dwell generation after generation."
He reiterated the command to Marshal Wòlǐlà, saying:
"Now you shall go.
Be faithful in reward and certain in punishment,
share the hardships and joys with the soldiers,
select good water and grass to establish camp,
measure the enemy before advancing,
and do not bring disaster and defeat upon yourselves."
They traveled more than ten thousand *lǐ* but achieved nothing.
Many oxen and horses died,
so he ordered the troops back.
Dàshí said:
"The August Heaven is not compliant;
this is fate!"
He died in the tenth year of Kāngguó,
having reigned for twenty years.
His temple name was Dézōng.
His son, Yíliè, was young,
so he left a dying instruction for the Empress to rule the state temporarily.
The Empress's name was Tăbuyān,
titled Găntiān Huánghòu.
She acted as regent,
changed the reign era to Xiánqīng,
and reigned for seven years.
His son Yíliè ascended the throne,
changing the reign era to Shàoxīng.
They registered the population aged eighteen and above,
obtaining 84,500 households.
He died after reigning for thirteen years.
His temple name was Rénzōng.
As his son was young,
a will was left for his younger sister, Pǔsùwán, to rule the state temporarily.
She acted as regent,
changed the reign era to Chóngfú,
and was titled Chéngtiān Tàihòu.
Later, she committed adultery with Pǔgǔ Zhīshālǐ, the younger brother of the Consort (Fùmǎ) Xiāo Wòlǔbù.
She had the Consort exiled as Prince of Dōngpíng,
and then framed and killed him.
Wòlǐlà, the Consort’s father, surrounded her palace with troops
and shot and killed Pǔsùwán and Pǔgǔ Zhīshālǐ.
Pǔsùwán reigned for fourteen years.
Rénzōng's second son, Zhílǔgǔ, ascended the throne,
changing the reign era to Tiānxī.
He reigned for thirty-four years.
One autumn, while he was out hunting,
Qūchūlǜ, the King of Nǎimán, captured him with eight thousand ambush troops
and seized his position.
Qūchūlǜ subsequently adopted the Liáo garments and cap,
honored Zhílǔgǔ as Tàishàng Huáng (Retired Emperor),
and the Empress as Huáng Tàihòu (Empress Dowager).
He inquired about their welfare morning and evening,
serving them until the end.
When Zhílǔgǔ died,
the Liáo line ended.
Yēlǜ Chún, during the reign of Tiānzuò,
governed great states in succession,
was granted a golden certificate,
and was allowed to be announced without stating his name during ceremonies.
The favors he received at that time
were unrivaled.
When Tiānzuò fled and dispersed,
Yēlǜ Chún was appointed Grand Marshal, tasked with guarding Nánjīng.
Why could he not have upheld great righteousness to inspire the people of Yān and the various ministers,
raised an army to aid the emperor,
resisted Jīn in the east, and welcomed Tiānzuò back?
Instead, he seized the position for himself;
this was usurpation.
Moreover, how could he bear to be king while Tiānzuò still lived?
Dàshí had already acknowledged Yēlǜ Chún as emperor and Tiānzuò as king,
but later returned to Tiānzuò.
Tiānzuò criticized him concerning great righteousness,
so he subsequently established himself as king and left.
Fortunately, relying on the residual might and enduring wisdom of his ancestors,
he established his reign tens of thousands of *lǐ* away.
Although succession passed among widowed mothers and weak sons,
replacing one another in turn,
for nearly ninety years,
this can also be considered remarkable.
However, the enthronement of Yēlǜ Chún, Yǎlǐ, and Dàshí
all occurred during the reign of Tiānzuò.
To have a sovereign and then establish another sovereign—
how can this be permissible?
The action of Zhūgě Wǔhóu in mourning Xiàndì
before installing Xiānzhǔ as emperor
cannot be mentioned in the same breath.
Therefore, this is recorded as a warning.
Eulogy says: Liáo arose in the northern wilderness.
The strength of their military forces,
advancing triumphantly beyond the passes,
sweeping over the region north of the Yellow River,
setting up the Jìn and establishing the Hàn—
how magnificent that was!
Tàizǔ and Tàizōng leveraged the momentum of a hundred battles,
brought together the newly established states.
Their heroic schemes and wise strategies
can be called far-reaching.
Even though Shìzōng had mediocre talent,
and Mùzōng was cruel and violent,
suffering repeated regicides and rebellions,
the divine mandate remained unshaken.
This was because the prestige and commands of the ancestors were still sufficient to overawe and subdue their countrymen.
Since Shèngzōng,
domestically, they cultivated governance,
and externally, they expanded the frontiers.
Subsequently, they renewed and solidified neighboring alliances,
and the four borders were peaceful.
The foundation that maintained the state for over two hundred years
had its origin there.
Down to Tiānzuò,
he encountered the final stage of fate,
yet he failed to satisfy the hopes of the people,
heavily trusted treacherous scoundrels,
thereby destroying the foundation of the state himself,
causing his subordinates to lose loyalty.
As soon as the Jīn troops gathered,
internal strife first arose.
Schemes of dethronement and installation,
and signs of rebellion and flight,
arose fiercely one after another.
This gradually led to utter collapse and fragmentation,
making it impossible to support the state again.
Truly lamentable!
The Yēlǜ and Xiāo clans
were related as nephews and maternal uncles through generations,
bound by shared fortune and misfortune.
Fèngxiān, motivated by private interest and neglecting public duty,
first instigated disaster and provoked trouble,
leading to this outcome.
When Tiānzuò was utterly desperate,
he finally realized that Fèngxiān had misled him.
Was it not too late?
the name being incorrect,
the words being illogical,
and the affairs failing.
Dà Shí (Yelü Dàshí) only prolonged [his state],
yet how much better
was that than this [situation]? Monograph One: Monograph on the Encampments and Guards (Part One)
In the age of high antiquity,
they wore grass and ate wood,
dwelling in nests and caves.
They were happy and content,
neither seeking nor contending.
Beginning when Yán Dì’s
governance declined, Chī Yóu
caused rebellion.
They first created shields and spears,
thereby poisoning the world.
Xuānyuán shì
executed him at the side of Zhuōlù.
When dwelling, the banner was fixed at the palace;
when traveling, the banner was suspended on the standard
—this served as a warning to the world for ten thousand generations.
Consequently, armies, soldiers, encampments, and guards
had to be established.
South of Jìzhōu,
after experiencing the changes of the great floods,
the Xià Hòu first established walled cities.
Their people settled and lived within the pacified territories (Suī Fú).
Externally, they raised military defenses;
internally, they managed civil education,
maintaining defense on all four borders.
The establishment of encampments and guards
was merely to prepare for emergencies.
North of Bīng and Yíng [provinces],
the fierce winds brought much cold.
[The people there] migrated following the sun,
having no settled abode year-round.
Over ten thousand *lǐ* of barren land,
bandits, thieves, and internal evildoers took advantage of the gaps and rose up.
The establishment of encampments and guards
was thus a permanent necessity.
The circumstances demanded it.
When Yǒu Liáo (The Liao state) first grew large,
their system of establishment was especially thorough.
When dwelling, they had palace guards,
which were called Wòlǔbō;
when traveling, they had mobile camps,
which were called Nàbō;
and those who garrisoned the frontiers
were called Bùzú (tribes).
When there was activity,
they focused on attack and battle;
when idle, they lived by hunting and fishing.
There was no day without encampment,
and no place without guard.
In establishing the framework of the state,
nothing was more important than this. Hence, this Monograph on Encampments and Guards was written.
Palace Guards
The law of the Liáo Guó was this: When the Son of Heaven ascended the throne, he established a palace guard (Gōng Wèi),
divided the prefectures and counties (Zhōu Xiàn),
separated the tribes (Bùzú),
established official bureaus (Guānfǔ),
registered the households (Hùkǒu),
and prepared soldiers and horses (Bīng Mǎ).
Upon death, the retinue of the empresses and concubines accompanied the royal tents
to attend to the imperial tombs (Língqǐn).
When a levy was ordered,
the able-bodied men (Dīng Zhuàng) followed military affairs,
while the old and weak remained behind to guard.
Tàizǔ (Emperor Tàizǔ) had the Hóngyì Gōng.
Yìngtiān Huánghòu (Empress Yìngtiān) had the Chángníng Gōng.
Tàizōng (Emperor Tàizōng) had the Yǒngxīng Gōng.
Shìzōng (Emperor Shìzōng) had the Jìqìng Gōng.
Mùzōng (Emperor Mùzōng) had the Yánchāng Gōng.
Jǐngzōng (Emperor Jǐngzōng) had the Zhāngmǐn Gōng.
Chéngtiān Tàihòu (Empress Dowager Chéngtiān) had the Chóngdé Gōng.
Shèngzōng (Emperor Shèngzōng) had the Xīngshèng Gōng.
Xīngzōng (Emperor Xīngzōng) had the Yánqìng Gōng.
Dàozōng (Emperor Dàozōng) had the Tàihé Gōng.
Tiānzuò (Emperor Tiānzuò) had the Yǒngchāng Gōng.
Furthermore, Xiàowén Huáng Tàidì (Imperial Younger Brother Xiàowén) had the Dūnmù Gōng,
and Chancellor Yélǜ Lóngyùn had the Wénzhōng Wáng Fǔ (Princely Establishment of Wénzhōng).
In total, there were thirty-eight Zhōu (prefectures),
ten Xiàn (counties),
forty-one Tíxiá Sī (Supervisory Agencies),
twenty-three Shíliè,
seventy-four Wǎlǐ,
ninety-eight Mòlǐ,
two Délǐ,
and nineteen Zhásǎ.
There were eighty thousand regular households (Zhèng Hù),
and one hundred twenty-three thousand Fan-Han transferred households (Fān Hàn Zhuǎnhù),
totaling two hundred three thousand households.
The Suàn Wòlǔbō
was established by Tàizǔ.
In the national language, the term for 'heart and stomach' (intimate trusted subjects)
is "Suàn,"
and the term for 'palace'
is "Wòlǔbō."
This was the Hóngyì Gōng.
It was established using guards composed of [the emperor’s] intimate trusted subjects,
augmented by captives from Bóhǎi
and households from Jǐnzhōu.
Its Wòlǔbō was located in Línhuáng Fǔ,
and the imperial tomb was twenty *lǐ* southeast of Zǔzhōu.
There were eight thousand regular households,
seven thousand Fan-Han transferred households,
supplying six thousand cavalry troops.
Five Zhōu: Jǐn, Zǔ, Yán, Qí, and Yín.
One Xiàn: Fùyì.
Four Tíxiá Sī: Nánjīng, Xījīng, Fèngshèng Zhōu, and Píngzhōu.
Two Shíliè: Xū
and Sùlǔ.
Four Wǎlǐ: Hébù,
Tàsǎ,
Mànyā,
and Hǔchí.
Four Mòlǐ: Shān,
Yùdūn,
Hútū,
and Jiūlǐchǎn.
Two Délǐ: Shùlěi Běi
and Shùlěi Nán.
The Guóāniǎn Wòlǔbō
was established by Tàizōng.
The term for 'gathering the state'
is "Guóāniǎn."
This was the Yǒngxīng Gōng,
originally named Gūwěn Wòlǔbō.
It was established using the captive households acquired by Tàizǔ upon pacifying Bóhǎi,
the Tíxiá Sī of Dōngjīng and Huáizhōu, and the households of Huáirén Xiàn in Yúnzhōu and Luánhé Xiàn in Zézhōu, and others.
Its Wòlǔbō was situated alongside the Yóugǔ Hé,
and the imperial tomb was thirty *lǐ* south of Huáizhōu.
There were three thousand regular households,
seven thousand Fan-Han transferred households,
supplying five thousand cavalry troops.
Four Zhōu: Huái, Qián, Kāi, and Lái.
Two Xiàn: Bǎohé and Luánhé.
Four Tíxiá Sī: Nánjīng, Xījīng, Fèngshèng Zhōu, and Píngzhōu.
One Shíliè: Běinǚgǔ.
Four Wǎlǐ: Mò,
Mǔ,
Hélǐzhī,
and Shùlěi.
Thirteen Mòlǐ: Shùlěizhěn,
Dàgémie,
Xiǎogémie,
Mǔ,
Guīhuàbùshù,
Tángkuò,
Tǔgǔ,
Bǎiěrgūatè,
Hélǔbùzhī,
Yímǎbùzhī,
Shān,
Qīngdài,
and Sùwěn.
Seven Zhásǎ: Bódébù,
Shǒuyù,
Xuégǔzhī,
Hébùpínní,
Hǔlǐyù,
Yēlǐzhǐ Jiáshì,
and Sēngyǐn Lìnggōng.
The Yělǔwǎn Wòlǔbō
was established by Shìzōng.
The term for 'great flourishing'
is "Yělǔwǎn."
This was the Jìqìng Gōng.
It was established using the escorting guards of Wénxiàn Huángdì
and the captive households of Tàizǔ,
as well as the Tíxiá Sī of Yúnzhōu,
and households from Gāo Zhōu, Yí Zhōu, and other prefectures.
Its Wòlǔbō was located east of the Tǔ Hé,
and the imperial tomb was north of the Chángníng Gōng.
There were five thousand regular households,
eight thousand Fan-Han transferred households,
supplying eight thousand cavalry troops.
Three Zhōu: Kāng, Xiǎn, and Yí.
One Xiàn: Shāndōng.
Four Tíxiá Sī.
One Shíliè: Xīlà.
Eight Wǎlǐ: Dá Sǎ,
Hébù,
Xīliè,
Bīlǐ,
Tánmǎ,
Shuòbù,
Yēlǐzhí, and Yělǔwùyě.
`Mòlǐ` ten: Namely `Hèsīzhí`,
namely `Mángě`,
namely `Juèlǐ`,
namely `Tánmǎtè`,
namely `Chūlǎn`,
namely `Sùhūlǔwǎn`,
namely `Diélǐdé`,
namely `Yánmǎ`,
namely `Diélītè`,
namely `Nǚgǔ`.
`Púsùwǎn Wòlǔwǔ`,
established by the Empress Dowager `Yìngtiānhuáng Tàihòu`.
