The Zhùzhàng Lángjūn:
The Zhùzhàng Lángjūn:
In the beginning,
Yáolián Héndéjǐn Kèhán harmed Yúyuè Shìlǔ with the three tribes including the Púgǔzhī;
their family members and property were confiscated and entered into the Wă lì.
Chúnqīn Huánghòu pardoned them
and made them Zhùzhàng Lángjūn.
Shìzōng completely exempted them.
Later, criminals from the imperial consort clans, relatives, and hereditary officials
were confiscated and inducted.
The Zhùzhàng Households:
The Zhùzhàng Households:
These were originally split off from the various Wōlǔwǎn,
as well as those confiscated due to various crimes.

They filled duties such as serving as junior staff, managing treasury stores, eagle handlers, preparing medicine, managing drinks, serving water and towels, managing meals, managing clothing, tailoring, and other services,
as well as accompanying palace officials and imperial princes,
and members of the musicians corps.
All of them were assigned these duties.
In total, the personnel of the various palaces and guards numbered four hundred eight thousand people,
with one hundred one thousand mounted troops.
The Zhùzhàng, released or confiscated,
were increased or decreased according to the time,
and had no fixed quota.
Treatise Two: On the Military and Guard System, Middle Section: The Traveling Court
According to the Zhōu official method of using the earth gnomon: When the sun is in the east,
the shadow in the evening is long and there is much wind;
when the sun is in the north,
the shadow is long and there is much cold.
Between heaven and earth,
the atmosphere and climate differ in suitability,
and people living therein
each adapt to their convenience.
The rulers regulate this based on the Three Powers (Heaven, Earth, and Man).
South of the Great Wall,
there is much rain and much heat;
the people here eat by farming,
dress in silk and hemp,
live in palaces and houses,
and govern through cities and walls.
In the midst of the Great Desert,
there is much cold and much wind;
It is called Yāzǐ Hélúo.
In the first third of the first month, the Huángdì [Emperor] sets up his felt tent,
arriving about sixty days later.
Before the swans arrive,
the tents are pitched on the ice,
and holes are cut in the ice to catch fish.
When the ice thaws,
they release the eagles and falcons to hunt swans and geese.
They go out at dawn and return at dusk,
engaging in archery and hunting.
Yāzǐ Hélúo is twenty *lǐ* east-to-west,
and thirty *lǐ* north-to-south,
located thirty-five *lǐ* northeast of Chángchūn Zhōu.
It is surrounded on four sides by sandy basins,
with many elm, willow, and apricot groves.
Whenever the Huángdì arrives,
the attending officials all wear dark green clothes,
each equipped with a linked mace,
a container of falcon food,
and a cone for stabbing geese.
They stand in rows around the *luò* (lake), spaced five to seven paces apart.
The Huángdì wears a cap and headscarf,
dons seasonal attire,
and fastens a jade belt,
watching from the upwind side.
A flag is raised where geese are spotted;
scout riders gallop to report,
and drums are beaten at the distant waters.
The geese are startled and fly up;
the surrounding riders on the left and right all raise banners to wave at them.
The Five Offices (Wǔ Fāng) bring forth the Hǎidōngqīng falcons,
which are presented through bows to the Huángdì, who releases them.
If a falcon catches a goose and they fall,
but the falcon's strength is insufficient,
the nearest officials standing in the line
raise their cones to stab the goose
and take its brain to feed the falcon.
Those who save the falcon are routinely rewarded with silver and silk.
When the Huángdì obtains the first goose,
it is offered to the ancestral temple;
all the officials present wine and fruit,
and music is played.
They exchange toasts,
offer words of congratulation,
and, for amusement, everyone inserts a goose feather into their headwear.
Wine is bestowed upon the attendants,
and the feathers are distributed everywhere.
After hunting, netting, and hooking,
they return only when spring ends.
Summer *Nàbō*:
There is no fixed location,
mostly at Tuěr Shān.
Dàozōng every year first visited Hēishān,
paid respects at the mausoleums of Shèngzōng and Xīngzōng,
appreciated the golden lotuses,
and then proceeded to Zǐ Hé to avoid the heat.
Tuěr Shān is three hundred *lǐ* northeast of Hēishān,
near Mántóu Shān.
Hēishān is thirteen *lǐ* north of Qìng Zhōu;
there is a pond on it,
and golden lotuses are in the pond.
Zǐ Hé is three hundred *lǐ* northeast of Tuěr Shān.
The Qīngliáng Diàn (Hall of Clear Coolness) in the western hills of Huáizhōu
is also a place for the imperial entourage to avoid the heat.
The felt tents are set up in the middle third of the fourth month,
choosing an auspicious spot for the cool retreat,
arriving in the last third of the fifth month or the first third of the sixth month.
They reside there for fifty days.
They discuss state affairs with officials from the North and South,
and hunt in their leisure time.
They depart in the middle third of the seventh month.
Autumn *Nàbō*:
It is called Fúhǔ Lín (Forest of the Submissive Tiger).
In the middle third of the seventh month, they set up the felt tents from the cool retreat area,
entering the mountains to shoot deer and tigers.
The forest is fifty *lǐ* northwest of Yǒngzhōu.
There was once a fierce tiger dwelling in the forest,
harming residents and livestock.
Jǐngzōng led a few horsemen to hunt there;
the tiger lay prone in the grass,
trembling and not daring to look up.
The sovereign spared it,
and the place was consequently named Fúhǔ Lín.
Every year when the imperial carriage arrives,
the imperial family and lower-ranking officials are distributed along the side of the *Luò* River.
When midnight approaches,
as the deer come to drink the salty water,
hunters are commanded to blow horns to imitate deer calls.
Once they have gathered, they are shot.
This is called
"Licking the Deer" (*Shì Lù*),
and also named
"Calling the Deer" (*Hū Lù*).
Winter *Nàbō*:
It is called Guǎngpíng Diàn.
It is thirty *lǐ* southeast of Yǒngzhōu,
originally named Báimǎ Diàn.
It stretches more than twenty *lǐ* east-to-west,
and more than ten *lǐ* north-to-south.
The terrain is very flat and level;
all views are sandy deserts,
and the trees are mostly elm and willow.
The area is rich in sand,
and the winter months are slightly warmer.
The felt tents often stay here for the winter,
where they meet with the ministers from the North and South to discuss state affairs,
occasionally conducting military exercises and hunts,
and simultaneously receiving ceremonial tributes from Southern Sòng and other states.
The Huángdì's felt tent uses spears to form a rigid encampment (*yìng zhài*),
connected by wool ropes.
Under each spear is one black felt umbrella,
to shield the guards from wind and snow.
Outside the spears is a layer of small felt tents;
each tent houses five people,
each armed with weapons to form the Forbidden Enclosure (*Jìn Wéi*).
To the south is the Shěngfāng Diàn (Hall for Inspecting the Regions).
About two *lǐ* north of the Hall is the Shòuníng Diàn (Hall of Longevity and Tranquility).
Both use wooden pillars and bamboo rafters,
covered with felt,
with colored paintings wrapped around the pillars,
brocade serving as wall coverings,
and embroidered crimson tablets added.
Furthermore, embroidered dragons on yellow cloth are used as floor screens.
The windows and lattices are also made of felt,
coated with yellow oiled silk.
The foundation is raised more than one *chǐ*.
The side corridors and galleries are also covered with felt,
without doors.
North of the Shěngfāng Diàn is a deerskin tent,
and north of that tent is the Bāfāng Gōngyòng Diàn (Eight-Directional Public Use Hall).
North of the Shòuníng Diàn is the Chángchūn Zhàng (Long Spring Tent),
guarded by the rigid encampment.
Four thousand Qìdān soldiers are used for the palace,
with one thousand rotating daily for guard duty.
Outside the Forbidden Enclosure, spears are set up to form a stockade;
at night, the spears are removed and moved to enclose the Huángdì's sleeping tent.
Barricades against horses are placed around it,
and guard stations (*pù*) are established outside,
using bells to relay the night watch.
Every year, the four seasons
cycle and repeat.
When the Huángdì tours and guards the realm throughout the four seasons,
all Qìdān officials, great and small, internal and external, and those belonging to the serving ranks,
as well as the hundred offices managed by the Hàn people's Xuānhuī Yuàn, all follow.
From the Hàn people's Shūmì Yuàn and Zhōngshū Shěng, only one Premier (*zǎixiàng*) is selected,
two Chief and Deputy Administrators (*dōufù chéngzhǐ*) from the Shūmì Yuàn,
ten clerks (*lìshǐ*),
one clerk from the Zhōngshū Shěng,
and one person selected from the Yùshǐ Tái and Dàlǐ Sì to accompany the procession.
Every year in the first third of the first month,
the imperial carriage begins its journey.
The Premier and officials below him
return to Zhōngjīng to reside and guard,
handling all public affairs of the Hàn people.
For appointing and dismissing officials,
only temporary assignments by ministerial orders (*táng tiě*) are issued;
after waiting for the conference at the traveling court location (*xíng zài suǒ*),
imperial decree is sought, and formal edicts are issued.
Civil officials, from the County Magistrate (*xiàn lìng*) and Record Keeper (*lù shì*) down, no longer need to report to the throne;
the Zhōngshū Shěng selects them.
Military officials must report to the throne.
In the fifth month,
there is a conference of Northern and Southern officials
at the cool retreat location (xíng zài suǒ).
In the tenth month,
there is also a conference at the winter court location (xíng zài suǒ),
conducted in the same manner.
Tribes and Clans (*Bù Zú*)
Settlements are called *Bù* (Tribe);
lineages are called *Zú* (Clan).
According to the ancient customs of the Qìdān,
they live divided by land,
but dwell together by clan.
Those who are clans but also tribes include
the Five Offices (*Wǔ Yuàn*), Six Offices (*Liù Yuàn*), and similar groups.
Those who are tribes but also clans include
the Xī Wáng and Shìwéi, and similar groups.
Those who are tribes but not clans include
the Tèlǐ Tèmiǎn, Shāowǎ, and Hézhú, and similar groups.
Those who are clans but not tribes include
the Yáoliǎn Nine Tents and the Three Father Branches of the Imperial Clan (Huángzú Sān Fù Fáng).
were invaded by Gāolì and Rúrǔ, and barely (with ten thousand mouths) submitted to Yuán Wèi.
Not long after they had multiplied,
they were invaded by Běi Qí,
who captured over one hundred thousand men and women.
They were subsequently pressed by the Tūjué,
and took temporary refuge in Gāolì,
numbering no more than ten thousand families.
The tribes scattered,
and they were no longer the ancient eight tribes.
Separate tribes submitted as vassals to the Tūjué,
while others submitted internally to the Suí,
settling along the Héchén Shuǐ.
As the tribes gradually grew numerous,
they divided into ten tribes,
holding territory over five hundred *lǐ* in Liáoxī.
During the Táng era, the Dàhè Shì remained eight tribes,
but Sōngmò and Xuán Zhōu were counted separately,
making them ten tribes in total.
The Yáoliǎn Shì, following the scattered defeat of Wànróng and Kětūyú,
reverted to being eight tribes;
however, as Yáoliǎn and Diélà were counted separately,
there were again ten tribes.
Zǔwǔ Kèhán split them into twenty tribes,
and the Qìdān began to grow strong.
When Liáo Tàizǔ came to power,
he divided the clans of the Nine Tents and Three Chambers,
listing them again as twenty tribes.
During the reign of Shèngzōng,
sixteen were established by division,
eighteen were newly added,
making a total of fifty-four tribes including the old ones;
internally, there were the clans of Bálǐ and Yǐshìyǐ, the imperial maternal uncles (guójiù),
and externally, ten vassal tribes.
It was a flourishing era!
Those clans whose lineage is known
are roughly listed in the two tables: the Imperial Clan and the Maternal Relatives.
For the remaining Wǔyuàn, Liùyuàn, and Yǐshì Bù, we only find Yìgǔ and Sālǐběn;
for the Nièlā and Wūgǔ Bù, we only find Sālǐbǔ and Nièlè;
and for the Tūlǚbù and Tūjǔ Bù, we only find Tǎgǔlǐ and Hángwò.
All were brothers.
Shísè and Zhélǐ of the Xī Wáng Fǔ Bù
were lord and vassal.
The Pǐn Bù had Nánǚ,
and the Chǔtè Bù had Wā.
Regarding the lineage and names of the rest,
none can be extensively verified.
The Old Records state:
"In the beginning of the Qìdān,
they lived in the grasslands and wild fields,
having no fixed abode.
It was not until Nièlǐ that tribes were first organized,
each having its own allocated territory.
When Tàizǔ arose,
because the Diélà Bù was strong and flourishing,
he divided it into the Wǔyuàn and Liùyuàn.
The Xī Six Tribes and those below them
were mostly established through capture and surrender.
Those skilled in arms
were registered in the military rolls
and assigned to the various Circuit Xiángwěn, Tǒngjūn, and Zhāotǎo Offices.
Those barbarians (fān) residing in the interior territories
farmed and pastured across the flat plains seasonally.
The households guarding the borders,
depending on animal husbandry
for their livelihood, spun wool and drank milk
for clothing and food.
Each maintained their old customs,
habitually laboring,
and were not changed by the sight of splendor or exotic goods.
Therefore, every family was self-sufficient and every person well-provided,
and military preparations were complete and well-ordered.
Eventually, they watched the four directions like a tiger,
forcing the powerful to court them and the weak to submit;
eastward crossing Pánmù,
westward traversing Liúshā,
none failed to comply and submit.
The tribes were truly their claws and teeth.'"
The Ancient Eight Tribes:
Xīwàndān Bù.
Hédàhé Bù.
Fúfúyù Bù.
Yǔlíng Bù.
Rìlián Bù.
Pǐjié Bù.
Lí Bù.
Tǔliùyú Bù.
The ancestor of the Qìdān
was called Qíshǒu Kèhán,
who had eight sons.
Later, their relatives gradually grew numerous,
dividing into eight tribes,
residing between Sōngmò.
Today, there is a temple for the founding ancestor of the Qìdān on Mùyè Shān in Yǒngzhōu,
where the statues of Qíshǒu Kèhán, his Kèdūn, and his eight sons are located.
West of the Huáng Hé
and north of the Tǔ Hé,
was the former territory of Qíshǒu Kèhán.
The Qìdān Ten Tribes during the Suí: In the late Yuán Wèi period,
Mòfú Hèwùyú, fearing invasion by Gāolì and Rúrǔ,
led three thousand chariots and ten thousand people to submit internally,
thus leaving the former territory of Qíshǒu Kèhán
and dwelling east of the Báiláng Shuǐ.
Emperor Wénxuān of Běi Qí invaded from three routes in Píngzhōu,
capturing over one hundred thousand men and women,
and settling them in various prefectures.
They were again pressed by the Tūjué,
and ten thousand families took temporary refuge within the borders of Gāolì.
In the fourth year of Kāihuáng of the Suí,
all the Mòfú Hè led their followers to request settlement near the border,
and were permitted to reside in the old land of Báiláng.
Another separate tribe that had taken refuge in Gāolì, led by Chūfú and others,
led their people to submit internally,
and an imperial edict placed them north of Dúxī Nāxié.
Furthermore, another separate tribe that had submitted as vassals to the Tūjué, numbering over four thousand households, came to surrender.
An imperial edict granted them provisions and ordered them back,
but they firmly refused to leave.
As the tribes gradually grew numerous,
they moved in search of water and pasture,
settling along the Héchén Shuǐ.
This was two hundred *lǐ* directly north of Liáoxī,
its territory extending five hundred *lǐ* east to west,
and three hundred *lǐ* north to south.
They divided into ten tribes,
whose names are lost.
The Táng Dàhè Shì Eight Tribes:
Dájī Bù,
Qiàoluò Zhōu.
Hébiàn Bù,
Tànhàn Zhōu.
Dúhuó Bù,
Wúféng Zhōu.
Fēnwèn Bù,
Yǔlíng Zhōu.
Tūbiàn Bù,
Rìlián Zhōu.
Ruìxī Bù,
Túhé Zhōu.
Zhuìjīn Bù,
Wàndān Zhōu.
Fú Bù,
with two prefectures (zhōu): Pǐlí and Chìshān.
Táng Tàizōng established Xuán Zhōu,
making Jùqǔ, the Qìdān commander, the Prefect (Cìshǐ).
He also established the Sōngmò Dūdū Fǔ,
making Kūgē the Commander-in-Chief (Dūdū).
He divided the eight tribes,
adding Xuán Zhōu to make ten prefectures.
Thus, the ten tribes were included therein.
The Yáoliǎn Shì Eight Tribes:
Dànlìjiē Bù.
Yǐshìhuó Bù.
Shíhuó Bù.
Nàwěi Bù.
Pínmò Bù.
Nàhuìjī Bù.
Jíjiě Bù.
Xīwà Bù.
During the Táng Kāiyuán and Tiānbǎo eras,
after the Dàhè Shì declined,
Liáo Shǐzǔ Nièlǐ established Díliǎn Zǔlǐ as Zǔwǔ Kèhán.
At that time, following Wànróng's defeat, the Qìdān
tribes were scattered and diminished.
The formerly existing populace was immediately divided into eight tribes.
The Diélà Bù, led by Nièlǐ, was made a separate tribe,
and was not included in this list.
Including Yáoliǎn and Diélà, there were also ten tribes.
The Twenty Tribes under Yáoliǎn Zǔwǔ Kèhán:
Yēlǜ Seven Tribes.
Shěnmì Five Tribes.
Eight Tribes.
Nièlǐ assisted Zǔwǔ Kèhán,
dividing the three Yēlǜ clans into seven,
and the two Shěnmì clans into five,
totaling twenty tribes along with the previous eight tribes.
The three Yēlǜ clans: first is Dàhè,
second is Yáoliǎn,
third is Shìlǐ,
who were the Imperial Clan.
The two Shěnmì clans: first is Yǐshìyǐ,
second is Bálǐ,
who were the imperial maternal uncles (guójiù).
How they were divided into tribes is not fully detailed;
those that are known are Diélà,
Yǐshì,
Pǐn,
Chǔtè,
Wūkuí,
Tūlǚbù,
Niēlā,
Tūjǔ,
and further, the Yòu Dà Bù and Zuǒ Dà Bù.
These total ten,
two of which are missing.
Dàhè and Yáoliǎn were divided,
while Shìlǐ was combined into one,
which is why the Diélà Bù remained strong and ungovernable throughout the era of the Yáoliǎn.
Treatise Three: Treatise on the Palace Guards and Army Camps (Part 2), Tribal Divisions (Part 2)
The Liáo arose from Sōngmò,
managed and absorbed,
and eventually possessed the instruments of emperors of the Táng and Jìn dynasties.
Their institutions, regulations, culture, and relics extended to the region of Huánghǎi.
Can historians still describe them using old customs and terminology?
The old histories contained treatises on tribal divisions,
which was something previous dynasties lacked.
In ancient times,
when the ruler toured the four great peaks,
the lords of the Five Zones each reported on their duties.
The tribal divisions of the Liáo truly resembled this.
Therefore, the Tribal Divisions section is placed after the Palace Guards and Army Camps section.
The Four Inner Tribal Divisions of the Liáo:
The Yáoniǎn Jiǔzhàng Tribe.
The Héngzhàng Sānfùfáng Tribe.
The Guójiù Zhàng Bálǐ and Yǐshǐyǐ Tribes.
The Guójiù Separate Divisions.
Tàizǔ had twenty divisions;
the two Guójiù ascended to Zhàng Fēn (Camp Divisions),
leaving only eighteen divisions.
The Wǔyuàn Division.
Its ancestor was called Yìgǔ.
It consisted of six camps.
During the time of Zǔwǔ Kèhán,
he and his younger brother, Sālǐběn, led them,
and it was called the Diélà Division.
When it passed to Tàizǔ,
he ascended the throne as Yílíjǐn.
In the first year of Tiānzàn,
because it was powerful and difficult to control,
he separated the Wǔ Shíliè into Five Yuàn,
and the Liù Zhǎo into Six Yuàn,
and established a Yílíjǐn for each.
In the first year of Huìtóng,
the Yílíjǐn title was changed to Dàwáng.
The division belongs to the Northern Administration (Běifǔ),
to guard the southern border.
The Dàwáng and Dūjiān (Commissioner) reside near the Wǔyuàn Division in spring and summer,
and in Yángmén Diàn in autumn and winter.
The four Shíliè are: Dàmiègū Shíliè,
Xiǎomiègū Shíliè,
Ōukūn Shíliè.
In the second year of Huìtóng of Tàizōng,
because the lands of the Wūgǔ were rich in water and grass,
they were ordered to settle there.
In the third year,
land near Hǎilè Shuǐ was added for farming.
Yǐxíběn Shíliè.
In the second year of Huìtóng,
they were assigned the land of Wūgǔ.
The Liùyuàn Division.
It belongs to the Běifǔ,
to guard the southern border.
Its Dàwáng and Dūjiān reside north of Tàidé Quán in spring and summer,
and in Dúlújīn in autumn and winter.
The four Shíliè are: Xiálǎn Shíliè,
Āsù Shíliè,
Wònàbō Shíliè,
Wònà'ālà Shíliè.
In the second year of Huìtóng,
they were ordered to settle in Wūgǔ.
In the third year,
land near Hǎilè Shuǐ was added.
The Yǐshǐ Division.
Its ancestor was called Sālǐběn.
In the time of Zǔwǔ Kèhán,
he and his elder brother Yìgǔ separated their camps and led them.
It was called the Yǐshǐ Division.
In the second year of Huìtóng,
the Yílíjǐn title was changed to Dàwáng.
It belongs to the Southern Administration (Nánfǔ).
Its Dàwáng and Dūjiān garrison the southwestern border.
The Sītú (Minister of Education) resides at Yuānyāng Pō,
and the Zhásàxiū resides at Chēzhóu Shān.
The two Shíliè are: Ālǐdá Shíliè,
and Yùzhǔ Shíliè.
The Pǐn Division.
Its ancestor was called Nánǚ.
Zǔwǔ Kèhán established its camp as a division.
Tàizǔ changed the Yílíjǐn of the various divisions to Lìngwěn.
During the Tǒnghé period,
it was again changed to Jiédùshǐ (Military Governor).
It belongs to the Běifǔ,
and is subordinate to the Northwest Circuit Pacification Command (Xīběilù Zhāotǎosī).
The Sītú resides at Tàizǐ Fén.
All garrison troops are subordinate to the Jiédùshǐ.
The resident households (Liúhòuhù) are subordinate to the Sītú.
The two Shíliè are: Běi Zhélǐzhǐ Shíliè,
and Nán Xiálǎn Shíliè.
The Chǔtè Division.
Its ancestor was called Wā.
Zǔwǔ Kèhán established its camp as a division.
It belongs to the Nánfǔ.
The Jiédùshǐ is subordinate to the Northwest Circuit Pacification Command (Xīběilù Zhāotǎosī).
The Sītú resides beside Bǎipō Shān and [Mò] Shān.
The two Shíliè are: Běi Shíliè,
and Nán Shíliè.
The Wūkuí Division.
Its ancestor was called Sālǐbǔ.
He shared a camp with his elder brother Nièlè.
Zǔwǔ Kèhán divided it into two: Sālǐbǔ became the Wūkuí Division,
and Nièlè became the Nièlà Division.
Both belong to the Běifǔ.
The Jiédùshǐ of the Wūkuí Division is subordinate to the Northeast Circuit Pacification Command (Dōngběilù Zhāotǎosī).
The Sītú resides beside Xúmǔ Shān and Hǎolǐ Hé.
The two Shíliè are: Běi Shíliè,
and Nán Shíliè.
The Nièlà Division.
Its ancestor was called Nièlè.
Zǔwǔ Kèhán divided his camp into a division.
The Jiédùshǐ is subordinate to the Southwest Circuit Pacification Command (Xīnánlù Zhāotǎosī),
and resides north of Hēishān.
The Sītú resides beside Hǎolǐ Hé.
The two Shíliè are: Běi Tālǐ Shíliè,
and Nán Chálǐ Shíliè.
The Tūlǚbù Division.
Its ancestor was called Tǎgǔlǐ,
who led three camps.
Zǔwǔ Kèhán ordered one camp to be separated and given to his younger brother, Hángwò, forming the Tūjǔ Division;
Tǎgǔlǐ retained the other two,
and it was renamed the Tūlǚbù Division.
It belongs to the Běifǔ.
The Jiédùshǐ is subordinate to the Northwest Circuit Pacification Command (Xīběilù Zhāotǎosī).
The Sītú resides west of Chángchūn Zhōu.
The two Shíliè are: Běi Tuōbù Shíliè,
and Nán Xū Shíliè.
The Tūjǔ Division.
Its ancestor was called Hángwò.
Zǔwǔ Kèhán separated the camp and established it as a division.
It belongs to the Nánfǔ.
It garrisons the Wūkuí Wūgǔ Division.
The Sītú resides beside Rǒng Quán.
The two Shíliè are: Běi Shíliè,
and Nán Shíliè.
The Office of the Xī King (Xīwáng Fǔ) Six Divisions and Five Camps Separation.
Its ancestor was called Shísè,
who served Zhélǐ, the Chief of the Eastern Yáolǐ Ten-Camp Division.
Later, he expelled Zhélǐ
and established himself as the Xīwáng.
When he died,
his younger brother Tǔlēsī succeeded him.
Yáoniǎn Xiānzhì Kèhán campaigned against him,
captured seven hundred households who resisted,
and collected those who surrendered.
Because of Shísè's former good relations,
only half of the tribal retainers were captured;
the rest were all left behind.
The power of the Xī subsequently declined.
Initially, there were five divisions: Yáolǐ,
Bódé,
Àolǐ,
Méizhǐ,
and Chǔlǐ.
Tàizǔ completely subjugated them,
and they were called the Five Divisions Xī (Wǔ Bù Xī).
In the second year of Tiānzàn,
there was Dōng Bālǐsī Húsǔn,
who, relying on the rugged terrain, fortified himself on Jiàngǎn Shān to resist orders.
He mocked, saying:
"What can the great army do?
I shall drink below Duòguī Mén!"
Tàizǔ destroyed him.
He used the Xī Fǔ assigned households,
and combined the hidden male adults (yǐn dīng) from various divisions,
gathering the scattered people,
to establish the Duòguī Division.
It was named after the phrase "Duòguī Mén,"
and thus called the Six Divisions Xī (Liù Bù Xī).
Bólǔ'ēn was ordered to govern it,
and was still titled Xīwáng.
When Tàizōng ascended the throne,
two Zǎixiàng (Chancellors) and two Chánggǔn (Chiefs) were established.
Shèngzōng merged the three divisions—Àolǐ, Méizhǐ, and Duòguī—into one;
and specially established two Kè Divisions to fulfill the number of six divisions.
The Xīwáng Héshuònú campaigned against the Wùrě,
but was defeated.
The six divisions were registered and subordinated to the Běifǔ.
The Tūlǚbù Shìwéi Division.
It was originally named the Great and Small Two Huáng Shìwéi Households.
When Tàizǔ was Dámǎxiū Shālǐ,
he used strategy to make them surrender.
He then established them as two divisions.
It belongs to the Běifǔ.
The Jiédùshǐ is subordinate to the Northeast Circuit Area Command (Dōngběilù Tǒngjūnsī),
and garrisons the area northeast of Tàizhōu.
The Nièlà Nágǔ Division.
It is the same as the Tūlǚbù Shìwéi Division.
The Jiédùshǐ garrisons the area east of Tàizhōu.
The Diélà Diédá Division.
It originated from the seven hundred Xī households captured by Xiānzhì Kèhán.
When Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
he made them into fourteen Shíliè,
and established them as a division.
It belongs to the Nánfǔ.
The Jiédùshǐ is subordinate to the Southwest Circuit Pacification Command (Xīnánlù Zhāotǎosī).
It garrisons the area north of Hēishān.
The tribal people reside south of Qìngzhōu.
The Yǐshì Āowěi (乙室奧隗) Tribe.
In Shéncè (神冊) 6th year (921),
Tàizǔ (太祖) established it with the captive Xī (奚) households.
It was subordinate to the Southern Chancellery (Nán Fǔ, 南府).
Its Jìedùshǐ (節度使, Military Commissioner) belonged to the Northeast Route Military Command (Dōngběi Lù Bīngmǎ Sī, 東北路兵馬司).
The Chǔtè Āowěi (楮特奧隗) Tribe.
Tàizǔ established it with Xī households.
It was subordinate to the Southern Chancellery.
Its Jìedùshǐ belonged to the Tokyo Command Headquarters (Dōngjīng Dū Bùshǔ Sī, 東京都部署司).
The Pǐndálǔguó (品達魯虢) Tribe.
Tàizǔ established it with the captured Dálǔguó (達魯虢) households.
It was subordinate to the Southern Chancellery.
Its Jìedùshǐ belonged to the Southwest Route Pacification Office (Xīnán Lù Zhāotǎo Sī, 西南路招討司).
They garrisoned north of Mount Hēishān (黑山).
The Wūgǔ Nièlá (烏古涅剌) Tribe.
It is also called the Nièlǐ (涅離) Tribe.
Tàizǔ took six thousand households from the Gǔlǐ (骨里) people.
In Shéncè 6th year (921),
he divided them into the Wūgǔ Nièlá and Túlǔ (圖魯) two tribes.
Both were subordinate to the Northern Chancellery (Běi Fǔ, 北府).
The Jìedùshǐ belonged to the Southwest Route Pacification Office.
The Túlǔ Tribe.
Its Jìedùshǐ belonged to the Northeast Route Supreme Military Command (Dōngběi Lù Tǒngjūn Sī, 東北路統軍司).
The above are the ten tribes that Tàizǔ established by dividing the old Yáoliǎn Shì (遙輦氏) tribes,
plus eight tribes he newly established.
Shèngzōng (聖宗) had thirty-four tribes:
The Sālǐgě (撒里葛) Tribe.
The Xī had three camps: Sālǐgě,
Yǎozhuǎ (窈爪),
and Nòuwǎnzhǎo (耨盌爪).
When Tàizǔ attacked the Xī,
they begged for surrender
and wished to become 'attendants in the tent' (zhù zhàng zǐ dì, 著帳子弟).
They were registered in the Imperial Division (Gōng Fēn, 宮分),
and each was headed by an Yílíjǐn (夷離菫).
Shèngzōng established each as a tribe
and changed the post to Jìedùshǐ.
All were subordinate to the Southern Chancellery,
to be prepared for hunting duties.
They resided east of Zézhōu (澤州).
The Yǎozhuǎ Tribe.
It was the same as the Sālǐgě Tribe.
They resided south of Tánzhōu (潭州).
The Nòuwǎnzhǎo Tribe.
Its Jìedùshǐ belonged to the Tokyo Command Headquarters.
The Épúkuò (訛僕括) Tribe.
It was the same as the three Sālǐgě tribes.
They resided east of Wàngyún (望雲) County.
The Tèlǐtèmiǎn (特里特勉) Tribe.
Initially, twenty households were separated from each of the eight tribes to garrison the Xī,
to scout and observe the banks of the Luòmǎ Hé (落馬河) and Sùlǔ Hé (速魯河).
Twenty Xiángwěn (詳穩) were established.
Since the population had flourished,
Shèngzōng established it as a tribe,
and appointed a Jìedùshǐ.
It was subordinate to the Southern Chancellery.
They garrisoned Dàotā Lǐng (倒塌嶺)
and resided at Tuótuó Gāng (橐駝岡).
The Shāowǎ (稍瓦) Tribe.
Initially,
the slaves of the imperial divisions and large families of the Horizontal Tent (Héng Zhàng, 橫帳) were taken to establish the Shāowǎ Shíliè (稍瓦石烈).
"Shāowǎ"
means 'eagle park' (yīng fāng, 鷹坊).
They resided east of the Liáo Shuǐ (遼水),
managing the netting and catching of birds.
As the population had flourished, Shèngzōng established it as a tribe.
Its Jìedùshǐ belonged to the Tokyo Command Headquarters.
The Héshù (曷朮) Tribe.
Initially,
the slaves of the imperial divisions and large families of the Horizontal Tent were taken to establish the Héshù Shíliè.
"Héshù"
means 'iron'.
They conducted smelting on the coast at Liǔshī Hé (柳濕河), Sānchùgǔsī (三黜古斯), and Shǒushān (手山).
As the population had flourished, Shèngzōng established it as a tribe.
It belonged to the Tokyo Command Headquarters.
The Yáolǐ (遙里) Tribe.
They resided between Tánzhōu and Lìzhōu (利州).
There were three Shíliè: Sālǐbì Shíliè (撒里必石烈),
Běi Shíliè (北石烈),
and Tiělǔ Shíliè (帖魯石烈).
The Bódé (伯德) Tribe.
Between Mount Sōngshān (松山) and Píngzhōu (平州),
the Grand Preceptor (Tàishī, 太師) and Grand Guardian (Tàibǎo, 太保) resided west of the Central Capital (Zhōngjīng, 中京).
There were six Shíliè: Chuòlè Shíliè (啜勒石烈),
Sùgǔ Shíliè (速古石烈),
Tiǎnní Shíliè (腆你石烈),
Diélǐ Shíliè (迭里石烈),
Xùtè Shíliè (旭特石烈),
and Yuèlǐ Shíliè (悅里石烈).
The Chǔlǐ (楚里) Tribe.
They resided north of Tánzhōu.
The Àolǐ (奧里) Tribe.
In Tǒnghé (統和) 12th year (994),
because their population was small along with the Mèizhǐ (梅只) and Duòguī (墮瑰) tribes,
they were combined into one tribe.
These three tribes, including the one above,
originally belonged to the Xī King's Residence (Xī Wáng Fǔ, 奚王府).
Shèngzōng divided and established them.
The Nánkè (南剋) Tribe.
The Běikè (北剋) Tribe.
In Tǒnghé 12th year (994),
they were established as two tribes by dividing the two Kè (剋) divisions of the Xī Residence.
The Wěiyǎn Tūjué (隗衍突厥) Tribe.
Shèngzōng established it by separating households from the four Pìshā (闢沙) and four Pōbèi (頗憊) tribes,
to guard the border of the Northeast Nǚzhí (女直).
In Kāitài (開泰) 9th year (1020),
the Jìedùshǐ submitted a memorial requesting the establishment of Shíliè.
It was subordinate to the Northern Chancellery,
belonging to the Huánglóng Fǔ Command Headquarters (Huánglóng Fǔ Dū Bùshǔ Sī, 黃龍府都部署司).
The Àoyǎn Tūjué (奧衍突厥) Tribe.
It was the same as the Wěiyǎn Tūjué.
The Nièlá Yuèwǔ (涅剌越兀) Tribe.
It was established with Nièlá Shìwéi (室韋) households.
It was subordinate to the Northern Chancellery.
Its Jìedùshǐ belonged to the Southwest Pacification Office (Xīnán Miàn Zhāotǎo Sī, 西南面招討司).
They garrisoned north of Mount Hēishān.
The Àoyǎn Nǚzhí (奧衍女直) Tribe.
Shèngzōng established it with Nǚzhí households.
It was subordinate to the Northern Chancellery.
Its Jìedùshǐ belonged to the Northwest Route Pacification Office (Xīběi Lù Zhāotǎo Sī, 西北路招討司).
They garrisoned the border of Zhènzhōu (鎮州).
From here to the Héxī (河西) Tribe,
all were captives from various states.
Initially subordinate to the Imperial Divisions,
they were established as tribes when the population flourished.
Up to the Five States (Wǔ Guó, 五國),
all had Jìedùshǐ.
The Yǐdiǎn Nǚzhí (乙典女直) Tribe.
Shèngzōng established it with Nǚzhí households.
It was subordinate to the Southern Chancellery.
They resided north of Gāozhōu (高州).
The Wòtūwǎn Wūgǔ (斡突盌烏古) Tribe.
Shèngzōng established it with Wūgǔ (烏古) households.
It was subordinate to the Southern Chancellery.
Its Jìedùshǐ belonged to the Southwest Pacification Office.
They garrisoned north of Mount Hēishān.
The Diélǔ Díliè (迭魯敵烈) Tribe.
Shèngzōng established it with Díliè (敵烈) households.
It was subordinate to the Northern Chancellery.
Its Jìedùshǐ belonged to the Wūgǔ Díliè Supreme Military Command (Wūgǔ Díliè Tǒngjūn Sī, 烏古敵烈統軍司).
The Shìwéi Tribe.
Shèngzōng established it with Shìwéi households.
It was subordinate to the Northern Chancellery.
Its Jìedùshǐ belonged to the Northwest Route Pacification Office.
The Zhúzhé Dálǔguó (朮哲達魯虢) Tribe.
Shèngzōng established it with Dálǔguó households.
It was subordinate to the Northern Chancellery.
Its Jìedùshǐ belonged to the Northeast Route Supreme Military Command.
They garrisoned within the border,
but resided outside the border.
The Méigǔxī (梅古悉) Tribe.
Shèngzōng established it with Tánggǔ (唐古) households.
It was subordinate to the Northern Chancellery.
Its Jìedùshǐ belonged to the Southwest Pacification Office.
The Jiédì (頡的) Tribe.
Shèngzōng established it with Tánggǔ households.
It was subordinate to the Northern Chancellery.
Its Jìedùshǐ belonged to the Southwest Pacification Office.
The Běi Díliè (北敵烈) Tribe.
Shèngzōng established it with Díliè households.
They garrisoned the Wěi Wūgǔ (隗烏古) Tribe.
The Nìqǐ Tánggǔ (匿訖唐古) Tribe.
Shèngzōng established it.
It was subordinate to the Northern Chancellery.
Its Jìedùshǐ belonged to the Southwest Pacification Office.
The Běi Tánggǔ (北唐古) Tribe.
Shèngzōng established it with Tánggǔ households.
It was subordinate to the Northern Chancellery.
Its Jìedùshǐ belonged to the Huánglóng Fǔ Command Headquarters.
They garrisoned south of the Residence.
The Nán Tánggǔ (南唐古) Tribe.
Shèngzōng established it.
It was subordinate to the Northern Chancellery.
The Hèlā Tánggǔ (鶴剌唐古) Tribe.
It was the same as the Nán Tánggǔ.
Its Jìedùshǐ belonged to the Southwest Pacification Office.
The Héxī Tribe.
Shèngzōng established it.
It was subordinate to the Northern Chancellery.
Its Jìedùshǐ belonged to the Northeast Route Supreme Military Command.
The Xuētè (薛特) Tribe.
In Kāitài 4th year (1015),
it was established with Huíhú (回鶻) households.
It was subordinate to the Northern Chancellery.
They resided north of Círén (慈仁) County.
The Bósībígǔdé (伯斯鼻骨德) Tribe.
Its households were originally from Bígǔdé (鼻骨德).
Initially subordinate to the Imperial Divisions,
Shèngzōng established it as a tribe when the population flourished.
It was subordinate to the Northern Chancellery.
Its Jìedùshǐ belonged to the Northeast Route Supreme Military Command.
They garrisoned within the border,
but resided outside the border.
The Dámǎ Bígǔdé (達馬鼻骨德) Tribe.
Shèngzōng established it with Bígǔdé households.
It was subordinate to the Southern Chancellery.
Its Jìedùshǐ belonged to the Northeast Route Supreme Military Command.
The Five Guó Tribe (Wǔ Guó Bù).
The state of Pōuālǐ Guó, Pénnúlǐ Guó,
Àolǐmǐ Guó, Yuèlǐdǔ Guó, and Yuèlǐjí Guó.
They came to submit during the time of Shèngzōng,
who ordered them to reside in their native lands,
to guard the northeastern frontier,
and placed them under the jurisdiction of the Huánglóng Fǔ Dū Bùshǔ Sī.
In the sixth year of Zhòngxī (1037),
because Shàng Hǎi and others, people of Yuèlǐjí Guó, complained that the chieftain Hún Bì was corrupt,
the chieftains of the Five Guó were dismissed,
and a Jiédùshǐ was established to govern them.
Of the tribes established by Shèngzōng from existing tribal units, the sixteen mentioned above,
eighteen were newly added.
The Ten External Tribes of Liáo Guó:
Wūgǔ Bù.
Díliè Bā Bù (The Eight Díliè Tribes).
Wěigǔ Bù.
Huíbá Bù.
Yānmǔ Bù.
Wútūwǎn Bù.
Diélàgě Bù.
Huíhú Bù.
Chángbáishān Bù.
Púlú Máoyán Bù.
These ten tribes were unable to form states independently;
they were vassals of Liáo,
sometimes rebelling, sometimes submitting.
They each had duties and presented tribute,
similar to the Jīmí Zhōu of the Táng people.
Zhì IV: Treatise on Military Defense, Part 1
Xūanyuán Shì (the Yellow Emperor) consolidated authority at the Eastern Sea,
establishing a capital at the edge of Zhuōlù.
He moved back and forth without a fixed dwelling,
using military strength for camping and defense.
North of Fēihú,
east of Wúlǜ,
and west reaching Liúshā,
this was land contested on all four sides.
Even the Sages could not dispense with military defense;
it was dictated by the topography.
Liáo Guó had Liáohǎi to the left (east),
and Zhuōlù to the right (west).
No state was stronger in military power.
During the Suí dynasty,
they lived along the Héchén Shuǐ,
divided into ten tribes.
The largest forces numbered three thousand,
the smallest over a thousand.
Following the heat and cold,
they pursued water and grass for herding.
If they launched an invasion, the ten tribes would confer together,
raise troops for the campaign,
and only act after reaching an agreement.
For hunting, each tribe acted independently.
By the Táng dynasty,
the Dàhè Shì had four hundred and thirty thousand fighting men,
divided into eight tribes.
When the Dàhè Shì declined,
only five tribes remained.
There was a man named Yēlǜ Yǎlǐ,
who divided the five tribes into eight,
established two government offices (fǔ) to administer them,
separated the three Yēlǜ clans into seven,
and the two Shěnmì clans into five,
totaling twenty tribes.
He carved notches in wood for contracts (qì),
and his political orders were widely implemented.
Sùn Bù did not rule the state;
instead, the Yáoliǎn Shì were established to replace the Dàhè Shì.
Their military strength increased further.
This was the sixth-generation ancestor of Tàizǔ.
When Tàizǔ met Lǐ Kèyòng in Yúnzhōng,
his forces numbered three hundred thousand—
a magnificent strength.
In the tenth year of Yáoliǎn Yēlán Kèhán (Khan),
which was the year Xīnyǒu,
Tàizǔ was given the battle-ax and the authority to lead campaigns.
He defeated the three states of Shìwéi, Yújué, and Xī,
capturing tents and livestock
too numerous to count.
In the tenth month,
he was appointed Yílíjǐn of the Dàdiéliè Fǔ.
He clarified rewards and punishments,
repaired armor and weapons,
gave rest to the common people,
encouraged the proliferation of herds,
and focused on ending military conflict.
In the eleventh year,
he commanded four hundred thousand troops to attack Dàiběi,
conquering nine commanderies and counties,
and capturing ninety-five thousand people.
In the twelfth year,
Dézǔ campaigned against the Xī,
capturing seven thousand households.
In the fifteenth year,
Yáoliǎn Kèhán died,
leaving an edict to yield the throne to Tàizǔ.
Five years after Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
he campaigned against the Western Xī and Eastern Xī,
completely pacifying them,
and taking full control of the populations of Xī and Xí.
In the spring of the sixth year,
he personally led a campaign against Yōuzhōu.
Banners stretched from east to west, visible to one another,
extending for hundreds of *lǐ*.
The commanderies and counties he passed through
all surrendered upon seeing his approach.
He captured a great many people,
and then returned with his troops.
In the autumn,
he personally campaigned against Bèiyīn Guó,
capturing tens of thousands.
In the first year of Shéncè (916),
he personally campaigned against the various tribes of Tūjué, Tǔhún, Dǎngxiàng, Xiǎofān, and Shātuó,
capturing fifteen thousand six hundred households.
He attacked Zhènwǔ,
and following up his victory, advanced eastward,
attacking the five prefectures of Wèi, Xīn, Wǔ, Guī, and Rú,
capturing countless people.
He beheaded fourteen thousand seven hundred who refused to submit.
He took complete possession of the populations of Dàiběi, Héqu, and Yīnshān,
and then seized the eight armies north of the mountains.
In the fourth year,
he personally campaigned against Yúgǔlǐ Guó,
capturing fourteen thousand two hundred people.
In the fifth year,
he campaigned against the Dǎngxiàng,
capturing two thousand six hundred people.
He attacked Tiāndé Jūn,
taking twelve fortified camps,
and relocated their inhabitants.
In the sixth year,
he emerged from Jūyōng Guān,
dividing his forces to raid Tán Zhōu and Shùn Zhōu,
as well as the counties of Ānyuǎn Jūn, Sānhé, Liángxiāng, Wàngdū, Lù, Mǎnchéng, and Suìchéng.
He captured their people and relocated them to the interior;
the Crown Prince raided Dìng Zhōu,
capturing a great many people.
In the first year of Tiānzàn (922),
because the population had greatly increased
and central control was lax over distant regions,
he divided the Běidà Nóngwù into two tribes,
establishing two Jiédùshǐ to govern them.
In the third year,
he campaigned west against the Dǎngxiàng and other states,
capturing countless people.
In the fourth year,
he personally campaigned against Bóhǎi again.
In the first year of Tiānxiǎn (926),
he extinguished Bóhǎi Guó,
which covered five thousand *lǐ* of territory,
had hundreds of thousands of soldiers,
five Capitals (Jīng), fifteen Prefectures (Fǔ), and sixty-two Departments (Zhōu).
He took possession of their entire population,
and the Qìdān state grew even larger.
Early in the Huìtóng era,
Tàizōng destroyed the Táng (Later Táng) and established the Jìn (Later Jìn).
Jìn offered the sixteen prefectures of Yān and Dài.
With a vast population and powerful military,
none could resist them.
Military System
Regarding the military system of Liáo Guó,
all commoners aged fifteen and above,
and fifty and below,
were registered on the military roster.
For every primary soldier,
there were three horses,
one retainer each for foraging (dǎ cǎo gǔ) and for guarding the camp,
nine items of iron armor for the man,
saddle and reins for the horses,
and horse armor of hide or iron,
depending on the soldier's means.
Four bows,
four hundred arrows,
one each of a long or short spear, ●●, battle-ax, small banner, hammer and awl, fire starter (steel and flint), horse basin, one *dǒu* of ●, ● bag, and covered ● umbrella.
Two hundred *chǐ* of rope for tethering horses,
all supplied by the soldier himself.
Neither man nor horse was supplied with rations or fodder.
Riders were sent out daily to forage (dǎ cǎo gǔ), raiding in all directions to provide supplies.
Golden fish tallies (jīnyú fú) were cast
to mobilize troops and horses.
Two hundred silver plaques (yín pái) were used for securing horses and transmitting orders.
Where the army made camp,
there were scouting horses (lánzimǎ) sent far ahead,
to listen for the sound of people and horses at night.
Tàizǔ ascended the throne for five years,
campaigning against the Western Xī and Eastern Xī.
He pacified them all,
and gained control of all the people of Xī and Xī.
In the spring of the sixth year,
he personally led an expedition to Yōuzhōu.
The banners of the east and west were visible to each other,
stretching for hundreds of lǐ.
The prefectures and counties he passed through
all submitted at the mere sight of his army.
He captured a great many,
then returned with his victorious army.
In the autumn,
he personally led an expedition against the Bèiyīn Guó,
capturing tens of thousands.
In the first year of Shéncè,
he personally led an expedition against the various tribes of Tūjué, Tǔhún, Dǎngxiàng, Xiǎofān, and Shātuó,
capturing 15,600 households.
He attacked Zhènwǔ,
and, taking advantage of his victory, marched eastward,
attacking the five prefectures of Wèi, Xīn, Wǔ, Guī, and Rú.
The number of captives was innumerable,
and 14,700 who resisted were beheaded.
He gained control of all the people of Dàiběi, Héqu, and Yīnshān,
and consequently seized the eight armies north of the mountains.
In the fourth year,
he personally led an expedition against the Gǔlǐ Guó,
capturing 14,200 people.
In the fifth year,
he campaigned against Dǎngxiàng,
capturing 2,600 people.
He attacked Tiāndé Jūn,
destroying twelve palisades,
and relocating their people.
In the sixth year,
he exited Jūyōng Guān,
and divided his troops to raid Tán, Shùn, and other prefectures,
as well as Ānyuǎn Jūn, Sānhé, Liángxiāng, Wàngdū, Lù, Mǎnchéng, Suìchéng, and other counties.
He captured their people and relocated them to the interior.
The Crown Prince attacked and pacified Dìngzhōu,
capturing a great many.
In the first year of Tiānzàn,
due to the increasing population
and the looseness of administration,
he divided the great Wūgǔ from the north into two parts,
establishing two military governors to govern them.
In the third year,
he led a western expedition against Dǎngxiàng and other states,
capturing innumerable people.
In the fourth year,
he again personally led an expedition against Bóhǎi.
In the first year of Tiānxiǎn,
he destroyed the Bóhǎi Guó,
which had a territory of five thousand lǐ,
an army of several hundred thousand,
five capitals, fifteen prefectures, and sixty-two districts.
He gained control of all its people,
and the Qìdān thereby grew larger.
At the beginning of Huìtóng,
Tàizōng destroyed Táng and established Jìn.
Jìn offered the sixteen prefectures of Yān and Dài.
With a numerous populace and strong army,
no one could resist them.
Military System
Regarding the military system of Liáo Guó,
all commoners aged fifteen and above,
and below fifty,
were registered in the military.
For each principal soldier,
there were three horses,
and one household attendant each for foraging, guarding the camp, and performing odd jobs.
Each person had nine items of iron armor,
horse saddles and bridles,
and horse armor made of leather and iron,
depending on their strength.
Four bows,
four hundred arrows,

one long and short spear, one *gē* (dagger-axe), one axe-halberd, one small banner, one hammer-awl, one fire-striker and flint, one horse trough, one *bǐng* (ration) of one dòu, one *xiá* (pouch), and one collapsible umbrella.
Two hundred chǐ of horse tethering rope
were all self-provided.
Neither men nor horses were supplied with rations or fodder.
Foraging cavalry were dispatched daily in all four directions to plunder and supply them.
Gold fish tallies were cast
to mobilize military horses.
There were two hundred silver plaques for capturing horses and transmitting orders.
At the army's encampment,
there were distant reconnaissance scouts on horseback
who listened for the sound of people and horses at night.
Whenever troops were raised,
the Emperor, accompanied by both civilian and military officials of the Fān and Hàn,
sacrificed a black ox and a white horse to heaven and earth and the sun god.
They did not bow to the moon.
He then commanded close officials to report to the tombs of Tàizǔ and his successors, as well as the Mùyè Shān deity,
and then issued edicts to various circuits to conscript soldiers.
Only the kings of Nán and Běi Xī,
the Bóhǎi troops of Dōngjīng,
and the統軍 troops of Yānjīng,
even upon receiving the edict,
would not dare to dispatch troops
without first reporting it.
The Emperor would send a great general carrying a gold fish tally,
and only when they matched
would the troops set out.
Upon first hearing the edict,
households and their able-bodied men were assembled.
Their household resources were assessed,
and registers were verified and people gathered to await orders.
From the ten-man commander and above,
they successively mustered and gathered military horses and weaponry.
When the tally arrived,
the military horses were led by their respective bureaus;
the envoy was not allowed to interfere.
Only after jointly reviewing the military horses
was another report made to the Emperor.
Based on the number of military horses,
an envoy was again appointed as the army commander,
who would supervise the respective bureaus.
They then requested to display the flags and drums of the five directions,
before the Emperor personally reviewed the generals and officers.
Furthermore, distinguished relatives and high-ranking ministers were selected
to serve as commander-in-chief, deputy commander-in-chief, and inspector-general of the field army, one of each.
In addition, thirty thousand of the most elite soldiers from various armies were selected as the imperial guard.
Three thousand brave and strong men were selected as the vanguard.
More than one hundred fierce and strong men were selected as distant reconnaissance scouts.
All of the above had their own commanders.
Furthermore, in each division of the various armies,
depending on its size,
ten or five men were drawn out
to form a squad,
with a separate commander established
to facilitate the requisition of soldiers and horses
and the transmission of official documents.
For southern expeditions, troop mobilization
often occurred at Yuānyāng Pō, a thousand lǐ north of Yōuzhōu.
When marching,
they generally took routes through Jūyōng Guān, Cáowáng Yù, Báimǎ Kǒu, Gǔběi Kǒu, Āndámǎ Kǒu, Sōngtíng Guān, and Yú Guān.
Upon approaching the borders of Píngzhōu and Yōuzhōu,
envoys were again dispatched to urge them on by separate routes,
not allowing them to stay long,
for fear of trampling crops.
Troops would not be deployed after September,
and would not return after December.
On the road, they were not allowed to see monks, nuns, or people in mourning attire.
the Emperor leads the civil and military officials, both Fān and Hàn,
and sacrifices a black ox and a white horse to announce the undertaking to Heaven and Earth and the Sun God.
However, the Moon is not worshipped.
He separately orders close officials to announce it to the various mausoleums from Tàizǔ down, and to the Mountain God of Mùyè.
Then he issues an imperial edict to the various circuits (dào) to levy soldiers.
Only the King of the South, the King of the North, and the King of Xī,
the troops and cavalry of Dōngjīng Bóhǎi,
and the troops and cavalry commanded by the Tǒngjūn of Yānjīng,
although they receive the edict,
do not dare dispatch troops
until they have reported it (to the throne).
The Emperor then sends a great general carrying a golden fish tally (Jīnyú fú).
When the two halves match,
then they proceed.
As soon as the edict is heard,
the able-bodied men (dīng) of the households are gathered,
the capacity of the households is assessed,
the registers are checked, and the populace is organized to await orders.
From the Shíjiàng (Commander of Ten) and above,
they sequentially review and gather the military personnel, horses, weapons, and equipment.
When the tally arrives,
the Bīngmǎ Běnsī (Office of Troops and Horses) takes charge directly.
The imperial envoy may not interfere.
Only after they have jointly reviewed the troops and horses again,
is a report submitted to the Emperor.
Depending on the number of troops and horses,
another envoy is appointed to serve as the Jūnzhǔ (Army Master),
who mutually supervises the Běnsī.
They also request permission to display the Five Directions' flags and drums,
and only then does the Emperor personally inspect the generals and officers.
Furthermore, honored relatives and high ministers are selected,
to serve as one person each for the Xíngyíng Bīngmǎ Dūtǒng (Area Commander-in-Chief of the Campaign Army), Fùdūtǒng (Deputy Commander), and Dūjiān (Supervisor).
In addition, thirty thousand exceptionally elite troops and cavalry are selected from the various armies to form the Hùjià Jūn (Imperial Guard Army).
Three thousand brave and fierce men are selected as the Xiānfēng Jūn (Vanguard Army).
More than one hundred skilled and powerful men are selected as the Yuǎntàn Lánzǐ Jūn (Far-ranging Scout and Screen Army).
All the aforementioned (units) have their own generals and leaders.
Moreover, within every division of the various armies,
judging the size of the force,
ten men or five men are drawn out
and combined into a separate unit (duì),
and separate commanders are established for them,
in preparation for drafting troops and horses
and relaying official documents.
When reviewing troops for the Southern Expedition (Nán Fá),
it is usually done at Yuānyāng Pō, a thousand lǐ north of Yōuzhōu.
When the army sets out,
they generally take the routes through Jūyōng Guān, Cáowáng Yù, Báimǎ Kǒu, Gǔběi Kǒu, Āndámǎ Kǒu, Sōngtíng Guān, and Yú Guān.
Upon reaching the borders of Píngzhōu and Yōuzhōu,
envoys are again dispatched to urge the troops forward along different paths,
and they are not allowed to stay long,
for fear of trampling the crops.
Troops are dispatched no later than the ninth month,
and the army returns no later than the twelfth month.
While on the march, they must not encounter monks, nuns, or people wearing mourning clothes.
If the Emperor personally campaigns,
one imperial prince (Qīnwáng) is left in Yōuzhōu,
to provisionally manage the great military and state affairs.
After entering the Southern territory,
the forces are divided into three routes,
one passing through Guǎngxìn Jūn, one through Xióngzhōu, and one through Bàzhōu.
The imperial chariot must travel the middle route,
followed by the Bīngmǎ Dūtǒng (Commander-in-Chief of Troops and Horses), the Hùjià Jūn, and other armies.
When the armies along the various routes encounter a county (xiàn) or a town (zhèn),
they attack immediately.
If it is a large prefecture (zhōu) or military command (jūn),
they must first estimate its strength or weakness and the proper sequence of attack before advancing troops.
Along the route, civilian dwellings, gardens, and mulberry groves
must be leveled, cut down, burned, and cleansed.
Upon reaching the Sòng capital of Běijīng,
the troops from all three routes converge,
to deliberate on the attack and capture (of the city).
The same applies when retreating.
The armies of the three routes have vanguards positioned to the front, rear, left, and right.
Ten or more cavalrymen from the Yuǎntàn Lánzǐ (Far-ranging Scouts)
move twenty or more lǐ ahead of and behind the vanguard.
They wear full armor and clothing.
During the night, they halt briefly every ten or five lǐ they march.
They dismount and listen carefully for any sounds of people or horses.
If there are sounds, they capture them;
if the force is overwhelming,
they swiftly report to the vanguard,
and the entire force attacks together.
If there is a large enemy army,
they race back to inform the main commander (zhǔshuài).
They ensure that the enemy's strength or weakness,
and every movement is known.
If the army encounters a prefectural city (zhōuchéng) along the route,
and its defenses are solid
and cannot be attacked,
they lead the troops past it.
Fearing the enemy might leave the city to intercept and obstruct them,
they surround it, shoot arrows, and raise a clamor with drums,
feigning an attack.
While the enemy is busy closing the gates and holding fast,
the road ahead is unobstructed.
The troops are led forward,
and detached forces are sent to bypass and cut off communications,
so that the prefectural cities along the way are isolated and unable to communicate,
becoming isolated and without support.
At every prefectural city, large or small, they pass,
when night falls,
fearing that forces might sortie from the city to launch a surprise attack,
or coordinate troops with neighboring prefectures,
during the first watch (jiǎyè),
for each city, one hundred cavalrymen are stationed about one hundred paces left and right of the city gates.
They wear armor and hold weapons,
standing mounted and awaiting.
If troops emerge,
and they cannot overpower them,
they gallop back to gather the main force and engage in combat.
To the left and right, along official roads, side paths, mountain trails, and river crossings,
troops are dispatched for night patrols and defense.
As for the jiādīng (servants/conscripts) engaged in Dǎ Cǎogǔ (foraging/pillaging),
each wears armor and carries weapons,
immediately grouping into units.
They must first chop down and destroy gardens and forests,
then drive and seize the old and young,
transporting earth and wood to fill moats and ditches.
During the siege of a city,
they are certainly made to climb first.
When arrows, stones, and rolling timbers are all cast down,
only the old and young are injured.
Furthermore, ten thousand Hàn commoner auxiliary troops (xiāngbīng) are raised in the prefectures and counties of their own country,
accompanying the army specifically to fell gardens and forests,
and block roads.
For the Imperial stockade (Yùzhài) and all the various camps and fortifications,
only mulberry, silkworm thorn, pear, and chestnut wood are used.
When the army retreats,
they set fire and burn them.
Once the enemy army has deployed formations (zhèn),
they assess the size of the formation,
the lay of the mountains and rivers,
the routes for advance and retreat,
the quick paths for reinforcement,
and the source of grain transport.
Each aspect must be controlled accordingly.
Then, around the four sides of the formation,
cavalry is lined up in units (duì),
each unit consisting of five or seven hundred men.
Ten units form one sector (dào),
and ten sectors cover one side.
Each (sector) has its own main commander (zhǔshuài).
The very first unit spurs its horses and shouts loudly,
charging and clashing with the enemy formation.
If they gain the advantage,
then all the units advance together;
if they do not gain the advantage,
they are led to retreat,
and the second unit follows.
Those who retreat
rest their horses and drink water.
All sectors operate in this manner.
They retreat in turn and advance alternately.
If the enemy formation remains stable
and does not fight forcefully.
After two or three days pass,
waiting until they are exhausted,
they then order the Dǎ Cǎogǔ jiādīng to tie double brooms to their horses,
and gallop swiftly into the wind,
kicking up dust toward the enemy formation,
moving back and forth in alternation.
Once (the enemy) is hungry and tired,
and cannot see each other clearly (due to dust),
victory can be achieved.
If the south side of the formation gains victory,
but the north side suffers defeat,
and the chief commander is in the center
and has no way to know,
then the names of the mountains and rivers corresponding to the four directions of their own country are used as signals,
sounded to be heard by each other,
allowing them to rescue and respond to one another.
If the Emperor does not personally campaign,
a high minister commands no less than one hundred and fifty thousand men.
They advance and return along three routes,
assemble troops at Běijīng,
advance in the ninth month,
and retreat in the twelfth month.
The sequence of operations is all carried out as above.
If it is Spring (in the first month),
or Autumn (in the ninth month),
and a Dūtǒng is not appointed,
only sixty thousand cavalry are dispatched.
They are not permitted to penetrate deeply,
nor to attack cities and walls,
nor to fell forests.
They merely operate within three hundred lǐ outside the border,
devastating the places where people live and gather,
and preventing them from planting or rearing livestock.
When the army entered the southern border,
the infantry, cavalry, chariots, and tents did not follow the main paths.
Each of the three routes had one commanding officer.
They led scouts (lānzǐ mǎ) of ten thousand cavalry each,
spreading out and maneuvering one hundred to ten *lǐ* away,
alternately watching and patrolling.
When evening approached,
the blowing of horns served as the signal,
and the troops immediately halted and established camp,
encircling the imperial tent (yùzhàng).
Starting from near and moving to far,
they broke off tree branches and bent them slightly,
to form temporary resting places (gōngzǐ pū),
without setting up defenses like spear camps, moats, or stockades.
Whenever the army marched,
the drum sounded three beats,
and regardless of day or night,
the entire host advanced simultaneously.
Before encountering a major enemy,
they did not ride their war horses;
waiting until they were near the enemy army,
they mounted newly bridled horses,
whose hooves still had strength remaining.
They did not fight when arrayed in formation;
if the enemy retreated, they pursued them.
They often used ambushes to cut off supply routes,
lit fires at night,
and dragged firewood upwind.
They provided their own provisions from their personal estates,
scattering and then regrouping.
They were skilled in combat
and resistant to cold.
This is why this army was strong.
Treatise V: Military and Guard Systems, Imperial Tent Personal Guard
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn conducted many tours and progresses,
and established the designations of the Qīmén, Cìfēi, and Yǔlín,
and thus the Son of Heaven first acquired a personal guard.
Emperor Tàizōng of Táng added the Wèi of Qīn, Xūn, Yì, and Qiānniú,
deploying them in critical areas,
making the defense system tight.
Emperor Tàizǔ of Liáo’s imperial clan (zōngshì) was greatly powerful,
and he divided the Diélà 部 into two,
leaving the Palace Guard (gōngwèi) internally weak.
Engaged in operations across the four directions,
he did not have time to gather troops.
During the period when Empress Shùlǜ Shì remained in charge of the defense,
she selected elite Khitan and Han troops to form the Shǔshān Jūn;
Emperor Tàizōng further selected the best armored troops from across the realm,
placing them as his trusted aides, forming the Píshì Jūn.
Together, the cavalry amounted to five hundred thousand,
and the national prestige was strengthened.
The Great Tent Píshì Jūn.
Established by Emperor Tàizōng,
it comprised thirty thousand cavalry in total.
The Shǔshān Jūn.
Established by the Empress Dowager (dì huánghòu),
it comprised twenty thousand cavalry.
Palace Guard Cavalry
Emperor Tàizǔ received the abdication (shòuchán) from the Diélà 部,
and divided his own tribe (běnbù) into the Five Circuits (Wǔ Yuàn) and Six Circuits (Liù Yuàn),
placing them under the command of the imperial relatives (huángzú),
but the personal guard was clearly lacking.
He then established the method of the Wòlǔmì (斡魯𩽆 fǎ),
splitting off prefectures and counties (zhōuxiàn),
and allocating households and adult males (hùdīng),
thereby strengthening the main branch (gàn) and weakening the auxiliary branches (zhī).
He planned for his successors
to establish the Palace Guards generation after generation.
When entering, they resided and guarded;
when traveling, they provided escort;
when buried, they served to guard the mausoleums.
Should there be military affairs,
the Tíxiá Sī (Commissioners' Offices) in the Five Capitals (Wǔ Jīng) and Two Prefectures (Èr Zhōu) were summoned by dispatch,
without waiting for the mobilization of prefectures, counties, or tribes (bùzú),
and ten thousand cavalry troops would be readily assembled.
The intent of the ruler’s grace was intimate,
the weapons and armor were sharp,
and training was comprehensive and practiced.
They selected the elite forces of the realm
and gathered them in the core region.
Those who cherished the old ways grew deep with the years,
and those who added new recruits thrived across generations.
This was an excellent military system.

Troops of the Vassal States
The vassal states of the Liáo that can be recorded number fifty-nine.
Tribute payment was irregular.
If there was military action, envoys were dispatched to conscript troops,
or imperial edicts were issued commanding dedicated campaigns;
those who did not comply were attacked.
The number of auxiliary troops
varied according to their respective conveniences,

When the Liáo established their state,
they bordered Liáng, Táng, Jìn, Hàn, Zhōu, and Sòng.
The Jìn, due to favors bestowed,
began as father and son, one family;
but eventually, they became enemies who attacked each other.
Liáng, Táng, and Zhōu were all implicitly hostile states.
Only when Sòng Tàizōng conquered Běihàn,
was the Liáo unable to rescue them,
otherwise, (the Sòng) mostly suffered defeats and setbacks;
even when gains were made, they did not compensate for the losses.
This was truly because Shí Jìn ceded territory,
causing the Central States to lose the fortifications of the Five Passes.
Gāolì, though a small state,
repeatedly defeated Liáo troops—
is this not because their natural defenses were sufficient to rely upon?
Xīxià, a land the size of a pill,
defeated the Sòng in the south,
and resisted the Liáo in the east.
Although the soldiers and horses of the northwest are strong and vigorous,
and Yuánhào and Liàngzuò possessed wisdom and courage surpassing ordinary men,
enabling them to restrain the great states using the Dǎngxiàng and Zǔbǔ,
it is probably also due to their territory being embraced by mountains and bordered by rivers,
having something to assist their power.
Nevertheless,
the Sòng had long lost geographical advantages,
and when the old records discuss military affairs,
they focus solely on opposing the Sòng.
When crossing the Three Passes,
and gathering for deliberation at Běijīng,
they still dared not advance lightly.
Is this not because the Great River was ahead,
and the Three Garrisons were behind,
and the assessment of the strategy before action was careful,
making it necessarily so?
The Two Tents, the Twelve Palaces, One Superior Prefecture, and Five Capitals,
have troops totaling 1,642,800.
The Palace adult males, the great leaders, and the various tribes,
Zhōngjīng and the counties/prefectures under the Head Tax Administration,
and the populace of the vassal states,
are all not included in this figure.
Not using them lightly,
is how the Liáo secured a long era.
Garrison Troops on the Borderlands
Furthermore, having obtained the accounts of Gāolì and Dàliáo affairs,
which record the garrison troops on the Eastern Border,
to guard against Gāolì, Nǚzhí, and other states,
we can see the structure of their defense of the state;
the deployment is concise and crucial,
by observing one, the situation of the three borders can be known.

Vassal state armies.
Emperor Yáo (Dì Yáo) divided All Under Heaven (Tiānxià) into Nine Provinces (Jiǔzhōu).
Shùn (Shùn) considered that Jì (Jì), Qīng (Qīng) had vast territories,
so he divided Yōu (Yōu), Bīng (Bīng), and Yíng (Yíng),
making Twelve Provinces (Shíyǒu Èr Zhōu).
Yōuzhōu lies between the Bohai (Bó) Sea and Jié (Jié) Mountain.
Bīngzhōu has Dài (Dài) and Shuò (Shuò) to the north.
Yíngzhōu extends eastward to the Liáohǎi Sea.
Its land relies on mountains and borders the sea.
Its people wield shields and spears,
excelling in martial defense.
The temperament (fēngqì) is fierce and strong;
since ancient times, it has been a place for military deployment.
Tàizǔ, using the masses of the Diélà (Diélà) tribe, replaced the Yáoliǎn (Yáoliǎn) clan,
arose in Línhuáng,
and established the Imperial Capital (Huángdū).
To the east, he annexed Bóhǎi,
obtaining one hundred and three settled cities and towns.
Tàizōng established the Jìn (Jìn) dynasty,

and possessed the sixteen prefectures (zhōu) of Yōu (Yōu), Zhuō (Zhuō), Tán (Tán), Jì (Jì), Shùn (Shùn), Yíng (Yíng), Píng (Píng), Wèi (Wèi), Shuò (Shuò), Yún (Yún), Yīng (Yīng), Xīn (Xīn), Guī (Guī), Rú (Rú), Wǔ (Wǔ), and Huán (Huán).
Thereupon, he partitioned the territory of the ancient Yōu, Bīng, and Yíng (Yíng) and took possession of it.
To the east, he held court over Gāolì;
to the west, the Xià (Xià) State was his subject;
to the south, he treated Shíjìn (Shí Jìn) as his son and Zhào Sòng (Zhào Sòng) as his brother.
Wúyuè and Nántáng sailed across the sea to deliver tribute.
Ah,
how flourishing it was!
The forefathers of the Liáo (Liáo) State were called Qìdān.
Their original land was that of the Xiānbēi,
dwelling in the center of the Liáozé Marsh.
It was 1,130 *lǐ* away from Yúguān,
and 714 *lǐ* away from Yōuzhōu.
To the south, it controlled Huánglóng;
to the north, it bordered the Huángshuǐ River.
Lěngxíng served as a screen on the right (west);
the Liáohé River acted as a moat on the left (east).
The high plains had many elms and willows;
the low, wet areas were abundant with reeds and rushes.
During the time of the Yuán Wèi (Yuán Wèi),
they possessed a territory of several hundred *lǐ*.
Reaching the Táng dynasty,
the Dàhè (Dàhè) clan gradually encroached upon the regions of Fúyú, Shìwéi, Xī, and Mòhé,
making the territory more than 2,000 *lǐ* square.
In the third year of Zhēngguān (Zhēngguān),
Xuánzhōu was established on its land.
Soon after, the Sōngmò Military Command (Sōngmò Dū Dū Fǔ) was established,
and the Eight Tribes were set up as prefectures (zhōu),
each appointing an administrator (cìshǐ): The Dájī (Dájī) tribe was named Qiàoluòzhōu,
the Hèbián (Hèbián) tribe was named Tánhànzhōu,
the Dúhuó (Dúhuó) tribe was named Wúféngzhōu,
the Fēnā (Fēnā) tribe was named Yǔlíngzhōu,
the Túbiàn (Túbiàn) tribe was named Rìliánzhōu,
the Ruìxī (Ruìxī) tribe was named Túhézhōu,
the Zhuìjīn (Zhuìjīn) tribe was named Wàndānzhōu,
and the Fú (Fú) tribe was named the two prefectures of Pǐlí and Chìshān.
Kūgē (Kūgē) of the Dàhè clan was made Commissioner with Credentials for the Military Affairs of Ten Prefectures (Shǐ Chí Jié Shí Zhōu Jūanshì).
The establishment of officials and division into prefectures
probably originated here.
By the time of the Five Dynasties (Wǔdài),
the territory expanded three thousand *lǐ* from east to west.
The Yáoliǎn clan reorganized the Eight Tribes, renaming them Dànlìjiē Bù, Yǐshìhuó Bù, Shíhuó Bù, Nàwěi Bù, Pínmò Bù, Nèihuìjī Bù, Jíjiě Bù, and Xīwà Bù.
They controlled forty-one subordinate counties (xiàn).
Each tribe established an administrator (cìshǐ),
and each county installed a magistrate (lìng).
Tàizōng designated the Imperial Capital (Huángdū) as Shàngjīng.
Yōuzhōu was promoted to Nánjīng.
Nánjīng was renamed Dōngjīng.
Shèngzōng built Zhōngjīng.
Xīngzōng promoted Yúnzhōu to Xījīng.
Thus, the Five Capitals (Wǔjīng) were complete.
Moreover, states (zhōu) were established in strategic locations using households captured in conquest,
mostly named after their original dwelling places.
Additionally, prefectures (Tóuxià Zhōu) administered by private slaves were established.
In total there were five Capitals (Jīng),
six Superior Prefectures (Fǔ),
one hundred and fifty-six Prefectures, Military Prefectures (Jūn), and Cities (Chéng),
two hundred and nine counties (xiàn),
fifty-two tribes (bùzú),
and sixty vassal states (shǔguó).
To the east, it reached the sea;
to the west, it reached Jīnshān Mountain
and extended to Liúshā (the Shifting Sands);
to the north, it reached the Lúqúhé River;
to the south, it reached Báigōu.
Its total area was ten thousand *lǐ* square.
Shàngjīng Circuit (Shàngjīng Dào)
Shàngjīng Línhuáng Fǔ [Superior Prefecture]
was originally the territory of Xī'ānpíng County, Liáodōng Commandery (Liáodōng Jùn) during the Hàn dynasty.
Xīn Mǎng (Xīn Mǎng) called it Běi'ānpíng.
Tàizǔ utilized the strategic position of the three mountains — Tiāntī, Méngguó, and Biélǔ — in Wěidiàn,
shot the Jīncuò Arrow to mark the place,
and called it Lóngméi Gōng [Palace].
In the third year of Shéncè, he built walls around it,
and named it the Imperial Capital (Huángdū).
In the thirteenth year of Tiānxiǎn,
it was renamed Shàngjīng,
and the superior prefecture was called Línhuáng.
The Láiliúhé River flows south from the northwest,
encircling the Capital on three sides,
and entering the Qǔjiāng River to the east.
To the north, it flows east and becomes the Ànchūhé River.
There are also the Yùhé River,
Shāhé River, Hēihé River, Huánghé River, Yāzǐhé River, Tāshǔhé River,
Lánghé River, Cāng'ěrhé River, Wǎngzǐhé River, Lúqúhé River, Yīnliánghé River, Zhūhé River, Yuānyāng Hú [Lake],
Xīngguó Huìmín Hú, Guǎngjì Hú, Yán Luò [Marsh], Bǎigǒu Luò, Huǒshéndiàn [Marsh],
Mǎyúshān Mountain, Tù'érshān Mountain,
Yěquèshān Mountain, Yánshān Mountain, and Záoshān Mountain.
It contains 36,500 households,
administering twenty-five Military Prefectures (Jūn), Superior Prefectures (Fǔ), Prefectures (Zhōu), and Cities (Chéng),
and governs ten counties (Xiàn):
Línhuáng Xiàn [County].
In the beginning of Tàizǔ's Tiānzàn era, when he attacked Yān (Yān) and Jì (Jì) to the south,
the captured households were scattered to reside north of the Huángshuǐ River.
The county borders the Huángshuǐ River,
hence its name.
The land is suitable for cultivation.
Households: 3,500.
Chángtài Xiàn.
Originally, its people were from Chángpíng County of the Bóhǎi State.
When Tàizǔ attacked Dà Yīnzhuàn,
he first captured this city
and moved its people to the northwest of the Capital,
where they lived mixed with Hàn people.
