Originally, its people were from Qiángshī County, Fúyú Fǔ.
When Tàizǔ conquered Fúyú,
he moved its people to the west of the Capital,
where they intermingled with Hàn people
and divided the land for farming.
In the eighth year of Tǒnghé,
it was established using the households administered by the Bureau of Various Palaces (Zhū Gōng Tíxiá Sī).
It is subordinated to Chángníng Gōng.
Households: 2,000.
Bǎohé Xiàn.
Originally, its people were from Fùlì County of the Bóhǎi State.
When Tàizǔ defeated Lóngzhōu,
he moved all the people of Fùlì County to scattered residences south of the Capital.
In the eighth year of Tǒnghé,
it was established using the households administered by the Bureau of Various Palaces.
It is subordinated to Zhāngmǐn Gōng.
Households: 4,000.
Lù Xiàn.
Originally, its people were from Lù County, Yōuzhōu.
In the first year of Tiānzàn,
Tàizǔ defeated Jìzhōu,
captured the people of Lù County,
and settled them east of the Capital,
where they intermingled with Bóhǎi people.
It is subordinated to Chóngdé Gōng.
Households: 3,000.
Yìsú Xiàn.
Originally, its people were Bóhǎi residents of Liáodōng.
In the ninth year of Tàipíng,
Dà Yánlín incited the eastern barbarians (yí) of Liáodōng to rebel.
After being besieged for a year,
they surrendered.
They were all moved north of the Capital,
and a county was established for their residence.
In the same year,
the families of Bóhǎi rebels were also moved and settled there.
Households: 1,000.
Qiānliáo Xiàn.
Originally, its people were Bóhǎi residents from various counties in Liáodōng.
When Dà Yánlín rebelled,
he selected those who were strategic and brave to be placed near him.
Later, he surrendered the city,
was executed,
and his family members were moved to the northeast of the Capital,
hence the name.
Households: 1,000.
Bóhǎi Xiàn.
Originally, its people were from Dōngjīng.
Because of rebellion,
they were moved and settled here.
Xīngrén Xiàn.
Established in the second year of Kāitài.
Xuānhuà Xiàn.
Originally, its people were from Shénhuà County, Liáodōng.
When Tàizǔ defeated Yālù Fǔ,
he moved all its people to reside south of the Capital.
In the eighth year of Tǒnghé,
it was established using the households administered by the Bureau of Various Palaces.
It is subordinated to Zhāngmǐn Gōng.
Households: 4,000.
Shàngjīng,
the place where Tàizǔ (太祖) founded his dynasty.
Backed by mountains and embraced by the sea,
its natural defenses were sufficient for fortification.
The land was fertile and suitable for cultivation,
and the water and grass convenient for animal husbandry.
With a single arrow shot by Jīn Chù (金齪),
a foundation of two hundred years
was established—magnificent indeed.
In the first year of Tiānxiǎn (天顯) [926 CE],
having pacified Bóhǎi (渤海) and returned,
he expanded the city walls and outer defenses,
built palaces,
and named it Tiānzàn (天贊).
He erected three great halls: Kēihuáng (開皇), Āndé (安德), and Wǔluán (五鸞).
Inside were the portraits of emperors throughout the generations.
On the first and fifteenth days of the lunar month, festival days, and memorial days,
all civil and military officials in the capital proceeded there to offer sacrifices.
Also, in the southeast corner of the inner city, he built Tiānxióng Sì (天雄寺, Temple of Heavenly Might),
where the posthumous portrait of the honored father, Xuānjiǎn Huángdì (宣簡皇帝), was enshrined.
Tàizǔ passed away that year,
and Yìngtiān Huánghòu (應天皇后) cut off her arm at Yìjié Sì (義節寺, Temple of Righteous Fidelity)
and placed it at Tàizǔ's mausoleum.
The Duànwǎn Lóu (斷腕樓, Severed Arm Tower) was constructed adjacent to the temple,
and a stele was erected there.
Tàizōng (太宗) provided aid to establish Jìn (晉) [Later Jìn],
and dispatched the chancellors Féng Dào (馮道), Liú Xù (劉昫), and others, bearing credentials,
to arrive here with the imperial regalia (lǔbù) and ceremonial robes (fǎfú),
to formally confer the honorary titles upon Tàizōng and Yìngtiān Huánghòu.
Tàizōng issued an edict that all Fān Bù (蕃部, Tribal Departments) must conform to Hàn (漢) institutions.
He presided at the Kāihuáng Diàn (開皇殿),
opened Chéngtiān Mén (承天門, Gate of Receiving Heaven) to receive the ceremonies,
and consequently renamed the Imperial Capital (Huángdū) as Shàngjīng (上京).
The city wall was twenty feet high,
without defensive towers (dílóu),
and spanned twenty-seven *lǐ* in circumference.
The gates
on the east were called Yíngchūn (迎春) [Welcoming Spring],
and Yàn'ér (雁兒) [Gosling];
on the south were Shùnyáng (順陽) [Following the Sun],
and Nánfú (南福) [Southern Fortune];
on the west were Jīnfèng (金鳳) [Golden Phoenix],
and Xīyàn'ér (西雁兒) [Western Gosling].
The northern part was called the Imperial City (Huángchéng),
thirty feet high,
with towers and turrets (lóulǔ).
The gates
on the east were called Āndōng (安東) [Pacifying the East],
on the south Dàshùn (大順) [Great Compliance],
on the west Qiándé (乾德) [Heavenly Virtue],
and on the north Gǒngchén (拱辰) [Worshipping the Dipper].
The Great Inner Palace (Dà Nèi) was located inside.
The Inner Palace's South Gate was called Chéngtiān (承天),
with upper storeys and pavilions (lóugé);
the East Gate was called Dōnghuá (東華),
and the West Gate Xīhuá (西華).
These were the places for entry and exit through the Inner Palace.
East of the main south street
was the office of the Liúshǒu Sī Yámén (留守司衙, Office of the Resident General),
next was the Yántiě Sī (鹽鐵司, Salt and Iron Bureau),
next was the South Gate,
and Lóngsì Jiē (龍寺街, Dragon Temple Street).
To the south was Línhuáng Fǔ (臨潢府),
and beside it Línhuáng Xiàn (臨潢縣).
To the southwest of the county was Chóngxiào Sì (崇孝寺, Temple of Exalting Filial Piety),
built by Chéngtiān Huánghòu (承天皇后).
West of the temple was Chángtài Xiàn (長泰縣),
and further west Tiāncháng Guàn (天長觀, Temple of Celestial Longevity).
To the southwest was the Guózǐ Jiān (國子監, Directorate of Education),
north of the Directorate was the Kǒngzǐ Miào (孔子廟, Temple of Confucius),
and east of the temple was Jiéyì Sì (節義寺, Temple of Fidelity and Righteousness).
Further northwest was Ānguó Sì (安國寺, Temple of Pacifying the State),
built by Tàizōng.
East of the temple was the former residence of Qítiān Huánghòu (齊天皇后),
and east of the residence was the residence of Yuán Fēi (元妃, Primary Consort),
which was built by Fǎtiān Huánghòu (法天皇后).
To the south were Bèishèng Ní Sì (貝聖尼寺, Nun’s Temple of the Sacred Cowrie),
the Língjǐn Yuàn (綾錦院, Silk and Brocade Workshop), Nèixǐng Sī (內省司, Inner Examination Bureau), and Qū Yuàn (麴院, Yeast Workshop),
and the two granaries, Zhànguó (贍國) and Xǐng Sī (省司).
All were located southwest of the Great Inner Palace.
The Bāzuò Sī (八作司, Eight Works Bureau) faced Tiānxióng Sì.
The southern city was called Hàn Chéng (漢城, Han City).
The main transverse street was to the south,
with towers confronting each other at the sides,
and below were markets and shops.
North of the East Gate was Lù Xiàn (潞縣),
and further southeast Xīngrén Xiàn (興仁縣).
East of the South Gate was the Huíhú Yíng (回鶻營, Uyghur Camp).
Uyghur merchants and traders residing in Shàngjīng
were settled in this camp.
To the southwest was Tóngwén Yì (同文驛, Same Writing Post Station),
where envoys from various states resided.
Southwest of the station was Línhuáng Yì (臨潢驛, Linhuang Post Station),
to accommodate the envoys from Xià Guó (夏國).
West of the station was Fúxiān Sì (福先寺, Temple of Foremost Fortune).
West of the temple was Xuānhuà Xiàn (宣化縣),
southwest Dìngbà Xiàn (定霸縣),
and west of the county Bǎohé Xiàn (保和縣).
North of the West Gate was Yìsú Xiàn (易俗縣),
and east of the county Qiānlíao Xiàn (遷遼縣).
During the Guǎngshùn (廣順) reign period of Zhōu (周) [951-954 CE],
Hú Qiáo (胡嶠) recorded: On the west tower of Shàngjīng
there were settlements, houses, markets, and shops.
Transactions used cloth instead of money.

There were various workshops for silk and brocade, eunuchs, members of the Hànlín (翰林) Academy, artisans, the Jiàofāng (教坊, Music Bureau), performers of *juédǐ* (角觝, wrestling/acrobatics), Confucians, Buddhist monks and nuns, and Daoist priests.
Most of the people from the Central Plains were from Bìng (幷), Fén (汾), Yōu (幽), and Jì (薊).
In the ninth year of Dàzhōng Xiángfú (大中祥符) of Sòng (宋) [1016 CE],
Xuē Yǐng (薛映) recorded: Shàngjīng
is eighty *lǐ* north of Zhōngjīng (中京) to Sōngshān Guǎn (松山館),
seventy *lǐ* to Chóngxìn Guǎn (崇信館),
ninety *lǐ* to Guǎngníng Guǎn (廣寧館),
fifty *lǐ* to Yáojiāzhài Guǎn (姚家寨館),
fifty *lǐ* to Xiánníng Guǎn (咸寧館),
thirty *lǐ* across the stone bridge over the Huáng Shuǐ (潢水).
Nearby is Ráozhōu (饒州).
The Táng (唐) court once established Ráolè Zhōu (饒樂州) among the Qìdān (契丹).
It is now inhabited by Bóhǎi people.
Fifty *lǐ* to Bǎohé Guǎn (保和館),
crossing the Hēishuǐ Hé (黑水河, Black Water River),
seventy *lǐ* to Xuānhuà Guǎn (宣化館),
fifty *lǐ* to Chángtài Guǎn (長泰館).
Twenty *lǐ* west of the station are Buddhist shrines and civilian dwellings,
which is Zǔzhōu (祖州).
Another forty *lǐ* to Línhuáng Fǔ.
From the point of crossing Chóngxìn Guǎn onwards is the old territory of the Qìdān;
south of that is the land of the Xī (奚).
Entering the West Gate,
the gate is named Jīndé (金德),
and inside is Línhuáng Guǎn.
The East Gate of the inner city (Zǐchéng) is named Shùnyáng (順陽).
Proceeding north to Jǐngfú Mén (景福門),
and then to Chéngtiān Mén.
Inside are the Zhāodé (昭德) and Xuānzhèng (宣政) halls, along with thatched dwellings (lú),
all facing east.
Two hundred *lǐ* northwest of Línhuáng is a place called Liángdiàn (涼淀),
south of Mántóu Shān (饅頭山),
a summer retreat area.
It has abundant grass,
and solid ice can be found by digging just over ten feet into the ground.
Zǔzhōu (祖州),
Tiānchéng Jūn (天成軍, Heavenly Accomplishment Commandery),
Superior (shàng) level,
governed by a Military Commissioner (jiédù).
It was originally the land of the Shìmòlǐ (世沒里) tribe, one of the eight sections of Liáoyòu (遼右).
Tàizǔ often hunted here in the autumn,
and first established the West Tower (Xī Lóu).
Later, a city was built on the site,
and named Zǔzhōu (Ancestral Prefecture).
It was so named
because it was the birthplace of Gāozǔ Zhāoliè Huángdì (高祖昭烈皇帝), Zēngzǔ Zhuāngjìng Huángdì (曾祖莊敬皇帝), Zǔkǎo Jiǎnxiàn Huángdì (祖考簡獻皇帝), and Huángkǎo Xuānjiǎn Huángdì (皇考宣簡皇帝).
The city wall was twenty feet high,
without defensive shelters (dí péng),
and spanned nine *lǐ* in circumference.
The gates
on the east were called Wàngjīng (望京) [Gazing at the Capital],
on the south Dàxià (大夏) [Great Xia],
on the west Yèshān (液山) [Liquid Mountain],
and on the north Xīngguó (興國) [Revitalizing the State].
In the northwest corner there was an inner city.
The halls were named Liǎngmíng (兩明) [Two Brightnesses],
where the portraits of the Ancestors (zǔkǎo) were enshrined;
and Èryí (二儀) [Two Principles],
where a statue of Tàizǔ was cast in white silver;
Hēilóng (黑龍) [Black Dragon],
and Qīngmì (清秘) [Pure Secrecy].
Each held Tàizǔ's weapons, implements, and fur and felt garments from his humble days (wēi shí),
preserved to show future generations,
so they would not forget their origins.
The Inner Palace's South Gate was called Xīngshèng (興聖) [Prospering Sages],
with three portals in total,
and upper storeys and pavilions above,
with corner towers to the east and west.
To the east were the prefecture office (zhōujiè) and the offices and residences of various officials,
the Língjǐn Yuàn (綾錦院),
the Bānyuàn Zhīhòu (班院祗候) for three hundred people from the Fān (蕃), Hàn (漢), and Bóhǎi groups,
who supplied and retrieved items for the Inner Palace (Nèifǔ).
The transverse street was to the southeast,
with towers confronting each other at the four corners,
and markets and shops connecting below.
To the east was Chángbà Xiàn (長霸縣),
and to the west Xiánníng Xiàn (咸寧縣).
There was Zǔ Shān (祖山, Ancestral Mountain),
on which stood the temple of Tàizǔ Tiānhuángdì (太祖天皇帝),
where his boots still remain.
There were also the mountains of Lóngmén (龍門), Lí Gǔ (黎谷), Yè Shān (液山), Yè Quán (液泉), Báimǎ (白馬), Dú Shí (獨石), and Tiāntī (天梯).
The rivers were the Nánshā Hé (南沙河) and the Xīyè Quán (西液泉) to the west.
Tàizǔ's mausoleum was carved into the mountain to form a palace,
named Míng Diàn (明殿).
On the ridge south of the hall was the Shàntáng (膳堂, Dining Hall),
to prepare for seasonal sacrifices.
The gate was called Hēilóng (黑龍).
On the east side was Shèngzōng Diàn (聖蹤殿, Hall of Sacred Traces),
where a stele was erected recounting Tàizǔ's hunting expeditions.
East of the hall was a tower,
where a stele was erected to record Tàizǔ's achievements in founding the dynasty.
All these were five *lǐ* west of the prefecture.
Constructed by Tàizōng during the Tiānxiǎn period,
it was administered by Hóngyì Gōng (弘義宮).
It governed two counties and one city:
Chángbà Xiàn.
Originally the people of Chángpíng Xiàn, Lóngzhōu,
moved here.
Households: two thousand.
Xiánníng Xiàn.
Originally Chángníng Xiàn.
After conquering Liáoyáng,
its people were moved and settled here.
Households: one thousand.
Yuèwáng Chéng (City of the Prince of Yuè).
Tàizǔ's paternal uncle, the Yúyuè Wáng (Prince of Yúyuè), Shùlǔ, campaigned westward against the Dǎngxiàng and Tǔhún.
Their captives were brought and pastured here,
and consequently, a city was established.
It is twenty *lǐ* southeast of the prefecture.
Households: one thousand.
Huáizhōu,
Fènglín Jūn (Army for Serving the Mausoleum),
Superior level,
Jìedù (Military Commissioner).
Originally the Guīchéng Zhōu of the Táng dynasty.
Tàizōng used his traveling tent to pasture livestock here.
During the Tiānzàn period,
he followed Tàizǔ in conquering Fúyú Chéng (Fúyú City),
subjugating Lóngquán Fǔ,
capturing its people,
and building a stockade for them to live in.
During the Huìtóng period,
captives seized from Yān and Jì were also settled here.
When Tàizōng died,
he was buried in Xīshān (West Mountain),
known as Huáilíng (Mausoleum of Huái).
In the first year of Dàtóng,
Shìzōng established the prefecture to serve it.
That year,
over ten horsemen,
hunting in the great mountains fifty *lǐ* west of Zǔzhōu,
saw Tàizōng riding a white horse,
single-handedly chasing a white fox.
He shot it;
one shot killed it.
Suddenly, he vanished,
but they recovered the fox and the arrow.
On that same day,
Tàizōng died at Luánchéng.
Later, a temple was built at that location,
and at the Fènghuáng Mén (Phoenix Gate) of the prefecture, a painting depicting Tàizōng galloping and shooting the fox was created.
After Mùzōng was assassinated,
he was buried next to Huáilíng,
and the Fènghuáng Diàn (Phoenix Hall) was built to serve his spirit.
There is the Qīngliáng Diàn (Cooling Hall),
which served as a retreat for the emperor during summer tours.
All these are twenty *lǐ* west of the prefecture.
It is subordinate to Yǒngxīng Gōng (Yǒngxīng Palace).
Governs two counties:
Fúyú Xiàn.
Originally part of Lóngquán Fǔ.
Tàizǔ relocated the surrendered households from Bóhǎi's Fúyú Xiàn here,
and Shìzōng established the county.
Households: one thousand five hundred.
Xiǎnlǐ Xiàn.
Originally the people of Xiǎnlǐ Fǔ.
When Tàizǔ campaigned against Bóhǎi,
he captured its king, Dà Yīnshuàn,
and moved the populace here.
Shìzōng established the county.
Households: one thousand.
Qìngzhōu,
Xuánníng Jūn,
Superior level,
Jìedù.
Originally the area of Hēihé (Black River) by Tàibǎo Shān (Mount Tàibǎo),
characterized by steep valleys and precipitous cliffs.
Mùzōng built a city,
naming it Hēihé Zhōu (Hēihé Prefecture).
Every year he would tour here,
shooting tigers and falconing,
leaving most military and state affairs to his high ministers.
He was later assassinated here.
Because the land was bitterly cold,
in the eighth year of Tǒnghé,
the prefecture was abolished.
When Shèngzōng hunted in autumn,
he admired its unusual beauty
and established it as Qìngzhōu.
The fifth generation ancestor of the Liáo state, Bótū,
had an unusual appearance,
possessed military strategy,
and had the strength to match a hundred men.
The masses nominated him as King.
He was born on Bótū Shān (Mount Bótū),
and thus was named after it.
When he died,
he was buried at the foot of the mountain.
It is two hundred *lǐ* from the prefecture.
Qìngyún Shān (Mount Qìngyún),
was originally Hēilǐng (Black Ridge).
When Shèngzōng stayed there,
he admired it and said:
"After I die,
I should be buried here."
Xīngzōng followed the dying wish
and established the Yǒngqìng Líng (Mausoleum of Yǒngqìng).
There are the Wàngxiān Diàn (Hall of Gazing at the Immortals) and the Yùróng Diàn (Hall of Imperial Portrait).
Three thousand households of Fān (Barbarian) and Hàn (Chinese) guards for the mausoleum were established,
all subordinate to the Dànèi Dū Zǒngguǎn Sī (Directorate General of the Imperial Household).
It is twenty *lǐ* west of the prefecture.
It has Hēishān (Black Mountain), Chìshān (Red Mountain), Tàibǎo Shān, Lǎowēng Lǐng, Mántóu Shān, Xīngguó Hú, Xiáshī Luò, and Hēihé (Black River).
It was re-established in the first year of Jǐngfú
and subsequently subordinated to Xīngshèng Gōng.
Governs three counties:
Xuándé Xiàn.
Originally the land of Hēishān and Hēihé.
In the first year of Jǐngfú,
the households of the Kuòluò tribe were gathered,
and settled there for convenience.
Households: six thousand.
Xiào'ān Xiàn.
Fùyì Xiàn.
Originally Yìzhōu.
Tàizōng moved the people of Bóhǎi's Yìzhōu here.
In the first year of Chóngxī, it was demoted to Yìfēng Xiàn,
and later renamed.
Subordinate to Hóngyì Gōng.
Tàizhōu,
Déchāng Jūn,
Jìedù.
Originally the grazing land of the twenty Qìdān tribes.
Because the Hēishǔ (Black Rat) tribe repeatedly raided Tōnghuà Zhōu,
and the people could not resist,
they subsequently moved six hundred *lǐ* to the southeast,
built a city, and settled there,
to be close to their own people.
The Hēishǔ live in holes,
have dark skin,
sharp snouts,
and resemble rats,
hence the name.
The prefecture is subordinate to Yánqìng Gōng;
military affairs belong to the Dōngběi Tǒngjūn Sī (Northeast Military Command).
Governs two counties:
Lèkāng Xiàn.
Adjacent to the prefectural seat.
Xīngguó Xiàn.
Originally the people from Shānqián.
Due to crimes, they were exiled and banished here.
Xīngzōng established the county.
Households: seven hundred.
Chángchūn Zhōu,
Sháoyáng Jūn,
Lower level,
Jìedù.
Originally the spring hunting grounds by the Yāzǐ Hé (Duck River).
Established by Xīngzōng in the eighth year of Chóngxī.
Subordinate to Yánqìng Gōng;
military affairs belong to the Dōngběi Tǒngjūn Sī.
Governs one county:
Chángchūn Xiàn.
Originally the area of Hùntóng Jiāng (Hùntóng River).
Criminals from Yān and Jì were exiled and banished here.
Households: two thousand.
Wūzhōu,
Jìng'ān Jūn,
Cìshǐ (Prefect).
Originally the land of the Wūhuán,
descendants of the Dōnghú.
Bōlà, the Great King of Liáoběi, occupied it for pasturage,
and built a city.
Later, it was taken back by the officials.
Subordinate to Xīngshèng Gōng.
It has the Liáohé (Liáo River), Yèhé (Night River), Wūhuán Chuān, and Wūhuán Shān.
Governs one county:
Àimín Xiàn.
King Bōlà followed the army on the Southern Campaign
and settled captured Hàn (Chinese) people here.
Households: one thousand.
Yǒngzhōu,
Yǒngchāng Jūn,
Guānchá circuit.
Established by Empress Dowager Chéng Tiānhuáng Tàihòu.
Tàizǔ placed the Nánlóu here.
In the third year of Qiánhēng (930 CE),
the prefecture was established beside the tomb of the Imperial Prince Hánbā.
The eastern Huáng Hé
and the southern Tǔ Hé,
the two rivers merge,
hence the name Yǒngzhōu.
In the winter months, the imperial traveling court often resided here;
this was called the Winter Nàbō.
There is Mùyè Shān.
The ancestral temple of the Qìdān founders was built on top of it.
Qíshǒu Kèhán is in the Southern Temple,
the Kèdūn is in the Northern Temple,
with painted and sculpted images of the Two Sages and their eight sons.
Legend has it that a divine man, riding a white horse,
floated east down the Tǔ Hé from Mǎyú Shān.
A heavenly maiden drove a green ox cart down the Huáng Hé from Píngdì Sōnglín.
They arrived at Mùyè Shān,
where the two rivers merged.
They met and became partners,
giving birth to eight sons.
After this, their clan gradually flourished
and was divided into eight tribes.
Whenever they mobilized the army or performed sacrifices in spring and autumn,
they always used a white horse and a green ox,
showing that they did not forget their origin.
Xīngwáng Sì
has a statue of Báiyī Guānyīn.
When Tàizōng assisted Shí Jìn in gaining control of Zhōngguó,
he returned from Lùzhōu,
entered Yōuzhōu,
and visited Dàbēi Gé.
Pointing to this statue, he said:
“I dreamt of a divine person ordering me to send Shíláng to be the emperor of Zhōngguó;
this is the one.”
Consequently, a temple was moved from Mùyè Shān
and established here.
Sacrificial ceremonies were held in spring and autumn,
and the figure was honored as the family deity.
Whenever an army was raised, they would certainly report to it,
then distribute tallies and arrows to the various tribes.
There are also Gāodiàn Shān and Liǔlín Diàn,
also called Báimǎ Diàn.
It is governed by Zhāngmǐn Gōng.
It administers three counties:
Chángníng Xiàn.
Originally the name of a county in Xiǎndé Fǔ.
Tàizǔ pacified Bóhǎi
and relocated its people here.
Four thousand five hundred households.
Yìfēng Xiàn.
Originally Yìzhōu of Tiělì Fǔ.
The Liáo troops defeated it,
moved its people to the northwest of Nánlóu,
and still named it Yìzhōu.
In the first year of Chóngxī (1032 CE),
the prefecture was abolished
and reorganized into the current county.
It is one hundred *lǐ* northwest of the prefecture seat.
It was also once renamed Fùyì Xiàn
and belonged to Tàizhōu.
The details of its beginning and end cannot be fully investigated,
but both names are retained today.
One thousand five hundred households.
Círén Xiàn.
Because the Imperial Prince Zhǐsāgǔ died,
Tàizōng established Cízhōu west of his tomb.
In the first year of Chóngxī (1032 CE),
the prefecture was abolished
and reorganized into the current county.
Four hundred households.
Yíkūn Zhōu,
Qǐshèng Jūn,
Jiédù circuit.
Originally the territory of the Qìdān Right Major Tribe.
Established by Empress Yìngtiān Huánghòu.
Huíhú Nuòsī lived there.
Down to his great-great-grandson Róngwǒ Méilǐ,
who gave birth to Empress Yìngtiān, Shùlǜ shì,
who married Tàizǔ.
Tàizǔ expanded the four directions
and pacified Bóhǎi,
and the Empress played an important role in this.
Many of the prisoners of war and those with technical skills were placed under her command;
these were called Shǔshān.
The prefecture was established on the land where she was born.
The Qǐshèng Yuàn was built in the prefecture,
and inside was the Yíníng Diàn,
where silver statues of Tàizǔ Tiānhuángdì and Yìngtiāndì Huánghòu are located.
It is governed by Chángníng Gōng.
It administers one county:
Guǎngyì Xiàn.
Originally the grazing land of the Huíhú Tribe.
Empress Yìngtiān settled the captives from her four campaigns here,
and consequently established the prefecture and county.
In the eighth year of Tǒnghé (990 CE),
Láiyuǎn Xiàn was established using households from the Tiwá Sì of the various palaces;
in the thirteenth year (995 CE), it was merged into this county.
Two thousand five hundred households.
Lónghuà Zhōu,
Xīngguó Jūn,
Subordinate level,
Jiédù circuit.
Originally the land of Běi Ānpíng Xiàn during the Hàn dynasty.
Qìdān ancestor Qíshǒu Kèhán resided here
and called it Lóngtíng.
Tàizǔ built the Dōnglóu here.
In the second year of Tiānfù of Táng (902 CE),
Tàizǔ, serving as the Yílíjǐn of the Diéliè Tribe,
defeated Dàiběi,
moved its people,
and built a city for them to live in.
The next year,
he attacked the Nǚzhí,
capturing several hundred households to populate it.
In the first year of Tiānyòu (904 CE),
the eastern city wall was expanded and repaired;
the structure was quite grand and beautiful.
In the thirteenth year (916 CE),
Tàizǔ accepted the revered title of Dàshèng Dàmíng Tiānhuángdì on Jīnlíng Gāng east of the city,
and established the era name Shéncè.
In the first year of Tiānxiǎn (926 CE),
he died in Dōnglóu.
Tàizōng promoted it to a Jiédù circuit.
It is governed by Zhāngmǐn Gōng;
military affairs belong to the Běilù Nǚzhí Bīngmǎ Sī.
There is one Cìshǐ Zhōu,
details unknown.
It administers one county:
Lónghuà Xiàn.
Tàizǔ campaigned east against the Nǚzhí
and south raided Yān and Jì,
establishing a city and district with the captives.
One thousand households.
Jiàngshèng Zhōu,
Kāiguó Jūn,
Subordinate level,
Cìshǐ circuit.
Originally the site of the Dà Bùluò Dōnglóu.
Tàizǔ’s spring traveling court often stayed here.
Empress Yìngtiān Huánghòu dreamed of a divine man wearing a golden crown and plain white clothes,
holding weaponry,
with a very dignified and beautiful appearance,
followed by twelve strange beasts.
Among them, a black rabbit leaped into the Empress’s bosom,
and consequently she became pregnant,
and then gave birth to Tàizōng.
At that time, black clouds covered the tent,
firelight illuminated the room,
and there was a sound like thunder,
which the various tribes regarded as extraordinary.
Mùzōng established the prefecture.
Thirty *lǐ* around in all four directions
were forbidden for firewood gathering and grazing.
It previously belonged to Yánchāng Gōng,
and later was governed by Zhāngmǐn Gōng.
It administers one county:
Yǒng'ān Xiàn.
Originally the name of a county in Qìngzhōu of Lóngyuán Fǔ.
Tàizǔ pacified Bóhǎi,
destroyed Yǒng'ān in Huáizhōu,
moved its people, established a stockade here,
and founded the county.
Eight hundred households.
Ráozhōu,
Kuāngyì Jūn,
Middle level,
Jiédù circuit.
Originally the land of the Ráolè Fǔ during the Táng dynasty.
Sōngmò Fǔ was established during the Zhēnguān era.
Tàizǔ fully restored the old fort.
It possesses the Huáng Hé, the Chángshuǐ Luò, the Méidǎ Hé, Qīng Shān, Dàfú Shān, and Sōng Shān.
It is governed by Yánqìng Gōng.
It administers three counties:
Chánglè Xiàn.
Originally the name of Liáochéng Xiàn.
Tàizǔ attacked Bóhǎi,
relocated its people,
and established the county for them to reside in.
Four thousand households,
including one thousand households that pay tax in iron.
Línhé Xiàn.
Originally people from Fēngyǒng Xiàn.
Tàizōng deployed troops to attack Bóhǎi
and relocated them to a bend in the Huáng Shuǐ.
One thousand households.
Ānmín Xiàn.
Tàizōng settled a mixture of captives from various towns in Bóhǎi here.
One thousand households.
Tóuxià Jūnzhōu.
were all established by the various princes (Zhū Wáng), imperial relatives by marriage (Wàiqī), high officials (Dàchén), and various tribes (Zhū Bù) using captives and spoils taken during campaigns,
or by settling slaves (shēngkǒu),
gathering them to establish Zhōuxiàn (prefectures and counties) to house them.
The various princes of the Héngzhàng (Horizontal Tents), the emperor's maternal uncles (Guójìu), and the princesses (Gōngzhǔ) were permitted to found Zhoūchéng (prefectural cities).
Others were not allowed to establish walled cities (chéngguō).
The imperial court (Cháotíng) bestowed the names (é) upon the prefectures and counties.
Their Jìedùshǐ (military commissioners) were appointed by the imperial court.
Officials below the level of Cìshǐ (prefect) were all filled by the private retainers (Bùqǔ) of the respective lords (Běn Zhǔ).
Taxes levied on those whose official rank was below the ninth rank, and on households of merchants and traders in towns and villages (Jǐng Yì Shanggǔ),
all went back to the Tóuxià (dependency lords);
only the liquor tax quota (Jiǔ shuì kè) was submitted to the Yántiě Sī (Salt and Iron Commission) in Shàngjīng.
Huīzhōu,
Xuāndé Jūn,
Jìedù.
Established by the daughter of Jǐngzōng, Qínjìn Dàcháng Gōngzhǔ.
The dependent households (Yìng Chén) totaled ten thousand.
It is 200 lǐ north of Yízhōu,
and thus a prefectural city was established.
700 lǐ north to Shàngjīng.
Officials below the Jìedùshǐ,
all belonged to the Princess’s administrative office (Gōngzhǔ Fǔshǔ).
Households: ten thousand.
Chéngzhōu,
Chángqìng Jūn,
Jìedù.
Established with the bestowed dependent households (Yìng Chén Hù) by the daughter of Shèngzōng, Jìn Guó Cháng Gōngzhǔ, and her superiors.
It is 160 lǐ north of Yízhōu,
and thus a prefectural city was established.
740 lǐ north to Shàngjīng.
Households: four thousand.
Yìzhōu,
Guǎngshùn Jūn,
Jìedù.
Established with the bestowed dependent households by the daughter of Shèngzōng, Yàn Guó Cháng Gōngzhǔ, and her superiors.
It is 200 lǐ northeast of Xiǎnzhōu,
and thus a prefectural city was established.
800 lǐ northwest to Shàngjīng.
Households: four thousand.
Wèizhōu,
Gāoyáng Jūn,
Jìedù.
Established by Fùmǎ Dūwèi Xiāo Chāngyì.
He married Qín Guó Wáng Lóngqìng's daughter, Hán Guó Cháng Gōngzhǔ,
and established the prefectural city using the bestowed dependent households.
250 lǐ northeast of Xiǎnzhōu.
According to the Liáo system,
the daughters of the emperor’s legitimate sons
were treated the same as the emperor’s daughters.
Households: one thousand.
Háozhōu.
Guójìu, the Chancellor (Zǎixiàng), campaigned in the south,
captured and plundered Hàn people,
and settled them on the former territory of Xī'ānpíng Xiàn in Liáodōng.
It is 220 lǐ northeast of Xiǎnzhōu,
720 lǐ northwest to Shàngjīng.
Households: six thousand.
Yuánzhōu.
Originally the territory of Běi'ānpíng Xiàn in Liáodōng.
300 lǐ northeast of Xiǎnzhōu.
Guójìu Jīn Dé captured and plundered Hàn people and established the city.
800 lǐ northwest to Shàngjīng.
Households: five hundred.
Fúzhōu.
Established by Guójìu Xiāo Níng.
He campaigned in the south, captured and plundered Hàn people,
and settled them on the former territory of Běi'ānpíng Xiàn.
It is 20 lǐ north of Yuánzhōu,
780 lǐ northwest to Shàngjīng.
Households: three hundred.
Héngzhōu.
Established by Guójìu Xiāo Kèzhōng.
His subordinate herdsmen settled on the former territory of the Hàn dynasty’s Liáoyáng Xiàn,
and thus the prefectural city was established.
It is 90 lǐ northwest of Liáozhōu,
720 lǐ northwest to Shàngjīng.
It has Héng Shān (Mount Heng).
Households: two hundred.
Fèngzhōu.
Former territory of the Mòlí Guó,
within the boundaries of the Bóhǎi’s Ānníng Jùn,
and the distributed territory of the five tents of the Nánwáng Fǔ (Southern King’s Residence).
It is 200 lǐ north of Hánzhōu,
900 lǐ northwest to Shàngjīng.
Households: four thousand.
Suìzhōu.
Originally Gāozhōu territory,
where the five tents of the Nánwáng Fǔ pastured their herds.
It is 200 lǐ west of Tánzhōu,
1,000 lǐ northwest to Shàngjīng.
Households: five hundred.
Fēngzhōu.
Originally a large tribe in Liáozé,
the pasturing ground of the Yáoniǎn Shì Sēngyǐn.
350 lǐ north to Shàngjīng.
Households: five hundred.
Shùnzhōu.
Originally the territory of Liáoduì Xiàn.
The Nánwáng Fǔ of the Héngzhàng captured and plundered the people of Yān, Jì, and Shùnzhōu,
established a city, and settled them there.
It is 120 lǐ northeast of Xiǎnzhōu,
900 lǐ northwest to Shàngjīng.
Households: one thousand.
Lǘzhōu.
Pasturing ground of Luógǔ Wáng,
near Yīwūlǘ Shān.
It is 130 lǐ west of Liáozhōu,
950 lǐ northwest to Shàngjīng.
Households: one thousand.
Sōngshān Zhōu.
Originally a large tribe in Liáozé,
the pasturing ground of the Héngzhàng Pǔgǔ Wáng.
It has Sōng Shān (Pine Mountain).
170 lǐ north to Shàngjīng.
Households: five hundred.
Yùzhōu.
Pasturing ground of the Héngzhàng Chén Wáng.
300 lǐ south to Shàngjīng.
Households: five hundred.
Níngzhōu.
Originally the Lèdé Shān of the Dàhè Shì clan,
the pasturing ground of the Héngzhàng Guǎnníng Wáng.
It is 80 lǐ east of Yùzhōu,
350 lǐ southwest to Shàngjīng.
Households: three hundred.
Border Defense Cities (Biānfáng Chéng)
The border defense cities on the northwest boundary of the Liáo State
were established for the purpose of military garrisoning,
aiming to occupy strategic terrain,
and did not rely on household tax revenue (dīngfù).
They are listed in detail as follows:
Jìngzhōu,
Guānchá (Observational Prefecture).
Originally Jīnshān in Tàizhōu.
Elevated in Tiānqìng 6 (1116 CE).
Zhènzhōu,
Jiàn'ān Jūn,
Jìedù.
Originally the ancient Kědūn Chéng (city).
Established by imperial decree/memorial (zòu zhì) from the Empress Dowager (Huáng Tàifēi) in Tǒnghé 22 (1004 CE).
More than 20,000 cavalry were selected from various tribes to serve as garrison troops (Tún Jūn),
specifically dedicated to defending against states like the Shìwéi and Yǔjué.
Whenever there were campaigns,
they were not permitted to be drawn away or transferred.
More than 700 households of Bóhǎi, Nǚzhí, and Hàn people who had been exiled,
were settled separately across the three prefectures: Zhèn, Fáng, and Wéi.
More than 3,000 lǐ southeast to Shàngjīng.
Wéizhōu,
Cìshǐ.
Fángzhōu,
Cìshǐ.
Hédǒng Chéng.
Originally the Huíhú Kědūn Chéng,
the pronunciation was corrupted to Hédǒng Chéng.
It had long been abandoned,
but the Liáo people restored it to guard against border troubles.
The Nǚzhí in the Gāozhōu boundary constantly engaged in banditry,
plundering travelers.
Their tribe was relocated here.
1,700 lǐ southeast to Shàngjīng.
Jìngbiān Chéng.
Originally the grassland (water and grass land) of the twenty tribes of the Qìdān.
It borders the Yǔjué to the north,
who regularly entered and committed banditry.
A city was built,
and over 1,000 cavalry were stationed there to defend it.
1,500 lǐ southeast to Shàngjīng.
Píbèi Hé Chéng.
Its location controls the northern border.
Five hundred soldiers are stationed here to guard and support the defense.
The Píbèi Hé originates north of the Huíhé,
flows southeast through the Yǔjué,
enters the Lúqú Hé,
runs north along Hédǒng Chéng,
flows east to join the Tuólu Hé,
and empties into the sea.
1,500 lǐ south to Shàngjīng.
Zhāozhōu,
Suīyuǎn Jūn,
Cìshǐ.
Established in Kāitài 3 (1014 CE) using Nǚzhí households.
Subordinate to the Xīběilù Zhāotǎo Sī (Northwest Route Pacification Commission).
Tǎlǎn Zhǔ Chéng.
Established in Dàkāng 9 (1083 CE).
Located on the Lúqú Hé.
Treatise 8, Geographical Treatise 2: Dōngjīng Dào (Eastern Capital Circuit)
was originally the land of Cháoxiān (Joseon).
Zhōu Wǔwáng released Jīzǐ from prison,
and he went to Cháoxiān,
where he was subsequently enfeoffed.
He established the eight prohibitions (bā tiáo zhī jiào),
valuing ritual and righteousness (lǐyì),
enriching agriculture and sericulture (nóngsāng),
keeping outside doors unlocked,
and people did not commit robbery.
This was transmitted for over forty generations.
Yān controlled Zhēnfān and Cháoxiān,
and first established officials and built defenses (zhàng).
Qín controlled the outer frontier (wài jiǎo) of Liáodōng.
In the early Hàn dynasty,
Mǎn, a man from Yān, ruled the former empty lands.
In the third year of Yuánfēng (108 BCE) under Wǔdì,
Cháoxiān was established as the four commanderies: Zhēnfān, Líntún, Lèlàng, and Xuántú.
During the Later Hàn (Hòu Hàn),
the two commanderies, Liáodōng and Xuántú,
their administrative changes were inconsistent.
Towards the end of the Hàn dynasty, the area was occupied by Gōngsūn Dù,
who passed it to his son Kāng;
his grandson Yuān,
proclaimed himself King of Yān (Yān Wáng),
established the era name Shàohàn,
but Wèi (Cao Wei) destroyed him.
Jìn fell to Gāolì (Koguryeo),
and later returned to Mùróng Chuí;
his son Bǎo,
installed Ān, King of Gōulì (Koguryeo), as Governor (mù) of Píngzhōu and settled him there.
Yuán Wèi Tàiwǔ sent an envoy to Píngrǎng Chéng (Pyeongyang City), where he resided.
Liáo's Eastern Capital (Tōujīng) originated from this location.
Táng Gāozōng pacified Gāolì,
and established the Āndōng Dūhù Fǔ (Protectorate General to Pacify the East) here;
later, it belonged to the Dà (Dae) clan of Bóhǎi.
The Dà clan first secured Dōngmóu Shān in Yìlóu.
During the Wànsuì Tōngtiān era of Wǔ Hòu (Empress Wǔ Zétiān),
being pressured by Qìdān Jìnzhōng,
there was a man named Qǐqǐ Zhòngxiàng,
who crossed the Liáo River (Liáoshuǐ) to secure himself.
Wǔ Hòu enfeoffed him as Duke of Zhèn Guó (Zhèn Guó Gōng).
He passed it to his son Zuòróng,
who established a capital city,
proclaimed himself King of Zhèn (Zhèn Wáng),
annexed the region north of the sea,
covering an area of five thousand *lǐ*,
with an army of several hundred thousand.
Zhōngzōng bestowed upon his capital the name Hūhàn Zhōu,
and enfeoffed him as Prince of Bóhǎi Commandery (Bóhǎi Jùnwáng).
After twelve generations, reaching Yízhèn,
he presumptuously adopted an imperial title and changed the era name,
planning to establish palaces and watchtowers.
It possessed five capitals (wǔ jīng), fifteen prefectures (shíwǔ fǔ), and sixty-two departments (liùshí'èr zhōu),
becoming the flourishing state of Liáodōng.
Hūhàn Zhōu was the former Píngrǎng Chéng,
and was called Zhōngjīng Xiǎndé Fǔ (Central Capital, Xiǎndé Prefecture).
Tàizǔ established the state,
attacked Bóhǎi,
captured Hūhàn Chéng,
took its king Dà Yīn Xuàn prisoner,
and established the Dōngdān Kingdom (Dōngdān Wángguó),
installing the Crown Prince Túyù as the Human Emperor (Rén Huángwáng) to govern it.
In the fourth year of Shéncè (919 CE),
the old city of Liáoyáng was repaired,
and Dōngpíng Jùn was established using Bóhǎi and Hàn households,
designated as a defensive department (fángyù zhōu).
In the third year of Tiānxiǎn (928 CE),
the people of the Dōngdān Kingdom were moved to reside there,
and it was elevated to Nánjīng (Southern Capital).
The city's name was Tiānfú.
It was three *zhàng* high,
equipped with towers and turrets (lóu lǔ),
and had a circumference of thirty *lǐ*.
There were eight gates: the East was Yíngyáng,
the Southeast was Sháoyáng,
the South was Lóngyuán,
the Southwest was Xiǎndé,
the West was Dàshùn,
the Northwest was Dàliáo,
the North was Huáiyuǎn,
and the Northeast was Ānyuǎn.
The Imperial City (gōngchéng) was in the northeast corner,
three *zhàng* high,
equipped with defensive towers (dí lóu).
The south side had three gates,
enhanced by layered towers and observatories (lóu guān).
The four corners had corner towers (jiǎo lóu),
separated from each other by two *lǐ*.
North of the palace wall was the Yàng Guó Huángdì Yùróng Diàn (Hall of the Imperial Countenance of the Abdicated Emperor).
Within the Great Palace (dà nèi), two halls were built,
but no palace women were installed.
It was guarded only by the envoys, deputies, and judges (pànguān) of the Inner Department (nèi shěng shǐ fù).
The inscription of the stele concerning the newly established Nánjīng of the Great Dōngdān Kingdom (Dà Dōngdān Guó Xīnjiàn Nánjīng Bēimíng)
was located south of the palace gate.
The outer city was called Hànchéng (Hàn City).
It was divided into the South Market and the North Market,
with a watchtower (kàn lóu) in the middle.
Morning gatherings took place in the South Market,
and evening gatherings in the North Market.
West of the street were Jīndé Sì (Jīndé Temple);
Dàbēi Sì (Dàbēi Temple);
Fùmǎ Sì (Fùmǎ Temple),
where the iron pennant pole (tiě fān gān) stood;
Zhào Tóu Tuó Sì (Zhào Tou Tuo Temple);
the Residence of the Commissioner (liúshǒu yá);
the Revenue Office (hùbù sī);
the Military Patrol Bureau (jūnxún yuàn),
where over a thousand soldiers of the Guīhuà Battalion (Guīhuà Yíng Jūn) were stationed.
Fugitives from Hé and Shuò
were all registered here.
To the east, it reached Běi Wūlǔhǔkè, four hundred *lǐ*;
to the south, it reached Tiěshān (Iron Mountain) by the sea, eight hundred and sixty *lǐ*;
to the west, it reached the river mouth (hǎikǒu) of Wàngpíng Xiàn, three hundred and sixty *lǐ*;
to the north, it reached Yìlóu Xiàn and Fànhé, two hundred and seventy *lǐ*.
The east, west, and south sides face the sea.
The Liáo River (Liáohé) flows out from the northeastern mountain pass as Fànhé,
flows southwest to form the Great Mouth (Dàkǒu),
and enters the sea.
The Dōngliáng River flows west from the eastern mountains,
joins the Hún River (Húnhé) to form the Small Mouth (Xiǎokǒu),
meets the Liáo River, and enters the sea.
It is also named Tàizǐ Hé (Crown Prince River),
and is also called Dàliáng Shuǐ.
The Hún River is between the Dōngliáng and Fàn Rivers.
The Shā River flows northwest from the southeastern mountains,
passes through Gàizhōu, and enters the sea.
There are Pú Hé;
Qīng Hé;
Pèishuǐ,
also called Ní Hé (Mud River),
and also called Xùnyù Luò,
whose waters contain much *xùnyù* grass.
Zhùbì Shān (Mountain of the Imperial Stop).
When Táng Tàizōng campaigned against Gāolì,
he stayed on its peak for several days
and carved a stone to commemorate his achievements.
It is commonly called Shǒu Shān (Hand Mountain).
On the flat rock atop the mountain, there are shapes resembling palms and fingers.
A spring flows from within it,
and is inexhaustible when drawn upon.
There are also Míngwáng Shān and Báishí Shān—also called Héngshān.
In the thirteenth year of Tiānxiǎn (938 CE),
Nánjīng was changed to Dōngjīng (Eastern Capital),
and the prefecture was named Liáoyáng.
There are forty thousand six hundred and four households.
It governs eighty-seven *zhōu*, *fǔ*, military units (jūn), and cities.
It controls nine counties (xiàn):
Liáoyáng Xiàn.
Originally the land of Jīndé Xiàn of the Bóhǎi Kingdom.
During the Hàn dynasty, it was Pèishuǐ Xiàn;
Gāolì changed it to Gōulì Xiàn;
Bóhǎi changed it to Chánglè Xiàn.
One thousand five hundred households.
Xiānxiāng Xiàn.
Originally Hàn Liáoduì Xiàn;
Bóhǎi changed it to Yǒngfēng Xiàn.
The *Shénxiān Zhuàn* (Biographies of Immortals) says:
"The Immortal Bái Zhònglǐ was able to refine divine elixirs,
and touch gold,
thereby saving the common people."
One thousand five hundred households.
Hèyě Xiàn.
Originally Hàn Jūjiù Xiàn;
Bóhǎi changed it to Jīshān Xiàn.
Formerly, Dīng Lìngwēi made his home here.
After leaving home for a thousand years,
he transformed into a crane and returned,
alighting on a ceremonial pillar (huábiǎo zhù).
He used his beak to scratch the pillar, saying:
"O bird, O bird, Dīng Lìngwēi!
Gone from home a thousand years, now I return.
The cities and walls are the same, but the people are not.
Why did you not study the Way of Immortals? Your tombs are piled high."
One thousand two hundred households.
Xīmù Xiàn.
Originally Hàn Wàngpíng Xiàn;
Bóhǎi changed it to Huāshān Xiàn.
One thousand households.
Zǐméng Xiàn.
Originally Hàn Lòufāng Xiàn.
Later, Fúniè Guó established Dōngpíng Fǔ,
which administered Méng Zhōu and Zǐméng Xiàn.
Later, it was moved to Liáochéng
and merged into Huánglǐng Xiàn.
Bóhǎi re-established it as Zǐméng Xiàn.
One thousand households.
Xīngliáo Xiàn.
Originally Hàn Píngguō Xiàn;
Bóhǎi changed it to Chángníng Xiàn.
During the Yuánhé era of Táng,
King Dà Rénxiù of Bóhǎi stabilized Sīllá in the south,
subdued various tribes in the north,
opened and established commanderies and cities,
and thus determined the current name.
One thousand households.
Sùshèn Xiàn.
Established using Bóhǎi households.
Guīrén Xiàn.
Shùnhuà Xiàn.
Kāizhōu,
Zhènguó Jūn,
Jǐedù (Military Governor).
Originally Huìmò territory.
Gāolí established Qìngzhōu,
Bóhǎi established Dōngjīng Lóngyuán Fǔ.
It had palaces.
It supervised the affairs of the four prefectures of Qìng, Yán, Mù, and Hè.
There were six former counties: Lóngyuán, Yǒng'ān, Wūshān, Bìgǔ, Xióngshān, and Báiyáng;
all were abolished.
A city wall was constructed of stacked stones,
with a circumference of twenty *lǐ*.
When Xuē Rén'guì of Táng campaigned against Gāolí,
he fought their great general Wēn Shāmén at Xióngshān,
and captured a master archer at the stone city;
this is that place.
When Tàizǔ pacified Bóhǎi,
he moved its inhabitants to large tribes,
and the city was subsequently abandoned.
When Shèngzōng returned from campaigning against Gāolí,
he surveyed the city foundations
and had them completely restored and repaired.
In the third year of Kāitài (1014),
more than a thousand households from the two prefectures of Shuāng and Hán were moved there to populate it,
and it was named Kāifēng Fǔ Kāiyuǎn Jūn,
with a Jǐedù;
it was later renamed Zhènguó Jūn.
It was subordinate to the Dōngjīng Liúshǒu (Resident Administrator),
and military affairs belonged to the Dōngjīng Tǒngjūn Sī (Military Command).

Record 9, Geography Record 3, Zhōngjīng Dào
Zhōngjīng Dàdìng Fǔ.
During Yú's time, it was Yíngzhōu;
during Xià, it belonged to Jìzhōu;
during Zhōu, it was part of Yōuzhōu.
Qín established prefectures throughout the land,
and this was Liáoxī.
During Hàn, it was Xīn'ānpíng Xiàn.
At the end of Hàn, Bùxī resided there,
with a territory of a thousand lǐ,
many great mountains and deep valleys,
its treacherous terrain sufficient for self-defense.
When Wèi Wǔ campaigned north,
he deployed his troops for a great battle,
and over 200,000 surrendered,
moving them to Sōngmò.
After that, the Tuòbá clan, taking advantage of Liáo, established their headquarters here,
south of the Ràolèhé River
and north of the Wēnyúhé River.
Emperor Tàizōng of Táng campaigned against Gāolì
and stopped here.
The tribal chief Sūzhī rendered meritorious service in the campaign.
The Xī chief Kědù led his people to submit,
and Ràolè Dūdūfǔ was established for them.
After Xiántōng,
Qìdān began to grow,
and the Xī ethnic group no longer dared to resist.
When Tàizǔ founded the nation,
the entire clan submitted as vassals.
Shèngzōng once passed by the banks of the Qīhīnshān Tǔhé,
and looking south, saw clouds
in the shape of city walls, gates, and towers,
and so discussed establishing a capital.
Skilled artisans were chosen from Yān and Jì,
and the work was overseen for two years,
with city walls, palaces, towers, government offices, markets, and corridors
modeled after the system of the divine capital.
In Tǒnghé 24th year,
the Wǔzhàng Yuàn presented the former Xī King's headquarters land.
In the 25th year,
the city was built,
filled with Hàn households,
named Zhōngjīng,
and its prefecture named Dàdìng.
Within the imperial city were the ancestral temple and the portraits of Jǐngzōng and Chéngtiān Huánghòu in the Yùróng Diàn.
The city moats were damp,
so many wells were dug to drain them,
which people found convenient.
There was Dàtóng Yì to receive Sòng envoys,
Cháotiān Guǎn to receive Xīnluó envoys,
and Láibīn Guǎn to receive Xià envoys.
There were Qīhīnshān, Mǎyúshān, Shuāngshān, Sōngshān, and Tǔhé.

we arrived at Wàngjīng Guǎn.
Fifty *lǐ* to Shùnzhōu.
Seventy *lǐ* to Tánzhōu,
gradually entering the mountains.
Fifty *lǐ* to Jīngōu Guǎn.
Approaching the station,
the river plains were flat and open,
called Jīngōu Diàn.
From here we entered the mountains,
winding and ascending,
there were no more mileage markers (hòus),
but we used the day's horse travel to record it,
estimating the mileage.
Ninety *lǐ* to Gǔběikǒu,
with steep cliffs on both sides,
barely allowing carriage tracks.
We then crossed Déshèng Lǐng,
the winding path having several levels (switchbacks),
commonly named Sīxiāng Lǐng (Homesickness Ridge),
eighty *lǐ* to Xīnguǎn.
We passed Diāokē Lǐng and Piānqiāng Lǐng,
forty *lǐ* to Wòrúlái Guǎn.
We crossed the Wūluán Hé,
to the east of which lies Luánzhōu,
and then crossed Mōdǒu Lǐng,
also named Dùyún Lǐng,
and Qíncài Lǐng,
seventy *lǐ* to Liǔhé Guǎn.
Sōngtíng Lǐng was extremely steep and dangerous,
seventy *lǐ* to Dǎzào Bùluò Guǎn.
Traveling fifty *lǐ* southeast to Niúshān Guǎn.
Eighty *lǐ* to Lù'érxiá Guǎn.
We passed Xiāma Líng,
ninety *lǐ* to Tiějiāng Guǎn.
We passed Shízǐ Lǐng,
and from here gradually exited the mountains,
seventy *lǐ* to Fùgǔ Guǎn.
Eighty *lǐ* to Tōngtiān Guǎn.
Twenty *lǐ* to Zhōngjīng Dàdìng Fǔ.
The city walls were low and small,
its circumference being merely four *lǐ*.
The gates were simply multi-story buildings,
lacking the structure of fortified gate towers (*zhú dú*).
The south gate was named Zhūxià,
inside the gate there were covered walkways,
and many residential block gates (fāngmén).
There were also four market towers: named Tiānfāng, Dàqú, Tōnghuán, and Wàngquè.
Next we reached Dàtóng Guǎn.
Its gates, directly north, were named Yángdé and Chānghé.
Inside the city, on a ridge in the southwest corner, there was a temple.
South of the city were gardens and fields,
a place for banquets and archery practice.
Since passing Gǔběikǒu,
the residents lived in thatched huts and plank houses,
farming,
but they lacked mulberry and cudrania trees (sāng zhè);
everything they planted was on ridges,
fearful of being choked by wind-blown sand.
In the mountains, tall pines were lush and dense,
in deep valleys, domestic cattle, horses, and camels were occasionally seen,
and there were many blue sheep and yellow pigs.
