then built Lóngchéng,
constructed palaces and temples,
changed Liǔchéng to Lóngchéng Xiàn,
and subsequently moved the capital,
naming it Hélóng Gōng.
Mùróng Chuí resided there again,
later it was destroyed by Féng Bá.
The Yuán Wèi captured it and made it Liáoxī Jùn.
When the Suí pacified Gāo Bǎoníng,
Yíngzhōu was established.
Emperor Yáng abolished the prefecture and established Liǔchéng Jùn.
At the beginning of the Wǔdé era of Táng,
Yíngzhōu was changed to a Zǒngguǎn Fǔ (General Commandery),
and soon after became a Dūdū Fǔ (Area Command).
During the Wànsuì Tōngtiān era,
it fell to Lǐ Wànróng.
At the beginning of the Shénlóng era,
the commandery was moved to Yōuzhōu.
In the fourth year of Kāiyuán, it was governed again from Liǔchéng.
In the eighth year, it moved west to Yúyáng.
In the tenth year, it returned to Liǔchéng.
Later it was occupied by the Xī.
When Tàizǔ pacified the Xī and captured the people of Yān,
intending to establish a city,
he commanded Hán Zhīfāng to select a location.
Thus, Liǔchéng was fully repaired,
named Bázhōu Zhāngwǔ Jūn,
Jìedù.
During the Tǒnghé era,
the Jìezhì (Commissioner) was established over the five prefectures of Jiàn, Bà, Yí, Jǐn, and Báichuān.
Soon after, the Jìezhì post was abolished,
and it became subordinate to Jīqìng Gōng.
Later it belonged to Xīngshèng Gōng.
In the tenth year of Chóngxī, it was upgraded to Xīngzhōng Fǔ.
It contains Dàhuá Shān, Xiǎohuá Shān, Xiānggāo Shān, Shèxiāng Yá (where an inscription by Tiānshòu Huángdì is located), Zhùlóng Yù, Shénshè Quán, and Xiǎolíng Hé.
It administers two prefectures and four counties:
Xīngzhōng Xiàn.
Originally the territory of Hàn's Liǔchéng Xiàn.
Tàizǔ captured Hàn people and settled them here,
establishing Bàchéng Xiàn.
During the Chóngxī era, the prefecture (Fǔ) was established,
and the name was changed.
Yíngqiū Xiàn.
Established by splitting off territory from Bàchéng.
Xiàngléi Xiàn.
Established in the second year of Kāitài using Màiwù Chuān.
Initially subordinate to Zhōngjīng,
it later belonged (to Xīngzhōng Fǔ).
Lǘshān Xiàn.
Originally Hàn's Qiělǜ Xiàn.
Established in the second year of Kāitài using Luójiā Jūn.
Subordinate to Zhōngjīng,
it later belonged (to Xīngzhōng Fǔ).
Āndé Zhōu,
Huàpíng Jūn,
Lower level,
Cìshǐ (Prefect).
Established from Āndé Xiàn of Bázhōu,
it came to belong (to Xīngzhōng Fǔ).
It administers one county: Āndé Xiàn.
Established in the eighth year of Tǒnghé by splitting off households in the territory of Lóngshān and Túhé southeast of Bàchéng.
Initially subordinate to Qiánzhōu,
then belonged to Bázhōu,
and was established as a prefecture (Zhōu) and came to belong (to Xīngzhōng Fǔ).
Qiánzhōu,
Fùchāng Jūn,
Lower level,
Cìshǐ.
Originally territory of Hàn's Liáoxī Jùn.
When Tàizǔ pacified Bóhǎi,
he settled the captured households here,
subordinate to the Hēishuǐ Hé Tíxiá Sī.
Emperor Ān established the prefecture,
and increased its population by splitting off Hàn households from Yí and Bà Prefectures.
Initially subordinate to Yǒngxīng Gōng,
then subordinate to Zhōngjīng,
later when the Fǔ was established,
it came to belong (to Xīngzhōng Fǔ).
It administers one county: Shèngjí Xiàn.
When Tàizǔ pacified Bóhǎi,
he brought back captured residents of Shèngjí Xiàn in Xīngzhōu to settle here,
and consequently established the county.
Yízhōu,
Chóngyì Jūn,
Upper level,
Jìedù.
Originally the territory of Liě Xiàn in Liáoxī.
The King of Dōngdān hunted here every autumn.
Xīngzōng established the prefecture using captured households from Dìngzhōu.
It contains Fén Shān,
where pines and cypresses stretch continuously for over a hundred *lǐ*,
gathering firewood is prohibited;
and Líng Hé,
where stones were piled up to form an embankment.
Subordinate to Jīqìng Gōng.
It administers two counties:
Hóngzhèng Xiàn.
Shìzōng established it using captured households from Dìngzhōu.
The residents are skilled in weaving cloth,
and are generally very skillful.
Wényì Xiàn.
Established by Shìzōng.
Initially subordinate to Hǎiběi Zhōu,
it later came to belong (to Yízhōu).
Jǐnzhōu,
Línhǎi Jūn,
Middle level,
Jìedù.
Originally Hàn's Wúlǜ Xiàn in Liáodōng.
Mùróng Huàng established Xīlè Xiàn.
Tàizǔ established the prefecture using captured Hàn people.
It contains Dà Húsēng Shān, Xiǎo Húsēng Shān, Dà Zhāyá Shān, Xiǎo Zhāyá Shān, and Táohé Dǎo.
Subordinate to Hóngyì Gōng.
It administers one prefecture and two counties:
Yǒnglè Xiàn.
Ānchāng Xiàn.
Yánzhōu,
Bǎosù Jūn,
a lower-class [xià] prefecture,
governed by an Cìshǐ (Prefect).
Its original territory was that of Hài-yáng Xiàn during the Hàn Dynasty.
When Tàizǔ pacified Bóhǎi,
he relocated Hàn households to live mixed within the territory of Xīngzhōu.
Shèngzōng established a city here.
It was subordinate to the Hóngyì Gōng palace
and later came under the prefecture.
It governs one county: Xīngchéng Xiàn.
Chuānzhōu,
Chángníng Jūn,
a middle-class [zhōng] prefecture,
governed by a Jiédù (Military Commissioner).
Its original territory was that of Qīngshān Zhōu during the Táng Dynasty.
Tàizǔ's younger brother, King Míng Ānduān, established it.
In the third year of Huìtóng (930 CE),
an imperial edict designated it as Báichuān Zhōu.
When Ānduān's son Cháge was executed for high treason,
the territory was confiscated
and reduced, being called Chuānzhōu.
Initially, it was subordinate to the Chóngdé Gōng palace,
but during the Tǒnghé era, it belonged to the Wénzhōng Wáng Fǔ (Prince Wénzhōng's Establishment).
It governs three counties:
Hónglǐ Xiàn.
Established in the eighth year of Tǒnghé (990 CE) using households from the various Palaces' Tíxiá Sī (Superintendencies of Control).
Xiánkāng Xiàn.
Yímín Xiàn.
Established during the Tǒnghé era.
Jiànzhōu,
Bǎojìng Jūn,
an upper-class [shàng] prefecture,
governed by a Jiédù (Military Commissioner).
During the Wǔdé era of the Táng Dynasty (618–626 CE),
Chānglè Xiàn was established.
Tàizǔ completely repaired the old ramparts
and established the prefecture.
In the first year of Qiányòu of the Hàn Dynasty (948 CE),
the former Empress Dowager of Shí Jìn traveled to see Shìzōng,
requesting to cultivate land next to the Hàn city to support herself.
Permission was granted to give her fifty qǐng (approx. 500 acres) of land forty lǐ south of Jiànzhōu,
where she constructed rooms and dwellings
and founded an ancestral temple.
The prefecture was south of the Líng Hé river,
and frequently suffered flood damage,
so Shèngzōng moved it north of the river to the former city of Táng's Chóngzhōu.
It was initially named Wǔníng Jūn,
subordinate to the Yǒngxīng Gōng palace,
and later belonged to the Dūnmù Gōng palace.
It governs two counties:
Yǒngbà Xiàn.
Yǒngkāng Xiàn.
Its original territory was that of Chānglí Xiàn during the Táng Dynasty.
Láizhōu,
Guīdé Jūn,
a lower-class [xià] prefecture,
governed by a Jiédù (Military Commissioner).
Because five departments of the Nǚzhí came and submitted during a famine,
Shèngzōng established this prefecture to settle them.
It was initially governed by a Cìshǐ (Prefect),
but was later promoted.
It is subordinate to the Yǒngxīng Gōng palace.
It contains Sānzhōu Shān, Liùzhōu Shān, and Wǔzhī Shān.
It governs two subordinate prefectures and
one county:
Láibīn Xiàn.
Its original territory was that of Láiyuǎn Xiàn during the Táng Dynasty.
Xízhōu,
Pínghǎi Jūn,
a lower-class [xià] prefecture,
governed by a Cìshǐ (Prefect).
Mùróng Huǎng established Jíníng Xiàn.
Shèngzōng took a census of the households and moved them to Xìnzhōu,
but they could not proceed due to heavy snow.
A city was built here,
and the prefecture was established.
It was subordinate to the Xīngshèng Gōng palace
and later came under the prefecture.
It governs one county: Hǎibīn Xiàn.
Its original territory was a Hàn Dynasty county.
It borders the sea,
and the land is mostly saline,
so a salt field was established here.
Qiānzhōu,
Xīngshàn Jūn,
a lower-class [xià] prefecture,
governed by a Cìshǐ (Prefect).
Its original territory was that of Yánglè Xiàn during the Hàn Dynasty.
When Shèngzōng pacified Dà Yánlín,
he relocated the people of Guīzhōu here and established the prefecture,
which later came under its authority.
It contains Jiàngǎn Shān.
It governs one county: Qiānmín Xiàn.
Rùnzhōu,
Hǎiyáng Jūn,
a lower-class [xià] prefecture,
governed by a Cìshǐ (Prefect).
When Shèngzōng pacified Dà Yánlín,
he relocated the people of Níngzhōu to settle here,
and established the prefecture.
It governs one county: Hǎiyáng Xiàn.
Its original territory was that of Yánglè Xiàn during the Hàn Dynasty,
relocated to Rùnzhōu.
The Bóhǎi households originally within the city of Dōngjīng
were moved here due to rebellion.
Treatise Ten: Geography, Part Four, Southern Capital Circuit (Nánjīng Dào)
Nánjīng Xījīn Fǔ (Southern Capital, Xījīn Prefecture),
originally the land of ancient Jìzhōu.
Gāoyáng Shì (Zhuanxu) called it Yōulíng;
Táo Táng (Yao) called it Yōudū.
Yǒu Yú (Shun) divided it and established Yōuzhōu.
The Shāng Dynasty merged Yōu into Jì.
The Zhōu Dynasty divided Bīng (Bīngzhōu) and established Yōu.
According to the Zhífāng (Official Geography section of the Rites of Zhou),
the northeast is Yōuzhōu.
Its mountain is Yīwūlǘ.
Its marsh is Kuìyǎng.
Its rivers are Hé and Jǐ.
Its inundations are Zāi and Shí.
Its advantageous products are fish and salt;
its livestock are horses, cattle, and swine;
its grains are millet, panicled millet, and rice.
King Wǔ enfeoffed Tài bǎo Shì in Yān.
The Qín Dynasty made this territory into the five commanderies: Yúyáng, Shànggǔ, Yòuběipíng, Liáoxī, and Liáodōng.
Under the Hàn Dynasty, it became the Kingdom of Yān.
Zāng Tú, Lú Wǎn, Liú Jiàn, Liú Zé, and Liú Dàn were successively enfeoffed there.
Zhuó Jùn and Guǎngyáng Guó were also established at times.
The Later Hàn Dynasty made it Guǎngpíng Guó and Guǎngyáng Jùn;
sometimes it was merged into Shànggǔ,
and Yōuzhōu was re-established.
The Later Zhōu Dynasty established Yān and Fànyáng Jùn.
The Suí Dynasty made it the Commander-in-Chief's seat of Yōuzhōu (Yōuzhōu Zǒngguǎn).
The Táng Dynasty established the Great Protectorate (Dà Dūdū Fǔ)
and later changed the title to Fànyáng Jiédùshǐ (Military Commissioner of Fànyáng).
Ān Lùshān, Shǐ Sīmíng, Lǐ Huáixiān, Zhū Tāo, Liú Pēng, and Liú Jì successively occupied the territory.
Liú Zǒng submitted to Táng.
Up to Zhāng Zhòngwǔ and Zhāng Yǔnzhòng,
they gained the people's support through justice.
Liú Rén-gōng and his son usurped and contended for power,
and subsequently it entered the period of the Five Dynasties.
From the Táng to the Jìn Dynasty,
Gāozǔ, because Liáo had assisted him in establishing his rule,
ceded Yōuzhōu and fifteen other prefectures as tribute.
Tàizōng promoted it to Nánjīng (Southern Capital),
also called Yānjīng (Capital of Yān).
The city walls measure thirty-six lǐ square,
thirty zhàng high,
and fifteen chí wide (at the base).
Enemy towers and battlements were all complete.
The eight gates are: Āndōng and Yíngchūn in the east;
Kāiyáng and Dānfèng in the south;
Xiǎnxī and Qīngjìn in the west;
Tōngtiān and Gǒngchén in the north.
The Great Palace (Dà Nèi) is in the southwest corner.
Inside the Imperial City (Huáng Chéng), there are two Imperial Portrait Halls (Yù Róng Diàn) for Jǐngzōng and Shèngzōng.
The eastern one is called Xuānhé,
and the southern one is called Dà Nèi.
The inner gate is called Xuānjiào,
later changed to Yuánhé;
the three outer gates are Nánduān, Zuǒyì, and Yòuyì.
Zuǒyì was changed to Wànchūn,
and Yòuyì was changed to Qiānqiū.
The gates have towers and pavilions.
The polo field is to the south of them,
and the Yǒngpíng Guǎn (Guest House) is to the east.
The west gate of the Imperial City is Xiǎnxī;
it was constructed but not opened.
The north gate is Zǐběi.
On the western ridge of the city wall, there is a Summer Palace (Liáng Diàn).
In the northeast corner, there is the Yànjiǎo Lóu tower.
The wards, markets, administrative offices, temples, and monasteries
are too numerous to record.
Outside [the city],
there are the passes of Jūyōng, Sōngtíng, and Yúlín,
the entrance of Gǔběi,
the Sānggān Hé, Gāoliáng Hé, Shízǐ Hé rivers, Dà'ān Shān, and Yān Shān—in which there is Yáoyǔ.
The prefecture is called Yōudū,
and the military command is named Lúlóng.
The military designation was established in the first year of Kāitài (1012 CE).
It governs six subordinate prefectures and eleven counties:
Xījīn Xiàn.
Originally Jì Xiàn under Jìn,
it was changed to Jìběi Xiàn.
In the first year of Kāitài (1012 CE), it was renamed to its current name.
It is named because the segment of Yān's stellar field (fēnyě) corresponding to the tiger constellation (lǚyín) is the Ford of Xīmù (Xīmù zhī Jīn).
Hence the name.
Twenty thousand households.
Wǎnpíng Xiàn.
Originally Yōudū Xiàn under Jìn,
in the first year of Kāitài (1012 CE), it was renamed to its current name.
Twenty-two thousand households.
Zhúzhōu,
Yǒngtài Jūn,
Superior Class (Shàng),
Magistrate (Cìshǐ).
In the 6th year of Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn, the region of Yān was divided to establish Zhuó Jùn.
Emperor Wéndì of Wèi changed it to Fànyáng Jùn.
During Jìn, it became Fànyáng Guó.
During Yuán Wèi (Northern Wei), it was restored as a commandery.
In the 2nd year of the Kāihuáng era of Suí, the commandery was abolished.
It belonged to Yōuzhōu.
In the 3rd year of the Dàyè era, Yōuzhōu was designated as Zhuó Jùn.
In the 1st year of the Wǔdé era of Táng, the commandery was abolished.
It became Zhuó Xiàn.
In the 7th year, it was changed to Fànyáng Xiàn.
In the 4th year of the Dàlì era, Zhuózhōu was established.
The Shí Jìn (Later Jin) submitted it to Tàizōng.
It contains Dàfáng Shān, Liùpìn Shān, Zhuó Shuǐ, Lóusāng Hé, Hénggōu Hé, Lǐxùn Hé, and Qígōu Hé.
Governs four counties: Fànyáng Xiàn.
Originally Hàn's Zhuó Xiàn.
During the Wǔdé era of Táng,
it was changed to Fànyáng Xiàn.
It contains Zhuó Shuǐ and Fàn Shuǐ.
10,000 households.
Gù'ān Xiàn.
Originally Hàn's Fāngchéng Xiàn.
Previously belonged to Guǎngyáng Guó.
In the 9th year of the Kāihuáng era of Suí,
it was moved and established from Láishuǐ Xiàn of Yìzhōu.
It belonged to Yōuzhōu.
The name was taken from the former Hàn county, Gù'ān Xiàn.
In the 4th year of the Wǔdé era of Táng, it belonged to Běiyì Zhōu.
The administration was moved to Zhāngxìn Bǎo.
In the 2nd year of the Zhēnguān era, Yìzhōu was abolished.
It was moved to its present administrative location.
It again belonged to Yōuzhōu.
It is ninety *lǐ* southeast of the prefecture.
10,000 households.
Xīnchéng Xiàn.
Originally Hàn's Xīnchāng Xiàn.
In the 4th year of the Dàlì era of Táng, it was established by separating territory from Gù'ān Xiàn.
Later abolished.
In the 4th year of the Tiānchéng era of Hòu Táng (Later Tang), it was again established by separating territory from Fànyáng Xiàn.
It is sixty *lǐ* south of the prefecture.
10,000 households.
Guīyì Xiàn.
Originally the territory of Hàn's Yì Xiàn.
During Qí, it was merged into Mà Xiàn.
In the 5th year of the Wǔdé era of Táng, Běiyì Zhōu was established.
When the prefecture was abolished,
the county was re-established and came under (this prefecture's) jurisdiction.
The civilian population resides south of Jùmǎ Hé.
Its provisional administration is located in Xīnchéng.
4,000 households.
Yìzhōu,
Gāoyáng Jūn,
Superior Class (Shàng),
Magistrate (Cìshǐ).
During Hàn, it was the territory of the two counties Yì and Gù'ān.
Suí established Yìzhōu.
At the end of Suí, it became Shànggǔ Jùn.
In the 4th year of the Wǔdé era of Táng, Yìzhōu was restored.
In the 1st year of the Tiānbǎo era, it reverted to Shànggǔ Jùn.
In the 1st year of the Qiányuán era, it was again changed to Yìzhōu.
During the Five Dynasties, it was subordinated to the Military Governor of Dìngzhōu.
In the 9th year of the Huìtóng era, Sūn Fāngjiǎn surrendered its territory and submitted.
In the 9th year of the Yìnglì era, it was taken by Shìzōng of Zhōu (Later Zhou).
Later, it belonged to Sòng.
In the 7th year of the Tǒnghé era, (the Liao) attacked and captured it.
It was elevated to Gāoyáng Jūn.
It contains Yì Shuǐ, Lái Shuǐ, Láng Shān, Tàiníng Shān, and Báimǎ Shān.
Governs three counties: Yì Xiàn.
Originally a Hàn county.
The old city is sixty *lǐ* southeast of the present county.
It was abolished in the 7th year of the Tiānbǎo era of Qí (Northern Qi).
In the 16th year of the Kāihuáng era of Suí,
a county was established at the northwest corner of the old Gù'ān city.
This is the seat of the present county administration.
25,000 households.
Láishuǐ Xiàn.
Originally Hàn's Dào Xiàn.
The old Dào city, one *lǐ* north of the present county, is this location.
The Yuán Wèi moved it south of the old city.
This is the location of the present county establishment.
Abolished in the 2nd year of the Dàxiàng era of Zhōu (Northern Zhou).
In the 18th year of the Kāihuáng era of Suí, it was changed to Láishuǐ Xiàn.
It is forty *lǐ* east of the prefecture.
It contains Lái Shuǐ.
27,000 households.
Róngchéng Xiàn.
Originally a Hàn county.
Previously belonged to Zhuó Jùn.
The old city is southwest of Xióngzhōu.
In the 5th year of the Wǔdé era of Táng, it belonged to Běiyì Zhōu.
In the 1st year of the Zhēnguān era, it reverted to its original jurisdiction.
In the 2nd year of the Shènglì era, it was changed to Quánzhōng Xiàn.
In the 1st year of the Tiānbǎo era, the name Róngchéng Xiàn was restored.
It is eighty *lǐ* east of the prefecture.
All households and residents live south of Jùmǎ Hé.
Its provisional administration is located in Xīnchéng Xiàn of Zhuózhōu.
5,000 households.
Jìzhōu,
Shàngwǔ Jūn,
Superior Class (Shàng),
Magistrate (Cìshǐ).
Territory of the two commanderies Yúyáng and Yòuběipíng during Qín.
During the Kāihuáng era of Suí, the administration was moved to Xuánzhōu General Administrative Office.
Emperor Yángdì changed it to Yúyáng Jùn.
In the 1st year of the Wǔdé era of Táng, it was abolished and merged into Yōuzhōu.
In the 18th year of the Kāiyuán era, Jìzhōu was separately established.
Governs three counties: Yúyáng Xiàn.
Originally a Hàn county.
Belonged to Yúyáng Jùn.
Abolished during Jìn.
Restored.
Abolished during Yuán Wèi.
During Táng, it belonged to Yōuzhōu.
In the 18th year of the Kāiyuán era, Jìzhōu was established.
It contains Bàoqiū Shuǐ.
4,000 households.
Sānhé Xiàn.
Originally the territory of Hàn's Línqú Xiàn.
In the 4th year of the Kāiyuán era of Táng, it was established by separating territory from Lùzhōu.
3,000 households.
Yùtián Xiàn.
Originally the State of Wúzhōng during the Spring and Autumn period.
Hàn established Wúzhōng Xiàn.
It belonged to Yòuběipíng Jùn.
During Yuán Wèi, it belonged to the administration of Yúyáng Jùn.
Abolished.
Restored in the 2nd year of the Wǔdé era of Táng.
Abolished early in the Zhēnguān era.
Restored during the Qiánfēng era.
In the 1st year of the Wànsuì Tōngtiān era, the name was changed to Yùtián.
It belonged to Yíngzhōu.
In the 4th year of the Kāiyuán era, it reverted to Yōuzhōu.
In the 8th year, it belonged to Yíngzhōu.
In the 11th year, it again belonged to Yōuzhōu.
In the 18th year, it came under (this prefecture's) jurisdiction.
Sōushén Jì (Record of Searching for Spirits) states:
“Yōng Bó,
a native of Luòyáng,
was filial by nature.
When his parents died,
he buried them on Wúzhōng Shān.
The mountain was eighty *lǐ* high.
There was no water on top.
Yōng Bó provided drinks.
For those who came to drink,
he gave them one *dǒu* of stones.
When planted, the stones produced jade.
Therefore, it was named Yùtián (Jade Field).”
3,000 households.
Jǐngzhōu,
Qīng'ān Jūn,
Inferior Class (Xià),
Magistrate (Cìshǐ).
Originally Zūnhuà Xiàn of Jìzhōu.
Established during the Zhòngxī era.
3,000 households.
Zūnhuà Xiàn.
Originally Mǎimǎ Jiān (Horse Purchasing Agency) of Píngzhōu during Táng.
It was made a county and came under (this prefecture's) jurisdiction.
Píngzhōu,
Liáoxīng Jūn,
Superior Class (Shàng),
Military Governor (Jiédù).
During Shāng, it was Gūzhú Guó.
During the Spring and Autumn period, it was Shānróng Guó.
During Qín, it was the territory of the two commanderies Liáoxī and Yòuběipíng.
Hàn followed this system.
At the end of Hàn,
Gōngsūn Dù occupied it.
(The territory) was passed down to his son Kāng and grandson Yuān.
(They eventually) submitted to Wèi.
During the Kāihuáng era of Suí, it was changed to Píngzhōu.
Early in the Dàyè era, it reverted to a commandery.
Early in the Wǔdé era of Táng, it was changed to a prefecture.
In the 1st year of the Tiānbǎo era, it reverted to Běipíng Jùn.
Hòu Táng (Later Tang) restored it as Píngzhōu.
In the 2nd year of the Tiānzàn era, Tàizǔ (of Liao) captured it.
The captured households from Dìngzhōu were settled throughout this region.
Governs two prefectures and three counties:
Lúlóng Xiàn.
Originally the State of Féirú.
During the Spring and Autumn period, Jìn destroyed Féi.
The Viscount of Féi fled to Yān.
He was enfeoffed here.
During Hàn and Jìn, it belonged to Liáoxī Jùn.
During Yuán Wèi, it was the administrative seat of the commandery.
And concurrently established Píngzhōu.
Běi Qí (Northern Qi) placed it under Běipíng Jùn.
During the Kāihuáng era of Suí,
Féirú was abolished
and merged into Xīnchāng.
In the 18th year, Xīnchāng was renamed Lúlóng.
During Táng, it was Píngzhōu.
Later dynasties followed this.
7,000 households.
Chāngpíng County.
Originally Hàng Jūndū County,
which in the Latter Hàn belonged to Guǎngyáng Commandery.
In the Jìn it belonged to Yān State.
During the Yuán Wèi, Dōngyān Prefecture, Píngchāng Commandery, and Chāngpíng County were established.
The commandery was abolished,
and the county was subordinate to Yōu Prefecture.
It is ninety lǐ north of the capital.
Seven thousand households.
Liángxiāng County.
During the Yān, it was Zhōngdū County.
The Hàn changed it to Liángxiāng County.
It formerly belonged to Zhuō Commandery.
In the seventh year of Tiānbǎo of the Běi Qí, it was merged into Jì County.
In the sixth year of Wǔpíng, it was re-established.
In the first year of Shènglì of the Táng, it was renamed Gùjiézhèn.
In the first year of Shénlóng, it was restored to Liángxiāng County.
Liú Shǒuguāng moved its seat here.
It is sixty lǐ south of the capital.
Seven thousand households.
Lù County.
Originally an old Hàn county,
it belonged to Yúyáng Commandery.
In the second year of Wǔdé of the Táng, Yuán Prefecture was established.
In the first year of Zhēngguān, the prefecture was abolished,
and it was restored as a county.
There is the Lù River.
It is sixty lǐ east of the capital.
Six thousand households.
Āncì County.
Originally an old Hàn county,
it belonged to Yúyáng Commandery.
In the fourth year of Wǔdé of the Táng, its seat was moved fifty lǐ southeast to Shíliáng City.
In the eighth year of Zhēngguān, it was again moved to Chángdào City, five lǐ west of the present county.
In the twenty-third year of Kāiyuán, it was again moved to the south of Gěngjiùqiáo Market.
It is one hundred twenty lǐ south of the capital.
Twelve thousand households.
Yǒngqīng County.
Originally Hàng Yìchāng County.
During the Suí, Tōngzé County was established.
During the Táng, Wǔlóng County was established,
then renamed Huìchāng.
In the early Tiānbǎo period, it became Yǒngqīng County.
It is one hundred fifty lǐ south of the capital.
Five thousand households.
Wǔqīng County.
In the Former Hàn, it was Yōngnú County,
belonging to Yúyáng Commandery.
The Shuǐjīng Zhù states:
Yōngnú
is the name of a marshy area.
Water on four sides is called "yōng,"
and non-flowing is called "nú."
In the early Tiānbǎo period of the Táng, it was renamed Wǔqīng.
It is one hundred fifty lǐ southeast of the capital.
Ten thousand households.
Xiānghé County.
Originally Sūncūn of Wǔqīng.
During the Liáo, a Salt Monopoly Office was established at Xīncāng.
Residents gathered there,
and so households were divided from Wǔqīng, Sānhé, and Lù counties to establish it.
It is one hundred twenty lǐ southeast of the capital.
Seven thousand households.
Yùhé County.
Originally the land of Quánshān.
[一０]Liú Rénqǐng established a palace-temple at Dà'ānshān,
learning the art of alchemy and transcendence from the Daoist master Wáng Ruònà.
Consequently, it was separated from Jì County
to supply him.
It is forty lǐ west of the capital.
One thousand households.
Huòyīn County.
Originally Huòcūntown of Hàng Quánshān.
Every spring, during the Liáo,
hunting took place at Yánfāngdiàn.
Residents formed a settlement,
locating it at the old Huòyīntown,
which was later changed to a county.
It is ninety lǐ southeast of the capital.
Yánfāngdiàn is several hundred lǐ in area.
In spring, geese and ducks gather there;
in summer and autumn, there are many water chestnuts and makhana.
When the ruler hunted in spring,
the guards all wore dark green,
each carrying a jointed flail, hawk food, and a goose-stabbing awl.
They lined up along the water's edge,
five to seven paces apart.
Drums were beaten upwind,
startling the geese slightly off the water.
The ruler personally released a Hǎidōngqīng falcon to catch them.
When a goose fell,
fearing the falcon might not be strong enough,
those in the line would stab the goose with their awls,
quickly taking its brain to feed the falcon.
Those who caught the lead goose
were typically rewarded with silver and silk.
The ruler, imperial family, and various ministers each had their own designated areas.
Five thousand households.
Sòng Wáng Zēng reported on Qìdān matters: "From Xióng Prefecture's Báigōuyì, cross the river,
forty lǐ to Xīnchéng County,
the ancient land of Dūkàngtíng.
Another seventy lǐ to Zhuō Prefecture.
Northward, cross the Fàn River and Liú-Lǐ River,
[一一]sixty lǐ to Liángxiāng County.
Cross the Lúgōu River,
sixty lǐ to Yōu Prefecture,
known as Yānjīng.
The inner city was built in the southwest of the outer wall.
The main south gate is called Qǐxiàmén.
Inside is the Yuánhédian.
The east gate is called Xuānhé.
All the wards and gates in the city have towers.
There is Mǐnzhōngsì Temple,
originally built by Táng Tàizōng for generals and soldiers who died in the campaign against Liáo.
There is also Kāitàisì Temple,
built by Wèi Wáng Yēlǜ Hànníng.
All envoys from the court were sent to tour and observe these.
Outside the south gate is the Yúyuè Wángjiè office,
a place for banquets and gatherings.
Outside the gate is Yǒngpíng Guǎn hostel,
formerly named Jiéshí Guǎn,
renamed after peace was sought.
To the south is the Sānggān River."
Shùn Prefecture,
Guīhuà Army,
Middle,
Prefectural Governor.
In Qín, it was Shànggǔ;
in Hàn, Fányáng;
in Běi Qí, the territory of Guīdé Commandery.
In the middle of Kāihuáng during the Suí,
when the Sùmò Mòhé were defeated in battle with Gāolì,
their chieftain Túdìjī led several thousand elite soldiers from eight tribes
from northwest of Fúyúchéng to defect and submit.
Shùn Prefecture was established to resettle them.
In the early Wǔdé period of the Táng, it was renamed Yān Prefecture.
In the middle of Huìchāng, it was renamed Guīshùn Prefecture.
At the end of the Táng, it reverted to Shùn Prefecture.
There is the Wēnyú River;
the Báisuì River;
Cáowángshān mountain,
where Cáo Cāo once stationed his army;
Shǔgǔshān mountain,
the place where Zōu Yǎn blew the pitch pipes.
To the south is the Qí Great Wall.
[一二]To the northeast of the city are Huálín and Tiānzhù estates,
where the Liáo built cool palaces
for appreciating flowers in spring
and enjoying coolness in summer.
The initial army was called Guīníng,
later renamed.
Governs one county: Huáiróu County.
Established in the sixth year of Zhēngguān of the Táng,
its seat was Wǔliǔchéng,
renamed Shùnyì County.
In the fourth year of Kāiyuán, Sōngmò Prefecture and Tánhàn Prefecture were established.
In the first year of Tiānbǎo, it was renamed Guīhuà Commandery.
[一三]In the first year of Qiányuán, it reverted to its present name.
Five thousand households.
Tán Prefecture,
Wǔwēi Army,
Lower,
Prefectural Governor.
Originally the territory of Yān Yúyáng Commandery.
In the Hàn, it was Báitán County.
The Wèi Shū states:
Cáo Gōng passed through Báitán
and defeated the Wūhuán at Liǔchéng.
The Xù Hàn Shū states:
Báitán is in Yòuběipíng.
During the Yuán Wèi, Mìyún Commandery was established,
along with Ān Prefecture.
During the Latter Zhōu, it was renamed Yuán Prefecture.
In the eighteenth year of Kāihuáng of the Suí, Tán Prefecture was established by carving out Yānlè and Mìyún counties.
In the first year of Tiānbǎo of the Táng, it was renamed Mìyún Commandery.
In the first year of Qiányuán, it reverted to Tán Prefecture.
The Liáo added its current military title.
There are Sāngxī, Bàodqiūshān mountain, Táohuāshān mountain, and Luóshān mountain.
Governs two counties: Mìyún County.
Originally Hàng Báitán County.
In the Latter Hàn, it was where the Tíxī resided.
During the Yuán Wèi, Mìyún Commandery was established,
governing Báitán, Yàoyáng, and Mìyún counties.
Gāo Qí abolished the commandery and the two counties.
It came to be subordinate.
Five thousand households.
Xíngtáng County.
Originally Xíngtáng County of Dìng Prefecture.
When Tàizǔ raided Dìng Prefecture
and defeated Xíngtáng,
he drove all its people
north to Tán Prefecture,
chose open land to settle them,
and established ten stockades,
still naming it Xíngtáng County.
It was subordinate to Zhāngmǐn Gōng.
Three thousand households.
Ānxǐ Xiàn.
Originally the territory of Lìngzhī Xiàn of the Hàn dynasty,
it had long been abandoned.
Tàizǔ established it using captured households from Ānxǐ Xiàn of Dìngzhōu.
It is sixty *lǐ* northeast of the Prefecture.
Five thousand households.
Wàngdū Xiàn.
Originally Hǎiyáng Xiàn of the Hàn dynasty,
it had long been abandoned.
Tàizǔ established it using captured households from Wàngdū Xiàn of Dìngzhōu.
It has Hǎiyáng Shān (Mount Hǎiyáng).
The County is thirty *lǐ* south of the Prefecture.
Three thousand households.
Luán Zhōu,
Yǒng'ān Jūn (Yǒng'ān Commandery),
Intermediate Class,
Administered by an *Cìshǐ*.
Originally the ancient Huángluò Chéng.
The Luánhé River encircles it,
lying south of Lúlóng Shān.
When Qí Huán Gōng attacked the Shānróng,
he saw the mountain spirit Yúguǐ;
this is that location.
During the Qín dynasty, it was Yòu Běipíng.
During the Hàn dynasty, it was Shíchéng Xiàn,
later named Hǎiyáng Xiàn.
At the end of the Hàn dynasty, it belonged to Gōngsūn Dù.
After the Jìn dynasty,
it belonged to Liáoxī.
When Shí Jìn ceded territory,
it was within the borders of Píngzhōu.
Tàizǔ established it using captured households.
Luán Zhōu rests against the mountains and is girded by the river,
serving as a strategically important
location for Shuòhàn (the northern Hàn territory).
It has Fúsū Quán (Fúsū Spring),
which is very sweet and delicious.
Qín crown prince Fúsū, when building the northern Great Wall, once resided here.
It has Línyú Shān (Mount Línyú),
whose peaks and ridges rise sharply,
over a thousand *rèn* high,
overlooking the Yúhé River below.
It administers three counties: Yìfēng Xiàn.
Originally the old city of Huángluò.
The Huángluò Shuǐ (Huángluò River) emerges from Lúlóng Shān to the north,
and flows south into the Rú Shuǐ (Rú River).
During the Hàn dynasty, it belonged to Liáoxī Jùn.
It had long been abandoned.
At the end of the Táng dynasty, it fell to the Qìdān.
Shìzōng established the County.
Four thousand households.
Mǎchéng Xiàn.
Originally the territory of Lúlóng Xiàn.
In the 28th year of Kāiyuán of the Táng dynasty (740 CE), it was separated and established as a county,
in order to facilitate water transport.
To the northeast is Qiānjīn Yě (Qiānjīn Metallurgical Works),
and to the east is Màoxiāng Zhèn (Màoxiāng Town).
The Liáo dynasty ceded it and assigned it to Luán Zhōu.
It is forty *lǐ* southwest of the Prefecture.
Three thousand households.
Shíchéng Xiàn.
Established during the Hàn dynasty,
it belonged to Yòu Běipíng Jùn.
It had long been abandoned.
During the Zhēnguān era of the Táng dynasty, Línyú Xiàn was established here.
In the first year of Wànsuì Tōngtiān (696 CE), it was renamed Shíchéng Xiàn.
It was thirty *lǐ* south of Luán Zhōu.
The Táng Yífèng stone inscription remains there.
The current county seat is fifty *lǐ* further south of that location.
The Liáo dynasty moved it to accommodate the salt official.
Three thousand households.
Yíng Zhōu,
Línhǎi Jūn (Línhǎi Commandery),
Lower Class,
Administered by an *Cìshǐ*.
Originally the Gūzhú Guó during the Shāng dynasty.
During the Qín dynasty, it belonged to Liáoxī Jùn.
During the Hàn dynasty, it was Chānglí Jùn.
Mùróng Huǎng of Former Yān moved his capital
here.
The Yuán Wèi (Northern Wèi) established Yíng Zhōu,
administering six commanderies: Chānglí, Jiàndé, Liáodōng, Lèlàng, Jìyáng,
and Yíngqiū.
Later, it was occupied
by Gāo Bǎoníng during the Hòu Zhōu (Northern Zhōu).
During the Kāihuáng era of the Suí dynasty, the Prefecture was established.
During the Dàyè era, it was changed to Liáoxī Jùn.
In the first year of Wǔdé of the Táng dynasty (618 CE), it was changed to Yíng Zhōu.
In the first year of Wànsuì Tōngtiān (696 CE), it first fell to the Qìdān.
In the second year of Shèng
lì (699 CE), the administrative seat was temporarily moved to Yúyáng.
In the fifth year of Kāiyuán (717 CE), it returned to Liǔchéng.
In the first year of Tiānbǎo (742 CE), it was renamed Liǔchéng Jùn.
The Later Táng restored it as Yíng Zhōu.
Tàizǔ used it to settle captured households from Dìngzhōu.
It administers one county: Guǎngníng Xiàn.
This was Liǔchéng Xiàn of the Hàn dynasty,
belonging to Liáoxī Jùn.
Its northeastern border connects with the Xī and Qìdān.
In the first year of Wànsuì Tōngtiān (696 CE),
it fell to Lǐ Wànróng of the Qìdān.
In the first year of Shénlóng (705 CE), it was moved to the border of Yōu Zhōu.
In the fourth year of Kāiyuán (716 CE), it returned to its old territory.
The Liáo dynasty changed it to its present name.
Three thousand households.
Treatise 11: Geographical Treatise 5, Xījīng Dào (Western Capital Circuit).
Xījīng Dàtóng Fǔ (Western Capital, Dàtóng Prefecture),
the region of Jì Zhōu during the Táotáng period.
The Yú dynasty divided it into Bīng Zhōu.
During the Xià dynasty, it reverted to Jì Zhōu.
According to the *Zhōuzhífāng* (Geography of Zhōu),
the due north region was called Bīng Zhōu.
During the Warring States period, it belonged to Zhào.
Wǔlíng Wáng first established Yúnzhōng Jùn here.
During the Qín dynasty, it belonged to Dài Wángguó.
Later, it became Píngchéng Xiàn.
During the Wèi (Cáo Wèi) dynasty, it belonged to Xīnxīng Jùn.
During the Jìn dynasty, it still belonged to Yànmén.
Liú Kūn petitioned to enfeoff Yīlú as the King of Dài,
who made Píngchéng his capital.
Dàowǔ of the Yuán Wèi (Northern Wèi) consequently established his capital city here.
Xiàowén Dì reformed it as Sī Zhōu Mù,
established Dài Yǐn,
moved the capital to Luòyì (Luòyáng),
renamed Wànnián,
and also established Dá Zhōu.
Wénxuān Dì of Gāo Qí abolished the prefecture and made it Ānzhèn.
This is now called Dōngchéng.
Soon after, the prefecture was restored.
During the Zhōu (Northern Zhōu) dynasty, it was restored as Ānzhèn
and renamed Shuò Zhōu.
During the Suí dynasty, it remained a garrison (*zhèn*).
In the fourth year of Wǔdé of the Táng dynasty (621 CE), Běi Zhōu was established.
It was abolished in the seventh year.
In the fourteenth year of Zhēnguān (640 CE), Dìngxiāng Xiàn of Yúnzhōng was moved here.
In the first year of Yǒngchún (682 CE), due to Mòchuò causing trouble for the people,
the inhabitants were moved to Shuò Zhōu.
In the eighteenth year of Kāiyuán (730 CE), Yún Zhōu was established.
In the first year of Tiānbǎo (742 CE), it was renamed Yúnzhōng Jùn.
In the first year of Qiányuán (758 CE), it was called Yún Zhōu.
In the third year of Qiánfú (876 CE),
Lǐ Guóchāng, *Jiédùshǐ* of the Dàtóng Army, had his son, Kèyòng, serving as the *Shǒuzhuōshǐ* (Defense Commissioner) of Yúnzhōng.
Kèyòng killed the *Fángyùshǐ* (Defense Commissioner),
occupied the prefecture, and reported it.
Xīzōng pardoned Kèyòng
and appointed Guóchāng as the *Fángyùshǐ* of the Dàtóng Army,
but he refused the appointment.
In the first year of Guǎngmíng (880 CE),
Lǐ Zhuó attacked Guóchāng.
Guóchāng’s forces were defeated,
and he fled north with Kèyòng.
When Huáng Cháo entered the capital,
an imperial edict summoned the Dàiběi forces.
Guóchāng was soon pardoned
and tasked with suppressing the rebels.
Kèyòng led thirty-five thousand cavalry south,
recovered the capital,
and achieved the greatest merit.
Guóchāng was enfeoffed as the Prince of Lǒngxī Jùn.
When Guóchāng died,
Kèyòng took Yún Zhōu.
Afterwards, having suffered losses wherever he attacked,
he used humble words and generous gifts
to meet with Tàizǔ at the East City of Yún Zhōu,
planning a major military offensive against Liáng.
It did not materialize.
Kèyòng's son, Cúnxù, destroyed Liáng,
becoming Táng Zhuāngzōng.
In the third year of Tóngguāng (925 CE),
Yún Zhōu was again designated as the headquarters of the Dàtóng Army *Jiédùshǐ*.
When Jìn Gāozǔ supplanted the Táng dynasty,
because the Qìdān had rendered service in assisting his establishment,
he ceded the Shānqián and Dàiběi regions as a bribe.
Dàtóng subsequently submitted
and was therefore established as the Xījīng (Western Capital).
Turrets and defensive towers were all constructed.
It is twenty *lǐ* in breadth and length.
The gates are:
The East is called Yíngchūn,
the South is called Cháoyáng,
the West is called Dìngxī,
and the North is called Gǒngjí.
The imperial walls of the Yuán Wèi occupied the north side of the city;
the twin watchtowers still remain.
Once the Liáo dynasty established the capital,
it treated this as a strategic location;
no one who was not an imperial prince was permitted to govern it.
In the eighth year of Qīngníng (1062 CE), Huáyán Sì (Huáyán Temple) was constructed,
housing stone and bronze statues of various emperors.
There are also Tiānwáng Sì (Tiānwáng Temple) and the residence of the *Liúshǒu Sī Yá*.
The south side is called Xīshěng (Western Department).
East of the North Gate is Dàtóng Fǔ,
and west of the North Gate is Dàtóng Yì (Dàtóng Post Station).
Initially, it was the Dàtóng Army *Jiédù* (Military Commission).
In the thirteenth year of Chóngxī (1044 CE), it was promoted to Xījīng (Western Capital).
The prefecture was called Dàtóng.
It administers two prefectures and seven counties:
Dàtóng County.
Originally the land of Dàtóngchuān.
In the 17th year of Chóngxī, Xī Xià invaded the border,
and it was established by separating territory from Yúnzhōng County.
Households: ten thousand.
Yúnzhōng County.
Established by Zhào.
Its history and changes are the same as those of the Capital Prefecture (Jīngfǔ).
Households: ten thousand.
Tiānchéng County.
Originally a land of the far frontier.
Emperor Dàowǔ of Wèi established Guǎngmù County;
in the 5th year of Wǔdé of Táng, Dìngxiāng County was established;
Liáo established it by separating territory from Yúnzhōng.
It is 180 *lǐ* north of the Capital.
Households: five thousand.
Chángqīng County.
Originally the land of Báidēng Terrace.
Mòdú Chányú led more than 300,000 elite cavalry and besieged Emperor Gāo of Hàn at Báidēng for seven days,
this is that location.
Liáo first established the county here.
It has Qīng Pō.
The Héngchuī Tune by Emperor Yuán of Liáng says:
“In the morning, traversing Qīng Pō,
In the evening, ascending Báidēng.”
It is 110 *lǐ* northeast of the Capital.
Households: four thousand.
Fèngyì County.
Originally the land of Táolín County of Hàn.
The Martial Emperor of Later Táng and Tàizǔ (of Liáo) met here.
Liáo established it by separating territory from Yúnzhōng.
Households: three thousand.
Huáirén County.
Originally Shānán County of Hàn.
During the chaos caused by Gě Róng in Yuán Wèi,
the county was abolished.
In the 2nd year of Kāihuáng of Suí, Yúnnèi was moved here.
In the 2nd year of Dàyè, Dàlì County was established,
belonging to Yúnzhōu,
then changed its affiliation to Dìngxiāng Commandery.
At the end of the Suí dynasty, it fell to the Tūjué.
Lǐ Kèyòng defeated Hèlián Duó,
and stationed troops here.
Liáo changed its name to Huáirén.
It is 60 *lǐ* south of the Capital.
Households: three thousand.
Huái'ān County.
Originally the land of Yíyú County of Hàn.
From the Wèi dynasty through the Suí dynasty,
it was occupied by the Tūjué.
When Táng overcame Xiélì,
the county was then abolished and became the Huáihuāng Garrison.
When Gāo Xūn governed Yān,
he requested that it be established by dividing territory from Wéndé County of Guīhuà Prefecture.
Initially, it was subordinate to Fèngshèng Prefecture,
but later came under (this jurisdiction).
It is 280 *lǐ* northwest of the prefecture.
Households: three thousand.
Hóngzhōu,
Bóníng Army Command,
Lower Class.
Governed by a Cìshǐ.
Emperor Jìng of Eastern Wèi established Běilíngqiū County.
In the early Táng dynasty, the land fell to the Tūjué.
During the Kāiyuán era, Ānbiān County of the Héngyě Army Command was established,
but it was abolished during the Tiānbǎo disturbances.
Later it became Xiāngyīn Village.
During the Tǒnghé era,
because Huánzhōu was close to the border,
and was defeated by the Sòng General Pān Měi,
it was abolished.
Hóngzhōu was then established here.
The initial military command was called Yǒngníng.
It has the Sānggān River, Báidào Spring, and Báidēng Mountain,
which is also called Huǒshāo Mountain.
It has fire wells.
Controls two counties: Yǒngníng County.
Households: ten thousand.
Shùnshèng County.
Originally the Ānsāi Army Command of Wèi.
It was abolished due to warfare during the Five Dynasties period.
When Gāo Xūn governed Yōuzhōu,
he memorialized Emperor Jǐngzōng to establish it by dividing territory from Yǒngxīng County.
Initially subordinate to Fèngshèng Prefecture.
It is 280 *lǐ* northwest of the prefecture.
Households: three thousand.
Dézhōu,
Lower Class.
Governed by a Cìshǐ.
During the Huìchāng era of Táng, Dézhōu was established at Xīdé Diàn.
In the 8th year of Kāitài, it was re-established using Hàn Chinese households.
It has Bùluò Spring, Jīnhé Mountain, Yěhú Ridge, and Báidào Slope.
One county: Xuāndé County.
Originally the land of Tóngguò County of Hàn,
belonging to Yúnzhōng Commandery,
later subordinated to Dìngxiāng Commandery,
it was abolished at the end of the Hàn dynasty.
Gāo Qí established the Zǐ'ā Garrison.
During the Huìchāng era of Táng, the county was established.
Households: three thousand.
Fēngzhōu,
Tiāndé Army Command,
Governed by a Jiédùshǐ.
During the Qín dynasty, it was the northern boundary of Shàng Commandery.
During the Hàn dynasty, it belonged to Wǔyuán Commandery.

Treatise 12: Treatise on Astronomy and Calendar, Part One
The Liáo dynasty established its state based on Yōu and Yíng,
and the structure of its rites, music, and institutions gradually matured.
They issued calendars and announced the start of months for over two hundred years.
We have received an imperial edict to compile the History of Liáo;
its structure should resemble those of Sòng and Jīn,
and thus the Dàmíng Calendar cannot be omitted.
The methods of the calendar system are legally forbidden and unobtainable.
Seeking the basis of the Dàmíng Calendar,
we obtained Zǔ Chōngzhī's methods from unofficial histories.
Is it possible that Zǔ Chōngzhī's method
is the source from which the Liáo calendar originated?
The ruling dynasty has also adopted it.
By calculating Zǔ Chōngzhī's method,
up to the year when the Liáo dynasty changed its calendar,
we derive the epochal numbers.
This is likely the Liáo Dàmíng Calendar.
Although the Liáo calendar could certainly be supplemented based on this,
we will not supplement it,
as historians value preserving omissions.
The unofficial histories record its method,
the Department of Astronomy maintains its function,
and this treatise in the History of Liáo is sufficient.
We compose the Treatise on Astronomy and Calendar.
The Calendar
In the 1st year of Dàtóng,
Emperor Tàizōng collected officials, staff, artisans, and calendar experts from the hundred departments in Biànjīng of the Jìn state,
and relocated them to Zhōngjīng.
It was then that the Liáo dynasty first possessed a calendar system.
Before this,
the Liáng and Táng dynasties still used the Jǐngfú Chóngxuán Calendar of the Táng dynasty.
In the 4th year of Tiānfú of the Jìn dynasty,
Mǎ Chóngjì, Director of the Department of Astronomy, presented the Yǐwèi Yuán Calendar,
named the Tiáoyuán Calendar,
which is what Emperor Tàizōng seized in Biàn.
In the 11th year of Yìnglì of Mùzōng,
Wáng Bái, Lǐ Zhèng, and others from the Department of Astronomy submitted a calendar,
which was presumably the Yǐwèi Yuán Calendar.
In the 12th year of Tǒnghé of Shèngzōng,
Jiǎ Jùn, the Cìshǐ (Prefect) of Kèhán Zhōu, presented a new calendar,
which was the Dàmíng Calendar.
The *Dàliáo Gǔjīn Lù* recorded by Gāolì states that the standard calendar was first issued and the calendar system changed in the 12th year of Tǒnghé,
which is verifiable.
The Dàmíng Calendar was originally Zǔ Chōngzhī's method from the Sòng dynasty,
fully detailed in Shěn Yuē's *Sòng Shū*.
The details are provided below.
In the 6th year of Dàmíng of Emperor Wǔdì of Sòng,
Zǔ Chōngzhī presented the Jiǎzǐ Yuán Calendar Method,
but it was not yet implemented,
so it was named the Dàmíng Calendar.
From the year Jiǎzǐ of Shàngyuán until the year Guǐmǎo, the seventh year of Dàmíng of Sòng,
51,939 years are excluded from the calculation.
Cycle divisor (Yuán fǎ): 592,365.
Epoch divisor (Jǐ fǎ): 39,491.
Period years (Zhāng suì): 391.
Period months (Zhāng yuè): 4,836.

Method for determining the New Moon (Tuī shuò shù):
Set aside the number of years since the Shàngyuán epoch,
multiply this by the Period months (Zhāng yuè).
Every time this reaches the Period years (Zhāng suì), it forms an accumulated month (Jī yuè).
The remainder is the intercalary remainder (Rùn yú).
If the intercalary remainder is 247 or more,
that year has an intercalary month.
Multiply the accumulated months by the Month divisor (Yuè fǎ).
Every time this reaches the Day divisor (Rì fǎ), it forms an accumulated day (Jī rì).
The remainder is the small remainder (Xiǎo yú).
Subtract cycles of sixty days (Lìu xún) from the accumulated days.
The remainder is the great remainder (Dà yú).
Use the great remainder to determine the day in the Jiǎzǐ cycle.
Excluded from calculation,
this is the New Moon (Shuò) of the 11th month (Tiānzhèng) of the required year.
If the small remainder is 1,849 or more,
that month is long.
To find the next month:
Add 29 to the great remainder,
and 2,090 to the small remainder.
If the small remainder reaches the Day divisor (Rì fǎ), carry over to the great remainder.
If the great remainder reaches a cycle of sixty days, subtract it.
Determine the day as before;
this is the New Moon (Shuò) of the subsequent month.
To find the quarter moons and Full Moon (Xián wàng):
Add 7 to the New Moon's great remainder,
1,507 to the small remainder,
and 1 to the small fraction (Xiǎo fēn).
If the small fraction reaches 4, carry over to the small remainder.
If the small remainder reaches the Day divisor (Rì fǎ), carry over to the great remainder.
Determine the day as before;
this is the day of the First Quarter Moon (Shàng xián).
Adding again gives the Full Moon (Wàng).
Adding again gives the Last Quarter Moon (Xià xián).
Adding again gives the New Moon (Shuò) of the following month.
Method for determining the intercalary month (Tuī rùn shù):
Subtract the intercalary remainder (Rùn yú) from the Period years (Zhāng suì).
If the remaining amount reaches the Intercalary divisor (Rùn fǎ), one month is obtained.
Determine the month based on Tiānzhèng.
Excluded from calculation,
this is where the intercalary month is located.
Intercalary months have advances and retreats;
the absence of a major solar term (Zhōng qì) is taken as the standard.
Determining the 24 Solar Terms (Tuī èr shí sì qì):
Set aside the number of years since the Shàngyuán epoch.
Multiply this by the Remainder number (Yú shù).
Every time this reaches the Epoch divisor (Jǐ fǎ), it forms an accumulated day (Jī rì).
The remainder is the small remainder (Xiǎo yú).
Subtract cycles of sixty days (Lìu xún) from the accumulated days.
The remainder is the great remainder (Dà yú).
Use the great remainder to determine the day in the Jiǎzǐ cycle.
Excluded from calculation,
this is the day of the Winter Solstice (Dōngzhì) in the 11th month (Tiānzhèng).
To find the next solar term:
Add 15 to the great remainder,
8,626 to the small remainder,
and 5 to the small fraction.
If the small fraction reaches 6, carry over to the small remainder.
If the small remainder reaches the Epoch divisor (Jǐ fǎ), carry over to the great remainder.
Determine the day as before;
this is the day of the subsequent solar term.
To find the period when the element Earth is dominant (Qiú tǔ wáng yòng shì):
Add 27 to the great remainder of the Winter Solstice,
and 15,528 to the small remainder.
This is the starting day of Earth's dominance in the final month of winter (Jìdōng).
Adding again 91 to the great remainder,
and 12,270 to the small remainder,
gives the starting day of the subsequent period of Earth's dominance.
Method for determining the invisibility (Tuī mò shù):
Multiply the Winter Solstice small remainder by 90.
Subtract this from the Eclipse parts (Mò fēn).
Every time this reaches the Eclipse divisor (Mò fǎ), it forms a day.
The remainder is the day remainder (Rì yú).
Determine the day based on the Winter Solstice.
Excluded from calculation,
this is the day of invisibility (Mò rì).
To find the next invisibility:
Add 69 days,
and 34,442 to the day remainder.
If the remainder reaches the Eclipse divisor (Mò fǎ), carry over to the days.
This is the day of the subsequent invisibility.
If the day remainder is exhausted, it is extinction (Miè).
Method for determining the Sun's position in degrees (Tuī rì suǒ zài dù shù):
Multiply the accumulated days of the New Moon (Shuò jī rì) by the Epoch divisor (Jǐ fǎ) to get the degree dividend (Dù shí).
Subtract the Revolution of the heavens (Zhōu tiān) from it.
Every time the remainder reaches the Epoch divisor (Jǐ fǎ), it forms an accumulated degree (Jī dù).
The remainder is the degree remainder (Dù yú).
Determine the position starting from the Xūyī (Xūyī) mansion.
Subtract the subsequent mansion (Sù).
Excluded from calculation,
this is the position of the Sun in degrees at midnight on the New Moon (Shuò) of the 11th month (Tiānzhèng).
To find the next month:
If it is a long month (Dà yuè), add 30 degrees.
If it is a short month (Xiǎo yuè), add 29 degrees.
Enter the Xū mansion (Rù Xū) and subtract the degree parts (Dù fēn).
To find the traveling fractions (Qiú xíng fēn):
Divide the degree remainder by the Small fraction divisor (Xiǎo fēn fǎ).
The quotient is the traveling fraction.
The remainder is the small fraction (Xiǎo fēn).
If the small fraction reaches its divisor, carry over to the traveling fraction.
If the traveling fraction reaches its divisor, carry over to the degrees.
To find the next day:
Add 1 degree.
Enter the Xū mansion (Rù Xū) and subtract 6 traveling fractions,
and 147 small fractions.
Method for determining the Moon's position in degrees (Tuī yuè suǒ zài dù shù):
Multiply the New Moon's small remainder (Shuò xiǎo yú) by 124 to get the degree remainder.
Also, multiply the New Moon's small remainder by 860 to get the fine fraction (Wēi fēn).
If the fine fraction reaches the Month divisor (Yuè fǎ), carry over to the degree remainder.
If the degree remainder reaches the Epoch divisor (Jǐ fǎ), it forms a degree.
Subtract this from the position of the Sun at midnight on the New Moon.
This is the Moon's position in degrees.
To find the next month:
If it is a long month, add 35 degrees,
a degree remainder of 31,834,
and a fine fraction of 77,967.
If it is a short month, add 22 degrees,
a degree remainder of 17,261,
and a fine fraction of 63,736.
Enter the Xū mansion (Rù Xū) and subtract the degrees.
Method for entering the Fast and Slow Calendar (Tuī rù chí jí lì shù):
Multiply the accumulated days of the New Moon (Shuò jī rì) by the Total divisor (Tōng fǎ) to get the total dividend (Tōng shí).
Subtract the Total circuit (Tōng zhōu).
Every time the remainder reaches the Total divisor (Tōng fǎ), it forms a day.
The remainder is the day remainder (Rì yú).
Determine the day, excluded from calculation,
this is the entry day into the calendar at midnight on the New Moon (Shuò) of the 11th month (Tiānzhèng).
To find the next month:
For a long month, add 2 days.
For a short month, add 1 day.
The day remainder is 11,746 in both cases.
When the calendar reaches 27 days,
and the day remainder is 14,631,
then subtract it.
To find the next day:
Add 1 day.
To find the corrected position in degrees for the day (Qiú rì suǒ zài dìng dù):
Multiply the remainder of the entry day at midnight by the Gain/Loss Rate (Sǔn yì lǜ).
Apply this gain or loss to the Accumulation of Advance/Retreat (Yíng suō jī fēn).
Divide the result by the Rate of difference (Chā lǜ).
Every time the quotient reaches the Epoch divisor (Jǐ fǎ), it forms a degree.
The remainder is the degree remainder.
Add the advance (Yíng) or subtract the retreat (Suō) from the mean degree and its remainder to obtain the corrected degree (Dìng dù).
If adding causes it to reach the divisor,
or if subtracting causes a shortfall,
adjust by advancing or retreating based on the Epoch divisor (Jǐ fǎ).
To find the degree and traveling fraction, use the method above.
To find the next day,
add according to the entry into the Fast and Slow Calendar.
For Xū mansion subtraction of parts,
use the method above.

To calculate the conjunction *Shuò* or lunar eclipse *Yuè Shí*:
Set the *Shuò* or *Wàng* midnight entered into the *Yīnyáng Lì* and its remainder.
If there is a half, remove it.
Set the minute fraction to three hundred and three,
and add the number of differences to it.
When the minute fraction is full (six hundred and six), it carries over to the day remainder.
When the day remainder is full (using the *Tōng Fǎ*), it carries over to the day.

which is the time of *Shuò* or *Wàng* added and entered into the calendar.
When the time of *Shuò* or *Wàng* added and entered into the calendar is one day,
the day remainder is four thousand one hundred and ninety-eight,

or twelve days,

then for *Shuò*, there is a conjunction (*Jiāohuì*),

To determine the exact major and minor remainders for the conjunction *Shuò* or lunar eclipse *Yuè Shí*:
Let the day remainder of the difference number be added to the remainder of the midnight entry into the deceleration/acceleration calendar (*Chí Jí Lì*).
When the day remainder is full (using the *Tōng Fǎ*), it carries over to the day.
This is the time of *Shuò* or *Wàng* added and entered into the calendar.
Multiply the remainder entered into the calendar by the loss/gain ratio (*Sǔn Yì Lǜ*).
Use this to calculate the integrated gain/loss (*Yíng Suō Jī Fēn*).
Divide by the difference divisor (*Chà Fǎ*).
Subtract the reduction or add the gain to the original *Shuò* or *Wàng* minute remainder to get the definitive minute remainder (*Dìng Xiǎo Yú*).
If the gain causes it to meet the divisor,
or if the loss causes it to be insufficient,
advance or retreat the day according to the day divisor (*Rì Fǎ*).
To calculate the added temporal hour (*Jiā Shí*) for the conjunction *Shuò* or lunar eclipse *Yuè Shí*:
Multiply the definitive minute remainder
by twelve. When full (using the *Rì Fǎ*), one temporal hour (*Chén*) is obtained.
Designate it as Zǐ (*Zǐ*),
outside the calculation,
which is the temporal hour where the added time is located.
If there is a remainder, multiply it by four.
When full (using the *Rì Fǎ*), one is obtained as lesser (*Shǎo*),
two as half (*Bàn*),
and three as greater (*Tài*).
If there is yet a remainder, multiply it by three.
When full (using the *Rì Fǎ*), one is obtained as strong (*Qiáng*).
Combine *Qiáng* with *Shǎo* to be lesser-strong (*Shǎo Qiáng*),
combine it with *Bàn* to be half-strong (*Bàn Qiáng*),
and combine it with *Tài* to be greater-strong (*Tài Qiáng*).
If two is obtained, it is lesser-weak (*Shǎo Ruò*).
Combine it with *Shǎo* to be half-weak (*Bàn Ruò*),
combine it with *Bàn* to be greater-weak (*Tài Ruò*),
and combine it with *Tài* to be one *Chén* weak.
Name it after the preceding *Chén*.
To find the degree of the Moon's distance from the Sun's path:

Divide the *Dìng Shù* by twelve to get the degree (*Dù*).
The remainder is divided by four,
giving lesser, half, and greater.
The remaining remainder is divided by three,
one is strong,
two is lesser-weak,
this is the number representing the Moon's distance from the Sun's path.

In the year of the Supreme Epoch (Shàngyuán),
the cyclic sign of the year was Jiǎzǐ.
The first day of the first lunar month (Zhēngyuè), Jiǎzǐ, at midnight, coincided with the winter solstice,
and the Sun, Moon, and Five Planets gathered at the beginning of the Xū Dù.
The lagging and swiftness (chí and jí) of Yīn and Yáng all start from this point.
In the third year of Tiānjiān of Liáng Wǔ Dì,
Zǔ Chōngzhī's son, Zǔ Gěng, submitted a memorial,
arguing that Hé Chéngtiān's calendar was erroneous and unusable.
In the first month of the ninth year,
an imperial edict commanded the use of the Jiǎzǐ Yuán Lì (Calendar of the Supreme Epoch, Jiǎzǐ) created by Zǔ Chōngzhī for issuing the calendar.
The Chén Dynasty followed the Liáng,
and also used Zǔ Chōngzhī's calendar.
Up until the Liáo Dynasty,
Shèngzōng used the New Calendar presented by Jiǎ Jùn,
and implemented it using the old title Dàmíng from the Sòng Dynasty.
The Jīn Dynasty called it the Rèngxīu Dàmíng Lì (Revised Dàmíng Calendar).
It was transmitted to the Imperial Yuán Dynasty, where it was also called the Rèngxīu Dàmíng Lì.
When the Shòushí Lì was later adopted,
the Sìtiānjīan (Directorate of Astronomy) was established separately to maintain and continue it,
and its methods were revised every year in which the winter solstice fell on Jiǎzǐ.
The documents are kept in the Tàishǐ Yuàn (Bureau of the Grand Astrologer),
and it is forbidden for anyone to know of them.
Treatise 13: Celestial Patterns (Lìxiàng Zhì) Middle Section: Examination of Intercalation (Rùnkǎo)
When the measure of the month is insufficient,
this gives rise to empty new moons (xuē).
When the celestial motion is in excess,
this is called full solar terms (qì yíng).
When the fullness and emptiness differ from one another,
the months and years become separated (pàn).
When these separations accumulate and cause errors,
winter and summer interchange,
the hundred grains fail to ripen,
and all government affairs become unclear.
The Sages verify this with the Dipper handle,
and standardize it by Suìxīng (Jupiter).
They thereupon established the method of intercalation,
which truly governs all officials.
Therefore, when the intercalation is rectified, the months are rectified;
when the months are rectified, the year is rectified.
Once the years and months are rectified,
in issuing commands and evaluating performance,
nothing is untimely.
For the State Historian to rectify the years and months in keeping with affairs,
nothing is more important than this.
The Liáo began tracking calendars using those of Liáng and Táng.
After entering Jìn,
they swiftly adopted the imperial system,
and the Yǐwèi and Dàmíng calendars,
represented a second change in calendrical methods.
In Mùzōng's Yìnglì sixth year (956 CE),
Zhōu used the Xiǎndé Qīntiān Calendar;
ten years later (966 CE),
Sòng used the Jiànlóng Yìngtiān Calendar.
In Jǐngzōng's Qiánhēng fourth year (982 CE),
Sòng used the Qiányuán Calendar.
In Shèngzōng's Tǒnghé nineteenth year (1001 CE),
Sòng used the Yítiān Calendar;
in Tàipíng first year (1021 CE),
Sòng used the Chóngtiān Calendar.
In Dàozōng's Qīngníng tenth year (1064 CE),
Sòng used the Míngtiān Calendar;
in Dàkāng first year (1075 CE),
Sòng used the Fèngyuán Calendar;
in Dà'ān seventh year (1091 CE),
Sòng used the Guāntiān Calendar.
In Tiānzuò Huángdì's Qiántǒng sixth year (1106 CE),
Sòng used the Jìyuán Calendar.
The Five Dynasties saw three changes in calendars;
Sòng saw eight changes;
Liáo only changed twice from start to finish.
Since the calendrical methods were not standardized,
the determinations of the new moon (Suò) and the placement of intercalary months (Rùn)
were sometimes inconsistent,
causing confusion for the reader.
Therefore, this investigation of the intercalary months (Rùn Kǎo) is presented.

Treatise Fourteen: Treatise on Astronomical Phenomena, Part Two: Investigation of the New Moon (Suò Kǎo).
In ancient times, the Grand Historian (Tàishǐ) was responsible for correcting the annual calendar (suì nián) based on events,
and the National Historian (Guóshǐ) correlated events with the days,
and correlated days, months, and seasons with the year.
If the seasons and months are incorrect,
then the records of events will not be unified.
Therefore, the two historian offices were combined into one post:
to manage the calendar and assign time,
which must prioritize great unification.
The Liáo, Hàn, Zhōu, and Sòng,
all followed the Xià calendar standard (beginning the year in the first month),
but each had its own calendar.
The new moon and intercalary months recorded by the National Historians
contain many discrepancies.
In the early Liáo period, they used the Yǐwèi Yuán Calendar,
which originated from Hé Chéngtiān’s Yuánjiā calendrical method;
later they used the Dàmíng Calendar,
which originated from Zǔ Chōngzhī’s Jiǎzǐ Yuán calendrical method.
Hé Chéngtiān’s method allowed solar eclipses to occur on the last day of the month (huì) or the first day (fěi),
requiring seven intercalary months per nineteen-year cycle (zhāng);
Zǔ Chōngzhī’s method required solar eclipses to occur only on the new moon (suò),
sometimes placing one intercalary month every four years.
When using the Yǐwèi Calendar,
it was mostly consistent with those of Hàn and Zhōu;
when using the Dàmíng Calendar,
it was occasionally different from Sòng.
In the records of the National Historian,
the sexagesimal cycle (Jiǎzǐ) days do not differ,
but the intercalary months (Rùn) and new moons (Suò) often differ.
This is the reason for that.
The records of Yēlǜ Yǎn use the Dàmíng method to retrospectively correct the monthly new moons (Suò) of the Yǐwèi period,
and sometimes they conflict with the records compiled by Chén Dàrèn.
Gentlemen who examine ancient matters
are often confused by this.
Using the precedents regarding the prefectures and armies of the Qìdān from the official history records of the five dynasties' bureaucratic geography,
this calendar of the first days of the months (Shuò) is compiled.
Differences in method are called
"Yì" (Different);
errors in transmission are called
"Wù" (Mistake).
The Liáo Shǐ (History of Liáo) does not record the country;
Yělǜ Yǎn and Yèlǜ Dàrèn's differing opinions are listed side by side under their respective names;
other histories prefix the country name to the Shuò.
All are noted below.

In the 12th month of Sòng Yuánfēng Year 1,
an imperial edict commanded the Directorate of Astronomy to compare the calendars of Liáo, Gāolì, and Japan with the Fèngyuán Calendar, noting similarities and differences.
The seasonal and lunar first days (Qìshùo) of Liáo in the year Jǐwèi
matched the Xuānmíng Calendar.
The year Wùwǔ of Japan was close to the Liáo calendar,
while the lunar first days of Gāolì in the year Wùwǔ
matched the Fèngyuán Calendar,
was Dàkāng Year 4 of Liáo;
Jǐwèi
was Year 5.
In the eras of Liáo and Sòng,
the directorates of astronomy of the two countries definitely cross-referenced [their calendars].
The records of the Great Liáo that Gāolì presented
contain the imperial edicts for enfeoffment of the various princes,
which frequently mention the lunar first days (Yuèshuò).
These are therefore attached.
Implication:
Mèngzǐ (Mencius) once said:
"The height of the heavens
and the distance of the stars
—if one truly seeks their causes,
the winter solstice of a thousand years from now can be determined while seated."
How profound!
The mental effort of the sage
can be called vast, great, subtle, and profound,
reaching the ultimate limit.
The sun has shadows cast by a gnomon,
the moon has brightness and darkness,
the Dǒu (Big Dipper) has positions indicating the seasons,
and the stars have times of visibility at dusk and dawn.
Observing the changes in the sky, instruments are created to monitor them:
an eight-chi (foot) gnomon,
a six-chi tube,
a water clock with a hundred *kè* (divisions),
and the sun, moon, stars, and planets are displayed as if in the palm of one's hand.
When the movements have been thoroughly observed,
and the degrees and divisions meticulously determined,
then, modeling the spherical heavens to display the movements,
and setting up a square base (earth chamber) to verify the rising and setting,
the Húnxiàng (Armillary Sphere) is constructed.
The constant laws of the heavenly way,
within a *xún* or *chǐ* (small measures), can be observed by looking down.
The instrument of Táo Táng (Yáo) is an example of this.
Setting up the three instruments (*sān yí*) to clarify the degrees and divisions,
and employing one pole (*yī héng*) to align the celestial pole,
the Húnyí (Armillary Instrument) is constructed.
The changes in the celestial phenomena,
can be observed by looking up at the standard instruments covering the six cardinal directions (*liù hé zhī biǎo*).
The *Jī* (Sphere) of Yǒu Yú (Shùn) is an example of this.
No substance is more solid than metal,
and no means is more effective than water.
Casting metal and setting water in motion,
one can know the way of Heaven without leaving the house.
This is how the sages achieve sagehood.
The instruments, spheres, gnomons, and water clocks of past dynasties
are each recorded in the monographs.
In the first year of Dàtóng (大同) of Tàizōng (太宗)
the Jin (晉) calendrical instrument, water clock, and armillary sphere were obtained.
By the second year of Qīngtài (清泰) of the Later Táng (後唐), they were already reported as damaged and unusable;
their condition when they reached the Central Capital (*Zhōngjīng*) can generally be inferred.
In antiquity, when refining copper,
the black, yellow, white, and green impurities were all removed
before it was used;
thus, it could be applied for long durations.
Yīxíng (一行), a Buddhist monk of the Táng (唐) dynasty, cast a Húntiānyí (渾天儀),
which was praised as exquisite and marvelous at the time,
but soon after, the copper and iron gradually became stiff,
it could not rotate by itself,
and was set aside and no longer used.
If the copper is not refined,
the nature of the water cannot flow (properly)—
how much worse if moved to a bitterly cold region?
The water clock
was constructed in the third year of Tiānfú (天福) of Jìn (晉).
The Zhou (周) officials, the *Qiè Hú Shì* (挈壺氏), would suspend the pot and must heat it with fire.
Even if the ground is bitterly cold,
it can still be used.
Official Stars (*Guān Xīng*)
In antiquity, there were over ten thousand names for official stars.
They were destroyed when the Qin (秦) burned the maps and records,
and the knowledge was kept secret by families and not transmitted.
The Hàn (漢) gathered what was scattered and lost,
obtaining the records and charts of the three schools: Gān Dé (甘德), Shí Shēn (石申), and Wū Xián (巫咸).
The combined warp and weft contained over a thousand official asterisms,
but barely a tenth remained.
They were divided into the Three Enclosures (*Sān Yuán*), Four Palaces (*Sì Gōng*), and Twenty-eight Mansions (*Èrshíbā Xiù*).
They were pivoted by the two poles,
established by the Běi Dǒu (North Dipper),
wefted by the five planets,
illuminated alternately by the sun and moon,
ranging from the most noble Tài Yī (太一)
down to the lowly *shǐkāng* (dung and chaff).
For the purpose of divination and judgment,
they were said to be comprehensive.
As Sīmǎ Qiān (司馬遷) recorded them all in the monograph on Celestial Offices (*Tiānguān Shū*),
subsequent generations of official astronomers, in observing and guarding the phenomena,
never went beyond the official stars of these three schools.
The celestial phenomena are clearly manifested
and have not changed throughout the dynasties,
yet the books of the Hàn, Jìn, Suí (隋), and Táng dynasties have repeatedly recorded astronomical matters,
which is close to superfluous.
Furthermore, concerning the portents and omens of celestial phenomena,
there are legal prohibitions (against indiscriminate recording).
If they are recorded in the histories of previous states,
they mislead scholars;
it is inappropriate to record them.
As for the auspicious omens of solar eclipses, stellar changes, winds, clouds, earthquakes, and snow,
they are fully contained in the Imperial Annals (*Dìjì*),
and will not be recorded again here.
Monograph Fifteen: Official Offices I
Offices originated from functions,
functions derived from affairs,
and then names were assigned to them.
Later generations perpetuated the names
without thoroughly investigating the reality.
The Ministry of Personnel (*Lìbù*) is one and the same as the Grand Tutor (*Tàizǎi*),
the Grand Minister of the Masses (*Dà Sītú*),
the Department of State Affairs (*Shàngshū*),
the Department of the Secretariat (*Zhōngshū*),
and the Department of the Chancellery (*Ménxià*).
The Ministry of War (*Bīngbù*) is one and the same as the Minister of War (*Sīmǎ*),
the Grand Marshal (*Dà Sīmǎ*),
the Grand Commandant (*Tàiwèi*),
and the Commissioner of Military Affairs (*Shūmìshǐ*).
By following ancient official titles
and allocating current functions and duties to match them,
the laws by which the former kings governed the realm
became like tangled threads,
and the names and realities were confused.
In the old customs of the Qìdān (契丹),
affairs were simple and functions specialized,
the official system was plain and practical,
and they were not confused by names;
thus, their rise was sudden and vigorous.
In the sixth year of Shéncè (神冊) of Tàizǔ (太祖),
an imperial edict ordered the rectification of ranks and titles.
When it came to Tàizōng,
who simultaneously governed the Central Plain (*Zhōngguó*),
officialdom was divided into Southern and Northern systems:
the National System was used to govern the Qìdān,
and the Hàn (Chinese) System was used to treat the Hàn people.
The National System was plain and simple,
but the Hàn System retained the tendency of perpetuating names.
The official system of the Liáo (遼) state
was divided into the Northern and Southern Courts.
The Northern Face administered the affairs of the imperial tents, tribal groups, and subordinate states.
The Southern Face administered the affairs of the Hàn people's prefectures and counties, taxation, and military horses.
Governing according to the customs
achieved what was appropriate for each.
Initially,
Tàizǔ divided the *Diélà Yílíjǐn* (迭剌夷離菫) into the two Great Kings, Northern and Southern,
calling them the Northern and Southern Courts.
The Chancellor (*Zǎixiàng*), Commissioner of Military Affairs (*Shūmì*), Commissioner of Palace Affairs (*Xuānhuī*), and Secretary (*Línyá*),
down to the Gentleman (*Lángjūn*) and Guard (*Hùwèi*),
were all divided into Northern and Southern,
though in reality, what they administered mostly pertained to the affairs of the Northern Face.
Those discussing the Liáo official system must distinguish this point.
In general, for the officials of the Liáo court:
the Northern Bureau of Military Affairs (*Běi Shūmì*) was equivalent to the Ministry of War, the Southern Bureau of Military Affairs (*Nán Shūmì*) was equivalent to the Ministry of Personnel,
the two Kings of the Northern and Southern Courts (*Běi, Nán Èr Wáng*) were equivalent to the Ministry of Revenue,
the *Yílíbì* (夷離畢) was equivalent to the Ministry of Justice,
the Commissioner of Palace Affairs (*Xuānhuī*) was equivalent to the Ministry of Works,
and the *Díliè Mádū* (敵烈麻都) was equivalent to the Ministry of Rites.
The Chancellors of the Northern and Southern Administrations (*Běi, Nán Fǔ Zǎixiàng*) oversaw them all.
The *Tìyǐn* (惕隱) governed the imperial clan.
The Secretary (*Línyá*) drafted literary pronouncements.
The *Yúyuè* (于越) sat and deliberated, symbolizing the Grand Mentor (*Gōng Shī*).
Within the imperial court,
affairs were simple and functions specialized;
this is why the Liáo flourished.
Northern Face (Běi Miàn) Officials of the Northern Face
Qìdān Northern Bureau of Military Affairs (*Běi Shūmì Yuàn*).
It managed military strategy, military personnel appointments, and the administration of the various herds.
All Qìdān armies and horses were subject to it.
Because its headquarters were situated north of the imperial tent-palace within the Great Inner Tent,
it was named the Northern Court.
This is what Yuán Hàowèn (元好問) meant when he said,
“The Northern Yámen does not manage the people.”

Dà Yúyuèfǔ.
Without specific duties,
it ranked above all other officials.
It was not conferred upon those without great merit and virtue.
It was a venerable office of the Liáo state,
like the Sāngōng (Three Dukes) in the Southern Dynasties.
Tàizǔ received the abdication from the Yúyuè of the Yáolián clan.
Throughout the Liáo dynasty,
three individuals gained great renown as Yúyuè: Yēlǜ Hélǔ, Wūzhì, and Rénxiān.
They were called the Sān Yúyuè (Three Yúyuè).

Dà Tìyǐnsī.
Established by Tàizǔ.
Manages the politics and education of the imperial clan.
Xīngzōng in Chóngxī twenty-first year (1052 CE),
Yēlǜ Yìxiān was appointed Tìyǐn,
and warned his clansmen, saying:
"The three paternal branches of the state are the most noble of clans.
All the cultural and moral influences of the realm originate from them;
disrespectful or unrighteous acts,
even minor ones, must not be committed."
His wife, the daughter of the Princess of Jìn State (Jìnguó Zhǎnggōngzhǔ),
always wore formal attire when meeting her relatives.
Yìxiān led by example,
and the imperial clan emulated him.

It has no specific managerial duties,
ranking above all officials.
It is not conferred upon anyone lacking great merit and virtue.
It is a respected official position of the Liáoguó,
akin to the Sāngōng of the Southern Dynasties.
Tàizǔ received the abdication from the Yùyuè of the Yáolián clan.
Throughout the era of Liáo,
three people gained great renown through the Yùyuè title: Yēlǜ Gélǔ, Wūzhì, and Rénxiān,
They are called the Sān Yùyuè.

In the twenty-first year of Chóngxī of Xīngzōng,
Yēlǜ Yìxiān was appointed Tìyǐn.
He cautioned his clansmen, saying:
"The Sān Fù Fáng of the State are the noblest clans.
All social customs and moral transformation in the realm originate from them.
Disrespectful or unjust acts,
however minor, must not be committed."
His wife, the daughter of the Grand Princess of Jìnguó,
always wore formal attire when meeting maternal relatives.
Yìxiān led by personal example,
and the imperial clan was reformed by his influence.

Officials of the Běimiàn Yùzhàng
Even the Sānhuáng and the Sages,
during the era of simple innocence,
used double gates and night-watch clappers,
remaining strict as if anticipating violent intruders.
In the early generations of Liáo,
they had no strong fortifications like walled cities, moats, or palaces.
Felt carts served as encampments;
strong stockades served as palaces.
Therefore, the Imperial Tent Officials (Yùzhàng Guān) necessarily had to be diligent.
Those selected from the imperial relatives were Shìwèi;
those stationed at the Tent were Jìnshì;
tribes from the North and South Departments formed Hùwèi;
military officials formed Sùwèi;
the Imperial Army formed Jìnwèi;
and officials rotating nightly formed Sùzhí.
The Fèngchén managed imperial supplies;
the Sānbān maintained order during court assemblies;
and the Strong Stockades maintained strict security day and night.
The system of governance can thus be called strict and rigorous.

In ancient times, criminals were not near the sovereign.
The family members of rebels were confiscated and made Zhuózhàng,
performing duties as imperial guards,
which could make one tremble with fear.
Is this why the Liáo dynasty often saw troubles arise close at hand?
Zhuózhàng Lángjūn Yuàn (Court of Zhuózhàng Gentlemen).
Yáoniǎn Héndéjǐn Kèhán killed Yúyuè Shìlǔ with the three clans of Púgǔzhǐ and others,
and their family members were confiscated into Wǎlǐ.
Yìngtiān Huángtàihòu governed the state,
and separated them out,
making them Zhuózhàng Lángjūn and Niángzǐ (Gentlemen and Ladies Assigned to the Tent),
always showing them pity and care.
Shìzōng pardoned them entirely.
Subsequently, offenders from the Inner Clan, Outer Relatives, and families of hereditary officials
were all confiscated into Wǎlǐ.
The number of households increased,
and thus the old name was restored.
The tents of the Huángtàihòu and Huángtàifēi (Imperial Concubines)
all had various Zhuózhàng Bureaus.

Běimiàn Huángzú Zhàng Guān (Northern Face Officials of the Imperial Clan’s Tents).
Sùzǔ’s eldest son, Qiàhé’s clan, was in the Five Courts Office (Wǔ Yuàn Sī);
his uncle’s son Gělá, youngest son Qiàlǐ, as well as Yìzǔ’s middle son Tièlā, and youngest son Niǎogǔzhí’s clans, were all in the Six Courts Office (Liù Yuàn Sī).
These five lineages
are called the Imperial Clan of the Two Courts (Èr Yuàn Huángzú).
Xuánzǔ’s eldest son, Mǎlǔ, had no heir;
the descendants of his second son, Yánmù, are called the Mèngfù Fáng (Elder Father’s Lineage);
his uncle’s son Shìlǔ is called the Zhòngfù Fáng (Middle Father’s Lineage);
his youngest son became Dézǔ.
Dézǔ’s first son was Tàizǔ Tiān Huángdì (Emperor Tàizǔ),
who is called the Héngzhàng (Horizontal Tent);
the second was Lāgě,
the third Diélā,
the fourth Yīndǐshí,
the fifth Ānduān,
and the sixth Sū,
all called the Jìfù Fáng (Younger Father’s Lineage).
These one tent and three lineages
are called the Imperial Clan of the Four Tents (Sì Zhàng Huángzú).
The Two Courts are governed by the Běi Wáng and Nán Wáng (Northern and Southern Princes);
the Four Tents are governed by the Dànèi Tìyǐn (Tìyǐn of the Great Inner Court),
all under the command of the Dà Tìyǐn Sī (Office of the Grand Tìyǐn).

Northern Imperial Tent Officials
The Three Sovereigns and Holy Sages,
in an era of pristine simplicity,
had double gates and clappers,
even stricter than for violent guests.
The ancestors of the Liáo,
before they had the security of cities, moats, and palaces,
used felt carts as camps,
and fortified stockades as palaces,
so the officials of the Imperial Tent had to be cautious.
Those from the imperial clan served as bodyguards;
Zhùzhàng served as close attendants;
Northern and Southern tribes served as guards;
military officials served as residential guards;
the imperial army served as imperial guards;
and all officials taking turns served as night watchmen.
Fèngchén oversaw imperial provisions;
the Three Divisions ensured solemnity at court assemblies;
and the fortified stockades maintained strictness day and night.
The legal system could be described as strict and meticulous.

Northern Front Zhùzhàng Officials
In ancient times, criminals were not kept by the ruler's side.
The families of rebels were confiscated and made into Zhùzhàng,
serving as imperial guards,
which could make one tremble with fear.
This is perhaps why the Liáo dynasty saw so many disturbances erupt from within.
Zhùzhàng Lángjūn Court.
Yáolián Héndéjīn Kèhán caused the three clans of Púgǔzhǐ and others to be harmed by Yuèshìlǔ,
and their families were confiscated and made into Wǎlǐ.
Yìngtiān Huángtàihòu, who managed state affairs,
separated them out,
making them Zhùzhàng Lángjūn and Niángzǐ,
and always treated them with compassion.
Shìzōng completely pardoned them.
Thereafter, those from the imperial clan, imperial relatives by marriage, and hereditary official families who committed crimes,
were all confiscated and made into Wǎlǐ.
As the number of households increased,
their original name was restored.
