Officials of the Various Northern Tents (Běimiàn Zhūzhàng Guān)
There were three marks of Tàizǔ of Liáo having the magnanimity of a sovereign: first, having replaced the Yáoliǎn clan,
he honored the Nine Tents (Jiǔzhàng) above the Imperial Camp;
this is the first;
second, having destroyed the Bóhǎi Kingdom,
he preserved their clan tents,
placing them second only to the Yáoliǎn;
this is the second;
third, having annexed the multitudes of the Xī King,
he soothed and protected their tent divisions,
treating them similarly to the Imperial Clan (guózú);
this is the third.
There were three marks of his heroic wisdom: appointing the imperial maternal relatives (Guójìu) to balance the Imperial Clan,
elevating the Yǐshì clan to counterbalance the Xī King,
and establishing the Two Courts (Èryuàn) to control the Yáoliǎn—that is all.
Observing the officials of the various Northern Tents,
one can perceive this.
The Grand Chánggǔn Office (Dà Chánggǔn Sī) of the Yáoliǎn Nine Tents.
Manages the palace division affairs of the nine generations of Yáoliǎn Khans: Wā Kèhán, Zǔwǔ Kèhán, Húlà Kèhán, Sū Kèhán, Xiānzhì Kèhán, Zhāogǔ Kèhán,
Yēlán Kèhán, Bālà Kèhán, and Héndéjǐn Kèhán.
Tàizǔ received the throne from the Yáoliǎn,
and placed the Nine Tents above the one tent of the Imperial Clan.
He established the Chánggǔn Office to serve them.
Other officials were not involved in this.
All of Liáo’s Twelve Palaces and Five Capitals,
were gained through conquest and campaigns since Tàizǔ’s time,
they were not inherited from the Yáoliǎn.
The generosity with which he treated the previous dynasty,
could not be surpassed.
According to Liáo custom, they faced East and honored the left.
The Imperial Tent faced East.
The Yáoliǎn Nine Tents faced South.
The Imperial Clan's Three Father Tents faced North.
East and West served as the warp (or longitude),
North and South as the weft (or latitude).
Therefore, the Imperial Camp was called the Transverse Tent (Héngzhàng).

Dominating for over two hundred years,

Emperor Tàizōng selected 300,000 elite armored troops from throughout the land to form the Pìshì Army.
Initially,
Emperor Tàizǔ used the traveling camp as his palace,
and selected over a thousand powerful and vigorous men from various tribes,
establishing them as the Inner Trust Division (Fùxīn Bù).
Yēlǜ Lǎogǔ, based on his merit, became the Right Pìshì Commissioner (Yòu Píshì Xiángwěn).
Thus, the Pìshì Army already existed since the time of Emperor Tàizǔ,
being the Inner Trust Division itself.
Emperor Tàizōng merely increased its number to 300,000.

Huáng Píshì,

Established by Empress Dowager Yìngtiān,

It selected elite troops of both Khitan (Fān) and Han origin,

Northern Border Defense Officials
Liao territory bordered Gāolí to the east,
was a powerful adversary to the six dynasties of Liáng, Táng, Jìn, Hàn, Zhōu, and Sòng to the south,
neighboring Zǔbù and Zhúbùgū to the north,
with a dozen large nations;
and controlled Xīxià, Dǎngxiàng, Tǔhún, Huíhú, etc., to the west,
with hundreds of strong nations.
Situated in a region of four wars,
it held its ground like a crouching tiger,
none daring to provoke it.
This was due to its effective methods of control.
Observing the border defense officials,
the grand ambitions of Tàizǔ and Tàizōng are evident.

The territory of Líao (遼) borders Gāolì (高麗) to the east,
to the south, it was a strong rival to the six dynasties of Liáng (梁), Táng (唐), Jìn (晉), Hàn (漢), Zhōu (周), and Sòng (宋);
to the north, it neighbors Zǔbǔ (阻卜) and Zhúbùgū (朮不姑),
great nations numbering in the tens;
to the west, it controls Xīxià (西夏), Dǎngxiàng (党項), Tǔhún (吐渾), Huíhú (回鶻), and others,
strong nations numbering in the hundreds.
Residing in a region of four-way warfare,
it crouched there like a tiger,
none daring to challenge it;
this was because of its skillful methods of control.
By observing the officials of the border defense,
the grand schemes of Tàizǔ (太祖) and Tàizōng (太宗) are evident.

Northern Marching Officials
According to Liáo regulations for marching officials,
the offices of Pílì Yuàn, Grand Commanders, and Commissioners of Military Affairs
supported each other from top to bottom.
The vanguard and two wings were formidable.
The central army was particularly cautious about distant reconnaissance and scouting.
During battle, heavy responsibility was entrusted to the battle supervisor.
Their duties were regular and
orderly and unhurried,
thus they were the means to victory.

Northern Subject States Officials
According to Liáo system,
officials of subject states and subject tribes,
the greater ones were designated as princely enfeoffments,
the smaller ones were treated as tribal commissioners.
Their chieftains were appointed with distinctions from Qìdān people,
governing with both benevolence and might,
achieving the way of conciliating distant peoples.

Northern Sector Field Army Officials:
In the Liáo Field Army Officials system,
the offices of the Privy Council (*Shūmì*), Supreme Commander (*Dūtǒng*), and Military Commissioner (*Bùshǔ*),
are mutually reinforcing (top and bottom),
the vanguard (*Xiānfēng*) and the two wings are disciplined and formidable,
the Central Army (*Zhōngjūn*) is especially careful regarding long-range scouting and reconnaissance,
and during battle, reliance is placed heavily on the Supervising General (*Jiānzhàn*).
The management of the offices is consistent,
systematically ordered and efficient,
which is the method for achieving victory.

Northern Sector Subject State Officials:
Under the Liáo system,
officials of subject states and subject tribes,
the greatest were designated as princes (*wáng*),
and the lesser were equivalent to tribal commissioners.
Their chiefs were appointed and utilized distinctly from the Qìdān people,
ruling by combining benevolence and might,
thereby obtaining the strategy of conciliating distant peoples.
Those that can be ascertained are listed below.
General List of Titles for Subject States:
Grand Prince (*Dà Wáng*) of State X.
*Yúyuè* of State X.
Left Chancellor (*Zuǒ Xiàng*) of State X.
Right Chancellor (*Yòu Xiàng*) of State X.
*Tìyǐn* of State X.
Also called Minister of Education (*Sītú*).
Grand Preceptor (*Tàishī*) of State X.
Grand Protector (*Tàibǎo*) of State X.
Minister of Works (*Sīkōng*) of State X.
Original name was *Tàlín*.
The Military Governor's Office for Tribe Y of State X.
Military Governor (*Jiédù Shǐ*) for Tribe Y of State X.
Vice Military Governor for Tribe Y of State X.
The *Xiángwěn* Office of State X.
*Xiángwěn* of State X.
Supreme Supervisor (*Dūjiān*) of State X.
General (*Jiāngjūn*) of State X.
Minor General (*Xiǎo Jiāngjūn*) of State X.
Titles for Grand Tribes:
All are the same as for Subject States.

Treatise 17, Part 1: Officialdom Treatise 3, Southern Face.
Qìdān Guó (Khitan State), since Táng Tàizōng established the Dūdu (Commander-in-Chief) and Cìshǐ (Prefect),
Wǔ Hòu (Empress Wǔ) added the title of royal enfeoffment (Wáng fēng),
Xuánzōng established the Jīnglüè Shǐ (Commissioner of Military and Civil Affairs),
and then they first received Táng official ranks and titles.
Thereafter, they habitually heard that the regional military governors (Fānzhèn) in Héběi received Táng official titles,
and consequently, the Tàishī (Grand Tutor), Tàibǎo (Grand Guardian), Sītú (Minister of the Masses), and Sīkōng (Minister of Works) were applied to the tribes.
Tàizǔ followed this practice.
In Dàtóng First Year (947 CE),
Shìzōng first established the Běi Yuàn Shūmì Shǐ (Commissioner of the Northern Chancellery of Military Affairs).
The following year,
Shìzōng appointed Gāo Xūn as Nán Yuàn Shūmì (Commissioner of the Southern Chancellery of Military Affairs).
Thus, the establishment of the Shūmì (Chancellery),
must have begun when Tàizōng entered Biàn (Kaifeng).
In Tiānlù Fourth Year (950 CE),
the Zhèngshì Shěng (Department of Governmental Affairs) was founded.
Therefore, the officials of the Southern Administration can be recorded.
In the beginning,
the Hàn Rén Shūmì Yuàn (Chancellery of Military Affairs for Han Chinese) concurrently managed the Shàngshū Shěng (Department of State Affairs).
The Offices of Personnel, Military, and Justice had Chéngzhǐ (Receivers of the Edict).
The Offices of Revenue and Works had Zhǔshì (Principals).
The Zhōngshū Shěng (Central Secretariat) concurrently managed the Lǐbù (Ministry of Rites).
There was also a separate Hùbù Shǐ Sī (Bureau of the Commissioner of Revenue).
Using the territory of Yíngzhōu plus half of Yōu and Jì (Provinces),
this arrangement was just sufficient.
In the middle period, officialdom flourished.
Yēlǜ Yángliù served as Tàifù (Grand Tutor),
signifying the existence of the Sānshī (Three Tutors).
Hūgǔ Zhì served as Tàiwèi (Grand Commandant),
signifying the existence of the Sāngōng (Three Dukes).
Yūwògǔdé served as Chángshì (Gentleman-in-Attendance),
Liú Jīng served as Lǐbù Shàngshū (Minister of Rites),
signifying the existence of the Ménxià Shěng (Chancellery) and Shàngshū Shěng (Department of State Affairs).
Kùbù (Storage Department), Yúbù (Forestry Department), and Cāngbù (Granary Department) had external mission officials (Yuán Wài Chū Shǐ),
signifying that the roster of Lángguān (Secretaries) and official posts was complete.
Shì Fǎng oversaw compilation,
signifying that the Guóshǐ (National History) had a bureau.
Chéng Zhù was a Shèrén (Secretarial Aide),
signifying that the Qǐjū Zhù (Diaries of Activity and Repose) existed.
Xíng Bàopǔ was a Chéngzhǐ (Receiver of the Edict),
Wáng Yánfū was an Xuéshì (Academician),
signifying the existence of the Hànlín Nèizhì (Inner Edicts of the Hanlin Academy).
Zhāng Gān was a Zhèngshì Shèrén (Secretarial Aide of Governmental Affairs),
signifying the existence of the Zhōngshū Wàizhì (External Edicts of the Central Secretariat).
The Dàlǐ (Court of Judicial Review) and Sīnóng (Court of the Imperial Granaries) had Qīng (Ministers),
the Guózǐ (Directorate of Education) and Shǎofǔ (Court of the Imperial Treasury) had Jiān (Directors),
thus the Jiǔ Qīng (Nine Ministers) and various Jiān (Directors) were present.
The Jīnwú (Guards of the Capital) and Qiānniú (Oxen Guards) had Dàjiàng (Generals),
thus the Shíliù Liè Wèi (Sixteen Divisions of Guards) were present.
The Tàizǐ (Crown Prince) had Shībǎo (Tutors and Guardians) above him,
and Fǔshuài (Commandants of the Guard) below him,
meaning the Dōng Gōng (Eastern Palace/Crown Prince's establishment) was fully staffed.
Jiédù (Military Commissioner), Guānchá (Investigating Commissioner), Fángyù (Defense Commissioner), Tuánliàn (Militia Commissioner), and Cìshǐ (Prefect),
all existed in the regional circuits (Fāng Zhōu),
following the Táng system.
All Táng official posts that can be verified and seen,
are listed in detail in this section;
those without evidence are not recorded.
Southern Administration Court Officials
Liáo already had Běi Miàn Cháo Guān (Northern Administration Court Officials),
but having obtained the Sixteen Prefectures of Yān and Dài,
they then utilized the Táng system,

and re-established the officials of the Southern Administration, including the Sān Shěng (Three Departments), Liù Bù (Six Ministries), Tái (Censorate), Yuàn (Courts), Sì (Courts), Jiān (Directorates), various Wèi (Guards), and Dōng Gōng (Eastern Palace).
They sincerely intended to emulate the grand systems of emperors and kings,
and also to attract people from the Central Plains (Zhōngguó).
The Residence of the Sānshī (Three Tutors).
Originally named Sāngōng (Three Dukes).
The Hàn Dynasty designated the Chéngxiàng (Chancellor), Tàiwèi (Grand Commandant), and Yùshǐ Dàfū (Grandee Secretary) as the Sāngōng.
Therefore, they were called the Sānshī.

Tàibǎo (Grand Protector).
In Huìtóng First Year (938 CE), Liú Xù served as Shǒu Tàibǎo (Acting Grand Protector).

Shàobǎo (Junior Protector).

during the Zhòngxī period, was the keeper of the seal for the Tàibǎo.
The Residence of the Sāngōng (Three Dukes).
The Former Hàn had the Chéngxiàng, Tàiwèi, and Yùshǐ Dàfū.
The Later Hàn changed the names to Dà Sītú (Grand Minister of the Masses), Dà Sīmǎ (Grand Minister of War), and Dà Sīkōng (Grand Minister of Works).
The Táng had Tàiwèi, Sītú, and Sīkōng.
They were also called Sānsī (Three Offices).
Tàiwèi (Grand Commandant).
In Tàizōng's Tiānxiǎn Eleventh Year (936 CE), Tàiwèi Zhào Sīwēn is recorded.
Sītú (Minister of the Masses).
In Shìzōng's Tiānlù First Year (947 CE), Sītú Huà Shè is recorded.
Sīkōng (Minister of Works).
In Shèngzōng's Tǒnghé Thirtieth Year (1012 CE), Sīkōng Xíng Bàozhì is recorded.
The Hàn Rén Shūmì Yuàn (Chancellery of Military Affairs for Han Chinese).
Its original function belonged to the Bīngbù (Ministry of War).
In the Zhōu Dynasty, it was the Dà Sīmǎ (Grand Minister of War).
In the Hàn Dynasty, it was the Tàiwèi.
In the late Táng period, palace eunuchs were influential.
The Shūmì Yuàn was established internally.
Later, it was changed to be staffed by scholars.
It was abolished during the Tiānfú period of the Jìn Dynasty,
and re-established in Kāiyùn First Year (944 CE).
Tàizǔ initially had the Hàn'ér Sī (Bureau for Han People).
Hán Zhīgǔ comprehensively managed the affairs of the Hàn'ér Sī.
When Tàizōng entered Biàn,
he consequently established the Shūmì Yuàn following the Jìn precedent,
managing the administration of the Han Chinese military,
and initially concurrently handling the Shàngshū Shěng.

In Tàizōng's Dàtóng First Year (947 CE), Shūmì Shǐ Lǐ Sōng is recorded.

Treatise 17, Part 2: Treatise on Officials 4: Southern-Facing Metropolitan Officials (Nánmiàn Jīngguān)
The Liáo had five capitals (Jīng).
Shàngjīng (Supreme Capital) was the Imperial Capital (Huángdū);
all court officials (Cháoguān) and metropolitan officials (Jīngguān) were established there.
In the remaining four capitals, officials were established as deemed appropriate,
and the system was not uniform.
Generally, Xījīng (Western Capital) had many border defense officials,
while Nánjīng (Southern Capital) and Zhōngjīng (Central Capital) had many fiscal and revenue officials.
Those (offices) established concurrently in all five capitals
are listed (in groups).
Those specifically established (in only one or some capitals)
are listed separately afterward.

Officials of the Fāngzhōu (Square Prefectures) in the Southern Division:
Liáodōng and Xī,
Yān, Qín, Hàn, and Táng had already established Commanderies and Districts,
and set up official posts.
Gāolì and Bóhǎi followed this system.
By the time of the Liáo,
the Five Capitals stood in array,
encompassing Yān and Dài,
all becoming the capital region (Jīdiàn).
For over two hundred years,
walls and ramparts faced each other,
and the fields and wilderness were increasingly cultivated.
They were headed by Jiédù (Military Governors),
followed by Guānchá (Inspectors), Fángyù (Defenders), Tuánliàn (Militia), and other Commissioners,
and subdivided by Cìshǐ (Prefects) and Xiànlìng (District Magistrates).
Generally, they adopted the Táng system.
During this time, the Imperial Clan, maternal relatives, and high ministers built cities and were granted plaques,
which were called
"Tóuxià Zhōujūn" (Feudal Prefecture/Garrison under a Noble's Jurisdiction);
only the Jiédù Shǐ were appointed by the court,
but later they frequently all reverted to the royal households.
Places too small to be a Zhōu (Prefecture) were called Jūn (Garrisons),
places too small to be a Xiàn (District) were called Chéng (Cities),
and places too small to be a Chéng were called Bǎo (Forts).
The establishment of officials in these places is not detailed.

The subordinate counties of the prefectures in the Five Capitals [Circuits]
are found in the Geography Treatise (Dìlǐ Zhì).

The county had various services (yì) such as courier stations (yìdì), horse and cattle management (mǎniú), flag and drum duties (qígǔ), village heads (xiāngzhèng), office attendants (tīnglì), and granary officials (cāngsī).
When people became bankrupt and could not supply these services,
the common people suffered from this.
Mǎ Rénwàng devised a method
allowing the people to pay money to be exempted from these services,
and the officials themselves hired people [to perform the duties].
Granary officials were given attendants to be paid for by public funds.
People considered this convenient.
Southern Administration Judicial Officials (Nánmiàn Fēnsī Guān)
were responsible for fairly administering general prisons,
and collecting information on the people's hidden grievances.
Since the Hàn and Táng dynasties,
wise rulers considered this a standard law for showing compassion to the people.
The position was not permanently established;
upon imperial decree,
officials with talent and reputation would be selected for it.
Commissioner for Separately Adjudicating Stalled Cases in Various Circuits (Fēn Jué Zhū Dào Zhì Yù Shǐ).
In the ninth year of Tǒnghé (991) of Shèngzōng,
Xíng Bàopǔ and five other officials were appointed,
and Mǎ Shǒuyīng and three other officials were also appointed,
to separately adjudicate stalled cases throughout the various circuits.
Commissioner for Inspecting Penal Cases in Various Circuits (Ànchá Zhū Dào Xíng Yù Shǐ).
In the fifth year of Kāitài (1016), Liú Jīng and others were dispatched to various routes to inspect penal cases.

Southern Administration Financial Officials (Nánmiàn Cáifù Guān)
The Liáo state relied on animal husbandry, agriculture, and fishing for its livelihood.
The financial offices
were initially very simple.
Since Nièlǐ taught farming and weaving,
the profits from salt, iron, and other sources grew daily.
After acquiring Yān and Dài [regions],
they became even more wealthy and prosperous.

Southern Administration Military Officials (Nánmiàn Jūnguān)
The commentary says:
"Though Chǔ has talent,
Jìn does indeed use it."
Since Tàizǔ, the Liáo,
in their attacks and raids on the territories of the Five Dynasties and Sòng,
acquired their people,
and promptly employed them.
In the two regions, East and North,
they were employed in agriculture and industry,
and when there was a military matter, they followed the military administration.
This was an excellent strategy.

The broad and lenient civilizing influence of the Sān Huáng and Wǔ Dì,
extended to the Hàn and Táng dynasties.
Loving life and abhorring killing,
custom became nature.
Even during the extreme chaos of the Five Dynasties,
only a few were accustomed to warfare.
The Sòng dynasty prevailed through culture,
yet Liáo's frontier defense was still more important on the southern front,
simply because of its vast territory and large population.
In the end, [they] befriended benevolent neighbors,
and the war drums were silent for nearly two hundred years.
This is perhaps what made the Liáo dynasty admirable.

Monograph XVIII: Rites I
Principles are established by Heaven,
emotions arise from human life.
By controlling emotions with principles,
the function of rites and music is enacted.
Forest wildcats and badger dogs,
gave rise to the suburban sacrifices and ancestral rites;
hollowed-out gourds and roasted millet,
gave rise to banquets;
bamboo sieves and earthenware coffins,
gave rise to funerals;
pairs of skins and black cloth,
gave rise to marriages and capping ceremonies.
The creation of emperors and the order of divinities,
were further refined by the Three Kings.
Alternating between refinement and simplicity,
indeed, has its root in sincerity.
Adapting to change and rectifying abuses,
it should conform to the times.
Only the sage can fully comprehend its meaning.
Those who cling to principles rigidly dispute endlessly,
not suiting human emotions;
those who yield to emotions produce mere chaff and weeds,
not aligning with heavenly principles.
From Qín and Hàn downwards,
the superior man finds no value in them.
Liáo originally was the old territory of Cháoxiǎn,
the eight articles of instruction of Jīzǐ,
its lingering customs and traditions,
likely still persisted.
From its ancient past,
adapting measures to suit emotions,
subtly there was a style that esteemed simplicity.
Yáoniǎn Húlà Khān established the Mountain Sacrifice Ceremony,
Sū Khān established the Sèsè Ceremony,
Zǔwǔ Khān established the Wood Register and Regeneration Ceremony.
Their emotions were simple,
their application frugal.
Respecting Heaven and showing concern for disasters,
extending benevolence based on filial piety,
originating from sincere devotion,
perhaps gained something beyond the rigid disputes.
In the remotest antiquity,
the rudimentary Five Rites,
how were they different from this?
When Tàizōng conquered Jìn,
he gradually adopted Hàn rites.
Currently, the National History Institute has Jīn Chén Dàrèn's Monograph on Liáo Rites,
which details its national customs,
and there are also miscellaneous Liáo dynasty rites,
many of which are Hàn ceremonies.
Another volume obtained from the Xuānwén Gé is Yēlǜ Yǎn's Monograph,
which is more detailed than Dàrèn's.
A summary is preserved,
and recorded in this chapter.

Treatise 18: Treatise on Rites I
Principle (Lǐ) is established by Heaven;
Emotion (Qíng) is born from man.
When principle governs emotion,
then the function of rites and music is practiced.
From the jackals of the forest and the badgers of the ravines,
arose the suburban and ancestral sacrifices;
From hollowed gourds and roasted millet,
arose feasts and banquets;
From straw mats and earthenware coffins,
arose funerals and burials;
From matched hides and black fabrics,
arose marriage and capping ceremonies.
The August ones created, and the Emperors arranged;
The Three Kings further refined them (Míwén).
One generation refined, the next was simple,
all fundamentally based on loyalty (Zhōng).
Changing and adapting, reforming abuses,
they were adjusted to fit the times.
Only the sage could truly grasp their intent.
Those who clung to principle were like adjusting a zither's pegs too tightly or engaging in endless legal disputes,
which did not suit human feelings;
Those who followed emotion were like tares and weeds, or grass mats,
which did not align with heavenly principle.
From the Qín and Hàn onward,
the noble-minded had little regard for them.
Liáo was originally the old territory of Cháoxiǎn (Joseon).
The eight articles of teaching by Jīzǐ,
their lingering customs and remaining habits,
perhaps still survived there.
From the time of their ancestors,
they established regulations based on natural feelings,
implicitly holding a tradition that favored simplicity (shàngzhì).
Yáoliǎn Húlà Kèhán established the rite for sacrificing to the mountains;
Sū Kèhán established the Sèsè Rite;
Zǔwǔ Kèhán established the Càicè and Regrowth Rite.
Their feelings were simple (pǔ),
their practices economical (jiǎn).
Revering Heaven and showing concern for calamities,
bestowing kindness based on filial piety,
coming from sincerity and earnestness (kǔnchén),
they perhaps achieved something beyond the constraint of adjusting a zither's pegs too tightly and endless legal disputes.
In the highest antiquity,
the rudimentary wheel and the Five Rites—
how were they different from this?
When Tàizōng conquered the Jìn,
he gradually adopted Hàn rites.
The National History Institute now possesses the "Treatise on Liáo Rites and Ceremonies" by Jīn Chén Dàrèn,
which covers the old customs of their state;
there is also "Miscellaneous Liáo Court Rites,"
where Hàn ceremonies predominate.
Separately, we obtained the treatise by Yēlǜ Yǎn preserved in the Xuānwén Gé,
which is more detailed than Dàrèn's work.
We present a summary of its contents
in this chapter.
Auspicious Rites
Mountain Worship Ceremony: The positions of the heavenly deities (Tiānshén) and earthly spirits (Dìzhī) are set up on Mùyèshān,
facing east.
A sovereign tree (jūnshù) is erected in the center,
with a cluster of trees planted in front,
to symbolize the court assembly.
Additionally, two trees are planted in pairs,
to serve as the spirit gate (shénmén).
When the emperor (Huángdì) and empress (Huánghòu) arrive,
the Yílíbì (夷離畢) prepares the ritual.
The sacrificial animals are a reddish-white horse, a black ox, and a reddish-white sheep,
all male.
The servant official, called Qígǔ Zhuàilá (旗鼓拽剌),
slaughters the animals,
carves the bodies,
and hangs them on the sovereign tree.
The Grand Shaman (Tàiwū) libates the animals with wine.
The ritual official, called Dílièmádū (敵烈麻都),
announces,
"The ceremony is complete."
The emperor wears a golden crown with golden patterns,
a white damask robe,
a crimson belt,
a hanging fish ornament,
three crimson tassels hanging from a mountain pattern,
decorated with rhinoceros horn and jade knives and whetstones,
and black boots with embroidered seams.
The empress wears a crimson skirt (or similar garment indicated by the ● character),
a red robe with embroidered seams,
a hanging jade pendant,
a double-knotted headscarf,
and black boots with embroidered seams.
The emperor and empress ride on saddled horses.
The officials stand to the south,
and the court ladies (mìngfù) to the north,
wearing the colors of their respective tribal banners.
The emperor and empress dismount in front of the sovereign tree,
ascend the southern altar, and sit on the imperial couch (yùtà).
The officials and court ladies arrange themselves in their respective ranks,
entering in order to take their positions;
they form a combined rank,
bow,
and return to their places.
The emperor and empress proceed to the positions of the heavenly deities (Tiānshén) and earthly spirits (Dìzhī),
and offer libations.
After the Héménshǐ (閤門使) finishes reading the prayer,
they return to their seats.
The Northern Chancellor (Běifǔ Zǎixiàng) and Tìyǐn (惕隱) then offer libations to the sovereign tree,
and then to all the cluster of trees.
Music plays.
The officials and court ladies withdraw.
The emperor, leading the clans of the Mèngfù (孟父), Zhòngfù (仲父), and Jìfù (季父),
circles the spirit gate trees three times.
Other clans circle seven times.
The emperor and empress bow twice,
and all those present also bow twice.
Incense is offered,
and they bow twice as before.
The emperor and empress ascend the altar,
and sit on a square cushion with a dragon pattern (lóngwén fāngyīn).
A warning is sounded twice,
and they proceed to the eastern place of sacrifice.
The officials and court ladies follow,
arranged in ranks as before.
The shaman (wū) wears white robes,
and the Tìyǐn (惕隱) bows and places a plain scarf (sùjīn) on his head.
The shaman delivers three addresses.
With each address,
the emperor and empress bow once,
and all those present also bow once.
The emperor and empress each offer two goblets of wine
and two dishes of meat,
making a second libation.
The ministers and court ladies, holding one dish of wine in their right hand
and one dish of meat in their left,
stand slightly behind,
and make one libation.
The Tìyǐn (惕隱) is instructed to throw them eastward.
The emperor and empress bow six times,
and all those present also bow six times.
The emperor and empress return to their positions,
and sit.
The Cáo Zhōngchéng (中丞) is ordered to present tea and fruit,
and two dishes each of cakes and pastries,
offering them to the positions of the heavenly deities (Tiānshén) and earthly spirits (Dìzhī).
Twenty Zhíshì Lángjūn (執事郎君) carrying auspicious wine (fújǐu) and sacrificial meat (zuòròu)
proceed before the emperor and empress.
After the Grand Shaman (Tàiwū) completes the libation,
the emperor and empress bow twice,
and all those present also bow twice.
The emperor and empress bow once,
drink the auspicious wine,
receive the sacrificial meat,
return to their positions,
and sit.
Those present drink in turn.
The emperor and empress lead the officials back to their ranks,
and bow twice.
A warning is sounded,
and they bow once.
They withdraw.
Tàizōng (太宗) visited the Dàbēigé (大悲閣) in Yōuzhōu (幽州),
moved the statue of the White-Robed Guānyīn (Báiyī Guānyīn),
built a temple on Mùyèshān,
and revered her as a household deity (jiāshén).
After the tree-circling part of the Mountain Worship Ceremony,
a section
"Proceeding to the Bodhisattva Hall Ceremony" (Yì Púsàtáng Yí)
was added,
after which the deities were worshipped.
This was not due to Húlà Kèhán (胡剌可汗).
Xīngzōng (興宗) first conducted ceremonies at the Bodhisattva Hall and for the deities of Mùyèshān
and the Liáohé (遼河),
and then performed the Mountain Worship Ceremony.
The crowns, robes, and ritual procedures were greatly changed,
and later became the norm.
Deities residing in trees,
the display of sacrificed animals announcing completion,
ritual positions for libations and prayers,
and the offering of blessings and drinking of auspicious wine
often coincidentally aligned with proper rites.
The principles of Heaven and human sentiment
are applicable universally
and truly so.
The reforms of Xīngzōng (興zōng),
not being based on canonical scholarship,
could not significantly surpass the past,
and therefore are not recorded.
Sèsè Ceremony: If there is a drought,
an auspicious day is chosen to perform the Sèsè Ceremony (Sèsè Yí) to pray for rain.
Before the day,
a hundred-pillar heavenly canopy (bǎizhù tiānpéng) is erected.
On the day itself,
the emperor offers libations to the imperial portraits of the former emperors (Xiāndì Yùróng),
and then shoots arrows at a willow.
The emperor shoots twice,
and the imperial princes (qīnwáng) and grand councilors (zǎizhí) each shoot once in turn.
Those who hit the willow stake their robes and hats,
while those who miss stake their robes and hats.
The loser offers a drink to the winner,
and then each reclaims their robes and hats.
The next day,
a willow is planted southeast of the heavenly canopy.
Shamans (wū) offer wine,
millet, and coarse grain to the planted willow,
and pray to it.
After the emperor and empress finish sacrificing to the east,
their children shoot arrows at the willow.
Imperial clan members (huángzú), maternal uncles of the emperor (guójìu), officials, and participants in the ceremony
are given gifts according to their rank.
If it rains for three days,
the Dílièmádū (敵烈麻都) is granted four horses and four sets of clothing;
otherwise, he is doused with water.
In the first year of Qīngníng (清寧) of Dàozōng (道宗),
after the emperor finished shooting the willow,
he proceeded to the Altar of the Wind Master (Fēngshī Tán),
and bowed twice.
The Ritual of Cháicè: Select an auspicious day.
Before that time,
the Cháicè Hall and the altar are set up.
Regarding the construction of the altar:
Firewood is piled up thickly,
a three-tiered altar made of wood is constructed,
and placed atop the firewood.
A felt rug one hundred *chǐ* is spread out,
and a square cushion patterned with dragons is placed.
Furthermore, the Chamber for the Rebirth and Search of the Empress Dowager is set up.
The Huángdì enters the Chamber of Rebirth,
and after the Ritual of Rebirth is completed,
the elders of the Eight Tribes lead in front and escort behind,
supporting the Huángdì on the left and right to the northeast corner of the Hall of the Charter.
After the bowing to the sun is completed,
he mounts a horse,
selecting an elder from the maternal relatives to drive the chariot.
The Huángdì gallops quickly,
falls,
and the driver and attendants cover him with felt.
The Huángdì proceeds to high ground.
The high ministers and the commanders of the various tribes line up the honor guards,
and bow from afar while gazing upon him.
The Huángdì dispatches an envoy with a decree, which states:
“The Xiāndì has ascended far away (passed away).
Since uncles, elder cousins, and elder brothers are present,
we ought to select a worthy person.
This youth is without virtue.
What plan shall be made?”
The assembled ministers reply, saying:
“Your subjects rely on the profound grace of the Xiāndì,
and Your Majesty’s brilliant virtue.
All of us are willing to devote our hearts entirely;
how would we dare to harbor any other plans?”
The Huángdì issues an order, saying:
“If I must comply with what you desire,
I shall faithfully and clearly administer rewards and punishments.
If you have merit,
I shall promote and employ you;
if you have committed a crime,
I shall dismiss and abandon you.
If you heed my command,
then we shall proceed with the plan.”
All assent, saying:
“We will follow only the command of the Dì.”
The Huángdì, at the recognizable spot,
piles up earth and stones to mark it.
He then proceeds.
He bows before the imperial portrait of the Xiāndì,
and feasts the assembled ministers.
The next day,
the Huángdì leaves the Hall of the Charter.
The Hùwèi Tàibǎo supports him as he ascends the altar.
The spirit tablets of the Seven Ancestral Temples are reverently placed upon the square cushion patterned with dragons.
The Zǎixiàng of the Northern and Southern Prefectures lead the assembled ministers to stand in a circle.
Each raises the edge of the felt rug.
After the invocation and prayers are completed,
the Shūmìshǐ reverently brings in the Jade Seal and the Jade Charter.
After the appropriate official reads the charter,
the Shūmìshǐ announces the esteemed title and presents it.
The assembled ministers call out three times,
“Wànsuì,”
and all bow.
The Zǎixiàng, the Dàwáng of the Northern and Southern Courts, and the commanders of the various tribes present one flock each of reddish-brown sheep and white sheep.
The Huángdì changes clothes,
and bows before the imperial portraits of the various Dì.
Thereupon, he feasts the assembled ministers;
gifts and rewards are bestowed according to various ranks.
The Ritual of Bowing to the Sun: The Huángdì ascends the uncovered terrace.
A rug is laid out.
Facing the sun, he bows twice,
and offers incense.
The Gate Keeper announces the arrival.
The Gěshǐ, or his deputy, and the officials who should participate in the bowing stand on the steps to the left and right of the hall as accompanying ranks,
and bow twice.
The Huángdì ascends to his seat.
After the memorial tablet is presented,
and the Northern Rank completes the salutations,
the Shíxiàng and those below announce their names and bow twice.
Without leaving their ranks,
they memorialize,
“May the Sagely Person be blessed with Wànfú,”
and bow twice again,
then each awaits orders respectfully.
The Xuānhuī and those below, standing in horizontal ranks, do the same.
The various Bureaus, the Gěmén, and those facing North first present their affairs;
the rest is the same.
The Jiàofāng performs the same as the officials.
The Ritual of Announcement at the Temple: Upon the designated day,
the officials, wearing court robes, arrive before dawn,
and proceed to the Tàizǔ Temple.
Next, the officials are ushered in.
They consolidate their ranks,
first viewing the imperial portrait.
After bowing twice,
the rank leader is ushered to the left and up,
to the position of the rug,
and bows twice.
The announcer prompts the offering of incense.
After bowing inside the railing and offering incense,
they return to the position of the rug,
and bow twice.
Each stands respectfully and still.
The attendants on the left and right raise the announcement plaque for the temple,
and kneel to hold it before the imperial portrait.
The Zhōngshū Shèrén kneels forward,
finishes reading,
rises forward,
and retires.
The rank leader is ushered down to the left,
returns to his original position,
and bows twice again.
They are ushered separately up to the hall,
and successively present wine three times.
They are ushered out in separate ranks.
The Ritual of Visiting the Temple: Upon the designated day, before dawn,
the officials of the Northern and Southern Administrations each prepare their court robes,
and proceed to the temple.
When the imperial carriage arrives,
the officials stand outside the gate according to their rank order,
and bow toward the carriage.
The rank leader does not leave the rank,
but memorializes,
“May the Sagely Person be blessed with Wànfú.”
After the Shèrén announces for everyone to stand respectfully,
the Huángdì descends from the carriage.
The officials of the Northern and Southern Administrations are ushered in separately to the left and right,
reaching the rug position on the Dānchí.
The ranks consolidate and settle.
The Huángdì ascends to the rug position on the uncovered terrace.
The Xuānhuī prompts the Huángdì to bow twice.
The accompanying officials both inside and outside the hall all bow twice.
After the offering of incense is completed,
they retire,
return to their positions,
and bow twice.
The officials are ushered separately to the left and right to stand in position on the hall.
The wine is offered before the imperial portrait according to regular rites.
If they retire immediately,
they bow twice.
The Shèrén prompts,
“Hǎo qù” (A safe journey),
and they are ushered out.
The rite is completed.
Gàomiào and Yèmiào,
are both called Bowing to the Portrait (Bàiróng).
Performing this rite on the birthdays and death anniversaries (jìchén) of the Xiāndì and the previous Empresses,
began with Tàizōng.
Thereafter, it was performed on the New Year (Zhèngdàn),
the Huángdì’s birthday, and all festival days.
If it is the death anniversary or if the imperial carriage is traveling (xíngxìng),
an envoy is also sometimes sent to perform the rite.
Generally, the rituals of Sèsè, Cháicè, and Rebirth,
and receiving the Empress (Nàhòu), are performed personally by the ruler.
Generally, for Cháicè or personal military campaigns (Qīnzhēng), the Announcement is made (gào);
when visiting the various Capitals (xìng zhū jīng), the Visit is made (yè).
In the four seasons, new offerings are presented.
The Ritual of Bowing at the Mausoleum on the First Day of the First Winter Month (Mèngdōng Shuò Bàilíng Yí): Officials prepare wine and food at the mountain mausoleum.
When the Huángdì and Huánghòu arrive by carriage,
the Dílièmádū reports,
“The rites are prepared.”
The Gěménshǐ prompts the Huángdì and Huánghòu to proceed to their positions and bow four times.
The shaman prompts the offering of prayers, the burning of sacrificial meat and seasonal clothing,
the pouring of libations, and the presentation of sacrificial animals.
High ministers
and court ladies burn the sacrificial meat in sequence,
and bow four times.
The Huángdì and Huánghòu lead the assembled ministers and court ladies,
to circle around the various mausoleums three times each.
They return to the palace.
The next day,
the assembled ministers enter to offer thanks.
The Ritual of Burning the Tally (Ruòjié Yí): When the Huángdì ascends the throne,
wherever rebellious states are campaigned against and their people captured,
or when subjects present population figures,
or when households forfeit their property due to crime,
the Huángdì personally inspects the available fields,
establishes prefectures and counties to house them,
and sets up officials to administer their affairs.
When the Dì passes away,
the households, official treasuries (fǔkù), money, and grain thus established,
are placed inside a small felt hall (zhàndiàn) within a yurt (qiónglú).
Golden statues of the Dì and the empresses and concubines (hòufēi) are cast and placed therein.
On festival days (jiéchén), death anniversaries, and the new and full moon (shuòwàng),
sacrifices are offered before the yurt.
Furthermore, a platform of earth is built,
more than ten *zhàng* high.
A large basin is placed on top.
The sacrificial wine and food are sprinkled into it,
and then burnt.
The custom of the state calls this *Ruòjié*.
Year-End Ceremony (Suì Chú Yí): On the evening before,
the imperial envoy (chì shǐ) and the Yílìbì led the attendant officers (zhí shì láng jūn) to the front of the hall,
placing salt and sheep fat in a brazier to burn it.
When the shamans (wū) and Grand Shamans (dà wū) had successively completed the prayers and praises to the Fire God (Huǒ Shén),
the Palace Gate Envoy (Gě Mén Shǐ) assisted the Emperor in facing the fire and performing two bows.
Originally,
the Emperors all bowed personally.
It was not until Emperor Dàozōng that the Yílìbì was first ordered to perform the bow.
Treatise 19, Ritual Treatises 2: Ominous Rites (Xiōng Yí)
Funeral and Interment Rites (Sāng Zàng Yí): When Emperor Shèngzōng died,
Emperor Xīngzōng wept and oversaw the rites (kū lín) at the Zōutú Hall.
When the fourth watch of the evening of the Great Departed finished,
the Emperor led the officials inside,
offering three libations before the coffin.
The coffin was borne out through the northwest gate of the hall,
placed upon the warm carriage (wēn liáng chē),
and covered with a plain mat.
Shamans performed purification rites (bá chú).
The next morning,
the procession departed.
Upon reaching the sacrificial place,
five libations in total were offered.
The Grand Shaman (tài wū) performed prayers and exorcisms (qí ráng).
The imperial clan (huáng zú), maternal relatives (wài qī), high ministers (dà chén), and officials from the various capitals (zhū jīng guān) offered sacrifices in turn.
Then, objects such as clothing, bows and arrows, saddles and bridles, paintings, horses and camels, and ceremonial guards (yí wèi) were all burned.
Arriving at the imperial tomb (shān líng),
after the interment was completed,
the Lamentation Scroll (āi cè) was presented.
The Emperor proceeded to the tent (yù wò),
ordered the changing of the fire (gǎi huǒ),
faced the fire and offered libations,
bowing three times.
Then, facing east,
and having performed two bows to Heaven and Earth,
he mounted his horse,
led those escorting the funeral procession past the wooden gate of the Spirit Gate (Shén Mén), and then dismounted.
Facing east, he bowed twice more.
On the morning of the following day,
he led the officials and the imperial ladies (mìng fù) to the imperial tomb,
performing the rite of the First Libation (chū diàn).
He ascended the Imperial Portrait Hall (Yù Róng Diàn),
and received the bequests (yí cì).
On the day after that,
the Second Libation (zài diàn) was performed as before.
When Emperor Xīngzōng died,
Emperor Dàozōng personally selected the site for the interment.
When Emperor Dàozōng died,
the corpse was temporarily placed (zōu tú) in the Yóuxiān Hall,
and the relevant officials presented the mourning attire.
Emperor Tiānzuò inquired about the rites from Yēlǜ Gù, the Director of the Hanlin Academy (Zǒng Zhī Hànlín Yuàn Shì).
He then began wearing the coarse hemp mourning garb (zhǎn cuī);
the imperial clan, maternal relatives, Envoys-Chancellor (shǐ xiàng), the Àiduān officials, and the officers (láng jūn) wore the same;
the remaining officials and attendants (chéng yìng rén) entered wearing white hemp garments and head coverings,
and performed the weeping oversight (kū lín).

The Tìyǐn, the Three Patriarchal Families (Sān Fù Fáng), the Chancellor of the Southern Administration (Nán Fǔ Zǎi Xiàng), the Yáoliǎn Chánggǔn, the officers of the Nine Xī Leaders (Jiǔ Xī Shǒu Láng Jūn), the Yílìbì, the Maternal Uncle Xiángwěn (Guójiù Xiángwěn), the officers of the Ten Zhásà (Shí Zhásà Láng Jūn), the Prince of the Southern Chancery (Nán Yuàn Dà Wáng), and the officers (láng jūn),
each offered sacrifices and libations in sequence,
presenting objects such as saddled horses, clothing, rhinoceros horn and jade belts (xī yù dài),
listing the quantity on a memorial (biǎo).
After reading it,
the memorial was burned.
The ritual vessels and clothing sent as funeral gifts (fù) by various kingdoms,
and the libations, sacrifices, and presentation of funeral gifts by the Imperial Princes (qīn wáng) and the Defenders (liú shǒu) of the various capitals, were handled similarly.
The day before the Former Emperor's Minor Encoffining (xiǎo liǎn),
the Emperor, in mourning attire, offered incense,
offered wine libations,
and performed the weeping oversight.
That night,
the Commissioner of Military Affairs of the Northern Chancery (Běi Yuàn Shūmì Shǐ) and the Grand Commissioner of the Khitan Traveling Palace (Qìdān Xínggōng Dū Bùshǔ) entered,
and performed the Minor Encoffining.
The following day,
the Vice Commissioner of Military Affairs of the Northern Chancery (Běi Yuàn Shūmì Fù Shǐ) and the Línyá were dispatched,
to place the received funeral vessels and clothing
inside the tomb chamber (yōu gōng).
When the spiritual coffin (líng jiù) was raised onto the carriage,
the Imperial Princes pushed it,
until it reached the station of Eating the Ram (shí gǔ zhī cì).
This was based on the old custom of the Liáo State,
where a ram was slaughtered here for sacrifice.
The imperial clan, maternal relatives, and officials from the various capitals and prefectures offered sacrifices in turn.
Upon reaching the burial site,
the spiritual coffin was lowered from the carriage,
and placed on the pallbearer's carriage (jū).
The Emperor removed his mourning attire,
and led the procession on foot to the embankment of the longevity tomb (cháng fú kān).
That evening,
the Emperor entered the mausoleum,
distributed the bequests to the imperial clan, maternal relatives, and various high ministers,
and then exited.
He ordered that the Former Emperor’s sleeping tent (qǐn wò)
be taken past the wooden gate of the Spirit Gate in front of the mausoleum.
The Emperor did not go personally,
but sent an attendant (jìn shì) in official dress to attend.
For the First Libation (chū diàn),

the Emperor and Empress led the imperial clan, maternal relatives, Envoys-Chancellor (shǐ xiàng), Military Commissioners (jié dù shǐ), and imperial ladies ranking Fūrén and above, to all perform bows and sacrifices.
They circled the tomb three times before descending.
For the Second Libation (zài diàn),
it was performed as before.
They took leave of the mausoleum and returned.
Ceremony for Presenting the Posthumous Name Scroll (Shàng Shì Cè Yí): One day prior,
an imperial tent (yù wò) and the ministers’ temporary quarters (mù cì) were set up in the west corridor of the Zōutú Hall.
The Director of the Grand Music (Tài Yuè Lìng) arranged the court music (gōng xuán) in the court yard,
and the Auxiliary Officer of Music (Xié Lǜ Láng) set up the position for raising the banner (jǔ huī wèi).
On the day itself,
the ministers of the Northern and Southern Administrations, in court attire,
proceeded to the Zōutú Hall before dawn.
The scroll case (cè) and the seal case (bǎo) were first placed below the west corridor.
The Palace Gate Envoy (gé shǐ) escorted the Emperor to the imperial tent,
where he put on a loose garment (kuān yī) and a black sash (zào dài).
When the rows of ministers were complete,
they were introduced in separate rows.
They merged ranks facing the hall and stood still.
The scroll case platform was guided up the hall to the mat position (rù wèi),
followed by the seal case platform.
They were placed on the west steps.
The Palace Gate Envoy escorted the Emperor up the hall via the west steps.
As he first moved,
music began.
Upon reaching his position and standing,
the music ceased.
The Commissioner of the Privy Council (Xuānhuī Shǐ) bowed to the Emperor, who bowed twice,
and all those in attendance bowed twice.
The Hanlin Envoy (Hànlín Shǐ) held the ceremonial cup (tái zhǎn) and advanced it.
The Emperor bowed twice.
He was escorted to the front of the divine seat (shén zuò),
knelt,
offered libations three times,
and the music began.
After the libations were presented,
he returned to his position.
The music ceased.
He bowed twice again,
and all those in attendance bowed twice.
The Emperor was escorted to the front of the divine seat,
and stood facing north.
The person holding the scroll box (cè hán) removed the lid,
advanced, and knelt.
The scroll platform was withdrawn,
and placed below the west wall of the hall.
The reader of the scroll was escorted forward,
bent down, lay prostrate, and knelt.
The official announced his full title and read the posthumous name scroll (shì cè).
After reading,
he lay prostrate and rose,
returning to his position.
The person holding the scroll box placed it upon the platform.
The person holding the seal box (bǎo hán) advanced and knelt.
The official reading the seal (dú bǎo guān) announced his title and knelt while reading; after he finished,
the Emperor was escorted to the mat position and bowed twice.
All those in attendance bowed twice.
When the rite was complete,
the Emperor was escorted back to the imperial tent.
As he first moved,
music began.
Upon reaching the imperial tent,
the music ceased.
The ministers were escorted out in separate rows.
If the Empress Dowager (Huáng Tàihòu) offered wine libations,
it followed the standard ritual.
Ceremony for the Mourning Day (Jì Chén Yí): One day prior,
a memorial tablet (bǎng zi) for the Mourning Day was presented,
and the name slips (míng zhǐ) were written in advance.
One large sheet of paper
used the back (yīn miàn), with the third line reading:
"Your servant, [Name], Chancellor, along with all civil and military officials, respectfully proceeds to the Western Upper Palace Gate (Xī Shàng Gě Mén) to present names and offer condolences."
On the day itself,
all officials, great and small, who were to bow, wore black robes and black sashes.
When the fourth watch arrived,
in front of the temporary quarters (mù cì),
or at a Buddhist monastery (sēng sì) if in the capital,
they formed ranks.
According to their rank, they stood facing the palace gate.
The Duty Attendant (zhí rì shè rén) knelt on the right,
holding the name slip in front.
The head of the ranks and those below him all bowed twice.
They were then escorted out.
The name slip was handed face-to-face by the Commissioner of the Privy Council (Xuānhuī Shǐ) to a palace attendant (nèi shì) for submission to the throne.
Song envoys’ funeral sacrifice, condolence, and comfort ceremony: The Grand Empress Dowager proceeded to the Cuōtú Diàn,
wearing mourning attire.
The Empress Dowager sat on the north side, facing south, with a curtain drawn.
The Emperor sat on the south side, facing north.
The Song envoys arrived at their temporary lodging.
They were granted plain clothes and black sashes.
After changing,
the northern and southern officials were led in to take their places
and stand still.
Those allowed to sit on low stools or below
all ascended the殿 (diàn) and stood in their positions.
First, the sacrificial envoy and deputy, holding the sacrificial text, entered through the south cave gate.
All officials above and below the殿 (diàn) raised a wail of sorrow,
and stood still at the Dānchí.
The Xīshàng Gémén Shǐ descended from the south steps,
received the sacrificial text,
ascended the殿 (diàn) to open the seal,
placed it on the incense table,
and the wailing ceased.
The sacrificial offerings were arranged in front of the殿 (diàn).
The envoy and deputy were led up the south steps to the殿 (diàn),
stood at the cushioned mat,
bowed,
and bowed twice again.
The Grand Envoy was led forward to offer incense,
then retreated,
and bowed twice again.
The Grand Envoy knelt forward,
held the ceremonial cup,
and offered three libations of wine.
The Jiàofāng played music.
He retreated,
and bowed twice again.
The two Zhōngshū Shèrén were beckoned to kneel and hold the sacrificial text.
The Grand Envoy was led forward to prostrate himself and kneel.
After the reading was finished,
a wail of sorrow was raised.
The envoy and deputy were led down the殿 (diàn) to stand still,
and the wailing ceased.
After the offering beds were all brought out,
the envoy and deputy were led to the south side,
facing north, to stand.
The condolence envoy and deputy were summoned to enter through the south cave gate.
The four envoys together saw the spirit of the late Emperor Dàxíng,
and bowed twice.
They were led out
to return to their temporary lodging.
The Empress Dowager sat in a separate殿 (diàn),
wearing mourning attire.
First, the northern and southern officials were led to stand in their places above and below the殿 (diàn).
The condolence envoy and deputy, holding the letter box, entered from the right,
and stood in the middle of the殿 (diàn).
The Gémén Shǐ descended from the right side of the殿 (diàn) to receive the letter box,
ascended the殿 (diàn) and reported,
“The seal is intact.”
After it was opened and read,
the envoy and deputy were led up the south steps to the殿 (diàn).
After conveying the condolences,
they retreated,
and descended the殿 (diàn) to stand.
After the offering beds were all brought past,
the envoy and deputy were led to the south side,
facing north, to stand.
The sacrificial envoy and deputy were summoned to enter.
The four envoys together presented themselves,
bowed,
and bowed twice again.
Without leaving their ranks,
they reported,
“May Your Majesty be blessed with ten thousand fortunes,”
and bowed twice again.
They left their ranks,
expressed gratitude for seeing the Emperor’s countenance,
and bowed twice again,
then stood still.
The Xuān Huī conveyed the imperial decree of comfort and inquiry.
They expressed gratitude in their positions,
and bowed twice again.
They were led out
to return to their temporary lodging.
The Emperor resided in the Nándiàn,
wearing mourning attire.
The envoy and deputy entered to have an audience,
following the ceremony for seeing the Empress Dowager,
with added expressions of gratitude for the distant reception, comfort, and medicines,
and bowed twice again.
Next, gifts were bestowed upon the envoy, deputy, and accompanying personnel.
The sacrificial envoy and deputy were separately granted customary items for reading the sacrificial text.
A banquet was hosted at the official residence on the same day.
The ceremonies for envoys from Gāolí and Xiàguó offering condolences and contributions
were generally similar.
When Dàozōng passed away,
Emperor Tiānzuò inquired about the rites from Yēlǜ Gù.
The State of Sòng dispatched envoys to offer condolences, present sacrifices, and return funerary gifts.
The Emperor wore mourning attire
and resided in a separate殿 (diàn) north of the Yóuxiān.
When the envoys entered the gate,
the Emperor wept.
The envoys proceeded to the coffin to offer incense.
After reading the sacrificial text,
they wept again.
The officials read the imperial will,
and wept uncontrollably.
The envoys exited.
A short while later,
they re-entered
and arranged the funerary gifts in front of the coffin.
The Emperor came to supervise and weep.
He retreated,
changed clothes,
and resided in the tent殿 (diàn) south of the Yóuxiān Diàn.
The envoys entered for an audience and to take their leave.
An imperial edict commanded officials to host a banquet at the official residence.
Song envoys’ announcement of sorrow ceremony: The Emperor wore plain cap and attire,
and the officials wore black robes and black sashes.
The Song envoy, holding the letter, entered from the right
and stood within the Dānchí.
The Xīshàng Gémén Shǐ descended from the right steps of the殿 (diàn),
received the letter box,
ascended the殿 (diàn),
bowed within the balustrade,
and reported,
“The seal is intact.”
After it was opened,
it was handed to the Zǎixiàng on a table west of the殿 (diàn) to be read.
The Emperor raised a wail of sorrow.
A Shèrén led the envoy up the right steps.
He prostrated and knelt within the balustrade.
After conveying greetings,
he rose from prostration
and stood.
The Emperor inquired,
“May the Emperor of the Southern Court be blessed with ten thousand fortunes?”
The envoy knelt and reported,
“When I departed, His Majesty was blessed with ten thousand fortunes.”
He rose
and retreated.
A Shèrén led the envoy down the right steps of the殿 (diàn).
West of the Dānchí,
he bowed facing east.
The Tōngshì Shèrén announced the envoy’s name for audience,
and he bowed twice.
Without leaving his ranks,
he reported,
“May Your Majesty be blessed with ten thousand fortunes,”
and bowed twice again.
He left his ranks,
expressed gratitude for seeing the Emperor’s countenance,
and bowed twice again.
He then left his ranks again
and expressed gratitude for the distant reception, comfort, and medicines,
and bowed twice again.
He was prompted to wait,
led out,
and proceeded to his temporary lodging,
where clothes and items were bestowed.
The accompanying personnel were led in.
Their names were announced for bowing,
and they reported,
“May Your Majesty be blessed with ten thousand fortunes.”
They left for their lodging,
where clothes were bestowed,
in a ceremony similar to that of the envoy.
The envoy was then led in again,
bowed facing the殿 (diàn),
and was prompted to express gratitude for the grace.
He was prompted again,
“There is an imperial decree to bestow a banquet,”
and bowed twice.
He was prompted to wait,
and proceeded to his temporary lodging for the banquet.
The accompanying personnel expressed gratitude for the grace
and bowed for the imperial decree bestowing a banquet,
all as before.
After the banquet,
they returned to the official residence.
Protocol for the Song Envoy presenting tribute and gifts: All officials, before dawn, in court attire,
stood in ranks before the palace hall.
The Song tribute envoy and the envoy for announcing the emperor's ascension, with their deputies, entered the inner gate.
The attendant vice-envoy (Guǎnbàn Fùshǐ) led the envoy for announcing the ascension (Xiè Dēngwèi Shǐ) to his tent for seating.
The attendant grand envoy (Guǎnbàn Dàshǐ) and the tribute envoy and his deputy presented a letter and entered,
stopping at the felt mat outside the western upper palace gate (Xīshàng Gémén).
The palace gate official (Géménshǐ) received the letter box,
placing it on a table below the western steps of the hall.
The usher (Yǐnjìnshǐ) led the tribute items through the western upper palace gate,
then out through the side gate in the corridor.
The emperor ascended the hall and took his seat.
The Xuanhuīshǐ (Commissioner of Military Affairs) led the ranks before the hall in paying respects.
Then the prime ministers (Zǎichén) led the civil and military ranks in paying respects.
The Zhōngshūlìng (Chancellor) was led up the western steps to the hall,
to present the Song envoy's memorial (Jiàn Bǎngzi).
The Qìdān officials paid their respects.
The Kònghèguān (Crane Controlling Officials) paid their respects.
The tribute envoy and his deputy entered through the western upper palace gate,
standing facing the hall.
The palace attendant (Shèrén) led the envoy and his deputy up the western steps to the hall,
where they verbally paid their respects.
They were then led down the western steps,
to the east of the vermilion courtyard (Dānchí),
bowed facing west,
announced their names, and reported,
"May the sacred person enjoy ten thousand blessings,"
following the protocol of the envoy for announcing mourning (Gào'āi Shǐ).
They offered thanks for seeing the celestial countenance,
and thanks for the distant reception, the inquiries, and the medicine.
The retinue of the tribute envoy also saw the emperor and followed the same procedure.
Next, the envoy for announcing the emperor's ascension (Gào Dēngwèi Shǐ) and his deputy presented the letter box,
entering through the eastern upper palace gate (Dōngshàng Gémén),
standing facing the hall.
The palace gate official went down the eastern steps,
to receive the letter box.
After the Zhōngshūlìng had read it,
the palace attendant led the envoy and his deputy up the eastern steps to the hall,
to verbally pay their respects.
They were then led down the hall,
standing facing south.
The gifts for announcing the ascension entered,
then exited through the side gate in the corridor.
They withdrew,
bowed facing west,
verbally paid their respects,
and gave thanks for seeing the celestial countenance, the distant reception, etc.,
all following the protocol of the tribute envoy.
Imperial gifts of clothing and other items were bestowed upon the tribute and ascension envoys and their deputies, and their retinues,
as for the envoy for announcing mourning.
All officials who were to be seated ascended the hall and stood in their places.
The two envoys and their deputies were separately led to stand in the two corridors.
The emperor asked the envoys and their deputies,
"Was the journey difficult?"
They prostrated five times within the vermilion courtyard.
Each was led up to the hall to stand in the imperial guard's waiting position.
High ministers presented wine.
The emperor drank wine.
A Qìdān interpreter (Tōng) spoke,
a Han Chinese official (Hànrén Zàn) delivered eulogies.
All officials in the hall bowed,
shouting
"Long live!"
After the eulogies, everyone took their seats.
After the serving of wine, delicacies, tea, meals, and steamed buns,
and after the retinue had finished their watered rice,
all officials rose.
The Qìdān interpreter spoke,
the Han Chinese official delivered eulogies,
all bowed twice,
shouting
"Long live!"
Everyone waited in attendance.
Only the Song envoys and their deputies were led down the hall to offer thanks,
prostrating five times.
They were then led out.
The Kònghèguān waited outside the gate,
reported to the palace gate official that there was no further business,
and the Gòngfèngguān (Officials of the Bureau of Supply) exited in formation.
Protocol for the Gāolì and Xiàguó envoys announcing a ruler's death: A few days in advance,
imperial tents were set up to the left and right of the temporary palace (Xínggōng),
and the envoys' tents were arranged to the southeast.
On the appointed day,
officials from the Northern Department (Běimiàn Chénliáo) wore their everyday attire,
while other officials wore court attire,
and entered for the audience.
When the envoys arrived at their tents,
the relevant authorities (Yǒusī) first presented the memorial of the successor (Sìzǐ Biǎozhuàng) to the Shūmìyuàn (Bureau of Military Affairs),
to be prepared for imperial presentation.
First, officials from the Northern Department and those of "Dwarf Mound" (Ǎiduàn) rank and above were led close to the imperial tent,
standing opposite each other.
Other officials stood according to their ranks and positions.
The envoy announcing the ruler's death (Gàozhōng Rénshǐ) was led in from the right,
reaching the vermilion courtyard,
and stood facing the hall.
He was led up to the right,
stood;
bowed slightly forward,
bowed,
knelt and presented his report.
An imperial inquiry was proclaimed.
If a successor had already been established,
he would humbly receive the imperial decree.
After the report,
he returned to his position.
If a successor had not yet been established,
no imperial inquiry was proclaimed.
He was led down to the vermilion courtyard on the right,
bowing facing north.
After calling out the ranks,
he was led to face the hall and bow twice.
He did not leave his rank,
but reported,
"May the sacred person enjoy ten thousand blessings,"
and bowed twice.
He left his rank,
thanked for seeing the celestial countenance,
returned to his position,
and bowed twice.
He left his rank,
thanked for the distant reception,
returned to his position,
and bowed twice.
After the eulogies, he waited,
then withdrew to his tent.
He re-entered,
as before, bowed facing north,
offered his condolences,
and bowed twice;
longing for the palace,
he bowed twice.
The eulogist said,
"May you have a good journey."
The ceremony concluded.
Collation Notes
Zhi (Treatise) 20, Rites Treatise 3: Military Protocol
Protocol for the Emperor's Personal Expedition: Usually in autumn and winter,
or whenever necessary to respond to the enemy and adapt to changes.
Before deploying the army,
the ancestors must first be informed at the ancestral temple.
Three spirit tablets were erected and sacrificed to: namely, the Former Emperors (Xiāndì),
the Roads (Dàolù),
and the Army (Jūnlǚ).
Blue oxen and white horses were sacrificed to Heaven and Earth.
The sacrifice
was usually performed under a solitary tree;
if there was no solitary tree,
it was performed at the place of encampment.
Sometimes the emperor wore armor,
sacrificed at the ancestral temples of the Former Emperors,
and then reviewed the troops.
Before marching,
one male and one female deer (Biāo) were offered for the "● sacrifice."
Before engaging the enemy,
horse tails were tied,
and Heaven and Earth were prayed to and bowed to before advancing.
After capturing a city or defeating the enemy,
Heaven and Earth were sacrificed to,
with white and black sheep as offerings.
Upon returning the army,
one captured stallion and one ox were sacrificed to Heaven and Earth.
When setting out, a condemned prisoner was used;
upon returning, a spy was used,
tied to a pillar erected for this purpose,
and shot at randomly in the direction from which he came.
Arrows covered him like a hedgehog,
which was called
"Shooting the Ghost Arrow" (Shèguǐjiàn).
Làyí (Winter Sacrifice Protocol): The Làyí was held on the Chen (辰) day of the twelfth month.
One day prior,
an imperial edict commanded the hunting officials to select a hunting ground.
On that day,
after the emperor and empress burned incense and bowed to the sun,
a hunting enclosure was set up,
and hunters were ordered to form the left and right wings.
After the hunting official (Sīlièguān) reported the formation was complete,
the emperor and empress ascended their palanquins.
The Dìlièmádū (a high official) presented two jars of wine and a platter of cooked meat (pánbì) to them,
and the grand kings (Dàwáng) of the Northern and Southern Chancellery (Běinán Yuàn) and below presented horses and clothing.
The emperor descended from his palanquin,
and after sacrificing to the east,
rode his horse into the hunting enclosure.
The crown prince (Huángtàizǐ) and imperial princes (Qīnwáng) led the assembled officials in presenting wine,
moving in two wings.
When the emperor first caught a rabbit,
the assembled officials presented wine as a toast,
and each was bestowed with wine.
At the time of the midday meal,
the imperial princes and high ministers each presented their catches.
After the wine concluded,
the assembled officials were granted drinks,
and returned to the palace.
In the winter of the first year of Yìnglì (951 CE),
Han envoys came to offer congratulations,
and from then on, this became a regular protocol.
In the Tǒnghé (983-1012 CE) period,
it was abolished.
Protocol for Dispatching the Army: Regulations are found in the Military Treatise.
Rites Treatise 4: Guest Protocol
Ritual for the Daily Morning Audience (Cháng Cháo Qǐ Jū Yí): At dawn,
the officials enter the court wearing court robes (cháo fú),
each according to his designated waiting area (mù cì).
The Palace Attendant (Nèi Shì) reports,
"The ranks are assembled (bān qí)."
First, the ranks of the Capital Officials (Jīng Guān) are led outside the Three Gates (Sān Mén).
The Attendant-in-Waiting on Duty (Dāng Zhí Shè Rén) announces the start of the greeting (qǐ jū).
They perform two full bows (zài bài),
and each waits respectfully (zhī hòu).
Next, the civil and military officials, from the Two Departments (Liǎng Fǔ) downward,
stand facing the hall within the Cinnabar Steps (Dān Chí).
The vertical ranks (shù bān) of various offices (zhū sī) and Attendants (gōng fèng guān),
stand facing each other outside the East and West paths.
The Commissioner and Deputy Commissioner of the Palace Gate on Duty (Dāng Zhí Gé Shǐ Fù) announce the start of the greeting.
They perform two full bows,
and each waits respectfully.
They withdraw and return to their waiting areas,
wearing official robes (gōng fú).
The Emperor (Dì) ascends the hall and sits.
The Liǎng Fǔ and the Jīng Guān offer a greeting (shēng nuò) within the Dān Chí,
and each waits respectfully.
After the Bureau of Music (Jiào Fāng Sī) and the Northern Ranks (Běi Bān) finish their greetings,
memorials are presented (zòu shì).
(In) Yānjīng (it is the) Jiāníng Diàn;
(in) Xījīng (it is the) Tóngwén Diàn.
Court Robes (Cháo Fú):
pǔtóu (head-cloth), robe, and hu (tablet);
Official Robes (Gōng Fú):
purple gown and cap.
Ritual for Formal Seating (Zhèng Zuò Yí): The Emperor ascends the hall and sits,
the warning sounds cease.
After the ranks of the Qìdān and Hàn people finish presenting themselves before the hall,
each stands waiting according to their position.
Next, after the Jiào Fāng ranks finish,
they roll up (their positions) and withdraw.
After the Jīng Guān ranks enter and finish bowing,
they bow (yī) west of the Right Transverse Street (Yòu Héng Jiē),
and stand in rank according to their position.
Next, after the Military Ranks (Wǔ Bān) enter and finish bowing,
they stand according to their position.
After the Civil Ranks (Wén Bān) enter and finish bowing,
they stand according to their position.
The Běi Bān enter,
finish their greeting,
and stand in ranked order east of the Left Transverse Street (Zuǒ Héng Jiē).
Next, the Liǎng Fǔ ranks enter,
bow deeply (jū gōng),
announce the greeting (qǐ jū) of the Grand Councilor (Zǎi Chén) [name] and those below him,
finish their bows,
and are led up the hall to present memorials.
The six ranks mentioned above for the Qǐ Jū,
all perform seven full bows.
If among them there is one who does not hold the title of Jìe Dù Shǐ,
the rank leader only announces the name,
and they still perform seven full bows.
The rolling up of ranks (juǎn bān),
is the same as the daily audience (cháng cháo).
Officials of the Zhí Yuàn who receive an imperial decree enter the Wén Bān.
The Residence Administration (Liú Shǒu Sī), the Three Bureaus (Sān Sī), the Army Command (Tǒng Jūn Sī), and the Policy Bureau (Zhì Zhì Sī) are called Jīng Guān;
The Supreme Military Command (Dū Bù Shǔ Sī), the Palace Commissioner (Gōng Shǐ), and the Deputy Palace Commissioner (Fù Gōng Shǐ),
the Clerks (lì shì) below the Capital Administrator (Dū Chéng),
and officials of various offices following the imperial carriage, from the Northern Face Director (Běi Miàn Zhǔ Shì) downward, are classified as Military Officials (Wǔ Guān);
The Academies (Guǎn, Gé), the Court of Judicial Review (Dà Lǐ Sì),
(officials) below the Táng Hòu,

the Censorate (Yù Shǐ Tái), unassigned personnel accompanying the carriage (xián yuán), clerks (lì shì), the Astronomical Bureau (Sī Tiān Tái), the Hàn Lín Academy, and the Medical Bureau (Yī Guān Yuàn) are classified as Civil Officials (Wén Guān).
In the winter of Tiānqìng 2nd year (1112 CE),
the Jiào Fāng were all required to wear robes.
Ritual for Receiving Officials (Chén Liáo Jiē Xiàn Yí): The Emperor occupies the throne,
after the roster (bǎng zi) for the audience is reported,
the officials enter from the left,
and bow deeply.
They announce the respectful audience (zhī hòu xiàn) of the civil and military officials (wén wǔ bǎi liáo), the Grand Councilor [name], and those below him.
They are led to face the hall and bow deeply,
performing the greeting (qǐ jū),
totaling seven bows.
The rank leader is led out of the rank,
offering thanks for facing the Celestial Countenance (Tiān Yán),
and returning to his position.
They perform the ceremonial dance (wǔ dǎo),
five bows,
and bow deeply.
The decree of imperial replies and inquiries (dá wèn zhì) is proclaimed.
They perform two full bows.
After the proclamation is finished,
they thank the Imperial Edict (Xuān Yù),
performing five bows.
After each has respectfully waited,
those who may sit on low stools (ǎi dūn) and above are led forward,
and they are asked,
"May the sacred person (shèng gōng) enjoy ten thousand blessings."
An attendant transmits the proclamation and asks,
"Was the journey (bá shè) not difficult?"
They bow deeply.
After the Attendant (shè rén) who leads the rank announces that all have respectfully waited,
they are led up on the right side,
preparing for the proclaimed inquiry.
The rest of the officials stand waiting on the right.
The proclamation replies, saying:
"You, sirs, have long resided in your districts (xiāng yì),
and have now come to serve the Imperial Carriage (chéng yú).
The season is cold with frost—or sometimes hot and humid—
We presume that you are greatly fatigued by your efforts.
May you all be
safe and well.
This should be properly known."
Ritual for Inquiring about the Emperor's Health (Wèn Shèng Tǐ Yí): When the Emperor travels,
and the Imperial Carriage arrives at the Nàbō (Imperial Traveling Court),
he sits in the imperial tent (yù zhàng).
The officials wear Gōng Fú,
and inquire,
"May the Shèng Gōng enjoy ten thousand blessings."
They announce the performance of two full bows,
and each waits respectfully.
They render service (fèng shì).
Officials from the Commissioner of Imperial Insignia (Xuānhuī) downward wear ordinary dress (cháng fú).
The Jiào Fāng are the same as the officials.
In the summer of Bǎodà 1st year (1121 CE),
by special decree, they announced their names and performed two full bows,
without referring to themselves as Zǎi Chén.
Ritual for the Return of the Imperial Carriage to the Capital (Chē Jià Huán Jīng Yí): One day prior,
the Xuānhuī and those below line up crosswise,
and the various offices (zhū sī) and Palace Gates (Gé Mén) all wear Gōng Fú,
waiting respectfully at the night camp (sù zhàng).
On the day itself, at dawn,
the Emperor rides the Imperial Chariot (Yù Lù).
After the Gé Mén proclaims the edict to the military and populace,
the carriage is escorted (dǎo jià).
The contemporary prime minister (shí xiàng) and those below advance to the Inner Gate (Nèi Mén).
After the Deputy Commissioner of the Palace Gate (Gé Fù) finishes examining the arrow (kān jiàn),
the Attendant of General Affairs (Tōng Shì Shè Rén) bows deeply,
and reports,
"Your servant announces the dismissal of the guards (fàng zhàng)."
The ritual is completed.
Ritual for Examining the Arrow (Kān Jiàn Yí): When the Emperor rides the Yù Lù,
arriving at the Nèi Mén.
The Northern and Southern officials stand in opposing ranks before the chariot.
The Arrow Examiner (Kān Jiàn Guān) holds the female arrow (cí jiàn),
standing in the middle of the gate.
The Eastern Upper Commissioner of the Palace Gate (Dōng Shàng Gé Mén Shǐ) goes before the chariot,
holding the male arrow (xióng jiàn) and standing to the left of the chariot,
summoning the Kān Jiàn Guān to advance.
The Kān Jiàn Guān bows and advances,
stopping about five paces from the chariot,
standing facing the chariot.
The Gé Shǐ says,
"Receive the arrow and perform the examination (xíng kān)."
The Kān Jiàn Guān bows, kneels,
and receives the arrow;
raising his hands, he completes the examination,
bows deeply,
and reports,
"The inner and outer examinations match."
The Gé Shǐ says,
"Proceed with the examination according to the imperial order (zhǔn chì)."
The Kān Jiàn Guān stands upright,
retreats to his former position in the middle of the gate,
holds the arrow close to his chest,
and announces,
"Military commanders (jūn jiāng) and gate guards (mén zhàng guān), step forward."
The Mén Zhàng Guān immediately opens the gate,
and upon the signal, they emerge simultaneously on both sides,
lining up side by side on the left and right,
standing still.
The Kān Jiàn Guān raises his right hand and announces,
"Present the arrow (chéng jiàn),"
then announces,
"The Imperial Arrow (Yù Jiàn) used to summon the guards has been produced from within,
and according to the imperial order (zhǔn chì), it is handed to the Left Imperial Guard (Zuǒ Jīn Zhàng) for examination."
He announces,
"Does it match or not match?"
They reply,
"Match, match, match,"
He announces,
"Is it the same or different?"
They reply,
"Same, same, same."
Completed.
The Kān Jiàn Guān advances again,
stands in position,
bows deeply,
announces his full title, saying, "Your servant [name] has matched the arrow before the Emperor,"
and retreats to stand in the middle of the gate.
He announces,
"The arrow is respectfully handed to the Gé Mén Shǐ to be brought in."
The affair is finished.
The arrow is handed to the Gé Shǐ,
who then transfers it to the Xuānhuī.
Protocol for the Audience of the Sòng Envoys with the Huáng Tàihòu: Sòng envoys offer congratulations on the birthday and New Year's Day.
On the appointed day,
officials enter the court at dawn.
The envoys arrive at their temporary lodging.
When the ranks of officials are arrayed,
the Huáng Tàihòu takes her seat on the main hall.
After the Xuānhuī Shǐ leads the officials in the front rank in performing the ritual obeisance,
the ranks disperse.
Next, the Qìdān officials perform their ritual obeisance and disperse.
Officials entitled to a seat are led up to the hall,
and stand in their positions.
The remaining officials not entitled to a seat
withdraw and stand attending on the east side.
Hàn-Chinese officials enter through the eastern side-gate,
facing west and bowing.
The Shèrén bows,
announces the ritual obeisance of Mǒu and those below him,
completing seven prostrations.
The announcer bids each to attend.
Officials entitled to a seat are led up to the hall,
and stand in their positions.
The Zhōngshū Lìng and Dàwáng ascend the hall via the western steps,
present the roster of Sòng envoys and their retinue,
and then stand in their positions.
The remaining officials not entitled to a seat
withdraw and stand attending on the west side.
Next, six Sòng envoys and their deputies are led in through the eastern side-gate,
and stand in a line facing the hall within the crimson courtyard.
The Géshǐ descends from the eastern steps,
receives the book-casket.
Those carrying the book-casket all kneel.
The Géshǐ holds his tablet of office inserted in his belt and stands,
receiving the book-casket.
He ascends the hall via the eastern steps,
bows within the railing,
announces
"Sealed and intact,"
then
hands it to the Shūmì for opening.
After the Zǎichén reads it aloud before the Huáng Tàihòu,
the six envoys and deputies are led up to the hall via the eastern steps,
and stand within the railing.
The envoy bows to the ambassador for the birthday festival to advance slightly.
The envoy prostrates himself and kneels,
makes a supplementary obeisance.
He rises,
and returns to his position to stand.
Next, the ambassador for congratulating the Huáng Tàihòu on New Year's Day is led forward,
performs a supplementary obeisance,
according to the previous protocol.
The Huáng Tàihòu asks,
"May the emperor of the Southern Court enjoy myriad blessings in his sacred person."
The Shèrén bows to the birthday ambassador and the New Year's Day ambassador to advance slightly.
They all kneel,
only the birthday ambassador reports,
"Upon my departure, his sacred person enjoyed myriad blessings."
They all prostrate themselves,
then rise.
They are led down the hall via the eastern steps,
and stand in a line facing the hall within the crimson courtyard.
The Yǐnjìn Shǐ leads the tribute items in through the western side-gate,
placing the carrying-beds in front of the hall.
The Kònghè Guān performs ritual obeisance,
four prostrations.
After the carrying-beds are taken out through the eastern side-gate,
the envoys and deputies are bowed to and withdraw to the east,
facing west,
all bowing.
The Shèrén bows,
announces that the State Envoy Mǒu Guān Mǒu and those below him from the Southern Court are to attend and present themselves,
perform a ritual dance,
completing five prostrations.
Without leaving their ranks,
they report,
"May the sacred person enjoy myriad blessings,"
and make two more prostrations.
The head of the rank is bowed to to step out of the rank,
expresses thanks for seeing the imperial countenance,
returns to position,
performs a ritual dance,
completing five prostrations.
The announcer bids each to ascend the hall and attend.
Each envoy and deputy is led up to the hall via the western steps and takes their position.
The retinue is called to enter through both side-gates,
bows facing the hall,
announces their names,
the announcer bids them to bow,
performs ritual obeisance,
completing four prostrations.
The announcer bids each to attend,
they are divided into ranks and led out through both side-gates.
If the Huáng Tàihòu asks the envoys and deputies,
"Was the journey not difficult?",
they are led down the hall via the western steps,
perform a ritual dance within the crimson courtyard,
completing five prostrations.
The announcer bids each to ascend the hall and attend,
they are led up to the hall via the western steps,
and stand in their positions.
The Qìdān Shèrén and Hàn-Chinese Géshǐ together announce the bowing.
The officials entitled to a seat and the envoys and deputies all bow,
exclaiming
"Long live!"
The announcer bids each to be seated.
