returns to his position,
and bows deeply (Jūgōng).
The herald announces the ceremonial dance,
performing five bows.
The herald announces that all should stand waiting.
One Grand Counselor (Zǎichén) is led up to the hall,
and reports the list of tributary items presented by the hundred officials (Bǎiliáo) and various circuits.
The Office of Music pays respects,
performing seven bows,
without offering congratulations.
The Palace Guards (Kònghè Guān) pay respects,
performing four bows.
The Military Commissioners (Yāyá) of the various circuits attach their respects to the report,
are granted a banquet,
totaling eight bows.
Khitan and Han officials form a unified line,
present the longevity wine (Shòujiǔ),
perform the ceremonial dance,
performing five bows.
One high minister is led up to the hall,
inserts his tablet (Hù) into his belt at the mat position (Rùwèi) outside the balustrade (Lánwài),
holds the cup on a tray (Tái) and presents the wine,
the Emperor and the Empress receive the cup.
He withdraws,
and returns to the mat position.
He hands over the tray and takes out his tablet,
bows and kneels inside the balustrade,
announces his full official title and offers birthday wishes, stating:
"We, your officials, respectfully present the wine of ten thousand thousand years of longevity (Qiānwànsuì Shòujiǔ),"
finishing,
he is led down the hall,
returns to his position,
performs the ceremonial dance,
performs five bows,
and bows deeply.
The Commissioner of the Bureau of Palace Affairs reports the imperial reply according to the ceremony,
is led up to the hall,
inserts his tablet and holds the tray.
The Emperor and the Empress drink,
the officials below the hall divide into lines,
the Office of Music plays music,
all bow,
and shout
"Ten Thousand Years (Wànsuì)!"
Upon finishing the drink,
the Emperor and the Empress hand over the cup.
He is led down the hall,
performs the ceremonial dance,
performs five bows.
The herald announces that all should stand waiting,
and he is led out.
Officials present tribute according to the ceremony,
and the banquet is announced according to the ceremony.
The Office of Music, the Overseer of Cups (Jiān Zhǎn), and the officials ascend the hall and stand waiting according to the ceremony.
The Empress presents wine to the Emperor,
the herald announces a bow upon the hall,
and the attending officials (Shì Chénliáo) all bow.
The Emperor receives the cup,
and all bow.
The Empress sits,
Khitan Gentlemen-in-Waiting and Han Palace Attendants (Hànrén Gěshǐ) announce a bow upon the hall,
all bow,
and shout
"Ten Thousand Years!"
The herald announces that all should take their seats.
High ministers present wine to the Emperor and the Empress,
and wine is served according to the ceremony.
Wine is served three times,
snacks are served,
and staple foods are served.
Wine is presented again to the Emperor and the Empress.
Wine is served twice more,
the large feast (Dà Zhuàn) is brought in,
and porridge is served.
The Office of Music offers felicitations,
and the officials all stand up.
When the shouted slogan (Kǒuhào) ends,
the herald announces a bow,
and shout
"Ten Thousand Years,"
they are led down the hall to thank for the banquet,
are led out,
all according to standard ceremony (Cháng Yí).
the *jǔrén*
follow the *shíxiàng* (current prime minister) to the side of the imperial tent,
present the list of names along with the *shíxiàng*'s list of names, and after they are submitted,
the *shíxiàng* has an audience following the usual
rites. When finished,
they bow to the *jìnshì* (first place and below) inside the *Dānchí* (Vermilion Steps) facing the hall and bow deeply,
announce their names,
and perform four prostrations.
The master of ceremonies instructs them to stand ready,
and all withdraw.
If there is someone presenting documents,
they do not withdraw,
but stand upright, holding the scroll.
The *Gěmén* (Palace Gate Official) requests permission to receive it,
kneels on the left knee and hands it over,
stands up straight, and withdraws.
The rites are concluded.
Rites for the Conferral of Imperial Edicts Categorized by Class upon the *Jìnshì*: After the officials pay their respects,
and the *dújuàn guān* (examiners) have submitted their reports,
they stand in sequence on the left side, having their names called out according to their classification,
and the *Gěmén* officials receive the imperial edicts.
The *gěshǐ* (Chief Palace Gate Official) requests permission to lead them to the *Dānchí*,
where they stand in sequence according to their classification.
The *gěshǐ* announces,
"There is an edict,"
they perform two prostrations,
and bow deeply.
The *Shèrén* (Attendant) proclaims the edict:
"To each of you, according to your classification, one imperial edict is granted.
You should know this,"
then bows and prostrates.
Each kneels on the left knee,
and after receiving the edict,
bows deeply.
All perform two prostrations.
Each stands ready,
and is led separately to the left and right to stand facing the center.
Waiting until the matters have been reported,
they are led up the two flights of steps onto the hall,
take their positions,
give a unified *nuò* aloud,
and are granted seats.
After three rounds of wine,
they stand up,
and utter *nuò* as before.
They bow and withdraw.
The rites are concluded.
The *Páiyìn Lángjūn* (Signet and Seal Gentlemen) serve the wine,
and the *gěshǐ* urges them to drink.
Rites for the Conferral of Official Attire upon the *Jìnshì*: The Emperor takes his seat in the hall,
and officials in court attire lead the *jìnshì* inside.
Facing west from the east side,
they perform two prostrations,
bow, and take their places at the *Dānchí* position,
facing the hall and bowing deeply.
The *gěshǐ*
announces, "There is an edict,"
they perform two prostrations,
and bow deeply.
The *Shèrén* proclaims the edict:
"To each of you, according to your classification, one imperial edict is granted,
and official attire is also bestowed.
You should know this,"
followed by a bow and two prostrations.
Kneeling, they receive the edict,
and perform two prostrations.
They withdraw,
are led to the place for official attire,
change their clothes,
bow, and return to the *Dānchí* position,
bowing deeply.
The master of ceremonies prompts them to offer thanks for the grace received,
perform a ritual dance (*wǔdǎo*),
and perform five prostrations.
Each stands ready,
and stands in sequence inside the pavilion east of the hall.
They utter *nuò*,
and are seated.
A banquet is granted,
and flowers are pinned in their hats (*zānhuā*).
One *gěshǐ* and three or two *Gěmén* officials are announced to urge them to drink for the whole day.
The rites are concluded.
Rites for the Mid-Term Thanks (*zhōngxiè*) of the *Zǎixiàng* (Chancellor): The Emperor wears casual attire and ascends the hall to sit,
and all classes of officials pay their respects according to the usual rites.
The officials entitled to seats ascend the hall,
while the remaining officials stand in attendance east and west below the hall,
all following the rites for the initial audience granted to the *Sòng* envoys.
The official offering *zhōngxiè* is led in from the left,
arriving at the *Dānchí* and standing facing west.
The *Shèrén* bows deeply in front of the hall,
announces the name of the newly appointed official, and awaits the *zhōngxiè*.
The *Xuānhuī* (Court Secretariat Official) summons the *Tōngbān Shèrén* (Roster-Announcing Attendant) in the hall to take the position of the master of ceremonies,
who prompts, "The official has arrived."
The *Xuānhuī* prompts the two *Tōngbān Shèrén* to stand opposite each other,
they bow to the *zhōngxiè* official, and he bows deeply.
The master of ceremonies prompts him to go to the prostration position,
and the two *Shèrén* lead him to face the hall and bow deeply.
The master of ceremonies prompts the prostration,
the *zhōngxiè* official performs the ritual dance (*wǔdǎo*),
performs five prostrations,
and without leaving the line of officials,
presents the report:
"May the Sacred Body enjoy ten thousand blessings."
The master of ceremonies prompts two prostrations.
He bows, leaves the line, and kneels.
The official
After giving the address,
he bows low, rises,
and returns to his position.
The master of ceremonies prompts the prostration,
the ritual dance (*wǔdǎo*),
and five prostrations.
He leaves the line again,
and the *zhōngxiè* official delivers the address according to the initial rites.
There are a total of seventeen prostrations.
The master of ceremonies prompts him to stand ready,
and he is led up the right steps onto the hall,
and takes his position.
He bows to the officials entitled to seats, they utter *nuò* aloud, and sit.
The *Gòngfèng Guān* (Officials in Attendance) serve the wine,
and an announcement is passed down that they must drink it all.
The officials tuck their tablets (*hù*) into their belts,
hold their goblets (*zhǎn*) and stand up,
drinking while standing behind their seats;
they place the goblets down,
and pull out their tablets.
The master of ceremonies prompts the prostration,
and all officials perform two prostrations.
The master of ceremonies prompts them all to sit,
tuck their tablets away,
hold their goblets,
and hand the goblets to the *Gòngfèng Guān*.
After three rounds of wine,
they bow to the seated officials, who stand up uttering *nuò*.
The *zhōngxiè* official is led down the right steps from the hall,
arrives at the *Dānchí*,
faces the hall, and bows deeply.
The master of ceremonies prompts the prostration,
the ritual dance (*wǔdǎo*),
and five prostrations.
He is led out to the right.
All officials withdraw.
The *Chéngxiàng* (Chancellor) and the *Shūmì Shǐ* (Chief Military Commissioner) follow the same rites,
but other officials do not ascend the hall.
Wine is granted,
officials without the title of *Jiédù Shǐ* (Military Governor) do not participate in the official rank formation,
but only announce their names,
and perform seven prostrations.
For general thanks (*zhòngxiè*),
one leader of the rank comes forward to offer *zhōngxiè*.
Rites for Presenting Memorials (*bài biǎo*): On that day,
felt mats are first laid out at the East Upper *Gěmén* (Palace Gate),
officials from the north and south and envoys and deputy envoys from various nations are led separately to the felt mats to form ranks.
Two *Tōngshì Shèrén* (Attendants of Communication) carry the memorial table,
place it in front of the rank leader,
bow and bow deeply,
perform two prostrations,
and stand upright.
A *Zhōngshū Shèrén* (Attendant of the Central Secretariat) stands by the side of the table.
The rank leader kneels,
tucks his tablet into his belt,
rises,
holds the memorial reverently,
kneels on the left knee,
and hands the memorial to the *Zhōngshū Shèrén*.
He pulls out his tablet,
proceeds to prostrate,
rises,
and performs two prostrations.
The *Zhōngshū Shèrén* places the memorial back onto the table.
The *Tōngshì Shèrén* carry the memorial table inside the East Upper *Gěmén*,
the ranks disperse,
and they are led out separately.
The rites are concluded.
On *Yuánrì* (New Year's Day),
the Emperor performs this ceremony without taking his seat.
All other instances where memorials must be submitted follow this pattern.
Ritual for Celebrating the Birth of an Imperial Son: On that day,
the imperial portrait of the late emperor is brought,
the main hall is prepared,
and the emperor sits on the octagonal dais.
When the signal sound concludes,
the Northern and Southern Xuānhuīshǐ stand to the left and right on the steps of the hall.
The Northern and Southern ministers and officials, wearing golden crowns and grand attire,
enter as a unified procession.
The two leaders of the procession hold up memorial essays and stand.
The official who reads the memorial essay first stands to the side on the left steps.
The two Xuānhuīshǐ receive the memorial essay on the eastern and western steps below the hall.
The person holding the memorial essay kneels on their left knee and presents it.
Then they bow,
rise,
and bow again.
All attend to their duties.
The two Xuānhuīshǐ both present it to the official who reads the memorial essay on the left steps above.
After it is read,
they bow and salute the ministers and officials.
The leader of the Northern faction is led up the hall via the left steps.
After offering congratulations within the railing,
they are led down the hall via the left steps,
return to their position,
perform ritual dances,
and bow five times.
The ritual concludes.
Ritual for Celebrating Auspicious Omens: When the signal sounds,
the Northern and Southern ministers and officials, wearing golden crowns and grand attire,
stand as a unified procession.
The two leaders of the procession each present a memorial essay to offer congratulations.
The Northern and Southern Xuānhuīshǐ receive the memorial essays on the left steps below the hall,
and ascend the hall to present them to the minister who reads the memorial essay.
After it is read,
they bow and salute the ministers and officials below the hall.
After bowing five times,
they bow.
The two leaders of the procession are led up the hall via the left steps.
Within the railing, they kneel and bow to offer congratulations.
After their address is concluded,
they are led down the hall via the left steps,
return to their position,
after bowing five times,
they bow.
After the imperial reply is proclaimed and the imperial decree is heard,
they bow again,
and bow.
They express gratitude for the imperial pronouncement.
After bowing five times,
all attend to their duties,
and stand in divided ranks.
The ritual concludes.
The two departments present affairs as usual.
In the 6th year of Qiántǒng,
when auspicious clouds appeared on Mùyè Shān,
this ritual was first performed.
In the 1st year of Tiānqìng,
when grain rained from the sky,
after expressing gratitude for the imperial pronouncement,
Zhào Wáng offered wine.
The
music bureau performed music,
and the ministers and officials were offered one round of wine.
After the ritual concluded,
affairs were presented.
Ritual for Celebrating the Suppression of Troubles: The emperor and empress ascend the hall and sit.
The Northern and Southern ministers and officials, along with the imperial wives, form a unified procession,
and bow five times.
The two leaders of the procession are saluted and step out of the ranks.
They kneel with bowed heads,
insert their tablets into their belts,
hold the memorial essay,
and move the table closer.
The Géshǐ receives the memorial essay,
places it on the table,
and all bow twice.
Two Tōngshì Shèrén carry the table,
ascend the hall via the left steps,
and place it on the exposed platform.
The official who reads the memorial essay receives it,
and enters to read the memorial essay.
After it is read before the emperor,
the ministers and officials below the hall bow five times,
and bow.
The two leaders of the procession are led up the hall via the left and right steps,
and stand side-by-side within the railing.
First, the leader of the Northern faction is led slightly forward,
kneels to deliver their address,
and then retreats to their kneeling mat position.
Next, the leader of the Southern faction does the same.
When finished,
they are separately led down the hall via the left and right steps,
return to their position,
bow five times,
and bow.
The Xuānhuī announces,
"There is an imperial edict!"
They bow twice.
The reply is proclaimed:
"The internal troubles have been quelled.
We will celebrate this with you all, both internally and externally."
They express gratitude for the imperial pronouncement,
and bow five times.
The ranks are dismissed.
The ministers and officials follow the emperor,
and the imperial wives follow the empress,
to the Empress Dowager's hall.
They view the imperial portrait of the late emperor,
take their accompanying positions,
and all bow twice.
The Empress Dowager sits properly.
Congratulations are offered,
totaling ten bows.
All are led up the hall,
and a banquet is bestowed as per ritual.
Regarding the Ritual for Quelling Troubles,
in the 9th year of Dàozōng's Qīngníng era,
the imperial uncle Zhòngyuán plotted rebellion.
Rén'yì Tàihòu personally led the imperial guards to battle the rebel faction.
When the matter was settled,
this ritual was
then established.
New Year's Day Morning Audience Ceremony: Ministers and envoys from various states enter the court at dawn.
They
report, "The ranks are all present."
The Huángdì ascends to the hall and sits.
The Qìdān attendants finish announcing from the hall.
They lead the Qìdān ministers in through the east side-gate.
They lead the Hàn people's ministers and envoys from various states in through the west side-gate.
They form ranks,
dance,
bow five times,
bow,
and straighten their bodies.
They lead the Qīnwáng up the east steps to the hall.
They prostrate themselves on their kneeling mats within the railing.
They announce their full titles, "Your ministers so-and-so," and complete their felicitations.
They rise from their prostration,
withdraw,
and are led down the east steps from the hall.
They return to their positions,
dance,
finish bowing five times,
and bow.
The Xuānhuīshǐ bows in the hall.
He
reports, "Your minister will convey the reply."
He announces,
"There is an imperial edict."
After the head of the ranks and those below him listen to the decree,
they bow twice,
and bow.
The Xuānhuīshǐ transmits the announcement, saying:
"The joy of the new year
is shared with all of you."
The attendant prompts them to express gratitude for the imperial announcement.
They bow,
dance,
and bow five times.
The attendant prompts everyone to stand by.
They are led out in separate ranks.
The head of the ranks is led up the west steps to the hall.
After reporting the table of contents of the memorials,
the Jiàofāng performs a salutation,
offers congratulations,
bows twelve times,
and, upon completion,
the attendant prompts everyone to stand by.
The Qìdān and Hàn people's ministers and envoys from various states are led in through the east and west side-gates.
They form ranks,
and bow twice.
The attendant prompts the offering of wine.
The Qīnwáng are led up the east steps to the hall.
They proceed to their kneeling mats within the railing,
insert their ceremonial tablets into their belts,
hold the ceremonial goblets,
complete the offering of wine,
withdraw,
and return to their kneeling mats.
They place down the stand,
take out their ceremonial tablets,
move slightly forward and kneel in a bowed posture.
They announce their full titles, "Your ministers so-and-so, respectfully present ten thousand years of longevity wine."
They rise from their prostration,
withdraw,
and return to their kneeling mats.
They, along with the ministers below the hall, all bow twice,
and bow.
They await the Xuānhuīshǐ bowing in the hall.
He
reports, "Your minister will convey the reply."
He announces,
"There is an imperial edict."
The Qīnwáng and those below them bow twice as in the initial ceremony.
The announcement is transmitted, saying:
"I drink your longevity wine,
and share the joy with all of you, both inside and outside."
The attendant prompts thanks for the imperial announcement as before.
The attendant prompts everyone to stand by.
The Qīnwáng insert their ceremonial tablets into their belts,
and hold the stand.
The ministers below the hall separate into ranks.
The Huángdì drinks the wine.
The Jiàofāng plays music.
The ministers above and below the hall all bow,
and exclaim,
"Long live!"
The attendant prompts everyone to stand by.
The music stops.
The Jiàofāng bows twice.
The Huángdì finishes drinking.
The Qīnwáng steps forward to receive the goblet,
returns to his kneeling mat,
places down the ceremonial goblet and stand,
and takes out his ceremonial tablet.
He bows to the ministers to form ranks.
The Qīnwáng is led down the east steps from the hall.
He returns to his position,
bows,
and bows twice.
The attendant prompts everyone to stand by.
They are led out in separate ranks.
The Huángdì rises,
and proceeds to the Huángtàihòu's hall.
The ministers and envoys from various states all follow.
The Huángtàihòu ascends to the hall.
The Huángdì sits on the east side.
The Qìdān and Hàn people's ministers and envoys from various states are led in through both side-gates.
They form ranks and offer congratulations.
They offer wine,
all according to the Huángdì's ceremony.
Upon completion,
they are led out.
The Jiàofāng enters.
The salutation and offering of wine are also as before.
The Huángtàihòu transmits her reply, announcing it as
"Imperial will."
The Qìdān ranks express gratitude for the imperial banquet,
ascend to the hall, and take their standing positions.
The Hàn people's ministers and envoys from various states enter through the east side-gate.
On the vermilion steps, towards the east,
they face west and bow.
The attendant bows,
conveys that the civil and military officials, the zǎichén so-and-so, and those below express gratitude for the imperial banquet,
and they bow twice.
After stepping out of rank and presenting their address,
they withdraw and return to their positions,
dance,
and bow five times.
The attendant prompts everyone to ascend to the hall and stand by.
The zǎichén and those below, along with the vice-envoys from various states, are led,
and the ministers in the hall who sit on square cushions
ascend the west steps to the hall and take their standing positions.
The ministers who are not allowed to sit all exit through the west side-gate.
Two people supervise the goblets.
The Jiàofāng bows twice.
The attendant prompts everyone to ascend the steps.
They descend from the hall to express gratitude for the banquet,
as in the Huángtàihòu's birthday ceremony.
following the procedure of the Zhèngdàn Ceremony.
The Huángdì and the Huánghòu pay homage to the sun,
and the officials, from their accompanying positions, bow twice.
The Huángdì and the Huánghòu ascend the hall and sit.
The Qìdān Shèrén announces,
the officials enter,
assemble in formation,
the Qīnwáng offers birthday wishes,
the reply is announced,
all following the procedure of the Zhèngdàn Ceremony.
After expressing thanks,
they perform the ceremonial dance,
bow five times,
and make a deep bow.
They step out of the formation and present
"May Your Sacred Person Enjoy Ten Thousand Blessings,"
return to their positions,
bow twice,
and make a deep bow.
The head of the formation steps out,
kneels prostrate,
finishes offering birthday wishes,
rises from the prostrate position,
performs the ceremonial dance,
bows five times,
and makes a deep bow.
The Usher commands, "All wait in attendance."
They separate into formations,
but do not exit,
and assemble the formations.
The Imperial Bed is brought in,
they bow twice,
and make a deep bow.
The Usher commands the presentation of wine.
The officials stand upright.
The Qīnwáng is led up the hall via the left steps,
proceeds to the cushioned spot inside the railing,
tucks the ceremonial tablet (hù) into his belt,
holds the wine cup on a stand,
and presents the wine.
After the Huángdì and Huánghòu receive the cup,
he retreats to the cushioned spot,
sets down the stand,
takes out the hù,
and kneels prostrate.
He steps slightly forward,
announces his full rank, stating, "Your servant [Name] and others respectfully present the wine for Ten Thousand Thousand Years of Longevity."
He rises from the prostrate position,
retreats,
returns to the cushioned spot,
bows twice,
and makes a deep bow.
All officials below the hall bow twice,
and make a deep bow.
The reply is announced following the Zhèngdàn Ceremony procedure.
The Qīnwáng tucks the hù into his belt,
holds the stand,
and separates from the formation.
The Huángdì and Huánghòu drink the wine,
music is played;
all officials above and below the hall bow,
proclaiming
"Ten Thousand Years of Longevity!"
The music stops.
The Jiàofāng bows twice,
and the officials assemble in formation.
The Qīnwáng steps forward to receive the cup,
proceeds to the cushioned spot,
sets down the wine cup on the stand,
takes out the hù,
and is led down the hall via the left steps.
The Imperial Bed is removed.
The Qīnwáng returns to his position on the Dānchí,
bows twice,
and makes a deep bow.
The Usher commands, "Wait in attendance."
They separate into formations and are led out.
The head of the formation ascends the hall via the right steps to present the memorial table of contents (biǎomù) and tributes.
Tributes from all Dào are presented,
and after the Jiàofāng finishes presenting tributes,
the Usher commands the collection of the tributes.
The head of the formation performs the ceremonial dance,
bows five times,
and makes a deep bow.
The Usher commands, "All wait in attendance."
The head of the formation exits,
the officials re-enter,
assemble in formation to express thanks,
perform the ceremonial dance,
bow five times,
and make a deep bow.
The Usher commands, "All wait in attendance."
They separate into formations and are led out.
The alarm signal sounds,
the Huángdì and Huánghòu rise,
and proceed to the North Hall (Běidiàn).
The Huáng Tàihòu is at the Yùróng Diàn (Hall of the Imperial Portrait),
and together with the Huángdì and Huánghòu, leads the officials in bowing twice.
The Huáng Tàihòu offers incense,
and all bow twice.
The Usher commands, "All wait in attendance."
Those of the rank of Kě Ǎidūn and above ascend the hall.
The Huáng Tàihòu presents wine three times before the Imperial Portrait,
and those in accompanying positions all bow.
The Huáng Tàihòu ascends the hall and sits.
The Huángdì proceeds to the cushioned spot on the open platform (Lùtái),
the Qīnwáng and the officials of the Northern and Southern Administrations stand lined up inside the Dānchí.
The Huángdì bows twice,
and the officials all bow,
and make a deep bow.
The Huángdì kneels inside the railing,
finishes offering birthday wishes to the Huáng Tàihòu,
returns to his position,
and bows twice.
Whenever they bow,
they all proclaim
"Ten Thousand Years!" (Wànsuì).
The Usher commands, "All wait in attendance."
The officials do not exit,
the Huángdì and Huánghòu sit to the side,
the Qīnwáng presents wine,
the officials accompany in bowing,
the Huáng Tàihòu announces the reply,
all following the procedure of the Zhèngdàn Ceremony.
The officials separate into formations,
but do not exit.
The head of the formation ascends the hall via the right steps to present the memorial table of contents (biǎomù),
they assemble in formation to thank for the announced feast,
ascend the hall, and take their places according to custom.
The Imperial Bed is brought in.
The Huángdì presents wine to the Huáng Tàihòu as before,
each proceeds to their seat to circulate the wine,
and a full drink is announced,
following the Huáng Tàihòu’s Shēngchén Ceremony procedure.
The Huánghòu presents wine,
following the Huángdì’s procedure.
Wine is presented three times,
tea is circulated,
the Jiàofāng offers felicitous remarks,
side dishes and meals are circulated,
the grand feast is served,
and wine is presented seven times.
The musical piece concludes (Qǔpò),
the officials rise,
the Imperial Bed is removed,
thanks for the feast are offered,
all following the Huáng Tàihòu’s Shēngchén Ceremony.
Lìchūn (Beginning of Spring) Ceremony: The Huángdì exits and proceeds to the Inner Hall (Nèidiàn),
pays homage to the portrait of the Former Emperor (Xiāndì),
and the officials of the Northern and Southern Administrations assemble in formation inside the Dānchí,
and bow twice.
Those of the rank of Kě Ǎidūn and above enter the hall,
and are granted seats.
The Dì presents wine before the Imperial Portrait,
and those in accompanying positions and standing attendants all bow twice.
After one presentation of wine,
the officials descend the hall,
and stand facing each other on the left and right.
The Huángdì wears the silk banner ornament (fānshèng),
and fānshèng are granted according to rank.
After the officials finish pinning them,
the Huángdì offers incense before the Clay Ox (Tǔniú),
pours wine three times,
but does not bow.
The Jiàofāng starts the music,
and the Shìyíshǐ (Usher of Ceremonies) kneels to present the decorated rod (cǎizhàng).
The Huángdì whips the Tǔniú,
and those of the rank of Kě Ǎidūn and above, being officials of the Northern and Southern Administrations, assemble in formation inside the Dānchí,
kneel on the left knee,
receive the cǎizhàng,
stand straight up,
and bow twice.
The Usher commands, "All wait in attendance."
The Sīchén (Time Official) reports that spring has arrived,
and whips the Tǔniú three circuits.
The Ǎidūn ceases whipping,
and the Jiédùshǐ (Military Commissioner) and those above him are led up the hall,
scatter grain and beans,
and strike the Tǔniú.
When the grain and beans are scattered,
the crowd is permitted to scramble for them.
The officials sit according to their positions,
wine is circulated twice,
and the Spring Platter (chūnpán) is brought in.
After the wine is circulated three times,
tea is circulated.
All rise.
The ceremony is concluded.
Dūanwǔ Yí (Ritual for the Double Fifth): On the designated day,
the ministers and officials proceed to the imperial tent at dawn.
The Huángdì (Emperor) ties a long-life colored thread and ascends to sit in the chariot.
The northern and southern ministers and officials are led to form ranks,
following the ritual of the Dānchí (Vermilion Terrace).
The relevant department grants each person a thread of longevity.
The ministers and officials bow, kneel to receive it,
and perform the repeated kowtow.
They are led to retire.
They follow the carriage to the dining area,
where three rounds of wine are served.
If a feast is to be granted,
it depends on the imperial decree at that time.
Chóngjiǔ Yí (Ritual for the Double Ninth): The northern and southern ministers and officials proceed to the imperial tent at dawn.
They follow the carriage to the hunting enclosure,
and are granted tea.
The Huángdì takes his seat,
and the ministers and officials are led to stand in ranks before the emperor.
The relevant department grants each person chrysanthemum wine.
They kneel to receive it
and perform the repeated kowtow.
After three rounds of wine,
they are signaled to rise.
Cángjiū Yí (Ritual for Drawing Lots): On the designated day,
the northern and southern ministers and officials enter the court in casual attire.
The Huángdì presides at the Tiānxiáng Diàn.
The ministers and officials are granted seats according to their rank.
The Qìdān (Khitan) face south,
and the Hàn people face north.
They divide into groups to draw lots.
There are sometimes five or sometimes seven tallies.
A meal is granted.
After the meal is finished,
everyone rises.
After a moment,
they sit down again to draw lots as before.
In the evening, tea is granted,
with three or five tallies.
The Jiàofāng (Music Bureau) performance ceases.
If the Emperor draws the lot,
the ministers and officials offer wine,
and then wine is granted to them in sequence.
This ritual was first performed on the twenty-second day of the twelfth month of
the tenth year of Dàkāng (1084 CE).
On this day, the court is not held.
Suìshí Záyí (Various Rites Throughout the Year):
On Zhēngdàn (New Year's Day),
it is the national custom to make cakes from glutinous rice mixed with white sheep marrow,
rolling them into balls the size of a fist.
Forty-nine pieces are granted to each tent.
At midnight,
everyone inside their tent throws a ball out through the window.
If the number is even,
music is played,
and they drink and feast.
If the number is odd,
twelve shamans are ordered to ring bells,
hold arrows,
and sing and shout around the tent.
Inside the tent, they explode salt in a brazier
and burn the ground to beat mice.
This is called "frightening the ghosts,"
and they stay inside for seven days before coming out.
The national language calls Zhēngdàn
"nǎi niē yī āi."
"Nǎi"
means "orthodox" (zhèng);
"niē yī āi"
means "dawn" (dàn).
On Lìchūn (Beginning of Spring),
women present spring scrolls (chūnshū),
and carve green silk into pennants,
shaping them like dragons to wear;
or they make them into toads.
The pennant scroll reads
"Yí Chūn" (Suitable for Spring).
Rénrì (Day of Man):
Of the days of the first lunar month,
the first is the day of the chicken, the second the dog, the third the boar, the fourth the sheep, the fifth the horse, the sixth the ox,
and the seventh day is the day of man.
For its divination,
clear weather is auspicious,
and cloudy weather is disastrous.
It is the custom to fry pancakes and eat them in the courtyard,
which is called
"Xūn Tiān" (Scenting the Heaven).
The first day of the second month is the Zhōnghé Jié (Central Harmony Festival).
The Guójiù (Imperial Maternal Relatives), the Xiāo clan, host a banquet
to receive the Guó Zú (Imperial Clan), the Yēlǜ clan.
This is done annually as a custom.
In the national language, this day is called
"li pǒ."
"Li"
means "to request" (qǐng);
"pǒ"
means "time/season" (shí).
The character [the first character],
is pronounced like xiá;
the character [the second character],
is pronounced like pǒ.
The eighth day of the second month is the birthday of Xīdá Tàizǐ (Prince Siddhārtha).
The capital prefecture and various circuits carve wooden images.
With honor guards and various performances leading the way,
they proceed around the city for entertainment.
Prince Siddhārtha
was the prince of Jìngfàn (Śuddhodana) in the Western Regions,
whose surname was Qútán (Gautama),
and personal name Shìjiāmóuní (Śākyamuni).
Because of his awakened nature,
he is called
"Fó" (Buddha).
The third day of the third month is Shàngsì (Upper Third).
It is the national custom
to carve wood into rabbits,
and divide into groups to race horses and shoot at them.
The group that hits first wins.
The losing group dismounts, kneels in a line, and offers wine.
The winning group drinks it on horseback.
The national language calls this day
"táo lǐ huà."
"Táo lǐ"
means "rabbit" (tù);
"huà"
means "to shoot" (shè).
On the Double Fifth of the fifth month,
at noon,
mugwort leaves are gathered, mixed with cotton, and sewn into clothing.
Seven items are presented to the Son of Heaven.
The northern and southern ministers and officials are each granted three items.
The ruler and subjects feast and enjoy themselves.
The Bóhǎi chefs present mugwort cakes.
Colored silk thread is twisted into ropes and wrapped around the arms,
which is called
"Héhuān Jié" (Joyful Union Knot).
Colored silk is also twisted to form human figures and worn as hairpins,
which is called
"Chángmìng Lǚ" (Longevity Thread).
The national language calls this day
"tǎo sài yī āi."
"Tǎo"
means "five" (wǔ);
"sài yī āi"
means "month" (yuè).
The day of Xiàzhì (Summer Solstice)
is popularly called
"Cháojié" (Court Festival).
Women present colored fans
and give each other sachets of powder and rouge.
On the eighteenth day of the sixth month,
it is the national custom
for the Yēlǜ clan to host a banquet
to receive the Guójiù, the Xiāo clan.
It is also called
"li pǒ."
On the thirteenth day of the seventh month,
at night,
the Son of Heaven pitches a tent thirty lǐ west of the palace and lodges there.
Before the appointed day,
wine and provisions are prepared.
The next day,
all the accompanying armies and tribes play barbarian music,
drinking and feasting until dusk.
Then they return to the traveling palace.
This is called
"Yíng Jié" (Welcoming the Festival).
On the fifteenth day, Zhōngyuán (Mid-Year Festival),
Chinese music is played,
and a grand banquet is held.
At dawn on the sixteenth day,
they return west.
The accompanying armies and tribes all shout loudly three times.
This is called
"Sòng Jié" (Sending Off the Festival).
In the national language, it is called
"sài yī āi shē."
"Shē"
means "good" (hǎo).
On the eighth day of the eighth month,
it is the national custom
to slaughter a white dog
and bury it seven paces in front of the sleeping tent,
leaving its snout exposed.
Seven days later, on Zhōngqiū (Mid-Autumn),
the sleeping tent is moved directly over it.
In the national language, it is called
"niē hè nài."
"Niē hè"
means "dog" (quǎn);
"nài"
means "head" (shǒu).
On the ninth day of the ninth month, which is the Double Ninth,
the Son of Heaven led his assembled ministers and tribal groups to shoot tigers.
The one who scored the fewest was deemed the loser,
and was penalized by hosting the Double Ninth banquet.
After the shooting was finished,
they selected high ground and pitched tents,
and bestowed upon the Fān (tribal) and Hàn (Chinese) officials chrysanthemum wine to drink.
Rabbit liver was prepared as preserved meat ('ní'),
and deer tongue as relish ('jiàng').
They also ground Cornus wine
and sprinkled it on doors and windows for protection and exorcism.
The national language calls this day
“Bìlǐ Chílí”,
which is the ninth day of the ninth month.
In the tenth month of the year,
the Five Capitals submitted 10,000 sets of small paper-made armor, spears, swords, and weaponry.
On the fifteenth day,
the Son of Heaven and his assembled ministers performed a distant sacrifice to Mùyè Shān.
They used written reports ('shū zhuàng') in the national script,
and subsequently burned them.
The national language calls this
“Dàlà”.
“Dài”
means to burn;
“là”
means armor.
On the day of the Winter Solstice,
it was the national custom
to slaughter white sheep, white horses, and white geese.
The blood of each was taken and mixed with wine,
and the Son of Heaven bowed towards Hēishān (Black Mountain) from afar.
Hēishān is located north of the border.
The custom holds that the souls and spirits of the people of the nation
are guarded by its deity,
just like Dàizōng (Mount Tài) in the Central Plains, it is said.
Every year on this day,
the Five Capitals submitted over 10,000 paper artifacts of people and horses,
which were sacrificed to the mountain and burned.
The custom was extremely solemn and fearful;
no one dared approach the mountain unless for the sacrifice.
On the day of the Làyīn (Winter Sacrifice),
the Son of Heaven led his officials from the north and south, all dressed in military attire,
and held court late at night ('wù yè').
They performed music and drank wine,
and bestowed armor, weapons, sheep, and horses according to rank.
The national language calls this day
“Chǎowǔ Érpuó”.
“Chǎowǔ Ér”
means war.
Rites of Rebirth: Every twelve years,
in the final winter month of the year preceding the Emperor’s natal year ('běn mìng'),
an auspicious day was selected.
Prior to this date,

ground was cleared north of the palace gate to set up the Chamber of Rebirth ('Zàishēng Shì'), the Chamber of the Empress Dowager ('Mǔhòu Shì'), and the carriage bearing the spirit tablet of the former Emperor ('Xiāndì Shénzhǔ Yú').
To the southeast of the Chamber of Rebirth,
a three-forked tree was planted upside down.
On that day,
a young boy and the birth-attendant matron ('chǎnyī yù') were placed inside the chamber.
One woman held wine,
and one old man held a quiver with arrows ('shǐ bō'),
standing outside the chamber.
The officials requested the spirit tablet to descend from the carriage
and offered sacrifices.
After the sacrifices were completed,
the Emperor exited his sleeping hall
and proceeded to the Chamber of Rebirth.
The assembled ministers welcomed him,
bowing twice.
The Emperor entered the chamber,
removed his clothes, and went barefoot.
With the young boy following him,
he passed under the forked tree three times.
Each time he passed,
the birth-attendant matron offered an address
and wiped and purified the Emperor’s body.
The young boy passed under the forked tree seven times.
The Emperor lay down beside the tree,
and the old man struck the quiver ('fú') and said:
“A son has been born.”
The Chief Shaman ('Tài Wū') covered the Emperor’s head.
He rose,
and the assembled ministers offered congratulations,
bowing twice.
The birth-attendant matron received wine from the woman holding the wine and presented it.
The Chief Shaman presented the swaddling clothes, silk knots, and other items, praising and offering prayers.
Seven old men had been previously selected.
Each wrote an imperial name ('yù míng') and attached it to a silk ribbon.
They all knelt and presented them.
The Emperor selected a laudable name and accepted it,
and bestowed gifts upon them.
They bowed twice
and withdrew.
All the assembled ministers then presented swaddling clothes, silk knots, and other items.
The Emperor bowed to the portraits of the former Emperors
and subsequently held a banquet for the assembled ministers.
How excellent
was Zhǔwǔ Kèhán's instructions bequeathed to his descendants!
There is no child who does not admire their parents;
but when desires deepen, love shallows,
and once wives and children are present, filial piety
declines.
This is true for everyone,
how much more so for the Son of Heaven?
The Rites of Rebirth,
performed once every twelve years,
compelled the Son of Heaven to perform this ceremony
to awaken his filial heart.
If
he embodies it truly,
then his reflection on it will be earnest.
The admiration of a child
will naturally well up from the depths of his heart.
The subtlety of this inspiration
is something that
cannot be achieved by mere spoken or written words.
How excellent
was Zhǔwǔ Kèhán's instructions bequeathed to his descendants!
Beginning with passing under the forked tree three times—
how could one not reflect on the toil and labor of the mother?
Concluding
with bowing to the portraits of the former Emperors—
how should one revere and maintain the ancestral temple?
The Odes say:
“Think of your ancestor,
and cultivate his virtue.”
Treatise Twenty-three: Treatise on Music
The Liáo had National Music ('Guó Yuè'),
Elegant Music ('Yǎ Yuè'),
Great Music ('Dà Yuè'),
Miscellaneous Music ('Sǎn Yuè'),
and Military Music ('Náogē Héngchuī Yuè').
The Old History states that Shèngzōng and Xīngzōng were both proficient in musical theory,
but records of the melodies, lyrics, and dance movements
—though sought from the Tàicháng (Court of Imperial Sacrifices), Yífèng (Imperial Music Bureau), and Jiàofāng (Music Academy)—could not be obtained.
We consulted the Annals, Treatises, and Miscellaneous Rites of the Liáo court,
referred to historical records,
and determined what could be known
to fill the gap in documentation for this dynasty.
Alas!
The music of Xián, Sháo, Xià, and Wǔ—
the sounds are lost and the scores dispersed.
When Hèjiān composed his record,
Sǐ Qiān merely used it for his book,
leaving a vast emptiness—how rare is completeness!
Observing the music of the Liáo is sufficient based on this.
National Music
The Liáo had National Music,
which resembled the customs ('fēng') of the ancient kings;
and their music of the various nations ('zhū guó yuè')
resembled the customs of the feudal lords.
Therefore, we record a summary.
On the first day of the first month, during the morning court greetings,
the Elegant Music with court chimes ('Gōng Xuán Yǎ Yuè') was used.
At the Grand Assembly ('Yuán Huì'),
the Great Music was used;
after the main tune ('qǔ pò'),
the Miscellaneous Music was used;
and wrestling ('jiǎo dǐ') concluded the event.
That night,
when the Emperor held a feast,
the National Music was used.
On the thirteenth day of the seventh month,
the Emperor traveled thirty lǐ from the traveling palace and pitched tents.
On the fourteenth day, a banquet was held,
and the accompanying troops followed the various tribes in performing music.
On the fifteenth day (Zhōngyuán Festival),
a grand banquet was held,
and music was used.
In the spring, during the release of the geese at Xìngguō,
when the Emperor shot and captured the lead goose,
it was offered to the ancestral temple during the feast.
Several dozen musicians played small instruments to accompany the wine.
Music of the Various Nations
In the third year of Hùitóng (Tàizōng’s reign),
when the Jìn Commissioners of the Privy Council, Yáng Duān and Wáng Tiǎo, and envoys from various nations came to pay court,
the Emperor held a banquet in the temporary palace ('Biàndiàn').
Duān and Tiǎo rose to propose a toast
and performed songs and dances.
The Emperor raised his cup for them and rejoiced greatly.
On the Duānwǔ day of the third year of Hùitóng,
all officials and envoys from the various nations offered congratulations.
A feast was held according to the established form,
and the envoys from Huíhú and Dūnhuáng were commanded to perform the dances of their respective nations.
Tiānzuò [Di]ānqìng’s second year,
the imperial carriage went on tour to the Hùntóng Jiāng.
At the banquet for the first fish,
being half drunk,
the Emperor commanded the various chieftains to take turns singing and dancing for entertainment.
The Nǚzhí Wánýán Āgǔdǎ stood straight and looked directly,
excusing himself by saying he could not.
The Emperor said to Xiāo Fèngxiān:
“Āgǔdǎ’s spirit and vigor are heroic and bold;
his gaze is unusual.
You could entrust him with border affairs and then execute him.
If not,
I fear he will become a future disaster.”
Fèngxiān responded:
“Āgǔdǎ has no major faults.
Killing him would injure the intention of those who turn toward transformation.
Merely a tiny country,
what trouble could it possibly cause?”
Regarding court music (yǎyuè):
From the Hàn dynasty onward,
the yǎyuè was inherited sequentially.
There were ancient eulogies (sòng) in it,
and there were ancient greater ōdes (Dàyǎ) in it.
The Liáo court lacked sòng music for suburban and temple rites.
In Dàtóng’s first year,
Tàizōng, returning from Biàn,
obtained the Tàicháng music scores, court suspension racks, and instrument stands of the Jìn dynasty.
He entrusted the relevant office to transport them first to the Central Capital (Zhōngjīng).
In Shèngzōng’s Tàipíng first year,
for the ceremony of honoring the imperial title: court suspension racks were set up in the palace courtyard.
The signal flag positions were placed on the western steps of the third tier of the palace.
The assistants to the Director of Music (Xiélǜ Láng) each entered and took up their signal flag positions.
The Tàicháng Doctoral Scholars (Bóshì) led the Tàicháng Minister (Qīng);
the Tàicháng Qīng led the Emperor.
When the imperial guard was about to move,
the Xiélǜ Láng raised the signal flag,
the Director of Grand Music (Tàiyuè Lìng) commanded the striking of the Huángzhōng bell,
and the left and right bells all responded.
The musicians raised the wooden music box (zhù),
and the music began;
when the Emperor took the imperial seat,
the screen was closed,
and the music stopped.
When the princes and dukes entered the gate,
the music began;
when they reached their positions,
the music stopped.
The attendant officials (Tōngshì Shèrén) led the minister who sealed the documents (yācè dàchén).
At the initial movement,
the music began;
after placing the documents on the incense table in front of the palace,
and taking their position,
the music stopped.
When the officials carrying the documents (yúcè guān) presented the documents,
at the initial movement,
the music began;
they ascended the palace,
placed the documents in front of the imperial seat,
and took their positions north of the west wall,
and the music stopped.
When the ministers ascended the palace,
the music began;
when they reached their positions inside the palace railing,
the music stopped.
When the ministers descended the palace steps,
the music began;
when they returned to their positions,
the music stopped.
When the princes and dukes of the third rank and above exited,
the music began;
the Tàicháng Bóshì led the Tàicháng Qīng,
and the Tàicháng Qīng led the Emperor to descend from the imperial seat and enter the side chamber,
and the music stopped.
In Xīngzōng’s Chóngxī ninth year,
during the ceremony of presenting the imperial documents to the Qìdān,
when the Emperor exited,
the Lóng’ān music was played.
In Shèngzōng’s Tǒnghé first year,
during the enthronement ceremony for Empress Dowager Chéngtiān:
court suspension racks were set up,
and instrument stands (xǔnjù).
Musicians of the Grand Music and Xiélǜ Láng entered.
When the Empress Dowager’s ceremonial guard moved,
the signal flag was raised,
and the Tàihé music began;
the Tàiyuè Lìng and Tàicháng Qīng led her to ascend to the imperial seat,
the curtain was rolled up,
and the music stopped.
When the civil and military officials of the third rank and above entered,
the Shūhé music began;
when they reached their positions,
the music stopped.
When the Emperor entered the gate,
the Yōnghé music began;
when he reached his position in front of the palace,
the music stopped.
When the chancellor sealed the documents (yācè),
and the Emperor followed the documents,
the music began;
when the documents were placed on the table in front of the palace,
the music stopped.
When the Academicians of the Hànlín Academy and the Grand Generals carried the documents,
the music began;
when they placed them in front of the imperial seat,
the music stopped.
When the Chancellor ascended the palace,
the music began;
when he reached the position for reading the documents,
the music stopped.
When the Emperor descended the palace,
the music began;
when he reached his position,
the music stopped.
After the Empress Dowager finished proclaiming her reply,
the music began;
when the Emperor reached the west side chamber,
the music stopped.
When the imperial princes and chancellor ascended the palace,
the music began;
when they retreated and exited the ranks,
the music stopped.
When the curtain was lowered,
the music began;
when the Empress Dowager entered the interior,
the music stopped.
The ceremony for the enthronement of the Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ): when the Crown Prince first entered the gate,
the Zhēn’ān music began.
Arrangement of musicians for the enthronement ceremony music:
in the four corners, one vertical drum (jiàngǔ) was placed, with one musician for each;
for the court suspension racks, nine sets were on each side,
with one musician for each set;
near the north of the instrument stands, one zhù and one yǔ (a tiger-shaped instrument scraped with a bamboo whisk) were placed,
with one musician for each;
inside the instrument stands sat the chamber ensemble musicians,
102 people on the left and 102 on the right;
southwest of the instrument stands were 64 military dancers,
and two people holding small flags;
southeast of the instrument stands were 64 civil dancers,
and two people holding small flags;
two Xiélǜ Láng;
one Tàiyuè Lìng.
The twelve Hé music pieces of the Táng dynasty
were used in the early Liáo: Yùhé for sacrificing to the celestial deities,
Shùnhé for sacrificing to the terrestrial deities,
Yǒnghé for offering sacrifices to the ancestral temples,
Sùhé for the ascending song and presenting jade and silk,
Yōnghé for entering the sacrificial vessels and welcoming the spirits,
Shòuhé for pouring libations and drinking with the spirits,
Tàihé for regulating ascent and descent,
Shūhé for regulating entry and exit,
Zhāohé for raising the cup of wine,
Xiūhé for offering cooked rice,
Zhènghé for the Empress receiving the imperial documents and proceeding,
Chénghé for the Crown Prince proceeding.
The twelve Ān music pieces of the Liáo: Initially,
the Liáng dynasty changed the Táng’s twelve Hé music pieces to the Nine Qìng music.
Later, the Hòu Táng dynasty established the Táng ancestral temples,
and still used the twelve Hé music pieces.
The Jìn dynasty changed them to the Twelve Tóng music pieces.
Miscellaneous rites of the Liáo:
“When the Son of Heaven enters or exits,
Lóng’ān is played;
when the Crown Prince proceeds,
Zhēn’ān is played.”
This means that the Liáo dynasty had at one time changed the names of the music pieces.
The names of the remaining ten Ān music pieces are missing.
The lyrics of the Liáo court music songs
are incomplete due to missing text;
the number of instruments in the eight sound categories
largely followed the old system of the Táng.
The eight sound categories: Metal:
Bó bell, Zhōng bell. Stone: Qíu jade chime, Qìng stone chime.
Silk: Qín zither, Sè zither.
Bamboo: Yuè transverse flute, Xiāo vertical flute, Chí transverse flute.
Gourd: Shēng mouth organ, Yú mouth organ.
Earth: Xūn ocarina.
Skin: Gǔ drum, Táo pellet drum.
Wood: Zhù wooden music box, Yǔ wooden tiger scraper.
The twelve pitch pipes (lǜ) used a pipe of nine inches, according to the Zhōu dynasty millet rule,
with a hollow diameter of three fen as the standard.
During Dàozōng’s Dàkāng era,
an imperial decree ordered the implementation of the measure for sheng and dou determined by the black millet (jùshǔ),
and fixed the pitch pipes.
This method largely employed the ancient pitch system.
Regarding Grand Music (dàyuè):
Since the Hàn dynasty,
the Music Bureau (Yuèfǔ) was established based on the sounds of Qín and Chǔ.
Reaching the time of Suí Gāozǔ, he issued a decree seeking those who understood music.
Zhèng Yì obtained the seven-tone (qīdàn) music of Sū Zhībō from the Western Regions.
He sought to harmonize the theory of seven notes and eighty-four modes (bāshísì diào).
From then on, both court and popular music
followed this system.
The music used in the court,
which was distinct from the court music (yǎyuè),
was called Grand Music (dàyuè).

Grand Musical Instruments: Originally they derived from the Qīdé and Jiǔgōng music of Táng Tàizōng.
Wǔ Hòu destroyed the Táng Imperial Ancestral Temple,
and the Qīdé and Jiǔgōng music and dances were consequently lost.
Thereafter, the ancestral temple used the two dances of Suí Wén and Wǔ.
The court used Gāozōng's Jǐngyún Yuè to replace them;
during the Grand Assemblage,
the first piece performed was the Jǐngyún Yuè dance.
Dù Yòu's Tōngdiǎn already stated that all other music was lost,
and only the Jǐngyún Yuè dance barely survived.
After the turmoil of the late Táng and Five Dynasties periods,
those surviving pieces were few.
The Grand Music of the Liáo state
was transmitted from the Jìn Dynasty.
Although the Miscellaneous Rites show 102 sitting musicians on both the left and right,
this was likely due to filling the ranks of the sitting section with remaining Jǐngyún performers;
as for the Sitting and Standing Music divisions,
they had been lost since the Táng Dynasty,
and only the Jǐngyún four-part dance music can be examined.

Grand Music Modes: Court music has seven notes (Qī Yīn),
Grand Music also has seven notes (Qī Shēng),
called the Qī Dàn: First is Suōlì,
the level tone (Píng Shēng);
Second is Jīshí,
the long tone (Cháng Shēng);
Third is Shāshí,
the plain, straight tone (Zhìzhí Shēng);
Fourth is Shāhóu Jiālàn,
the responsive tone (Yīng Shēng);
Fifth is Shālā,
the responsive and harmonious tone (Yīnghé Shēng);
Sixth is Bānzhàn,
the five tones (Wǔ Shēng);
Seventh is Sìlì
the Húniú tone.
Since the Suí Dynasty,
the Music Bureau adopted these notes,
forming the Grand Music with four Dàn and twenty-eight modes (Diào).
