Above are the four Dàn and twenty-eight modes.
They do not use the Míllét measurement (shǔlǜ),
but are matched using Pípá strings.
All proceed from turbid to clear,
changing their sounds successively,
lower notes are more turbid,
higher notes are clearer.
There are seven times seven, forty-nine modes,
but the remaining twenty-one modes have lost their transmission.
They supposedly originated from the Qiūcí Bù of the Jiǔ Bù Yuè.
Grand Music Notes: Within each mode,
when composing tunes and harmonizing sounds,
there are ten notes (Shēng),
named: Wǔ, Fán, Gōng, Chǐ, Shàng, Yī, Sì, Liù, Gōu, Hé.
They approximate the twelve orthodox pitches (Yǎ Lǜ),
lacking one note from each of the Lǜ and Lǚ,
just as the court music (Yǎ Yīn) falls short of the Shāng mode.
Informal Music (Sǎnyuè)
The Yīn people created decadent music (Mǐmǐ zhī Yuè),
whose sound goes forth and does not return,
flowing into the music of Zhèng and Wèi.
Between the Qín and Hàn
dynasties, the music of Qín and Chǔ arose,
and the music of Zhèng and Wèi gradually faded.
Hàn Wǔdì appointed Lǐ Yánnián to manage the Music Bureau (Yuèfǔ),
gradually incorporating the sounds of Xīliáng.
Today's Sǎnyuè,
with actors, singing, and dancing presented together,
often retains echoes of the Hàn Yuèfǔ.
In the third year of the Tiānfú
era of Jìn, Liú Xù was sent with court musicians to submit (to Liáo).
The Liáo state thus acquired Sǎnyuè,
originating from this.
Liáo Protocol for Installing an Empress: They presented various performances (Bǎixì), wrestling (Juédǐ), and horse-play as entertainment.
The sequence of music for the Emperor's birthday: During the first round of drinks, the Bìlì begins,
followed by singing.
During the second round of drinks, there is singing,
and hand performers enter.
During the third round of drinks, the Pípá is played solo.
Cakes, tea, and formal felicitations (Zhì Yǔ).
Food enters,
and Zájù (variety plays) are presented.
The fourth round of drinks is omitted (Què).
During the fifth round of drinks, the Shēng is played solo,
and the drum and flute performers advance.
During the sixth round of drinks, the Zhēng is played solo,
followed by Cùqiú (kickball).
During the seventh round of drinks, the melody is interrupted by singing (Gēqǔ Pò),
followed by Juédǐ (wrestling).
The sequence of music for the celebratory banquet for the envoy of the Sòng Guó: During the first round of drinks, the Bìlì begins,
followed by singing.
During the second round of drinks, there is singing.
During the third round of drinks, there is singing,
and hand performers enter.
During the fourth round of drinks, the Pípá is played solo.
Cakes, tea, and formal felicitations (Zhì Yǔ).
Food enters,
and Zájù (variety plays) are presented.
The fifth round of drinks is omitted (Què).
During the sixth round of drinks, the Shēng is played solo,
followed by harmonized tunes (Héfǎ Qǔ).
During the seventh round of drinks, the Zhēng is played solo.
During the eighth round of drinks, there is singing,
followed by Jījià Yuè (instrumental rack music).
During the ninth round of drinks, there is singing,
followed by Juédǐ (wrestling).
Sǎn Yuè (popular entertainment/secular music),
using the three tones to embody the meaning of the Three Powers (Sāncái),
and the four sounds to regulate the vital energy of the four seasons,
corresponding to the number of the twelve pipes.
Bamboos are cut to make four-holed flutes (dí),
in order to harmonize the notes and sounds,
and they are accompanied by stringed instruments and singing.
The three tones (Sān Yīn) are: the tone of Heaven (Tiān Yīn) is ascending (Yáng),
the tone of Earth (Dì Yīn) is suppressed (Yì),
the tone of Man (Rén Yīn) is central (Zhōng),
all of which have sound but no formal notation (Wén).
The four seasons (Sì Shí): the sound of spring is called Level (Píng),
the sound of summer is called Rising (Shàng),
the sound of autumn is called Departing (Qù),
and the sound of winter is called Entering (Rù).
Instruments of Sǎn Yuè: Bìlì, Xiāo, Dí, Shēng, Pípá, Wǔxián, Kōnghóu, Zhēng, Fāngxiǎng, Zhànggǔ, Second Drum, Third Drum, Yāogǔ, Dàgǔ, Kòng, and Pāibǎn.
Variety performances (Zá Xì): Starting from Qí Jǐng Gōng employing singers, actors, and dwarves,
up to Hàn Wǔ Dì establishing the Yúlóng Mànyán performances,
and in the Later Hàn dynasty having rope dancers and self-disemboweling acts (Zì Kū zhī Jì),
Dù Yòu considered many of these to be magic tricks (Huànshù),
all originating from the Western Regions (Xīyù).
Being vulgar, rustic, and improper (Wā Lǐ Bù Jīng),
they are therefore not described in detail.
Gǔchuī Yuè (Drum and Wind Music)
Gǔchuī Yuè,
also called Duǎnxiāo Náogē Yuè (Short Flute and Cymbals Music),
has existed since the Hàn dynasty,
and is referred to as military music (Jūn Yuè).
In the miscellaneous rites of the Liáo dynasty,
during court assemblies, twelve stands (àn) featuring bears and brown bears (Xióng Pí) were set up;
the imperial carriage (Fǎ Jià) had front and rear Gǔchuī sections,
and the Lǔbù (honor guard) of all officials also included Gǔchuī Yuè.
Front Section (Qián Bù): Two Gǔchuī Lìng (Commanders of Drum and Wind Music),
twelve Gānggǔ (shoulder drums),
twelve Jīnzhēng (metal gongs),
one hundred twenty Dàgǔ (large drums),
one hundred twenty Chángmíng (long-sounding horns),
twelve Náocymbals,
twelve Gǔ (drums),
twenty-four singers (gē),
twenty-four Guǎn (pipes),
twenty-four Xiāo (vertical flutes),
and twenty-four Jiā (reeds/horns).
Rear Section (Hòu Bù): Two Gǔchuī Chéng (Assistants of Drum and Wind Music),
one hundred twenty Dàjiǎo (large horns),
twelve Yǔbǎo (feathered canopies),
twelve Gǔ (drums),
twenty-four Guǎn (pipes),
twenty-four Xiāo (vertical flutes),
twelve Náocymbals,
twelve Gǔ (drums),
twenty-four Xiāo (vertical flutes),
and twenty-four Jiā (reeds/horns).
The aforementioned front and rear Gǔchuī
are played to precede the imperial carriage when traveling,
but during court assemblies, they form ranks
and are displayed but not played.
Héngchuī Yuè (Transverse Flute Music)
Héngchuī is also military music (Jūn Yuè),
used together with Gǔchuī but organized into separate sections,
and both are overseen by the Gǔchuī Lìng.
Front Section (Qián Bù): One hundred twenty Dà Héngchuī (large transverse flutes),
two Jiégǔ (time-keeping drums),
twenty-four Dí (flutes),
twenty-four Bìlì (oboes),
twenty-four Jiā (reeds/horns),
twenty-four Táopí Bìlì (peach-bark oboes),
twelve Gānggǔ (shoulder drums),
twelve Jīnzhēng (metal gongs),
one hundred twenty Xiǎogǔ (small drums),
one hundred twenty Zhōngmíng (middle-sounding horns),
twelve Yǔbǎo (feathered canopies),
twelve Gǔ (drums),
twenty-four Guǎn (pipes),
twenty-four Xiāo (vertical flutes),
and twenty-four Jiā (reeds/horns).
Rear Section (Hòu Bù): One hundred twenty-four Xiǎo Héngchuī (small transverse flutes),
twenty-four Dí (flutes),
twenty-four Xiāo (vertical flutes),
twenty-four Bìlì (oboes),
and twenty-four Táopí Bìlì (peach-bark oboes).
The Gǔchuī and Héngchuī Yuè for the various officials,
starting from the fourth rank (sì pǐn) and above,
each had variations in additions and subtractions,
as seen in the Yíwèi Zhì (Treatise on Ceremonial Guard).
Since the decline of the Zhōu dynasty,
the music of the former kings gradually disappeared and became incomplete,
and the melodies of Zhōu Nán transformed into the airs of Qín Fēng.
When the First Emperor (Shǐ Huáng) possessed the realm,
the sounds of Zhèng, Wèi, Qín, Yān, Zhào, and Chǔ successively advanced,
and the elegant music (Yǎ Shēng) was lost.
During the prosperity of the Hàn and Táng dynasties,
civil affairs mostly employed Western music (Xī Yīn),
which became Dà Yuè (Grand Music) and Sǎn Yuè (Secular Music);
martial affairs all employed Northern music (Běi Yīn),
which became Gǔchuī and Héngchuī Yuè.
As for the elegant music (Yǎ Yuè) that remained,
its instruments were refined,
but its sound was also considered Western.
Treatise Twenty-Four: Treatise on Ceremonial Guard One (Yíwèi Zhì Yī)
Liáo Tàizǔ rose up from Shuòfāng,
and Tàizōng continued his aspiration and completed his work,
thereby establishing the dynasty's foundation.
Consequently, they conquered Bóhǎi,
established Jìng Táng (Shí Jìng Táng),
defeated Chóng Guì (Shí Chóng Guì),
and acquired all the remaining material civilization (Wénwù) from the Zhōu, Qín, the two Hàn dynasties, Suí, and Táng dynasties and occupied them.
They used imperial carriages (Lùchē) and ritual artifacts (Fǎwù) to emphasize hierarchical prestige,
and golden tallies (Jīnfú) and jade seals (Yùxǐ) to issue commands.
Thus, it was passed down through nine rulers for over two hundred years.
How could this rely solely on the advantage of weapons
and the strength of soldiers and horses?
The civil aspects are called Ceremony (Yí),
the martial aspects are called Guard (Wèi);
these were sufficient to complete the institutional structure of a dynasty.
An examination of all the carriages and robes (Yúfú), tallies and seals (Fúxǐ), and ceremonial weapons (Yízhàng) possessed by the Liáo,
forms the basis of the Yíwèi Zhì.
Carriages and Robes (Yúfú)
Since the time of Huáng Dì (the Yellow Emperor),
the system of carriages and robes
has a long history.
Yǔ rode the four kinds of transport and created the small cart (Xiǎochē);
the Shāng people, upon receiving the auspicious sign of the mulberry root, created the Grand Carriage (Dà Lù);
the Zhōu people added gold and jade,
and the ornamentation and decoration became more elaborate.
The Qín acquired the ceremonial objects of the six states
and differentiated their uses,
but the systems of the former kings
were set aside and not employed.
By the middle of the Hàn dynasty,
they eagerly studied antiquity;
however, regarding ritual affairs,
the names remained but the substance was lost,
perhaps retaining only one or two percent.
The carriages of the Táng dynasty followed the inherited systems of the Zhōu and Suí dynasties,
the additions and subtractions of which are recognizable.
Their sacrificial robes were all cyan (Qīng),
their court robes were all crimson (Jiàng),
and their everyday wear followed the Yǔwén system,
using purple (Zǐ), scarlet (Fēi), green (Lǜ), and dark green/blue (Bì) to distinguish official ranks (Pǐn Zhì).
During the Five Dynasties (Wǔ Dài), everyday wear was often used in place of court robes.
In the Liáo Guó, after Tàizōng entered Jìn,
the Emperor and the Southern Bureau (Nán Bān) Han officials wore Hàn dress;
the Empress Dowager and the Northern Bureau (Běi Bān) Khitan officials wore national dress (Guó Fú);
the Hàn dress was the inherited system of the Five Dynasties' Jìn.
Examining the verifiable historical records,
we compose the chapter on Carriages and Robes (Yúfú Piān),
placing it at the beginning of the Yíwèi Zhì.
National Carriages (Guó Yú)
According to the ancient customs of the Qìdān,
they favored saddles and horses.
When migrating to follow water and pasture,
they used felt carts (Zhānchē);
for heavy transport, they had large carts (Dàchē);
women rode horses,
but also had small carts (Xiǎochē);
the wealthy and noble added extravagant ornamentation to them.
Regulations were loose and broad,
prioritizing practicality only.
It was naturally necessary
that those for the Emperor and Empress were more elaborate.
We compile what is known and record it in this chapter.
The Grand Carriage (Dà Yú)
is seen in the Cháicè Zàishēng ceremony carrying the spirit tablet (Shénzhǔ).
The Carriage (Yú)
is seen in the Là Yí ceremony when the Emperor and Empress ascend and descend the carriage.
The Zǒngdào Chē (Standard-Bearing Chariot),
drawn by imperial camels.
In the Mountain Sacrifice ceremony, the Huáng Tàihòu is seen ascending the Zǒngdào Chē.
The chariot,
in the Empress Reception ceremony, the Huánghòu is seen entering the chariot.
The Qīngxiǎn Chē (Blue Curtained Chariot),
its two chi-head decorations and roof section are all adorned with silver,
drawn by camels.
It is bestowed upon a Princess upon her marriage.
In ancient times, when a king's daughter married,
her carriage and attire were not subordinate to her husband,
but were one rank below the Empress.
Is this the surviving intention of that tradition?
The Sòngzhōng Chē (Funeral Chariot),
the superstructure of the chariot is entirely adorned with brocade,
the chi-heads with silver,
bells hang below,
and a large felt curtain hangs down at the back.
It is drawn by oxen.
One sheep is carried on top,
called the sacrificial sheep,
to simulate the usage for funerals.
This is also bestowed upon a Princess.
The Yǐ (Chair/Sedan).
In the Investiture of the Huáng Tàihòu ceremony,
the Huángdì rides the Yǐ,
carried by bearers from the Biàndiàn (Side Palace) to the Xībiànmén (West Side Gate).
Saddle and horse.
In the Mountain Sacrifice ceremony,
the Huángdì rides a horse,
accompanying the Huáng Tàihòu.
In the Làyí (Winter Sacrifice ceremony),
the Huángdì descends from the sedan,
and after completing the eastern sacrifice,
rides a horse into the hunting ground.
In the Sèsè Yí (Sèsè ceremony),
all ride horses proceeding east,
the officials are positioned in the south,
and the noble ladies in the north.
Hàn Style Sedans and Chariots.
In the first year of Huìtóng (938 CE), under Tàizōng Huángdì,
Jìn envoys Féng Dào, Liú Xǔ, and others prepared the chariots, imperial carriages (lù), and ritual objects,
for the ceremony of conferring the honorable titles upon the Huángdì and Huáng Tàihòu.
From this point, the Son of Heaven’s carriages and attire began to appear in Liáo.
During the Tàipíng era, the Hàn-style investiture ceremony was performed.
The Chénghuáng Lìng arranged the chariots and imperial carriages,
and the Shàngniǎn Fèngyù arranged the sedans and palanquins.
The palanquins and imperial carriages of High Táng
were all present at the Liáo court.
The Five Imperial Carriages (Wǔ Lù): The Zhōu Guān Diǎn Lù (Record of Chariots in the Rites of Zhōu) describes five imperial carriages.
After the fall of Qín,
Hàn created its own systems.
The Yù Lù (Jade Carriage),
used for sacrificing to Heaven, sacrificing to Earth, offering sacrifices in the ancestral temple, holding court audiences, and receiving an Empress.
It is blue in substance,
adorned with jade,
with a yellow cover,
and a banner on the left.
Twelve bells (luán) are on the crossbar (héng),
two small bells (líng) are on the footboard (shì).
The dragon shaft has a pennant erected on the left side,
with twelve streamers,
all painted with ascending dragons,
dragging on the ground.
Drawn by Cāng Lóng (Azure Dragons—horses),
the harness is gold,
chiseled and inlaid with tin,
with twelve sections of pendant tassels.
In the Liáo Guó Kǎnjiàn Yí (Arrow Inspection Ceremony),
the Huángdì rode the Yù Lù to the inner gate.
In the tenth year of Kāitài (1021 CE), under Shèngzōng,
he ascended the Yù Lù and entered the Wànshòu Diàn (Hall of Ten Thousand Ages) from the three inner gates,
offering wine to the imperial portraits in the seven ancestral temples.
The Jīn Lù (Gold Carriage),
used for banquets, archery practice, returning from sacrifices, and celebratory drinking.
Red in substance,
adorned with gold,
the rest is the same as the Yù Lù,
the color follows its basic substance.
Drawn by chìliú (red horses).
The Xiàng Lù (Ivory/Elephant Carriage),
used when traveling on the road.
Yellow in substance,
adorned with ivory,
the rest is the same as the Jīn Lù.
Drawn by huángliú (yellow horses).
The Gé Lù (Leather Carriage),
used for inspection tours and military affairs.
White in substance,
covered with leather.
Drawn by báihàn (white horses).
The Mù Lù (Wood Carriage),
used for hunting.
Black in substance,
decorated with lacquer.
Drawn by hēiluò (black horses).
Chē (Chariots): Their structure is smaller than the imperial carriage (lù),
and they are ridden for minor affairs.
The Gēnggēn Chē (Plowing Chariot),
used for the ritual plowing ceremony.
Blue in substance,
the cover has three layers,
the rest is the same as the Yù Lù.
The Ān Chē (Comfortable Chariot),
also named the Jìnxián Chē (Promoting Worthies Chariot),
used for imperial visits.
Adorned with gold,
a double cabin,
curved side panels,
eight bells (luán) on the crossbar,
purple oilcloth, dark red netting, and curtains,
with a red silk net covering.
Drawn by chìliú (red horses),
with red pendant tassels.
The Sìwàng Chē (Four-Direction Viewing Chariot),
also named the Míngyuǎn Chē (Clear Distant Viewing Chariot),
used for visiting imperial tombs,
or for overseeing mourning ceremonies.
Adorned with gold,
with blue oilcloth, dark red netting, and connecting curtains.
Drawn by oxen,
the rest is the same as the Ān Chē.
The Liáng Chē (Cool Chariot),
red in substance,
used for inspecting regions and ceasing the hunt.
Red in substance,
coated in gold,
and mounted with silver.
Woven with five-colored dragons and phoenixes,
rattan oilcloth side panels,
crimson silk tassels,
and a lotus seat.
Drawn by camels.
Niǎn (Palanquin/Sedan): Pulled by men,
originally ridden within the palace.
Táng Gāozōng first established the system of seven palanquins.
The Zhōu Guān Jīn Chē (Official Records of the Cap-Chariot) includes palanquins,
pulled by groups of men.
In the Tàipíng investiture ceremony,
the Huángdì rode a palanquin.
The Dà Fèng Niǎn (Great Phoenix Palanquin),
red in substance,
with a gold phoenix on the roof,
and cloud vapor and golden wings painted on the side panels.
It has a footboard in front,
and railings below.
The harnesses and belts are all embroidered with clouds and phoenixes,
and it has silver steps.
Eighty men are needed to manage the palanquin.
The Dà Fāng Niǎn (Great Fragrant Palanquin).
The Xiānyóu Niǎn (Immortal Journey Palanquin).
The Xiǎo Niǎn (Small Palanquin).
In the Yǒngshòu Jié ceremony,
the Huáng Tàihòu rode the Xiǎo Niǎn.
The Fāngtíng Niǎn (Fragrant Pavilion Palanquin),
black in substance,
with scarlet railings and a curtained roof,
all embroidered with clouds and phoenixes.
Red and green layered windows,
flowered panels and red netting,
two curtains and four poles,
and silver-decorated steps.
One hundred and twenty men are needed to manage the palanquin.
The Dà Yù Niǎn (Great Jade Palanquin).
The Xiǎo Yù Niǎn (Small Jade Palanquin).
The Xiāoyáo Niǎn (Wandering Palanquin),
used constantly.
Palm fiber roof,
red in substance,
coated in gold,
mounted with silver,
with red silk cords.
Twelve palanquin attendants,
wearing scarlet robes in spring and summer,
and plain brocade clothing in autumn and winter.
The Píngtóu Niǎn (Flat-Top Palanquin),
used for common travel.
Its construction is like the Xiāoyáo Niǎn,
but without a roof.
In the Investiture of Chéngtiān Huáng Tàihòu ceremony,
the Huáng Tàihòu rode the Píngtóu Niǎn.
The Bù Niǎn (Walking Palanquin).
In the third year of Tǒnghé (985 CE), under Shèngzōng,
while halting at Tǔ Hé,
he rode the Bù Niǎn to attend to governance.
The Yáng Chē (Goat/Auspicious Sheep Chariot),
an ancient carriage/palanquin.
Red in substance,
the two side panels bear tortoise patterns and phoenix wings,
with scarlet curtains.
The harnesses and door curtains are all embroidered with auspicious sheep,
with painted wheels.
Originally drawn by oxen,
the Suí Dynasty changed this to guǒxiàmǎ (small horses).
Eighteen youths,
dressed in embroidered garments,
pull the auspicious sheep (carriages).
Yú (Palanquin): Carried on the shoulders of men.
The Tiānzǐ (Son of Heaven) uses braided coverings, wrist bands, and bracelets.
Yāoyú (Waist Palanquin):
Two long poles each in front and back,
with gold and silver chī (hornless dragon) heads,
embroidered crimson phoenix borders,
a brocade cushion placed on top,
and a separate small seat established.
Sixteen men bear the palanquin.
Xiǎoyú (Small Palanquin):
Red foundation,
blue canopy,
curved handles,
braided straps embroidered in crimson.
Its style is like the Fèngniǎn (Phoenix Chariot) but smaller.
It has an Imperial Seat (Gùozuò) on top.
Twenty-four men bear the palanquin.
Huáng Tàizǐ (Crown Prince) Chariots and Carriages:
Jīnlù (Gold Chariot).
Used when participating in sacrifices and offerings, the great court assembly in the first month of winter (Zhèng Dōng Dàcháo), and receiving a consort (nàfēi).
During the ceremony of investing the Huáng Tàizǐ,
the Officer in Charge of Yellow Horses (Chénghuáng Lìng) arranges the Jīnlù.
The Huáng Tàizǐ ascends and descends the Jīnlù.
Yáochē (Light Chariot):
Used for the regular court assembly on the fifth day (Wǔ Rì Chángcháo), feasting palace officials (Gōngchén), and traveling out and about.
Decorated with gold,
purple curtains and vermilion front screen.
Drawn by one horse.
Sìwàngchē (Four-Gazing Chariot):
Used when visiting the distressed or attending funerals (diàolín).
Decorated with gold,
purple oiled silk full curtains.
Drawn by one horse.
Treatise Twenty-five: Treatise on Ceremonial Guards, Part Two: National Dress (Guófú)
The people of high antiquity
netted and trapped birds and beasts,
ate meat and wore skins,
using paired deer hides to cover the front and back,
which was called bì.
Only then did the custom of wearing hemp cloth in summer and furs in winter arise.
When Zhōugōng established the royal enterprise,
the poem "Seventh Month" (Qī Yuè)
mentions going out to hunt badgers (máo) on the first day,
stripping the mulberry trees in the third month,
and spinning thread in the eighth month.
Public and private needs emerged from these activities.
The Qìdān resided among the grazing lands,
and the customs of deep antiquity were not far removed from them.
Tàizǔ's paternal uncle, Shùlán,
held the office of Yūyuè of the Yáoniǎn clan.
He settled in the fertile soil of the Huáng Hé area,
and first established cities and towns.
He instituted teachings on cultivation, planting mulberry and hemp, and weaving.
The flourishing royal enterprise of Liáo
must have also originated here!
Tàizǔ ruled the north (Běifāng);
Tàizōng controlled the Central Plain (Zhōngguó).
Mice of purple silver (Zǐyín zhī shǔ),
and baskets of silk gauzes (luó qǐ)
arrived in numerous loads.
Fine and beautiful silks and soft furs
covered the land and adorned the trees.
Thereupon, the system of garments and headwear was established:
The Northern Division (Běibān) used the Qìdān national system (Guózhì),
and the Southern Division (Nánbān) used the Hàn (Chinese) system (Hànzhì).
Each followed what was convenient for them.
Details of the national dress (Guófú) are recorded here to make known its beginning.
Sacrificial Robes (Jìfú): The state of Liáo considered mountain sacrifice (Jì Shān) a grand ceremony,
and the clothing and adornments were particularly splendid.
For the Great Sacrifice (Dàsì):
The Huángdì (Emperor) wore a gold-patterned gold crown (jīnwén jīnguān),
a white damask robe (bái líng páo),
a red belt,
a hanging fish pendant (xuányú),
and three red mountain pendants (sānshān hóng chuí).
Adorned with rhinoceros horn and jade knife ornaments (dāocuò),
and black boots with braided seams (luòfèng wū xuē).
For the Minor Sacrifice (Xiǎosì):
The Huángdì wore a hard cap (yìngmào),
and a red silk robe with turtle patterns (hóng kè sī guīwén páo).
The Huánghòu (Empress) wore a red kerchief,
a red robe with braided seams,
hanging jade pendants (xuán yù pèi),
a double heart-shaped kerchief (shuāng tóngxīn pà),
and black boots with braided seams.
The clothing of officials (chénliáo) and noblewomen (mìngfù)
followed the colors of their respective tribal banners (qízhì).
Court Robes (Cháofú): In the year Bǐngyín, Tàizǔ ascended the Imperial Throne,
and his court robes concealed armor
to prepare for emergencies.
Subsequently, when performing the Sèsè ritual (Sèsè Lǐ) and the Great Willow Shooting (Dà Shèliǔ),
this attire was worn.
In the first year of Tǒnghé (983 CE), when Shèngzōng invested the Empress Dowager Chéngtiān,
officials of the third rank (sānpǐn) and above were granted the Hàn (Chinese) ceremonial robes (Fǎfú),
and those below the third rank used the attire for the Great Willow Shooting.
The Huángdì wore a Shílǐxuē ceremonial crown (gǔn guān),
a red robe with braided seams,
a belt decorated with rhinoceros horn and jade ornaments,
and boots with braided seams.
This was called the Gǔnmiǎn (Imperial Ceremonial Dress) of the national attire (Guófú).
Tàizōng later changed this to a brocade robe and a gold belt.
Officials wore felt caps (zhān guān),
decorated with gold flowers,
sometimes augmented with pearls, jade, and kingfisher feathers.
Gold flowers hung down behind the forehead,
with a woven lined strap
containing a bundle of hair inside.
Alternatively, a gauze cap (shā guān),
styled like the Wūshāmào (Black Gauze Cap),
but without a brim,
and not pressing against the ears.
A gold flower was attached to the front of the forehead,
tied above with a purple strap,
with pearls affixed at the end.
They wore a narrow purple robe,
fastened with a kèdié belt
made of yellow and red cords wrapped around leather,
adorned with gold, jade, crystal, and indigo stone.
This was
called "Pánzǐ."
Tàizōng later changed this to a brocade robe and a gold belt.
In the first year of Huìtóng (938 CE),
all high-ranking older officials
were granted these items.
Official Uniforms (Gōngfú):
Called "Zhǎnguǒ,"
they were purple in color.
In the twenty-second year of Zhòngxī (1053 CE), Xīngzōng
issued an edict regarding the headscarf (jīnzé) for the Eight Family Clans (Bāfáng Zú).
In the first year of Qīngníng (1055 CE), Dàozōng
decreed that those who were not descendants of meritorious relatives, nor the Vice Commissioner (Fùshǐ) of the Yílíjǐn, nor employees who held functional positions,
should not wear the headscarf (jīn).
The Huángdì wore a purple satin hood,
a narrow purple robe,
a jade girdle,
or a red jacket.
Officials also wore the hood
and purple clothing.
Informal Attire (Chángfú):
During the ceremony when prime ministers offered their second thanks,
the Emperor wore informal attire.
During the ceremony when the Gāolì envoys were received,
officials wore casual clothes,
which were
called "Pánguǒ."
Narrow robes with green patterns.
The inner garment was mostly red and green.
The noble wore sable furs,
considering purplish-black the most valuable,
with dark blue second.
There were also silver mice furs,
which were exceptionally pure white.
Those of lower status wore furs of sable hair, sheep, rodents, or sand fox.
Hunting Attire (Tiánlièfú):
The Huángdì wore a hood,
donned armor and military dress (róngzhuāng),
using sable, goose neck, or duck head fur as waist protection.
All Commissioners and above, both Qìdān (Fān) and Hàn, wore military dress.
Their clothing was all folded left over right (zuǒrèn),
and dark green or black in color.
Mourning Attire (Diàofú): When Tàizǔ's rebellious younger brother, Làgē, and others surrendered,
he received them wearing plain white clothes.
He wore plain white clothes
and rode a reddish-white horse.
Hàn (Chinese) Attire (Hànfú)
Huángdì (The Yellow Emperor) first instituted the Miǎn ceremonial cap and patterned robes,
which later kings used for ancestral worship, sacrifices, and offerings.
The Xià wore the shōu, the Yīn wore the xǔ, and the Zhōu wore the biàn for court audiences.
They wore caps for dwelling and everyday life,
thus distinguishing rank and differentiating ritual objects.
Subsequently, the Táng Dynasty used the miǎn cap and green garments as sacrificial robes,
the Tōngtiān crown and scarlet robes as court robes,
and the Píngjīnzé (flat headcloth) and hemmed robe as informal attire.
On the first day of the first month of Dàtóng (947 CE),
Emperor Tàizōng entered Jìn,
prepared the ceremonial carriage,
and received the congratulations of all civil and military officials at the Chóngyuán Diàn in Biànjīng.
From that day forward, this became customary.
Returning north that same year,
the ritual artifacts and culture of the Táng and Jìn Dynasties
were adopted by Liáo.
We selected and compiled from all sources,
recording in this chapter those items which were commonly used.
Sacrificial Robes (Jìfú): Throughout the Liáo Dynasty,
the Altars for Heaven and Earth were not established,
so the Dàqiú Miǎnfú (Great Fur Robe and Miǎn Cap) attire is not recorded here.
The Gǔnmiǎn (Imperial Ceremonial Robe and Crown),

is worn during the ancestral temple sacrifices (jìsì zōngmiào), when sending a high general (shàngjiàng) out on campaign (chūzhēng), during the Yìnzhì ceremony, accession to the throne (jiànzuò), the capping ceremony (jiā yuánfú), the installation of an Empress (nà hòu), or when holding court (shòu cháo) on New Year's Day (Yuánrì).
It is adorned with gold ornaments (jīnshì).
Twelve streams (liú) of white pearls hang down.
The chin strap (yīng) is made of braided cords (zǔ).
The color is the same as its ribbon (shòu).
Yellow floss (tǔ kuàng) is used for the ear plugs (chōng ěr).
It features a jade hairpin (yù zāndǎo).
The robe is black (xuán yī) and the skirt is reddish-yellow (xūn cháng), featuring twelve insignias (shí'èr zhāng): eight insignias are on the robe (yī):
Sun (rì), Moon (yuè), Stars (xīng), Dragon (lóng), Flowery Insect (huáchóng), Fire (huǒ), Mountain (shān), and Sacrificial Vessels (zōngyí);
four insignias are on the skirt (cháng):
Waterweed (zǎo), Grains of Rice (fěnmǐ), Axe (fǔ), and Bow-shaped design (fú).
The cuff (biǎo) and collar (lǐng) of the robe,
are woven with ascending dragon (shēnglóng) patterns,
arranged in six ranks (liù děng) for each.
Below the dragon and mountain patterns,
each insignia occupies one line,
twelve items per line.
The inner garment (zhōngdān) is white gauze (bái shā),
with an Axe-patterned collar,
and green cuffs, hems (zhuó), and border (jū).
The leather belt (gédài) and great sash (dàdài) are embroidered with the Bow-shaped design.
A sword (jiàn), girdle pendants (pèi), and ribbon are worn.
The ceremonial shoes (xì) are adorned with gold ornaments.
For the court assembly (cháohuì) ceremony on New Year's Day (Yuánrì),
the Emperor (Huángdì) wears the Gǔnmiǎn.
Court Attire (Cháofú): In the fifth year of Qiánhēng,
Shèngzōng conferred the title upon Empress Dowager Chéngtiān,
and provided ceremonial robes (fǎfú) to officials of the third rank (sānpǐn) and above.
For miscellaneous ceremonies (zálǐ),
specifically the ceremony for granting the title to Empress Dowager Chéngtiān,
the Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng) approached the mat,
removed his sword and took off his shoes.
During the enthronement ceremony (zūnhào cèlǐ) in the fifth year of Zhòngxī,
the Emperor wore the Dragon Gǔn (lónggǔn).
Officials from both the Northern (běi) and Southern (nán) administrations all wore court attire.
This was generally the rule of the Liáo dynasty.
During the Hùitóng era,
the Empress Dowager (Tàihòu) and officials of the Northern administration (běimiàn chénliáo) wore the national dress (guófú);
the Emperor and officials of the Southern administration (nánmiàn chénliáo) wore Hàn attire (Hànfú).
After the Qiánhēng era,
during grand ceremonies (dàlǐ), even Northern officials of the third rank and above used Hàn attire;
after the Zhòngxī era,
Hàn attire was used for all grand ceremonies.
However, for routine court assemblies (cháng cháo), the Hùitóng system was still followed.
The Emperor's Tōngtiān Crown (Tōngtiān guān).

It is worn when returning from all sacrifices, when holding court on the Winter Solstice (Dōngzhì) and the first day of the lunar month (Shuòrì), when greeting princes and dukes (wánggōng) from the imperial viewing platform (lín xuān), and during the Spring (Yuánhuì) and Winter (Dōnghuì) assemblies.
The crown is topped with a gold Bóshān ornament (jīn bóshān).
It has twelve attached cicadas (fù chán).
The top is adorned with pearls and kingfisher feathers (zhū cuì).
A black jièzé headband is worn.
Hair cord (fàyīng) and kingfisher tail ornaments (cuì ruí).
A jade (yù) or rhinoceros horn (xī) hairpin (zāndǎo) is used.
A reddish-purple gauze robe (jiàng shā páo).
A white gauze inner garment (bái shā zhōngdān).
Cuffs and collar.
Vermilion hems and borders.
A white skirt (qún) and shirt (rú).
A reddish-purple ceremonial apron (bìxī).
A white ornamental sash (jiǎdài) and a curved collar (qū lǐng) with a square-heart shape (fāngxīn).
He wears the leather belt, sword, and ribbon.
And stockings (wà) and ceremonial shoes.
If he has not yet undergone the capping ceremony,
then he wears his hair in twin boy knots (shuāng tóng jì),
with an empty top (kōng dǐng),
a black jièzé headband,
a double jade hairpin (shuāng yù dǎo),
and added precious ornaments (bǎoshì).
For the New Year's Day longevity offering ceremony (shàng shòu yí),
the Emperor wears the Tōngtiān Crown,
and the reddish-purple gauze robe.
The Crown Prince's (Huáng Tàizǐ) Yuǎnyóu Crown (Yuǎnyóu guān).
It is worn when visiting the ancestral temple (yè miào), returning to the palace, and attending court on New Year's Day, Winter Solstice, and the first day of the lunar month.
It is a three-bar crown (sān liáng guān),
adorned with nine gold attached cicadas,
the top decorated with pearls and kingfisher feathers.
A black jièzé headband.
Hair cord and kingfisher tail ornaments.
A rhinoceros horn hairpin.
A reddish-purple gauze robe.
A white gauze inner garment.
Black collar and cuffs,
hem and border.
White skirt and shirt.
A white ornamental sash and a curved collar with a square-heart shape.
A reddish-purple gauze ceremonial apron.
His leather belt, sword, girdle pendants, and ribbon,
as well as his stockings and ceremonial shoes, are the same as above.
Later, this was changed to white stockings and black ceremonial shoes.
If he has not yet been capped (wèi guān),
then he wears twin boy knots,
with an empty top,
a black jièzé headband,
a double jade hairpin,
and added precious ornaments.
For the ceremony conferring the title of Crown Prince,
the Crown Prince wears the Yuǎnyóu Crown,
and the reddish-purple gauze robe.
The Yuǎnyóu Crown of the Imperial Princes (Qīnwáng).
It is worn when assisting in sacrifices (péi jì), attending court banquets (cháo xiǎng), presenting memorials (bài biǎo), and during grand affairs (dà shì).
The crown has three bars.
It is adorned with gold attached cicadas.
A black jièzé headband.
Blue tail ornaments (qīng ruí) and a hairpin.
A single reddish-purple gauze robe (jiàng shā dānyī).
A white gauze inner garment.
Black collar,
hem and border.
White skirt and shirt.
A leather belt with a buckle (gōu) and clasp (pī).
An ornamental sash with a curved collar and square heart.
A reddish-purple gauze ceremonial apron.
Stockings and ceremonial shoes,
sword, girdle pendants, and ribbon.
Officials of the second rank (èrpǐn) and above wear the same.
The Yuǎnyóu Crown of the various Princes (Zhūwáng).
Three bars.
Black jièzé headband.
Blue tail ornaments.
Officials of the third rank and above wear the Jìnxián Crown (Jìnxián guān),
with three bars,
and precious ornaments.
Officials of the fifth rank (wǔpǐn) and above wear the Jìnxián Crown,
with two bars,
and gold ornaments.
Officials of the ninth rank (jiǔpǐn) and above wear the Jìnxián Crown,
with one bar,
and no ornaments.
Officials of the seventh rank (qīpǐn) and above dispense with the sword, girdle pendants, and ribbon.
Those of the eighth rank (bāpǐn) and below wear the same as the Official Robe (Gōngfú).
Official Robe (Gōngfú): For the Kànjiàn ceremony (inspection of arrows),
the Palace Envoys (Gěshǐ) wore the Official Robe,
and tied their shoes.
The Liáo state had previously used the Official Robe.
The Emperor's Yìshàn Crown (Yìshàn guān).
It is worn when holding routine court (shì cháo) on the first day of the lunar month (shuò).
A gamboge yellow robe (zhè huáng páo).
A nine-ring belt (jiǔ huán dài).
A white silk skirt and shirt.
Liùhé boots.
The Crown Prince's Yuǎnyóu Crown.
Worn for routine court every fifth day (wǔ rì cháng cháo), and when receiving court on New Year's Day and Winter Solstice.
A single reddish-purple gauze robe.
White skirt and shirt.
Leather belt with a gold buckle and clasp.
Ornamental sash with a square heart.
Hanging ribbon (fēn) and pouch (pánnáng).
White stockings.
Black leather shoes (wū pí lǚ).
For officials below the first rank and above the fifth rank,
they wear a crown, headband (zé), and cord (yīng),
and a hairpin.
This attire is worn when having an audience with the Crown Prince (Dōnggōng) and for other public duties (gōngshì).
A single reddish-purple gauze robe.
White skirt and shirt.
A belt with a buckle and clasp.
Ornamental sash with a square heart.
Stockings and shoes.
Hanging ribbon and pouch.
For officials below the sixth rank,
they wear a crown, headband, and cord,
and a hairpin,
but omit the hanging ribbon and pouch,
the rest is the same.
Informal Attire (Chángfú): The Liáo state called this
"Chuānzhí."
During the daily life rituals (qǐjū lǐ),
officials wore Chuānzhí.
This means wearing boots (chuān xuē) and holding a ceremonial tablet (zhí hú).
The Emperor wears a gamboge yellow robe (zhè huáng páoshān),
a folded-top headdress (zhé shàng tóujīn),
a nine-ring belt,
Liùhé boots.
This practice originated with the Yǔwén clan.
After the Zhēnguān era of Táng Tàizōng,
unless it was holding court on New Year's Day or Winter Solstice, or for grand sacrifices,
all officials simply wore Informal Attire.
The Crown Prince's Jìndé Crown (Jìndé guān),
nine qǐ ornaments,
and gold ornaments.
A single reddish-purple gauze robe.
White skirt and shirt.
White stockings.
Black leather shoes.
Officials of the fifth rank and above:
Pūtóu (turban),
also called the folded-top headdress,
purple robe (zǐ páo),
ivory tablet (yá hú),
and gold and jade belt.
Civil officials (wénguān) wear a handkerchief (shǒujīn), calculation bag (suàndài), small knife (dāozǐ), whetstone (lì shí), and a gold fish purse (jīnyúdài);

Military officials (wǔguān) wear the Qīchá Qīshì (seven accessories for the belt): saber (pèi dāo), small knife, whetstone (mó shí), Qìbìzhēn (a type of pouch/belt), Huìjué (a type of tool/whistle), needle case (zhēntǒng), and tinder bag (huǒshídài).
Black leather Liùhé boots.
Officials below the sixth rank:
Pūtóu,
scarlet robe (fēi yī),
wooden tablet (mù hú),
silver belt,
silver fish purse (yínyúdài) pendant,
and the boots are the same.
Eighth and ninth ranks:
fútóu,
green robes,
brass belts,
and boots.
Collation Notes
Zhi 26: Yíwèi Zhì 3: Fúyìn
In the era of the Yáoniǎn Shì,
they received their seal from the Huíhú.
When Yēlán Kèhán requested a seal from the Táng,
Emperor Wǔzōng first bestowed
the "Fèngguó Qìdān Yìn" (Seal of Qìdān, Defender of the State).
In the first year of Tàizǔ's Shéncè reign,
the Liáng Governor of Yōuzhōu defected,
and an imperial edict bestowed upon him a seal and ribbon.
At this time,
Tàizǔ had already held the Yáoniǎn position for ten years.
In the ninth year of Huìtóng,
Tàizōng campaigned against Jìn,
and the last emperor presented the State-Transmitting Treasure (Chuánguó Bǎo) and
three golden seals,
whereupon the auspicious symbols of the Son of Heaven returned to Liáo.
The Chuánguó Bǎo
was made by Qín Shǐhuáng,
using blue jade,
with a chí (hornless dragon) knob,
six sides,
and the inscription on its front face read:
"Received Mandate from Heaven,
May it Endure in Everlasting Prosperity."
It was in fish-bird seal script,
and Zǐyīng presented it to Hàn Gāozǔ.
When Wáng Mǎng usurped the Hàn,
Empress Píng threw the imperial seal down the palace steps,
and a corner of the chí was slightly chipped.
Emperor Xiàn lost it,
Sūn Jiān found it in a well,
it was passed down to Sūn Quán,
who then surrendered it to the Wèi.
Emperor Wèi Wénlì engraved on its shoulder:
"The Great Wèi Receives the State-Transmitting Treasure of Hàn."
The Táng renamed it
"Shòumìng Bǎo" (Seal of Receiving the Mandate).
After the fall of Jìn, it returned to Liáo.
Since the Three Kingdoms period,
the usurping and false states often imitated and privately manufactured seals,
and the seals stored in the imperial treasuries of successive dynasties varied,
making it impossible to distinguish genuine from fake.
In the tenth year of Shèngzōng's Kāitài reign,
an express messenger was dispatched to retrieve the jade seal presented by Shí Jìn from Zhōngjīng.
In the seventh year of Xīngzōng's Chóngxī reign,
those possessing the Chuánguó Bǎo were deemed legitimate to sit for the imperial examinations for jinshì.
In the second year of Tiānzuò's Bǎodà reign,
the Chuánguó Xǐ was lost in the Sānggān Hé.
The Jade Seal:
When Tàizōng returned north after defeating Jìn,
he obtained it from the Biàn Palace
and stored it in the imperial carriage treasury.
In the second year of Mùzōng's Yìnglì reign,
an edict commanded the use of Tàizōng's old treasure.
The Yùqián Bǎo (Front-of-Emperor Seal)
was cast in gold,
with the inscription
"Yùqián Zhī Bǎo" (Treasure of the Emperor's Presence),
used to seal imperial proclamations to officials.
The Zhàoshū Bǎo (Edict Seal)
was inscribed
"Shūzhào Zhī Bǎo" (Treasure for Edicts and Rescripts),
and was used for all edicts, rescripts, and replies.
The Qìdān Bǎo (Qìdān Seal):
During the ceremony for enfeoffing the Qìdān,
the Fúbǎo Láng (Director of Tallies and Seals) placed the seal to the east of the imperial throne.
Three Golden Seals:
Presented by the Jìn emperor;
their inscriptions are not detailed.
The Huáng Tàihòu Bǎo (Empress Dowager's Seal):
Its specifications are not detailed.
In the second year of Tiānxǐn,
Empress Dowager Yìngtiān assumed regency,
and her ministers presented seals and ribbons.
During the ceremony for enthroning Empress Dowager Chéngtiān,
the Fúbǎo Láng presented the seal and placed it to the right of the Empress Dowager's throne.
The Huánghòu Yìn (Empress's Seal)
was inscribed
"Huánghòu Jiàoyìn" (Empress's Teaching Seal).
The Huáng Tàizǐ Bǎo (Crown Prince's Seal):
Its specifications are not detailed.
In the ninth year of Chóngxī, during the ceremony for enthroning the Crown Prince,
the Zhōngshū Lìng (Director of the Central Secretariat) presented the Huáng Tàizǐ Bǎo to the Crown Prince.
Seals:
The Lìbù Yìn (Seal of the Ministry of Personnel)
was inscribed
"Lìbù Zhī Yìn" (Seal of the Ministry of Personnel),
cast in silver,
used to seal official appointments and edicts for civil officials.
The Bīngbù Yìn (Seal of the Ministry of War)
was inscribed
"Bīngbù Zhī Yìn" (Seal of the Ministry of War),
cast in silver,
used to seal military appointments and edicts.

The seals of the Qìdān Shūmìyuàn (Qìdān Bureau of Military Affairs), Qìdān Zhū Xíngjūn Dūbùshǔ (All Qìdān Field Army Commanders), Hànrén Shūmìyuàn (Hàn Chinese Bureau of Military Affairs), Zhōngshūshěng (Central Secretariat), and Hànrén Zhū Xínggōng Dūbùshǔ (All Hàn Chinese Field Palace Commanders),
were all cast in silver.
Their inscriptions did not exceed six characters,
and were colored with cinnabar.
The seals of the Nánběi Wáng (Northern and Southern Kings) and below, and of the hundred internal and external offices,
were all cast in bronze,
colored with minium,
while those of the various tax offices were colored with red ocher.
The Sháowā Yìn (Sháowā Seal):
Sháowā
is a general term for birds of prey,
used as a seal knob,
to symbolize speed.
It was used for imperial decrees issued to generals and commanders on military campaigns.
Dàozōng bestowed an eagle-knob seal upon Yēlǜ Rénxiān,
which was this type.
Tallies and Credentials:
Since the time the eight tribes of the Dàhè Shì engaged in warfare,
they would join tallies to mobilize,
which was merely carving wood to form matching halves.
When Tàizǔ received the Mandate,
he replaced them with golden fish.
Seven golden fish tallies,
cast in gold,
six inches long,
each bearing a character and number.
Each fish was divided into left and right halves that matched.
When there was an affair,
the left half was first given to the defending general,
the envoy held the right half,
and when the size, length, and character numbers matched,
troops would then be dispatched.
Upon completion of the matter,
they were returned to the imperial treasury.
Two hundred silver plates,
one chi (foot) long,
engraved with the national characters,
with the inscription
"Yí Sù" (Urgent Speed),
and also
"Chì Zǒumǎ Pái" (Imperial Galloping Horse Plate).
When the state faced important matters,
the emperor personally bestowed a plate upon an envoy,
and a handwritten note allocated a certain number of relay horses.
If relay horses were lacking,
other horses were used as substitutes.
By law,
they galloped seven hundred li day and night,
or five hundred li for the next fastest.
Wherever they arrived, it was as if the Son of Heaven himself was present;
they could request changes and replacements,
and no one dared to defy them.
Upon the envoy's return,
the emperor personally received it,
and the Pái Yì Lángjūn (Officer in Charge of Plates and Seals) sealed and stored it by hand.
The wooden tally (mùqì):
The front side is Yáng;
the back side is Yīn.
It is used when the Gémén calls for the imperial guards (zhàng).
During the Cháohè ceremony,
the Xuānhuī Shǐ requests the Yáng side of the wooden tally and descends the hall.
Upon reaching the palace gate,
he hands the tally to the Xīshàng Gémén Shǐ, saying:
"The tally is delivered for inspection."
The Kānqì Guān announces affirmation (shēng nuò),
kneels to receive the tally,
raises his hand to confirm the tallies match,
bows low and rises,
then bows deeply (jūgōng),
and reports:
"The tallies match inside and out."
The Gémén Shǐ says:
"According to the imperial decree (zhǔn chì), inspect the tally;
proceed with the inspection."
The Kānqì Guān holds the Yīn side of the wooden tally and announces affirmation (shēng nuò),
stands upright,
steps back slightly,
and calls out loudly:
"Commanders and Gate Guard Officials (Ménzhàng Guān)!"
They all announce affirmation (qí shēng nuò).
The Kānqì Guān says:
"One wooden tally for calling the guards has been issued from inside.
According to the imperial decree, it is delivered to the guards of the Left and Right Jīnwú for inspection."
The Kānqì Guān says:
"Do they fit (hé bù hé)?"
The Ménzhàng Guān says:
"They fit (hé)."
This is repeated once more.
The Kānqì Guān says:
"Are they identical (tóng bù tóng)?"
The Ménzhàng Guān says:
"Identical (tóng)."
This is also repeated once more.
The Kānqì Guān moves forward and bows deeply (jūgōng),
reporting:
"The inspector, (Mǒu Guān Mǒu, filling in the blanks for the unnamed official) the Gōuhuà Dūzhī of the Zuǒ Jīnwú Yǐnjià Zhàng,
has inspected them before Your Majesty and found them to be identical."
He stands upright,
steps back slightly,
raises the tally in his right hand and says:
"This tally is respectfully delivered to the Gémén Shǐ to be returned."
The Gémén Shǐ calls out affirmation (shēng nuò),
and the Ménzhàng Guān lowers their voices in affirmation.
The Kānqì Guān kneels and hands over the tally.
The Gémén Shǐ ascends the hall to present the tally,
and the Xuānhuī Shǐ receives the tally.
The Gémén Shǐ descends the hall,
and by imperial decree, calls for the guards.
The wooden arrow (mùjiàn):
The inner arrow is Xióng (male);
the outer arrow is Cí (female).
It is used when the Emperor travels.
Upon returning to the palace,
the Kānjiàn Guān holds the Cí arrow,
and the Dōngshàng Gémén Shǐ holds the Xióng arrow.
The ceremony is the same as the tally inspection,
detailed in the Lǐyí Zhì.
Treatise Twenty-Seven, Yíwèi Zhì Four: Yízhàng.
When the Emperor resides, the gates are locked and watchmen beat their clappers;
when he goes out, troops are used as guards and escorts.
Such toil for the people and movement of the masses—
how can this be avoided?
The great troubles of the world arise from great desires,
necessitating far-sighted consideration and deep defense.
The wise, the heroic, the pre-eminent officials (kuí chén), and the powerful vassals (xióng fān) are all present here.
The military preparedness is concealed within the civil institutions (wénwù).
This is why the Yízhàng are established.
The guards of the Jīnwú and the Huánghuī Liù Jūn,
Liáo received them from Jìn,
Jìn received them from Hòu Táng,
Hòu Táng received them from Liáng and Táng.
Their origins are well-established.
Yēlǜ Yǎn and Chén Dàrèn’s former treatises had omissions,
so we have also examined the records in the Liáocháo Zálǐ.
Guózhàng.
Wáng Tōng said that
when Shùn made his annual tours throughout the four great mountains (sì yuè),
the people did not complain of toil,
because the guards and escorts were few and the requisitions were light.
Liáo Tàizǔ, with a single horse and a single standard,
expanded territory for ten thousand *lǐ*,
managing affairs in all four directions.
He never settled down in peace,
yet wherever he went, people willingly followed.
He used this same principle (dào).
When Tàizōng conquered and controlled Zhōngguó,
the ceremonial regulations of Qín Huáng and Hàn Wǔ arrived daily,
and later generations continued to use them.
With banners of yak tails and leopard tails (máo tóu bào wěi),
they drove frequently between the Wǔ Jīng.
They were constantly active throughout the year,
their tracks overlapping.
The people were exhausted and the treasury depleted;
was this the reason why?
Starting from the time Liáo's Dàhè Shì Móhuì received the gift of drums and standards from the Táng Dynasty,
these constituted the Guózhàng.
Its system was very simple.
Before Tàizōng attacked Táng and Jìn,
these were the only things used.
We record this at the beginning of the chapter
to show that a ruler who founded the state amid hardship
did not necessarily need heavy personal protection.
Twelve Shéndú,
twelve banners,
twelve drums,
curved-handled Huágài,
straight-handled Huágài.
The last ruler of the Yáoniǎn (clan) commanded
that the twelve Shéndú and the Son of Heaven’s banners and drums be brought and placed before Tàizǔ's tent.
When the younger brothers, including Lāgē, rebelled,
Yúndéshí set fire to the temporary palace.
The Empress ordered Hégǔlǔ to save them,
but only the Son of Heaven's banners and drums were recovered.
When Tàizōng ascended the throne,
he placed the banners, drums, and Shéndú in front of the palace hall.
Shèngzōng used the light carriage and ceremonial guard to offer sacrifice at Dìshān.
Bóhǎi Zhàng.
In the fourth year of Tiānxiǎn,
Tàizōng traveled to Liáoyáng Fǔ.
The Rén Huángwáng prepared the imperial carriage and feathered guards to welcome him.
In the fifth year of Gānhēng,
Shèngzōng toured the East,
and the Dōngjīng Liúshǒu prepared the ceremonial guard to welcome the imperial carriage.
These were the former Bóhǎi ceremonial guards.
Hàn Zhàng.
Dàhè Shīhuó had an audience with the Táng court,
and Suōgù and his brothers succeeded him.
They married princesses and were enfeoffed as kings,
feasting their eyes on the superior nation.
During the Kāiyuán Dōngfēng,
Shàogù accompanied the Emperor,
and further witnessed the grandeur of the Great Peace.
From then on, they paid annual tribute to Táng.
Nièlǐ, the Liáo Shǐzǔ, helped establish the Yáoniǎn clan,
serving as Imperial Chancellor (Guó Xiāng) for generations.
What they saw with their eyes and heard with their ears
had long inspired their ambition for the glory of imperial rule.
Although the Yáoniǎn clan brought drums and standards before Tàizǔ's tent,
how could this ever suffice to match the vast ambition and commanding presence he gazed upon?
Afterward, they exchanged envoys with Liáng and sent tribute to Táng,
not fearing the toil.
When it came to Tàizōng,
he established Jìn to demand the official investiture (cè lǐ),
and entered Biàn to seize the imperial regalia (Fǎwù).
Only then did he obtain in one stroke
what previous generations had longed for.
Tàiyuán seized power,
not because its military strength was inferior.
Yet (Tàizōng) swept up the Fǎwù
and first delivered them to the Zhōngjīng,
tossing aside the lands and rivers
with barely a second thought.
His ambition is evident.
Consequently, the imperial regalia and cultural artifacts (wénwù) from the Qín and Hàn dynasties onward all entered Liáo.
Zhōu and Sòng subsequently had to remake them according to diagrams;
they were not the original objects.
What Liáo valued,
this was the main point,
hence it is specifically recorded here.
In the first year of Huìtóng of Tàizōng,
Féng Dào, the envoy from Jìn, prepared the carriages and Fǎwù
to present the cè lǐ (investiture ceremony) for the Huáng Tàihòu.
Liú Xù and Lú Zhòng prepared the ceremony
to present the honored title to the Emperor.
In the third year,
His Majesty was in Jìzhōu viewing the diagrams for the guided imperial ceremonial guard.
He subsequently prepared the Fǎjià and traveled to Yān,
where he presided in Yuánhé Diàn to perform the rite of entering the gates (rù gé lǐ).
In the sixth year,
the Fǎjià was prepared for travel to Yān,
and the procession was welcomed and guided to Yuánhé Diàn.
On the first day of the first month of the first year of Dàtóng,
the Fǎjià was prepared and arrived at Biàn.
His Majesty presided in Chóngyuán Diàn
to receive the Cháohè from all civil and military officials.
From this point on, it became a daily custom.
On the first day of the second month,
His Majesty presided in Chóngyuán Diàn,
prepared the rites, and received the Cháohè.
In the third month,
His Majesty was about to travel to Zhōngjīng Zhènyáng,
and ordered the collection of the Lǔbù and Fǎwù,
delegating the relevant officials to escort them ahead.
Not long after, Zhènyáng fell to the Hàn (dynasty),
and the Lǔbù and Fǎwù returned with Shìzōng to Shàngjīng.
In the fourth month,
the Huáng Tàidì Lǐ Hú sent an envoy to inquire about military affairs.
His Majesty replied:
"The court audience and daily life proceed according to the rites."
In this month,
Tàizōng died.
Shìzōng ascended the throne,
but the Lǔbù and Fǎwù were prepared yet not used.
First Year,
an edict commanded that court assemblies follow the precedents of Emperor Sìshèng Huángdì,
using Hàn rites.
In the second month of Jǐngzōng Qiánhēng Fifth Year,
the sacred coffin was placed upon the covered carriage (wēnliáng chē),
complete with the imperial guard and honor guard (lǔbù yíwèi).
In the sixth month,
Shèngzōng arrived at Shàngjīng.
The Residency Administrator (Liúshǒu) prepared the ceremonial carriage (fǎjià) to greet and guide him.
Shèngzōng Tǒnghé First Year,
the imperial entourage returned to Shàngjīng,
and the ceremonial escort and guard followed the standard form.
In the third year,
the entourage proceeded to Shàngjīng,
and the Liúshǒu prepared the guards and escort for the reverent welcome.
In the fourth year,
the Liúshǒu of Yānjīng prepared the escort to guide the imperial entourage into the capital,
His Majesty ascended the Yuánhé Diàn,
and the myriad officials offered court congratulations.
After this,
the ceremonial escorts became commonplace matters,
and historians did not record them again.

This information was obtained from the miscellaneous Liao Dynasty rites preserved in the family collection of Xú Shìlóng, the Tàicháng Qīng of our dynasty.
As for the detailed procedures of the ceremonies,
we dare not compile or synthesize them (based on conjecture). Treatise 28: Treatise on Food and Money, Part One (Zhì Dì Èrshíbā Shíhuò Zhì Shàng)
According to the ancient customs of the Qìdān,
their wealth was based on horses,
and their strength was based on soldiers.
They allowed their horses to roam the wilderness,
and kept their soldiers dispersed among the people.
When there was a matter requiring battle,
the armored, strong cavalry (guōqí jièfū),
were ordered to muster at *mǎo* and assemble by *chén*.
Horses followed water and grass,
people relied on mare's milk and dairy,
drawing strong bows to hunt,
in order to supply daily needs.
Dried rations and fodder,
the guiding principle lay in this.
By this they achieved victory,
and wherever they went, they were unopposed.
When they finally established a state,
internally they established ancestral temples and court government,
externally they set up commanderies, districts, governors, and administrators,
regulations increased daily,
and expenditures expanded daily.
Superiors and inferiors imitated each other,
and clothing and accoutrements became increasingly extravagant,
thus the management of food and money became urgent.

Therefore, in the Five Capitals (Wǔjīng) and in Chángchūn, Liáoxī, and Píngzhōu, offices were established for Salt and Iron (Yántiě), Transport (Zhuǎnyùn), State Finance (Dùzhī), and Money and Silk (Qiánbó),
to manage revenue and expenditure.
Although the precise scale and hierarchy of these regulations cannot all be detailed,
the main points are generally found scattered throughout the old histories.
Such matters as agriculture and grain (nónggǔ), taxes and levies (zūfù), salt and iron (yántiě), commerce and trade (màoyì), mines and smelting (kēngyě), currency (quánbì), and state herds (qúnmù),
are collected category by category,
and compiled into this chapter,
to preserve the outline of food and money management for that dynasty.
Initially,
the Imperial Ancestor Yún Déshí served as the Yílíjǐn of Dàlièfǔ;
he delighted in farming and harvesting,
was skilled in animal husbandry,
and assessed the land benefits to teach the people how to farm.
His second uncle, Shù Lán, became the Yúyuè (Grand Minister),
and ordered the people of the state to plant mulberries and hemp,
and practice weaving.
Tàizǔ suppressed the rebellion of his younger brothers,
pacified the military, lightened the taxes,
and focused entirely on agriculture.
He observed that the population was proliferating,
and oversight was lax and distant.
He divided the Běidà Nóngwù into two tribes (bù),
and mandated them to cultivate crops.
The various tribes imitated this.
At the beginning of Tàizōng's Huìtóng era,
when he was about to hunt eastward,
Sān Kè submitted a memorial requesting the reduction of baggage trains,
to quickly rush to the Northern Mountains to gather supplies,
in preparation for state needs,
without harming agricultural labor.
Soon after, an edict commanded officials to encourage agriculture and sericulture,
and teach spinning and weaving.
Since the land of Wūgǔ had abundant water and rich grass,
he ordered the Ōukūn Shíliè (tribe) to reside there,
and added good land near the Hǎilè Shuǐ for use as farmland.
In the third year,
an edict granted land near the Xiélǐ Hé and Lúqú Hé
to the three Shíliè tribes: Ōujǐn Tūlǚ, Yǐsībó of the Southern Chancellery (Nányuàn), and Wēnnà Hélà of the Northern Chancellery (Běiyuàn),
so that they might undertake farming.
In the eighth year,
he paused his journey at Chìshān,
and hosted a banquet for his accompanying ministers,
asking about essential matters of the military and the state.
His attendants replied:
“Regarding the matters of the military and the state,
loving the people is the foundation.
If the people are wealthy, the troops will be sufficient;
if the troops are sufficient, the state will be strong.”
His Majesty greatly approved of this.
In this same year,
an edict summoned troops from all circuits (dào),
and simultaneously warned that anyone daring to damage grain and crops would be judged according to military law.
During the Yìnglì period,
Yúnzhōu presented auspicious grain (jiāhé).
At the time, this was attributed to the emphasis placed on agriculture.
Bǎoníng Seventh Year,
the Hàn territory (of the Liao) had Sòng troops (present),
and an envoy came to beg for rations.
An edict granted them 200,000 *hú* of millet to assist them.
If state finances had not been abundant,
how could they have done this?
Shèngzōng (聖宗), in the fifth year of Qiānhēng (乾亨) (983 CE), issued an edict saying:
“When the five grains fail to ripen,
we open the imperial treasury to remit the people’s taxes;
when armyworms and locusts cause disaster,
we abolish corvée labor to show pity for the hungry and poor.”
In the third year of Tǒnghé (統和) (985 CE),
the Emperor once passed through Ānchéng (䤝城).
Seeing that the sorghum of the women of the Yǐshì (乙室) and Àowěi (奧隗) tribes, such as Díliǎn (迪輦), was overripe and unharvested,
he sent men to help reap it.
Tàishī (太師) Hán DéRàng (韓德讓) said
that after the war, absconding commoners abandoned their livelihoods,
and their crops remained lodged in the fields.
He proposed recruiting people to harvest them,
giving half of the yield to the harvesters.
Zhèngshì Lìng (政事令) Shì Fǎng (室昉) also said
that the prefectures west of the mountains (Shānxī) had been providing for military campaigns,
and the people’s strength was depleted.
Their fields and crops were largely trampled by border soldiers,
and he requested remission of this year's rent.
In the sixth year (988 CE),
there was frost and drought,
and the afflicted people were starving.
An edict was issued to the Three Offices (Sān Sī), stating:
The old method of commuting tax money for grain
did not accurately reflect the market price.
The value should be increased to benefit the people.
They also moved three hundred households of residents from Jíbì Zhài (吉避寨) to the three prefectures of Tán (檀), Shùn (順), and Jì (薊),
selected fertile land,
and provided them with oxen and grain seeds.
In the thirteenth year (995 CE),
an edict ordered the establishment of Righteous Granaries (Yìcāng) in all circuits (dào).
In autumn of each year,
the community members (shè mín), according to their harvest,
would have their households contribute grain to stockpile in the granaries,
and the community officials (shè sī) would register the details.
In lean years,
the grain would be distributed to relieve the people.
In the fifteenth year (997 CE),
an edict exempted Nánjīng (南京) from old debts of grain owed to the Righteous Granaries,
and also prohibited various military officials from hunting or grazing outside the proper season, thereby interfering with farming.
In the first year of Kāitài (開泰) (1012 CE),
an edict stated:
“We believe that when the common people’s corvée burdens are heavy,
they should be given more payment for their labor;
when the year's harvest fails to ripen,
granaries should be opened for loans;
and for those whose fields and gardens are overgrown and ruined,
oxen and seeds should be provided to assist them.”
In the early years of Tàipíng (太平) (1021–1031 CE), the Emperor visited Yān (燕).
The people of Yān offered local rare and valuable products because of the bountiful year.
The Emperor showed courtesy to the elderly,
bestowed favor upon the widowed and orphaned,
and granted feasts for consecutive days.
In the ninth year (1029 CE),
there was famine in the Yān region.
Hùbù Fùshǐ (戶部副使) Wáng Jiā (王嘉) requested the construction of ships,
recruiting those skilled in sea transport,
to move grain from Liáodōng (遼東) to supply Yān.
However, the proposal was shelved after critics claimed the route was dangerous and inconvenient.
Upon Xīngzōng’s (興宗) accession (1031 CE),
he sent envoys to inspect the crops in all circuits.
In that same year,
a comprehensive census of households was conducted.
An edict stated:
“In Our early years,
We learned about farming.
Those who labor efficiently widely engage in plowing and weeding,
but seldom report their yields for tax;
those dependent on official stipends completely neglect planting,
often leading to flight and dispersion.
It is appropriate to conduct a thorough inspection
to achieve universal fairness and equity.”
It was prohibited for officials of various ranks to arbitrarily use grain for brewing alcohol;
for weddings and sacrifices,
permission was granted only after the authorities issued a written document.
In the early years of Dàozōng (道宗) (1055–1101 CE),
grain rained down from the northwest for thirty *lǐ*,
and a *dǒu* of grain cost six *qián* in Chūnzhōu (春州).
At that time, the Western Fān (蕃) often rebelled.
The Emperor, wishing to establish defense measures,
ordered Yēlǜ Tánggǔ (耶律唐古) to supervise farming to supply the Western Army.
Tánggǔ led the multitude to cultivate fields beside the Lúqú Hé (臚朐河),
and the annual harvest was abundant.
He moved the garrison to Zhènzhōu (鎮州).
For fourteen years,
they accumulated several hundred thousand *hú* of grain,
each *dǒu* costing no more than a few *qián*.
When Mǎ Rénwàng (馬人望) previously served as the Dùzhī Pànguān (度支判官) of Nánjīng,
both public and private finances were ample.
He inspected the households
and applied the law fairly and leniently.
He was then promoted to Dùzhī Shǐ (度支使) of Zhōngjīng (中京).
After holding office for half a year,
he accumulated 150,000 *hú* of grain,
and was promoted to Zuǒ Sànqí Chángshì (左散騎常侍).
The grain agriculture of Liáo (遼) reached its peak at this time.
And in Tōnjīng (東京), within the more than fifty cities like Xián (咸), Xìn (信), Sū (蘇), Fù (復), Chén (辰), Hǎi (海), Tóng (同), Yín (銀), Wū (烏), Suì (遂), Chūn (春), Tài (泰), etc.,
and the various prefectures along the borders,
each had Harmonized Purchase Granaries (Hé Dí Cāng).
Following the laws of the ancestors,
they exchanged old grain for new,
and permitted the common people to voluntarily borrow money,
collecting an interest of twenty percent (two *fēn*).
The total stock in various locations was estimated to be two to three hundred thousand *shí*.
Even through consecutive military campaigns,
they never ran short.
By the Tiānqìng (天慶) period (1111–1121 CE),
when the Jīn (金) troops invaded in force,
it was all taken over.
When Tiānzuò (天祚) was forced to flee,
Yēlǜ Díliè (耶律敵烈) and others compelled the enthronement of Prince of Liáng, Yǎlǐ (梁王雅里).
They ordered the households under the herdsmen's administration to transport grain from the Yánluò Cāng (鹽濼倉).
The households suffered damage and loss to the grain.
It was proposed that their assets be registered to compensate for the loss.
Yǎlǐ personally set the compensation value: one sheep for one cartload of grain,
one ox for three cartloads,
one horse for five cartloads,
and one camel for eight cartloads.
His followers said:
“Currently, two *dǒu* of grain are hard to obtain for one sheep;
this valuation is far too low.”
Yǎlǐ replied:
“If the people have it, I have it.
If they are made to compensate fully,
how can the multitude endure?”
Though the matter was ultimately unresolved,
had Heaven not yet cut off Liáo,
these words would have been sufficient to win the hearts of the people.
Regarding the system of taxation,
it was initiated by Tàizǔ (太祖), when he employed Hán YánHuī (韓延徽),
who first established the national expenditure regulations.
Tàizōng (太宗) registered the households and adults (*dīng*) of the Five Capitals (Wǔ Jīng) to determine taxes,
but the exact number of households and adults is unverifiable.
During Shèngzōng’s Qiānhēng (乾亨) period,
it was determined that in Shàngjīng (上京),
the “cloud-dependent households” (*yún wéi hù*),
who possessed substantial wealth according to property assessment,
were adept at evading corvée labor,
thereby harming the poor commoners.
Consequently, an order was issued compelling these households
to deliver all accrued interest and principal
to the government,
and distribute the levies equally among the people.
In the middle of Tǒnghé (統和) (983–1012 CE),
Yēlǜ Zhāo (耶律昭) reported
that among the population of the Northwest,
each year during the farming season,
one man was used for lookout duty,
one man cultivated public fields,
and two men were assigned corvée duty for the investigation officials (*jiū guān*).
At that time, military farm garrisons (*túntián shù bīng*) were established along the border,
cultivating fields and accumulating grain to provide military rations.
Therefore, an edict in the seventh year of Tàipíng (太平) (1027 CE) stipulated that
the grain accumulated in official granaries at the military farms must not be lent out arbitrarily,
and those in the garrisons who vigorously cultivated public fields
were exempt from taxes and levies.
This was the system of Public Fields (gōngtián).
Other commoners who volunteered
either cultivated unused land (xián tián)
or cultivated private land (sī tián).
In these cases, they paid taxes based on the measurement of the land by contributing grain to the state.
In the fifteenth year of Tǒnghé (統和) (997 CE),
people were recruited to cultivate the fallow land along the Luán Hé (灤河),
and rent collection began ten years later.
This was the system of Official Fallow Land (guān xián tián).
An edict also ordered households north and south of the mountains (Shān Qián Hòu) who had not yet paid taxes
to register land and establish holdings for taxation
in the two counties of Mìyún (密雲) and Yānlè (燕樂).
This was the system of Private Land (sī tián).
The ministers of various tribes followed the emperor on campaigns,
captured and seized households,
and established their own walled settlements,
forming Head-Under Military Prefectures (Tóuxià Jūnzhōu).
All taxes from market transactions
went to the Head-Under administrations,
except for the alcohol tax, which was submitted to Shàngjīng.
This divides the taxes of the Head-Under Military Prefectures into two categories.
Previously,
the newly annexed territory of Liáodōng (遼東) did not have a monopoly on brewing and vending alcohol,
and restrictions on salt and yeast (*yán qū*) were also relaxed.
Féng YánXiū (馮延休) and Hán ShàoXūn (韓紹勳) successively engaged in commercial exploitation,
attempting to apply the rules of Píngshān (平山) in the Yān region to impose strict regulations.
The common people resented this,
which consequently led to the rebellion of Dà YánLín (大延琳).
After consecutive years of edicts restoring their previous tax system,
the people finally became peaceful and stable.
Nánjīng annually submitted salt and iron tax money to the Three Offices, commuted into silk.
Dàtóng (大同) annually submitted tax money to the Three Offices, commuted into grain.
According to the precedent of Kāiyuǎn Jūn (開遠軍),
the commoners annually paid their taxes,
with one *dǒu* of grain commuted for five *qián*.
When Yēlǜ Mǒzhī (耶律抹只) governed the prefecture,
he submitted a memorial requesting commutation at six *qián*.
These were all benevolent policies beneficial to the people.
Treatise Twenty-Nine: Food and Goods, Part Two
originated when Tàizǔ (太祖) established Yángchéng (羊城) north of Tànshān (炭山),
establishing monopoly offices (Quèwù) to facilitate market exchanges across all circuits (dào).
When Tàizōng (太宗) acquired Yān (燕),
he established Nánjīng (南京).
North of the city was a market,
where hundreds of goods were piled up like mountains.
He commanded the responsible officials to manage the taxation thereof.
In the other four capitals (jīng) and in other prefectures (zhōu) and counties (xiàn) where goods were produced and traded,
offices were established similarly.
A watchtower (kànlóu) was established within the city of Dōngpíng Jùn (東平郡),
dividing it into Southern and Northern Markets.
Trade took place in the Northern Market around Yǔzhōng (禺中);
after Wǔlòu (午漏), trade shifted to the Southern Market.
Xióngzhōu (雄州), Gāochāng (高昌), and Bóhǎi (渤海) also established mutual markets (hùshì),
to facilitate trade with Nánsòng (南宋), the various Northwestern tribes, and Gāolì (高麗).

Thus, the Nǚzhí (女直) used gold, silks, cloth, honey, wax, various medicinal materials, and tribes like Tiělí (鐵離), Mòhé (靺鞨), and Yújué (于厥) used clamshell pearls, blue squirrel fur, sable fur, aquatic animal hides (jiāoyú zhī pí), cattle, sheep, camels, horses, and felted wool (cuìjì) products,
which they brought to exchange in Liáo (遼);
the roads were packed [with traders].
In the early Tǒnghé (統和) era of Shèngzōng (聖宗), the Yānjīng Liúshǒusī (燕京留守司) reported that
the common people faced difficulty obtaining food.
They requested to relax the duties at Jūyōng Guān (居庸關),
in order to facilitate the procurement and exchange of grain from Shānxī (山西).
Officials were also ordered to inform the various traveling palaces (xínggōng) that
textiles (bùbó) that were short, narrow, and did not meet the required measurements
should not be sold in the market.
The following year,
an edict was issued stating that the markets of the Southern and Northern Palaces (Nán Fǔ, Běi Fǔ) lacked sufficient people,
and it was fitting to lead a hundred carriages from the relevant departments to attend the assembly.
Qífēng Lù (奇峰路) was opened to facilitate trade with Yìzhōu (易州).
In the twenty-third year [of Tǒnghé],
Zhènwǔ Jūn (振武軍) and Bǎozhōu (保州) both established monopoly markets (quèyì).
At that time, Yēlǜ Shǐlǔ (耶律室魯), the Grand King of the Northern Chancellery (Běiyuàn Dàwáng), noted that there were frequent deficiencies in the sheep provided as stipends,
and his tribal people were impoverished.
He requested permission to exchange old, weak sheep and their hides and wool for silks from the Southern region,
which would be convenient for all parties.
By the time of Tiānzuò's (天祚) rebellion/turmoil,
taxes and levies were already heavy,
and the laws of commerce were broken.
Wealth daily dwindled, and the people daily suffered.
Regarding the laws of salt administration (yán cè),
Tàizǔ (太祖), due to the large number of Hàn (漢) people he had acquired,
immediately separated the ancient Hànchéng (漢城) from the eight tribes, forming a separate department to govern it.
The city was south of Tànshān (炭山).
It had the benefit of salt ponds.
This was the former Huáyán Xiàn (滑鹽縣) of the Later Wèi (Hòu Wèi).
All eight tribes obtained and consumed salt from it.
When [Tàizǔ] returned from campaigning against Yōu (幽) and Jì (薊),
he stopped at Hèlà Luò (鶴剌濼),
and ordered salt to be retrieved there and provided to the army.
Thereafter, the salt in the lake (luò) became increasingly abundant,
sufficient for both the upper and lower classes.
In the early Huìtóng (會同) era,
Tàizōng (太宗) provided great assistance to Jìn (晉).
Jìn offered sixteen prefectures (zhōu) as tribute land,
and Yíng (瀛) and Mò (莫) were among them.
Thus, [Liao] first acquired the benefit of boiling seawater for salt at Héjiān (河間).
A Salt Monopoly Office (Quèyán Yuàn) was established in Xiānghé Xiàn (香河縣).
Consequently, the regions of Yān (燕) and Yún (雲) and areas further north temporarily consumed Cāng (滄) salt.
At that time, salt-producing areas, such as Bóhǎi (渤海), Zhènchéng (鎮城), Hǎiyáng (海陽), Fēngzhōu (豐州), Yángluò Chéng (陽洛城), and Guǎngjì Hú (廣濟湖),
were placed under the jurisdiction of the Accounting Bureaus (Jìsī) of the Five Capitals (Wǔ Jīng).
Regarding the system for boiling and extracting [salt],
and the annual output quota,
the details cannot be fully ascertained.
As for mining and smelting (kēng yě),
Tàizǔ (太祖) began by annexing the Shìwéi (室韋).
Their land produced copper, iron, gold, and silver,
and their people were skilled at making copper and iron implements.
Moreover, the Hézhú (曷朮) tribe had much iron.
"Hézhú" (曷朮)
means "iron" in the national language.
This department established three smelting sites (yě): called Liǔshī Hé (柳濕河),
Sānchù Gǔsī (三黜古斯),
and Shǒushān (手山).
In the early Shéncè (神冊) era,
when Bóhǎi (渤海) was pacified,
Guǎngzhōu (廣州) was acquired.
This was originally Bóhǎi's (渤海) Tiělì Fǔ (鐵利府),
and was renamed Tiělì Zhōu (鐵利州).
The area also produced much iron.
Dōngpíng Xiàn (東平縣) was originally the former land of Hàn's Xiāngpíng Xiàn (襄平縣).
Iron ore was produced there.
Three hundred households dedicated to mining and refining were established,
and they provided tribute based on their assessments.
Since most mining and smelting sites were in the eastern part of the state,
the Hùbù Sī (戶部司, Ministry of Revenue Bureau) was established in Dōngjīng (東京),
and the Qiánbó Sī (錢帛司, Bureau of Coinage and Silk) was established in Chángchūn Zhōu (長春州).
When Tàizǔ (太祖) campaigned against Yōu (幽) and Jì (薊),
the army returned,
stopping at the foot of a mountain.
Silver and iron ore were discovered,
and he ordered smelting sites to be established.
During the Tàipíng (太平) era of Shèngzōng (聖宗),
gold and silver mines were discovered north of the Huáng Hé (潢河) at Yīnshān (陰山), and at the source of the Liáo Hé (遼河),
respectively.
Smelting was initiated for mining and refining.
From this time until the end of Tiānzuò (天祚),
the state relied on these profits.
Regarding the laws of coinage (gǔ zhù),
in the preceding generation, Sālàde (撒剌的) was Yílíjǐn (夷離菫).
Since the land produced much copper,
he began minting currency.
Tàizǔ (太祖) was his son,
and he inherited and used this currency,
thereby achieving wealth and power,
which led to the founding of the imperial enterprise.
Tàizōng (太宗) established the Five Smelting Grand Masters (Wǔyě Tàishī),
to supervise the coinage and iron production across the four regions.
Shí Jìngtáng (石敬瑭) also presented the accumulated coinage along the border,
to provision the army.
Jǐngzōng (景宗), finding the old coins insufficient for use,
began casting the new Qiánhēng (乾亨) coins.
The currency circulated widely.
Shèngzōng (聖宗) dug into Dà'ān Shān (大安山),
recovering the coins hidden by Liú Shǒuguāng (劉守光).
These were distributed among the Five Accounting Bureaus (Wǔ Jìsī).
He also minted the Tàipíng (太平) coins,
using both the new and old interchangeably.
Because of this, the state's currency
spread throughout the realm.
Thus, during the Tǒnghé (統和) era, coins from the imperial treasury were released,
and granted to the various military headquarters in Nánjīng (南京).
In the Kàitài (開泰) era,
an edict was issued to all circuits (dào),
stating that for poor and destitute people
who had pawned or mortgaged their sons or daughters,
the hire price should be calculated at ten coins per day.
Once the debt was cleared,
they should be returned to their parents.
Every spring and autumn,
official funds were used to feast the officers and soldiers.
The abundance of coins was overwhelming;
consequently, those minted in Dōngjīng (東京) were only put into use starting in the Qīngníng (清寧) era.
At this time,
an edict prohibited trading copper and iron in all circuits,
to prevent private minting.
It was also forbidden to sell copper and iron to the Huíhú (回鶻).
The law became increasingly strict.
During Dàozōng's (道宗) reign,
there were four types of coins: Xiányōng (咸雍),
Dàkāng (大康),
Dà'ān (大安),
and Shòulóng (壽隆).
All were renamed following changes in the reign title (yuán).
Details regarding their inner rim (ròu hǎo) or weight in zhū cannot be verified.
Furthermore, Yáng Zūnxù (楊遵勗) was commanded by edict to collect old coins from households delinquent to the Hùbù Sī (戶部司).
He recovered over 400,000 strings (qiǎng) of coins,
and was appointed Academician of the Bureau of Military Affairs (Shūmì Zhí Xuéshì).
Liú Shēn (劉伸), serving as Minister of Revenue (Hùbù Shǐ),
brought in an excess of 300,000 strings of coins annually,
and was promoted to Commissioner of Military Affairs of the Southern Chancellery (Nányuàn Shūmìshǐ).
Due to disasters and plagues,
money was released to relieve the poor and destitute, and the households stationed at various palaces and border garrisons.
At this time,
although there were not yet accumulations so vast that the strings rotted and defied counting,
the state could still be called wealthy.
However, in his later years,
expenditures were vast and numerous,
and coinage remained the same,
but the state's resources were insufficient.
Although aid amounting to ten million [coins] from the Hǎiyún Fósì (海雲佛寺)
was accepted without refusal,
soon after, the export of commoners' money outside the borders was prohibited.
During Tiānzuò's (天祚) reign,
two types of new coins, Qiántǒng (乾統) and Tiānqìng (天慶), were minted,
yet both the elite and the common people were poor and suffering,
and the state treasuries held no surplus savings.
When Tàizǔ first served as the Yílíjǐn of Diéliè Fǔ,
he was mindful of the singularity and weakness of the Yáoniǎn clan,
and therefore pacified all the tribes.
He made rewards and punishments clear,
did not launch reckless military expeditions,
and benefited the people by utilizing their advantages.
Livestock bred in great numbers,
and both superiors and subordinates had sufficient supplies.
When he ascended the throne,
he attacked Hédōng,
and conquered the commanderies and counties of Dàiběi,
capturing over 100,000 cattle, sheep, camels, and horses.
The Grand Councilor Yēlǜ Xiézhěn campaigned against the Nǚzhí,
and subsequently captured over 200,000 horses.
These were divided up and pastured in locations convenient for water and grass;
the increase over several years was countless.
At that time,
when counting the horses of the rich,
none were added [in the official count],
