and when granting more than ten thousand horses to the Dà Hú and Xiǎo Hú armies,
none were deducted [from the official count].
This was certainly because the livestock management system was regulated.
In the fifth year of Xiányōng (1069),
Xiāo Táokuí, serving as the Grand Guardian of the Horse Herds,
submitted a memorial still arguing that the system of herding existed only in name but not in reality,
with superiors and subordinates deceiving each other.
He suggested that the actual numbers should be counted to establish a fixed registry.
Subsequently, Dōngdān Guó annually contributed a thousand horses,
the Nǚzhí ten thousand horses,
Zhíbùgǔ and other states ten thousand horses,
Zǔbǔ and Wúdúwǎn and Tìdé each twenty thousand horses,
Xī Xià and Shìwéi each three hundred horses,
and Yuèlǐdǔ, Pōuālí, Àolǐmǐ, Púnúlǐ, Tiělí, and other various tribes three hundred horses.
Furthermore, the sale of sheep and horses from Shuòzhōu Lù into Sòng was forbidden,
as was the sale of Tǔhún and Dǎngxiàng horses into Xià.
Because of this, the herds flourished and multiplied,
reaching a count of over a million head.
The officials managing the pastures in all the offices were promoted in turn.
From Tàizǔ until Xīngzōng, for nearly two hundred years,
the prosperity of the herds was constant.
In the early years of Tiānzuò,
there were still tens of thousands of horse herds,
with each herd comprising no fewer than a thousand horses.
According to the ancestral statutes,
tens of thousands of horses intended for Southern campaigns were always selected,
and pastured between Xióng, Bà, Qīng, and Cāng,
to be prepared for emergencies in Yān and Yún.
Several tens of thousands more were selected
for seasonal hunting expeditions;
the remainder were divided up for regional pasturing.
This system was perfectly sound.
By the final years [of the dynasty],
repeated battles with Jīn resulted in
losses of sixty or seventy percent of the Khitan and Han warhorses.
Although prices were raised several times over,
it was impossible to purchase replacements.
Consequently, people illegally bought government horses for military service.
Private sales among the herdsmen increased daily,
and even hunting expeditions lacked sufficient mounts.
They were subsequently defeated by Jīn.
Abandoning the populace and being forced to move,
they finally perished.
The old horses north of Sōngmò
all fell into the possession of Dàshí Línyá.
What can be seen regarding the sustenance and wealth of Liáo is thus.
As for the annual tribute paid by neighboring states,
and the annual submission of local produce by vassal states,
although the military and state expenditures of successive courts largely relied upon these,
they were not products of the home country.
Moreover, the names and quantities have already appeared in the Annals (Běnjì),
so they are not recorded here again.
Now, Jìběi is suitable for horses,
and the seashore is suitable for salt.
There is no need to debate this.
Half of the Liáo territory is sandy desert,
and three seasons are mostly cold.
Plowing and harvesting in spring and autumn must be done precisely on time,
and millet and rice planting relies on the topography of the land.
Therefore, it cannot be the same as the Central Lands (Zhōngtǔ).
However, from the beginning years of Liáo,
agricultural grain was abundant and surplus,
relief for famine and aid for the distressed
was dispensed without stinginess,
extending even to neighboring states,
with a generous surplus.
What method was employed to achieve this prosperity?
It was nothing other than
selecting the right people to encourage agriculture,
and having regulated planning and arrangements.
Those who discuss currency in the world
always worry that heavy metals are hard to transport
and that casting cannot meet the demand.
This is why the expedient method of paper currency arose.
The use of boats and oars for transport in the Northwest,
compared to the Southeast,
is barely one or two tenths.
When Liáo was flourishing,
metallic currency circulated widely,
the state finances were robust.
They provided for garrisons and rewarded campaigns,
granting gifts in the hundreds of millions,
yet we never heard of what is called paper currency.
What method, then, allowed them to achieve this convenience?
It was nothing other than
both old reserves and newly minted coins,
being permitted for use by the people.
Mèngzǐ said:
“He who is sufficient in managing resources
cannot be destroyed by a year of famine.”
If human effort is brought to bear,
a single man is still sufficient to overcome seasonal calamities,
let alone managing a nation.
From this, we know that those who plan well for the state
have a method to govern the suitability of heavenly timing and earthly advantages,
and they never fail to achieve their ambitions.
No provision is greater than grain,
and no commodity is greater than currency.
We especially record these two things
to show that the officials who held power early in Liáo
were skilled in enriching their nation.
Treatise Thirty: Treatise on Penal Law, Part One
Punishment (Xíng)
is that which begins with force (bīng) and ends with propriety (lǐ).
In the age of primal chaos,
the nascent populace had force,
like a bee has a sting,
purely for self-defense.
It was only when Chīyóu first began to cause trouble,
and these people acted cruelly,
with villainy and criminality arising together,
how could the use of punishment cease?
Emperor Yáo sought information clearly from the common people,
and then ordered the Sān Hòu (Three Chiefs) to supervise services for the people.
Bó Yí established the statutes,
and restrained the people by means of punishment.
Therefore, it is said that punishment (xíng)
is that which begins with force (bīng) and ends with propriety (lǐ).
The ancient kings followed Heaven, Earth, and the Four Seasons to establish the Six Ministers.
Autumn,
is the season of the penal official,
symbolizing the time when things are completed.
Autumn transfers its energy from Summer,
and changes color from Spring.
By extension, this can be understood.
Liáo established its state through military power,
and the control of violence and suppression of wickedness
started with punishment.
When the state first enacted laws,
some measures exceeded the rules of the Five Mourning Attires (Wǔ Fú) and the Three Degrees of Punishment (Sān Jiù).
As the momentum of force (bīng) was still surging,
there was no time yet for the application of propriety (lǐ).
When Zǔwǔ Kèhán recognized the worthiness of the imperial kinsman Yǎlǐ,
he appointed him Yílíjǐn to oversee penalties and executions.
Was this not because the position of Judicature Official (Shìshī)
cannot be held by anyone but the worthy?
When Tàizǔ and Tàizōng managed the territories,
the armored soldiers had no peaceful rest year-round.
Awe must overcome love—
this was the necessity of the situation.
As their descendants succeeded them,
the laws varied in severity;
but those who could prudently assess expedience in the interim,
and conclude matters with propriety (lǐ),
were only the two sovereigns, Jǐngzōng and Shèngzōng, who excelled.
However, the general categories for imposing penalties are four: namely, death,
namely, banishment (liú),
namely, penal servitude (tú),
and namely, beating with a rod (zhàng).
Death sentences include categories such as strangulation (jiǎo), decapitation (zhǎn), and slow slicing (língchí).
There is also the method of confiscation (jímò).
For the penalty of banishment (liúxíng), judging the severity of the crime,
they were settled in the territories of border cities or tribes.
If further, they were cast beyond the borders.
If even further, they were punished by being sent to remote lands.
Penal servitude (túxíng) is categorized first as lifelong,
second as five years,
and third as one and a half years.
Those sentenced to lifelong servitude were beaten five hundred strokes;
the subsequent categories were reduced by one hundred strokes successively.
There was also the method of tattooing (qīngcì).
Punishment by rod (zhàngxíng) ranged from fifty to three hundred strokes.
Generally, those who received fifty or more strokes,
were beaten with a sandbag (shādài).
There were also the methods involving the wooden sword (mùjiàn), the large club (dàbàng), and the iron bone hammer (tiěgǔgāng).
The number of strokes for the wooden sword (mùjiàn) and the large club (dàbàng) was three,
ranging from fifteen to thirty.
The number of strokes for the iron bone hammer (tiěgǔgāng),
was either five or seven.
For those with heavy offenses,
who were about to be beaten with a sandbag (shādài),
they were first struck above and around the coccyx.
Instruments for torture and interrogation
included the *zàng* rod, the thin rod (xìzhàng), and the methods of whipping (biān) and branding (lào).
The number of strokes for the *zàng* rod (zàngzhàng) was twenty;
the number of strokes for the thin rod (xìzhàng) was three,
ranging from thirty to sixty.
Regarding the number of strokes for whipping (biān) and branding (lào):
generally, thirty brandings incurred three hundred whip strokes,
and fifty brandings incurred five hundred whip strokes.
If the accused, regarding various matters, should have submitted but did not comply,
they were interrogated using these methods.
If ranking officials made mistakes while handling public affairs,
or if commoners aged seventy or above, or fifteen or below, committed crimes,
they were permitted to redeem the punishment (shú) with a fine.
The amount of copper (tóng) for redemption was:
for one hundred strokes of the rod,
one thousand coins were submitted.
There were also the principles of the Eight Deliberations (Bāyì) and the Eight Allowances (Bāzòng).
The method of confiscation (jímò),
began when Tàizǔ (太祖) was the Tàimǎcháshālǐ (撻馬狘沙里),
receiving the order of Héndéjǐn Kèhán (痕德菫可汗),
to investigate the murder of Yúyuè Shìlǔ (于越釋魯).
The families of the principal offenders were confiscated and placed under Wǎlǐ (瓦里).
When Chúnqīn Huánghòu (淳欽皇后) was reigning, they were separated out
to become Attendant Gentlemen (Zhùzhàng Lángjūn).
It was not until Shìzōng (世宗) issued an edict to pardon them.
After that, the families of imperial relatives, both internal and external, and hereditary officials,
who committed crimes such as rebellion (fǎnnì),
were again subject to confiscation (mòrù).
Other people were confiscated to become Attendant Households (Zhùzhàng Hù).
There were also cases where property was confiscated into the Palace Division (Gōngfēn) or distributed as gifts to subordinates.
The wooden sword (Mùjiàn) and the large club (Dàbàng)
were established during the reign of Tàizōng (太宗).
The wooden sword (mùjiàn) was flat on one side and convex on the back.
If high ministers committed grave crimes,
and leniency was desired, they were struck with it.
The sandbag (shādài)
was established during the reign of Mùzōng (穆宗).
Its construction used cured leather sewn together,
six *cùn* long,
two *cùn* wide,
and the handle was about one *chǐ* long.
The details of the number of years for penal servitude (túxíng) are elaborated in the Zhòngxī (重熙) statutes.
The details for the number of strokes for punishment by rod (zhàngxíng) and lesser penalties are elaborated in the Xiányōng (咸雍) statutes.
As for the rest, which were not commonly used and had no fixed form,
they cannot all be recorded.
In the early years of Tàizǔ (太祖),
miscellaneous affairs were initially improvised.
Offenders were punished based on the assessed severity of their crime.
Later, when punishing the rebellious faction of his younger brothers,
ad hoc laws were created expediently.
If an imperial prince followed the rebellion,
he was not distinguished from common people;
sometimes he was thrown from a high cliff and killed.
Those who engaged in sexual depravity and defiance of norms
were torn apart by five chariots (huánshā).
Those who rebelled against their parents were treated similarly.
Those who slandered, cursed, or offended superiors
were killed by having their mouths pierced with a hot iron awl.
Accessories to the crime
were subjected to the rod (zhàngjué) based on the severity of their involvement.
There were two types of rods: the large one weighed five hundred *qián*,
and the small one three hundred *qián*.

There were also the punishments of displaying the head on a pole (xiāozhé), burying alive (shēngyì), shooting with ‘ghost arrows’ (shèguǐjiàn), launching by catapult (pàozhì), and dismemberment (zhījiě).
The reliance on harsh laws
was merely to restrict the populace and prevent disturbances.
In the *Guǐyǒu* year,
an imperial edict stated:
“Since I began the Northern Campaigns,
lawsuits and prisons across the four regions
have accumulated considerably.
Now that the fighting has ceased and the people are resting,
let all my officials fulfill my intention,
deliberate and resolve these cases carefully,
so that no one suffers injustice.”
Thereupon, he ordered the Chancellor of the Northern Administration, Xiāo Dílǔ (蕭敵魯), and others to divide up the task and expedite the resolution of the cases.
The sympathetic and merciful intent of the Liáo (遼) Dynasty
began to be evident here.
In the sixth year of Shéncè (神册),
after subduing and pacifying the various barbarian tribes,
the Emperor (Shàng) addressed his attendants, saying:
“All miscellaneous matters of the state,
whether great or small, are distinct.
If the legal codes and standards are unclear,
how can governance be achieved,
and how can the subordinates know what is prohibited?”
He then commanded the high ministers to establish laws for governing the Qìdān (契丹) and the various other barbarians (zhūyí).
Hàn (漢) people were judged according to the regulatory statutes (lǜlìng),
and a Bell Bureau (Zhōngyuàn) was established to allow the common people to present their grievances.
During the reign of Tàizōng (太宗),
the governance of the Bóhǎi (渤海) people entirely followed the Hàn (漢) legal system,
but there were no other changes.
In the fourth year of Huìtóng (會同),
Shèlì Lángjūn (舍利郎君) of the imperial clan plotted to poison the interpreter Jiělǐ (解里) and others.
Two individuals had already been poisoned.
An order was given to heavily flog him,
and his wife was banished (liú) to the Juébálímǐ Hé (厥拔離弭河).
The family of the person who manufactured the poison was executed (zú).
In the second year of Tiānlù (天祿) during the reign of Shìzōng (世宗),
Tiāndé (天德), Xiāo Hàn (蕭翰), Liú Gē (劉哥), and his younger brother Péndōu (盆都), among others, plotted rebellion.
Tiāndé (天德) was executed.
Xiāo Hàn (蕭翰) was beaten with the rod (zhàng).
Liú Gē (劉哥) was banished (liú).
Péndōu (盆都) was dispatched as an envoy to the Xiágāsī Guó (轄戞斯國).
Now, the crimes of these four people were equal, yet their punishments differed.
During the Liáo (遼) dynasty, there were often cases
where the same crime was adjudicated differently.
In the twelfth year of Mùzōng’s Yìnglì era,
Hǎilǐ, the slave of the Imperial Uncle (Guójiù) and Bureau Chief (Zhàng Lángjūn) Xiāo Yánzhī, forcibly violated the minor daughter of Zhuāi Là Tūlǐ.
As there was no existing law concerning this matter,
he was punished with castration (gōng xíng)
and returned to Tūlǐ to serve as a slave.
Because of this incident, a decree was instituted.
In the sixteenth year,
an edict was issued to the relevant authorities (yǒu sī):
“Since the time of the previous dynasty, wherever the imperial procession stopped and rested,
tall markers must be erected to prohibit passage.
Recently, it has been heard that the likes of Chǔgǔ,
deliberately place these markers low down in the deep grass,
hoping that people will mistakenly enter,
and then use this to seize wealth.
From now on, anyone who repeats this offense
shall be executed.”
However, the Emperor was addicted to wine and hunting,
and paid no attention to governing (zhèngshì).
The staff of the Wǔfāng (Five Bureaus), the Animal Keepers (Zhǎng Shòu), Attendants (Jìnshì), Food Servers (Fèng Shàn), and Wine Servers (Zhǎng Jiǔ), etc.,
if deer, wild boar, falcons, or pheasants were lost, injured, or killed,
or if servants privately escaped and absconded,
or if a summoned person exceeded the reporting deadline,
or failed to arrive on time when summoned,
or if their petition or answer was slightly unsatisfactory,
or because of a small matter concerning food or drink,
or because he transferred his anger onto innocent people due to the offenses of others,
he would immediately inflict the torture of branding (páolào) and the iron comb (tiě shū).
The worst cases were countless.
Sometimes he stabbed them personally with a blade,
or had them executed, struck, shot, or burned;
hands and feet were cut off,
shoulders and thighs were lacerated,
waists and shins were broken,
mouths were gashed, teeth were smashed,
and bodies were abandoned in the wilderness.
Furthermore, he ordered the construction of mounds over these sites.
The number of dead reached over a hundred people.
In the capital (Jīngshī), a hundred-foot prison (láo) was established to house the detained prisoners.
It is said that shortly after he ascended the throne,
he was misled by the words of the sorceress Xiàogǔ,
and took human gall bladders to compound medicine for longevity,
so he killed quite a large number of people.
Later, realizing her deception,
he killed her by shooting her with a cluster of whistling arrows and having her trampled by horses.
When Hǎilǐ died,
the Emperor held prolonged night drinking sessions.
The executions and killings of staff from the Wǔfāng, the Animal Keepers, and personal attendants (zuǒyòu gěishì)
followed one after another without cessation.
Although he sometimes regretted his excessive punishments due to anger,
and decreed that his high officials (dàchén) should strongly remonstrate;
those at court were fearful and timid,
and few were able to offer correction or salvation.
Even if they did remonstrate, he could not listen.
When he was about to kill Shòugē and Niàngǔ,
the Grand Inspector-in-Chief of the Palace Front (Diànqián Dōu Diǎnjiǎn), Yēlǜ Yīlàgě, remonstrated, saying:
“Shòugē and the others ran away out of fear of punishment
after killing the pheasant under their care.
According to the law, they should not die.”
The Emperor grew angry,
beheaded Shòugē and the others,
and dismembered their bodies.
He ordered the relevant authorities to gather all sixty-five deer-keepers who were currently detained,
beheaded the forty-four whose offenses were serious,
and severely beat the rest.
Among those whom the Emperor intended to kill,
they were spared thanks to the remonstrance of Prince Bìshè and others.
Soon after, he became angry that Pōdé had fed the deer irregularly,
causing them injury and death,
and consequently killed him.
In his later years,
his tyranny grew worse.
He once told the Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi) Huàgě:
“If I execute someone inappropriately while drunk,
report it to me when I am sober.”
Yet, he only spoke these words;
he showed no intention of repenting in the end,
and thus met his downfall (nàn).
Although it is said that his cruelty was limited to his personal servants (xiè yù),
not extending up to the high officials
nor down to the common people (bǎixìng),
how could the judicial system and laws
be instruments for a ruler to indulge his emotions and follow his desires?
Jǐngzōng, while still a prince (zài qián),
had already observed his faults.
Upon ascending the throne,
he executed the Grand Inspector-in-Chief of the Palace Front (Diànqián Dōu Diǎnjiǎn) Yēlǜ Yīlàgě
for dereliction of duty in the palace guard (sù wèi).
Xǐyǐn, the Prince of Zhào, arbitrarily removed his shackles from the confinement area
and requested an audience to defend himself.
The Emperor addressed him, saying:
“Right and wrong have not yet been determined,
how can there be a principle of leaving prison to defend oneself?”
He ordered him to be bound again.
Afterward, he personally reviewed the records of the prisoners
and summoned and released them all.
In the third year of Bǎoníng,
because Mùzōng had abolished the Complaint Bureau (Zhōng Yuàn),
leaving wronged poor people nowhere to appeal,
he decreed its restoration.
He also commanded that a bell be cast
and the decree inscribed upon it,
explaining the rationale for its abolition and restoration.
Shāo, the Prince of Wú, was falsely accused by a slave.
The authorities requested an investigation.
The Emperor said:
“I know this is a fabrication.
If we interrogate the case,
I fear that others will imitate this behavior.”
He ordered the execution of the slave as a warning.
In the fifth year,
the attendant Shílǔlǐ accidentally touched the sacred banner (shén dǔ).
The law dictated death,
but he was beaten and released.
This suggests an inclination toward balancing leniency and strictness.
However, he was slow in prosecuting rebels;
the Yìnglì era conspirators were only captured and executed at this point.
Commentators use this point to find him wanting.
Shèngzōng inherited the throne in his youth.
The Empress Dowager Ruìzhì acted as regent (chēng zhì),
paying careful attention to judicial decisions.
She often advised the Emperor that the laws should be lenient.
When the Emperor reached maturity,
he became even more adept at state affairs,
and was focused on good governance.
At that time, more than ten laws and statutes were amended and fixed,
mostly aligning with public sentiment,
and he applied punishments with detailed caution.
Previously,
when Qìdān (Khitan) and Hàn (Han) people injured each other causing death,
the severity of the laws applied was unequal.
From this time on, they were judged equally.
In the twelfth year of Tǒnghé,
a decree stated that if Qìdān people committed the Ten Abominations (shí è),
they should also be judged according to the standard laws.
The old law dictated that
the bodies of executed prisoners were to be displayed in the market for three days.
From this time on, they could be collected and buried after just one night.
In the twenty-fourth year,
a decree stipulated that if a master had not committed the crimes of plotting rebellion, high treason, or offenses punishable by exile or death,
their slaves and maidservants were not allowed to denounce them;
conversely, if a slave or maidservant committed a crime punishable by death,
they must be handed over to the authorities,
and their master was not permitted to kill them arbitrarily.
In the twenty-ninth year,
because the old law stated that
if descendants of families whose Chancellors (Zǎixiàng) or Military Governors (Jiédùshǐ) were hereditary appointments committed a crime,
they would suffer exile or beating like commoners (qí mín),
but were exempted from tattooing the face (qíng miàn),
a decree mandated that from now on, whenever an offense required facial tattooing,
they must be subjected to the same punishment as required by law.
In the eighth year of Kāitài,
the law stated that theft involving ten strings of cash (shí guàn) or more
resulted in the execution of the ringleader.
This law was considered too severe,
so the amount was raised to twenty-five strings of cash (èrshíwǔ guàn).
The ringleader would be executed,
and accomplices sentenced to beating and exile.
He once ordered that if there were grievances in any regional legal case or prison
that could not be resolved,
the aggrieved party was permitted to go to the Censorate (Yùshǐ Tái) to submit a complaint,
and officials would be assigned to review the case.
In the past, lawsuits in the Supreme Court (Dàlǐ Sì)
that required official review and memorialization
were resolved in detail by the Academicians of the Hànlín (Hànlín Xuéshì), Attendant Censors (Gěishì Zhōng), and Secretarial Aides for Political Affairs (Zhèngshì Shèrén);
at this time, the posts of Vice Minister (Shào Qīng) and Chief Administrator (Zhèng Zhǔ) were established to manage this.
Still concerned that not every case had been thoroughly addressed,
he personally reviewed the prisoners’ records.
He frequently dispatched envoys to various circuits to examine and decide cases of injustice and backlog,
such as Xíng Bàopǔ.
Wherever he went,
people felt that they had no outstanding grievances.
Among the people of the Wǔyuàn Bù, there was one who deliberately destroyed his armor.
Fónú, their chief, beat him to death.
The Emperor was angry that his application of the law was too severe,
and decreed that he be dismissed from office.
Because of this, officials did not dare to be cruel.
Tàlàgān Nǎifāngshí, being drunk, spoke about affairs concerning the imperial inner chambers.
By law, he should have died,
but his crime was specially pardoned.
A commoner of the Wǔyuàn Bù accidentally started a fire,
which spread to the ancestral burial grounds (zhàoyù) on Mùyè Shān.
He should also have died,
but he was beaten and released.
This incident was subsequently established as law.
As for Díbāgē, he first stole property from Wáng Lìngqiān's house in Jìzhōu.
When he was discovered,
he stabbed Lìngqiān with a knife,
who fortunately did not die.
The relevant authorities proposed sentencing him for robbery (dào lùn),
but he was only given the punishment of flogging.
Furthermore, Nàmǔgǔ committed theft thirteen times.
Since the circumstances of all his offenses were unforgivable,
he was sentenced to public execution.
Consequently, an imperial decree stated that henceforth, anyone who commits theft three times
shall be tattooed (qíng) on the forehead and sentenced to penal servitude for three years;
four offenses result in tattooing on the face and five years of penal servitude;
and five offenses lead to execution.
Such measures,
where severity and leniency were appropriate,
were sufficient to serve as a warning.
The attendants Liú Gē and Wūgǔsī once eloped with the wife of the Qí Wáng.
They were granted amnesty.
Later, they surrendered during the Qiānlíng Jié festival.
Thereupon, an edict commanded all attendants and imperial guards to assemble and watch them be cut in half at the waist (yāozhǎn).
Consequently, the nation harbored no citizens expecting impunity.
Regulations and discipline were maintained.
Most officials attended to their duties.
People hesitated greatly before violating the law.
Therefore, during the Tǒnghé era,
Nánjīng, Yìzhōu, and Píngzhōu were reported to have empty prisons.
By the fifth year of Kàitài,
prisons in all circuits (dào) were empty,
achieving a state where punishments were set aside.
According to former precedent,
the Shūmì Shǐ (Commissioner of Military Affairs), unless dealing with major state affairs,
never personally made rulings.
All legal cases and lawsuits were managed solely by the Yílíbì.
When Xiāo Hézhuó and Xiāo Pǔ successively became Shūmì Shǐ,
they exclusively valued official talent
and began to hear lawsuits themselves.
People at the time began to imitate this practice,
competing with each other in cunning and cleverness.
Customs and morality declined from this point onward.
Therefore, in the sixth year of Tàipíng, an imperial edict stated:
"Seeing that Our state comprises both Qìdān and Hàn people,
We thus employed the Southern and Northern Bureaus (Yuàn) to govern them separately,
intending to eliminate corruption and injustice
and remove troubles and disturbances.
However, if the noble and the humble are subject to different laws,
resentment will surely arise.
When common people commit crimes,
they are certainly unable to influence the relevant authorities to reach the court.
Only imperial relatives and consort families often rely on imperial favor and engage in bribery
in an attempt to escape punishment temporarily.
If this continues, the law will be abolished.
Henceforth, whenever noble relatives are accused in a case,
regardless of the magnitude of the matter,
the local officials where they reside shall investigate and interrogate them,
and fully report the case to the Northern and Southern Bureaus (Yuàn) for re-interrogation to verify the facts before reporting them to Us.
Those who report without investigation,
or those who accept requests for influence and memorialize on their behalf,
shall be punished with the same penalty as the original offender."
In the seventh year,
an edict was issued to ministers within and outside the court, saying:
"If there are deficiencies in the regulations or instances where the severity or leniency is imbalanced,
memorialize them clearly,
so that they may be discussed, augmented, or revised."
Treatise Thirty-One: Treatise on Penal Law, Part Three
When Xīngzōng ascended the throne,
Empress Qīn'āi first gained influence,
and her brothers seized control of the government.
Féng Jiānú and others, seeking to cater to Qīn'āi's desires,
falsely accused Xiāo Zhuóbǔ and others of plotting rebellion,
implicating the primary consort, Empress Réndé.
Xiāo Zhuóbǔ and more than ten others, along with over forty relatives and dependents of Réndé, were convicted.
All were sentenced to capital punishment,
and their families’ properties were confiscated.
Réndé was imprisoned in Shàngjīng.
Afterward, someone was sent to assassinate her.
Having been forced to a premature death,
indignation arose both within and outside the court.
Empress Qīn'āi later plotted to depose the Emperor and install another.
She was moved to Qìngzhōu.
When she was later welcomed back,
she again participated considerably in state affairs,
but her cruelty and tyranny could no longer prevail.
However, Xīngzōng loved reputation,
enjoyed making changes,
and was also devoted to Buddhism (Fútú Fǎ).
He aimed to grant minor favors,
frequently issued amnesties and pardons,
and released a great number of death row inmates.
In the first year of Zhòngxī,
an edict permitted officials in active service who committed official crimes (gōngzuì) to commute their sentences by fine,
while private crimes (sīzuì) were to be handled according to the original laws.
If a man’s sons, younger brothers, or household members accepted bribes,
but the man was unaware,
only the perpetrator was to be punished.
Previously,
those in the Nánjīng Sānsī who melted down currency to make utensils weighing three *jīn*,
those carrying ten *guàn* of cash out of Nánjīng,
and those who stole property worth five *guàn* from a house damaged by accidental fire, were sentenced to death.
Now,
those whose melted copper exceeded three *jīn*,
and those carrying cash or stolen goods worth twenty *guàn* or more were sentenced to death.
In the second year,
the relevant authorities memorialized:
"The edict of the first year stated that
those who commit severe crimes punishable by life penal servitude
shall be subject to flogging and beatings (chuí chǔ)
and also tattooed on the face (qíng miàn).
This constitutes three penalties for a single crime,
so the tattooing should be waived.
Furthermore, for descendants of officials in active service and families hereditarily chosen for the roles of Zǎixiàng (Chancellor) and Jiédù Shǐ (Military Governor),
who commit adultery (jiānzuì) leading to penal servitude,
is it decided whether they should be tattooed or not?"
The Emperor merely replied with an instruction, saying:
"Those who commit a crime but repent and reform themselves
are still people who can be used.
If their face is tattooed,
they endure shame for life.
We deeply pity them."
Thereafter, those sentenced to life penal servitude
were only tattooed on the neck.
When slaves (núbì) committed escape,
or stole their master’s property,
masters were not allowed to privately tattoo their faces.
Tattooing the arm or the neck was permitted.
Those who committed theft
were initially tattooed on the right arm;
a second offense was tattooed on the left arm;
a third offense was tattooed on the right side of the neck;
a fourth offense on the left side;
and a fifth offense led to execution.
In the fifth year (of Zhòngxī),
the newly revised statutes and regulations were completed.
An edict commanded the relevant authorities to apply them starting from the next day of the imperial audience.
They were also promulgated throughout all the circuits (dào).
These were compiled and revised from the laws and regulations dating back to Tàizǔ,
incorporating ancient systems.
The punishments included death, exile (liú), flogging (zhàng), and three grades of penal servitude (tú).
There were five major categories and five hundred forty-seven articles.
At that time, there was a government herdsman who secretly replaced an official seal and gave a horse to someone.
By law, he should have been executed.
The Emperor said:
"To kill two people over one horse,
is this not excessive?"
The sentence was reduced from death.
Furthermore, there were brothers who committed armed robbery and were due to be executed.
Considering that the younger brother followed the older,
and that neither had sons,
the younger brother was specially pardoned.
As for [crimes such as] violating the law for personal gain and accepting bribes,
fraudulently using imperial orders to run the relay post,
falsely imitating imperial handwriting,
and stealing tribute items from foreign nations,
they were generally exempted from the death penalty.
Mílǐjí, a household slave of the Jùnwáng Tiēbù, accused his master of speaking words that implied resentment and grievance.
The investigation found no proof.
He should have been punished with the inverse crime (fǎnzòu, counter-sentencing),
but because of the secretive words (yǔyán) of Empress Qīn'āi,
he was ultimately not punished
nor was he handed over to his master for judgment.
He was merely stripped of his property and status.
Xiāo Bái, the Níngyuǎn Jūn Jiédù Shǐ, forcibly abducted the daughter of the Wūgǔdíliè Dūxiángwěn Dílǔ to be his wife.
He was also exempted from the death penalty due to the Empress's intercession,
being flogged and stripped of his office.
Méilǐ Gǒudān, having become drunk and killed a person, fled.
During the Yǒngshòu Jié festival, he surrendered.
His crime was specially pardoned.
On the birthday of the Imperial Younger Sister, the Qín Guó Gōngzhǔ,
the Emperor visited her residence.
The entertainer Zhāng Suí,
who was originally a spy (zhuó) sent by Sòng,
was discovered by a high minister, who reported it to the throne.
He was summoned and interrogated.
He confessed fully.
He was immediately released.
Later, an edict stated that all officials who privately took government property
shall be treated as committing outright theft (zhèng dào lùn).
Gentlemen of the various *zhàng* (tribal banners) who hunted deer in forbidden areas
were punished with three hundred strokes of the rod
but were not required to pay compensation.
Minor generals were punished with two hundred strokes or less.
However, common people who committed the offense were punished with three hundred strokes.
The principles established by Shèngzōng had vanished.
Qīngníng (1055 CE),
an edict was issued to all Palace Commanders (Dū Bùshǔ), saying:
"Regarding any matters of military secrecy
, they should be immediately reported to Us face-to-face;
all other matters that are petitioned
should be handled according to existing laws.
If anyone submits a book containing slander or libel
, those who receive or read it shall all be executed publicly (Qìshì)."
In the second year (1056 CE),
He ordered the chief officials (Zhǎnglì) of all commanderies, following the precedent of the various departments
, to decide capital cases jointly with their subordinates
, so that no one should wrongfully die in prison.
An edict was issued, stating:
"Previously, all death sentences across the circuits (Lù) awaited final judgment by the court
, thus causing stagnation in judicial proceedings
. From now on, concerning all confirmed cases of armed robbery (Qiángdào)
, officials are permitted to execute the sentence immediately."
In the fourth year (1058 CE)
, He again issued an edict to the Chancellor of the Left (Zuǒ Yílíbì), saying:
"Previously, We commanded that death sentences in the outer circuits
be executed immediately by the local authorities.
However, We fear that the full circumstances may not have been completely understood
, which might result in miscarriages of justice.
From now on, even if the person has confessed
, nearby authorities must still be ordered to review the interrogation.
Only if there is no injustice (yuān) should the sentence be carried out
; if there is injustice, report the details immediately."
In the first year of Xiányōng (1065 CE)
, it was decreed that prisoners who had no family
should be provided with rations.
In the sixth year (1070 CE)
, the Emperor considered that since the customs of the Qìdān and Hàn people differed
, the laws of the state could not be uniformly applied
. Thereupon, he ordered Tìyǐn Sū and Privy Councilor (Shūmìshǐ) Yǐ Xīn, among others, to revise the statutes
. All matters conforming to the codes and ordinances (Lǜlìng)
were fully recorded;
those that did not conform
, were separately reserved.
The officials responsible for verification and amendment at that time took the old statutes of Chóngxī
, and changed the statute where theft of goods worth 25 Guàn resulted in the death penalty
, increasing the threshold to 50 Guàn for the death penalty;
they also deleted two redundant articles
, for a total of 545 articles;
they extracted 173 articles from the codes (Lǜ)
, and newly created 71 articles
, making a grand total of 789 articles
, while the compiled punitive articles (biān) increased to over a thousand.
All were categorized and listed.
During the Dàkāng period, these statutes were finalized
, and revised again against the codes (Lǜ) and regulations (Tiáolì)
, subsequently adding 36 articles.
Thereafter, amendments continued based on circumstances
, stopping in the third year of Dà'ān (1087 CE)
, having added another 67 articles.
As the statutes became overly complicated
, officials responsible for the law could not master them all
, and ignorant commoners did not know how to avoid violating them
. Consequently, the number of offenders increased
, and officials were able to commit corrupt acts by exploiting loopholes
. Therefore, in the fifth year (1089 CE) an edict stated
: "Law (Fǎ) is used to show faith to the people
, and achieve national order.
It should be simple and easy like Heaven and Earth
, and unwavering like the four seasons
, so that the people know how to avoid it and not commit transgression.
Recently, We ordered the relevant authorities to compile and revise the penal laws
, but they failed to embody Our intent clearly
. They created many detailed articles
, thereby entrapping the people in crime
, which We deeply disapprove of.
From now on, the old laws shall be used again
, and all others are abolished."
However, starting from the first year of Dàkāng (1075 CE)
, the Northern Administration Privy Councilor Yēlǜ Yǐ Xīn gained power.
Palace maid Shāndēng and others falsely accused Empress Xuānyì
. Yǐ Xīn reported this to the throne
. The Emperor immediately ordered Yǐ Xīn to investigate and detail the charges
, and he used this opportunity to confirm the fabrication.
The Emperor became furious
, executed the family of the actor Zhào Wéiyī
, executed Gāo Chángmìng
, confiscated the property of both their families
, and granted the Empress the decree to commit suicide.
In the third year (1077 CE)
, Yǐ Xīn and his associates again plotted to frame Crown Prince Zhāohuái
. They secretly ordered the Grand Guardian of the Right Guards, Yēlǜ Chálà
, to inform Shūmìyuàn affairs official Xiāo Sùsà and eight others of a plot to install the Crown Prince.
An edict was issued to investigate, but no evidence was found
. Sùsà and Dábùyě were sent out to provincial postings
, and six others, including the guard Sābō, were exiled.
The Emperor decreed that anyone reporting the instigators of the rebellion
would be heavily rewarded with official rank and gifts
; otherwise, they would all be executed.
Yǐ Xīn instructed the Tablet Seal Director Xiāo Éduōwò to confess himself
: "Your servant was formerly privy to the plot of Sùsà and the others"
, and then listed their names and reported them.
The Emperor believed him
, and ordered Yǐ Xīn and his associates to conduct the interrogation
, leading to the flogging of the Crown Prince
, who was then imprisoned in a separate room within the palace
. Thirty-five people, including Tàbùyě and Sālà, were killed
, and the sons of Sùsà and others were also killed;
their young children, women, slaves, and household property
were all confiscated
, or distributed among the officials.
Yānge and others fraudulently produced a written confession (Yuánshū) in the name of the Crown Prince and submitted it
. The Emperor grew extremely angry
, deposed the Crown Prince
, and moved him to Shàngjīng.
Yǐ Xīn soon sent people to assassinate him in his place of confinement
. The Emperor remained unenlightened
, and above and below the court
, discipline was utterly lost.
In the first year of Tiānzuò Qiántǒng (1101 CE)
, all those who had suffered harm due to Yǐ Xīn in the third year of Dàkāng were fully restored to their ranks and titles
. Their confiscated property was returned
, and those exiled were returned to their homes.
In the second year (1102 CE)
, Yǐ Xīn's grave and those of his associates were finally unearthed
, their coffins were split open and their corpses mutilated
. Their sons and grandsons were executed
, while the sons and grandsons of the remaining associates were granted a reduction in sentence from death
, and exiled to the border
. Their families, including slaves, were distributed to the families of the victims.
However, particularly cunning and wicked members of the faction, such as Yēlǜ Tàbùyě and Xiāo Dálǔgǔ
, were bribed to avoid punishment
. Regarding those who lost armies or surrendered cities
, they were merely stripped of office
. The Traveling Generals (Xíngjūn Jiāngjūn) Yēlǜ Nièlǐ and two others were executed publicly (Qìshì) for the crime of hunting deer in a prohibited area
If officials in various bureaus and those in attendance committed faults
, besides being demoted or punished
, they were all drafted into the army.
Rewards and punishments were inconsistent
, and resentment and criticism arose daily;
major bandits incited each other
, and desertions and rebellions followed one after another.
Tiānzuò became greatly afraid
, and became more dedicated to enforcing strict harshness
. Consequently, the punishments of being thrown off a cliff, blasted by a cannon, being nailed and cut, or having the body slowly sliced (Luǎnshā) were revived
. Sometimes, bodies were dismembered and distributed among the Five Capitals (Wǔ Jīng)
, and in extreme cases, the heart was even extracted and offered to the ancestral temple (Zǔmiào).
Although this was partly due to Tiānzuò having no strategy to remedy the crisis
, leading him toward cruelty
, it was also because the ancestors had provided the precedents that allowed it.
The earlier generations of the Liáo dynasty
were already strict in their application of the law.
Even if their descendants all possessed the capacity of a ruler
, and knew how to choose wisely
, this harshness was still not the proper way of governance inherited from the ancestors (Zǔzōng Yímóu zhī Dào)
; unfortunately, should there be one ruler who is foolish and violent
, drawing slightly upon these precedents as an excuse
, there is nothing he would not do.
Yet, why is it that the application of punishment in the late Liáo period
was the same as in the earlier generations
, but the outcome (rise or fall) was different?
Generally, when applied by a founding ruler
, before the law has been stabilized
, the people still dare not judge its intent;
but when applied by a ruler of a doomed state
, after the law has already been established
, what dependence can the people still have
? This is why the outcomes differed.
The *Zhuàn* says
: "A new state (Xīn Guó) should have lenient regulations (Qīng Diǎn)"
. How could this merely pertain to temporary expediency?
In Tiānzuò's final years
, his hunting and travel became excessive
, and he showed signs of becoming weary of governing.
Among his sons, Āolúwò, born to Consort Wénfēi, was the most virtuous.
Xiāo Fèngxiān was the brother of the Principal Consort (Yuánfēi)
, and he deeply resented Āolúwò.
Coincidentally, Consort Wénfēi's elder sister was married to Yēlǜ Táhálǐ
, and her younger sister was married to Yēlǜ Yú Dǔ.
Fèngxiān then falsely accused Yú Dǔ and others of plotting to establish the Prince of Jìn (Jìn Wáng)
, and to honor Tiānzuò as the Retired Emperor (Tàishàng Huáng).
Consequently, Táhálǐ and his wife were executed
, and Consort Wénfēi was granted the decree to commit suicide.
Āolúwò escaped harm because he was not involved in the alleged conspiracy.
When Tiānzuò was hunting west in Fèngshèng Zhōu
, Fèngxiān again alleged that Yēlǜ Sābā and others intended to kidnap and install Āolúwò
. Sābā was immediately executed
, and all his associates were annihilated.
Because Āolúwò had the hope (support) of the people
, he was granted the decree to commit suicide that very day.
All the attending officials, various bureau personnel, and military men who heard this while following the Emperor
, all wept bitterly.
Generally, starting from the time of Xīngzōng,
a great purge suddenly arose;
Empress Réndé was murdered in a secluded place,
and the administration of the Liáo began to decline.
Dàozōng killed Empress Xuānyì,
and banished Crown Prince Zhāohuái;
the Crown Prince was subsequently murdered.
Tiānzuò knew of his father's injustice,
and he himself was almost killed;
yet at this point, he also killed his son, Áolúwò.
The Commentary says:
“To treat lightly those whom one ought to treat generously,
means one will treat nothing generously.”
During the two hundred plus years of the Liáo,
kinsmen repeatedly annihilated each other.
Tiānzuò was especially depraved and tyrannical,
and consequently led the state to ruin.
Alas!
Table One: Genealogy
Heaven opened at zǐ,
Earth unfolded at chǒu,
and Humanity arose at yín.
In the beginning of Heaven, Earth, and Humanity,
there was only unity.
Heaven moves,
it has constant measure;
Earth is still,
it has constant form;
Humankind’s movement and stillness are not fixed,
and their residence is not permanent.
Heaven presides over flow and circulation,
Earth presides over storage and release.
The two Qì never go anywhere without reaching,
and they are bestowed wherever humans reside.
When Páoxī Shì descended,
the descendants of Yándì Shì and Huángdì Shì were numerous.
The feudal grants within the royal domain were limited,
but the dissemination of royal governance was inexhaustible.
Therefore, those who ruled the four quarters
were often descendants of the two Dì,
but those who governed the central lands fundamentally came from the same origin.
Consulting the records of Yǔwén Zhōu,
the Liáo originally descended from Yándì,
but Yēlǜ Yǎn claimed the Liáo were descendants of Xuānyuán.
Yǎn’s record appeared later;
why not follow the Zhōu record?
Now, a descendant of Yándì named Gěwūtú,
was a hero on the northern frontier for generations.
Later, he was attacked by Mòdú Kèhán,
and he sought refuge and dwelt in Xiānbēi Shān,
adopting the name Xiānbēi Shì.
Subsequently, Mùróng Yàn defeated them,
and divided their tribes: Yǔwén,
Kùmò Xī,
and Qìdān.
The name Qìdān
first appeared here.
During the Súi and Táng eras,
the ruler of the Qìdān was named Dàhè Shì.
Empress Wǔ sent a general to attack and scatter their forces,
and the Dàhè Shì declined.
Guòzhé, the chief of another tribe, replaced them.
Guòzhé was soon destroyed.
Nièlǐ, the chief of the Diélà tribe, established Díniǎnzǔlǐ as Zǔwǔ Kèhán,
and changed the designation to Yáoniǎn Shì.
The Táng granted them the Imperial surname,
calling him Lǐ Huáixiù.
Subsequently, Huáixiù rebelled against the Táng,
and Kǎiluò was newly enfeoffed as King.
Meanwhile, Nòulǐsī, a descendant of Nièlǐ,
assisted Huáixiù.
Kǎiluò lasted until Qūshù for nearly a hundred years,
and the national power revived.
Up to Ābǎojī, the grandson of Nòulǐsī,
his achievements and enterprise greatly flourished,
and he adopted the name Shìlǐ Shì.
This was Liáo Tàizǔ.
Thereupon, the Shìlǐ Shì, along with the Dàhè and Yáoniǎn, were called
“The Three Yēlǜ.”
From that time onward,
the state grew increasingly large.
Beginning in the late Táng dynasty,
spanning the Five Dynasties and the Sòng dynasty,
for over two hundred years.
Names shifted according to the changing eras,
characters were transmitted and sounds rotated.
This is how their spoken and written languages communicate with each other,
which can be investigated and known.
Those who cannot be known
are figures like Qíshǒu Kèhán, Húlà Kèhán, Sū Kèhán, and Zhāogǔ Kèhán.
All were ancestors of the Liáo,
but their generational order cannot be investigated.
Gathering what can be known,
I composed the Liáo Shìbiǎo (Genealogical Table of Liáo).
Imperial Lineage: The Ancestral Generations of the Qìdān.
Hàn Dynasty: Màodùn Kèhán attacked the Dōnghú with troops
and destroyed them.
The remaining masses sought refuge in Xiānbēi Shān,
and were consequently named Xiānbēi.
Wèi Dynasty: In the middle of the Qīnglóng era,
the chieftain Bǐnéng became somewhat unruly,
and was killed by Wáng Xióng, the Cìshǐ of Yōuzhōu.
They dispersed and migrated south of the Huáng Shuǐ,
and north of Huánglóng.
Jìn Dynasty: A descendant of the Xiānbēi Gě Wūtú was named Pǔhuí.
Pǔhuí had a son named Mònà,
who migrated south from Yīnshān,
and first settled in Liáoxī.
After nine generations, they were destroyed by Mùróng Huǎng.
The Xiānbēi people scattered, forming the Yǔwén Shì,
some becoming the Kùmò Xī,
and others becoming the Qìdān.
Yuán Wèi Dynasty: The Qìdān state was east of the Kùmò Xī;
they were different tribes but the same kind of people,
a separate branch of the Dōngbù Xiānbēi.
It was at this time they first named themselves Qìdān.
They were defeated by the Mùróng Shì,
and both fled between Sōngmò.
During the Dēngguó era of Emperor Dàowǔ Dì,
they were greatly defeated,
and consequently split away from the Kùmò Xī.
After several decades,
they gradually spread out,
having tribes several hundred *lǐ* north of Hélóng.
Since the Tàipíng Zhēnjūn era of Emperor Tàiwǔ Dì,
they annually delivered famous horses.
During the time of Xiànwén,
they sent Mòfú Gēhéchén to present tribute.
They were first ranked at the end of the various nations,
and were delighted and submissive.
The Wàndān Bù, Hédàhé Bù, Fúfúyù Bù, Yǔlíng Bù, Rìlián Bù, Pǐjié Bù, Lí Bù,
and Tǔliùyú Bù came to pay tribute with famous horses and patterned furs.
They were allowed to trade between Hélóng and Mìyún.
In the third year of Tàihé,
Gāogōulì and the Rúrú conspired to seize Dìdòuyú and divide the land.
The Qìdān were afraid.
Mòfú Hèwùyú led his tribe, three thousand chariots and more than ten thousand people, to submit,
settling east of the Báiláng Shuǐ.
Běi Qí Dynasty: In the ninth month of the fourth year of Tiānbǎo,
the Qìdān violated the frontier.
Emperor Wénxuān Dì personally went to suppress them.
When he reached Píngzhōu,
he then rushed onward.
The Sītú Pān Xiànglè led five thousand elite cavalry
and rushed toward Qīngshān via the eastern route.
The Prince of Āndé, Hán Guǐ, led four thousand cavalry eastward to cut off their escape route.
The Emperor personally crossed the mountain ridges and launched a fierce attack,
capturing more than one hundred thousand men and women,
and hundreds of thousands of livestock.
Xiànglè also greatly defeated a separate tribe at Qīngshān.
The captured people were distributed among various prefectures.
They were again pressed by the Tūjué,
and ten thousand households were placed temporarily within the borders of Gāolì.
Suí Dynasty: In the fourth year of Kāihuáng,
they led the various Mòfú Hè to come and pay respects.
In the fifth year,
the entire populace requested submission at the frontier.
Gāozǔ accepted them,
allowing them to reside in their former lands.
In the sixth year,
the various tribes incessantly attacked one another,
and they also invaded the Tūjué.
Gāozǔ sent envoys to instruct them to reconcile.
Chūfú and others from a separate tribe abandoned Gāolì,
and led their people to submit.
They were settled north of Kěxīnàxié.
At the end of the Kāihuáng era,
more than four thousand households from a separate tribe abandoned the Tūjué and came to surrender.
Gāozǔ provided food and ordered them to return;
they firmly refused to leave,
and their tribe gradually increased in number.
They subsequently migrated north,
following water and grass,
situated two hundred *lǐ* directly north of Liáoxī,
and settled near the Gēchén Shuǐ.
They stretched five hundred *lǐ* east to west,
and three hundred *lǐ* north to south,
divided into ten tribes.
The largest military contingent was three thousand,
the smallest over one thousand.
When there were military campaigns,
the chieftains would consult with one another.
When raising troops, they would join the tally.
Shābōlüè Kèhán of the Tūjué sent Tǔtún Pāndié to govern them,
but the Qìdān killed the Tǔtún.
In the seventh year of Dàyè,
they offered local produce as tribute.
Táng Dynasty: The Qìdān territory was five thousand *lǐ* and more directly northeast of the Jīngshī (Capital).
To the east, it bordered Gāolì;
to the west, Xī;
to the south, Yíngzhōu;
to the north, Mòhé and Shìwéi.
They relied on Lěngxíng Shān for defense.
Their dwelling places for hunting were not fixed.
Their ruler, of the Dàhè Shì clan, commanded forty thousand effective troops.
They were divided into eight tribes.
They served the Tūjué
and were designated as Sìjīn.
Whenever troops were mobilized for attack or war,
all the tribes would assemble.
For hunting, the tribes were allowed to act independently.
They were not at peace with the Xī.
Whenever they fought and lost,
they would flee and secure themselves in Xiānbēi Shān.
At the beginning of the Wǔdé era,
the great chief Sūn Áocáo and the Mòhé leader Tūdìjī both came to court.
In the second year,
they invaded the border of Píngzhōu.
In the sixth year,
the ruler Duōluó presented famous horses and abundant sable furs.
In the second year of Zhēnguān,
Móhuì came to surrender.
The Tūjué requested to exchange Liáng Shīdū for the Qìdān.
Tàizōng said:
"The Qìdān and the Tūjué are not the same kind of people.
Shīdū is a registered household of the Táng.
I will capture him;
I cannot exchange those who have surrendered."
In the third year,
Móhuì came to court.
He was granted drums and standards,
and thereafter provided regular tribute.
When the Emperor campaigned against Gāolì,
he mobilized all the Qìdān and Xī chieftains to join the army.
Upon returning and passing Yíngzhōu,
Kūgē was appointed Zuǒ Wǔwèi Jiāngjūn (General of the Left Militant Guard).
The great chief Rǔgē Zhǔ Jùqǔ led his people to submit.
His tribe was immediately established as Xuánzhōu,
with Jùqǔ as the Cìshǐ,
subordinate to the Yíngzhōu Dūdu Fǔ (Area Command).
Kūgē offered his entire tribe for internal allegiance.
The Sōngmò Dūdu Fǔ was then established,
with Kūgē as the Dūdu,
titled Wújí Nán (Baron of Wújí),
and granted the surname Lǐ.
The Dáqī Tribe was made Qiàoluò Zhōu;
the Gēbiàn Tribe was made Tánhàn Zhōu;
the Dúhuó Tribe was made Wúféng Zhōu;
the Fēnwèn Tribe was made Yǔlíng Zhōu;
the Tūbiàn Tribe was made Rìlián Zhōu;
the Ruìxī Tribe was made Túhé Zhōu;
the Zhuìjīn Tribe was made Wàndān Zhōu;
the Fú Tribe was made Pǐlí and Chìshān two prefectures.
All were subordinate to the Sōngmò Fǔ,
with Rǔgē Zhǔ serving as the Cìshǐ.
After Kūgē died,
they rebelled alongside the Xī.
The Field Army Commander Āshǐdé Shūbīn captured Ābùgù, the Sōngmò Dūdu,
and presented him to the Dōngdū (Eastern Capital).
Kūgē had two grandsons: one was Kūmòlí,
Cìshǐ of Tánhàn Zhōu and Prince of Guīshùn Commandery;
the other was Jìnzhōng,
Sōngmò Dūdu.
Áocáo’s great-grandson was Wànróng,
Cìshǐ of Guīchéng Zhōu.
At that time, Zhào Wénhuì, the Yíngzhōu Dūdu, frequently harassed and insulted his subordinates.
Jìnzhōng and others harbored resentment.
They jointly raised troops with Wànróng,
killed Wénhuì,
and occupied Yíngzhōu.
Jìnzhōng proclaimed himself
"Wúshàng Kèhán,"
and supported Wànróng as the commander.
In less than twenty days,
their forces numbered tens of thousands.
They attacked Chóngzhōu
and captured Xǔ Qīnjì, the Deputy Envoy for Suppression.
Empress Wǔ Hòu was enraged.
She issued an edict ordering General Cáo Rénshī and twenty-seven other generals to attack them.
She renamed Wànróng
"Wànzhǎn" (Ten Thousand Slashes),
and Jìnzhōng
"Jìnmiè" (Utter Destruction).
They fought at Xīxiáshí Huángzhāng Gǔ,
where the imperial army suffered a defeat.
They advanced to attack Píngzhōu,
but could not conquer it.
Empress Wǔ Hòu further mobilized troops to attack the Qìdān.
Wànróng launched a night attack on Tánzhōu.
Zhāng Jiǔjié, the Deputy Commander-in-Chief of the Qīngbiāndào, resisted the attack.
Wànróng was defeated and fled.
Soon after, Jìnzhōng died,
and Mòchuò of the Tūjué attacked and shattered his tribe.
Wànróng gathered the scattered soldiers,
it rallied again.
The detached generals Luò Wùzhěng and Hé Āxiǎo entered Jìzhōu,
killed the Regional Inspector Lù Bǎojī,
and plundered several thousand people.
Wǔ Hòu, hearing of Jìnzhōng's death,
commanded Wáng Xiàojié, Minister of the Summer Office, and others to lead 170,000 troops to suppress Wànróng.
They fought at Dōng Xiáshí,
were defeated,
and Xiàojié died there.
Wànróng advanced and massacred Yōuzhōu.
She further commanded Lóu Shīdé, Grand Master of Remonstrance, and others to lead 200,000 troops to attack him.
Wànróng, capitalizing on his sharp momentum,
marched south to the beat of drums,
ravaging the dependent counties of Yíngzhōu.
Yáng Xuánjī, Grand Controller of the Divine Forces Route, led Xī troops in a surprise attack,
thoroughly defeating Wànróng,
and capturing Hé Āxiǎo.
The detached generals Lǐ Kǎigù and Luò Wùzhěng surrendered.
Wànróng abandoned his army and fled.
Xuánjī and the Xī attacked him jointly from all four sides.
Wànróng's troops collapsed,
and fled east.
Zhāng Jiǔjié set three ambushes and waited for him.
Wànróng, exhausted and desperate,
fled eastward to Lùhé with a light cavalry escort and his household slave.
He was extremely weary
and lay down under a tree.
The slave cut off his head and presented it,
and Jiǔjié sent it to the Eastern Capital (Dōngdū).
The remaining Qìdān populace could not establish themselves
and subsequently attached themselves to the Tūjué.
In the second year of Kāiyuán (714),
Jìnzhōng’s cousin, Shīhuó, led his tribe back to Táng.
To Shīhuó,
Xuánzōng granted an Iron Certificate inscribed in red (dānshū tiěquàn).
In the fourth year of Kāiyuán (716),
he came together with the Xī chieftain Lǐ Dàpú.
An imperial edict reestablished the Sōngmò Fǔ,
making Shīhuó the Military Governor (dūdū),
and enfeoffing him as Prince of Sōngmò Commandery (Sōngmò Jùnwáng).
Furthermore, the Jìngxī Jūn was established,
with Shīhuó acting as the Commissioner of Pacification and control (jīnglüè dàshǐ).
The eight tribal chiefs were all made Regional Inspectors (cìshǐ).
In the fifth year (717),
a woman of the Yáng Shì family was created Princess Yǒnglè (Yǒnglè Gōngzhǔ) and married off to Shīhuó.
In the sixth year (718),
he died.
Suōgù
was Shīhuó's younger brother.
The Emperor allowed Suōgù to inherit the title.
In the eleventh month of the seventh year of Kāiyuán (719),
Suōgù came to court with the Princess.
The official Kětūyú was brave and fierce,
and gained popular support.
Suōgù wanted to eliminate him.
When the matter was leaked,
Kětūyú attacked him,
and Suōgù fled to Yíngzhōu.
The Military Governor Xǔ Qīndàn and the Xī ruler Lǐ Dàpú attacked Kětūyú,
but were defeated.
Suōgù and Dàpú both died.
(Hán Yù wrote Kětūgān,
but Liú Xù, Sòng Qí, and the Táng Huìyào all wrote Kětūyú.)
Yùyú
was Suōgù's cousin.
Kětūyú supported him and installed him as ruler,
and sent an envoy to apologize for the offense.
Xuánzōng formally installed him to succeed Suōgù's position.
In the tenth year of Kāiyuán (722),
Yùyú entered court.
A woman of the Mùróng Shì family was created Princess Yànjùn (Yànjùn Gōngzhǔ) and married off to Yùyú.
He died.
Duōyú
was Yùyú's younger brother,
and inherited the office and title.
In the thirteenth year of Kāiyuán (725),
Duōyú again became suspicious of and alienated from Kětūyú.
He fled with the Princess,
and was renamed Prince of Liáoyáng (Liáoyáng Wáng).
Shàogù
was Duōyú's younger brother.
The people of the state jointly established him.
In the winter of the thirteenth year of Kāiyuán (725),
he came to pay homage at the temporary capital (Xíngzài).
He participated in the Feng and Shan sacrifices at Tài Shān,
was renamed Prince of Guǎnghuà Commandery (Guǎnghuà Jùnwáng),
and a woman of the Chén Shì family was created Princess Dōngguāng (Dōngguāng Gōngzhǔ) and married off to Shàogù.
In the eighteenth year (730),
he was assassinated by Kětūyú,
who took his followers and surrendered to the Tūjué.
Princess Dōngguāng fled to Pínglú.
Qūliè,
whose lineage is unknown,
was installed by Kětūyú.
In the sixth month of the twenty-second year of Kāiyuán (734),
Zhāng Shǒuguī, the Jiedushi of Yōuzhōu, greatly defeated Kětūyú.
In the twelfth month,
he defeated them again,
beheading Qūliè, Kětūyú, and others,
and sending their heads to the Eastern Capital (Dōngdū).
The remaining followers scattered and fled into the mountains and valleys.
Guòzhé
was originally a Qìdān tribal chief,
and served as an official of the Sōngmò Fǔ.
He killed Kětūyú and Qūliè, and returned to Táng.
Zhāng Shǒuguī, the Jiedushi of Yōuzhōu, installed him,
and he was enfeoffed as Prince of Běipíng Commandery (Běipíng Jùnwáng).
In that same year,
Nílǐ, a remnant follower of Kětūyú, assassinated Guòzhé,
and massacred his family.
One son, Làgān, fled to Āndōng
and was appointed General of the Left Swift Cavalry Guard (Zuǒ Xiāowèi Jiāngjūn).
From this point onward,
the Qìdān entered a period of decline.
The Dàhè Shì became vassals to the Xī kings
in order to maintain contact with Táng,
and annual tribute missions arrived.
During the Zhìdé and Bǎoyìng eras, missions arrived twice;
during the Dàlì era, thirteen times;
during the ninth, tenth, and eleventh years of Zhēnyuán, three times;
during the Yuánhé era, seven times;
and during the Tàihé and Kāichéng eras, four times.
Nílǐ
is written as Nièlǐ in the Liáo Shǐ by Yēlǜ Yǎn,
and written as Yǎlǐ by Chén Dàrèn.
He was likely the founding ancestor of Liáo Tàizǔ.
Lǐ Huáixiù
was given his name and surname by the Táng.
His Qìdān name was Díliǎn Zǔlǐ.
He was originally the great commander of the eight tribes.
In the fourth year of Tiānbǎo (745), he surrendered to Táng
and was appointed Military Governor of Sōngmò (Sōngmò Dūdū).
Ān Lùshān presented a memorial requesting to campaign against the Qìdān.
Huáixiù mobilized 100,000 troops
and fought Lùshān south of Huáng Shuǐ,
where Lùshān suffered a great defeat.
From this point, the conflict between him and Lùshān's forces never ceased.
The records of Yēlǜ Yǎn state that
Nòulǐsī, the great-great-grandfather of Tàizǔ, was the Yílíjǐn of the Diélà Bù,
and sent generals Zhǐlǐgū and Kuòlǐ
to heavily defeat Ān Lùshān of Fànyáng at Huáng Shuǐ.
This coincides exactly with the generation of Huáixiù.
Thus, it is clear that Huáixiù was indeed the initial ruler of the Yáoliǎn Shì
and was Zǔwǔ Kèhán.
Kǎiluò
was enfeoffed by Táng as Prince Gōngrén (Gōngrén Wáng),
replacing the Military Governor of Sōngmò,
and thereafter styled himself King of Qìdān.
Subsequently, his power gradually grew.
In the fourth year of Zhēnyuán (788),
he violated the northern border,
which was reported by Yōuzhōu.
Since Lùshān rebelled,
Héběi had been carved up and occupied,
making the route blocked and impassable.
Therefore, the succession order cannot be fully ascertained.
The King of Qìdān, Qūshù,
was granted the title General of the Cloud Cavalry (Yúnhuī Jiāngjūn) in the second year of Huìchāng (842) under Wǔzōng.
He was Yēlán Kèhán.
Zhāng Zhòngwǔ, the Jiedushi of Yōuzhōu, memorialized that the Qìdān formerly used a Huíhú seal
and requested that an imperial seal be granted.
An edict
specified the inscription
as "Qìdān Who Serves the State" (Fèngguó Qìdān).
(The Gāolì Gǔjīnlù writes Qūxū.)
The King of Qìdān, Xí'ěr,
was Bālà Kèhán.
During the Xiántōng era,
he sent envoys again to offer tribute.
His tribe gradually grew strong.
The King of Qìdān, Qīndé,
who was of Xí'ěr's clan,
was Héndéjǐn Kèhán.
During the Guāngqǐ era,
he plundered and raided the Xī and Shìwěi tribes,
subjugating them all.
He frequently attacked Liú Réngōng.
In his later years, the government declined.
According to law, the leader of the eight tribes
was usually succeeded every three years.
Yēlǜ Ābǎojī of the Diélà Bù raised his banner and drums,
formed his own tribe,
refused to accept substitution,
proclaimed himself King,
took control of the entire Qìdān state,
and thus the Yáoliǎn Shì perished.
Xiāo Hánjiānú had a saying that
after the earlier Yáoliǎn Kèhán Wā,
the dynastic lineage was broken.
Only after the Yílíjǐn Yǎlǐ established Zǔwǔ Kèhán
did the great position become settled.
Now, referencing the Táng Shǐ and the Liáo Shǐ,
the Dàhè Shì line ended with Shàogù.
The one established by Yǎlǐ was Huáixiù.
Between them were only two generations: Qūliè and Guòzhé.
Qūliè was installed by Kětūyú,
and Guòzhé, as another tribal chief, was killed by Yǎlǐ.
The Táng Shǐ states that Nílǐ was a remnant follower of Kětūyú.
Therefore, was Kèhán Wā
perhaps Qūliè?
Table Two: The Table of Imperial Sons
The Emperor oversees All Under Heaven,
and the King establishes his family.
As for cherishing the nine kin groups [jiǔzú],
and respecting the five ancestral temples [wǔzōng],
the principle is singular.
In the times before the Three Dynasties [Sāndài],
the feudal system was long-lasting.
Therefore, concerning Wú, Lǔ, Yān, Cài, Wèi, Jìn, and Zhèng,
Tài Shǐ Qiān [Sīmǎ Qiān] not only compiled Hereditary Houses [Shìjiā],
but also listed Chronological Tables [Niánbiǎo],
not finding the detail excessive.
Since the Hàn Dynasty,
the feudal system has truly perished,
though its name remains.
Those who ruled for a long time were included in the Hereditary Houses,
and those whose lines ended were placed in the Biographies [Lièzhuàn].
However, the princes and marquises could still be covered by Chronological Tables.
Bān Gù believed that the text lacked substance,
and instead merged the feudal lords, omitting their years, and listed them in tables.
Gentlemen of later generations approved of this.
Since the Wèi Dynasty,
they were neither recognized as Emperors [dì] nor established as hereditary houses [shì],
and kings and marquises often moved and received several enfeoffments,
not knowing what the next day would bring.
Therefore, they were listed and described in Biographies.
Their merits were insufficient to serve as standards,
and their faults were insufficient to serve as warnings.
They were merely mediocre [lùlùrán],
or even worse.
Now, we extract those whose merits and faults were outstanding and list them in Biographies;
for those who were characterized by the grace of familial affection [qīnqīn zhī ēn]
and the duty of respecting elders [jìngzhǎng zhī yì],
but had nothing else worthy of record,
we briefly display them in a table,
creating the Table of Imperial Sons [Huángzǐ Biǎo].
Table Three: The Table of Princesses
According to the principle of the Spring and Autumn Annals [Chūnqiū],
when a royal lady [wángjī] married down, it was recorded in the documents,
because the state of the Duke of Lǔ was of the same surname as the King and thus presided over the marriage.
In ancient times,
a woman's name was avoided and she did not leave the inner quarters;
words from the interior did not go beyond the threshold [kǔn].
Listing all princesses in the Biographies [Lièzhuàn]
is contrary to propriety.
However, the State of Liáo relied heavily on the maternal relatives [wàiqī],
and princesses frequently appeared throughout the Annals [Jì] and Biographies [Zhuàn].
Therefore, we must display them in a table.
According to Rites [Lǐ],
males and females are accorded separate priority,
and they should not be listed together with the imperial sons.
Therefore, a separate appended table is made for the princesses [Gōngzhǔ Fùbiǎo].
Table Four: The Table of the Imperial Clan
When Liáo Tàizǔ established the state,
his younger brothers coveted the throne.
He was tolerant, supportive, and guiding,
not bearing to execute them.
Even the ancient sages found this difficult.
Although his tolerance and magnanimity [dùliàng huīkuò] were great,
his consideration for governing the state was far-reaching.
Throughout the entire Liáo period,
among those who originated from the Yělü Hèngxàng [Héngzhàng] and the Five Courts [Wǔyuàn] and Six Courts [Liùyuàn],
though great villains were present,
founding ministers [yuánxūn] were truly numerous.
If we do not display them in a table,
we cannot know their origins and developments.
Therefore, the Table of the Imperial Clan [Huángzú Biǎo] is made.
Table Five: The Table of Maternal Relatives
The Hàn Dynasty had the disaster of Xīn [Wáng Mǎng]'s rise from maternal relatives [wàiqī],
and the Jìn Dynasty imperial clan [zōngshì] had the Calamity of the Eight Princes [Bā Wáng zhī Nán].
In the history of Liáo, the Yělü [Yēlǜ] and Xiāo [Xiāo] clans occupy eight or nine tenths.
The Imperial Clan and the Maternal Relatives [Wàiqī],
equal in influence and power,
acted as lips and teeth for each other,
thereby strengthening the state and family.
This might be considered one way [to rule].
However, just as they rose through this method,
they also perished through it,
which indicates the fault of this system.
The maternal relatives of the Qìdān [Qìdān wàiqī]
were primarily the two Shěn Mì [Shěnmì] clans: Bálǐ [Bálǐ],
and Yǐshìyǐ [Yǐshìyǐ].
Up to the time of Liáo Tàizǔ,
he married the Shùlǜ [Shùlǜ] clan.
The Shùlǜ,
originally descendants of the Huíhú [Huíhú] Nuòsī [Nuòsī].
In the first year of Dàtóng [Dàtóng Yuánnián] (947 CE),
Tàizōng was preparing to return from Biàn [Biàn],
and left the maternal relative Xiǎo Hàn [Xiǎo Hàn] as the Military Commissioner [Jiédùshǐ] of Biàn Zhōu,
granting him the name Xiāo Hàn [Xiāo Hàn],
in order to follow the customs of the Central Plains [Zhōngguó].
From this point, the three clans Bálǐ, Yǐshìyǐ, and Shùlǜ all took the surname Xiāo.
The Bálǐ had two branches:
Dàfù [Dàfù] and Shàofù [Shàofù];
the Yǐshìyǐ also had two branches:
Dàwēng [Dàwēng] and Xiǎowēng [Xiǎowēng];
Shìzōng made his maternal uncle Tǎliègé [Tǎliègé] the Guójiù Biébù [Guójiù Biébù].
These three clans were consistently chosen for the selection of the Northern Chief Minister [Běi Zǎixiàng].
This began in the second year of Shéncè [Shéncè Èrnián] (917 CE) under Tàizǔ, when Āgǔzhǐ [Āgǔzhǐ] was appointed.
Shèngzōng combined the two Guójiù branches of Bálǐ and Yǐshìyǐ into one,
making two groups together with the Biébù.
This is the complete history of the Liáo maternal relatives.
Therefore, the Table of Maternal Relatives [Wàiqī Biǎo] is made.
Table Six: The Table of Imperial Tours and Hunts
In the Northern Desert [Shuòmò], animal husbandry, shooting, and hunting constitute the primary occupation,
just as agriculture is important to the Hàn people.
The means of livelihood derive from this.
Since Liáo established its state,
it constructed the Five Capitals [Wǔjīng],
set up the Northern and Southern Courts [Nánběi Yuàn],
and controlled all the Chinese states [Zhū Xià].
Yet, the custom of touring and hunting [yóutián zhī xí],
still followed its original tradition.
Tàizǔ was preoccupied with managing affairs in all four directions,
having no time for leisure;
but in the reigns of Mùzōng and Tiānzuò,
history cannot record all the instances.
Now, drawing upon Sīmǎ Qiān's precedent of separately recording the Feng and Shan sacrifices [Fēng Shàn lì],
we list them in a table,
which is certainly sufficient for readers to gain insight.
Therefore, the Table of Imperial Tours and Hunts [Yóuxìng Biǎo] is made.
Table Seven: The Table of Tribes and Clans
Sīmǎ Qiān, when compiling the Records of the Grand Historian [Shǐjì],
placed the Four Barbarian Quarters [Sì Yì] at the end of the volume.
Since the Qín and Hàn dynasties,
each state had its own territory,
with boundaries marking one domain against another,
and the distances were vast.
One could not unite all under heaven [huányǔ]
or fully know every single tribe [zhǒnglào].
Regarding the neighboring states that came and went for tributary missions,
how could one view all of them sequentially?
One could only record them through oral accounts and memories,
sketching a rough outline.
Liáo bordered the Five Dynasties [Wǔdài],
and the near and far lands of the Hàn territory [Hàndì]
are recorded and verifiable in the documents.
Regarding the northwestern desert regions,
the cultivation of the five grains,
the clothing, carriages, horses, rites, and refinement [lǐwén],
the institutional regulations and composition [zhìdù wénwéi],
and the native products,
we grasp the superficial but miss the essential.
Regarding the names of the tribal settlements [bùluò zhī míng]
and the designations of surnames and clans [xìngshì zhī hào],
we capture the sound but have not captured the corresponding characters.
Successive generations have perpetuated errors,
making detailed investigation difficult.
The Liáo clan communicated with various tribes,
who came and went to pay tribute.
The places reached by the Western Liáo [Xī Liáo]
also appear frequently in the Annals and Biographies.
Their events are recorded in the Annals [Jì],
and the tribes and clans are listed in the table.
When Tiānzuò fled and wandered,
Yēlǜ Dàshí established Yān, Jìn Guówáng Chún [Yān Jìn Guówáng Chún];
when Chún died,
he fled with Consort Xiāo [Xiāo Fēi] to Tiāndé Jūn.
The Emperor executed the consort [fēi]
and censured Dàshí.
Dàshí led his followers westward,
and established himself as Emperor.
The various tribes he encountered
are appended below:
Table Eight: The Table of Subject States
When the Zhōu possessed All Under Heaven,
more than eight hundred states assembled without being summoned.
Liáo resided in Sōngmò,
and was extremely powerful and prosperous.
When the Mandate of Heaven [Tiānmìng] returned,
it established the state and changed the reign title.
The decrees and regulations [fǎdù],
all followed the Hàn system.
It commanded generals and dispatched armies,
subjugating various states.
The populace was all registered in the census,
and taxes and tributes were all paid into the inner treasury.
From east to west, north to south,
it covered more than ten thousand *lǐ*.
Compared to the ancients who started with a state of a hundred *lǐ* and achieved the great peace [tàipíng] enterprise,
Liáo was nearly equivalent.
Thus, the flourishing of the Liáo must be recorded.
Therefore, the Table of Subject States [Shǔguó Biǎo] is made.

Biographies One: Empresses and Consorts Sùzǔ Zhāoliè Huánghòu Xiāo Shì, Yìzǔ Zhuāngjìng Huánghòu Xiāo Shì, Xuánzǔ Jiǎnxiàn Huánghòu Xiāo Shì, Dézǔ Xuānjiǎn Huánghòu Xiāo Shì, Tàizǔ Chúnqīn Huánghòu Shùlǜ Shì, Tàizōng Jìng’ān Huánghòu Xiāo Shì, Shìzōng Huáijié Huánghòu Xiāo Shì, Shìzōng Fēi Zhēn Shì, Mùzōng Huánghòu Xiāo Shì, Jǐngzōng Ruìzhì Huánghòu Xiāo Shì, Shèngzōng Réndé Huánghòu Xiāo Shì, Shèngzōng Qīn'āi Huánghòu Xiāo Shì, Xīngzōng Rényì Huánghòu Xiāo Shì, Xīngzōng Guìfēi Xiāo Shì, Dàozōng Xuānyì Huánghòu Xiāo Shì, Dàozōng Huìfēi Xiāo Shì, Tiānzuò Huánghòu Xiāo Shì, Tiānzuò Défēi Xiāo Shì, Tiānzuò Wénfēi Xiāo Shì, Tiānzuò Yuánfēi Xiāo Shì.
The [Shū] Book (of Documents) began with the consort of Yú [Shù shǐ pín Yú],
and the [Shī] Odes were inspired by [Guān Jū] [Shī xìng Guān Jū].
The records of the state historians [Guó shǐ jìzǎi],
often start from the family and extend to the state [wǎngwǎng zì jiā ér guó],
in order to establish the foundation of All Under Heaven [yǐ lì tiānxià zhī běn].
However, the distinction between the honored and the lowly [rán zūnbēi zhī fēn],
must not be altered [bù kě yì yě].
Sīmǎ Qiān placed Empress Lǚ [Lǚ Hòu] in the Basic Annals [Sīmǎ Qiān liè Lǚ Hòu yú Jì];
Bān Gù followed suit [Bān Gù yīn zhī],
but transmitted the biography of Empress Yuán [Yuán Hòu] in the section on Imperial Affines [ér chuán Yuán Hòu yú Wàiqī zhī hòu];
Fàn Yè elevated the Empresses and Consorts to the Imperial Annals [Fàn Yè dēng Hòufēi yú Dìjì].
The annals [jì] are what record the events of the Son of Heaven’s [Tiānzǐ] years [Tiānzǐ jì nián yǐ shì wèi zhī jì],
so why should the Empress [Hòu] be recorded in the annals [Hòu hé wèi ér jì zhī]?
Since the history of Jìn [Jìn Shǐ] listed the empresses at the beginning of their biographies [Zì Jìn Shǐ liè zhū Hòu yǐ shǒu chuán],
from the Suí and Táng dynasties onward [Suí, Táng yǐlái],
no one has been able to change this [mò zhī néng yì yě].
Liáo, following the tradition of the Tūjué [Liáo yīn Tūjué],
called the Empress [chēng Huánghòu yuē]
"Kèdūn" [Kědūn],
and in the national language, called her [Guóyǔ wèi zhī]
"Mōlǐ jiǎn" [Mōlǐ jiǎn],
and the honorific title was [zūnchēng yuē]
"Nòuwò mō" [Nòuwò mō],
which perhaps meant to match her with the Sovereign Earth [Hòutǔ] and mother the people [gài yǐ pèi Hòutǔ ér mǔ zhī yún].
When Tàizǔ proclaimed himself Emperor [Tàizǔ chēng Dì],
he honored his grandmother as the Grand Empress Dowager [Tài Huáng Tàihòu] [zūn zǔmǔ yuē Tài Huáng Tàihòu],
his mother as the Empress Dowager [Huáng Tàihòu] [mǔ yuē Huáng Tàihòu],
and his consort as the Empress [Huánghòu] [pín yuē Huánghòu].
They were designated with honorable appellations [Děng yǐ huī chēng],
and given beautiful titles [jiā yǐ měi hào],
which were simple compared to the Suí and Táng [zhì yú Suí, Táng],
and refined compared to the old customs [wén yú gù sú].
The Empress’s clan only included the Yǐshì and Bálǐ clans [Hòuzú wéi Yǐshì, Bálǐ shì],
and for generations, they were entrusted with the affairs of the state [ér shì rèn qí guóshì].
Tàizǔ admired Emperor Gāo of Hàn [Hàn Gāo Huángdì] [Tàizǔ mù Hàn Gāo Huángdì],
thus the Yēlǜ [Yēlǜ] clan also adopted the surname Liú [gù Yēlǜ jiān chēng Liú shì];
and because the Yǐshì and Bálǐ were comparable to Chancellor Xiāo [Xiāo Xiāngguó] [yǐ Yǐshì, Bálǐ bǐ Xiāo Xiāngguó],
they consequently became the Xiāo clan [suí wéi Xiāo shì].
Yēlǜ Yǎn and Chén Dàrèn’s Biographies of Empresses and Consorts in the Liáo History [Yēlǜ Yǎn, Chén Dàrèn Liáo Shǐ Hòufēi Chuán],
are largely the same with minor differences [dàtóng xiǎoyì],
and we have judiciously selected the appropriate parts to be included in this chapter [zhuó qǔ qí dàng zhù yú piān].
Empress Zhāoliè [Zhāoliè Huánghòu] Xiāo [Xiāo shì] of Sùzǔ [Sùzǔ],
whose milk name was Zhuōzhēn [Xiǎozì Zhuōzhēn].
She married Sùzǔ [Guī Sùzǔ],
and bore four sons [shēng sì zǐ],
as seen in the Table of Imperial Sons [jiàn Huángzǐ Biǎo].
In the third year of Qiántǒng (1103) [Qiántǒng sān nián],
she was posthumously honored as Empress Zhāoliè [zhuī zūn Zhāoliè Huánghòu].
Empress Zhuāngjìng [Zhuāngjìng Huánghòu] Xiāo [Xiāo shì] of Yìzǔ [Yìzǔ],
whose milk name was Yālǐxīn [Xiǎozì Yālǐxīn].
Sùzǔ once visited her family and said [Sùzǔ cháng guò qí jiā yuē]:
"Those of the same surname can form alliances [Tóngxìng kě jiéjiāo],
those of different surnames can intermarry [yìxìng kě jiéhūn]."
Knowing she was from the Xiāo clan [Zhī wèi Xiāo shì],
she was engaged for Yìzǔ [wèi Yìzǔ pìn yān].
She bore seven children, both male and female [Shēng nánnǚ qī rén].
In the third year of Qiántǒng (1103) [Qiántǒng sān nián],
she was posthumously honored as Empress Zhuāngjìng [zhuī zūn Zhuāngjìng Huánghòu].
Empress Jiǎnxiàn [Jiǎnxiàn Huánghòu] Xiāo [Xiāo shì] of Xuánzǔ [Xuánzǔ],
whose milk name was Yuèlǐgū [Xiǎozì Yuèlǐgū].
Xuánzǔ was harmed by Hěndé [Xuánzǔ wèi Hěndé suǒ hài],
and the Empress lived as a widow [Hòu lí jū],
fearing she would not be spared [kǒng bù miǎn],
she ordered her four sons to go and rely on the neighboring family Yēlǜ Táiyā [mìng sì zǐ wǎng yī línjiā Yēlǜ Táiyā],
and thus obtained peace [nǎi huò ān].
When Tàizǔ was born [Tàizǔ shēng],
the Empress, seeing his unusual bone structure [Hòu yǐ gǔ xiàng yìcháng],
