feared there were hidden plotters who might harm him [jù yǒu yīntú hài zhě],
and raised him in a separate tent [jū zhī bié zhàng].
In the twenty-first year of Chóngxī (1052) [Chóngxī èrshíyī nián],
she was posthumously honored as Empress Jiǎnxiàn [zhuī zūn Jiǎnxiàn Huánghòu].
Empress Xuānjiǎn [Xuānjiǎn Huánghòu] Xiāo [Xiāo shì] of Dézǔ [Dézǔ],
whose milk name was Yánmǔjīn [Xiǎozì Yánmǔjīn].
She was the daughter of Tìlá, the Prime Minister [zǎixiàng] of the Yáoliǎn clan [Yáoliǎn shì zǎixiàng Tìlá zhī nǚ].
She had six children, male and female [Nán, nǚ liù rén],
Tàizǔ being the eldest son [Tàizǔ cháng zǐ yě].
She passed away in the eighth year of Tiānxiǎn (933) [Tiānxiǎn bā nián bēng],
and was interred at Délíng [fù Délíng].
In the twenty-first year of Chóngxī (1052) [Chóngxī èrshíyī nián],
she was posthumously honored as Empress Xuānjiǎn [zhuī zūn Xuānjiǎn Huánghòu].
Empress Chūnqīn [Chūnqīn Huánghòu] Shùlǜ [Shùlǜ shì] of Tàizǔ [Tàizǔ],
whose taboo name was Píng [huì Píng],
and milk name was Yuèlǐgū [xiǎozì Yuèlǐgū].
Her ancestor was Nuòsī [Nuòsī], a Huíhú [Huíhú] person [Qí xiān Huíhú rén Nuòsī],
who bore Wèiníng Shèlì [shēng Wèiníng Shèlì],
Wèiníng bore Shènsī Méilǐ [Wèiníng shēng Shènsī Méilǐ],
Shènsī bore Pó’gū Méilǐ [Shènsī shēng Pó’gū Méilǐ],
Pó’gū married the daughter of King Yúndégǎ [Pó’gū qǔ Yúndégǎ wáng nǚ],
and bore the Empress in the Right Grand Department of Qìdān [shēng Hòu yú Qìdān Yòu Dàbù].
Pó’gū's name was Yuèwǎn [Pó’gū míng Yuèwǎn],
who served the Yáoliǎn clan as Āzhā gēzhǐ [shì Yáoliǎn shì wèi Āzhā gēzhǐ].
The Empress was reserved, serious, and resolute [Hòu jiǎnzhòng guǒduàn],
and possessed great strategy [yǒu xiónglüè].
She once reached the junction of the Liáo and Tǔ Rivers [Cháng zhì Liáo, Tǔ èr hé zhī huì],
where a woman riding a green ox-cart [yǒu nǚzǐ chéng qīng niú chē],
hurriedly avoided the path [cāngcù bì lù],
and then suddenly disappeared [hū bù jiàn].
Before long [Wèijǐ],
a children's rhyme said [tóngyáo yuē]:
"The green ox matron [Qīng niú yù],
once avoided the path [céng bì lù]."
It is said that the common saying referred to the Earth Deity as the Green Ox Matron [Gài yàn wèi dìqí wèi qīng niú yù yún].
When Tàizǔ ascended the throne [Tàizǔ jíwèi],
the officials presented the honorific title, Empress of the Earth [Qúnchén shàng zūn hào yuē Dì Huánghòu].
In the first year of Shéncè (916) [Shéncè yuán nián],
during the grand investiture [dà cè],
the title Yìngtiān Dàmíng Dì Huánghòu (Empress of the Earth, Corresponding to Heaven and Greatly Enlightened) was added [jiā hào Yìngtiān Dàmíng Dì Huánghòu].
When leading troops and commanding the masses [Xíng bīng yù zhòng],
the Empress always participated in the planning [Hòu cháng yǔ móu].
Tàizǔ once crossed the desert to attack the Dǎngxiàng [Tàizǔ cháng dù qì jī Dǎngxiàng],
and the Huángtóu and Chòubó branches of the Shīwěi took advantage of the emptiness to attack [Huángtóu, Chòubó èr Shīwěi chéng xū xí zhī];
the Empress knew this [Hòu zhī],
mustered the troops to await them [lè bīng yǐ dài],
fought fiercely [fènjī],
and greatly defeated them [dà pò zhī],
making her fame shake all the barbarians [míng zhèn zhū yí].
At that time, Lǐ Cúnxù, the King of Jìn [Jìn Wáng Lǐ Cúnxù], wished to form an alliance [Shí Jìn Wáng Lǐ Cúnxù yù jié yuán],
and treated the Empress as his paternal aunt [yǐ shúmǔ shì Hòu].
Liú Shǒuguāng of Yōuzhōu sent Hán Yánhuī to request assistance [Yōuzhōu Liú Shǒuguāng qiǎn Hán Yánhuī qiú yuán],
but he did not perform the full prostration [bù bài],
Tàizǔ was angry [Tàizǔ nù],
detained him [liú zhī],
and made him herd horses [shǐ mù mǎ].
The Empress said [Hòu yuē]:
"To maintain integrity and not yield [Shǒu jié bù qū],
is the mark of a worthy person [xiánzhě yě].
He should be treated with courtesy and employed [Yí lǐ yòng zhī]."
Tàizǔ then summoned Yánhuī to speak with him [Tàizǔ nǎi zhào Yánhuī yǔ yǔ],
was greatly pleased [dàyuè],
and appointed him as his chief strategist [yǐ wéi móuzhǔ].
Lord Lǐ of Wú [Wú Zhǔ Lǐ Yuán] presented fierce fire oil [xiàn měnghuǒ yóu],
which only intensified when water was poured on it [yǐ shuǐ wò zhī yù chì].
Tàizǔ selected thirty thousand cavalry to attack Yōuzhōu [Tàizǔ xuǎn sān wàn jì yǐ gōng Yōuzhōu].
The Empress said [Hòu yuē]:
"How can one test oil and then attack another's country [Qǐ yǒu shì yóu ér gōng rén guó zhě]?"
She pointed to a tree in front of the tent and said [Zhǐ zhàng qián shù yuē]:
"Can a tree without bark survive [Wú pí kěyǐ shēng hū]?"
Tàizǔ said [Tàizǔ yuē]:
"No [Bù kě]."
The Empress said [Hòu yuē]:
"Yōuzhōu, with its territory and people [Yōuzhōu zhī yǒu tǔ yǒu mín],
is just like this [yì yóu shì ěr].
If we use three thousand cavalry to raid its four borders [Wú yǐ sān qiān jì luè qí sì yě],
in no more than a few years [bù guò shù nián],
it will be exhausted and submit to us [kùn ér guī wǒ yǐ],
why must we do this [hé bì wéi cǐ]?
If by chance we do not win [Wànyī bù shèng],
we will be laughed at by the Central States [wéi Zhōngguó xiào],
would our tribes not also disintegrate [wú bùluò bù yì jiětǐ hū]!"
In the pacification of Bóhǎi [Qí píng Bóhǎi],
the Empress was involved in the planning [Hòu yǔ yǒu móu].
When Tàizǔ passed away [Tàizǔ bēng],
the Empress proclaimed herself regent [Hòu chēng zhì],
and managed the military and state affairs [shè jūnguó shì].
When the burial took place [Jí zàng],
she wished to be buried alive with him [yù yǐ shēn xùn],
but her relatives and all the officials strongly remonstrated [qīnqī bǎiguān lì jiàn],
so she cut off her right wrist and placed it in the coffin [yīn duàn yòu wàn nà yú jiù].
When Tàizōng ascended the throne [Tàizōng jíwèi],
she was honored as the Empress Dowager [zūn wèi Huáng Tàihòu].
At the beginning of Huìtóng (938) [Huìtóng chū],

the honorific title Guǎngdé Zhìrén Zhāoliè Chóngjiǎn Yìngtiān Huáng Tàihòu (Empress Dowager, Vast Virtue, Utmost Benevolence, Illustrious Ardor, Sublime Simplicity, Corresponding to Heaven) was conferred [shàng zūn hào yuē Guǎngdé Zhìrén Zhāoliè Chóngjiǎn Yìngtiān Huáng Tàihòu].
Previously [Chū],
Tàizǔ had said that Tàizōng would surely bring prosperity to their family [Tàizǔ cháng wèi Tàizōng bì xīng wǒ jiā],
and the Empress wished to make the Crown Prince Bèi avoid him [Hòu yù lìng Huáng Tàizǐ Bèi bì zhī],
but Tàizǔ invested Bèi as King of Dōngdān [Tàizǔ cè Bèi wèi Dōngdān Wáng].
When Tàizǔ passed away [Tàizǔ bēng],
Tàizōng was enthroned [Tàizōng lì],
and the King of Dōngdān fled to Táng [Dōngdān Wáng bì zhī Táng].
The Empress Dowager always favored her youngest son, Lǐ Hú [Tàihòu cháng shǔyì yú shǎozǐ Lǐ Hú].
When Tàizōng passed away [Tàizōng bēng],
Shìzōng ascended the throne in Zhènyáng [Shìzōng jíwèi yú Zhènyáng],
and the Empress Dowager, enraged [Tàihòu nù],
sent Lǐ Hú with troops to meet and attack him [qiǎn Lǐ Hú yǐ bīng nì jī].
Lǐ Hú was defeated [Lǐ Hú bài],
and the Empress Dowager personally led the army to meet Shìzōng at the Cross Ford of the Huáng River [Tàihòu qīn shuài shī yù yú Huáng Hé zhī Héngdù].
Thanks to the remonstrance of Yēlǜ Wūzhì [Lài Yēlǜ Wūzhì jiàn],
the troops were withdrawn [bà bīng].
The Empress Dowager was relocated to Zǔzhōu [Qiān Tàihòu yú Zǔzhōu].
She passed away in the third year of Yìnglì (953) [Yìnglì sān nián bēng],
at the age of seventy-five [nián qīshíwǔ],
and was interred at Zǔlíng [fù Zǔlíng],
with the posthumous title Zhēnliè [shì yuē Zhēnliè].
In the twenty-first year of Chóngxī (1052) [Chóngxī èrshíyī nián],
her posthumous title was changed to the present one [gēng jīn shì].
Tàizōng Jìng'ān Empress Xiāo shì,
whose *xiǎozì* was Wēn,
was the daughter of Chúnqīn Empress's brother Shìshìlǔ.
When the Emperor was Grand Marshal,
she was taken as a consort,
and gave birth to Mùzōng.
Upon his accession,
she was made Empress.
She was intelligent, pure, and simple by nature,
and was especially favored.
Even during military campaigns and hunts, she would always accompany him.
In Tiānxiǎn 10, she passed away,
posthumously named Zhāngdé,
and buried in Fènlíng.
In Chóngxī 21,
her posthumous name was changed to the current one.
Shìzōng Huáijié Empress Xiāo shì,
whose *xiǎozì* was Sāgězhǐ,
was the daughter of Chúnqīn Empress's brother Āgǔzhǐ.
When the Emperor was Prince of Yǒngkāng,
she was taken,
and gave birth to Jǐngzōng.
At the end of Tiānlù,
she was made Empress.
In the autumn of the following year,
she gave birth to Princess Ménggǔ.
While she was in confinement,
Chágē rebelled,
assassinating the Empress Dowager and the Emperor.
The Empress rode a litter
directly to Chágē,
requesting to complete the collection and interment.
The next day she was killed.
She was posthumously named Xiàoliè Empress.
In Chóngxī 21,
her posthumous name was changed to the current one.
Shìzōng's consort, Zhēn shì,
was a palace woman from the Later Táng dynasty,
possessing beauty.
The Emperor obtained her when he followed Tàizōng on his southern expedition.
She was greatly favored,
and gave birth to Níngwáng Zhǐmò.
Upon his accession,
she was made Empress.
She was strict and clear, dignified and serene,
with an elegant demeanor.
She managed the inner palace with rules,
allowing no personal interference.
Liú Zhīyuǎn and Guō Wēi proclaimed themselves emperors,
while Shìzōng, possessing strong and prosperous talents,
lingered for years.
The Empress participated in the imperial tent,
secretly assisting in grand strategies,
but they were not adopted.
When Chágē rebelled,
she was killed.
Upon Jǐngzōng's enthronement,
the two Empresses were buried on Yīwūlǘ Shān,
and temples were built beside their mausoleums.
Mùzōng Empress Xiāo shì,
whose father Zhīfán,
was a Chamberlain for Court Ceremonials and Hanlin Academician.
When the Empress was born,
auspicious clouds and a fragrant aroma lingered for a long time.
As a child, she had proper deportment.
When the Emperor was a regional prince,
she was taken as a consort.
Upon ascending to the central palace,
she was gentle and compliant by nature,
unable to correct others.
She had no children.
Jǐngzōng Ruìzhì Empress Xiāo shì,
whose given name was Chuò,
and *xiǎozì* Yànyàn,
was the daughter of the Northern Chancellor Sīwēn.
She was intelligent from an early age.
Sīwēn once observed his daughters sweeping the ground,
and only the Empress swept it clean.
He happily said:
"This daughter will surely be able to establish a family!"
Upon the Emperor's accession,
she was chosen as noble consort.
Soon after, she was enfeoffed as Empress,
and gave birth to Shèngzōng.
Upon Jǐngzōng's death,
she was honored as Empress Dowager,
and managed the affairs of the state.
The Empress wept, saying:
"The mother is a widow, the son is weak,
the clan members are powerful,
and the border defenses are not yet settled. What shall we do?"
Yēlǜ Xiézhěn and Hán Dé ràng stepped forward and said:
"If you trust your servants,
what worries are there?"
Thereupon,
the Empress, along with Xiézhěn and Dé ràng, deliberated on major state affairs,
entrusting the southern border affairs to the Prince Yúyuè Xiūgē.
In Tǒnghé 1,
she was granted the honorable title of Chéngtiān Empress Dowager.
In Tǒnghé 24,
she was further granted the honorable title of Ruìdé Shénlüè Yìngyùn Qǐhuà Chéngtiān Empress Dowager.
In Tǒnghé 27, she passed away,
posthumously named Shèngshén Xuānxiàn Empress.
In Chóngxī 21,
her posthumous name was changed to the current one.
The Empress was intelligent and understood the ways of governance,
always following good advice,
thus all her officials exerted their loyalty.
She was skilled in military administration.
During the Battle of Chányuān,
she personally rode the war chariot,
commanding the three armies.
Rewards and punishments were clear and trustworthy,
and the generals and soldiers fought bravely.
Shèngzōng was called a prosperous ruler of Liáo,
much of which was due to her teachings and guidance.
Shèngzōng Réndé Empress Xiāo shì,
whose *xiǎozì* Púsàgē,
was the daughter of Ruìzhì Empress's brother Kuíyīn.
At the age of twelve,
beautiful and talented,
she was selected into the imperial harem.
In Tǒnghé 19,
she was enfeoffed as Qítiān Empress.
She once made a palace model with straw reeds,
secretly giving it to the relevant officials,
ordering the construction of the three halls: Qīngfēng, Tiānxiáng, and Bāfāng.
Upon completion,
she was even more favored and distinguished.
Her carriage was adorned with dragon heads and *chīwěi*,
decorated with gold.
She also built a nine-dragon carriage and carriages for various princes,
and made stupas of white gold,
each with ingenious designs.
In summer and autumn, she traveled through mountains and valleys,
where flowers and trees were like embroidery,
and carriages and attire intertwined,
making people look upon her as a goddess.
She gave birth to two imperial princes,
both of whom died young.
In Kāitài 5,
the palace woman Nòujīn gave birth to Xīngzōng,
whom the Empress adopted as her son.
When the Emperor was gravely ill,
Nòujīn cursed the Empress, saying:
"Old hag, does your favor have an end?"
Attendants helped the Empress out.
Upon the Emperor's death,
Nòujīn enthroned herself as Empress Dowager,
becoming Qīn'āi Empress.
Guards Fēng Jiānú and Xǐsūn, seeking imperial favor,
falsely accused Northern Chancellor Xiāo Zhuóbǔ and Imperial Uncle Xiāo Pǐdí of treason.
An imperial decree ordered an investigation,
which implicated the Empress.
Xīngzōng heard of it and said:
"The Empress served the late Emperor for forty years,
and nurtured my humble self.
She should be Empress Dowager;
now, not only is she not,
but she is also being accused.
Is this acceptable?"
Qīn'āi replied:
"If this person remains,
I fear future troubles."
The Emperor said:
"The Empress has no children and is old.
Even if she remains,
she can do nothing."
Qīn'āi did not agree,
and moved the Empress to Shàngjīng.
When the imperial carriage went on a spring hunt,
Qīn'āi, fearing that the Emperor harbored gratitude for her upbringing,
dispatched someone to harm her.
When the envoy arrived,
the Empress said:
"I am truly innocent,
as the whole world knows.
Sir, please allow me to bathe,
and then I will die.
May I?"
The envoy withdrew.
By the time he returned,
the Empress had already passed away,
at the age of fifty.
On that day,
some people saw the Empress in the shade of Mùyè Shān,
riding a blue-canopied carriage,
with a very strict escort.
She was posthumously honored as Réndé Hòu Huáng.
She was buried together with Qīn'āi in Qìnglíng.
of Shèngzōng,
whose informal name was Nòujīn,
was a fifth-generation descendant of Āgǔzhǐ, the younger brother of Empress Chúnqīn.
She had a dark complexion
and a fierce gaze.
Her mother once dreamed of a golden pillar supporting the sky,
and though her other children wished to ascend it, they could not;
when the Empress arrived later,
she and her attendants all ascended,
which was considered extraordinary.
After a long time,
she entered the palace.
She once cleaned the couch of Empress Dowager Chéngtiān,
and found a golden chicken.
She swallowed it,
and her complexion became more luminous than usual.
The Empress Dowager was astonished and said:
“She is certain to bear a miraculous son!”
Subsequently, she gave birth to Xīngzōng.
Empress Réndé had no sons,
so she took him and raised him as if he were her own.
The Empress was displeased
that Xīngzōng served Empress Réndé so respectfully.
When Shèngzōng died,
she ordered Féngjiānú and others to falsely accuse Empress Réndé of plotting rebellion with Xiāo Zhuóbǔ, Xiāo Pǐdí, and others.
She was exiled to Shàngjīng
and subsequently killed.
She established herself as Empress Dowager
and acted as Regent,
designating her birthday as the Yìngshèng Festival.
In the first year of Chóngxī,
she was honored with the title Réncí Shèngshàn Qīnxiào Guǎngdé Ānjìng Zhēnchún Kuānhòu Chóngjué Yītiān Huáng Tàihòu.
In the third year,
the Empress Dowager secretly summoned her younger brothers to plot,
wishing to establish her youngest son, Chóngyuán.
Chóngyuán reported the scheme to the Emperor.
The Emperor confiscated the Empress Dowager’s seals and insignia
and exiled her to the Qīkuò Palace in Qìngzhōu.
In the autumn of the sixth year,
the Emperor regretted this,
personally drove the carriage to welcome her back,
and offered increasingly filial and respectful attendance and care.
The Empress Dowager was often unhappy.
When the Emperor died,
she showed absolutely no signs of grief.
Seeing Empress Chóngshèng weeping mournfully according to the rites,
she addressed her, saying:
“You are still young;
why such profound sorrow?”
In the beginning of the Qīngníng era,
she was honored as Grand Empress Dowager.
When she died,
her posthumous title was Empress Qīn'āi.
When the Empress Dowager first became Regent,
she posthumously enfeoffed her great-grandfather as the Prince of Lánlíng Commandery,
her father as the Prince of Qí State,
and all her younger brothers were made princes;
even the Five Marquises of the Hàn Dynasty could not have surpassed this.
Empress Rén'yì Xiāo Shì of Xīngzōng,
whose informal name was Tàlǐ,
was the eldest daughter of Xiàomù, the younger brother of Empress Qīn'āi.
Her nature was generous and tolerant,
and her appearance was dignified and beautiful.
When the Emperor ascended the throne,
she entered the palace
and gave birth to Dàozōng.
In the fourth year of Chóngxī,
she was established as Empress.
In the twenty-third year,
she was given the title Empress Zhēnyì Cíhé Wénhuì Xiàojìng Guǎng'ài Chóngshèng.
When Dàozōng ascended the throne,
she was honored as Empress Dowager.
In the second year of Qīngníng,
she was offered the honorary title Cíyì Rénhé Wénhuì Xiàojìng Guǎng'ài Zōngtiān Huáng Tàihòu.
In the autumn of the ninth year,
Yēlǜ Liáng, Director of the Dūnmù Palace, secretly informed the Empress Dowager of the signs of rebellion by Chóngyuán and his son Nièlǔgǔ.
She then reported this to the Emperor.
The Emperor doubted the claim,
but the Empress Dowager said:
“This is a major affair concerning the state,
so we should plan early.”
The Emperor then declared martial law.
When the battle ensued,
the Empress Dowager personally commanded the guards,
and defeated the rebel faction.
She died in the second year of Dàkāng.
Her posthumous title was Empress Rén'yì.
She was benevolent, kind, virtuous, and cautious,
and universally praised both within and outside the court.
Whenever tribute funds arrived from various states on New Year's Day or her birthday,
she distributed them entirely to the impoverished.
She once dreamed that Chóngyuán said:
“My bones are north of Mount Tàizǐ,
and I cannot endure the severe cold.”
When she awoke,
she immediately ordered a shelter built over the burial site.
Her compassion was of this kind.
Noble Consort Xiāo Shì of Xīngzōng,
whose informal name was Sān,
was the daughter of Fùmǎ Dūwèi Pǐlǐ.
She was selected to enter the Eastern Palace.
When the Emperor ascended the throne,
she was established as Empress.
In the beginning of the Chóngxī era,
she was demoted to Noble Consort due to an offense.
Empress Xuānyì Xiāo Shì of Dàozōng,
whose informal name was Guānyīn,
was the daughter of the Commissioner of Military Affairs Huì, the younger brother of Empress Qīn'āi.
Her appearance was unparalleled;
she was skilled in poetry
and good at conversation.
She composed her own lyrics,
and was especially skilled at the Pípá.
During the Chóngxī era,
when the Emperor was Prince of Yānzhào,
he accepted her as a consort.
In the beginning of the Qīngníng era,
she was established as Empress Yìdé.
The wife of the Imperial Uncle Chóngyuán
prided herself on her glamorous beauty.
When the Empress saw this,
she warned her, saying:
“As a wife of a noble family,
why must you be like this!”
The Empress gave birth to Crown Prince Jùn,
and monopolized the Emperor’s affection.
She loved music,
and the musician official Zhào Wéiyī was permitted to attend her closely.
In the beginning of the Dàkāng era,
the palace maid Shàndēng and Zhū Dǐnghè of the Music Bureau falsely accused the Empress of having a private affair with Wéiyī.
The Commissioner of Military Affairs, Yēlǜ Yǐxīn, reported this to the Emperor.
An imperial decree ordered Yǐxīn and Zhāng Xiàojié to investigate the charges,
and they subsequently affirmed them as true.
Wéiyī and his clan were executed,
and the Empress was granted the favor of committing suicide.
Her body was returned to her family.
In the beginning of the Qiántǒng era,
she was posthumously titled Empress Xuānyì
and interred together at Qìnglíng Mausoleum.
Consort Huì Xiāo Shì of Dàozōng,
whose informal name was Tǎnsī,
was the younger sister of Fùmǎ Dūwèi Xiámò.
In the second year of Dàkāng,
Yǐxīn recommended her,
and she was selected to enter the Imperial Harem
and established as Empress.
She resided there for several years
but had not produced an imperial heir.
The Empress's younger sister, Wòtèlǎn, had previously married Yǐxīn’s son, Suíyě.
The Empress spoke to the Emperor, claiming Wòtèlǎn was suitable for bearing a son,
so she was divorced
and brought into the palace.
In the eighth year,
when the Imperial Grandson Yánxǐ was enfeoffed as the Prince of Liáng,
she was demoted to Consort Huì
and moved to Qiánlíng;
Wòtèlǎn was returned to her family.
Shortly thereafter,
her mother, the Lady of Yān State, practiced black magic against the Prince of Liáng
and was executed.
The Consort was degraded to commoner status
and imprisoned in Yízhōu.
Her younger brothers were confiscated by the Xīngshèng Palace.
In the sixth year of Tiānqìng,
she was summoned back
and enfeoffed as Grand Imperial Consort Dowager.
Two years later,
she fled to Mount Hēidǐng
and died,
and was buried at Mount Tàizǐ.
Empress Xiāo Shì of Tiānzuò,
whose informal name was Duōlǐlǎn,
was a fifth-generation descendant of Chancellor Jìxiān.
She entered the palace in the third year of Dà’ān.
The following year,
she was enfeoffed as the Princess Consort of Yān State.
In the beginning of the Qiántǒng era,
she was formally installed as Empress.
Her nature was quiet and virtuous,
and she maintained proper decorum.
Her brothers, Fèngxiān, Bǎoxiān, and others, relied on the Empress’s favor to hold important positions.
During the Jurchen rebellion,
she followed Tiānzuò on his flight west,
and died of illness.
Virtuous Consort Xiāo Shì of Tiānzuò,
whose informal name was Shīgū,
was the daughter of Chánggē, Chancellor of the Northern Administration.
She entered the palace in the second year of Shòulóng,
was enfeoffed as Consort of Yān State,
and gave birth to her son Tàlǔ.
In the third year of Qiántǒng,
her title was changed to Virtuous Consort.
Through the Chái Enfeoffment Ceremony,
Tàlǔ was enfeoffed as the Prince of Yān State,
and the Consort’s title was supplemented with Zànyì.
When the Prince died,
she died of sorrow and grief.
Tiānzuò Wén Fēi Xiāo Shì (Consort Xiāo, the Accomplished Consort of Tiānzuò),
whose childhood name was Sèsè,
was the daughter of the Guójiù Dàfù Fáng (the lineage of the Maternal Grandfather).
In the beginning of the Qiántǒng reign,
the Emperor visited Yēlǜ Tàgé's residence,
saw her and was pleased by her,
and concealed her in the palace for several months.
The Imperial Grand-Uncle Hélǔwò urged the Emperor to formally select and accept her according to ritual.
In the winter of the third year (of Qiántǒng),
she was established as Wén Fēi (Accomplished Consort).
She bore the Princess of Shǔguó and the Prince of Jìn, Āolúwò,
and was particularly favored.
Using the ritual of burning firewood (in a ceremony),
she was granted the added title Chéngyì (Inheriting and Assisting).
She was skilled at singing poetry.
When the Nǚzhí rebellion broke out,
the intrusions and aggressions were visible daily.
The Emperor hunted and roamed, showing no concern,
and many loyal officials were estranged and dismissed.
The Consort composed a song to satirize and remonstrate,
the lyrics of which said:
"Do not lament the dark crimson dust along the frontier,
do not grieve over great difficulties, fearing the barbarian men;
it is better to block the path of the wicked and treacherous,
and select worthy ministers.
You must truly sleep on brushwood and taste gall,
to inspire brave gentlemen to sacrifice their lives;
in the morning, you can clear the northern deserts,
and in the evening, rest upon Yān and Yún (territories)."
She sang another song, saying:
"When the Prime Minister comes to court, his sword-pendants clang,
a thousand officials look askance, and there is silence.
If external troubles are fostered—alas, how can it be remedied!
Misfortune befalls loyal ministers, yet punishments are unclear.
Relatives all occupy positions of screening and defense,
private households secretly raise soldiers for their claws and teeth.
Pitiable was the Son of Heaven of Qín in times past,
still hoping for Great Peace within his palace."
Tiānzuò saw this and bore a grudge.
Since the dispersion and removal (of the capital),
nearly half of the commanderies and counties had been lost,
and the sovereign harbored an inclination to tire of his duties.
Among the imperial princes, Āolúwò was the most worthy,
and he had long been held in high public esteem.
The elder brother of the Primary Empress, Xiāo Fèngxiān, deeply resented him,
and falsely accused Yú Dǔ, the Commander-in-Chief of the Southern Army, of plotting to install the Prince of Jìn.
They alleged that the Consort was complicit,
and she was granted death.
Tiānzuò Yuán Fēi Xiāo Shì (Primary Consort Xiāo of Tiānzuò),
whose childhood name was Guìgē,
was the younger sister of the Consort of Yānguó.
At seventeen years old,
she was enfeoffed as the Primary Consort (Yuán Fēi).
She was naturally deep and calm.
Once, while sleeping during the day,
a close attendant stole a sable mat.
The Consort noticed but did not speak of it,
and the palace chambers praised her tolerance and generosity.
She followed Tiānzuò on his western hunt,
and died of illness.
A comment says: The Liáo treated the saddle and horse as their home,
and empresses and consorts were often skilled in archery and horsemanship,
in military affairs and in hunting expeditions,
they never failed to follow.
Such as Yìngtiān’s fierce assault on the Shìwēi,
Chéngtiān’s leading of the army at Chányuān,
and Rényì’s personal defeat of Zhòngyuán—
these were unprecedented in antiquity,
and were also part of their custom.
Jìng'ān had neither censure nor praise;
Qítiān’s clever thinking,
was merely the gradual spread of extravagance;
Xuānyì’s composing music and understanding melodies,
how could this have led to the steps of false slander?
Wén Fēi was capable of singing poetry to remonstrate,
yet to say she plotted private benefit for her son,
is wrong.
As for Jiǎnjiàn’s protecting the orphan during perilous difficulties,
and Huáijié’s calm acceptance of righteousness,
even a fierce hero could not surpass them.
Qīn'āi was cruel and refractory,
and murdered the primary empress.
But Xīngzōng was unable to restrain his mother—
what a pity!
Biographies, Chapter Two: Imperial Relatives: Yìzōng Bèi (son Píng Wáng Lóngxiān, Jìn Wáng Dàoyǐn), Zhāngsù Huángdì Lǐ Hú (son Sòng Wáng Xǐyǐn), Shùnzōng Jùn, Jìn Wáng Āolúwò.
Yìzōng,
personal name Bèi,
childhood name Túyù,
was the eldest son of Tàizǔ,
his mother was Empress Chúnqīn Xiāo Shì.
As a child, he was intelligent, quick-witted, and fond of learning,
outwardly generous but inwardly sincere.
In the spring of the first year of the Shéncè reign,
he was established as the Crown Prince.
At that time, Tàizǔ asked his attending officials, saying:
"A sovereign who has received the Mandate (of Heaven),
should serve Heaven and respect the spirits.
I wish to sacrifice to those who have great achievements and virtue.
To whom should I sacrifice?
Whom should I place first?"
All replied with the Buddha.
Tàizǔ said:
"Buddhism is not a central Chinese teaching."
Bèi said:
"Kǒngzǐ (Confucius) is a great sage,
respected by ten thousand generations,
he should be first."
Tàizǔ was greatly pleased,
and immediately built a Temple of Confucius,
and ordered the Crown Prince to perform the ritual sacrifices (shìdiàn) in spring and autumn.
He once followed Tàizǔ on campaigns against the Wūgǔ and the Dǎngxìang,
serving as the Commander-in-Chief of the Vanguard,
and also managed the Yān territories.
When Tàizǔ campaigned in the west,
he left Bèi to guard the capital.
Bèi then presented a plan for conquering Bóhǎi.
In the first year of the Tiānxiǎn reign,
he accompanied Tàizǔ on the campaign against Bóhǎi.
After capturing Fúyú City,
the sovereign wished to register the households and population.
Bèi remonstrated, saying:
"We have just acquired this land, yet if we begin counting the people,
the people will surely become unsettled.
If we seize the momentum of splitting the bamboo,
and proceed straight to Hūhàn City,
we will certainly conquer it."
Tàizǔ followed his advice.
Bèi, along with the Grand Marshal Déguāng, served as the vanguard,
and besieged Hūhàn City by night.
Dà Yīnchuàn was reduced to desperation,
and requested surrender.
Soon after, they rebelled again,
and Tàizǔ defeated them.
The state was renamed Dōngdān (Eastern Dan),
its city was named Tiānfú (Heavenly Blessing),
and Bèi was made the Rén Huáng Wáng (Human Emperor King) to govern it.
He was also granted the crown and robes of the Son of Heaven,
established the Gānlù era name,
proclaimed imperial decrees (chēng zhì),
and installed the Zǔoyòu Dàcì Four Ministers and all officials,
all employing Hàn (Chinese) methods.
He was to annually contribute 150,000 bolts of cloth,
and 1,000 horses.
The sovereign instructed him, saying:
"This land borders the sea,
it is not a place where one can reside long.
I leave you to comfort and govern (this region),
to show my heart's love for the people."
When the imperial carriage was about to return,
Bèi composed a song and presented it.
When taking leave from the steps of the throne,
Tàizǔ said:
"Having you govern the Eastern Territory,
what further worries do I have?"
Bèi wailed loudly and departed.
He then proceeded to Yíkūn Prefecture.
Not long after,
many tribes revolted,
and the Grand Marshal (Déguāng) suppressed and pacified them.
When the news of Tàizǔ’s death arrived,
Bèi immediately rushed to the imperial mausoleum.
Bèi knew that the Empress Dowager intended to enthrone Déguāng,
so he addressed the nobles and ministers, saying:
"The Grand Marshal’s achievements and virtue reach men and spirits,
and the center and outside (court and provinces) are attached to him;
he should preside over the state (shèjì)."
He then, along with the multitude of officials, petitioned the Empress Dowager and ceded the throne.
Thereupon, the Grand Marshal ascended the throne,
this was Tàizōng.
After Tàizōng was established,
(Bèi) came to be suspected.
Dōngpíng was made the Southern Capital (Nánjīng),
and Bèi was relocated to reside there,
and all his people were moved away.
Guards were also installed to secretly monitor his activities.
After Bèi returned to his state,
he ordered Wáng Jìyuǎn to compose the inscription for the monument establishing the Southern Capital,
erected a library tower at the Western Palace,
and composed music and pastoral poetry.
Táng Míngzōng heard of this,
and dispatched a messenger across the sea carrying a letter to secretly summon Bèi.
Bèi happened to be hunting by the sea.
When the messenger arrived again,
Bèi said to his attendants:
"I yielded the empire to the sovereign,
yet now I am suspected in return;
it is better to go to another state,
to achieve the renown of Wú Tàibó."
He erected a wooden post by the sea,
and carved a poem on it, saying:
"The small mountain presses the great mountain,
the great mountain is completely powerless.
Ashamed to see the people of my former home,
from now on, I flee to a foreign land."
Taking Gāo Měirén (Beauty Gāo),
and carrying his books, he floated across the sea and departed.
Táng used the imperial honor guard of the Son of Heaven to welcome Bèi,
Bèi sat in a boat palace,
and all the officials lined up to offer greetings for long life.
When he reached Biàn,
he met Míngzōng.
Míngzōng gave him Xià Shì, the Empress of Zhuāngzōng, as a wife,
granted him the surname Dōngdān,
and named him Mùhuá.
Ruìzhōu was renamed Huáihuà Jūn,
and he was appointed Huáihuà Jūn Jiédùshǐ (military commissioner), and Commissioner of Observation for prefectures including Ruìzhōu and Shènzhōu.
Later, he was again granted the surname Lǐ,
and named Zànhuá.
He was transferred to command at Huázhōu,
and remotely led the Qiánzhōu Jiédùshǐ post.
Although Bèi was in a foreign country,
he constantly thought of his kin,
and envoys sent to inquire about their welfare never ceased.
Later, Cóngkē, Míngzōng's adopted son, murdered his ruler and established himself,
Bèi secretly informed Tàizōng, saying:
"Cóngkē murdered the sovereign,
Why not chastise him?"
When Tàizōng established Shí Jìngtáng as the Lord of Jìn,
and advanced troops upon Luò.
Cóngkē wished to immolate himself,
and summoned Bèi to join him;
Bèi refused to follow,
so [Cóngkē] dispatched the strongman Lǐ Yànshēn to murder him,
He was thirty-eight years old at the time.
A monk collected and buried his remains.
When Jìngtáng entered Luò,
he wore mourning attire and wept at the grave,
and temporarily interred him with the rites of a Wáng (Prince).
Later, Tàizōng reburied him at Yīwūlǘ Shān,
giving him the posthumous title Wénwǔ Yuánhuáng Wáng.
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
he was posthumously titled Ràngguó Huángdì (Emperor Who Yielded the State),
and his mausoleum was named Xiǎnlíng.
During the Tǒnghé period,
the posthumous title was changed to Wénxiàn.
In the twentieth year of Chóngxī,
the posthumous title was augmented to Wénxiàn Qīnyì Huángdì,
and his temple name was Yìzōng.
The two Empresses were posthumously titled Duānshùn,
and Róuzhēn.
Bèi initially bought up to ten thousand scrolls of books,
storing them in the Wànghǎi Táng on the highest peak of Yīwūlǘ Shān.
He mastered Yīnyáng (cosmology/divination),
knew musical theory,
and excelled in the arts of medicine, acupuncture, and cauterization.
He was proficient in Liáo and Hàn writings,
and once translated the Yīnfú Jīng.
He was skilled at painting people from his native land,
such as *Shèqí*, *Lièxuěqí*, and *Qiānlùtú*,
all of which entered the imperial archive of Sòng.
However, his nature was severe, impulsive, and bloodthirsty;
if a maid or concubine made a minor error,
he often inflicted cuts or burns.
Xià Shì was frightened and requested to shave her head and become a nun.
He had five sons: the eldest was Shìzōng,
the others were Lóuguó, Shāo, Lóngxiān, and Dàoyǐn,
each having his own biography.
Píng Wáng Lóngxiān,
courtesy name Tuányǐn,
his mother was Dà Shì.
When Jǐngzōng ascended the throne,
he was first enfeoffed as Píng Wáng.
Not long thereafter,
he concurrently served as Zhèngshì Lìng,
and served as Garrison Commander of Dōngjīng.
He reduced levies and taxes,
reduced punishments and imprisonment,
showed compassion to the orphaned and the widowed,
and frequently recommended worthy and capable scholars.
Later, he achieved merit by campaigning against Gāolì alongside Tǒngjūn Yēlǜ Shìlǔ,
and died upon his return.
He was buried in Dàoyǐngǔ in Yīwūlǘ Shān.
Píng Wáng was an intelligent person,
widely learned, and capable of writing poetry;
his *Làngyuàn Jí* circulated throughout the world.
In the final years of the Bǎoníng period,
his son Chén Gē and Bóhǎi officials plotted to murder his father,
raised troops and created chaos.
The Emperor ordered him to be torn apart by chariots in the marketplace.
Jìn Wáng Dàoyǐn,
courtesy name Liúyǐn,
his mother was Gāo Shì.
Dàoyǐn was born during the Táng period,
when Rén Huáng Wáng suffered harm at the hands of Lǐ Cóngkē,
he was still young at the time,
and a monk in Luòyáng hid and raised him.
Hence he was named Dàoyǐn.
When Tàizōng destroyed Táng,
and returned to the capital,
an imperial decree granted him land at Wàiluó Shān for his residence.
His nature was quiet and calm,
possessing both civil and military talent,
and people of the time praised him.
When Jǐngzōng ascended the throne,
he was enfeoffed as Shǔ Wáng,
and served as Garrison Commander of Shàngjīng.
In the first year of Qiánhēng,
he was transferred to guard Nánjīng.
His decrees were severe and solemn,
and the people attained peaceful livelihoods.
After residing there for several years,
he was transferred and enfeoffed as Jīng Wáng.
In the beginning of the Tǒnghé period,
he died of illness.
He was posthumously enfeoffed as Jìn Wáng.
The commentary states: Since ancient times, among newly established states,
that a Crown Prince yields [the throne] in the first succession,
how could this be easily found?
Yìzōng of Liáo,
can be called truly magnificent!
Yet, having yielded and still being suspected,
was this not already foreshadowed at the time he established his era name and claimed imperial authority?
This was the fault of the ruler and ministers of that era who were ignorant of ritual systems.
Binding his books and crossing the sea,
lodging his presence in another country,
remembering his parents without forgetting them,
sending incessant inquiries about their health—
his heart had much that truly deserves to be understood.
Observing how he initially admired the virtue of Tàibó and made plans for distant relocation,
and finally loathed the wickedness of [Lǐ Cóng]kē and took the action of requesting a punitive expedition,
the eminence of his ambition and outlook,
was perhaps already revealed in his early years by his statement about first offering sacrifices to Kǒngzǐ.
That goodness does not lead to a good end,
the Way of Heaven is hard to question;
could it not have been caused by his harsh nature and craving for killing!
Nevertheless,
throughout the Liáo dynasty,
worthy and sagely rulers inherited the lineage,
all of whom were his descendants.
The reward for his paramount virtue,
is clearly manifested in this fact.
Zhāngsù Huángdì,
childhood name Lǐ Hú,
also named Hónggǔ,
courtesy name Xīyǐn,
was the third son of Tàizǔ,
his mother was Empress Chúnqīn Xiāo Shì.
As a youth, he was fierce, aggressive, and powerful,
but his nature was ruthless and cruel.
Upon slight provocation, he would immediately tattoo people's faces,
or throw them into water or fire.
Tàizǔ once observed his sons asleep.
Lǐ Hú slept inside, drawing his neck in;
[Tàizǔ] said:
"This one will surely rank below all his sons."
Also, during a great cold spell,
he ordered his three sons to gather firewood.
Tàizōng took whatever came to hand without selection,
and arrived the earliest;
Rén Huáng Wáng selected the dry pieces, bundled them, and returned,
arriving later;
Lǐ Hú took little and abandoned much,
and upon arriving,
he stood with his hands in his sleeves.
Tàizǔ said:
"The eldest is quick, and the second will achieve completion,
but the youngest is deficient."
But his mother dearly loved Lǐ Hú.
In the fifth year of *Tiānxiǎn*,
he was sent to patrol the territory of *Dàiběi*,
and attacked *Huánzhōu*.
He captured many prisoners and returned.
Consequently, he was established as Imperial Younger Brother,
also holding the title Grand Marshal of All Military Forces under Heaven.
When *Tàizōng* personally campaigned,
he habitually remained to guard the capital.
When *Shìzōng* ascended the throne at *Zhènyáng*,
the Empress Dowager was enraged.
She sent *Lǐ Hú* to lead troops to attack him.
Upon reaching *Tàidé Quán*,
they were defeated by *Ān Duān* and *Liú Gē*.
The Empress Dowager and *Shìzōng* arrayed their forces, separated by the *Huáng Hé*.
Each explained their reasons for raising arms.
*Yēlǜ Wūzhì* entered and remonstrated with the Empress Dowager, saying:
“The Lord above has already been established;
it is proper to permit this.”
At that time, *Lǐ Hú* was beside her.
He changed color and said:
“As long as I exist,
how can *Wùyù* be established?”
*Wūzhì* replied:
“What about your Lordship’s cruelty and tyranny, by which you have lost the hearts of the people!”
The Empress Dowager looked at *Lǐ Hú* and said:
“In the past, *Tàizǔ* and I loved you differently from our other sons.
The proverb says: ‘The overly cherished son does not secure the inheritance,
and the hard-won wife does not govern the household.’
It is not that I did not wish to establish you;
you are simply unable to do it yourself.”
When the conference was held,
*Shìzōng* commanded him to ungird his sword before speaking.
Once the peace agreement was settled,
he hastened to *Shàngjīng*.
Someone subsequently reported that *Lǐ Hú* and the Empress Dowager were plotting to depose the emperor and establish a replacement.
*Lǐ Hú* was banished to *Zǔzhōu*,
and his movements were restricted.
During the reign of *Mùzōng*,
his son *Xǐyǐn* plotted rebellion.
The testimony implicated *Lǐ Hú*.
He was incarcerated,
and died in prison
at the age of fifty.
He was buried in the western valley of *Yùfēng Shān*.
During the *Tǒnghé* period,
he was posthumously given the title Emperor *Qīnshùn*.
In the twenty-first year of *Chóngxī*,
the posthumous title was changed again to *Zhāngsù*,
and his Empress was titled *Héjìng*.
He had two sons: *Sòng* King *Xǐyǐn*, and *Wèi* King *Wǎn*.
*Xǐyǐn*,
courtesy name *Wándé*,
was heroic and adept at horsemanship and archery.
He was enfeoffed as the Prince of *Zhào*.
During the *Yìnglì* period,
he plotted rebellion.
When the affair was discovered,
the Emperor personally questioned him, finding the evidence conclusive.
He was released due to their kinship.
Not long after,
he rebelled again
and was imprisoned.
When *Jǐngzōng* ascended the throne,
hearing there was an amnesty,
he removed his own shackles and went to court.
The Emperor angrily said:
“You are a criminal.
How dare you leave your place of confinement without authorization.”
An imperial decree ordered the execution of the guards,
and he was returned to the prison.
When the era name was changed to *Bǎoníng*,
he was subsequently pardoned.
He married the Empress’s elder sister,
and his noble rank was restored.
He was created Prince of *Sòng*.
*Xǐyǐn* was frivolous, reckless, and lacked constancy.
The slightest success made him arrogant.
The Emperor once summoned him,
but he failed to arrive promptly.
In anger, the Emperor whipped him.
Due to this, he was filled with resentment and plotted rebellion.
He was demoted, but later summoned again.
He happened to see a letter from the Emperor addressed to *Liú Jìyuán*.
The tone and meaning were humble and deferential.
He remonstrated, saying:
“Our present court is the ancestor to the Hàn [Kingdoms].
If the content of the letter is like this,
I fear it will harm the dignity of the state.”
The Emperor immediately revised it.
He was appointed Commissioner of Recruitment and Pacification for the Southwest Front,
and commanded to retrieve *Tǔfān* households in *Hédōng*.
He was gradually promoted and given employment.
He again incited minor officials to plot treason.
The Emperor ordered that his hands and feet be chained,
and imprisoned him in a circular earthen structure (*Yuántǔ*) at *Zǔzhōu*.
More than two hundred surrendered *Sòng* soldiers wished to kidnap and establish *Xǐyǐn*.
Because the city defenses were strong, they could not enter.
Instead, they established his son *Liú Lǐshòu*.
*Chúshì*, the Commander of *Shàngjīng*, captured him.
*Liú Lǐshòu* was executed.
*Xǐyǐn* was granted death.
A commentary says: *Lǐ Hú* was cruel, violent, arrogant, and conceited.
*Tàizǔ* knew he lacked ability but failed to properly instruct him,
and the Empress Dowager did not recognize his wickedness and loved him excessively.
Initially, the establishment of *Shìzōng* was settled based on *Wūzhì*’s counsel,
yet she later again plotted deposition and establishment.
His descendants were successively executed for treason,
which also affected his own person.
How lamentable this is!
Indeed, since the age of *Tàizǔ*,
*Làgě* and *Ān Duān* first initiated calamity and rebellion.
*Tàizǔ*, far from executing them,
also employed them again.
This was indeed the measure of a true sovereign.
However, only *Tàizǔ*’s talent was sufficient to manage them,
making the situation barely tolerable.
From *Lǐ Hú* onward,
the imperial princes were restive,
and there was no generation without this occurrence.
The internal difficulties of *Liáo*,
accompanied the state from beginning to end.
The subsequent succeeding rulers,
though they tried to control them strictly by law,
ultimately could not stop it.
Alas!
The sovereign who founds the enterprise and establishes the lineage,
in the plans he leaves for his descendants,
must surely exercise great caution!
*Shùnzōng*,
given name *Jùn*,
nickname *Yēlǔwò*,
was the eldest son of *Dàozōng*.
His mother was Empress *Xuānyì*, of the *Xiāo* clan.
He spoke well even as a child,
loved learning, and understood literature.
*Dàozōng* once said:
“This child is wise and intelligent.
It must be a gift from Heaven!”
At six years old,
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of *Liáng*.
The following year,
he accompanied the Emperor hunting.
His arrows were shot consecutively, hitting three targets.
The Emperor looked at his attendants and said:
“Since the time of Our ancestors,
our horsemanship and archery have been unparalleled,
shaking the world.
Although this boy is young,
he does not fall short of that standard.”
Later, having encountered ten deer,
he shot and captured nine.
The Emperor was delighted
and held a banquet.
At eight years old,
he was established as the Crown Prince.
In the first year of *Dàkāng*,
he concurrently managed the affairs of the Northern and Southern Chancellery Bureaus.
When his mother, the Empress, was murdered,
the Crown Prince looked distressed.
*Yēlǜ Yǐxīn* was the Commissioner of the Northern Chancellery.
He was constantly ill at ease.
Coincidentally, the Imperial Guard *Xiāo Hūgǔ* plotted to murder *Yǐxīn*.
When the matter was discovered,
he was imprisoned.
The Deputy Inspector *Xiāo Shísān* said to *Yǐxīn*:
“The hearts of the officials and commoners belong to the Crown Prince.
Your Lordship is not of distinguished lineage.
If he were to be established one day,
where would we find a place for ourselves!”
Therefore, he plotted with *Xiāo Tèdádá*, Co-Manager of the Bureau of Northern Affairs, to frame the Crown Prince.
He secretly instructed *Yēlǜ Zhālà*, Grand Guardian of the Right Imperial Guard,
to falsely accuse Palace Commissioner *Yēlǜ Sālā*, Administrator *Xiāo Sùsā*,
and Imperial Guard *Xiāo Hūgǔ* of plotting deposition and establishment.
An edict was issued for investigation, but no evidence was found.
No prosecution was carried out.
Yǐxīn (乙辛) again commanded Lìngpái Yìn Lángjūn (令牌印郎君) Xiāo Éduō (蕭訛都斡) and others, who said:
"Zhālà's (查剌) previous accusation was not baseless.
Your servant truly participated in the plot,
wishing to kill Yēlǜ Yǐxīn (耶律乙辛) and others,
and then enthrone the Heir Apparent.
If your servant had not spoken,
I feared that once the matter was revealed, I would be implicated."
The Emperor believed them.
He confined the Heir Apparent in a separate chamber,
and ordered Yēlǜ Yàngē (耶律燕哥) to conduct the investigation.
The Heir Apparent fully detailed the injustice, saying:
"As the designated heir,
what more could I possibly seek?
You, sir, should discern the truth for me."
Yàngē (燕哥) was a partisan of Yǐxīn (乙辛),
and changed his statement into an admission of guilt.
The Sovereign was greatly angered,
and deposed the Heir Apparent, reducing him to a commoner.
As he was about to leave,
he said:
"What crime have I committed to deserve this!"
Shísān (十三) shouted at him to board the carriage,
and dispatched guards to seal the door.
He was moved to Shàngjīng (上京),
and imprisoned within circular walls.
Yǐxīn (乙辛) soon sent Dálǔgǔ (達魯古) and Sābā (撒八) to murder him.
The Heir Apparent was just twenty years old.
Xiāo Tǎdé (蕭撻得), the Resident General of Shàngjīng (上京), falsely reported that he had died of illness.
The Sovereign mourned him,
and ordered the appropriate authorities to bury him at Lóngmén Shān (龍門山).
When the Emperor wished to summon his consort,
Yǐxīn (乙辛) secretly sent men to kill her.
Later, the Emperor realized the injustice,
but his remorse came too late.
He bestowed the posthumous title Zhāohuái Tàizǐ (昭懷太子),
and reburied him with the rites of an emperor at Yùfēng Shān (玉峯山).
Early in the Qiántǒng (乾統) era,
he was posthumously honored as Dàxiàoshùn Shèng Huángdì (大孝順聖皇帝).
His temple name was Shùnzōng (順宗),
and his consort, Consort Xiāo (蕭氏), was titled Zhēnshùn Huánghòu (貞順皇后).
He had one son,
Yánxǐ (延禧),
who became Emperor Tiānzuò (天祚皇帝).
Commentary states: Although Dàozōng (道宗) knew of the Heir Apparent's worthiness,
he was unable to discern Yǐxīn’s (乙辛) deceit,
ultimately severing the bond between father and son.
This is regrettable for ten thousand generations.
Yǐxīn (乙辛) knew only how to scheme for his own self-interest,
ignorant of the principle of loyalty between ruler and minister.
How could he possibly acknowledge the existence of the Heir Apparent?
Treacherous and wicked ministers cause disruption to family and state in this manner.
Should one not take warning!
Should one not take warning!
The Prince of Jìn (晉王),
given the infant name Áolúwò (敖盧斡),
was the eldest son of Emperor Tiānzuò (天祚皇帝).
His mother was Consort Wén (文妃) Xiāo Shì (蕭氏).
While still a youth,
he rode horses and excelled at archery.
He was adopted as a son by the Grand Chancellor Yēlǜ Lóngyùn (耶律隆運),
and was enfeoffed as the Prince of Jìn (晉王).
By nature, he enjoyed speaking of people's virtues,
but was condescending toward those who were incapable.
At that time, anyone seen reading books in the palace was immediately rejected.
Áolúwò (敖盧斡) once entered the sleeping quarters,
and saw the attendant Xiǎodǐ Chálà (小底茶剌) reading a book.
He took it to look at it.
Just then, the various princes arrived.
He secretly hid it in his sleeve and returned it,
saying:
"Don't let anyone else see it."
He was universally called a gentleman.
When he grew up,
he accumulated great popularity,
and people inside and outside the court were devoted to him.
In the first year of Bǎodà (保大) (1121 CE),
the Southern Military Governor Yēlǜ Yúdǔ (耶律余覩) secretly plotted with his mother, Consort Wén (文妃), to enthrone him.
When the plot was discovered,
Yúdǔ (余覩) surrendered to the Jīn (金) Dynasty.
Consort Wén (文妃) was executed.
Áolúwò (敖盧斡) had actually not been involved in the plot,
and was spared.
In the second year (1122 CE),
Yēlǜ Sābā (耶律撒八) and others again plotted to enthrone him,
but failed.
The Sovereign knew that Áolúwò (敖盧斡) had won the hearts of the people,
and could not bear to execute him personally.
He ordered him to be strangled to death.
Someone advised him to flee,
but Áolúwò (敖盧斡) said:
"How can I, for the sake of this puny body,
lose the great principle of loyalty owed by a minister and son?"
He then accepted death.
Those who heard of it were saddened.
Commentary states: Tiānzuò (天祚) failed as a sovereign,
and when his subordinates plotted to enthrone his son,
it merely led to the son's death.
Áolúwò (敖盧斡) valued the command of his sovereign and father,
and died without fleeing.
He was indeed as dutiful as Shēnshēng (申生)!
Biographies, Number Three: Yēlǜ Gělǔ (耶律曷魯), Xiāo Dílǔ (蕭敵魯) (Āgǔzhǐ - 阿古只), Yēlǜ Xié Nièchì (耶律斜涅赤) (Lǎogǔ - 老古, Pōdé - 頗德), Yēlǜ Yùwěn (耶律欲穩), Yēlǜ Hǎilǐ (耶律海里).
Yēlǜ Gělǔ (耶律曷魯),
courtesy name Kòngwēn (控溫),
also named Hóngyǐn (洪隱),
was a man of the Diélà (迭剌) tribe.
His grandfather, Xiámǎgě (匣馬葛),
was the elder brother of Emperor Jiǎnxiàn (簡憲皇帝).
His father, Ǒusī (偶思),
served as the Yílíjǐn (夷離菫) of his tribe during the Yáoliǎn (遙輦) period.
Gělǔ (曷魯) was his eldest son.
His character was honest and generous.
While still a youth,
he associated with Tàizǔ (太祖).
His paternal uncle Shìlǔ (釋魯) considered them extraordinary and said:
"Those who will bring prosperity to our family
must be these two lads."
When Tàizǔ (太祖) grew up,
they exchanged furs and horses as tokens of friendship,
but Gělǔ (曷魯) served Tàizǔ (太祖) with even greater respect.
When Huágē (滑哥) assassinated his father Shìlǔ (釋魯),
Tàizǔ (太祖) turned to Gělǔ (曷魯) and said:
"Huágē (滑哥) murdered his father.
He expects that I surely cannot tolerate this,
and he will soon turn to attack me.
Now he blames Táixǐn (臺哂) as an excuse.
I will temporarily indulge him.
But I will not forget this villain!"
From then on,
Gělǔ (曷魯) constantly carried a sword and followed Tàizǔ (太祖),
in preparation for unforeseen events.
After a long time,
Gělǔ's (曷魯) father, Ǒusī (偶思), fell ill.
He summoned Gělǔ (曷魯) and said:
"Ābǎojī's (阿保機) genius and strategy are Heaven-sent.
You must lead your younger brothers in serving him wholeheartedly."
Soon after, Tàizǔ (太祖) came to inquire about his illness.
Ǒusī (偶思) held his hand and said:
"You are a singular talent destined for greatness.
My son Gělǔ (曷魯),
may be entrusted with great responsibilities in the future,
and I have already instructed him."
Following this, he entrusted all his sons to Tàizǔ (太祖).
When Tàizǔ (太祖) was Tàmǎyuè Shālǐ (撻馬狘沙里),
and involved in tribal affairs,
Gělǔ (曷魯) led several cavalrymen and summoned the Xiǎohuáng Shìwéi (小黃室韋) to submit.
Tàizǔ (太祖) had long harbored great ambitions,
and knowing Gělǔ (曷魯) was worthy,
no military or state affair was carried out without Gělǔ's (曷魯) counsel.
During the campaign against the Yuèwù (越兀) and Wūgǔ (烏古) tribes,
Gělǔ (曷魯) served as the vanguard
and achieved merit in battle.
When Tàizǔ (太祖) became the Yílíjǐn (夷離菫) of the Diélà (迭剌) tribe,
he attacked the Xī (奚) tribe.
Their leader, Zhúlǐ (朮里), fortified himself in a dangerous position.
The attack could not succeed in taking the position.
Tàizǔ (太祖) ordered Gělǔ (曷魯) to take a single arrow shaft (as a symbol) and go persuade them.
After entering,
he was seized by them.
He then addressed the Xī (奚) people, saying:
"The Qìdān (契丹) and Xī (奚) share a common language,
and are essentially one nation.
How could our Yílíjǐn (夷離菫) have any intention of bullying the Xī (奚)?
The Hàn (漢) people killed our ancestor, the Xīshǒu (奚首).
The Yílíjǐn (夷離菫) harbors deep, bone-piercing resentment,
and thinks day and night about avenging himself upon the Hàn (漢) people.
However, his strength is slight and weak,
so he sent me to seek aid from the Xī (奚),
sending the arrow to show sincerity.
The Yílíjǐn (夷離菫) has received the mandate of Heaven,
and governs his subordinates through virtue.
That is why he is able to command this host.
Now, if the Xī (奚) kill me,
they will be defying Heaven and betraying virtue;
there is no greater misfortune.
Furthermore, a chain of conflict and disaster
will begin right here.
How can this benefit your state!"
Zhúlǐ (朮里) was moved by his words,
and surrendered.
When Tàizǔ (太祖) became Yúyuè (于越)
and held the reins of state power,
he wished to appoint Gělǔ (曷魯) as the Yílíjǐn (夷離菫) of the Diélà (迭剌) tribe.
Gělǔ (曷魯) declined, saying:
"Since the villain is near Your Lordship,
I dare not leave for a distant post."
Tàizǔ (太祖) campaigned against the Hēichēzǐ Shìwéi (黑車子室韋).
Liú Rén'gōng (劉仁恭) of Yōuzhōu (幽州) sent his adopted son Zhào Bà (趙霸) to lead troops to their rescue.
Gělǔ (曷魯) concealed troops at Táo Shān (桃山),
waited until more than half of Bà's (霸) forces had passed, and then intercepted them.
They combined forces with Tàizǔ (太祖) in an attack,
achieving a great number of kills and captures,
subsequently forcing the Shìwéi (室韋) to surrender.
Tàizǔ (太祖) met with Lǐ Kèyòng (李克用) at Yúnzhōu (雲州).
At that time, Gělǔ (曷魯) was in attendance.
Kèyòng (克用) looked at him, impressed, and said:
"Who is that magnificent man?"
Tàizǔ (太祖) replied:
"He is Gělǔ (曷魯) of my clan."
died.
The assembled officials, honoring the dying command, requested the elevation of Tàizǔ.
Tàizǔ declined, saying:
“Formerly, my ancestor Yílíjǐn Yǎlǐ once refused the throne, judging that he ought not to be established.
Now you all repeat this suggestion.
Why is this?”
Hélǔ stepped forward and said:
“The refusal of your ancestor in the past
did not involve a dying command,
nor had auspicious signs yet appeared;
he was merely supported and championed by the people of the state.
Now, the words of the former sovereign are still fresh in our ears,
granted by Heaven and man,
as if matching a tally.
Heaven cannot be disobeyed,
man cannot be resisted,
and the sovereign’s command must not be disregarded.”
Tàizǔ said:
“The dying command is indeed so,
but how do you know the Way of Heaven (Tiāndào)?”
Hélǔ said:
“I heard that when Yúyuè was born,
divine light reached the sky,
an unusual fragrance filled the tent,
he received divine instruction in a dream,
and a dragon bestowed a golden pendant.
The Way of Heaven (Tiāndào) is impartial;
it must respond to virtue.
Our state has been weakened,
oppressed and nibbled at by neighboring tribes for a long time.
Therefore, a sage was born to raise it up.
The Kèhán knew the intent of Heaven (Tiānyì),
hence this command.
Moreover, among the nine camps of Yáo Niǎn,
it is not that there is no one who could be established;
yet the minor officials, great ministers, and the common people all incline their hearts toward Yúyuè.
This is Heaven.
Formerly, Yúyuè’s paternal uncle, Shìlǔ, once said: ‘I am merely a snake,
but my son is a dragon.’
The opportune time from Heaven (Tiānshí) and the affairs of man
— this chance must not be lost.”
Tàizǔ still did not consent.
That night,
he privately summoned Hélǔ and reproached him, saying:
“The multitude pressure me using the dying command.
Do you not understand my heart,
that you also bow down and follow them?”
Hélǔ said:
“In the past, although Yílíjǐn Yǎlǐ had many supporters,
he declined,
and Zǔwǔ was established as Kèhán.
After this succession of more than ten generations,
the demarcation between sovereign and minister became confused,
and the framework of governance collapsed.
We offered submission to other states,
like streamers being hung up.
Urgent military dispatches flew back and forth,
and the people were exhausted rushing about on missions.
The destiny for establishing a royal lineage
truly lies in this day.
Responding to Heaven and according with man,
in order to fulfill the dying commission,
must not be missed.”
Tàizǔ then consented.
The next day,
he ascended the Imperial throne,
and commanded Hélǔ to oversee all military and state affairs.
At that time, the institutional regulations were not yet established,
state resources were insufficient,
and the imperial entourage was incomplete;
and his younger brothers, such as Làgě, frequently harbored illicit ambitions.
Tàizǔ established the Fùxīnbù (Trusted Core Division) in the imperial mobile camp,
selecting more than two thousand powerful and robust men from various tribes to fill it,
with Hélǔ and Xiāo Dílǔ commanding them.
Subsequently, the rebellion of his younger brothers erupted.
Tàizǔ ordered Hélǔ to take supreme command of military affairs,
and he suppressed it.
For this merit, he was made Yílíjǐn of the Diélà Bù.
At that time, the people, having suffered war, burning, and plunder,
were daily worn out and exhausted.
Hélǔ had effective methods for pacification and consolidation,
livestock increased,
and the people became rich and prosperous.
He then attacked the Wūgǔ Bù
and defeated them.
From then on, they were terrified
and dared not rebel again.
He then requested the establishment of court ceremonies and the declaration of a reign title (Jiànyuán),
and led the multitude of officials in presenting the honorific title (Zūn Hào).
After Tàizǔ had prepared the rites and received the patent,
he appointed Hélǔ as Ālǔdūn Yúyuè.
“Ālǔdūn”
is
Liao language for “great reputation.”
Later, when Tàizǔ campaigned against the various southwestern non-Han tribes (Zhū Yí),
Hélǔ often served as the vanguard.
In Shéncè Second Year (917),
he followed Tàizǔ in pressing Yōuzhōu,
and fought a defensive battle against Zhōu Déwēi, the Táng Jǐedùshǐ, west of Kèhánzhōu.
They defeated his army
and subsequently besieged Yōuzhōu,
but did not capture it.
Tàizǔ, citing the summer heat, ordered the army to return,
leaving Hélǔ and Lú Guóyòng to guard the siege.
Soon after, relief troops arrived successively.
Hélǔ and others, due to their limited forces and lack of support,
withdrew.
In the third year, in the seventh month,
after the Imperial Capital (Huángdū) was completed,
a banquet was held for the assembled officials to celebrate its inauguration.
On that very day, Hélǔ fell ill and died,
at the age of forty-seven.
After the burial,
his burial path was granted the name Yàndá,
the mountain was named Yúyuè Yù,
and an imperial edict commanded the erection of a stele to record his merits.
During the Qīngníng period (1055–1064),
an order was given to establish a shrine for him in Shàngjīng.
Previously,
when Hélǔ was critically ill,
Tàizǔ personally visited him
and asked what he wished to say.
Hélǔ replied:
“Your Majesty's sagely virtue is generous and benevolent;
all creatures are prosperous,
and the imperial enterprise is flourishing.
Since your servant has received such gracious favor,
I have no regrets, even upon closing my eyes.
Only the proposal to divide the Diélà Bù remains undecided.
I wish it to be carried out quickly.”
When he died,
Tàizǔ wept and said:
“If this man had lived for three or five more years,
there is nothing I planned that would not have succeeded!”
Later, among the twenty-one meritorious officials of Tàizǔ,
each was assigned a representative body part;
Hélǔ was referred to as the heart.
His sons, Tìlà and Sālā,
neither held office.
The Commentary says: Hélǔ, relying on his close familial ties,
was entrusted with the responsibilities of the strategizing tent.
His words were like milfoil and tortoise shell (prophetic),
his strategies succeeded, and he won battles.
It can be said that his calculations never failed to produce a strategy.
The sincerity of the mutual affinity between this sovereign and minister
was perhaps like that of Wú Hàn toward Guāngwǔ.
Indeed, to trust whom one ought to trust
is wisdom,
and Tàizǔ possessed it.
Thus it is said,
only the sage knows the sage,
only the worthy knows the worthy;
this is close to that truth.
Xiāo Dílǔ,
courtesy name Dínliǎn.
His mother was Dézǔ’s younger sister,
and Empress Chúnqīn was his elder sister.
His fifth generation ancestor was Húmǔlǐ.
During the time of the Yáo Niǎn Shì, he was once sent as an envoy to Táng,
and Táng detained him in Yōuzhōu.
One night,
he broke the gate and fled back to his state.
Because of this, his family for generations served as judicial officers.
Dílǔ was generous and tolerant by nature,
his physical strength surpassed others,
and he was skilled in military affairs.
When Tàizǔ was a regional lord,
Dílǔ served him daily,
and whenever there was a punitive expedition, Dílǔ was always involved in the lines of battle.
After Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
Dílǔ, together with his younger brother Āgǔzhǐ, Yēlǜ Shìlǔ, and Yēlǜ Hélǔ, jointly commanded the imperial guard.
Dílǔ was appointed Northern Prime Minister (Běi Fǔ Zǎixiàng),
and the position was made hereditary.
When Tàizǔ campaigned against the Xī and attacked Liú Shǒuguāng,
Dílǔ seized territory along the coast,
slaying and capturing many people.
After a short time,
Làgě and others launched a rebellion;
they were routed and fled north.
Dílǔ led light cavalry in pursuit,
traveling both day and night.
When they reached the Yúhé River,
he defeated Làgě's faction,
captured Làgě, and presented him.
Tàizǔ praised him
and bestowed extremely generous gifts.
Later, in the campaign against the southwestern non-Han tribes (Xīnán Yí),
his merits ranked foremost among the various generals.
He died in the twelfth month of Shéncè Third Year (918).
Dílǔ possessed courage and strategy.
Upon hearing where the enemy was, he immediately rushed there,
personally enduring arrows and stones.
In battles, he never suffered the slightest setback,
stopping only when victory was secured.
Therefore, in the list of Tàizǔ’s meritorious officials,
he was symbolized by the hand.
His younger brother was Āgǔzhǐ.
Āgǔzhǐ,
courtesy name Sābĕn.
He was outstanding in his youth,
acting freely and without restraint.
When he grew up, he was fierce and brave, skilled in archery,
and dared to advance against the enemy.
Every time he shot at armor or shields, he would pierce them completely.
When Tàizǔ (Emperor Tàizǔ) was Yúyuè (a tribal chief title),
he used him for service because of his talent and bravery.
After Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
he was placed with Dírǔ and Zŏng as a trusted member of the inner circle.
During Lāgĕ’s rebellion,
Empress Chúnqīn’s army was at Hēishān (Black Mountain),
securing themselves by relying on the dangerous terrain.
As Tàizǔ was planning campaigns in the Xī territory,
he ordered Āgǔzhǐ to command one hundred cavalry to go and guard her.
The rebel leaders Diélĭtè and Yēlǜ Huágē had long feared his bravery and strategy,
and warned each other, saying:
“He is not to be challenged!”
When Lāgĕ fled north,
Āgǔzhǐ and Dírǔ pursued and captured him at Yúhé (Elm River).
In the first year of Shéncè (916 CE),
he had merit in suppressing the Southwestern Yí;
he campaigned through the various commanderies and counties west of the mountains,
and also conquered them,
defeating Zhōu Déwēi’s army.
In the third year,
for his merit, he was appointed Prime Minister (Zăixiàng) of the Northern Prefecture,
making the position hereditary.
In the beginning of Tiānzàn (922 CE),
he collaborated with Wáng Yù to seize territory in Yān and Zhào,
and crushed Cíyáo Zhèn (Cíyáo Garrison).
When Tàizǔ marched west,
he entrusted all matters concerning the southern border to him.
He attacked Bóhăi,
and broke Fúyú Chéng (Fúyú City).
Leading five hundred cavalry alone,
he defeated an army of thirty thousand led by Lăo Xiàng (the Old Minister).
After Bóhăi was pacified,
it was renamed the state of Dōngdān.
Soon after,
the commanderies and counties that had surrendered rebelled again,
and bandits rose up like swarms of bees.
Āgǔzhǐ and Kāng Mòjì suppressed them,
and wherever they went, the enemy collapsed.
It happened that seven thousand enemy light cavalry came from Yālù Fŭ to reinforce the rebels,
and their strength greatly increased.
Āgǔzhǐ led the elite troops under his command
and charged straight into their vanguard.
He defeated them in a single battle,
beheading or capturing more than three thousand,
and subsequently advanced to break Huíbá Chéng (Huíbá City).
He died from illness.
Among the meritorious ministers, Āgǔzhǐ was likened to an ear (a vital organ).
His son, Āntuán,
reached the office of Right Píshì Xiángwĕn.
Yēlǜ Xiéinièchì,
courtesy name Sālà,
was from the clan of Shèlì Niăogŭzhí of the Six Yüan (Liù Yuàn) Division.
His initial courtesy name was Duówăn.
He was early attached to Tàizǔ’s headquarters.
Once, when he was ill,
Tàizǔ granted him a jar of wine to drink, and he recovered.
The Khitan word for wine jar is
“Sālà,”
so Tàizǔ ordered his courtesy name to be changed to that.
When Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
he was placed in charge of the Inner Circle Division (Fùxīn Bù).
In the beginning of Tiānzàn,
the Diélà Division was separated into the Northern and Southern Yuàn (Yards/Courts),
and Xiéinièchì became the Yílíjĭn of the Northern Yuàn.
When the Emperor marched west and reached Liúshā (Moving Sands),
his prestige greatly shook the region,
and the various barbarian tribes scattered.
Tàizǔ then ordered Xiéinièchì to console and gather them.
When Bóhăi was suppressed,
and Fúyú Chéng was broken,
Xiéinièchì followed the Crown Prince Grand Marshal (Dàyuánshuài) and led troops to besiege Hūhàn Chéng by night,
and Dà Yīnxuăn surrendered.
Later, when Dà Yīnxuăn rebelled again,
the generals were ordered to attack the various territories.
The next morning,
Xiéinièchì encouraged and motivated his soldiers,
beating drums and shouting to ascend the ramparts.
The enemy was struck with terror
and dared not resist,
so the city was captured.
He died during the Tiānxiăn era (926–938 CE),
at the age of seventy,
and was one of the meritorious ministers who assisted in the founding of the state.
His nephews were Lăogŭ and Pŏdé.
Lăogŭ,
courtesy name Sălăn,
was the son of Empress Chúnqīn’s elder sister.
Lăogŭ was raised in the palace quarters during his youth.
When he grew up,
he was profound, resolute, and possessed bravery and strategy,
serving under Tàizǔ’s banner.
After Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
he frequently achieved military success.
During Lāgĕ’s rebellion,
Lāgĕ intended to use the chance when we were unprepared to launch a surprise attack,
and pretended to surrender.
Tàizǔ was about to accept the surrender,
but ordered Lăogŭ and Yēlǜ Yùwĕn to enforce strict discipline,
restrain the soldiers,
and hold the reins to prevent any sudden change.
The rebel party realized that precautions had been taken,
became afraid, and fled.
For his merit, Lăogŭ was granted the position of Right Píshì Xiángwĕn,
managing the Imperial Guard.
When Tàizǔ invaded Yān and Zhào,
he encountered the Táng army at Yúnbì Diàn.
Lăogŭ, relying on his bravery, underestimated the enemy
and charged straight into their vanguard.
After a long battle,
he suffered several wounds
and died upon returning to the camp.
Tàizǔ grieved deeply and cherished him.
He was another of the meritorious ministers who assisted in the founding of the state.
Pŏdé,
courtesy name Wùgŭlín.
He served Tàizǔ when he was only twenty.
In the beginning of Tiānxiăn,
he served as Left Píshì Xiángwĕn,
managing the Imperial Guard,
and was promoted to Southern Yuàn Yílíjĭn.
His administration earned him a good reputation.
When Shí Jìngtáng defeated Zhāng Jìngdá’s army north of Tàiyuán,
Pŏdé commanded troops as reinforcement at that time,
but Jìngdá had already fled.
Jìngtáng pursued him to Jìn’ān Zhài and besieged it.
Pŏdé led light cavalry to raid Lùzhōu,
cutting off the enemy’s supply route.
The various Táng generals were terrified
and killed Jìngdá, offering surrender.
In the beginning of Huìtóng (938 CE),
the title of Yílíjĭn of the Diélà Division was changed to Great King (Dàwáng),
and Pŏdé was immediately appointed to it,
and later given the added position of Inspector (Căifăng Shĭ).
According to the old system,
the Imperial Clan members below Sùzŭ were called Yuàn;
the Imperial Clan members of Dézŭ were called Sān Fù Fáng (Three Fathers’ Houses),
and were referred to as Héngzhàng (Horizontal Tent);
while the sons and younger brothers of officials and those who were registered as captives were called Zhùzhàng (Attached Tent).
Yēlǜ Xiédì said
that the ranking order of the Héngzhàng
should not be equated with the Northern and Southern Yuàn.
Tàizōng ordered the court officials to deliberate,
and they all agreed.
Consequently, an edict decreed that the Héngzhàng should be ranked highest.
Pŏdé memorialized, saying:
“I have respectfully observed the official system,
where the Great Kings of the Northern and Southern Yuàn rank above the Tìyĭn.
Now the Héngzhàng initially sought the high rank,
and desired to serve concurrently with the Northern and Southern Yuàn;
but now they are ashamed to be ranked equally.
The Héngzhàng, like all other tribes, are subjects;
how should their ranking be different?”
The Emperor then instructed the officials, saying:
“If I do not know something,
you should not just agree face to face.”
He decreed a return to the old system.
His strength and integrity in not compromising were like this.
Pŏdé’s appearance was outstanding and imposing.
When Tàizǔ first saw him, he said:
“The spiritual quality and bone structure of this son are extraordinary;
he will surely become a vessel for the state.”
Later events proved this to be true.
He died at the age of forty-nine.
Yēlǜ Yùwĕn,
courtesy name Xiálàgān,
was a native of the Tūlǚbù Division.
His grandfather, Tái Yā,
was the Northern Border Zhuàilá during the Yáoliĕn period.
When Empress Jiănxiàn and her sons encountered misfortune,
she relied on him for protection and thus escaped.
Tàizǔ, mindful of his merit and never forgetting it,
and also appreciating Yùwĕn’s gravity and seriousness,
and his ambition to save the world,
ordered him to take charge of the nearby divisions
to deter any thoughts of encroachment from other tribes.
Since Yùwĕn saw that he was highly regarded,
he was further motivated to repay the kindness.
When Tàizǔ first established the Palace Division (Gōng Fèn) for self-defense,
Yùwĕn led his retainers to be the first to enroll in the palace register.
The Emperor increasingly praised his loyalty
and decreed that Tái Yā should be enshrined and sacrificed to in the ancestral temple.
After suppressing the rebellion of Lāgĕ and others,
he was promoted, for his merit, to Yílíjĭn of the Xī Diélà Division.
He had merit in following the campaign against Bóhăi.
He died in the beginning of the Tiānxiăn era.
Later emperors, due to Tàizǔ's desire for stability,
often took his descendants as allies.
In the palace divisions, they were called
the "Eight Families" (Bā Fáng),
all being his lineage.
His younger brother, Xiálǐ,
ultimately served as the Tūlǐ of the six Xī divisions.
Yēlǜ Hǎilǐ,
courtesy name Nièlākūn,
was a descendant of Yáoliǎn Zhāogǔ Kèhán.
When Tàizǔ passed on the throne,
Hǎilǐ was highly instrumental.
When the mandate was first received,
his lineage relatives harbored ambitions,
and the former clans of Yáoliǎn were particularly discontented.
Hǎilǐ had the foresight of the late emperor regarding knowing men,
and he had always submitted to the prestige and virtue of Tàizǔ,
offering his sole allegiance to him.
Therefore, Tàizǔ relied on him as his eyes and ears,
and he frequently followed Tàizǔ on campaigns.
After the internal disturbances were quelled,
the post of Yáoliǎn Chǎngwěn was established,
and Hǎilǐ was ordered to hold the office.
At the beginning of Tiānxiǎn era,
during the campaign against Bóhǎi,
Hǎilǐ led the Yáoliǎn Jiū,
and defeated Hūhàn Chéng.
When the army returned,
he died.
Biographies, Chapter Four: Yēlǜ Dílà, Xiāo Héndǔ, Kāng Mòjì (Yánshòu), Hán Yánhuī (Déshū, Shàoxūn, Shàofāng, Zīràng), Hán Zhīgǔ (Kuāngsì, Déyuán, Déníng).
Yēlǜ Dílà,
courtesy name Hélǔyǐn,
was the son of Yáoliǎn Xiānzhì Kèhán.
When Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
he assisted in governance whole-heartedly, along with Chǎngwěn Hǎilǐ.
Tàizǔ, knowing his loyalty and trustworthiness,
ordered him to manage rites and ceremonies,
and also entrusted him with military affairs.
Later, based on his merit in quelling internal disturbances,
he replaced Xiálǐ as the Tǔlǐ of the six Xī divisions,
and died thereafter.
Dílà was skilled in riding and archery,
and rather fond of ritual and literature.
Xiāo Héndǔ,
courtesy name Wūlǐzhěn,
was a man of the Diélà Tribe.
His ancestors had served as chancellors to the Yáoliǎn clan.
Héndǔ was spirited in his youth,
and took responsibility based on his ability and talent.
Early on, he was attached to Tàizǔ's headquarters,
and frequently followed him on campaigns.
After Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
he was appointed Prime Minister of the Northern Administration (Běi Fǔ Zǎixiàng).
Héndǔ was filially pious toward his parents,
and valued leniency and simplicity in governance.
Kāng Mòjì,
original name Zhào.
In his youth, he was a subordinate official (yáxiào) in Jìzhōu.
When Tàizǔ invaded Jìzhōu and captured him,
Tàizǔ admired his talent
and attached him to his command.
All matters concerning both Fān (barbarians) and Hàn (Chinese)
were settled by Mòjì through compromise,
and they all accorded with the Emperor's wishes.
At that time, various tribes had newly submitted,
and the legal system was incomplete.
Mòjì analyzed and inferred the intent of the laws,
determining the severity or lightness of judgments,
without the slightest error.
Those who incurred legal penalties
all felt that they had not been wronged.
Shortly thereafter,
he was appointed Minister of the Left (Zuǒ Shàngshū).
In the third year of Shéncè,
when the capital city was first established,
Mòjì oversaw the project,
and everyone willingly participated;
the work was completed in one hundred days.
In the fifth year,
he became the Yílíbì of the Imperial Capital.
When Tàizǔ led an army out through Jūyōng Guān,
he ordered Mòjì to lead the Hàn troops and advance upon the water fortresses at Chánglú,
taking many captives and heads.
In the fourth year of Tiānzàn,
when Tàizǔ personally campaigned against Bóhǎi,
Mòjì followed along with Hán Zhīgǔ.
Later, Dà Yīn Xuàn rebelled,
and the generals were ordered to attack him.
Mòjì was assigned to attack the eastern gate
and led the brave and fierce men in the initial ascent.
After the city was taken,
he captured Chánglǐng Fǔ along with Hán Yánhuī.
When the army returned,
many of the recently subdued cities and towns rebelled.
Mòjì pacified them along with Āgǔzhī.
After defeating Huíbá Chéng,
and upon returning to the camp after the completion of Tàizǔ's imperial mausoleum,
he died.
He was one of the meritorious officials who aided in the foundation of the state.
His grandson, Yánshòu,
courtesy name Yìnchāng,
was unconventional in his youth.
He said to his intimates:
"A true man serving as a general
ought to dedicate himself to the frontier,
his corpse wrapped in horse hide."
Jǐngzōng specially appointed him Grand General of the Qiānniú Guard.
When the Sòng people attacked Nánjīng,
after the various generals had formed ranks,
Yánshòu alone fought fiercely at the front of the formation,
and the enemy consequently suffered a great defeat.
For his merit, he was granted the position of Military Commissioner of the Bǎodà Army (Bǎodà Jūn Jiédùshǐ) from afar.
He died in the third year of Qiánhēng.
Hán Yánhuī,
courtesy name Cángmíng,
was a native of Āncì, Yōuzhōu.
His father, Mèngyīn,
successively held the post of Regional Inspector (Cìshǐ) for the three prefectures of Jì, Rú, and Shùn.
Yánhuī was distinguished in his youth.
Liú Réngōng, the commander of Yān, thought highly of him,
summoning him to serve as Literary Scholar (Wénxué) of Yōudū Fǔ and Registrar and Military Advisor (Lùshì Cānjūn) of Píngzhōu.
He served in the Zhīhòu Yuàn alongside Féng Dào,
and was appointed Surveillance Commissioner for Finance (Guānchá Dùzhīshǐ) of Yōuzhōu.
Later, when Shǒuguāng became commander,
Yánhuī came on a mission.
Tàizǔ was angered by his refusal to yield
and detained him.
Empress Shùlǜ admonished, saying:
"He holds fast to integrity and does not bend;
he is a worthy man.
Why must he be distressed and humiliated?"
Tàizǔ summoned him for a discussion,
finding his opinions agreeable,
and immediately ordered him to serve as Military Advisor (Cānjūnshì).
In attacking the Dǎngxiàng and the Shìwēi,
and subjugating the various tribes,
Yánhuī's planning contributed greatly.
He then requested the establishment of walled cities,
dividing them into markets and residential areas,
to settle the surrendered Hàn people.
He also arranged marriages for them
and taught them cultivation methods,
thus ensuring their livelihood and growth.
Because of this, few people ran away.
After residing there for a long time,
he felt a deep longing for his hometown,
expressed his sentiments through poetry,
and consequently fled back to Táng.
Soon thereafter, having a conflict with another general, Wáng Jiān,
and fearing ensuing trouble,
he visited his parents in Yōuzhōu
and hid in the dwelling of his old acquaintance, Wáng Démíng.
Démíng asked where he intended to go.
Yánhuī replied:
"I intend to run back to Qìdān."
Démíng disapproved of this idea.
Yánhuī laughed and said:
"Their loss of me
is like losing their left and right hands;
when they see me, they will surely be delighted."
Upon arrival,
Tàizǔ asked the reason for his return.
Yánhuī replied:
"To forget one's parents is not filial piety;
to abandon one's sovereign is not loyalty.
Although I risked my life to flee,
my heart remained with Your Majesty.
It is for this reason that I have returned."
The Emperor was greatly pleased,
and bestowed upon him the name Xiáliè.
"Xiáliè"
means "returned" in the Liáo language.
He was immediately appointed Acting Director of Political Affairs (Shǒu Zhèngshì Lìng) and Grand Academician of the Chóngwén Palace (Chóngwén Guǎn Dà Xuéshì),
and was authorized to participate in and decide all internal and external matters.
In the fourth year of Tiānzàn,
