he followed Tàizǔ in the campaign against Bóhǎi,
and Dà Yīn Xuàn requested surrender.
Afterwards, Dà Yīn Xuàn rebelled again.
He and the other generals defeated the city,
and for this merit, he was appointed Minister of the Left (Zuǒ Púyè).
He also attacked Chánglǐng Fǔ with Kāng Mòjì
and captured it.
When the army returned,
Tàizǔ died,
and grief affected all those around him.
During the reign of Tàizōng,
he was enfeoffed as the Duke of Lǔ (Lǔ Guó Gōng),
and remained Director of Political Affairs (Zhèngshì Lìng).
After returning from a mission to Jìn,
he was transferred to be the Commissioner of the Three Departments (Sānsī Shǐ) of Nánjīng.
During the reign of Shìzōng,
he was transferred to be the Grand Councilor (Zǎixiàng) of the Southern Prefecture (Nánfǔ),
and established the Department of Governmental Affairs (Zhèngshì Shěng).
He implemented methods of governance,
and was praised as a conscientious official (jìnlì lì).
In the sixth month of the fifth year of Tiānlù [951 CE],
the envoy from Hédōng requested that the investiture ceremony be performed.
The Emperor (Dì) commanded Yánhuī (Liú Yánhuī) to determine the regulations for it.
Yánhuī memorialized that they should strictly follow the ceremony Tàizōng used to invest the Jìn Emperor (Jìn Dì).
This was adopted.
During the Yìnglì period,
he retired from office (zhì shì).
His son, Déshū (Liú Déshū), was garrisoned at Dōngpíng,
and the Emperor permitted him by decree to return east every year to visit his parents.
He died in the ninth year [of Yìnglì, 959 CE],
at the age of seventy-eight.
The Emperor (Shàng) was deeply grieved upon hearing the news,
and posthumously granted him the title Grand Secretary (Shàngshū Lìng).
He was buried in Lǔguō outside Yōuzhōu.
He was known to the world as Chóngwén Lìng Gōng (Duke of the Director of Exalted Culture).
Previously,
when Yánhuī fled south,
Tàizǔ dreamt that a white crane flew out from within his tent.
When he returned,
it flew back into the tent.
The next morning,
he said to his attending officials:
“Yánhuī has arrived.”
Soon after, it proved true.
When Tàizǔ first took power,
most affairs were rudimentary.
All matters regarding establishing the capital (dū yì),
constructing palaces,
rectifying the relationship between ruler and minister,
and settling ranks and titles (míng fèn)—
the clarity and orderliness of the laws and institutions (fǎ dù),
were due to Yánhuī’s efforts.
He was one of the meritorious officials who aided the founding of the dynasty (zuǒ mìng gōngchén).
His son was Déshū (Liú Déshū).
When Déshū was just fifteen years old,
Tàizōng saw him,
and said to Yánhuī:
“This child is a blessing to your house,
a treasure to My state,
truly a hero!”
Before he reached manhood,
he was given the concurrent post of Grand General of the Left Yǔlín (Zuǒ Yǔlín Dà Jiāngjūn).
He was promoted to Grand Master of Court Discussion (Tèjìn) and Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi).
At that time, many Hàn people who had surrendered or migrated,
were housed in Dōngpíng.
They suffered annual calamities,
famine, and epidemics.
Déshū requested to go and pacify and nurture them.
He was appointed Regional Governor of the Liáoxīng Army (Liáoxīng Jūn Jiédùshǐ).
Upon arrival, he regulated disorder and eliminated corruption.
His kindness and warmth inspired trust,
he encouraged agriculture and sericulture,
and promoted education.
Within a year, the people recovered and found peace.
He entered the court to become the Commissioner of the Southern Chancery (Nányuàn Xuānhuī Shǐ),
concurrently holding the title of Regional Governor of the Tiānpíng Army (Tiānpíng Jūn Jiédùshǐ),
Inspector and Administrator of the circuits within Píng, Luán, and Yíng Prefectures (Píng, Luán, Yíng sān zhōu guǎn nèi Guānchá Chǔzhì děng Shǐ),
and Administrator of the Affairs of the Secretariat-Chancellery (Ménxià Píngzhāngshì).
Later, he was granted the title Kāifǔ Yítóng Sān Sī (Opening the Palace with the Honors of the Three Dukes) and acting Minister of the Palace Gate (Shìzhōng).
He was enfeoffed as the Duke of Zhào (Zhào Guó Gōng).
He died in the first year of Bǎoníng [969 CE].
His grandsons were Shàoxūn (Liú Shàoxūn) and Shàofāng (Liú Shàofāng).
Shàoxūn
served as the Commissioner of the Ministry of Revenue (Hùbù Shǐ) in the Eastern Capital (Dōngjīng).
When Dà Yánlín rebelled,
he was captured.
He refused to yield when questioned.
The bandits used a saw to dismember him;
he cursed them indignantly until his death.
Shàofāng (Liú Shàofāng)
was an Associate Administrator of Governmental Affairs (Cānzhī Zhèngshì) during the Chóngxī period,
and was concurrently granted the title of Minister of the Palace Gate (Shìzhōng).
When the court debated launching a campaign against Lǐ Yuánhào,
he strongly remonstrated against it, but was not heeded.
He was sent out to serve as the Regional Governor of the Guǎngdé Army (Guǎngdé Jūn Jiédùshǐ).
Upon hearing of the defeat,
he vomited blood and died.
His grandson was Zīràng (Liú Zīràng).
At the beginning of the Shòulóng period, he was appointed Vice Director of the Chancellery (Zhōngshū Shìláng) and Administrator of the Affairs of the Secretariat-Chancellery (Píngzhāngshì).
When Sòng Huīzōng succeeded to the throne,
an envoy was sent to report the succession.
The officials concerned checked the official document,
and found the phrase
“ascended the precious throne” (dēng bǎo wèi)
in the text.
Because of this error, he was dismissed and made Regional Governor of the Chóngyì Army (Chóngyì Jūn Jiédùshǐ).
He was later reassigned to govern Liáoxīng,
where he died.
Hán Zhīgǔ,
a native of Yùtián in Jìzhōu,
was good at strategy and possessed great foresight.
When Tàizǔ pacified Jì [Jìzhōu],
Zhīgǔ was six years old,
and was captured by Yùwěn, the elder brother of Empress Chúnqīn (Chúnqīn Huánghòu).
When the Empress later married,
Zhīgǔ followed her,
but was not often seen or noticed.
After a long time,
relying on his abilities,
he felt disgruntled and frustrated.
He bravely escaped to serve as a menial worker (yōng bǎo),
to earn money for his needs.
His son, Kuāngsì (Hán Kuāngsì), was able to become close to Tàizǔ,
and spoke of his father during a private moment.
Tàizǔ summoned Zhīgǔ for an audience and spoke with him.
Deeming him worthy,
he ordered him to participate in planning and deliberation.
At the beginning of the Shéncè period,
he was given the concurrent title of Regional Governor of the Zhāngwǔ Army (Zhāngwǔ Jūn Jiédùshǐ).
After a long time,
trust in him grew stronger.
He supervised all affairs of the Department of Hàn People (Hàn'ér Sī),
and concurrently managed the diplomatic protocols of various nations.
At that time, rituals and statutes were loose and broad.
Zhīgǔ drew upon old classical texts,
blended them with national customs,
and developed them by mixing them with Hàn rituals,
making them easy for the people of the state to understand and follow.
After a short while,
he was appointed Left Director of the Department of State Affairs (Zuǒ Púshè).
He achieved merit leading the Hàn Army with Kāng Mòjì in the campaign against Bóhǎi.
He was promoted to Director of the Chancellery (Zhōngshū Lìng).
He died during the Tiānxiǎn period,
and was one of the meritorious officials who aided the founding of the dynasty.
His son was Kuāngsì (Hán Kuāngsì).
Kuāngsì was skilled in medicine,
and served duty at the Chánglè Palace (Chánglè Gōng).
The Empress treated him like her own nephew.
In the tenth year of Yìnglì [960 CE],
he became the Temple Supervisor (Xiángwěn) for the temple of Tàizǔ.
Later, Sòng Wáng (King of Sòng) Xǐyǐn plotted rebellion,
and implicated Kuāngsì in his deposition,
but the Emperor (Shàng) ignored the matter.
Initially,
when Jǐngzōng was still in his princely residence,
he was fond of Kuāngsì.
Upon ascending the throne,
he appointed Kuāngsì Garrison Commander of the Supreme Capital (Shàngjīng Liúshǒu).
Soon after,
he was made King of Yàn (Yàn Wáng),
and transferred to be the Garrison Commander of the Southern Capital (Nánjīng Liúshǒu).
At the end of the Bǎoníng period,
he concurrently held the position of Commissioner of Military Affairs (Shūmì Shǐ) while serving as Garrison Commander.
At that time, Yēlǜ Hǔgǔ returned from an embassy to Sòng,
and said that the Sòng people would surely seize Hédōng,
and that preparations should be made beforehand.
Kuāngsì criticized this, saying:
“How could that happen!”
Soon after, the Sòng people indeed captured Tàiyuán,
and pressed toward Yàn (Yōuzhōu) with their momentum.
Kuāngsì, along with the Southern Prefecture Grand Councilor Shā and the Tìyǐn (a tribal leader title) Xiūgē (Yēlǜ Xiūgē), invaded Sòng,
and encamped at Mǎnchéng.
During the battle formation,
the Sòng people requested surrender.
Kuāngsì intended to accept it.
Xiūgē said:
“Their military spirit is very sharp;
I suspect they are trying to lure us.
We should reorganize our troops to defend.”
Kuāngsì did not listen.
Suddenly, the Sòng army charged, beating drums and shouting toward us.
The troops trampled over each other in panic,
and dust rose up and filled the sky.
Kuāngsì hurriedly instructed his generals
not to resist their vanguard.
Once the troops had scattered,
they encountered Sòng ambush forces blocking the main roads.
Kuāngsì abandoned his flags and drums and fled.
His followers ran toward the mountains of Yìzhōu.
Only Xiūgē collected the abandoned weapons and equipment,
and returned with his army intact.
The Emperor was angry at Kuāng Sì,
listing his faults, saying:
"You violated the general counsel,
deeply penetrating enemy territory,
that is your first crime;
orders and commands were not strict,
the ranks were not disciplined,
that is your second crime;
you abandoned my troops,
saving yourself by fleeing like a rat,
that is your third crime;
scouting missed opportunities,
defense was not prepared,
that is your fourth crime;
you abandoned flags and drums,
damaging prestige and disgracing the state,
that is your fifth crime."
He immediately ordered him executed.
The Empress gathered the imperial relatives, slowly pleading for his release.
The sovereign was reluctant to refuse their request.
After a long while,
his anger slightly subsided,
so he had him flogged and spared him from execution.
Afterward, he was remotely appointed as Jìnchāng Jūn Jiédùshǐ.
In Qiánhēng third year (929),
he was transferred to Xīnánmiàn Zhāotǎoshǐ,
and died.
Empress Ruìzhì heard of this,
and sent an envoy to mourn him,
giving extremely generous funeral gifts.
Later, he was posthumously granted Shàngshū Lìng.
He had five sons: Déyuán,
Déràng—who was later granted the name Lóngyùn,
Déwēi,
Décóng,
Déníng.
Biographies of Déyuán and Déníng are attached here;
the others each have their own biographies.
Déyuán
was foolish and greedy by nature,
and served Jǐngzōng's residence early on.
When Jǐngzōng ascended the throne,
he was ranked among the close attendants.
During the Bǎoníng period,
he held the posts of Chóngyì and Xīngguó Èrjūn Jiédùshǐ,
and was granted Jiǎnxiào Tàishī.
Due to his reputation for bribery,
Déràng sent him a letter of remonstrance,
but he ultimately did not reform.
Therefore, commentators scorned him.
Later, he was granted Tóng Zhèngshì Ménxià Píngzhāngshì,
remotely governing the Bǎoníng Jūn Jiédùshǐ.
He died early in the Qiánhēng period.
Déníng
was humble, modest, honest, and cautious.
In the middle of the Bǎoníng period,
he was promoted to Hùjūn Sītú.
In the middle of the Kāitài period,
he was successively promoted to Hùwèi Tàibǎo, Dūgōngshǐ, and Chóngyì Jūn Jiédùshǐ.
He was transferred to govern Guǎngdé.
When his term of office was complete,
the local people requested him to remain,
and permission was granted.
He was transferred to Xīnánmiàn Zhāotǎoshǐ.
When the Dǎngxiàng Lóngyìdā rebelled,
he suppressed them.
He was promoted to Dàtóng Jūn Jiédùshǐ,
and died while in office.
His son Guōsān
ended his career as Tiāndé Jūn Jiédùshǐ.
His grandson Gāojiānú
ended his career as Nányuàn Xuānhuīshǐ;
Gāoshí
ended his career as Liáoxīng Jūn Jiédùshǐ.
Biographies, Volume Five: Yēlǜ Díliè (Yǔzhī) Yēlǜ Duózēn (Gǔ Tūlǚbù) Wáng Yù Yēlǜ Túlǔjiǒng
Yēlǜ Díliè,
courtesy name Wùlǐzhěn,
was a descendant of Púgǔzhǐ Yílíjǐn of the Liùyuànbù.
His father Ǒusī
was also an Yílíjǐn.
Initially,
when Tàizǔ was Yúyuè,
Díliè was trusted and employed for his caution, sincerity, tolerance, and forgiveness.
When Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
his elder brother Hélǔ managed the palace guard,
and thus Díliè entered to attend in the imperial tent,
participating in governmental affairs.
In Shéncè third year (918),
Hélǔ died.
Díliè was appointed Diélà Bù Yílíjǐn,
and entrusted with affairs concerning the south.
Coincidentally, when Dǎngxiàng were being subdued,
the Crown Prince served as the vanguard,
and Díliè was his deputy.
The army reached Tiāndé and Yúnnèi,
splitting the routes and advancing simultaneously.
Díliè led his crack troops across the river and fought fiercely,
achieving many decapitations and captures.
Early in the Tiānzàn period (922),
the Diélà Department was divided into the North and South Bureaus,
where Díliè served as Yílíjǐn.
At that time, the Grand Marshal led troops from Gǔběikǒu to invade Yāndì,
and Díliè swept through Shānxī.
All the castles he reached surrendered.
Tàizǔ praised his achievements
and bestowed upon him generous rewards.
He followed in the campaign against Bóhǎi,
capturing Fúyú Chéng.
Díliè and Yǐndǐshí were left to guard it.
In Tiānxiǎn second year (927),
he was made Resident General of Nánjīng.
He died in the tenth year (935),
aged fifty-six.
His younger brother was Yǔzhī.
Yǔzhī,
childhood name Wùlǐ,
courtesy name Yǐndǐshěn.
As a child, he was heroic, straightforward, and stood out from the crowd.
When he grew older, he was fond of learning
and was fluent in the languages of various tribes.
Early in Tàizǔ's plans and endeavors,
he frequently participated in military strategies.
In Tiānxiǎn first year (926),
Bóhǎi was pacified,
and the Crown Prince was established as Dōngdān Wáng.
Yǔzhī was made Zhōngtáishěng Yòu Cì Xiàng.
At that time, the hearts of the people were unsettled.
Zuǒ Dà Xiàng Diélà died within the month.
Yǔzhī handled affairs diligently and sincerely,
utilizing both authority and trustworthiness.
When Tàizōng ascended the throne,
Yǔzhī submitted a memorial, saying:
"Our Dàshèng Tiānhuáng first possessed the Eastern Land,
choosing capable officials to govern these people,
and did not discard me, your humble subject, for my foolishness, but employed me.
Regarding the advantages and disadvantages of the state,
how dare I not report what I know?
Bóhǎi previously feared the Southern Dynasty,
relying on hazardous terrain for self-defense,
residing in Hūhàn Chéng.
Now, they are far and distant from Shàngjīng.
Since they are not being utilized,
and yet their garrisons are not dismissed,
what purpose does this serve?
The former emperor took advantage of their fragmented morale,
seizing the opportunity to act,
thus conquering them without a fight.
Heaven granted this and men assisted;
that was an opportunity specific to that time.
The remaining descendants are gradually flourishing,
and now reside in a distant border region.
I fear they will become a future disaster.
The land of Liángshuǐ is their former home.
The land is expansive and the soil fertile,
possessing benefits of wood, iron, salt, and fish.
While they are still weak,
move their people back there;
this is a long-term strategy for ten thousand generations.
If they recover their homeland,
and furthermore obtain the bounty of wood, iron, salt, and fish,
they will surely live peacefully and enjoy their livelihoods.
After that, select troops to flank our left,
while the Tūjué, Dǎngxiàng, and Shìwěi assist our right,
allowing us to comfortably control the Southern States,
unifying the entire realm,
thus completing the achievements not yet finished by the Sage Ancestor,
and bequeathing endless blessings to future generations."
When the memorial was presented,
the Emperor praised and accepted it.
In that year,
an imperial edict moved the people of Dōngdān Guó to Liángshuǐ.
People at the time acclaimed the wisdom of this measure.
When Rén Huángwáng fled to Táng,
Yǔzhī stabilized and comforted the people of the state,
maintaining everything as it was before.
For his achievements, he was granted Shǒu Tàifù,
and promoted to Zhōngtáishěng Zuǒ Xiàng.
Early in the Huìtóng period,
he went to the capital for the investiture ceremony,
and was granted Tèjìn.
He submitted a memorial detailing the corruption and unlawful activities of the Zuǒ Cì Xiàng, Bóhǎi Sū.
He died.
His son Hélǐ
ended his career as Dōngjīng Liúshǒu.
Yēlǜ Duózēn,
courtesy name Dínǐn,
was a native of the Liùyuànbù.
His grandfather Púgǔzhǐ
had twice served as Yílíjǐn of his department during the Yáoliěn Shì era.
After Yēlǜ Lángdé and others assassinated Xuánzǔ,
they became increasingly tyrannical and unrestrained.
Púgǔzhǐ used a strategy to lure their faction,
and executed all of them.
Duō Zhēn, since childhood, possessed aspiration and integrity.
When Tàizǔ was the Yúyuè,
he often stayed by his side.
After he ascended the throne,
the people of Liáng sent an envoy requesting materials for shafts and axles.
Tàizǔ found this difficult.
Duō Zhēn said:
“Liáng is nominally requesting materials,
but is actually observing our strength.
We should answer saying: ‘Where the material grows,
it is certainly in deep mountains and remote valleys,
and there is a spirit that oversees it.
We must offer sacrifices and pray using a red donkey with a white nose,
and only then can it be felled.’
If we do this,
then their words will naturally be stopped.”
Later, it was exactly as he said.
In the third year of Tiānzàn,
when they were about to attack Bóhǎi,
Duō Zhēn advised:
“If Your Majesty attends to Bóhǎi first,
then Xīxià will surely trail behind us.
Please campaign in the west first,
so that we might have no worries about the rear.”
Tàizǔ agreed with him.
When Empress Chúnqīn governed as regent,
she disliked Duō Zhēn,
and imprisoned him,
swearing:
“When the iron lock rusts,
I shall release you!”
Later, when she summoned him,
the messenger wanted to remove the lock.
Duō Zhēn refused, saying:
“The iron has not yet rusted,
should I be released?”
The Empress heard this,
admired and praised him,
and quickly summoned and released him.
He died in the second year of Tiānxiǎn.
His younger brothers were Gǔ and Tūlǚbù.
Gǔ,
courtesy name Nièlākūn,
was initially named Xiámǎgé.
When Tàizǔ was the Yúyuè,
he once followed him to seize territory west of the mountains.
He met Lǐ Kèyòng at Yúnzhōu.
Gǔ was in attendance,
and Kèyòng was impressed by him, saying:
“This child’s bone structure is extraordinary;
he should not be kept close by.”
For this reason, Tàizǔ was rather wary of him.
At that time, when he was campaigning in the west,
his younger brothers staged a rebellion.
Upon hearing of the change,
Tàizǔ asked if Gǔ was involved.
The reply was no.
He rejoiced, saying:
“I have no worries anymore!”
He quickly summoned Gǔ to consult.
Gǔ presented a strategy for their annihilation,
and later everything happened as he said,
and thus he was bestowed with very generous rewards.
At the end of Shéncè,
during the southern campaign,
Gǔ was appointed to assist Lǎogǔ, the Yòu Píshì Xiángwěn.
They fought the Táng troops at Yúnbìdiàn.
Lǎogǔ was struck by a stray arrow,
and was severely wounded.
Tàizǔ suspected that Gǔ had secretly harmed him.
Gǔ knew the emperor’s intention,
and knelt, saying:
“Does Your Majesty suspect that your servant was ashamed to serve under Lǎogǔ?
While Lǎogǔ is alive now,
please send an envoy to ask him.”
Tàizǔ sent someone to question Lǎogǔ,
who replied:
“Your servant has nothing to suspect regarding Gǔ.”
The emperor’s doubt was thus dispelled.
Lǎogǔ died,
and Gǔ was subsequently made the Yòu Píshì Xiángwěn.
After he died,
Tàizǔ said to his attendants:
“Gǔ’s death
is like a tall pine tree falling over by itself;
I did not fell it.”
Tūlǚbù,
courtesy name Duóguǎn,
was intelligent and studious as a child.
He served Tàizǔ and was greatly valued.
When the large Qìdān characters were devised,
Tūlǚbù’s contributions were significant.
Not long after,
he became the Wén Bān Línyá,
concurrently holding the positions of Guózǐ Bóshì and Zhī Zhìgào.
The following year,
he received an imperial edict to compile laws for judicial decisions.
Tàizǔ attacked Yān,
and ordered him, along with the Crown Prince and Wáng Yù, to attack Dìngzhōu.
When the army returned and reached Shùnzhōu,
Wáng Qiān, the Commander of Cavalry and Infantry of Yōuzhōu, led his troops to launch a surprise attack.
Tūlǚbù shot his horse, causing it to stumble,
and captured him.
In the second year of Tiānzàn,
the Imperial Prince Yáogǔ was made the Dà Yuánshuài.
Tūlǚbù was his deputy.
After conquering Píngzhōu,
they advanced on Yān and Zhào,
attacking and taking Qǔyáng and Běipíng.
When they reached Yìzhōu,
the people of Yì came to resist,
crossing the moat and forming ranks.
Lǐ Jǐngzhāng came out and surrendered,
saying the people inside the city had no will to fight.
The Dà Yuánshuài was about to repair the siege equipment,
but Tūlǚbù advised:
“Our army has traveled far,
and both men and horses are exhausted;
it is strategically impossible to stay long.”
So, they stopped.
When the army returned,
the Dà Yuánshuài reported his counsel.
Tàizǔ was greatly pleased,
and granted generous rewards.
When the imperial retinue campaigned in the west,
Tūlǚbù and the Dà Yuánshuài served as the vanguard.
They achieved merit attacking the Dǎngxiàng.
Tàizǔ rewarded the army at Shuǐjīngshān.
The Dà Yuánshuài returned east,
but Tūlǚbù remained stationed in the southwest,
and again campaigned against the Dǎngxiàng.
He captured many and returned.
When Tàizǔ campaigned in the east,
Dà Yīnzhuàn surrendered and then rebelled again.
When attacking him,
Tūlǚbù was the first to ascend the walls.
After Bóhǎi was pacified,
he received an imperial edict to inscribe Tàizǔ’s achievements and virtue upon the walls of Yǒngxīngdiàn.
When the army returned,
the prefectures and counties that had already submitted often rebelled again.
Tūlǚbù followed the Dà Yuánshuài and defeated them.
When Empress Chúnqīn governed as regent,
there were slanderous rumors defaming him.
The Empress grew angry,
and Tūlǚbù fled in fear.
Tàizōng knew he was innocent
and recalled him.
In the third year of Tiānxiǎn,
he campaigned against the Wūgǔ tribe,
capturing many prisoners.
When attacking Táng,
Tūlǚbù was made the commander of the Left Wing.
He attacked the Táng army’s Xiáshāzhài,
forcing its surrender.
In the eleventh year,
he escorted the Prince of Jìn, Shí Jìngtáng, into Luò.
During the great enfeoffment ceremony,
Tūlǚbù oversaw the rites and ceremonies,
and was promoted to Tèjìn Jiǎnxiào Tàiwèi.
He died in the fifth year of Huìtóng.
Wáng Yù,
was a native of Wànnián County, Jīngzhào.
He was the illegitimate son of Chǔ Zhí, the Táng Yìwǔjūn Jiédùshǐ.
His uncle Chǔ Cún governed Yìwǔ.
When he died,
the entire army supported his son Gào to succeed him.
Chǔ Zhí was the Dū Zhī Bīngmǎ Shǐ.
In the third year of Guānghuà,
Zhū Quánzhōng, the Prince of Liáng, attacked Dìngzhōu.
Gào sent Chǔ Zhí to resist them at Shāhé.
The army was defeated,
and he entered the city and drove out Gào.
Gào fled to Tàiyuán.
The mutinous soldiers supported Chǔ Zhí as Liúhòu,
and sent people to request service under the Prince of Liáng.
Liáng had severed ties with Kèyòng, the Prince of Jìn,
and submitted a memorial appointing Chǔ Zhí as the Yìwǔjūn Jiédùshǐ.
Initially, when Gāo Mólán [Gāo Mólán] was overthrown,
Yù [Yù] followed him.
The Jìn [Jìn] king Lǐ Kèyòng [Lǐ Kèyòng] gave him his daughter as a wife,
and Yù [Yù] was made Defense Commissioner of Xīnzhōu [Xīnzhōu].
Chǔ Zhí [Chǔ Zhí] expected that Jìn [Jìn] would certainly attack Zhāng Wénlǐ [Zhāng Wénlǐ],
and that if Zhèn [Zhèn] fell,
he would certainly not survive alone.
He became increasingly suspicious.
He secretly sent Yù [Yù] to guide the Qìdān [Qìdān] into the pass from the north to tie down the Jìn [Jìn] troops,
and also promised to make him his successor.
Yù [Yù], having fled to Jìn [Jìn],
was always afraid of losing his father's favor.
When he received the envoy,
he was overjoyed.
In the sixth year of Shéncè [Shéncè] (921),
he presented a memorial, sent [Fā] [Fā],
and brought his entire household to surrender.
Tàizǔ [Tàizǔ] adopted him as a son.
Not long after,
Yù's [Yù's] elder brother Dū [Dū] imprisoned their father
and made himself Administrator-in-Chief.
The Emperor dispatched Yù [Yù] to accompany the Crown Prince to attack him.
When they reached Dìngzhōu [Dìngzhōu],
Dū [Dū] held his ground firmly and did not sally forth.
They plundered the inhabitants and returned.
The following year,
he accompanied the Crown Prince to attack Zhènzhōu [Zhènzhōu],
encountered Táng [Táng] troops at Dìngzhōu [Dìngzhōu],
and defeated them.
In the autumn of the second year of Tiānzàn [Tiānzàn] (923),
Yù [Yù] and Āgǔzhī [Āgǔzhī] raided the lands of Yān [Yān] and Zhào [Zhào],
and captured Cíyáowù [Cíyáowù].
He accompanied Tàizǔ [Tàizǔ] in pacifying Bóhǎi [Bóhǎi],
and distinguished himself in battle.
He was promoted to Co-Administrator of Governmental Affairs and Grand Councilor,
and changed to Military Commissioner of Chóngyì [Chóngyì] Command.
When Tàizǔ [Tàizǔ] died,
Yù [Yù] and his wife attended the funeral.
His wife tearfully pleaded with Empress Chúnqīn [Chúnqīn],
requesting to return to her homeland,
which was granted.
Yù [Yù] memorialized, saying:
"Your servant was originally the son-in-law of the Táng [Táng] ruler.
The ruler has already been assassinated.
How can my wife and I protect each other on this journey?
I wish to always serve the Empress Dowager."
The Empress was pleased and said:
"Among the Hàn [Hàn] people,
only Lord Wáng [Wáng] is truly loyal and filial."
This was because Tàizǔ [Tàizǔ] had once made an oath of brotherhood with Lǐ Kèyòng [Lǐ Kèyòng].
Soon after, he was promoted to Administrator of Governmental Affairs.
He returned to Yízhōu [Yízhōu]
and died.
Yélǜ Túlǔjiǒng [Yélǜ Túlǔjiǒng],
courtesy name Ālǔyǐn [Ālǔyǐn],
was the grandson of Sùzǔ's [Sùzǔ] son Qiàkē [Qiàkē].
He was brave and resourceful.
During Tàizōng's [Tàizōng's] campaign to establish Jìn [Jìn],
his father Dírǔgǔ [Dírǔgǔ] was the Yílíjǐn [Yílíjǐn] of the Five Courts,
and died in battle.
The Emperor immediately appointed Túlǔjiǒng [Túlǔjiǒng] to his position.
In the first year of Huìtóng [Huìtóng] (938),
he was made Grand King of the Northern Court.
He often dismissed his attendants to discuss important matters with the Emperor,
and his replies always pleased the Emperor.
He accompanied the expedition against Shí Chóngguì [Shí Chóngguì].
Dù Chóngwēi [Dù Chóngwēi], commanding over 100,000 troops, resisted at Hūtuó [Hūtuó] Bridge,
fighting fiercely for several days,
preventing their advance.
The Emperor said:
"Both armies are exhausted from fighting over the crossing,
men and horses are weary.
What plan should we adopt?"
The generals requested to slow the army
and make plans for later,
which the Emperor approved.
Túlǔjiǒng [Túlǔjiǒng], with a stern expression, stepped forward and said:
"Your foolish servant humbly believes that if Your Majesty delights in peace and comfort,
then guarding the four borders is sufficient;
but since you wish to expand the territory
and launch distant campaigns,
how can you be without worries?
If we stop midway,
it will only benefit the enemy,
who will then certainly invade Nánjīng [Nánjīng]
and destroy our subordinate cities.
If this happens,
the fighting will never cease,
and our people will never have a moment of peace.
Moreover, they are infantry and we are cavalry,
why should we worry about not succeeding?
Furthermore, the Hàn [Hàn] people's leg strength is weak and their movements slow.
If we select light, elite cavalry to first cut off their supply lines,
then nothing will fail to be accomplished."
The Emperor was pleased and said:
"When a country is strong, its people are wise;
when the sea is vast, its fish are large."
Thereupon, they cut off their supply lines,
and frequently launched sorties to harass their forces.
Dù Chóngwēi [Dù Chóngwēi] indeed surrendered as predicted.
For his merits, he was richly rewarded.
The following spring,
he died in the army.
Commentary: In the early years of Shéncè [Shéncè],
the generals, prime ministers, and high officials, raised from obscurity,
supported the royal destiny,
and those who gained renown through their service
were indeed talents of their time;
this was also due to Tàizǔ's [Tàizǔ's] sincerity in governing his subordinates,
not relying on sole discretion,
thus being able to gather all strategies and utilize them!
Their seizing of opportunities to establish great deeds,
even leading to analogies of 'heart and belly,' 'ears and eyes,' 'hands and feet,'
how could it be mere chance!
Attacking the Dǎngxiàng [Dǎngxiàng],
routing Dírǔ [Dírǔ],
pacifying Lāgě [Lāgě],
and settling Bóhǎi [Bóhǎi],
their achievements were truly great.
If Mòjì [Mòjì] is remembered for administering justice without wrongdoing,
Pōdé [Pōdé] for maintaining his arguments without wavering,
Yánhuī [Yánhuī] for establishing principles and setting regulations,
Shàoxūn [Shàoxūn] for upholding integrity unto death,
Túlǔjiǒng [Túlǔjiǒng] for anticipating the enemy and achieving victory,
could it be that those with broad talents are not useful in close quarters,
and those with far-reaching ways have distant achievements?
It is fitting to call them founders of the dynasty.

Yélǜ Jiělǐ [Yélǜ Jiělǐ],
courtesy name Pōdān [Pōdān],
was from the Tūlǚbù [Tūlǚbù] tribe.
His family had been minor officials for generations.
Jiělǐ [Jiělǐ] served under Tàizōng [Tàizōng] early on
and was promoted to military officer.
During the Tiānxiǎn [Tiānxiǎn] period (926-938),
Táng [Táng] attacked Dìngzhōu [Dìngzhōu].
After it fell,
Jiělǐ [Jiělǐ] was captured by Táng [Táng] troops;
when Jìn Gāozǔ [Jìn Gāozǔ] ascended the throne,
he first returned to his country.
Tàizōng [Tàizōng] pardoned his crime
and appointed him Imperial Censor-in-chief.
In the ninth year of Huìtóng [Huìtóng] (946), during the campaign against Jìn [Jìn],
the army reached Hūtuóhé [Hūtuóhé],
seized the Zhongdu Bridge,
and forced the surrender of its general Dù Chóngwēi [Dù Chóngwēi].
The Emperor ordered Jiělǐ [Jiělǐ] and the surrendered general Zhāng Yànzé [Zhāng Yànzé] to lead three thousand cavalry to quickly advance to Hénán [Hénán];
wherever they went, no one dared to resist their vanguard.
After entering Biàn [Biàn],
Jiělǐ [Jiělǐ] and others moved the Jìn [Jìn] ruler Chóngguì [Chóngguì] to Kāifēng [Kāifēng] Prefecture.
Yànzé [Yànzé] indulged in killing and plundering,
and caused chaos in the imperial palace.
Jiělǐ [Jiělǐ] could not restrain him.
The common people were agitated,
and all were resentful.
When the imperial carriage arrived at the capital,
Yànzé's [Yànzé's] crimes were enumerated
and he was executed in the marketplace.
The people of Biàn [Biàn] rejoiced;
Jiělǐ [Jiělǐ] was also reprimanded,
but soon released.
During the Tiānlù [Tiānlù] period (947-951),
he was granted the additional title of Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince.
In the early years of Yìnglì [Yìnglì] (951-969),
he established the Lìngwěn [Lìngwěn] of his own tribe,
and Jiělǐ [Jiělǐ] inherited this position.
He died.
Yélǜ Bálǐdé [Yélǜ Bálǐdé],
courtesy name Háilín [Háilín],
was the son of Tàizǔ's [Tàizǔ's] younger brother Lāgě [Lāgě].
When Tàizōng [Tàizōng] ascended the throne,
he was entrusted with important tasks due to his close affection.
In the seventh year of Huìtóng [Huìtóng] (944),
during the campaign against Shí Chóngguì [Shí Chóngguì],
Bálǐdé [Bálǐdé] advanced to besiege Dézhōu [Dézhōu],
captured it,
and seized Governor Shī Jūfán [Shī Jūfán] and twenty-seven others.
In the ninth year (946),
the army was raised again,
reached Hūtuóhé [Hūtuóhé],
forced Dù Chóngwēi [Dù Chóngwēi] to surrender,
and contributed greatly in battle.
When Tàizōng [Tàizōng] entered Biàn [Biàn],
he was granted the position of Military Commissioner of Ānguó [Ānguó] Command for his merits,
and overall command of the Héběi [Héběi] Circuit.
When the army returned,
the prefectures and commanderies often rebelled
in response to Liú Zhīyuǎn [Liú Zhīyuǎn].
Bálǐdé [Bálǐdé] could not defend them and returned.
When Shìzōng [Shìzōng] ascended the throne,
he was transferred to Resident Commissioner of Zhōngjīng [Zhōngjīng],
and died.
, courtesy name Mígǔdǐng

, capturing their general Sài Xiàngyǔ
. When the army was stationed at Yuánchéng
, the Jìn generals Lǐ Shǒuzhēn and Gāo Xíngzhōu led troops to intercept them
, but Yánshòu defeated them
. Upon reaching Dùnqiū
, heavy continuous rain fell
, and the Emperor wanted to withdraw the army
. Yánshòu remonstrated, saying
: "The Jìn army is stationed on the riverbank
but dares not engage in battle
. If we penetrate directly into Chánzhōu
and seize their bridge
, then Jìn will not be difficult to pacify
." The Emperor agreed with this
. Coincidentally, the Jìn army had already retreated to Chánzhōu
. When Gāo Xíngzhōu reached Xichéng
, Yánshòu led light troops to meet and fight him
. The Emperor personally supervised the cavalry charge through their formation
, and the enemy immediately scattered
. When the army returned
, Yánshòu was left behind to pacify the three prefectures of Bèi, Jì, and Shēn
. In the eighth year
, when they campaigned against Jìn again
, the Jìn ruler sent Zhào Xíngshí
, a member of Yánshòu's clan, with a letter to entice him to defect
. At that time, the Jìn people held fast behind their fortifications and refused to come out
. Yánshòu lied, saying
: "I have been held captive for a long time
, but how could I forget the land of my fathers
? If you send an army to meet me
, I will immediately return
." The Jìn people believed him
, and dispatched Dù Chóngwēi to lead troops to receive him
. Yánshòu reached the Hūtuó River
and occupied the Zhōngdù Bridge
. He fought fiercely with the Jìn army
, personally killing their general Wáng Qīng
. The two armies were locked in confrontation
. Tàizōng secretly crossed the river at another ferry
, leaving Yánshòu and Yēlǜ Shuògǔ to hold the bridge
. The enemy could not seize it
, and they were repeatedly defeated
. Dù Chóngwēi subsequently surrendered with all his forces
. The Emperor was pleased
, and bestowed upon Yánshòu a scarlet robe embroidered with dragons and phoenixes
, saying
: "All the Hàn soldiers are now yours
. You should personally go and comfort them
." Yánshòu went to the camp
, where Dù Chóngwēi and Lǐ Shǒuzhēn came to greet him at the head of his horse
. Later, after Tàizōng conquered Biàn
, Yánshòu, through Lǐ Sōng
, sought to be made Crown Prince
. The Emperor said
: "For the Prince of Wèi, I would not hesitate even to cut off my own flesh
. However, the Crown Prince must be the son of the Son of Heaven
. How could the Prince of Wèi be made Crown Prince
?" The reason was that the Emperor had previously promised that after the destruction of Jìn
, Yánshòu would rule the Central Plains as Emperor
. Therefore, in breaking through strong defenses and defeating the enemy
, Yánshòu always placed himself in the vanguard
. When he subsequently used Lǐ Sōng to convey his wish
, the Emperor ordered Yánshòu's rank to be promoted
. Zhāng Lì

, Academician of the Hànlín Academy and Chief Editor, proposed titles for him: Resident Commissioner of Zhōngjīng, Grand Chancellor, Director of the Affairs of the Department of State Affairs, and Overall Commander of Domestic and Foreign Military Affairs
. The Emperor crossed out
"Director of the Affairs of the Department of State Affairs and Overall Commander of Domestic and Foreign Military Affairs"
. When Shìzōng ascended the throne
, based on his merit in supporting the accession
, he was appointed Shūmìshǐ
. He died in the second year of Tiānlù
Gāo Móhàn
. Initially
, when Tàizǔ pacified Bóhǎi
, Móhàn fled to Gāolì (Goryeo)
, and the King married his daughter to him
. Due to an offense, he fled back
. He was imprisoned for killing a man while drunk
. Tàizǔ, knowing his talent
, pardoned him
In the seventh month of Tiānxiǎn (天顯) 11th year (936 CE),
Táng (唐) dispatched Zhāng Jìngdá (張敬達) and Yáng Guāngyuǎn (楊光遠) to lead an army of 500,000 to attack Tàiyuán (太原).
The momentum was very sharp.
Shí Jìngtáng (石敬瑭) sent messengers to request aid,
Tàizōng (太宗) granted it.
In the ninth month,
troops were mobilized and left Yànmén (雁門).
Móhàn (模翰) engaged Jìngdá’s (敬達) army,
and defeated it.
The siege of Tàiyuán (太原) was lifted.
Jìngtáng (敬瑭) came out at night to pay his respects to the Emperor,
and they agreed to a relationship of father and son.
The Emperor summoned Móhàn (模翰) and others and bestowed wine and food upon them,
personally feasting the soldiers.
The morale of the troops was further boosted.
The following day,
they fought again,
and defeated them again.
Jìngdá (敬達) fled like a rat to Jìn'ān Zhài (晉安寨).
Móhàn (模翰) presented captives to the Emperor.
At that time, Jìngtáng (敬瑭) established himself as the Emperor of Jìn (晉帝).
Guāngyuǎn (光遠) killed Jìngdá (敬達) and surrendered,
and all the prefectures submitted.
The Emperor instructed Móhàn (模翰), saying:
“Since I raised troops,
in over a hundred battles,
your merit is the greatest.
Even famous generals of antiquity could not surpass you.”
Thereupon, he was appointed Shàng Jiāngjūn (上將軍, Grand General).
In the first year of Huìtóng (會同, 938 CE),
the investiture ceremony was completed.
A feast was held for all officials and envoys from various states at the Èryí Diàn (二儀殿).
The Emperor pointed at Móhàn (模翰) and said:
“This is the brave general of the state.
My unification of the realm,
is due to the strength of this man.”
All the ministers shouted "Ten thousand years!"
When Jìn (晉) later betrayed the alliance,
an army was sent out to campaign in the south.
Móhàn (模翰) served as Tǒngjūn Fùshǐ (統軍副使, Deputy Commissioner of Military Command),
and acted as vanguard with Sēng'è (僧遏).
They captured Chìchéng (赤城),
and destroyed the stockades in Dé (德) and Bèi (貝).
That winter,
he concurrently commanded the Left and Right Iron Osprey Armies (Zuǒyòu Tiěyàozi Jūn, 左右鐵鷂子軍),
and took several dozen cities and towns south of the pass (Guānnán, 關南).
In the third month,
an imperial decree ordered the Tiger Official Yáng Tán (楊覃) to proceed to Qiánníng Jūn (乾寧軍),
but he was besieged by the Cāngzhōu Jiédùshǐ (滄州節度使, Military Commissioner of Cāngzhōu) Tián Wǔmíng (田武名).
Móhàn (模翰) met with Zhào Yánshòu (趙延壽) to discuss going to the rescue.
Suddenly, a light emanated from Móhàn’s (模翰) eyes,
circling around the banners and spears,
flickering like a meteor for a long time.
Móhàn (模翰) rejoiced and said:
“This is an auspicious sign of heavenly support!”
They then advanced their troops,
killing and capturing a great many men.
For his merit, he was promoted to Shìzhōng (侍中, Palace Attendant).
He seized territory at Yánshān (鹽山),
and defeated Ráo'ān (饒安).
The Jìn (晉) people were terrified,
and dared not engage in battle.
He was promoted to Tàifù (太傅, Grand Tutor).
Jìn (晉) sent the Wèifǔ Jiédùshǐ (魏府節度使) Dù Chóngwēi (杜重威) with 300,000 troops to resist them.
Móhàn (模翰) said to his staff:
“Military strategy lies in righteousness, not in numbers.
Using large numbers to overwhelm few,
if unjust, must result in defeat.
Is this not what Jìn (晉) is doing!”
At dawn the next day,
he counter-attacked with 300 men under his banner,
killing their vanguard Liáng Hànzhāng (梁漢璋).
The remaining troops were defeated and fled.
An imperial handwritten edict praised him highly,
comparing him to Lǐ Líng (李陵) of Hàn (漢).
A short while later,
Dù Chóngwēi (杜重威) and others returned to the Hūtuó Hé (滹沱河).
The Emperor summoned Móhàn (模翰) and asked for his strategy.
The Emperor approved of his words and said:
“None of the generals can match this.”
He then ordered Móhàn (模翰) to guard the Zhōngdù Qiáo (中渡橋, Middle Crossing Bridge).
When they fought,
they defeated them again.
The Emperor said:
“I observed the momentum of the two armies from a height,
and saw that your bravery and sharpness were unrivaled,
like a hawk pursuing pheasants and rabbits.
Your portrait should be drawn in the Língé (麟閣, Unicorn Pavilion),
and your titles passed down to your descendants.”
Soon after, Dù Chóngwēi (杜重威) and others surrendered.
When the Emperor entered Biàn (汴),
he was promoted to Tèjìn Jiǎnxiào Tàishī (特進檢校太師, Specially Advanced Grand Tutor/Acting Grand Preceptor),
and enfeoffed as the Zhé Jùn Kāiguó Gōng (悊郡開國公, Founding Duke of Zhé Commandery).
He was granted an imperial sealed document and sword ornaments.
He served as Biànzhōu Xúnjiǎn Shǐ (汴州巡檢使, Inspector of Biàn Prefecture),
pacifying the local bandits in the Sìshuǐ (汜水) mountains.
He was transferred to guard Zhōngjīng (中京, Central Capital).
In the second year of Tiānlù (天祿, 948 CE),
he was promoted to Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (開府儀同三司, Grand Commissioner, Equal to the Three Dukes),
and granted court robes, saddles and bridles, and famous horses.
In the beginning of Yìnglì (應曆, 951 CE),
he was summoned to serve as Yòuxiàng (右相, Right Chancellor) of the Zhōngtái Shěng (中臺省, Central Terrace Department).
When he arrived at Dōngjīng (東京, Eastern Capital),
the elders welcomed him, saying:
“You rose from military service,
achieved wealth and honor,
bringing glory to the village.
Figures like Xiāngrú (相如) and Mǎichén (買臣) cannot surpass you.”
In the first month of the ninth year (959 CE),
he was transferred to Zuǒxiàng (左相, Left Chancellor),
and died.
Zhào Sīwēn (趙思溫),
courtesy name Wénměi (文美),
was a native of Lúlóng (盧龍).
In his youth he was bold and sharp,
with strength exceeding ordinary men.
He served under the banner of the Yàn Commander Liú Rén'gōng (劉仁恭).
When Lǐ Cúnxù (李存勗) campaigned against Yàn (燕),
Sīwēn (思溫) led a detached force to resist him.
A stray arrow hit his eye.
He tore his clothing to soak up the blood,
but continued fighting.
He was captured by Cúnxù’s (存勗) general Zhōu Déwēi (周德威).
Cúnxù (存勗) admired his bravery and released his bonds.
Over time,
he became increasingly trusted.
He fought against Liáng (梁) at Shēnxìan (莘縣),
and became famous for his fierce courage.
He was appointed Píngzhōu Cìshǐ (平州刺史, Prefect of Píng Prefecture),
concurrently serving as Dūzhǐhuīshǐ (都指揮使, Commander-in-Chief) of the three prefectures of Píng (平), Yíng (營), and Jì (薊).
In the second year of Shéncè (神冊, 917 CE),
Tàizǔ (太祖) sent a great general to pacify the Yān region (Yāndì, 燕地).
Sīwēn (思溫) came and surrendered.
When Bóhǎi (渤海) was attacked,
Sīwēn (思ēn) was made Hànjūn Dūtuánliàn Shǐ (漢軍都團練使, Commissioner-in-Chief of Militia of the Han Army).
He fought fiercely and captured Fúyú Chéng (扶餘城).
He sustained several wounds on his body.
Tàizǔ (太祖) personally prepared medicine for him.
When Tàizōng (太宗) ascended the throne,
for his merit, he was promoted to Jiǎnxiào Tàibǎo (檢校太保, Acting Grand Guardian) and Bǎojìng Jūn Jiédùshǐ (保靜軍節度使, Military Commissioner of Bǎojìng Command).
In the eleventh year of Tiānxiǎn (天顯, 936 CE),
when Táng (唐) troops attacked Tàiyuán (太原),
Shí Jìngtáng (石敬瑭) sent an envoy to request aid.
The Emperor ordered Sīwēn (思溫) to mobilize troops between Lán (嵐) and Xiàn (憲) prefectures to reinforce the siege.
After the military campaign ended,

he was reassigned as Nánjīng Liúshǒu (南京留守, Defender-in-Chief of the Southern Capital), Lúlóng Jūn Jiédùshǐ (盧龍軍節度使, Military Commissioner of Lúlóng Command), Guǎnnèi Guānchá Chǔzhì Děng Shǐ (管內觀察處置等使, Commissioner of Observation and Affairs within the Circuit), and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (開府儀同三司, Grand Commissioner, Equal to the Three Dukes),
concurrently holding the post of Shìzhōng (侍中, Palace Attendant).
He was granted the title Xiémóu Jìngluàn Yìshèng Gōngchén (協謀靜亂翊聖功臣, Meritorious Official who Planned Together, Pacified Disorder, and Aided the Sage).
Soon after, he was reassigned as Línghǎi Jūn Jiédùshǐ (臨海軍節度使, Military Commissioner of Línghǎi Command).
At the beginning of Huìtóng (會同, 938 CE),
he followed Yēlǜ Diéhǎ (耶律牒●) as an envoy to Jìn (晉) to conduct the investiture ceremony.
Upon returning,
he was promoted to Jiǎnxiào Tàishī (檢校太師, Acting Grand Preceptor).
In the second year (939 CE),
a star fell in his courtyard,
and he died.
The Emperor sent an envoy to bestow gifts and offer sacrifices.
He was posthumously granted the titles Tàishī (太師, Grand Preceptor) and Wèi Guó Gōng (魏國公, Duke of Wèi State).
His sons, Yánzhào (延照) and Yánjìng (延靖),
rose to the rank of Shǐxiàng (使相, Envoy-Chancellor).
Yēlǜ Ōulǐsī (耶律漚里思),
was a descendant of the Liùyuàn Yílíjǐn (六院夷離菫, Ilijin of the Six Courts) Púgǔzhī (蒲古只).
He possessed courage and strategy.
In every battle he wore heavy armor,
and wielded an iron spear.
Wherever he went, the enemy scattered.
During the Huìtóng (會同) period,
when Jìn (晉) was campaigned against,
the Emperor reached a river and hunted there.
Just then, a Hǎidōng Qīng Hú (海東青鶻, Sea Eastern Blue Falcon) attacked a pheasant.
A Jìn (晉) soldier on the other side of the water used a pigeon to lure the falcon away.
The Emperor looked at his attendants and said:
“Who can capture this man for me?”
Ōulǐsī (漚里思) requested a swift horse,
crossed the river and captured him,
and returned after killing several men who came to his aid.
The Emperor was greatly pleased,
and generously rewarded him.
Later, the Jìn (晉) general Dù Chóngwēi (杜重威) opposed them at Wàngdū (望都),
holding the river and compelling a fight.
Ōulǐsī (漚里思) charged into the formation on an armored horse.
The rest of the army followed.
He was surrounded.
The troops suggested they could break out where the formation was weak,
but Ōulǐsī (漚里思) said:
“I fear they have other preparations there.”
He ultimately led his troops to charge through the strongest point and escape.
Looking back at the place the troops had pointed to,
it was all large ditches.
His predictions regarding the enemy were often like this.
That year,
he was put in overall command of the Díliè Pīshì Jūn (敵烈皮室軍, Diliè Pishi Army).
He was impeached for privately excusing his subordinates,
stripped of office,
and died.
Zhāng Lì,
a native of Cízhōu,
initially served the Táng [Dynasty] as an attendant secretary (Zhǎngshūjì),
and was promoted to Hànlín Xuéshì (Academician of the Hanlin Academy).
When Shí Jìngtáng raised troops,
the Táng ruler appointed Lì as the pacification commissioner's deputy (Zhāotǎo Pànguān),
and he followed Zhào Déjūn to reinforce Zhāng Jìngdá in Hédōng.
When Jìngdá was defeated,
Lì entered Qìdān (the Khitan state).
Later, Tàizōng, seeing that Lì was resolute and upright,
and possessed literary talent,
promoted him to Hànlín Xuéshì.
Lì always spoke his mind completely when addressing matters,
avoiding nothing,
and the Emperor esteemed him even more.
Not long after,
he plotted to flee home,
but was captured by pursuing cavalry.
The Emperor reproached him, saying:
"Why did you run away?"
Lì replied:
"I am unaccustomed to the customs, food, and dwelling conditions of the north.
My heart was constantly melancholy,
and that is why I fled."
The Emperor looked at the interpreter, Gāo Yànyīng, and said:
"I once warned you to treat this man well.
Why did you cause him to feel unsettled and flee?
If Lì leaves,
can he be obtained again?"
Thereupon, he beat Yànyīng with a staff and apologized to Lì.
Early in the Huìtóng period,
Lì was promoted to Hànlín Chéngzhǐ (Academician-in-Waiting),
concurrently serving as Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū),
and followed Tàizōng to attack Jìn.
Upon entering Biàn [Liang],
the generals Xiāo Hàn, Yēlǜ Lángwǔ, Mádá, and their like indulged in slaughter and plunder.
Lì memorialized, saying:
"Now that Dà Liáo has just gained Zhōngguó (China proper),
it is appropriate to govern it with Zhōngguó people.
We must not exclusively employ people of the state (Khitan) or the close attendants of the emperor.
If governance and decrees are flawed or errant,
then the people's hearts will not submit,
and though we have gained it, we will surely lose it."
The Emperor did not heed him.
Lì was relocated to Right Executive Assistant (Yòu Púyè),
concurrently serving as Palace Gate Vice Minister (Ménxià Shìláng) and Grand Councilor (Píngzhāng Shì).
After a while,
the Emperor's carriage returned north,
and he died at Luánchéng.
At that time, Lì was in the prefecture.
Xiāo Hàn and Mádá surrounded his residence with troops.
Lì was ill in bed,
but he came out to see them.
Hàn enumerated his faults, saying:
"Why did you tell the former emperor that Khitan people should not be made military governors (Jiédùshǐ)?
I, relying on my kinship as the maternal uncle of the Emperor (Guójǐu),
and having merits in campaigns,
was kept by the former emperor to guard Biàn [Liang],
and appointed as the Jiédùshǐ of Xuānwǔ Commandery.
Yet you alone deemed it improper.
Furthermore, you slandered me, saying that I and Xièlǐ enjoyed plundering people's possessions, wealth, daughters, and sons.
Today, you must die!"
He immediately ordered Lì to be bound.
Lì raised his voice and said:
"This concerned the great structure of the state,
relating to its stability or peril.
I spoke honestly about it.
If you wish to kill me, then kill me.
Why bother binding me?"
Mádá, considering Lì a high minister,
and that he could not be killed without authorization,
stepped in and stopped him.
That evening,
Lì died of indignation and fury.
The commentary states: Initially,
Jìn, relying on Liáo's troops, gained the empire.
Therefore, [Jìn] treated Liáo both with the rites of a vassal and served it as a father,
ceded territory as a tribute of longevity,
and transported silks as tribute.
Not long after,
the army of the Huìtóng period reached the Hūtuó [River].
Could this outcome have been caused by the collective generals being greedy for glory and fond of war?
Or was it because, as the saying goes, their fidelity did not come from the heart?
Mú Hàn finished his life with merit and fame,
and may be called a good general.
As for Yánshòu, although his achievements were notable,
his ambition for the position of heir apparent [Chǔ Wèi]
was a mistake.
Driven by profit, his wisdom was clouded,
and there is certainly no need to discuss him further.
If one were to create a minor feud that diminished great merit,
like Xièlǐ,
what criticism is there of him?
Biographies VII: Yēlǜ Wūzhì, Yēlǜ Hǒu (Hélǔbù), Yēlǜ Āntuán, Yēlǜ Wā, Yēlǜ Tuíyù, Yēlǜ Tàliè
Yēlǜ Wūzhì,
courtesy name Dínǐan,
descended from the Mèngfù branch.
His demeanor was simple and tranquil,
he possessed ability and insight,
and he valued promises.
When encountering urgent matters,
he handled them calmly;
people could not fathom him.
He was broadly learned,
and understood astronomy.
During the Huìtóng period,
he served as Tìyǐn (Chief of the Shàngshě Tribe).
When Tàizōng died,
the various high ministers installed Shìzōng.
The Empress Dowager (Tàihòu) heard of this
and was extremely angry.
She dispatched the Imperial Son Lǐ Hú with troops to attack the opposing side.
He met Ānduān and Liú Gē at Tàidé Quán,
and returned defeated.
Lǐ Hú seized all the family members of Shìzōng's officials and subordinates,
and told the guards:
"If I fail to win the battle,
I will first slaughter these people!"
Everyone was terrified, saying among themselves:
"If we truly fight,
then fathers, sons, and brothers will destroy each other!"
The army reached the Huáng Hé River crossing,
confronting each other across the banks.
At that time, Wūzhì followed the Empress Dowager.
Shìzōng, knowing Wūzhì was good at strategizing,
wished to sow discord.
He thus created a situation and presented a letter
to test the Empress Dowager.
The Empress Dowager received the letter
and showed it to Wūzhì.
After Wūzhì finished reading,
he spoke, saying:
"The Empress Dowager assisted Tàizǔ in settling the empire,
therefore your servant is willing to exhaust his utmost effort.
If the Empress Dowager harbors suspicion toward me,
even if I wish to fulfill my loyalty,
will I be able to?
As for the current plan,
nothing is better than reconciliation through dialogue,
and success is assured;
otherwise, we should fight quickly
to decide the outcome.
However, once the people's hearts waver,
the disaster to the state will not be minor.
I urge the Empress Dowager to consider and decide."
The Empress Dowager said:
"If I suspected you,
how could I have shown you the letter?"
Wūzhì replied:
"Lǐ Hú and the Prince of Yǒngkāng are both descendants of Tàizǔ.
The divine instruments [throne] have not been transferred to another clan;
what is there to deem improper?
The Empress Dowager should consider a long-term strategy,
and negotiate peace with the Prince of Yǒngkāng."
The Empress Dowager said:
"Who can be dispatched?"
Wūzhì replied:
"If the Empress Dowager does not suspect your servant,
I request to go.
If by chance the Prince of Yǒngkāng listens,
it will be a blessing to the ancestral temples and the state."
The Empress Dowager then dispatched Wūzhì to deliver a letter to the Emperor.
The Emperor sent the Commissioner of Court Affairs (Xuānhuīshǐ), Yēlǜ Hǎisī, to reply,
the language of which was largely disrespectful.
Wūzhì remonstrated, saying:
"The intent of the letter is like this,
and the worries of the state will not cease.
If we can relinquish hatred to bring peace to the altars of soil and grain (state),
then your servant believes nothing is better than peace and harmony."
The Emperor said:
"That crowd is merely a rabble;
how can they stand against us?"
Wūzhì said:
"Even if they cannot stand against us,
what about our blood relatives?
Moreover, we do not yet know who will win.
Suppose we are fortunate enough to win,
the clans of all those officials who have been seized by Lǐ Hú will be utterly wiped out.
Considering this,
only peace is the best course."
Those nearby who heard this changed color.
The Emperor was silent for a long time,
and then asked:
"How should we achieve peace?"
Wūzhì replied:
"Meet with the Empress Dowager,
and each side relieves their anger and resentment;
peace will not be difficult.
If not,
a decisive battle will not be too late."
The Emperor agreed,
and then dispatched Hǎisī to go to the Empress Dowager to arrange peace.
After several days of exchange,
the agreement was settled.
When they first met,
feelings of resentment and blame were mutually expressed,
utterly lacking any harmonious intent.
The Tàihòu said to Wūzhì:
"You ought to plan this for me."
Wūzhì stepped forward and said:
"If the Tàihòu and the Dàwáng are able to release their resentment, your servant then dares to offer advice."
The Tàihòu said:
"You just speak it."
Wūzhì borrowed the usher's tally and held it,
saying to the Tàihòu:
"In the past, when the Rén Huáng Wáng was alive,
why was the Sīshèng established?"
The Tàihòu said:
"The establishment of the Sīshèng
was the dying wish of Tàizǔ."
She further said:
"Why did the Dàwáng arbitrarily install himself,
without consulting the revered elders?"
The Emperor said:
"The Rén Huáng Wáng ought to have been established but was not,
therefore he was removed."
Wūzhì spoke sternly:
"The Rén Huáng Wáng abandoned his parents' state and fled to Táng.
Is the duty of a son supposed to be like this?
The Dàwáng, upon seeing the Tàihòu,
showed no modesty or apology,
but only sought out grievances.
The Tàihòu, influenced by biased affection,
relied on the late emperor’s dying command,
wrongly granting the sacred vessel (shénqì).
If this is the case, how can harmony be hoped for?
You should quickly engage in battle!"
He threw down the tally and withdrew.
The Tàihòu wept and said:
"Previously, when Tàizǔ encountered the rebellion of his younger brothers,
the world was poisoned and suffered greatly,
the wounds have not yet healed.
How can this be repeated!"
Thereupon, she requested a tally.
The Emperor said:
"If the father did not act, but the son does,
who is there to blame?"
He also took a tally and held it.
Those around them were deeply moved,
and wept loudly.
The Tàihòu again said to Wūzhì:
"Now that the discussion is settled,
to whom should the sacred vessel ultimately belong?"
Wūzhì said:
"If the Tàihòu grants it to Yǒngkāng Wáng,
it will accord with Heaven and satisfy the people.
What further doubt is there?"
Lǐ Hú said in a fierce voice:
"While I am alive,
how can Wùyù be established!"
Wūzhì said:
"The rites dictate that succession follows the hereditary legitimate line,
and is not passed to younger brothers.
In the past, the establishment of the Sīshèng
was still considered wrong,
let alone that you, Lord, are violent, cruel, and ruthless,
and the people have many complaints.
Ten thousand mouths speak one word,
desiring the establishment of Yǒngkāng Wáng;
this cannot be denied."
The Tàihòu looked at Lǐ Hú and said:
"Have you also heard these words?
You truly brought this upon yourself!"
Thus, she permitted the establishment of Yǒngkāng.
The Emperor said to Wūzhì:
"Your family connections are particularly close to Mine,
why did you instead assist the Tàihòu?"
Wūzhì replied:
"Your servant considers the Altars of Soil and Grain to be extremely important,
and it cannot be entrusted lightly,
therefore I acted thus."
The Emperor was pleased by his loyalty.
In Tiānlù 2nd Year,
Yēlǜ Tiāndé and Xiāo Hàn were imprisoned for plotting rebellion.
The Tìyǐn Liú Gē and his younger brother Péndōu joined Tiāndé and others to cause trouble.
Yēlǜ Shílà secretly informed Wūzhì.
Wūzhì immediately brought him in to see the Emperor,
and reported the matter.
Liú Gē and the others did not admit guilt,
so the matter was dropped.
Before long,
Liú Gē invited the Emperor to watch a dice game,
raised a goblet to offer longevity,
and advanced with a blade hidden in his sleeve.
The Emperor perceived it,
ordered him to be seized,
and personally interrogated him about the matter.
Liú Gē swore an oath,
and the Emperor again did not press the matter.
Wūzhì submitted a memorial, saying:
"We must have Liú Gē confront Shílà with the evidence,
he should not be lightly pardoned."
The Emperor said:
"You, Minister, shall investigate it for Me."
Wūzhì led swordsmen to interrogate them.
Tiāndé and the others confessed guilt.
Tiāndé was executed,
Hàn was beaten with rods,
Liú Gē was exiled,
and Péndōu was sent as an envoy to the Xiágānsī state.
In the 3rd Year,
(Wūzhì) memorialized, listing the conspiracies of Tàiníng Wáng Chágē.
The Emperor did not heed him.
In the 5th Year,
he was made the Yòu Píshì Xiángwěn.
That autumn,
the Emperor was sacrificing to the Ràng Guó Huángdì at the traveling palace.
He and all his ministers were drunk,
and Chágē assassinated the Emperor.
Wūzhì heard a report that said,
"Those wearing purple must not be allowed to escape,"
so he changed his clothes and went out.
He quickly sent people to summon the various princes,
and instructed the leaders of the Imperial Guard and Píshì to unite their efforts to eliminate the rebels.
At that time, Shòu'ān Wáng was returning to his tent.
Wūzhì sent his younger brother Chōng to welcome him.
When the Prince arrived,
he was still hesitant.
Wūzhì said:
"Your Highness is the son of the Sīshèng.
If the rebels capture you,
they certainly will not spare you.
Whom will the ministers then serve?
On whom will the Altars of Soil and Grain rely?
If by chance you fall into the rebels' hands,
what use will regret be?"
The Prince finally understood.
When the generals heard that Wūzhì had gone out,
they arrived one after another.
At dawn, the troops were organized,
catching the rebels unexpectedly.
They surrounded them,
and subsequently executed Chágē.
Once the chaos was settled,
Mùzōng ascended the throne,
and said to Wūzhì:
"My life
truly comes from your hands, Minister."
He ordered him to oversee state affairs,
and gave him all the property of the rebel faction,
but Wūzhì firmly declined.
In Yìnglì 5th Year,
he was made Běiyuàn Dàwáng,
overseeing the affairs of Shānxī.
Early in Bǎoníng,
Sòng besieged Tàiyuán.
Wūzhì was ordered to lead troops to reinforce it.
Upon reaching Báimǎ Lǐng,
he sent elite soldiers out via secret paths at night,
who galloped quickly to station themselves west of Tàiyuán,
beating drums and lighting fires.
The Sòng army, thinking a large army had arrived,
became afraid and fled during the night.
Due to his merit, he was promoted to Yúyuè.
In the 4th Year,
Liú Jìyuán of Hàn sent an envoy to offer tribute.
He presented silks to Wūzhì.
Wūzhì reported this,
and the Emperor ordered that they be accepted.
In the 5th Year, fifth month, he died,
aged fifty-seven.
The Emperor grieved deeply,
and suspended court for three days.
Later, Dàozōng issued an imperial decree to establish a shrine and offer sacrifices in Shàngjīng,
and erected a stele to commemorate his achievements.
Yēlǜ Hǒu,
courtesy name Hélǔ,
was a descendant of Pú Gǔzhī, the Yílíjǐn of the Six Yüan tribes.
He was upright and sincere, and charitable,
and did not engage in production.
Tàizōng especially relied upon and appointed him.
In Huìtóng 6th Year,
he was made Nányuàn Dàwáng.
He handled affairs with clarity and simplicity,
and people did not dare to slight him on account of his youth.
At that time, Shí Chóngguì, the ruler of Jìn, did not acknowledge vassalage in his memorials;
his language was mostly arrogant and rude.
Hǒu stated that Jìn's crime meant they must be punished.
When the Emperor personally led the campaign,
(Hǒu) followed with the troops under his command.
After entering Biàn,
all the generals took treasures and rarities from the imperial treasury.
Hǒu alone took horse armor.
The Emperor praised him for this.
When the Emperor collapsed and died in Luánchéng,
there was no dying imperial edict,
and the army was anxious and fearful, not knowing what to do.
Hǒu went to see the Northern Chancellery King Yēlǜ Wā and deliberated, saying:
"The imperial throne cannot be vacant for a single day.
If we ask the Empress Dowager,
then the throne will certainly go to Lǐ Hú.
Lǐ Hú is violent and cruel;
how can he be a father to the people?
If we must satisfy the popular will,
then we should establish the Prince of Yǒngkāng."
Wā agreed.
At that time, Yēlǜ Āntuán arrived,
and his intention aligned with Hǒu's,
so they settled on establishing the Prince of Yǒngkāng,
who became Shìzōng.
Soon after,
for his meritorious service, he was promoted to Cǎifǎngshǐ,
and bestowed with treasures and goods.
Hǒu declined, saying:
"My position is already high;
how dare I again seek wealth!
My cousin Délù's sons were implicated in an incident and had their property confiscated.
If Your Majesty would pity them and release them,
then I would have received a great reward!"
The Emperor said:
"Hǒu renounces a great reward
to plead for his kinsmen;
his virtue is far superior."
He granted it,
and moreover bestowed fifty palace households.
At that time, there were those who compiled biographies of "Seven Worthies" from prominent figures of the era,
and Hǒu was one of them.
He died in Tiānlù 3,
aged thirty-nine.
His son was Hélǔbù.
Hélǔbù,
whose courtesy name was Xiézhòng,
once assisted Yēlǜ Wūzhì in pacifying the Zhāgē rebellion.
Mùzōng, because his father Hǒu had first proposed establishing Shìzōng,
did not employ him prominently.
In his later years, he served as Chǎngshǐ for his own tribe.
When Jǐngzōng ascended the throne,
for his meritorious service in pacifying Zhāgē,
he was appointed Zhāodéjūn Jiédùshǐ
and became the Northern Chancellery King.
At that time, Yàn Pǒ, a military commander of Huánglóng Fǔ, killed the defending official and rebelled.
Hélǔbù suppressed him
and defeated him at the Yālù Jiāng.
He was punished with a beating
for not personally pursuing the enemy,
which led to the loss of the rebel.
He died during the Qiánhēng era.
Yēlǜ Āntuán's
great-grandfather was Yánmù,
the eldest son of Xuánzǔ;
his grandfather, Chǔbùlǔ,
was Yílíjǐn of his tribe.
His father, Diélǐ,
was often ill when young,
and at that time, Tàizǔ, who was Tàmǎ Kuòshālǐ,
often cared for him.
In Shéncè 6,
he became Tìyǐn,
and followed Tàizǔ, leading the Dragon Army to campaign against the Zǔbǔ and Dǎngxiàng with merit.
In Tiānzàn 3,
he became Southern Chancellery Yílíjǐn,
campaigning against Bóhǎi,
attacking Hūhàn Chéng,
capturing and executing many.
When Tàizǔ died,
Empress Chúnqīn proclaimed herself regent,
wishing to have the Grand Marshal succeed to the throne.
Diélǐ argued
that the imperial throne should first go to the eldest legitimate son;
now that the Prince of Dōngdān has arrived at court,
he should be established.
Because of this, he displeased the Empress.
For associating with the Prince of Dōngdān,
an edict was issued to imprison him,
interrogate him,
and torture him with fire and branding.
He did not yield,
so he was killed,
and his household was confiscated.
Āntuán was like an adult from a young age.
During his father's mourning,
his grief and emaciation exceeded the proper rites,
and those who saw him were moved.
Tàizōng repeatedly offered comfort and advice,
once saying:
"This child will surely become a capable vessel."
Once grown,
he was sparing with words and laughter,
valued his promises,
always followed rules and regulations,
and was extremely filial to his mother.
Because his father died unjustly
and was not yet buried,
he did not participate in feasts or entertainments.
When Shìzōng was still in his princely residence,
he showed him particular pity and care,
and Āntuán secretly built ties with him.
When Tàizōng returned from campaigning against Jìn,
he collapsed and died in Luánchéng.
The generals wanted to establish Shìzōng,
but because Lǐ Hú and the Prince of Shòu'ān were at court,
they hesitated and could not decide.
At that time, Āntuán was on duty as a guard,
and Shìzōng secretly summoned him to ask for advice.
Āntuán said:
"Your Highness is intelligent, wise, and magnanimous,
and the eldest legitimate son of the Human Emperor;
although the late Emperor had Shòu'ān,
the hearts of the realm are largely inclined towards Your Highness.
If a decision is not made now,
regret will be too late."
Just then, someone came from the capital.
Āntuán falsely reported the death of Lǐ Hú to the army,
and all believed it.
Thereupon, Āntuán went to consult with the Northern and Southern Chancellery Kings.
The Northern Chancellery King Wā heard this and immediately rose, saying:
"We two were just discussing this matter.
The late Emperor once intended to make the Prince of Yǒngkāng his heir apparent,
and today, with us here,
who would dare not obey!
My only fear is that establishing him without informing the Empress Dowager
will cause trouble for the state."
Āntuán replied:
"Since Your Highness knows that the late Emperor intended to make the Prince of Yǒngkāng his heir apparent,
and moreover, the Prince of Yǒngkāng is virtuous and sagacious,
and people are happy to follow him.
Now that the realm is just settled,
a slight delay will lead to the loss of the great affair.
If we inform the Empress Dowager,
she will certainly establish Lǐ Hú.
Furthermore, Lǐ Hú is cruel and violent,
a fact known to all passersby;
if he truly succeeds to the throne,
what will become of the state and its altars?"
The Southern Chancellery King Hǒu said:
"This statement is correct.
My decision is made!"
Then he arrayed the army,
summoned the generals, and enthroned Shìzōng before Tàizōng's coffin.
When the Emperor was established,
he made Āntuán his confidant
and overall director of the imperial guards.
That year,
a peace treaty was concluded at the crossing of Huánghé.
The Empress Dowager asked Āntuán:
"What grievance do you and I have?"
Āntuán replied by referring to his father's death,
and the Empress Dowager fell silent.
When the Northern Chancellery Shūmìshǐ was established,
the Emperor ordered Āntuán to take the position,
bestowing upon him a hundred slaves,
and entrusting him with unparalleled favor,
with all matters being decided by him.
However, his nature was too lenient,
and he handled matters with perfunctory simplicity,
unable to control the powerful and arrogant who acted without restraint.
Towards the end of Tiānlù,
Zhāgē's army attacked the imperial encampment,
and he was again unable to suppress them,
whereupon he was criticized both domestically and abroad.
When Mùzōng ascended the throne,
because of his role in establishing Shìzōng,
he was no longer given important responsibilities.
In Yìnglì 3,
someone falsely accused Āntuán of plotting rebellion with Qí Wáng Yǎnsāgē,
and he died in prison.
His nephew was Sājǐ,
the Zuǒ Píshì Xiángwěn.
Yēlǜ Wā,
courtesy name Díchǔ,
was the grandson of Suíguó Wáng Shìlǔ,
and the son of Southern Chancellery Yílíjǐn Wǎn Sī.
From a young age, he possessed insight and discernment;
people expected him to become a high minister.
During Tàizǔ's time,
though not yet an official,
he was often entrusted with affairs.
When Tàizōng ascended the throne,
he became Tìyǐn.
Towards the end of Tiānxiǎn,
the Emperor supported Hédōng,
and Wā served as the vanguard,
defeating Zhāng Jìngdá's army north of Tàiyuán.
During Huìtóng,
he was promoted to Northern Chancellery King.
When Jìn was again attacked,
he again served as vanguard,
and fought Xiáng Hànzhāng at Yíngzhōu,
defeating him.
the prefectures and commanderies of the south largely rebelled,
the soldiers and horses were exhausted and depleted,
and the army did not know what to do.
Wā and Yēlǜ Hǒu decided on the strategy to enthrone Shì zōng,
and then ordered the generals, saying:
"The Great Departed has ascended as a guest (of the heavens),
the sacred implements (of rule) have no master.
The Prince of Yǒngkāng, the legitimate eldest son of Rén huáng wáng,
is favored by Heaven and the people;
he ought to be established (as Emperor).
Those who do not comply
will be dealt with according to military law."
All the generals replied,
"Yes."
Shì zōng ascended the throne,
granted him fifty palace households,
and appointed him Yú yuè.
He died
at the age of fifty-four.
Yēlǜ Tuíyù,
courtesy name Tuánníng,
was a descendant of Mèngfù Chǔ guó wáng.
His father, Mòduō,
once served as Yílíjǐn.
Tuíyù was upright and straightforward by nature.
During the Huìtóng period,
he led the Jiǔshíliè tribe,
administering governance through a balance of leniency and strictness.
When Shì zōng ascended the throne,
he became Tìyǐn.
In the third year of Tiānlù (949 CE),
he concurrently held the post of Zhèngshì lìng,
and was enfeoffed as the Jùnwáng of Qīshuǐ.
When Mù zōng was established,
for his meritorious support,
he had previously been promised the title of Dàwáng of his original tribe.
Later, when Shì zōng was about to be interred,
Tuíyù pleaded with the Emperor, saying:
"Your servant received great grace from the preceding Emperor,
but I have not been able to repay it.
Fortunately, I can attend the grand funeral,
and I request permission to take a place (in the procession)."
The Emperor was displeased by this,
and dropped the matter.
He passed away.
Yēlǜ Tàliè,
courtesy name Nièlǔgǔn,
was a descendant of the Magistrate (Lángjūn) Niǎogǔzhí of the Liùyuàn Tribe.
He was serious, profound, and highly intelligent,
possessing the talent to bear heavy responsibilities.
He was forty years old before he held office.
During the Huìtóng period,
he served as Biānbù Lìngwěn.
In the beginning of Yìnglì,
he was promoted to Nányuàn Dàwáng,
equalizing taxes and corvée labor,
and encouraging cultivation and planting.
The tribesmen were transformed by his influence,
and the number of households increased greatly.
At that time, the Zhōu people (Later Zhōu) invaded Hàn (Northern Hàn),
and Tàliè was appointed General-in-Chief (Dū tǒng) of the Southwestern Circuit army to assist them.
Zhōu had already captured several cities around Tàiyuán,
and the Hàn people dared not fight.
When they heard Tàliè’s troops had arrived,
the Zhōu ruler dispatched Guō Cóngyì, Shàng Jūn, and others, leading elite cavalry to resist them at Xīnkǒu.
Tàliè defeated them in battle,
capturing their general Shǐ Yànchāo.
The Zhōu army fled back,
and the captured cities and towns were recovered.
The Hàn ruler went to Tàliè to offer thanks.
When the Hàn ruler passed away,
the Sòng army came to attack.
The Emperor commanded Tàliè to be the General-in-Chief of the Campaigning Army (Xíngjūn Dū tǒng),
sending troops from various circuits to rescue (Hàn).
After he emerged from Yànmén,
the Sòng spies learned of it and retreated.
In the first year of Bǎoníng (969 CE),
he was additionally granted the concurrent post of Zhèngshì lìng,
and retired from office.
At the beginning of Qiánhēng,
he was summoned.
The Emperor saw that his hair and beard were white,
but his vital energy was still strong.
He questioned him about governmental affairs
and treated him with great respect.
He passed away due to illness,
at the age of seventy-nine.
Whenever Tàliè commanded troops,
rewards and punishments were trustworthy and clear,
winning the hearts of the officers and soldiers.
That Hédōng, being isolated and weak,
was not annexed by Zhōu or Sòng,
Tàliè had a hand in it.
While in office, he paid little attention to his personal appearance,
but the people were without complaint,
and the harvests were consistently abundant.
At that time, Yēlǜ Wūzhì resided in the Northern Chancellery (Běiyuàn),
and Tàliè resided in the Southern Chancellery (Nányuàn).
Both had notable administrative achievements,
and the court consensus was that
he was a "Dàwáng who Enriched the People."
The Eulogy states: Establishing the heir by legitimacy
is the proper rite (Lǐ).
When Tài zōng died,
had Ān Tuán, Hǒu, and Wā not plotted and decisively acted,
devising the strategy to enthrone Shì zōng,
and had Wūzhì not been straightforward and able to remonstrate,
suppressing the self-interest of the Empress Dowager Dù,
and curbing the violence of Lǐ Hú,
thereby accomplishing the covenant of Héngdù,
then who would have stabilized the chaos?
These four officials
nearly achieved the merit of the initial stabilization lauded in the *Chūnqiū*.
Biographies, Chapter Eight: Yēlǜ Yīlàgě, Xiāo Hǎilí, Xiāo Hùsī, Xiāo Sīwēn, Xiāo Jìxiān
Yēlǜ Yīlàgě,
courtesy name Sūsǎn,
was a native of the Palace Division (Gōng fēn rén) and the son of the Acting Grand Preceptor (Jiǎnjiào Tài shī) Hélǔ.
In the beginning of Yìnglì,
he entered service based on his father's rank.
After several years,
he first served as Commander-in-Chief of the Palace Guard (Diànqián Dū Diǎnjiǎn).
At that time, the Emperor had just ascended the throne
and suspected the various princes of having rebellious intentions.
He brought Yīlàgě in as a commoner confidant,
and consulted him on all confidential matters.
He was promoted to Jìbān Dūzhī,
and granted palace households.
At that time, the Emperor was addicted to alcohol
and frequently killed people over minor offenses.
There was a Superintendent of Pheasants (Jiān zhì) who ran away after accidentally injuring a pheasant.
When he was captured and the Emperor intended to execute him,
Yīlàgě remonstrated, saying:
"This crime does not merit death."
The Emperor nevertheless killed him
and handed the corpse to Yīlàgě, saying:
"Take care of your old friend!"
Yīlàgě was ultimately unable to stop (the killing).
Furthermore, a Xiángwěn overseeing the deer lost a deer,
was imprisoned, and was due to die.
Yīlàgě again remonstrated, saying:
"Human life is extremely valuable;
how can a man be killed for the sake of one beast?"
After a long while,
the man was spared.
According to Liáo law,
only the Son of Heaven (Emperor) was permitted to shoot a stag
with branched antlers.
During a joint autumn hunt,
someone skilled in imitating deer calls summoned a stag to approach.
The Emperor ordered Yīlàgě to shoot it,
and the stag fell immediately upon the sound of the bowstring.
The Emperor was greatly pleased,
bestowed upon him one hundred *liǎng* of gold and one hundred *liǎng* of silver,
one hundred famous horses,
and the land of Mòzhēn east of Hēishān.
Later, when Mù zōng was assassinated,
Yīlàgě was implicated for his lax guarding duties
and was executed.
Xiāo Hǎilí,
courtesy name Yíndeshěn.
His ancestors served as Yílíjǐn of their tribe during the Yáoliǎn clan period.
His father, Tǎliè,
served as Lìngwěn of the tribe during the Tiānxiǎn period.
Hǎilí was physically imposing
and possessed superhuman strength.
During the Tiānlù period,
he married Princess Àiyīn, daughter of the Prince Míngwáng Ānduān.
In the beginning of Yìnglì,
because of Chá Gē's rebellion,
Àiyīn was implicated.
He subsequently married Princess Cháoguī.
The Emperor regarded him as a close relative
and commended his diligence and faithfulness.
He was ordered to be considered for selection as Chancellor of the Northern Chancellery (Běifǔ Zǎixiàng).
Soon after,
he took overall charge of military and state affairs.
At that time, many princes were implicated in rebellion.
Hǎilí was known for being honest and cautious,
and he understood the mechanisms of government.
Whenever he was ordered to investigate a case,
he usually succeeded in uncovering the truth,
and no one suffered injustice.
Because of this, he became well-known.
The Hàn ruler Liú Chéngjūn often sent envoys to offer tribute.
He always separately presented gifts and valuables (to Hǎilí),
and an imperial decree permitted him to accept them.
He died at the age of fifty.
The Emperor lamented and mourned him,
suspending court for two days.
Xiāo Hùsī, courtesy name Yánníng.
His family had for generations served as officials in the Northern Chancellery (Běiyuàn).
He was successively promoted to Palace Deputy Censor-in-Chief (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng),
and took overall charge of the registers of the herds and flocks.
, he was promoted to Zuǒ Kèshěng Shǐ
. Before long
, he was appointed Yùshǐ Dàfū
. At that time
, many princes were imprisoned due to various offenses.
The Emperor, seeing that Hùsī (護思) possessed talent and capability
, ordered a thorough investigation.
He satisfied the Emperor’s wishes.
He was appointed Běiyuàn Shūmì Shǐ,
and furthermore, it was decreed that his descendants should be eligible for selection as chief ministers.
Hùsī declined, saying:
“The worthiness of my sons and grandsons is yet unknown;
to obtain the rank of Kèshěng Shǐ is sufficient
.” The Emperor agreed.
In the Emperor’s later years, he indulged heavily in alcohol
and often administered punishments excessively.
Although Hùsī occupied an important position
, he merely protected himself
and never offered a single word of correction or rescue
. Commentators therefore belittled him for this.
He died at the age of fifty-seven
Xiāo Sīwēn (蕭思溫),
courtesy name Yíngǔ (寅古),
was the son of Hūmòlǐ (忽沒里), who was a cousin of the chief minister Dílǔ (敵魯).
He was well-versed in texts and history.
During the reign of Tàizōng (太宗), he served as Xītúlǐ Tàiwèi (奚禿里太尉)
and married the Yānguó Gōngzhǔ (燕國公主).
He served as Qúnmù Dū Línyá (羣牧都林牙).
While Sīwēn was in the military
, he was meticulous and highly self-disciplined.
His colleagues all said he lacked the talent of a commander.
Soon after, he became Nánjīng Liúshǒu (南京留守).
Previously
, when the people of Zhōu (周) attacked Yángzhōu (揚州)
, the Emperor sent Sīwēn to follow closely behind them.
Fearing the heat, he dared not advance
, but he captured several border towns before returning.
Later, the Zhōu army invaded
and besieged Fēngmǔ Zhèn (馮母鎮)
, displaying great strength.
Sīwēn requested reinforcements.
The Emperor replied
: “If the enemy comes
, join forces with the Tǒngjūnsī (統軍司) to resist them;
if the enemy leaves
, focus on agricultural production
and do not exhaust the troops and horses.”
Coincidentally, the enemy entered Shùchéng (束城)
, and our army retreated, crossed the Hūtuó (滹沱) River, and set up camp.
Sīwēn constrained his troops and proceeded slowly
. The Zhōu army remained motionless for several days.
Sīwēn discussed this with his generals, saying
: “The enemy is numerous and sharp.
If we fight unsuccessfully, there will be future trouble.
It is better to halt our troops to wear out their army
, then follow and strike them
, ensuring victory
.” The generals agreed.
Consequently, he met with the forces of the Tǒngjūnsī
and fabricated a request for further reinforcements.
The Zhōu forces withdrew
, and Sīwēn also returned
. Not long after
, the ruler of Zhōu invaded the north again
