, advancing along separate routes with his generals Fù Yuánqīng (傅元卿) and Lǐ Chóngjìn (李崇進), among others.
They besieged Yíngzhōu (瀛州)
and captured the three passes: Yìjīn (益津), Wǎqiáo (瓦橋), and Yūkǒu (淤口).
They were almost upon Gù'ān (固安).
Sīwēn did not know what strategy to adopt
, saying only that the imperial carriage would arrive momentarily.
The soldiers under his command eagerly begged to fight
, but he did not permit it
. Soon after
, Yì (易), Yíng, Mò (莫), and other prefectures fell.
The people in the capital region, Jīngjī (京畿), were all terrified
, often fleeing into the Xīshān (西山) mountains.
Sīwēn, due to the failure of the border defenses
, feared the court would punish him
, and submitted a memorial requesting the Emperor to personally lead the campaign.
Coincidentally, the ruler of Zhōu, Róng (榮), returned due to illness.
Sīwēn retreated to Yìjīn
and falsely claimed ignorance of the enemy’s whereabouts.
He encountered over two thousand foot soldiers coming to resist him
and defeated them.
That year
, upon hearing of the death of the Zhōu ruler
, the people of Yān (燕) finally felt secure
, and he withdrew his army.
At that time, Mùzōng (穆宗) was habitually drunk and fond of killing.
Although Sīwēn participated in government as a close imperial relative
, he offered no assistance or correction
. Public opinion did not favor him.
In the nineteenth year
, during the spring hunt
, the Emperor shot a bear and hit it.
Sīwēn, along with Yílíbì Yálǐsī (夷離畢牙里斯) and others, offered wine to wish the Emperor longevity.
The Emperor, drunk, returned to the palace.
That night
, he was assassinated by the cook Sīnúgǔ (斯奴古) and others.
Sīwēn, along with Nányuàn Shūmì Shǐ Gāo Xūn (南院樞密使高勳) and Fēilóng Shǐ Nǚ Lǐ (飛龍使女里), among others, established Jǐngzōng (景宗) on the throne.
In the early years of Bǎoníng (保寧)
, he became Běiyuàn Shūmì Shǐ
, simultaneously serving as Běifǔ Zǎixiàng (北府宰相).
It was further decreed that his descendants should be eligible for selection for these roles.
The Emperor appointed Sīwēn’s daughter as Empress
, granted him the title of Shàngshū Lìng (尚書令)
, and enfeoffed him as Wèi Wáng (魏王).
While accompanying the Emperor on a hunt at Lǘ Shān (閭山)
, he was murdered by bandits
. Xiāo Jìxiān (蕭繼先)
, courtesy name Yángyǐn (楊隱)
, childhood name Liúzhǐgē (留只哥).
He was sharp and intelligent as a child.
His uncle Sīwēn designated him as his son
, and Empress Ruìzhì (睿智皇后) especially cherished him.
In the early years of Qiángēng (乾亨)
, he married the Qíguó Gōngzhǔ (齊國公主)
and was appointed Fùmǎ Dūwèi (駙馬都尉).
In the fourth year of Tǒnghé (統和)
, when the Sòng (宋) people invaded
, Jìxiān led his reconnaissance cavalry to intercept them at the border
and captured many prisoners.
The Emperor praised him
and appointed him Běifǔ Zǎixiàng.
From then on, whenever an army was dispatched
, Jìxiān would surely lead the troops from his own administration to follow first.
He captured the stone fort at Lángshān (狼山)
and participated in defeating the Sòng army at Yìngzhōu (應州).
When the Emperor campaigned south to seize Tōnglì Jūn (通利軍)
, his efforts in battle were hailed as swift and powerful.
When the Emperor personally campaigned against Gāolì (高麗)
, Jìxiān was deemed too old
and was left to guard Shàngjīng (上京).
He died
at the age of fifty-eight.
Although Jìxiān occupied a position of wealth and honor
, he advocated frugality and simplicity.
Wherever he served, he was known for his good governance.
Therefore, when leading troops in attack and battle
, he never suffered a defeat
, and his reputation was highly valued among the imperial relatives.
Commentary says: Alas!
Of the faults of a ruler
, none is greater than killing the innocent.
When Tāng (湯) waged war against Jié (桀)
, he enumerated his crimes, saying
: “He has charged the innocent before the gods of heaven and earth.”
When Wǔ Wáng (武王) waged war against Zhòu (紂)
, he enumerated his crimes, saying
: “The innocent cry out to Heaven.”
When Yáo (堯) waged war against the Miáomín (苗民)
, Lǚ Hóu (呂侯) posthumously enumerated their crimes, saying
: “They slaughtered the innocent.”
Judging by these words
, the counsel of Yílàgě (夷臘葛)
was awe-inspiring and closely approached the style of the ancient virtuous gentlemen.
Nevertheless
, those skilled in remonstrance do not remonstrate regarding what is already done.
They must first address the subtle root of the mental disposition
, like a pulse diagnostician
who treats the ailment before it takes hold
; then success is easily achieved.
Mùzōng's addiction to drink and moral decline
was surely due to having long relied on his status of wealth and power to indulge himself.
If his ministers, in the course of his every action and movement
, had offered continuous remonstrance and counsel
, raising their voices to warn him
and prevent his excess
, how could it have come to this?
From this, we know that Hùsī and Sīwēn, occupying high and important positions
, indulged in stipends and sought favor
; they were truly base fellows!
As for Hǎilí’s (海瓈) clear judgments in legal cases
and Jìxiān’s good governance
, they can be called capable officials.
Collected Biographies, Number Nine: Shì Fǎng (室昉), Yēlǜ Xiánshì (耶律賢適), Nǚ Lǐ, Guō Xí (郭襲), Yēlǜ Āmòlǐ (耶律阿沒里).
Shì Fǎng
, courtesy name Mèngqí (夢奇)
, was a native of Nánjīng.
From childhood, he was cautious, honest, and dedicated to study.
He did not leave his home for twenty years
, such that even his neighbors did not recognize him.
His dedication was thus profound.
Huìtóng era,
he passed the *jìnshì* examination,
and served as the Lúlóng Patrol Officer.
When Tàizōng entered Biàn to receive the investiture ceremony,
an imperial edict appointed Fǎng as Zhī Zhìgào,
managing all ceremonial affairs.
During the Tiānlù era,
he served as the Nánjīng Liúshǒu Pànguān.
During the Yìnglì period,
he was repeatedly promoted to Hànlín Xuéshì,
serving within the Forbidden Precincts for over ten years.
During the Bǎoníng period,
he also held the post of Zhèngshì Shèrén.
He was frequently summoned and questioned regarding the successes and failures of governance and disorder, past and present,
and his memorials and replies accorded with the imperial will.
The Emperor greatly appreciated Fǎng's talent for handling complex affairs,
and changed his post to Nánjīng Deputy Liúshǒu.
He judged lawsuits fairly and justly,
which benefited everyone.
He was promoted to Gōngbù Shàngshū,
and shortly thereafter changed to Shūmì Fùshǐ,
and Cānzhī Zhèngshì.
After a short while,
he was appointed Shūmì Shǐ,
concurrently Běifǔ Zǎixiàng,
and given the additional title Tóng Zhèngshì Ménxià Píngzhāng Shì.
In the beginning of the Gānhēng era,
he supervised the compilation of the National History.
In the first year of Tǒnghé,
he requested retirement due to old age,
but was refused.
He presented the *Shàngshū Wúyì Piān* (Chapter on Avoiding Ease) as a remonstrance,
and the Tàihòu heard of it and praised him.
In the autumn of the second year,
an edict ordered the repair of all mountain roads.
Fǎng mobilized two hundred thousand civilian laborers,
and completed the work in one day.
At this time,
Fǎng was on friendly terms with Hán Déràng and Yēlǜ Xiézhěn,
and they aided the government with one mind,
streamlining and analyzing detrimental abuses.
If they knew something, they did not fail to speak of it,
and worked diligently to bring relief to the people and lighten taxes.
Due to this, laws and regulations were reformed and made clear,
and there was no dissent at court.
In the eighth year,
he again requested to retire from public life.
An imperial edict permitted him to attend court without kneeling,
bestowed a small table and a staff upon him,
and the Tàihòu sent the Gémén Shǐ Lǐ Cóngxùn bearing an edict to convey appreciation and inquire after his health.
He was ordered to reside permanently in Nánjīng,
and was enfeoffed as Zhèng Guó Gōng.
Previously,
Jìn Guó Gōngzhǔ established a Buddhist monastery in Nánjīng,
and the Emperor permitted the granting of a plaque (imperial title).
Fǎng memorialized, saying:
"The imperial edict previously condemned all unregistered monasteries.
Now, if we grant a plaque based on the Princess's request,
not only does it violate the former edict,
but I fear this trend will become even more rampant."
The Emperor agreed with him.
He submitted the twenty scrolls of the *Shílù* (Veritable Records) he had compiled.
The Emperor honored him with a personally written edict,
added the title Zhèngshì Lìng,
and bestowed six hundred rolls of silk.
In the ninth year,
he recommended Hán Déràng as his replacement,
but this was not followed.
Because the Emperor knew Fǎng was elderly and suffered from the cold,
he bestowed sable fur quilts and blankets,
and permitted him to ride in a carriage when attending court.
When his illness worsened,
the Hànlín Xuéshì Zhāng Gàn was dispatched to his residence to confer upon him the title of Zhōngjīng Liúshǒu,
with the additional title Shàngfù.
He died
at the age of seventy-five.
The Emperor lamented his passing,
suspended court for two days,
and posthumously granted him the title Shàngshū Lìng.
His dying words cautioned against an elaborate funeral.
Fearing that others would overpraise him,
he wrote his own tomb inscription.
Yēlǜ Xiánshì,
courtesy name Āgǔzhēn,
was the son of the Yúyuè Lǔbùgǔ.
He was fond of learning and harbored great ambitions,
yet he was witty and flippant about the world,
so few understood him.
Only the Yúyuè Wūzhì appreciated his ability.
He once said to others:
"If this man governs the country,
it will be a great fortune for the realm."
During the Yìnglì era,
many court officials incurred censure due to their speech.
Xiánshì found pleasure in quiet retreat,
entertaining himself with hunting,
and when speaking with relatives and friends, he never touched upon current affairs.
When he returned from the campaign against the Wūgǔ,
he was promoted to Yòu Píshì Xiángwěn.
When Jǐngzōng was in the Fāndǐ,
he often associated with Hán Kuāngsì and Nǚlǐ.
His words occasionally contained sarcasm or criticism.
Xiánshì advised him to promptly distance himself from them.
Because of this, Mùzōng never suspected him in the end,
which was due to Xiánshì's effort.
When Jǐngzōng ascended the throne,
for his merit, he was granted the additional title Jiǎnxiào Tàibǎo,
and shortly thereafter was remotely appointed Níngjiāng Jūn Jiédùshǐ,
and bestowed the honorary title Tuī Zhōng Xiélì Gōngchén.
At that time, the Emperor had just ascended the throne,
and was greatly suspicious that the various princes might harbor rebellious ambitions.
He secretly treated Xiánshì as his confidant,
and added the title Tèjìn Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāng Shì.
In the autumn of the second year of Bǎoníng,
he was appointed Běiyuàn Shūmì Shǐ,
concurrently Shìzhōng,
and bestowed the honorary title Bǎojié Gōngchén.
In the third year,
he became the Xīběi Lù Bīngmǎ Dū Bùshǔ.
Xiánshì was loyal, straightforward, and astute.
He treated others with utmost sincerity,
and even when resting he did not forget government affairs.
For this reason, all officials in charge of departments
dared not be lazy or neglectful,
and delayed lawsuits that had dragged on for years were all resolved.
The Dà Chéngxiàng Gāo Xūn and the Qìdān Xínggōng Dū Bùshǔ Nǚlǐ relied on imperial favor to act unrestrainedly,
and the Emperor's maternal aunt and wet nurse wielded immense influence.
At that time, people offered bribes and sought interviews,
making their gates look like market districts.
Xiánshì was concerned about this,
and spoke to the Emperor,
but received no response.
He tried to resign on account of illness,
but this was also disallowed,
and he was ordered to continue his duties using a cast hand-seal.
In the beginning of the Gānhēng era,
his illness became critical,
and he finally obtained permission (to retire).
The following year,
he was enfeoffed as Xīpíng Jùnwáng,
and died
at the age of fifty-three.
His son, Guānyīn,
was the Dàtóng Jūn Jiédùshǐ.
Nǚlǐ,
courtesy name Nièliègǔn,
his clan name is lost.
He was appointed as a servant in the Jìqìng Gōng.
In the beginning of the Yìnglì era,
he was Xímǎ Xiǎodǐ (an apprentice groom).
He left due to mourning his mother.
One day he went to Yǎbó Shān,
and saw a giant.
He fled in panic.
The giant stopped him and said:
"Do not fear.
I am the Earth Spirit.
Bury your mother here,
and you must quickly go to the Palace;
you will certainly achieve nobility."
Nǚlǐ followed this advice,
and was repeatedly promoted to Mǎqún Shìzhōng.
At the time Jǐngzōng was in the Fāndǐ,
because Nǚlǐ originated from that same residence,
he was treated with exceptional generosity,
and Nǚlǐ likewise devoted himself to fostering relations.
When Mùzōng was assassinated,
Nǚlǐ rushed to Jǐngzōng.
That night,
he gathered five hundred palace guards to protect him.
After Jǐngzōng ascended the throne,
due to his merit in assisting the succession,
Nǚlǐ was granted the additional titles Zhèngshì Lìng and Qìdān Xínggōng Dū Bùshǔ.
He was extremely richly rewarded.
Soon after, he was given the additional title Shǒu Tàiwèi.
Liú Jìyuán, ruler of Northern Hàn, heard that Nǚlǐ was trusted by the Emperor
and would always send gifts on Nǚlǐ’s birthday.
Nǚlǐ was habitually greedy,
and his colleague Xiāo Ābùdǐ was also fond of bribes.
The two were on good terms.
If someone's felt coat or fur garment was covered with burrs,
people would jokingly say:
"If Nǚlǐ and Ābùdǐ encounter you,
they will certainly take every last one!"
This anecdote spread as a source of laughter.
His rapacious greed was like this.
Towards the end of the Bǎoníng era,
he was implicated for secretly possessing five hundred sets of armor.
When the authorities were investigating him,
a letter concerning the murder of the Shūmì Shǐ Xiāo Sīwēn was found hidden in Nǚlǐ's sleeve,
and he was sentenced to death.
Nǚlǐ was good at judging horses.
Once, when traveling in the countryside,
he saw several hoof prints.
He pointed to one and said:
"This belongs to a truly superb steed!"
He exchanged his own horse for the one that made the print,
and it proved to be true.
Guō Xī,
was from an unknown prefecture.
His nature was upright and proper,
and he understood the principles of governance.
He was long delayed in minor external postings.
When Jǐngzōng ascended the throne,
he was summoned for an audience.
His responses accorded with the emperor's wishes,
who recognized that he could be entrusted with responsibilities.
He was appointed Minister of the Southern Chūmì Institute (Shūmìshǐ).
Soon after, he was additionally granted the concurrent post of Director of Political Affairs (Zhèngshìlìng).
Because the Emperor frequently went hunting,
Xī submitted a memorial advising against it, saying:
“In the past, when Táng Gāozǔ was fond of hunting,
Sū Shìcháng stated that less than ten periods of ten days (shùn) was not enough to consider it enjoyment.
Gāozǔ immediately ceased the activity that day,
and historians praise this virtue.
I humbly reflect that the Sacred Ancestor (Shèngzǔ) faced great difficulty in founding the state,
cultivating virtue and promulgating policies,
working diligently day and night without slackening.
Mùzōng indulged his insatiable desires,
and failed to attend to state affairs,
causing distress and resentment throughout the land.
When Your Majesty succeeded to the rule, the whole country eagerly looked forward to a revival of good governance (zhōngxīng zhī zhì).
Over the past ten or more years,
campaigns have not ceased,
yet bandits and rebels have not been suppressed;
though harvests have been good,
the scars and wounds [of the people] have not yet healed.
It is precisely the time to be cautious, fearful, and to examine oneself and cultivate virtue,
in order to ensure a lasting future.
I have heard that Your Majesty indulges in hunting,
more so than in former days.
Should there unfortunately be a peril of being injured by antlers (xián zhī biàn),
or the danger of being mauled (bóshì zhī yú),
what use will regret be?
Moreover, there is a powerful enemy to the south watching for opportunities to act;
hearing of this, would it not give them designs [against us]?
I humbly implore Your Majesty to restrain the pleasures of pursuing game and drinking wine (cóngqín hānyǐn zhī lè),
for the sake of the common people and the altars of the land (shèjì).
Then there will be boundless prosperity.”
The Emperor read it, praised its excellence,
and bestowed upon him the title 'Collaborative and Assisting Meritorious Official' (Xiézàn Gōngchén).
He was appointed Military Commissioner (Jiédùshǐ) of Wǔdìng Prefecture,
and then died.
Yēlǜ Āmèilǐ,
courtesy name Púlín,
was the fourth-generation descendant of Yáoliěn Cháogǔ Kèhán.
He was intelligent and keen in his youth.
During the Bǎoníng era, he served as the Commissioner of the Southern Xuānhuī Institute (Xuānhuīshǐ).
In the beginning of the Tǒnghé era,
when the Empress Dowager assumed the regency (chēng zhì),
he participated in state discussions (guólùn) with Yēlǜ Xiézhěn,
and was appointed Grand Commander (Dūtǒng).
For his merit in the campaign against Gāolì,
he was promoted to Commissioner of the Northern Xuānhuī Institute,
and additionally granted the post of Director of Political Affairs.
In the spring of the fourth year,
the Sòng generals Cáo Bīn, Mǐ Xìn, and others invaded Yān.
The Emperor personally led the campaign,
with Āmèilǐ serving as Inspector General (Dūjiān).
They repeatedly defeated the enemy forces.
In the twelfth year,
there were many thieves where the court resided (xíngzài).
Āmèilǐ established a law prohibiting and apprehending them,
and the thievery then ceased.
Before this,
in families of rebels,
brothers who were unaware of the plot were also implicated (liánzuò).
Āmèilǐ advised against this, saying:
“Although brothers are of the same womb (tóngbāo),
their natures are distinct.
If one executes a rebellious plan,
and the others, though unaware,
are nevertheless punished by law,
this is punishing the innocent.
From now on,
even brothers living together,
if unaware of the plot, shall be exempted from implication.”
The Empress Dowager praised and accepted this,
and had it established as law.
He retired due to old age,
and died.
Āmèilǐ was fond of accumulation and gathering wealth (jùliǎn).
Every time he participated in a campaign, he would gather the captured people (rénkǒu),
and assemble them to establish a city.
He requested it be named Fēngzhōu,
and immediately appointed his household slave, Yán Guì, as Prefect (Cìshǐ).
The opinions of the time disdained this.
His son, Xiángē,
was the Grand Minister of the Left (Zuǒ Yílíbì).
The appraisal states: During the reign of Jǐngzōng,
people looked forward to a revival (zhōngxīng).
Was this because he diligently worked on all state matters (shùjī)?
Rather, having succeeded Mùzōng's drunken tyranny (yìngnuè zhī yú),
doing good was easily apparent.
It was also due to the presence of many worthy ministers
who assisted and harmonized with the court.
Shì Fǎng presented the chapter on 'Avoidance of Ease' (Wú Yìl zhī piān),
Guō Xī submitted the memorial advising against hunting (jiànliè zhī shū),
and Āmèilǐ requested the exemption of relatives from implication (tóngqì zhī zuò).
These are what are called the words of benevolent men,
and their benefit is extensive indeed.
Xián Shì was loyal and proper,
also a famous official of recent times.
Nǚ Lǐ was greedy and vulgar,
someone from whom later generations should draw a lesson.
Biographical Account 10: Zhāng Jiǎn, Xíng Bǎopǔ, Mǎ Déchén, Xiāo Pǔ, Yēlǜ Bāgē.
Zhāng Jiǎn,
a native of Wǎnpíng,
was upright and honest,
and did not engage in outward show.
In the fourteenth year of Tǒnghé,
he achieved the highest rank in the civil service examination (jìnshì),
and was appointed an auxiliary official (mùguān) in Yúnzhōu.
According to custom,
when the imperial carriage passed through,
the local chief official should offer something.
When Shèngzōng hunted in Yúnzhōng,
the Military Commissioner advanced and said:
“Within my territory, there are no other products;
only my auxiliary official Zhāng Jiǎn,
a treasure of his generation.
I wish to present him as an offering.”
Previously,
the Emperor had dreamed that four men attended him,
and he bestowed upon each man two mouths of food (kǒu).
Upon hearing Jiǎn's name,
he suddenly understood the dream.
He summoned him for an audience.
His demeanor and deportment were simple and rustic.
When asked about contemporary state affairs (shìwù),
he reported and memorialized on more than thirty topics.
From this, the Emperor treated him with exceptional regard,
and he advanced through prestigious posts,
renowned for his clear competence.
During the Kāitài era,
he was successively promoted to Deputy Commissioner of the Chūmì Institute (Tóngzhī Shūmìyuàn Shì).
In the fifth year of Tàipíng,
he was sent out to serve as the Military Commissioner of Wǔdìng Prefecture,
and then transferred to govern Dàtóng.
In the sixth year,
he was recalled to serve as Minister of the Southern Chūmì Institute.
The Emperor greatly favored and relied upon him.
Wú Shūdá, who participated in managing political affairs (Cānzhī Zhèngshì), did not get along with Jiǎn.
The Emperor grew angry,
dismissed Shūdá to be the Prefect of Kāngzhōu,
and appointed Jiǎn Left Chancellor (Zuǒ Chéngxiàng),
and enfeoffed him as King of Hán (Hán Wáng).
When the Emperor became ill,
he received the dying instructions to assist in establishing the Crown Prince,
who became Xīngzōng.
He was bestowed the title 'Loyal, Upright, Vastly Tranquil, Safeguarding Righteousness, Maintaining Integrity, Venerable Virtue Meritorious Official' (Zhēnliàng Hóngjìng Bǎoyì Shǒujié Qídé Gōngchén),
appointed Grand Tutor (Tàishī) and Director of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Lìng),
and given the honorific title Shàngfù.
He was transferred to be the King of Chén.
In the fifth year of Chóngxī,
when the Emperor visited the Ministry of Rites examination hall (gòngyuàn) and personally tested the civil service candidates,
it was Jiǎn who initiated all of this.
When granted an audience, he was not referred to by his personal name (bùmíng).
The Emperor bestowed a poem praising his excellence.
Jiǎn's clothing consisted only of coarse silk (chóubó),
and his meals were not doubled in variety.
When his monthly salary had a surplus,
he used it to aid relatives and old acquaintances.
In the middle of winter,
when he presented memorials in the side hall (biàndiàn),
the Emperor saw that his robe was worn and shabby.
He secretly ordered a close attendant to use fire tongs to clip and burn holes to mark it,
but saw that it was repeatedly not changed.
The Emperor asked the reason,
and Jiǎn replied:
“Your servant has worn this robe for thirty years.”
As the fashion of the time was extravagant and luxurious (shēmǐ),
he used this subtle manner to admonish them.
The Emperor pitied his integrity and poverty (qīngpín),
and ordered him to take whatever he wished from the Imperial Treasury (nèifǔ).
Jiǎn accepted the decree and left with three bolts of cloth (bù sān duān),
which earned him even greater praise and respect.
Jiǎn had five younger brothers.
The Emperor wanted to grant them all the rank of advanced scholar (jìnshì dì),
but Jiǎn firmly declined.
The relevant authorities captured eight thieves.
After executing them,
the actual ringleader was then caught.
The families appealed their injustice (yuān).
Jiǎn thrice pleaded for the case to be reviewed (shēnlǐ).
The Emperor angrily said:
“Do you want me to pay for their lives (chángmìng)!”
Jiǎn replied:
“The elderly and young of the eight families have no one to appeal to.
If Your Majesty shows a little care and solicitude for them,
allowing them to collect and bury the bodies,
it would be enough to comfort both the living and the deceased (cún mò).”
The Emperor then complied.
Jiǎn held the position of Chancellor for more than twenty years,
and his contributions were extensive.
He retired from governance and returned to his mansion.
It happened that Sòng's letters were lacking in propriety,
and the Emperor was about to lead a personal expedition.
He visited Jiǎn's mansion.
The Director of Imperial Cuisine (Shàngshí) went ahead to prepare the feast,
but he refused it.
He presented mallow soup and dry rice.
The Emperor ate it and found it excellent.
He slowly asked him for strategy.
Jiǎn fully presented the advantages and disadvantages,
and further said:
"You need only dispatch an envoy to question them,
why must you fatigue the imperial carriage by traveling far?"
The Emperor was pleased and stopped the plan.
He later went to his mansion again and granted a banquet,
giving him all the vessels and trinkets.
In the twenty-second year, he passed away.
He was ninety-one years old.
An imperial decree ordered him to be buried in Wǎnpíng Xiàn.
Xíng Bàopǔ,
was a man from Yīngzhōu,
and the son of Xíngbù Lángzhōng Jiǎn.
Bàopǔ was naturally intelligent and perceptive,
fond of learning, and widely knowledgeable about antiquity.
Early in the Bǎoníng era,
he served as Zhèngshì Shèrén and Zhī Zhìgào.
He was successively promoted to Hànlín Xuéshì,
and granted the title of Lǐbù Shìláng.
In the fourth year of Tǒnghé,
the prefectures and counties of Shānxī were ravaged by war.
Bàopǔ was ordered to pacify and comfort them.
The people began to settle down,
and he was granted the title of Hùbù Shàngshū.
He was promoted to Hànlín Xuéshì Chéngzhǐ,
and together with Shì Fǎng, he compiled the Veritable Records.
When he returned after settling the backlog of cases in Nánjīng,
he received a distinguished imperial edict praising him.
In the tenth year,
he was appointed Cānzhī Zhèngshì.
Following the recommendation of the Grand Councilor Hán Déràng,
he investigated the competency of the prefects and magistrates across various circuits and either dismissed or promoted them.
This greatly met public expectation.
Soon after, he resigned his post due to mourning for his mother.
An edict ordered him to resume his duties.
He presented a memorial requesting to complete the mourning period,
but this was not followed.
The chief ministers secretly relayed the Emperor's intention,
whereupon he resumed his duties.
People praised him for his filial piety.
When Yēlǜ Xiūgē served as the Resident General of Nánjīng,
there was again a large accumulation of unsettled legal cases.
An edict once more ordered Bàopǔ to settle and resolve them.
No one suffered injustice.
He was transferred to be the Nányuàn Shūmìshǐ,
and died.
He was posthumously granted Shìzhōng.
Previously,
Bàopǔ and his younger brother, Bàozhì, studied the classics under their mother, Lady Chén.
Both became prominent through Confucian scholarship.
Bàozhì also achieved the office of Shìzhōng.
People of the time honored them.
Mǎ Déchén,
a man from Nánjīng,
was fond of learning and knowledgeable about antiquity,
skilled at writing,
especially adept at poetry.
During the Bǎoníng era,
he was successively promoted to Zhèngshì Shèrén and Hànlín Xuéshì.
He often participated in court deliberations,
and was praised for his uprightness.
Early in the Qiánhēng era,
since the Sòng armies repeatedly violated the border,
he was ordered to serve as the Deputy Resident General of Nánjīng,
and later reappointed as Hànlín Xuéshì Chéngzhǐ.
When Shèngzōng ascended the throne,
the Empress Dowager assumed regency.
He also served as Shìdú Xuéshì.
The Emperor reviewed the annals of Táng Gāozǔ, Tàizōng, and Xuánzōng (the Three Reigns).
Déchén then recorded the deeds that could serve as models and presented them.
When he accompanied the Emperor on the expedition against Sòng,
he advanced the opinion that those who surrendered should not be killed,
those who flee should not be pursued,
and those who are fickle in their loyalty should be separately considered.
An edict mandated compliance with this.
Soon after, he concurrently served as Jiànyì Dàfū,
and Zhī Xuānhuī Yuàn Shì.
At that time, the Emperor indulged excessively in polo.
He submitted a memorial remonstrating, saying: "Your subject humbly observes that Fáng Xuánlíng and Dù Rúhuì,
were mere scholars at the end of the Suí dynasty.
If they had not met Tàizōng,
how could they have become famous chancellors of an age?
Although your subject is untalented,
when Your
Majesty was in the Eastern Palace,
I was fortunate enough to be counted among your attendants.
Now I am again permitted to attend the sacred reading,
yet I have not yet been able to aid Your sagacity.
Your Majesty once asked your subject about the affairs of Zhēnguān and Kāiyuán.
Your subject requests permission to briefly present them.
Your subject has heard that when Táng Tàizōng finished attending the Supreme Emperor at a banquet,
he would pull the imperial carriage to the inner chamber.
Xuánzōng, when happily drinking with his brothers,
observed all the rites due to family members.
Your Majesty inherits
the legacy of your ancestors,
and personally attends the Empress Dowager.
This can be called the highest filial piety.
Your subject further hopes that, besides the morning and evening greetings,
you will harmonize the six types of relatives,
and increase love and respect for them.
Then Your Majesty's way of cherishing relatives,
will rival that of those two emperors.
Your subject also heard that those two emperors immersed themselves in the classics and histories,
frequently summoning dukes and ministers to discuss scholarship,
lasting until late afternoon.
Therefore, the world at that time unanimously inclined toward these examples,
thus promoting cultured
governance.
Now Your Majesty directs your heart toward the canons and records,
analyzing chapters and sentences.
Your subject wishes you to investigate the principles of the classics,
delve deeply into them, and earnestly practice them.
The governance of the two emperors would then not be difficult to achieve.
Your subject also heard that when Tàizōng shot a boar,
Táng Jiǎn remonstrated with him.
When Xuánzōng carried a hawk on his arm,
Hán Xiū spoke out against it.
Neither of the two emperors failed to joyfully comply.
Now Your Majesty takes pleasure in polo and horses,
your foolish subject considers this,
and finds three points of impropriety.
Therefore, I do not shrink from the ax and battle-ax to speak of it.
I humbly believe that when ruler and minister play together,
they cannot avoid rivalry and contention.
If the ruler wins, the minister is ashamed;
if one loses, the other rejoices.
This is the first impropriety.
Leaping on horses and wielding sticks,
galloping wildly back and forth,
disregarding the distinction between high and low,
struggling to be first and obtain victory,
violates the propriety due from a minister.
This is the second
impropriety.
Taking lightly the dignity of the Son of Heaven,
seeking momentary pleasure,
if by chance there is a mishap with the bridle or reins,
what would happen to the state and the Empress Dowager?
This is the third impropriety.
Should Your
Majesty not consider your subject's words impractical,
and graciously grant them a brief review,
it would be a blessing for the realm,
and the desire of your ministers."
After the memorial was presented,
the Emperor praised and sighed admiringly for a long time.
Not long after, he died.
He was posthumously granted Tàizǐ Tàibǎo.
An edict instructed the appropriate office to provide funeral arrangements.
Xiāo Pǔ,
courtesy name Yánníng,
was a member of the clan of the maternal uncle (Guójìu) Shàofù Fáng.
His father, Láo Gǔ,
was skilled at writing,
and served as a poetry companion to Shèngzōng.
Pǔ, even in youth, was like an experienced adult.
When he grew up,
he was widely learned and highly intelligent.
reign period, he was appointed *Pái'yìn Lángjūn*.
He served as *Nányuàn Chéngzhǐ*,
and temporarily managed the affairs of the *Zhuǎnyùn Shì*.
Soon after, he was transferred to *Nánmiàn Línyá*.
The Emperor questioned him regarding governance.
*Pǔ* fully laid out the sufferings of the common people
and the sufficiency or depletion of state finances.
The Emperor was pleased and said:
"I have found the right man!"
He was promoted to *Zuǒ Yílíbì*.
At that time, Xiāo Hézhuō was the *Shūmìshǐ*.
*Pǔ* managed the affairs of the Bureau of Deployment (*Bùshǔ Yuàn Shì*),
but neglected his duties due to drinking,
and was sent out to be the Military Governor (*Jiédùshǐ*) of Xīngguó Jūn.
Soon after, he was recalled to serve as *Nánmiàn Línyá*.
In the third year of *Tàipíng* (1023),
he was appointed Acting Grand Mentor of the Crown Prince (*Tàizǐ Tàifù*).
The following year,
he was appointed Prime Minister of the Northern Administration (*Běifǔ Zǎixiàng*),
and later transferred to *Běiyuàn Shūmìshǐ*.
As the era of *Tàipíng* had lasted a long time,
the Emperor devoted his attention to literature and painting,
and began drawing up genealogies (*pǔdié*) to distinguish between legitimate and illegitimate lineage (*díshù*).
Because of this, disputes and lawsuits arose frequently.
*Pǔ* possessed administrative talent,
and could grasp the intentions of the ruler.
His presentations and reports were satisfying to the Emperor,
and the court deliberations often deferred to his judgment.
He was enfeoffed as the Prince of Lánlíng Jùn,
promoted to Prince (*Wáng*),
and given the additional title of *Zhōngshū Lìng*.
When Dà Yánlín rebelled,
an edict ordered him to pacify Dōngjīng (the Eastern Capital),
and to act according to expediency.
When Xīngzōng ascended the throne,
the Empress Dowager served as regent (*chēngzhì*),
and all state affairs were entrusted to her younger brother, Xiāo Xiàoxiān.
At this time, Empress Fāng Réndé had been wrongly framed and killed by Fēng Jiānú.
*Pǔ* repeatedly spoke about her injustice,
but received no response.
Whenever he thought of this,
he would vomit blood.
In the beginning of *Chóngxī*,
his princely title was changed to Prince of Hán,
and he was appointed Garrison Commander of Dōngjīng (*Dōngjīng Liúshǒu*).
When the Empress Dowager was moved to Qìngzhōu,
*Pǔ*'s princely title was moved to Prince of Chǔ,
and he was promoted to *Nányuàn Shūmìshǐ*.
In the fourth year (of *Chóngxī*, 1035),
he was made Prince of Wèi.
He passed away
at the age of fifty.
He was posthumously granted the title Prince of Qí.
His son, Duólà,
was a *Guójìu Xiángwěn*.
Yēlǜ Bāgē,
courtesy name Wūgǔlín,
was a man of the Wǔyuàn Tribe.
He was intelligent in youth;
he could recite a book after merely glancing at it.
During the *Tǒnghé* period,
based on hereditary service, he became a clerk in his own tribe.
Not long after,
he was promoted to *Zhásà Yuè*,
and soon transferred to be a *Shìyù* in the Bureau of Military Affairs (*Shūmì Yuàn*).
When the Sòng generals Cáo Bīn and Mǐ Xìn invaded Yān,
*Bāgē* gained merit while attending the Emperor,
and was promoted to Garrison Commander of Shàngjīng (*Shàngjīng Liúshǒu*).
In the fourth year of *Kāitài* (1015),
he was summoned to serve as Vice Commissioner of Military Affairs of the Northern Administration (*Běiyuàn Shūmì Fùshǐ*).
After a while,
he served as Garrison Commander of Dōngjīng.
In the seventh year (1018),
the Emperor ordered Xiāo Páiyā, Prince of Dōngpíng, to lead an army to attack Gāolì (Koryŏ),
and *Bāgē* served as the Supervisor General (*Dūjiān*).
When they reached Gāijīng (Kaesŏng),
they plundered extensively and returned.
Crossing the two rivers, Chá and Tuó,
the pursuing Gāolì army arrived.
All the generals wanted to let the enemy cross both rivers before attacking them,
but *Bāgē* alone believed this was unwise.
He said:
"If the enemy crosses both rivers,
they will certainly fight desperately;
that would be a dangerous strategy.
It is better to attack them between the two rivers."
*Páiyā* followed his advice,
but in the battle,
they suffered a defeat.
The following year,
upon returning to Dōngjīng,
he reported that the *Bóhǎi* Attendant Officials (*Chéngfèng Guān*) ought to have someone to manage them.
The Emperor followed his suggestion,
and established the position of *Dūzhī Yābān*.
Later, because of the defeat at Chá and Tuó Rivers,
he was stripped of his title as Commissioner-Chancellor (*Shǐxiàng*),
demoted to Supervisor General of the Northwest Route (*Xīběi Lù Dūjiān*),
and died there.
Commentary says: Zhāng Jiǎn’s name matched the Emperor's dream,
and thus gained the Emperor’s deep trust.
He wore a tattered robe and did not change it,
aiming to strengthen the declining moral standards.
His achievements shone across two reigns,
and people universally called him a worthy chancellor;
this was not excessive praise.
Xíng Bàopǔ evaluated and distinguished local magistrates and governors (*Shǒulìng*),
greatly satisfying the public expectation.
He twice resolved complex, stagnant lawsuits,
leaving the populace free from injustice or wrongful conviction.
Mǎ Déchén cited the governance of the Flourishing Táng to advise his ruler.
Xiāo Pǔ grieved over the Empress’s wrongful accusation,
to the point of vomiting blood.
These four men,
all reached high office through understanding the classics (*Míngjīng*),
and their loyalty and devotion were like this.
This is fitting.
The human resources available to Shèngzōng,
were particularly plentiful in this period.
Biographies, Chapter 11: Yēlǜ Shìlǔ (Ōulǐsī), Wáng Jìzhōng, Xiāo Xiàozhōng, Chén Zhāogǔn, Xiāo Hézhuō
Yēlǜ Shìlǔ,
courtesy name Yǐxīnyǐn,
was a man of the Liùyuàn Tribe.
He was tall and robust,
and possessed a handsome appearance.
He was born in the same year as Emperor Shèngzōng,
and the Emperor favored him.
Immediately upon reaching adulthood (capping ceremony),
he was appointed *Zhīhòu Lángjūn*.
Not long after,
he became a Palace Guard Officer (*Sùzhí Guān*).
When the army was deployed to attack Sòng,
he served as a troop commander (*Duìshuài*).
He followed *Nánfǔ Zǎixiàng* Yēlǜ Núguā and Commander-in-Chief (*Tǒngjūnshǐ*) Xiāo Tàlǎn in seizing territory in Zhào and Wèi (regions),
and gained merit.
He was granted the additional title of Grand Preceptor (*Tàishī*), concurrently serving (*Jiǎnxiào*),
and was made Grand Prince of the Northern Administration (*Běiyuàn Dàwáng*).
He attacked and captured Tōnglì Jūn.
When the peace agreement with Sòng was concluded,
he was specially advanced to *Ménxià Píngzhāngshì*,
and bestowed the meritorious title *Tuīchéng Jiéjié Bǎoyì Gōngchén*.
Since the sheep provided as stipends to his tribe were often insufficient,
and the tribesmen were impoverished,
he requested permission to use thin, old sheep, hides, and fur
to annually exchange for silk from the south (China Proper).
This benefited both parties.
He was appointed *Běiyuàn Shūmìshǐ*,
and enfeoffed as the Prince of Hán.
Since Hán Dé'ràng managed the Northern Administration (*Běiyuàn*),
many duties had been neglected and left undone.
On the day *Shìlǔ* accepted the appointment,
the court and the countryside mutually rejoiced.
He accompanied the Emperor on a hunt in Sōnglín,
and died at Shā Lǐng,
at the age of forty-four.
He was posthumously granted the titles Acting Minister of Education (*Shǒu Sītú*) and Director of Political Affairs (*Zhèngshì Lìng*).
He had two sons: Shíshénnú and Ōulǐsī.
Shíshénnú
was the Grand Prince of the Southern Administration (*Nányuàn Dàwáng*).
Ōulǐsī,
courtesy name Liúyǐn,
had great ambitions in his youth.
Before reaching adulthood,
he was appointed *Zhīhòu Lángjūn*.
In the beginning of *Kāitài*,
he became Minister of Education (*Sītú*) of his tribe.
After his term of office was completed, he lived in leisure,
but was recruited to be the *Lángjūn Bān Xiángwěn*.
He was transferred to *Yòu Píshì Xiángwěn*,
leading the troops of his tribe.
He followed Xiāo Páiyā, Prince of Dōngpíng, in attacking Gāolì.
When they reached the two rivers, Chá and Tuó,
the battle went unfavorably.
*Ōulǐsī* alone returned with his entire force intact.
The Emperor highly praised him.
He eventually held the post of Commissioner of Pacification for the Southwest Frontier (*Xīnánmiàn Zhāotǎoshǐ*).
Wáng Jìzhōng,
his place of origin is unknown.
He served Sòng as Prefect (*Cìshǐ*) of Yùnzhōu and Supreme Commander of the Palace Army (*Diànqián Dūyúhòu*).
In the twenty-first year of *Tǒnghé* (1003),
Sòng dispatched *Jìzhōng* to station troops at Wàngdū in Dìngzhōu.
Leading light cavalry to spy on our forces,
he encountered *Nánfǔ Zǎixiàng* Yēlǜ Núguā and others,
who captured him.
The Empress Dowager, recognizing his talent,
appointed him Commissioner of the Ministry of Revenue (*Hùbùshǐ*).
She gave him a woman from the clan of Kāng Mòjì as his wife.
*Jìzhōng* also became greatly inspired,
and always devoted his full effort to his duties.
Since Sòng regarded *Jìzhōng* as a former official of their court,
whenever they sent an envoy,
there were always extra gifts sent along.
Emperor Shèngzōng permitted him to accept them.
In the twenty-second year,
an envoy from Sòng came to offer congratulations.
He presented Jìzhōng with a solitary bow and arrows, a whip and riding crop, and a diplomatic letter requesting peace.
It said:
"Since ascending the great throne,
I have cherished and nurtured the common people.
How could I wish to exhaust military resources?
I only desire to cease hostilities.
I always issue edicts concerning border affairs,
strictly instructing the frontier officials.
Regarding the people of the northern territories,
I do not permit even slight intrusions or harassment.
This is fully known by everyone,
and you are also fully aware of it.
Previously, I relied on Hé Chéngjǔ, the Prefect of Xióngzhōu, to communicate this sincerity,
but since then, there has been no news whatsoever.
You may speak privately (to the envoy).
If peace and reconciliation are permitted,
I shall immediately send a separate envoy to make the formal request."
An imperial edict commanded Jìzhōng to meet with the Sòng envoy,
and permitted the negotiations for peace.
Since Jìzhōng had no slaves in his household,
he was granted thirty palace households (as servants).
He was promoted to Superior General of the Left Militant Guard (Zuǒ Wǔwèi Shàng Jiāngjūn),
and served concurrently as the Resident General of Zhōngjīng (Zhōngjīng Liúshǒu).
In the fifth year of Kāitài (1016),
he was made the Grand Commissioner of the Hán Rén (Han Chinese) Traveling Palace,
and enfeoffed as the Prince of Lángxié Commandery (Lángxié Jùnwáng).
In the sixth year (1017),
he was promoted to Prince of Chǔ (Chǔ Wáng),
and granted the imperial surname (Xiāo).
The Emperor once held a banquet,
discussing appointing Xiāo Hézhuó as the Commissioner of Military Affairs of the Northern Chancellery (Běiyuàn Shūmìshǐ).
Jìzhōng said:
"Although Hézhuó has talent in drafting documents,
he is ignorant of the greater scheme of things.
Xiāo Díliè possesses both talent and conduct;
he is suitable for the post."
The Emperor did not accept (this advice),
and ultimately employed Hézhuó.
When Hézhuó was dispatched to campaign against Gāolì (Koryŏ),
Jìzhōng served as the Deputy Commissioner of the Expeditionary Army (Xíngjūn Fù Dūbùshǔ).
They attacked Xīnghuà Zhèn,
but failed to take it after more than a month.
When the army returned,
the Emperor acknowledged Jìzhōng’s discernment in knowing men,
and appointed him Commissioner of Military Affairs (Shūmìshǐ).
He retired (Zhìshì) in the third year of Tàipíng (1023),
and died.
His son, Huáiyù,
served up to the position of Defense Commissioner (Fángyùshǐ).
Xiāo Xiàozhōng,
courtesy name Sābǎn,
given diminutive name Túgǔsī,
was high-spirited and generous.
During the Kāitài period,
he was appointed Attendant Gentleman (Zhīhòu Lángjūn).
He married the Princess of Yuè State (Yuègúo Gōngzhǔ),
and was appointed Commandant-in-Chief of the Imperial Son-in-Law (Fùmǎ Dūwèi),
and successively promoted to Grand Inspector of the Palace Front (Diànqián Dū Diǎnjiǎn).
During the Tàipíng period,
he was promoted to Chancellor of the Northern Administration (Běifǔ Zǎixiàng).
In the seventh year of Chóngxī (1038),
he served as the Resident General of Dōngjīng (Dōngjīng Liúshǒu).
At that time, people of Bóhǎi were forbidden from playing polo (Jīqiú).
Xiàozhōng argued:
"Dōngjīng is the most important strategic town,
and there is no place for hunting birds and beasts.
If they do not practice with polo and horses,
how can they practice martial skills?
Furthermore, the Son of Heaven regards all four seas as his home;
why make distinctions between 'us' and 'them'?
It is appropriate to lift this prohibition."
This was adopted.
In the twelfth year (1043),
he entered the court,
was enfeoffed as the Prince of Chǔ (Chǔ Wáng),
and appointed Commissioner of Military Affairs of the Northern Chancellery (Běiyuàn Shūmìshǐ).
According to the national system,
the Qìdān and Hàn Rén (Han Chinese) affairs were governed separately by the Northern and Southern Chancellery Commissioners of Military Affairs.
Xiàozhōng memorialized, saying:
"One state having two Commissioners of Military Affairs
is the reason why customs differ.
If they could be merged into one,
it would be a great fortune for the empire."
Before this matter could be implemented,
he passed away.
He was posthumously enfeoffed as Prince of Chǔ State (Chǔ Guówáng).
The Emperor wore plain clothes and wept at the funeral,
pardoned several condemned prisoners,
in order to accumulate merit (Jiànfú) for Xiàozhōng.
On the day of the burial,
the Emperor personally attended,
and granted palace households (as servants) to guard the tomb.
His son, Āsù,
ended his career as Commissioner of Military Affairs of the Southern Chancellery (Nányuàn Shūmìshǐ).
Chén Zhāogǔn,
diminutive name Wángjiǔ,
was a native of Yúnzhōu.
He was skilled at interpreting Qìdān (Yìdí),
was brave, and an excellent archer.
During the Tǒnghé period,
he was appointed Attendant Gentleman (Zhīhòu Lángjūn),
and became the Commander (Xiángwěn) of the Xī Zhuàlè (Xi Yueluo) tribe,
and was successively promoted to Grand Guardian of the Dūnmù Palace (Dūnmù Gōng Tàibǎo),
concurrently overseeing affairs of the Imperial Hunting Grounds (Wéichǎng).
In the autumn of the fifth year of Kāitài (1016),
during a great hunt,
the Emperor shot at a tiger.
Because his horse raced too fast,
the arrow could not be loosed in time.
The tiger grew furious,
gathering its strength to attack the Emperor's carriage (Fànbì).
Those around the Emperor fled in panic.
Zhāogǔn abandoned his horse,
grabbed the tiger by its two ears, and mounted it.
The tiger was startled,
and ran away.
The Emperor ordered the guards to chase and shoot it.
Zhāogǔn shouted loudly, stopping them.
Although the tiger sped off into the mountains,
Zhāogǔn never fell to the ground.
Watching for an opportunity,
he drew his belt-knife and killed it.
When he was brought before the Emperor's presence in a palanquin (or cart),
he was consoled and praised for a long time.
A banquet was held that same day,
and all the gold and silver vessels on the tables were bestowed upon him.
He was specially granted a banner and axe (mark of military authority, Jiéyuè),
promoted to Grand Preceptor of the Imperial Hunting Grounds (Wéichǎng Dū Tàishī),
and granted the imperial surname (Xiāo).
Zhāng Jiǎn and Lǚ Démào were ordered to compose odes to praise him.
He was promoted to Military Commissioner of the Guīyì Army (Guīyì Jūn Jiédùshǐ),
served concurrently as Administrator of the Resident General of Shàngjīng (Tóng Zhī Shàngjīng Liúshǒu),
and subsequently served as Commander-General for Pacification of the Southwest Sector (Xīnán Miàn Zhāotǎo Dūjiān),
and died.
Xiāo Hézhuó,
courtesy name Hélǔyǐn,
was a man of the Tūlǚbù tribe.
He began as a clerk in his own tribe.
Early in the Tǒnghé period,
owing to his prudence and diligence,
he was appointed Vice Minister of the Southern Chancellery (Nányuàn Shìláng).
In the eighteenth year (1000),
Hán Déràng, the Commissioner of Military Affairs of the Northern Chancellery, recommended Hézhuó as Censor (Zhōngchéng),
and sent him on a mission to Sòng with gifts from the Empress Dowager.
Upon his return,
he was promoted to Deputy Commissioner of Military Affairs of the Northern Chancellery (Běiyuàn Shūmì Fùshǐ).
In the third year of Kāitài (1014),
he was made Left Yílíbì (Chief Justice).
Hézhuó had long held positions close to the Emperor;
he was thoroughly familiar with precedents and established procedures,
and skilled in conversation and reply.
Because of this, he was especially favored,
and promoted to Commissioner of Military Affairs of the Northern Chancellery (Běiyuàn Shūmìshǐ).
Contemporary opinion held that he lacked perfect conduct,
and should not be greatly employed.
Wáng Jìzhōng, the Commissioner of Military Affairs of the Southern Chancellery, attending a banquet,
also mocked his flaws.
The Emperor was somewhat displeased.
In the sixth year (1017),
Hézhuó was dispatched to campaign against Gāolì (Koryŏ).
Upon his return,
those seeking advancement often attached themselves to him;
however, his clothing, food, servants, and horses were no more luxurious than before.
The Emperor, knowing his integrity,
gave a woman from the imperial clan to marry his son,
and issued an edict permitting relatives and friends to present gifts (Kuìxiàn).
Wealthy and powerful nobles rushed to his gate.
In the fifth year of Tàipíng (1025),
he fell ill.
The Emperor wanted to visit him,
but Hézhuó declined, saying:
"I, your subject, am unworthy,
yet I have improperly received great responsibilities.
Now my appearance is ravaged and exhausted;
I fear Your Majesty might be moved emotionally upon seeing me."
The Emperor agreed.
When Xiāo Pǔ, the Chancellor of the Northern Administration (Běifǔ Zǎixiàng), visited him during his illness,
Hézhuó held his hand and said:
"When I die,
you will surely become the Commissioner of Military Affairs.
Be careful not to recommend anyone superior to yourself."
Pǔ left and scorned him (for this remark).
He died that same day.
His son, Wūgǔ,
ended his career as Military Commissioner (Jiédùshǐ) of his native tribe.
The appraisal states: Among the various officials during the Tǒnghé reign,
many brought fame to the imperial house.
When Shì Lǔ (室魯) was appointed Commissioner of Military Affairs (Shūmìshǐ),
the court and the common people celebrated together;
this must have been due to his winning the hearts of the people.
Since Jì Zhōng (繼忠) was unable to die for the state,
although he facilitated peace between the North and the South,
and possessed the discernment to recognize talent,
how is he worthy of esteem?
Xiàozhōng (孝忠) and Zhāogǔn (昭袞),
both have commendable qualities.
When Hé Zhuó (合卓) was near death,
he instructed Xiāo Pǔ (蕭朴) not to nominate anyone more capable than himself for the post of Commissioner of Military Affairs (Shūmì),
his crime of misleading the state was grave!
Biographies, Chapter 12: Yēlǜ Lóngyùn (耶律隆運) (Déwēi 德威, Dí Lǔ 滌魯, Zhìxīn 制心), Yēlǜ Bógǔzhé (耶律勃古哲), Xiāo Yángāwǔbái (蕭陽阿武白), Xiāo Chánggē (蕭常哥), Yēlǜ Hǔgǔ (耶律虎古) (Mólǔgǔ 磨魯古).
Yēlǜ Lóngyùn
originally bore the surname Hán (韓),
with the given name Déràng (德讓).
He was the son of Kuāngsì (匡嗣), the Commissioner for Pacification (Zhāotǎoshǐ) of the Southwest Circuit.
In the 19th year of Tǒnghé,
he was granted the name Déchāng (德昌);
in the 22nd year,
he was granted the surname Yēlǜ;
in the 28th year,
he was again granted the name Lóngyùn.
He was dignified, substantial, and possessed strategic intelligence.
He clearly understood the governmental structure,
and was fond of achieving merit and establishing works.
While serving Emperor Jǐngzōng (景宗),
he became renowned for his caution and propriety,
and was promoted to Attendant Official (Chéngfèngguān) of the Eastern Department,
appointed Interpreter (Tōngshì) in the Bureau of Military Affairs (Shūmì Yuàn),
transferred to Prefect (Huángchéngshǐ) of the Supreme Capital (Shàngjīng),
and remotely commissioned as Military Commissioner (Jiédùshǐ) of the Zhāngdé (彰德) Army.
He succeeded his father Kuāngsì as Resident Administrator (Liúshǒu) of the Supreme Capital,
and provisionally managed the affairs of the capital,
acquiring a great reputation.
Soon after, he again succeeded his father in guarding the Southern Capital (Nánjīng);
the people of the time considered this an honor.
When Sòng (宋) troops captured Hédōng (河東),
and invaded Yān (燕),
Xī Dǐ (奚底), the Xiángwěn (詳穩) of the Five Divisions, and Xiāo Tǎogǔ (蕭討古), the Commander, etc., returned defeated.
The Sòng troops besieged the city,
recruiting and threatening with great urgency,
and people harbored disloyal thoughts.
Lóngyùn ascended the city walls,
day and night defending the city.
When reinforcement troops arrived,
the siege was lifted.
When they fought at Gāoliáng Hé (高梁河),
Sòng troops were defeated and fled.
Lóngyùn intercepted and attacked them,
and defeated them again.
For his merit, he was appointed Military Commissioner (Jiédùshǐ) of the Liáoxīng (遼興) Army,
and recalled to serve as Commissioner of Military Affairs (Shūmìshǐ) of the Southern Bureau (Nányuàn).
When Emperor Jǐngzōng’s illness worsened severely,
Lóngyùn and Yēlǜ Xiézhěn (耶律斜軫) together received the dying commission.
They enthroned the Prince of Liáng (Liáng Wáng) as Emperor,
and the Empress as Empress Dowager (Huáng Tàihòu),
who administered the government.
Lóngyùn took charge of the Imperial Guards (Sùwèi) affairs.
The Empress Dowager entrusted and favored him even more.
In the first year of Tǒnghé,
he was granted the honorific title Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī,
concurrently serving as Director of Governmental Affairs (Zhèngshì Lìng).
In the 4th year,
Sòng dispatched Cáo Bīn (曹彬) and Mǐ Xìn (米信) to lead a hundred thousand troops to invade.
Lóngyùn followed the Empress Dowager in leading the army and defeated them,
promoted to Acting Minister of Works (Shǒu Sīkōng),
and enfeoffed as Duke of Chǔ (Chǔ Guógōng).
Upon returning with the army,
he jointly administered state affairs with Shì Fǎng (室昉), the Chancellor of the Northern Bureau (Běifǔ Zǎixiàng).
He memorialized that the four prefectures of Shānxī (山西) had frequently suffered warfare,
and were afflicted by famine,
suggesting that taxes should be lightened to attract displaced people.
This was followed.
In the 6th year,
the Empress Dowager was watching a polo match.
Hú Lǐ Shì (胡里室) charged Lóngyùn, causing him to fall from his horse.
She ordered Hú Lǐ Shì to be instantly executed.
By imperial decree, he led the army to attack Sòng, besieging Shā Duī (沙堆).
The enemy launched a surprise night attack.
Lóngyùn maintained strict military formation and waited,
defeated and routed them.
He was enfeoffed as Prince of Chǔ (Chǔ Wáng).
In the 9th year,
he again stated that the people of Yān engaged in fraud,
falsely avoiding taxes and labor service,
and that nobles were profiting greatly from this.
He requested sending Zhào Zhì (趙智), the Commissioner of Envoys (Xuānhuīshǐ) of the Northern Bureau, to admonish and instruct them.
This was followed.
In the 11th year,
he observed mourning for his mother,
but an imperial decree forced him to resume his duties.
The following year,
Shì Fǎng resigned from office (Zhìzhèng).
Lóngyùn was appointed Chancellor of the Northern Bureau in his place,
still holding the post of Commissioner of Military Affairs (Shūmìshǐ),
and concurrently supervising the compilation of the National History.
He was granted the title Meritorious Official for Promoting Transformation (Xīnghuà Gōngchén).
In the sixth month of the 12th year,
he memorialized that the officials responsible for judicial interrogations in the three capitals,
often accepted entreaties and bribes,
granting leniency unfairly,
or arbitrarily administering flogging and torture.
He petitioned for these practices to be prohibited.
The Emperor approved his petition.
He also submitted a memorial requesting the appointment of the virtuous and the removal of the wicked.
The Empress Dowager was delighted and said:
“Promoting the virtuous to assist in governance
is truly the duty of a great official.”
He was bestowed with generous rewards.
When the mourning period concluded,
he was promoted to Acting Grand Tutor (Shǒu Tàibǎo) and concurrently Director of Governmental Affairs (Zhèngshì Lìng).
Coincidentally, Yēlǜ Xiézhěn, the Commissioner of Military Affairs of the Northern Bureau, passed away.
An imperial decree ordered Lóngyùn to assume that concurrent post.
After a long time,
he was appointed Grand Chancellor (Dà Chéngxiàng),
promoted to Prince of Qí (Qí Wáng),
and oversaw the affairs of both Bureaus of Military Affairs.
Because Nánjīng and Píngzhōu (平州) suffered poor harvests,
he memorialized for the people to be exempted from the tax on agricultural tools,
and requested the standardization of prices charged by merchants in all prefectures.
All were followed.
In the 22nd year,
he accompanied the Empress Dowager on the southern campaign.
Upon reaching the [Yellow] River,
they agreed to peace with Sòng and returned.
He was transferred to Prince of Jìn (Jìn Wáng),
granted the imperial surname,
removed from the court registry,
and registered under the lineage of the youngest paternal uncle of the Horizontal Tent (Héngzhàng Jìfǔ Fáng).
He was then renamed with his current name (Lóngyùn),
ranking above all imperial princes (Qīnwáng),
and granted lands, residences, and a burial plot for accompanying the imperial tomb.
Returning from the campaign against Gāolì (高麗),
he contracted a chronic illness.
The Emperor and the Empress Dowager personally visited him, overseeing his medical care.
He passed away,
at the age of seventy-one.
He was posthumously granted Minister (Lìng) of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū),
with the posthumous title Wénzhōng (文忠).
The government provided burial equipment,
and a temple was built near Qián Líng (乾陵).
He had no sons.
In the 3rd year of Qīngníng (清寧),
Yēlǔ (耶魯), the son of the Prince of Wèi (Wèi Wáng) Tiēbù (貼不), was made his heir.
When Tiānzuò (天祚) ascended the throne,
the Imperial Prince Áolúwò (敖盧斡) succeeded him.
His younger brother was Déwēi (德威),
and his nephew was Zhìxīn (制心).
Déwēi
was firm and straightforward by nature,
and skilled in riding and archery.
Early in the Bǎoníng (保寧) reign,
he successively held the posts of Prefect (Huángchéngshǐ) of the Supreme Capital,
Defense Commissioner (Fángyùshǐ) of Rúzhōu (儒州),
and was transferred to Commissioner of Envoys (Xuānhuīshǐ) of the Northern Bureau.
At the end of the Qiánhēng (乾亨) reign,
he mourned his father's death,
but was compelled to resume his post,
provisionally acting as Commissioner for Pacification of the Southwest.
Early in the Tǒnghé reign,
when the Dǎngxiàng (党項) raided the border,
he repelled them in a single battle.
He was granted a sword, allowing him to act according to circumstance,
and commanded the troops of the Tūlǚbù (突呂不) and Diélà (迭剌) divisions.
Due to his merit in suppressing Shāogǔgě (稍古葛),
he was officially appointed Commissioner for Pacification (Zhāotǎoshǐ).
Lǐ Jìqiān (李繼遷) of Xiàzhōu (夏州) rebelled against Sòng and pledged allegiance [to the Liao].
Déwēi requested permission to accept him.
Once Jìqiān was accepted,
all the surrounding barbarians followed suit.
He was praised and rewarded by imperial letter.
Together with the Tìyǐn (惕隱) Yēlǜ Shànbǔ (耶律善補), he defeated the Sòng general Yáng Jìyè (楊繼業),
and was promoted to Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī and concurrently Manager of Affairs (Píngzhāngshì) in the Department of Governmental Affairs (Zhèngshì Ménxià).
Not long after,
because many cities and towns in Shānxī were captured,
he was stripped of his military authority.
Lǐ Jìqiān accepted bribes,
and secretly harbored disloyalty.
Déwēi received an imperial decree to lead troops to go and warn him.
Jìqiān used the pretext of campaigning in the west and refused to come out.
Déwēi reached Língzhōu (靈州), took captives and loot, and returned.
He died at the age of fifty-five.
He was posthumously granted concurrent Grandee Remonstrant (Shìzhōng).
His son Pāngjīn (雱金),
ended his career as Military Commissioner (Jiédùshǐ) of the Zhāngguó (彰國) Army.
He had two grandsons: Xiè Shí (謝十) and Dí Lǔ.
Xiè Shí ended his career as Tìyǐn.
Dí Lǔ,
courtesy name Zūnníng (遵寧).
He was raised in the palace when young,
and was granted the title Minor General (Xiǎo Jiāngjūn).
In the early period of Chóngxī,
he successively served as Xūanhūi Shǐ of the Northern Bureau, Yòu Línyá, and Fù Diǎnjiǎn.
He was appointed Tìyǐn,
then changed to Zhāotǎo Shǐ of the Northwest Route,
and enfeoffed as the Prince of Qīshuǐ Commandery.
He requested to reduce 3,280 men from the military roster.
Later, because he privately took a otter fur coat from a Huíhú envoy
and privately took tribute items from the Zǔbǔ,
the matter came to light.
He was given a severe beating with a large staff,
deprived of his title, and dismissed from office.
Soon after, he was reinstated as Xūanhūi Shǐ of the Northern Bureau.
In the nineteenth year,
he was reassigned as Dū Xiángwěn of the Wūgǔ Díliè Department,
and soon after became Xiángwěn of the Northeast Route,
enfeoffed as the Prince of Húntóng Commandery.
In the early Qīngníng period,
he was transferred to be the Prince of Dèng,
and promoted to Nánfǔ Zǎixiàng.
Because of his old age, he requested to retire,
and was then made Prince of Hàn.
He passed away during the Dàkāng period
at the age of eighty.
Dí Lǔ had a refined and perceptive mind.
Shèngzōng regarded him as a son,
and Xīngzōng treated him with the courtesy due to an elder brother.
Though highly placed, he grew all the more humble.
When he first served as Dū Diǎnjiǎn,
he accompanied the emperor on a hunt to Hēilǐng,
where a bear was caught.
The emperor, enjoying a celebratory drink,
said to Dí Lǔ:
"Do you have any requests?"
He replied:
"Your servant's wealth and status far exceed my merits,
and I dare not ask for more.
However, my uncle received preferential treatment in the previous reign.
After his death,
his unworthy son was convicted and had his property confiscated.
For the seasonal sacrifices,
if one grandson could be pardoned to officiate the rites,
my wish would be fulfilled."
An edict pardoned the confiscation
and restored his property.
His son Yānwǔ
rose to the office of Nánjīng Bùjūn Dū Zhīhuīshǐ.
Zhìxīn,
whose pet name was Kèhánnú.
His father Déchóng
was skilled in medicine.
By observing a person's appearance and complexion,
he could diagnose their illness.
He successively rose to the office of Wǔdìngjūn Jiédùshǐ.
Zhìxīn was skilled in training eagles and falcons.
During the Tǒnghé period,
he served as Guīhuàzhōu Cìshǐ.
During the Kāitài period,
he was appointed Shàngjīng Liúshǒu,
promoted to Hànrén Xínggōng Dū Bùshǔ,
and enfeoffed as the Prince of Qīshuǐ Commandery.
As the Empress's maternal younger brother,
his favor and trust grew daily.
When the Privy Council Vice-Commissioner Xiāo Hézhuó was in power,
Zhìxīn reported that Hézhuó lacked judgment
and proper conduct.
The emperor remained silent.
Whenever there was a joyful inner banquet,
he would avoid it.
The Empress was displeased and said:
"Are you not happy?"
Zhìxīn replied:
"Few can long maintain such favor and status.
This is what worries me!"
During the Tàipíng period,
he successively served as Zhōngjīng Liúshǒu,
Tìyǐn, and Nánjīng Liúshǒu,
was transferred to be the Prince of Yān,
and then promoted to Nányuàn Dàwáng.
Someone advised Zhìxīn to worship Buddha.
He replied:
"I do not understand Buddhist teachings.
Only if one's heart is selfless,
then one is close to it."
One day,
he bathed, changed his clothes, and lay down to rest.
His family heard music from string and wind instruments,
and, surprised, entered to check,
only to find that he had already passed away.
He was fifty-three years old.
He was posthumously granted the title of Zhèngshìlìng
and posthumously enfeoffed as the Prince of Chén.
While serving as Shàngjīng Liúshǒu,
the alcohol prohibition was very strict.
When someone was caught privately brewing alcohol,
he drank it all himself,
smiled, and did not question the person.
On the day of his death,
the local people mourned as if for their parents.
Yélǜ Bógǔzhé,
courtesy name Púnúyǐn,
a descendant of Púgǔzhī, the Yílíjǐn of the Six Departments.
He was brave, fierce,
and skilled in managing livelihood.
During the Bǎoníng period,
he served as Tiāndéjūn Jiédùshǐ,
and successively as Nánjīng Shìwèi Mǎbùjūn Dū Zhīhuīshǐ.
For suppressing and pacifying the Dǎngxiàng Qiāng Álǐsāmǐ and Púlíbiē Mǐ,
he was promoted to Nányuàn Dàwáng.
When Shèngzōng ascended the throne,
the Empress Dowager exercised imperial power.
When she convened a meeting of officials to discuss military and state affairs,
Bógǔzhé submitted a memorial listing several advantageous proposals.
It pleased the emperor,
and on the same day, he was concurrently appointed to oversee the various prefectures of the Shānxī Route.
In the fourth year of Tǒnghé,
when the Sòng generals Cáo Bīn and others invaded Yān,
Bógǔzhé attacked them vigorously.
He was bestowed the title 'Shūzhōng Bǎojié Zhìzhǔ Gōngchén'
and given overall command of the five prefectures of Shānxī.
Later, there was an accusation that Bógǔzhé distorted the law and oppressed the people.
Upon investigation, the accusations were found to be true.
He was punished with a severe beating with a large staff.
In the eighth year,
he became Nánjīng Tǒngjūnshǐ
and died.
His son Yáolǐ
rose to the office of Xiángwěn.
Xiāo Yáng'ā,
courtesy name Shāoyǐn.
He was resolute, dignified, and strict,
understood Khitan and Chinese characters,
and was knowledgeable in astronomy and physiognomy.
When his father died,
he personally pulled the hearse from the Wǔfānbù to Xīwánglǐng.
People praised his filial piety.
At nineteen,
he became Běnbān Lángjūn.
He successively served as Xiángwěn of the Tiělín, Tiěyáo, and Dàyīng armies.
In the first year of Qiántǒng,
from Wūgǔ Dílièbù Túntián Tàibǎo, he became Yìzhōu Cìshǐ.
The favored official Liú Yànliáng once came to the prefecture on official business,
and, relying on imperial favor, acted arbitrarily.
He was thwarted by Yáng'ā.
Upon his return, Yànliáng
maliciously slandered him,
and soon sent someone to replace Yáng'ā.
Over a thousand prefecture residents went to the palace gate to request his retention.
On the same day, he was appointed Wǔ'ānzhōu Guāncháshǐ.
He successively served as Jiédù Shǐ of Wūgǔnièlǐ, Shùnyì, Zhāngxìn, and other armies,
and provisionally oversaw the affairs of the Tǒngjūnshǐ of the Northeast Route.
Hearing that Yélǜ Lángbù, Duóluówò, and others had rebelled,
he alone led over thirty men from his command to pursue and capture them.
He suffered two wounds,
captured more than ten people alive,
and sent them to the traveling court.
He was dismissed from office
for failing to capture the main culprits.
Not long after,
he provisionally served as Nánjīng Liúshǒu
and died.
Wǔ Bái,
his place of origin is unknown.
He served as a Guózǐ Bóshì in the Sòng dynasty,
and was assigned as Zhī Xiàngzhōu.
Upon reaching Tōnglìjūn,
he was captured by our army.
An imperial edict appointed him Shàngjīng Guózǐ Bóshì.
He was then changed to Línhuáng Xiànlìng,
and promoted to Guǎngdéjūn Jiédù Fùshǐ.
Previously,
there was a lawsuit alleging an illicit relationship between the Zǎixiàng Liú Shènxíng and his daughter-in-law Yáo Shì.
The authorities found him guilty.
Shèngzōng ordered Bái to investigate it.
Bái rectified the matter.
After returning from an envoy mission to Gāolì,
he provisionally served as Zhōngjīng Liúshǒu.
At that time, all of Shènxíng's sons held important positions of power.
Because Bái ruled unfairly on a case of the common people's land registration,
he was demoted.
Not long after,
he was promoted to Shàngshū Zuǒchéng,
then Zhī Shūmì Shì,
and appointed Liáoxīngjūn Jiédùshǐ.
He retired
and died.
Xiāo Chánggē,
courtesy name Húdúgǐn,
from the family of the Guójìu.
His grandfather Yuēzhí
was Tóng Zhèngshì Ménxià Píngzhāngshì.
His father Shílǎo
successively rose to the office of Jiédùshǐ.
Cháng Gē was burly and taciturn.
When he was over thirty years old,
he first served as a Zhīhòu Lángjūn.
He successively held the positions of Běn Zú Jiāngjūn and Cìshǐ of Sōngshān Zhōu.
In the second year of Shòulóng,
he gave his daughter as the consort of the Yàn Wáng,
and was appointed Yǒngxīng Gōng Shǐ.
When the consort gave birth to a son,
he was made Nányuàn Xuānhuī Shǐ,
and soon after, this was changed to Hànrén Xínggōng Dū Bùshǔ.
At the beginning of Qiántǒng,
he was promoted to Tàizǐ Tàishī,
and became Guójiù Xiángwěn.
In the second year,
he was transferred to be the Jiédùshǐ of Liáoxīng Jūn,
then summoned to serve as Běifǔ Zǎixiàng.
Due to the Cháicè Lǐ ceremony,
he was additionally granted the title of Jiān Shìzhōng.
In the first year of Tiānqìng,
he retired from office,
passed away,
and was posthumously named Qīnsù.
Yēlǜ Hǔgǔ,
courtesy name Hǎilín,
was the grandson of Liùyuàn Yílíjǐn Díliè.
In youth, he was clever and insightful,
and valued keeping his promises.
At the beginning of Bǎoníng,
he was appointed Yùzhǎn Lángjūn.
In the tenth year,
he returned after serving as an envoy to Sòng,
and informed the Emperor of Sòng’s intention to seize Hédōng.
Hán Kuāngsì, the Yàn Wáng, asked:
“How do you know this?”
Hǔgǔ replied:
“Sòng has already annexed all the states
that usurped titles,
only Hédōng has not yet been taken.
Now Sòng is practicing military arts and training for war;
their intent must be directed toward Hàn.”
Kuāngsì strongly discouraged (the Emperor from believing him),
and the matter was dropped.
The next year,
Sòng indeed attacked Hàn.
The Emperor, seeing that Hǔgǔ could predict events,
valued him greatly,
and said:
“Kuāngsì and I failed to consider this.”
He was appointed Cìshǐ of Zhuō Zhōu.
At the beginning of Tǒnghé,
the Empress Dowager assumed regency,
and summoned him to the capital.
He clashed with Hán Déràng over an affair.
Déràng grew angry,
took a weapon carried by a guard, and struck him on the head,
and he died.
His son was Mólǔgǔ.
Mólǔgǔ,
courtesy name Yáoyǐn,
possessed wisdom and discernment,
and was skilled in archery.
At the beginning of Tǒnghé,
he was appointed Nánmiàn Línyá.
In the fourth year,
when Sòng invaded Yān,
the Empress Dowager personally led the punitive expedition.
Mólǔgǔ served as the vanguard,
and was struck by a stray arrow in the hand.
He pulled it out and charged forward again.
When the Empress Dowager arrived,
Mólǔgǔ, due to his wound, was unable to fight,
and was assigned to patrol the border alongside Xiāo Jìxiān, the Běifǔ Zǎixiàng.
He was repeatedly promoted, eventually becoming Běiyuàn Dàwáng.
In the sixth year,
when attacking Sòng, he served as the vanguard,
and, together with Yēlǜ Núguā, defeated the enemy general Lǐ Zhōngjí at Dìng Zhōu.
He died of illness while in the army.
The Commentary states: Déràng, during the Tǒnghé period,
held ranks combining those of general and chancellor.
His accomplishments in conquering enemies, achieving victories,
recommending the worthy, and assisting the state
were magnificent.
As for being granted the imperial surname,
and being enfeoffed as the Prince of Qí and Jìn,
was this not due to the favor shown by the Empress Dowager?
Regarding the clan members, such as Déwēi, who pacified the Dǎngxiàng,
Dílǔ, who completed the ancestral sacrifices,
and (others) whose minds were controlled and who did not blindly comply,
their family prestige was increasingly prominent.
How could these achievements lack a source!
As for the loyalty of Bógǔ,
the filial piety of Yáng'ā,
and the straightforwardness of Wǔbái,
they were indeed admirable good ministers of their generation.
Biographies, Chapter 13: Yēlǜ Xiūgē (Yēlǜ Mǎgē), Yēlǜ Xiézhěn, Yēlǜ Xī dī, Yēlǜ Xuégǔ (Yēlǜ Wūbùlǚ)
Yēlǜ Xiūgē,
courtesy name Xùnníng.
His grandfather, Shìlǔ,
was the Suí Guówáng.
His father, Wǎnsī,
was the Nányuàn Yílíjǐn.
In youth, Xiūgē possessed the qualities of a statesman and assistant to the ruler.
Initially, when the two tribes of Wūgǔ and Shìwěi rebelled,
Xiūgē followed Xiāo Gān, the Běifǔ Zǎixiàng, to suppress them.
At the end of Yìnglì,
he became Tìyǐn.
In the first year of Qiánhēng,
when Sòng invaded Yān,
Běiyuàn Dàwáng Xī dī and Tǒngjūn Shǐ Xiāo Tǎogǔ suffered a defeat,
and Nánjīng was besieged.
The Emperor ordered Xiūgē to replace Xī dī,
leading the troops of the Five Circuits to relieve the siege.
They encountered a large enemy force at Gāoliáng Hé.
He and Yēlǜ Xiézhěn divided into left and right wings,
and defeated the enemy.
They pursued and slaughtered (the enemy) for over thirty *lǐ*,
beheading more than ten thousand.
Xiūgē sustained three wounds.
The next morning,
the Sòng ruler fled.
Xiūgē, due to his wounds, could not ride a horse,
so he chased in a light chariot as far as Zhuō Zhōu,
but failed to catch him and returned.
In the winter of that year,
the Emperor ordered Hán Kuāngsì and Yēlǜ Shā to attack Sòng,
in retaliation for the siege (of Nánjīng).
Xiūgē led his divisional troops and fought alongside Kuāngsì and the others at Mǎn Chéng.
The next day, when they were about to fight again,
the Sòng troops requested surrender.
Kuāngsì believed them.
Xiūgē said:
“Their troops are organized and sharp;
they certainly will not submit.
This is merely a deception to lure us.
We should prepare our soldiers strictly and wait.”
Kuāngsì did not listen.
Xiūgē led his troops to high ground to observe.
A moment later, the Southern (Sòng) troops arrived in great numbers,
beating drums, shouting, and charging rapidly.
Kuāngsì was flustered and did not know what to do,
and his officers and soldiers abandoned their flags and drums and ran,
and were utterly defeated.
Xiūgē organized his troops and counterattacked,
and the enemy withdrew.
An edict ordered him to take command of all garrison troops facing the south,
and he was made Běiyuàn Dàwáng.
The following year,
the imperial carriage personally led an expedition,
and besieged Wǎqiáo Guān.
Sòng troops came to relieve the siege.
The defending general, Zhāng Shī, broke through the encirclement.
The Emperor personally supervised the battle.
Xiūgē killed Zhāng Shī,
and the rest of the enemy troops retreated back into the city.
The Sòng army formed ranks south of the water.
As they were about to fight,
the Emperor, concerned that Xiūgē’s armored horse was distinctively yellow,
might be recognized by the enemy,
therefore bestowed upon him black armor and a white horse to replace it.
Xiūgē led his elite cavalry across the water,
defeated them,
and pursued them as far as Mò Zhōu.
Corpses covered the road,
and both lances and arrows were exhausted.
He captured several generals alive and presented them.
The Emperor was pleased,
bestowed upon him an imperial horse and a golden bowl,
and praised him, saying:
“Your bravery exceeds your reputation.
If everyone were like you,
what need would we have to worry about failing to conquer?”
When the army returned,
he was appointed Yūyuè.
Emperor Shèngzōng ascended the throne,
the Empress Dowager (Tàihòu) assumed regency and ruled,
ordering Xiūgē to take overall command of the southern military affairs,
acting according to expediency.
Xiūgē standardized the garrison troops,
established a rotation system for rest,
encouraged agriculture and sericulture,
repaired military defenses,
and the border region was greatly secured.
In the fourth year of Tǒnghé [986 CE],
Sòng invaded again.
Their generals Fàn Mì and Yáng Jìyè emerged from Yúnzhōu;
Cáo Bīn and Mǐ Xìn emerged from Xióng and Yì [zhou],
taking Qígōu and Zhuōzhōu,
capturing Gù'ān,
and setting up garrisons.
At that time, the soldiers of the Northern and Southern Courts and the Xī tribes had not yet arrived,
Xiūgē's forces were few,
and he dared not engage in open battle.
At night, he sent light cavalry between the two armies,
killing their isolated or weak units to intimidate the remaining troops;
by day, he displayed his strength using elite troops,
causing the enemy to exhaust themselves in defense,
thereby wearing down their strength.
He also set up ambushes in the forests and thickets,
cutting off their supply routes.
Cáo Bīn and others, due to the failure of food transportation,
retreated to secure Báigōu.
After more than a month,
they returned.
Xiūgē used light forces to approach them,
watching for them eating their morning meal,
attacking those who were separated from their ranks or marching alone,
fighting while gradually withdrawing.
Because of this, the Southern Army were too busy defending themselves,
forming square formations,
digging trenches on both sides of their march.
The army was thirsty and lacked wells;
they strained the muddy water to drink,
only reaching Zhuō [zhou] after four days.
Hearing that the Empress Dowager's army had arrived,
Bīn and the others fled in the rain.
The Empress Dowager reinforced [Xiūgē] with elite soldiers,
and they pursued them.
Their strength exhausted,
they circled their supply carts to defend themselves.
Xiūgē surrounded them.
That night,
Bīn and Xìn fled with a few riders,
and the remaining troops completely collapsed.
The pursuit reached east of Yìzhōu,
where they heard that tens of thousands of Sòng troops still remained,
cooking by the Shā Hé (Sand River).
[Xiūgē] hurried his troops to attack them.
The Sòng army, seeing the dust cloud, scattered and fled,
falling down banks and trampling each other; more than half died,
and the flow of the Shā Hé was obstructed by them.
The Empress Dowager returned her banners.
Xiūgē collected the Sòng corpses and built a Jīngguān (monument of enemy dead).
He was enfeoffed as Sòng Guówáng (Prince of Sòng).
He further reported to the throne,
stating that they should take advantage of Sòng's weakness
to seize territory up to the Hé (Yellow River) as the border.
The memorial was submitted,
but it was not accepted.
When the Empress Dowager campaigned south,
Xiūgē served as the vanguard,
defeating the Sòng forces at Wàngdōu.
At that time, the Sòng general Liú Tíngràng, with tens of thousands of cavalry, marched out along the sea,
planning to join forces with Lǐ Jìngyuán,
publicly declaring they would take Yān [zhōu].
Xiūgē heard this
and first blocked their strategic location with troops.
When the Empress Dowager's army arrived,
they engaged in battle,
killing Jìngyuán,
and Tíngràng fled to Yíngzhōu.
In the seventh year,
Sòng sent Liú Tíngràng and others to attack Yìzhōu, taking advantage of the summer heat and flooding.
All the generals feared them;
only Xiūgē led elite troops to strike them preemptively north of the Shā Hé,
killing and wounding tens of thousands,
capturing an incalculable amount of military supplies,
and presenting them to the court.
The Empress Dowager praised his achievements,
issuing an edict exempting him from formal prostration and permitting him not to be addressed by name.
From then on, Sòng dared not move north.
At that time, when the Sòng people wanted to stop children crying,
they would say:
"The Yúyuè (Supreme Commander) has arrived!"
Xiūgē, seeing that the people of Yān [zhōu] were exhausted,
reduced taxes and corvée,
provided relief to orphans and widows,
and warned the garrison soldiers not to trespass into Sòng territory.
Even horses and cattle that had strayed north were all returned.
People near and far were drawn to his influence,
and the border regions were peaceful.
In the sixteenth year,
he died.
That night,
freezing rain fell.
Emperor Shèngzōng decreed the establishment of a shrine for him in Nánjīng.
Xiūgē's wisdom and strategies were grand and far-reaching;
he predicted the enemy like a spirit.
Whenever he won a battle,
he deferred credit to his generals,
thus the soldiers and officers happily served under him.
He personally experienced a hundred battles,
yet never killed a single innocent person.
He had two sons: Gāo Bā,
whose official position reached Jiédùshǐ (Military Governor);
and Gāo Shí,
who ended his career as Yúyuè (Supreme Commander).
His grandson was Mǎgē.
Mǎgē,
courtesy name Ètèlǎn.
During the reign of Xīngzōng,
he was received in audience while holding an untitled position.
The Emperor asked:
"Do you serve the Buddha, Sir?"
He replied:
"Every morning, your servant recites the dying instructions of Tàizǔ (Emperor Tàizǔ), Tàizōng (Emperor Tàizōng), and my late father,
and has not yet had time to serve the Buddha."
The Emperor was pleased.
During the Qīngníng era,
