he was transferred to become the Jiédùshǐ of the Tánggǔ Department.
During the Xiányōng era,
he was successively promoted to Jiédùshǐ of the Kuāngyì Army.
Early in the Dàkāng era,
he retired,
and died.
Yēlǜ Xiézhěn,
courtesy name Hányǐn,
was the grandson of Yúyuè Hélǔ.
He was naturally intelligent and perceptive,
and did not focus on production.
In the first year of Bǎoníng,
the Chief Administrator of the Bureau of Military Affairs, Xiāo Sīwēn, recommended that Xiézhěn possessed talent for governing the state.
The Emperor said:
"I know this,
but he is carefree and wild.
How can he be constrained?"
[Xiāo Sīwēn] replied:
"Although outwardly carefree and wild,
his inner qualities are immeasurable."
[The Emperor] then summoned him and questioned him about current affairs,
and his responses were precise and penetrating.
The Emperor highly valued him.
He gave him the Empress's niece in marriage,
ordered him to command all the armies of the southwestern sector,
and furthermore, to provide aid to Hédōng.
He was later appointed as the Nányuàn Dàwáng (Great King of the Southern Court).
Early in the Qiánhēng era,
Sòng again attacked Hédōng.
[Xiézhěn] followed Yēlǜ Shā to Báimǎ Lǐng (White Horse Ridge) where they encountered the enemy.
Shā and the others were unsuccessful in battle;
Xiézhěn rushed to assist,
ordering ten thousand arrows to be loosed simultaneously by his troops.
The enemy's spirit flagged, and they retreated.
In the autumn of that year,
Sòng conquered Hédōng,
and capitalizing on their victory, raided Yān [zhōu].
The Běiyuàn Dàwáng (Great King of the Northern Court), Yēlǜ Xīdì, and Xiāo Tǎogǔ fought them,
suffered a defeat,
and retreated to garrison north of the Qīng Hé.
Xiézhěn took the Green Banner troops of Xīdì and others and used them at Déshèng Kǒu (Victory Pass) to lure the enemy.
The enemy indeed rushed to the spot.
Xiézhěn emerged behind them,
struck fiercely, and defeated them.
And in the Battle of Gāoliáng,
he divided the left and right wings with Yēlǜ Xiūgē and attacked from both sides,
heavily defeating the Sòng army.
In the beginning of the Tǒnghé era,
the Empress Dowager (Huáng Tàihòu) assumed regency,
and [he] was increasingly entrusted with duties,
serving as the Northern Chancellery Military Commissioner (Běiyuàn Shūmìshǐ).
At that time, Sòng generals Cáo Bīn and Mǐ Xìn marched out from Xióng and Yì [Prefectures],
and Yáng Jìyè marched out from Dàizhōu.
The Empress Dowager personally led the army to rescue Yān,
appointing Xiézhěn as the Commander-in-Chief of Cavalry and Infantry of the Shānxī Route (Shānxī Lù Bīngmǎ Dūtǒng).
Jìyè captured various commanderies in Shānxī,
assigning troops to defend each one,
and personally garrisoned Dàizhōu.
Xiézhěn reached Dìng'ān,
encountered the army of Hè Lìngtú,
defeated them,
pursued them to Wǔtái,
and beheaded tens of thousands [of enemies].
The next day,
he arrived at Yùzhōu.
The enemy dared not come out.
Xiézhěn wrote on silk and shot it onto the city walls,
conveying his intention to offer amnesty and conciliation.
Secretly hearing that the Sòng army was coming to reinforce,
he ordered the Supervising Commissioner Yēlǜ Tízǐ to lay an ambush in a dangerous defile during the night,
waiting for the enemy to arrive before striking.
The defenders of the city, seeing the reinforcements arrive,
sallied forth.
Xiézhěn attacked their rear,
and both armies collapsed.
He pursued them to Fēihú,
beheaded over twenty thousand [enemies],
and subsequently captured Yùzhōu.
Hè Lìngtú and Pān Měi returned again with troops.
Xiézhěn intercepted them at Fēihú,
and defeated them.
Those Sòng forces located in Húnyuán and Yìngzhōu
all abandoned the cities and fled.
Xiézhěn heard that Jìyè had mobilized troops,
and ordered Xiāo Tà● to lay an ambush on the road.
At dawn the next day,
Jìyè’s troops arrived.
Xiézhěn massed his forces in a battle formation.
Jìyè advanced, waving his banner.
Xiézhěn feigned retreat.
The ambush struck,
and Xiézhěn advanced to attack.
Jìyè was defeated and fled,
reaching Lángyácūn.
All his forces collapsed.
Jìyè was struck by a stray arrow
and was captured.
Xiézhěn rebuked him, saying:
"You have competed for supremacy with our country for over thirty years.
How dare you show your face to me today!"
Jìyè only replied, confessing his capital crime.
Originally,
Jìyè was famous in Sòng for his fierce bravery,
and people called him Yáng Wúdí (Yang the Peerless).
He was the first to establish the policy of obstructing the border.
When he reached Lángyácūn,
he inwardly disliked the place,
and wished to avoid it but could not.
After being captured,
he died three days later.
Xiézhěn returned to the capital,
and due to his merit, was given the additional title of Grand Guardian (Tàibǎo).
He followed the Empress Dowager on the southern campaign,
and died in the army.
The Empress Dowager personally mourned for him
and provided funeral materials.
His concubine-born son, Gǒu'ér,
achieved the office of Minor General (Xiǎo Jiāngjūn).
Yēlǜ Xīdī
was a descendant of the Prince of Chǔ (Chǔguówáng), Mèngfù.
He was skilled in archery and horsemanship,
and courageous in attack and battle.
During the reign of Jǐngzōng,
he was frequently appointed to military matters.
In the fourth year of Tǒnghé (Tǒnghé sì nián),
he became the Xiángwěn (Commander) of the Right Pìshì Guard (Yòu Píshì Xiángwěn).
At that time, the Sòng general Yáng Jìyè had captured commanderies and counties in Shānxī.
Xīdī followed the Military Commissioner Xiézhěn to subdue him.
In every battle, he personally took the lead.
His arrows never missed their mark.
Jìyè was defeated south of Shuòzhōu
and hid deep in the forest.
Xīdī saw the shadow of his robe and shot,
causing Jìyè to fall from his horse.
Previously,
the military order required Jìyè to be captured alive.
For this reason, Xīdī was unable to claim the merit [of killing him].
Later, when the Empress Dowager campaigned south,
he repeatedly achieved military success.
He died of illness.
Yēlǜ Xuégǔ,
courtesy name Yǐxīnyǐn,
was the concubine-born grandson of Yúyuè Wā.
He was intelligent and fond of learning,
and skilled in translation and poetry.
During the Bǎoníng era,
he was appointed Palace Cup Attendant (Yùzhǎn Lángjūn).
In the first year of Qiánhēng,
after Sòng had captured Hédōng,
they pressed their advantage and invaded Yān.
Xuégǔ received an imperial order to go provide aid.
Just as he arrived at the capital,
the Sòng had defeated Yēlǜ Xīdǐ and Xiāo Tǎogǔ, among others.
Their momentum increased.
They surrounded the city three times,
digging tunnels to advance,
and the common people within the city harbored disloyalty.
Xuégǔ used tactics to stabilize those who were wavering,
prepared defenses according to circumstances,
and did not slacken day or night.
Just then, over three hundred enemy soldiers climbed the city walls at night.
Xuégǔ fought and repelled them.
When the relief army arrived,
the siege was consequently lifted.
Xuégǔ opened the gates and arrayed his forces.
Drums sounded on all four sides.
The residents shouted loudly,
their noise shaking heaven and earth.
Soon after came the victory at Gāoliáng.
Due to his merit, he was remotely granted the title of Military Commissioner of Bǎojìng Commandery (Bǎojìng Jūn Jiédùshǐ),
and became the Commander-in-Chief of Cavalry and Infantry of Nánjīng (Nánjīng Mǎbù Jūn Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ).
In the second year [of Qiánhēng],
during the campaign against Sòng,
he requested command over the Hàn troops.
This was granted,
and his title was changed to Military Commissioner of Zhāngguó Commandery (Zhāngguó Jūn Jiédùshǐ).
At that time, the southern border was not yet peaceful,
and the people desired rest.
Xuégǔ prohibited raiding and looting to pacify them.
At the time, the Sòng general Pān Měi led troops to invade by various routes.
As Xuégǔ had few soldiers,
he exaggerated his forces by displaying many flags and banners,
and mixed common villagers among the troops to act as a diversionary force.
That night,
coincidentally, a beacon fire was raised at Dúhǔ Yù (Solitary Tiger Gorge).
He dispatched men to scout,
who saw the enemy capturing and looting the villages.
He attacked them,
recovered all the stolen goods,
and captured their commander.
From then on, Xuégǔ and Pān Měi each adhered to the border agreement,
neither crossing into the other's territory,
and the people secured their livelihood.
Due to his merit, he was appointed Tìyǐn,
and died.
His younger brother was Wūbùlǚ.
Wūbùlǚ,
courtesy name Liúyǐn.
He was serious and dignified,
possessed great physical strength,
and was skilled in composition.
During the Tǒnghé era campaign against Sòng,
he was repeatedly entrusted with military matters.
He once clashed with Yáo Zhí,
and consequently said:
"You slave,
what do you know?"
Yáo Zhí complained to the Northern Chancellery Military Commissioner Hán Déràng.
Déràng became angry
and asked:
"How did you acquire such a slave?"
Wūbùlǚ replied:
"They were easily obtained even in the era of Sānfù Yìjí (the time of fragmented clans and registers)."
Déràng laughed and released him.
Later, he followed Xiāo Dé in campaigning against the Púlú Máochǔ tribe,
and due to his merit, became the Supervising Commander of the Eastern Route (Dōnglù Tǒngjūn Dūjiān).
When Déràng became Grand Chancellor (Dà Chéngxiàng),
he recommended Wūbùlǚ as talented enough to serve as Commander (Tǒngjūnshǐ).
The Empress Dowager said:
"Wūbùlǚ was once disrespectful to you, Lord.
Why do you recommend him?"
Déràng reported:
"Though I hold the Chancellor’s position,
he remains unyielding even toward me,
let alone toward others.
By this, I know he is capable of service.
If he is appointed and utilized,
he will surely be able to govern and pacify the various foreign tribes."
The Empress Dowager agreed,
and bestowed upon him the titles Grand Master of Court Discussion with Gold and Purple (Jīnzǐ Chónglù Dàfū) and Acting Grand Commandant (Jiǎnxiào Tàiwèi).
However, his younger brother Guóliú fled due to a crime,
and Wūbùlǚ and his mother were both imprisoned (delivered to the authorities).
Fearing disaster would reach his mother,
he secretly sent someone to summon Guóliú,
deceiving him by saying:
"The Empress Dowager knows the case was fabricated.
Just come, don't be afraid."
When Guóliú arrived,
he was handed over to the relevant department
and executed for his crime.
After this,
he retired and returned to his hometown,
and died of illness.
led their armies to besiege Yān,
and subsequently dispatched Cáo Bīn, Yáng Jìyè, and others to launch attacks via separate routes.
In these two campaigns,
the Liáo was indeed perilously close to ruin!
Yēlǜ Xiūgē fought valiantly at Gāoliáng,
and the enemy troops scattered and collapsed;
Yēlǜ Xiézhěn captured Yáng Jìyè at Shuò Zhōu,
and soon the former territory was recovered.
From then on, the Sòng did not penetrate deeply again;
the state was stabilized and the borders were peaceful.
Even when compared to famous generals of antiquity,
they are without shame.
However, if it were not for Yēlǜ Xuégǔ stabilizing the internal unrest while located at Nánjīng,
then the achievements of the two generals
would likely have been difficult to attain.
Therefore it is said:
The state is made important by its people—
truly faithful words.
Biographies, Chapter Fourteen: Yēlǜ Shā, Yēlǜ Mǒzhī, Xiāo Gān (Tǎogǔ), Yēlǜ Shànbǔ, Yēlǜ Hǎilǐ
Yēlǜ Shā,
courtesy name Ānyǐn.
His ancestors once served as chancellor for the Yáoniǎn clan.
During the Yìnglì period,
he was successively promoted to Chancellor of the Southern Administration.
When Emperor Jǐngzōng ascended the throne,
he was put in overall charge of border affairs in the south.
During the Bǎoníng period,
when Sòng attacked Hédōng,
Shā led troops to relieve them,
achieved merit,
and was granted the honorary title Grand Guardian (Tàibǎo).
Early in the Gānhēng period,
Sòng again invaded the north.
Shā led troops via a side route to Báimǎ Lǐng,
where they were halted by a large stream and met the enemy.
Shā and the various generals wished to wait for the rear troops to arrive before engaging in battle,
but the Prince of Jì, Díliè, and the Army Supervisor Yēlǜ Mǒzhī
believed that an immediate attack was opportune.
Shā could not overrule them.
Díliè and the others led the vanguard across the stream,
but before they were halfway across,
they were attacked by the Sòng forces,
and the army collapsed. Díliè, along with his son Wāgē, Shā's son Délǐ, Lìngwěn Dūmǐn, and Xiángwěn Tángkuò—these five generals all perished.
Just then, the Northern Chancellor Yēlǜ Xiézhěn arrived with his troops;
ten thousand arrows were fired simultaneously,
and the enemy army finally retreated.
Shā was about to hurry to Tàiyuán,
when the Hàn Commander and Imperial Son-in-Law Lú Jùn came defecting,
saying Tàiyuán had already fallen.
He then restrained his troops and returned.
Sòng, riding the momentum, invaded Yān.
Shā engaged them in battle at the Gāoliáng River,
and was slightly pushed back.
However, upon meeting Yēlǜ Xiūgē and Yēlǜ Xiézhěn, who intercepted the enemy,
they defeated the Sòng army.
The Sòng ruler fled under cover of night;
upon reaching Zhuō Zhōu,
he wore common clothes, rode a donkey cart,
and escaped via a side road.
The Emperor pardoned his previous fault due to his merit.
That year,
he again followed Hán Kuāngsì in the campaign against Sòng,
but suffered a crushing defeat.
The Emperor wished to execute him,
but the Empress intervened and he was spared.
When Empress Ruìzhì assumed regency,
she summoned him and bestowed upon him a small table and a staff,
in honor of his advanced age.
He subsequently followed in the campaign against Sòng,
defeated the armies of Liú Tíngràng and Lǐ Jìngyuán,
and received exceedingly generous rewards.
He died in the sixth year of Tǒnghé.
Yēlǜ Mǒzhī,
courtesy name Liúyǐn,
was a descendant of the King of Suí, his paternal uncle.
Initially, as a member of the imperial clan, he entered service.
When Emperor Jǐngzōng ascended the throne,
he became Palace Secretary (Línyá),
and was known for his efficiency and competence.
During the Bǎoníng period,
he was promoted to Vice Commissioner of Military Affairs.
In the spring of the first year of Gānhēng,
when Sòng attacked Hédōng,
the Chancellor of the Southern Administration Yēlǜ Shā was made Generalissimo
and led troops to aid them;
Mǒzhī served as Army Supervisor.
At the defeat at Báimǎ Lǐng,
he barely escaped with his life.
When Sòng rode their momentum to attack Yān,
he led Xī troops alongside Yēlǜ Xiūgē
and defeated the Sòng forces.
The Emperor pardoned his previous fault due to this merit.
That winter,
he followed Generalissimo Hán Kuāngsì in the campaign against Sòng,
fighting at Mǎnchéng.
He was deceived by the Sòng general,
and the various armies scattered and collapsed;
only Mǒzhī's division did not fall into disorder.
He slowly reformed his banners and drums and returned.
An imperial edict praised and commended him,
and he was transferred to become Military Governor (Jiédùshǐ) of Nánhǎi Command.
In the second year of Gānhēng,
he was appointed Vice Commissioner of Military Affairs.
Early in the Tǒnghé period,
he served as Resident General (Liúshǒu) of the Eastern Capital.
When Sòng generals Cáo Bīn and Mǐ Xìn invaded the border,
Mǒzhī led troops to the Southern Capital
and first repaired and prepared the defenses.
When the Imperial Carriage subsequently arrived,
Mǒzhī and Yēlǜ Xiūgē engaged the enemy east of Zhuō,
defeated them,
and Mǒzhī was promoted to Military Governor of Kāiyuǎn Command.
According to custom,
the commandery people paid taxes annually,
where one *dǒu* of grain was commuted to five coins.
Mǒzhī memorialized requesting commutation to six coins,
which the local populace found beneficial.
He died toward the end of the Tǒnghé period.
Xiāo Gān,
juvenile name Xiàngliè,
courtesy name Pōdiǎn,
was the son of the Chancellor of the Northern Administration, Dílǔ.
His nature was honest and straightforward.
Initially,
during Chá Gē’s rebellion,
his partisan Húgǔzhī was friendly with Gān
and sent someone to summon him.
Gān said:
“How could I follow a rebellious subject!”
He bound the messenger and sent him to the Prince of Shòu'ān.
When the rebellion was quelled,
the Emperor praised his loyalty
and appointed him Chief Palace Secretary of the Imperial Herds.
Furthermore, due to his merit in campaigning against the Wūgǔ,
he was promoted to Chancellor of the Northern Administration,
and then transferred to be Military Governor of the Túlǚbù Tribe.
Early in Gānhēng,
Sòng attacked Hédōng
and rode their victory to invade Yān.
Gān was ordered to resist them,
and fought at the Gāoliáng River.
Yēlǜ Shā retreated,
but Gān, along with Yēlǜ Xiūgē and others, joined forces to fight and defeat the Sòng army.
The Emperor personally sent an imperial letter expressing appreciation.
From then on, he necessarily participated in deciding military affairs in every campaign.
He was promoted to Director of Government Affairs.
In the second year,
Sòng troops besieged Wǎqiáo
and launched a night attack on our camp.
Gān and Yēlǜ Yúngǔ fought and repelled them.
At that time, the Empress addressed Gān as “father” (a term of honor).
When the Empress later became Empress Dowager and assumed regency,
Gān often presented memorials outlining advantageous measures,
and many of these were accepted and implemented.
He died in the fourth year of Tǒnghé.
His nephew was Tǎogǔ.
Tǎogǔ,
courtesy name Kuòníng,
had an honest and simple nature.
Early in the Yìnglì period,
he first entered service.
When the Prince of Jì, Díliè, and the Commissioner of the Privy Council, Hǎisī, plotted rebellion,
Tǎogǔ and Yēlǜ Āliè secretly reported this to the Emperor.
The Emperor praised his loyalty
and decreed that he marry Princess Pǔjǐn.
Toward the end of the Bǎoníng period,
he became Commander of the Southern Capital.
Early in Gānhēng,
when Sòng invaded Yān,
Tǎogǔ and the Northern Chancellor Xīdǐ resisted them,
but were unsuccessful,
and the army collapsed.
Tǎogǔ and the others dared not fight again
and retreated to garrison at Qīng Hé.
The Emperor heard of the defeat
and sent an envoy to rebuke them, saying:
“You did not strictly maintain scouting and lookouts,
your deployment of troops lacked strategy,
and upon meeting the enemy, you immediately lost.
What purpose do you serve as generals!”
Tǎogǔ was afraid.
A short time later,
relief troops arrived,
and Tǎogǔ fought hard to defeat the Sòng army.
The Emperor pardoned his crime,
but demoted him to Commander-in-Chief of the Palace Guard at the Southern Capital.
He died in the fourth year (of Tǒnghé).
Yēlǜ Shànbǔ,
courtesy name Yáoshēng,
was a descendant of the King of Chǔ, his paternal elder.
He was honest, diligent, and possessed talent and wisdom.
Jǐngzōng ascended the throne,
he was granted the title of Qiānniú Wèi Dà Jiàngjūn,
and was transferred to be the Jiédùshǐ of Dàtóng Jūn.
When Sòng was attacked,
Hán Kuāngsì and Yēlǜ Shā led troops advancing via the eastern route;
Shànbǔ, serving as the Nánjīng Tǒngjūnshǐ, advanced
via the western route. Shànbǔ, hearing that Kuāngsì
had suffered a defeat, gathered his troops and returned.
At the end of Qiánhēng
(era), he fought the Sòng army at Mǎnchéng.
He was surrounded by the attacking forces,
but Xiézhěn rescued him, allowing him to escape.
Because of his lack of preparation,
he was punished with a severe caning.
At the beginning of Tǒnghé
(era), he became the Tìyǐn.
When Sòng subsequently invaded,
Shànbǔ served as Dū Yuánshuài to repel them.
He dared not engage in battle,
so many prefectures and counties west of the ridge fell.
He was dismissed as Tìyǐn.
Because his uncle, Ānduān, had rendered service
in assisting Shìzōng, the Emperor pitied him.
Shànbǔ was summoned to serve as the Nánfǔ Zǎixiàng,
and later transferred to be Nányuàn Dàwáng.
When the campaign against Sòng
was launched again, intending to attack Wèifǔ,
the masses were summoned for a collective discussion.
The generals and officers, believing Wèichéng lacked preparation,
all argued that it could be attacked.
Shànbǔ said:
"Attacking is certainly easy,
but the city is immense and incalculable.
If we capture the city,
the soldiers will be greedy for captives and plunder,
and their momentum will surely be impossible to restrain.
Moreover, there are many major garrisons nearby;
each will send out reinforcements.
If we face serious enemies internally,
how can we withstand them?"
Thereupon, the Emperor stopped the plan.
Shànbǔ’s character was cowardly
and cautious. He preserved tranquility.
In all campaigns,
he dreaded offense and warfare,
and hastily returned.
Because of this, his battles were often unsuccessful.
He died at the age of seventy-four.
Yēlǜ Hǎilǐ,
courtesy name Liúyǐn,
was the eldest son of Lìngwěn Bálǐdé.
During the rebellion of Chá Gē,
his mother, Dìlǔ, was involved.
People were sent to summon Hǎilǐ,
but Hǎilǐ refused them.
When the rebellion was quelled,
Dìlǔ was spared because of her son.
Hǎilǐ was frugal and simple,
and did not pursue fame or profit.
He entertained himself through archery and hunting.
Although he lived in idleness,
people respected him as if he were a high official.
In the beginning of Bǎoníng
(era), he was appointed Zhāngguó Jūn Jiédùshǐ,
and later transferred to Tìyǐn.
When his tenure was complete,
he claimed illness and retired from office.
After a long time,
he was reinstated as Nányuàn Dàwáng.
When Cáo Bīn, Mǐ Xìn,
and others invaded, Hǎilǐ achieved merit in repelling the enemy,
and was granted the title Zīzhōng Bǎoyì Kuāngguó Gōngchén.
The Emperor personally campaigned frequently,
Hǎilǐ served in the Nányuàn for more than ten years,
stabilizing the region through leniency and tranquility.
The population increased,
and contemporary opinion held him in high regard.
He was enfeoffed as Qīshuǐ Jùnwáng,
transferred to Shàngjīng Liúshǒu,
and passed away.
An imperial edict commanded that due to his family's poverty, funeral supplies should be provided.
Commentary states: During the victories at Gāoliáng and Shuòzhōu,
subordinate generals such as Shā and Mǒzhǐ,
saw their merit realized through Xiūgē and Xiézhěn—
what is called “losing it in the East Corner
and retrieving it at the Mulberry and Elm.”
As for Xiāo Gàn and Hǎilǐ, refusing the summons of Chá Gē,
and suppressing the rebellion of Gǔ Gào Hǎisī,
their merit was not merely in military achievements.
Compared to the fearful cowardice of Shànbǔ,
were they not superior?
Biographies Fifteen: Xiāo Tàlǐn, Xiāo Guānyīn Nú, Yēlǜ Tízǐ, Yēlǜ Xiélǐ, Yēlǜ Núguā, Xiāo Liǔ, Gāo Xūn, Xī Héshuò Nú, Xiāo Tǎliègé, Yēlǜ Sāhé.
Xiāo Tàlǐn,
courtesy name Tuóníng,
was the son of a second cousin of Sīwēn.
His father, Zhúlǔliè,
was skilled in judging horses.
During the Yìnglì era, he served as Mǎqún Shìzhōng.
Tàlǐn was upright and sincere in youth,
possessed talent and strategy,
and understood astronomy.
In the beginning of Bǎoníng
(era), he served as a Sùzhí Guān,
and was repeatedly appointed to difficult posts.
In the fourth year of Tǒnghé
(986 CE), Yáng Jìyè of Sòng led troops to invade via Dàizhōu,
capturing towns and cities.
Tàlǐn, as Fù Bùshǔ of the various armies,
followed the Pīmìshǐ Yēlǜ Xiézhěn and defeated them,
capturing Jìyè at Shuòzhōu.
In the autumn of the sixth year,
he was appointed Nányuàn Dūjiān,
followed the imperial cortege on the Southern Campaign,
and attacked Shāduī.
He fought hard and was wounded,
and the Empress Dowager personally came to check on him.
The following year,
he was granted the titles Yòu Jiānmén Wèi Shàng Jiàngjūn and Jiǎnxiào Tàishī,
and was concurrently granted the title of Zhāngdé Jūn Jiédùshǐ from afar.
In the eleventh year,
he and the Dōngjīng Liúshǒu Xiāo Dé campaigned against Gāolì,
defeating them.
Gāolì acknowledged vassalage and paid tribute.
In the twelfth year,
the Xià people caused trouble at the border.
The Imperial Grand Consort received the mandate to command the armies of the Wūgǔ and Yǒngxīng Palaces to suppress them.
Tàlǐn was made the Zǔbǔ Dū Xiángwěn.
All orders and commands in the army
were entrusted entirely to Tàlǐn by the Grand Consort.
When the army returned,
due to his merit, he was additionally granted the concurrent position of Shìzhōng,
and enfeoffed as Lánlíng Jùnwáng.
In the fifteenth year,
the people of the Díliè Tribe killed their Xiángwěn and rebelled,
fleeing to the northwestern wilderness.
Tàlǐn led light cavalry to pursue them,
and subsequently suppressed those Zǔbǔ who had not yet submitted.
The yearly tribute of local products from the various foreign states filled the state coffers,
and thereafter, their comings and goings were like that of a single family.
The Emperor bestowed a poem in commendation,
and furthermore ordered the Línyá Yēlǜ Zhāo to compose a rhapsody (fù)
to narrate his achievements.
Tàlǐn, observing that the submission and rebellion of the various tribes was unstable,
presented a memorial requesting the construction of three cities to eliminate border troubles.
This was approved.
Soon after, he was summoned to serve as Nánjīng Tǒngjūnshǐ.
In the twentieth year,
he campaigned against Sòng again.
He captured their general Wáng Xiānzhī,
defeated their army at Suíchéng,
and took Qízhōu.
The Emperor issued a personal decree of praise and encouragement.
He advanced to Chányuān.
The Sòng ruler commanded the army between the city walls and the moat.
Before engaging in battle,
Tàlǐn inspected the terrain,
and while taking Sòng's Shènglǎnguān, Yánduī, and Fúyàn (locations/resources),
he was struck by an arrow from a hidden crossbowman.
The next day,
the funerary chariot arrived.
The Empress Dowager wept bitterly over him,
and suspended court for five days.
His son, Zàogǔ,
served as Nánjīng Tǒngjūnshǐ.
Xiāo Guānyīn Nú,
courtesy name Yēníng,
was the grandson of Xī Wáng Dāhé.
In the twelfth year of Tǒnghé,
he became Yòu Zhīhòu Lángjūn Bān Xiángwěn,
and was transferred to Xī Liù Bù Dàwáng.
Previously,
in addition to their regular salaries and ranks,
they were given a hundred deer and roe deer,
all taken from the populace.
Guānyīn Nú memorialized for this practice to be abolished.
When Sòng was attacked,
he served as vanguard alongside Xiāo Tàlǐn,
securing the surrender of Qízhōu,
and taking Déqīng Jūn.
The Emperor bestowed generous rewards upon him.
He served as Tóngzhī Nányuàn Shì,
and died.
Yēlǜ Tízǐ,
courtesy name Shèngyǐn,
was the grandson of Běifǔ Zǎixiàng Wùlǐ.
He was skilled in archery
and adept at painting.
During the Bǎoníng era,
he served as Yù Zhǎn Lángjūn.
In the ninth year,
he was sent on a mission to Hàn,
and fully explained the plan for lasting peaceful relations between the two states.
Its ruler, Jìyuán, treated him with great respect and honor.
In the second year of Tǒnghé [984 CE],
he led troops with the Western Xiángwěn, Yēlǜ Sùsǎ, to suppress the Tuóluójīn,
and greatly defeated them.
In the fourth year [986 CE],
the Sòng general Yáng Jìyè occupied cities and towns in Shānxī.
Tízǐ followed the Northern Court Grand Councilor and Commissioner of Military Affairs, Yēlǜ Xiézhěn, to attack him,
and defeated Hè Lìngtú at Dìng'ān.
He was appointed Deputy Commissioner-in-Chief of Recruitment and Pacification for the Southwest Region.
The Sòng army defending Wèizhōu was hard-pressed
and called for external reinforcements.
Tízǐ heard of this
and ambushed troops by the road at night.
At dawn,
the Sòng troops indeed arrived;
he attacked them before they had passed halfway.
The army within the city sallied forth,
and Xiézhěn subsequently intercepted them.
Both Sòng armies completely collapsed
and fled towards Fēihú.
As the terrain was narrow, they could not advance,
and the casualties were heavy.
Hè Lìngtú reassembled the routed soldiers to raid Wèizhōu again.
Tízǐ met them in battle
and defeated them.
The defending general of Yìngzhōu fled on his own.
He advanced to besiege Huánzhōu,
climbed the city wall under a hail of arrows and stones,
and the Sòng army was utterly defeated.
When Xiézhěn captured Jìyè at Shuòzhōu,
Tízǐ’s achievement was the greatest.
In the winter of that year,
he again joined Xiāo Tàlǐn to attack Sòng via the eastern route,
capturing many prisoners and booty.
Later, hearing that Sòng troops were garrisoned at Yìzhōu,
he led troops to intercept them,
but died upon reaching the border of Yìzhōu.
Previously,
when Tízǐ defeated Lìngtú,
there was a Sòng general who fell due to wounds.
Tízǐ painted his likeness to show the Sòng people,
and all lamented its wondrous resemblance.
Yēlǜ Xiélǐ,
courtesy name Wūgǔlín,
was a man from the Tūjǔ tribe.
In the fourth year of Tǒnghé [986 CE],
the Sòng general Yáng Jìyè came to attack Shānxī.
Xiélǐ followed Yēlǜ Xiézhěn to attack him,
always serving as the vanguard,
and achieved merit in reconnaissance and scouting.
In that year [986 CE],
when Sòng was attacked,
the Sòng people resisted at the Hūtuó Hé.
Xiélǐ led elite cavalry to cross first via a shortcut,
capturing their general Kāng Bǎowēi.
In recognition of this merit, an imperial decree stipulated that his lineage should be eligible for selection as Jiédùshǐ forever.
In the first year of Tàipíng [1021 CE],
he was gradually promoted to Jiédùshǐ of his own tribe.
In the sixth year [1026 CE],
he followed Xiāo Huì to attack Gānzhōu,
but failed to take it.
At that time, the Zǔbǔ attacked and besieged Sānkè Jūn.
Xiélǐ went to rescue them with the Deputy Commissioner-in-Chief Yēlǜ Nièlǔgǔ.
Upon reaching the southwest of Kědūn Chéng,
they encountered the enemy.
He could not form a battle array
and died from a stray arrow.
Yēlǜ Núguā,
courtesy name Yánníng,
was the grandson of the Southern Court Chancellor Sū, who was Tàizǔ’s half-brother.
He possessed great physical strength
and was skilled at training hawks and falcons.
In the fourth year of Tǒnghé [986 CE],
when Sòng's Yáng Jìyè invaded,
Núguā served as the Deputy Commissioner-in-Chief of the Huángpíshì Jiū,
defeated him,
and completely recovered the lost cities and towns.
When the army returned,
he was promoted to Minor General of the Various Guards.
When Sòng was later attacked,
he gained merit
and was promoted to Huángpíshì Xiángwěn.
In the sixth year [988 CE],
the campaign was renewed.
He led the vanguard forces,
defeated the Sòng skirmishers at Dìngzhōu,
and was made Commander-in-Chief of Dōngjīng,
and was awarded the grade of Gold and Purple Grand Master for Supervising Good Fortune.
He followed the King of Xī, Héshuònú, to attack the Wùrě.
Due to a loss in battle,
his Gold and Purple Grand Master rank was stripped.
In the nineteenth year [1001 CE],
he was appointed Chancellor of the Southern Court.
In the twenty-first year [1003 CE],
he attacked Sòng again,
capturing their general Wáng Jìzhōng at Wàngdū,
and capturing and killing many soldiers.
In recognition of this merit, he was promoted to Joint Manager of Affairs with the Secretariat-Chancellery.
In the twenty-sixth year [1008 CE],
he served as Jiédùshǐ of Liáoxīng Jūn,
and soon after was again made Chancellor of the Southern Court.
At the beginning of Kāitài [1012 CE],
he was granted the title Shàngfù,
and then passed away.
Xiāo Liǔ,
courtesy name Túmén,
was the fifth-generation descendant of Āgǔzhǐ, the younger brother of Empress Chúnqīn.
He was raised in the household of his paternal uncle Páiyā when young.
He was widely knowledgeable,
skilled in writing,
and his physical strength surpassed others.
During the Tǒnghé period [983–1012 CE],
his uncle Délín, on his deathbed,
recommended his talent,
and an imperial decree summoned him to serve in the Imperial Guard.
In the seventeenth year [999 CE],
during the southern campaign,
the Sòng general Fàn Tíngzhào arranged a square formation and waited.
At that time, the Imperial Brother Lóngqìng served as the vanguard
and asked the assembled generals and aides who dared to take the lead.
Liǔ said:
“If I can obtain a swift horse,
then I am willing to go first.”
Lóngqìng provided him with armored cavalry.
Liǔ grasped the reins
and said to the generals:
“If the enemy formation wavers,
you gentlemen must attack quickly.”
He then galloped forward,
and the enemy slightly retreated.
Lóngqìng seized the opportunity to attack them,
and the Southern (Sòng) army immediately fell into disorder.
Liǔ was struck by a stray arrow,
but bound his wound and continued fighting.
Everyone scattered before him.
At that time, Páiyā was serving as Resident General of Dōngjīng
and submitted a memorial recommending Liǔ as Commander-in-Chief of the Four Armies.
The following year [1000 CE],
he was appointed Northern Nǚzhí Xiángwěn.
His governance balanced leniency and strictness,
and the people of the tribe respected and loved him.
He was promoted to Commander-in-Chief of the Eastern Route.
When his term was completed,
the populace requested that he be allowed to remain and serve another term,
which was granted.
He followed the campaign against Gāolì (Koryŏ).
When they encountered a large snake blocking the road,
the forerunners requested to avoid it.
Liǔ said:
“How can a brave man fear this?”
He drew his sword and cut the snake in two.
When the army returned,
he retired from office.
Liǔ enjoyed humor and jesting.
Even during private feasts between ruler and ministers,
he made jokes without reserve.
People at the time compared him to an actor.
On his deathbed,
he said to someone:
“When I was young, I aimed to serve the ruler well,
but since I could not succeed directly,
I proceeded with humor.
Hoping to achieve one ten-thousandth of something beneficial,
why should I avoid the name of an actor!”
A moment later,
he sat up dressed in his sleeping clothes
and shouted:
“I am leaving!”
He died immediately after speaking.
Yēlǜ Guānyīnnu collected a thousand poems written by Liǔ
and titled the collection *Suìhán Jí*.
Gāo Xūn,
courtesy name Dǐngchén,
was the son of Gāo Xìntāo, the King of Běipíng in Jìn.
He was naturally perceptive and clever.
He served Jìn as Palace Gate Prefect.
In the ninth year of Huìtóng [946 CE],
he surrendered along with Dù Zhòngwēi.
When Tàizōng entered Biàn,
he was appointed Prefect of the Four Quarters Hall.
He liked to associate with the powerful and noble
and was able to serve the senior ministers diligently,
often promoting and praising them.
During the Tiānlù period,
he served as the Shūmìshǐ (Commissioner of Military Affairs),
overseeing the military affairs of Hàn.
In the fifth year,
Liú Chóng sent an envoy seeking enfeoffment and investiture.
An imperial decree ordered Xūn to invest Chóng as Dà Hàn Shénwǔ Huángdì (Great Hàn Divine Martial Emperor).
Early in the Yìnglì period,
he was enfeoffed as Zhào Wáng (Prince of Zhào).
He was sent out to serve as the Liúshǒu (Defense Commissioner) of Shàngjīng,
soon relocating to Nánjīng.
When Sòng intended to build a city at Yìjīn,
Xūn submitted a memorial requesting permission to patrol and scout to harass them.
The Emperor approved his memorial,
and Sòng consequently failed to complete the city.
In the seventeenth year,
Sòng seized territory near Yìjīn Guān (Yìjīn Pass).
Xūn defeated them,
and was appointed Zhī Nányuàn Shūmì Shì (Manager of Southern Chancellery Military Affairs).
When Jǐngzōng ascended the throne,
based on his merit in securing the succession plan,
he was promoted to Wáng (Prince) of Qín.
During the Bǎoníng period,
noting that there was much vacant land within the outskirts of Nánjīng,
he requested permission to dig ditches and plant rice.
The Emperor intended to grant this.
Línyá Yēlǜ Kūn declared in court:
"This memorial by Gāo Xūn
must hide ulterior motives.
If we truly allow rice cultivation,
drawing water and creating fields,
should the capital rebel,
how would the imperial forces enter?"
The Emperor was suspicious,
and did not accept the proposal.
Soon after, he was transferred to Nányuàn Shūmìshǐ (Commissioner of the Southern Chancellery).
He presented poison to Fùmǎ Dūwèi Xiāo Chuòlǐ.
When the matter was discovered,
he was exiled to Tóngzhōu.
Soon after, he also plotted to murder Shàngshū Lìng Xiāo Sīwēn.
He was executed by imperial decree in prison,
his property confiscated,
and all given to the family of Sīwēn.
Xī Héshuònú,
courtesy name Chóuníng,
was a descendant of the Xī Kèhán (Khan of Xī).
During the Bǎoníng period,
he served as the Chief of the Six Departments of the Xī.
Early in the Tǒnghé period,
the Empress Dowager assumed regency.
Yēlǜ Xiūgē was put in charge of the southern border affairs,
and Héshuònú was made the Fù Bùshǔ (Vice Commander) of the Southern Campaign Army.
In the fourth year,
Sòng forces led by Cáo Bīn, Mǐ Xìn, and others invaded.
Héshuònú and Xiūgē defeated the Sòng troops south of Yān,
and received handwritten edicts praising them.
When the army returned,
relying on his power, he beat the innocent man Lǐ Hào to death.
The Emperor pardoned him because of his achievements.
In the winter of the sixth year,
during the southern campaign,
he led his departmental troops along a separate route to attack the enemy forces at Lángshān,
capturing a great number of prisoners.
In the eighth year,
he submitted a memorial, saying:
"I humbly observe that during the time of Tàizōng,
the Six Departments of the Xī had two Zǎixiàng (Chancellors) and two Chánggǔn.
By imperial decree, the position of the Senior Chánggǔn ranked beside the Chief,
and the Vice Chánggǔn oversaw the kinship groups of the Chief’s five branches.
The two Zǎixiàng supported and assisted the Chief,
proposing virtuous policies.
Currently, the duties of the Zǎixiàng remain the same,
but the two Chánggǔn have no specific jurisdiction.
I request that the old system be reinstated."
This was granted.
In the autumn of the thirteenth year,
he was transferred to Dū Bùshǔ (Commander-in-Chief),
and campaigned against Wùrě.
He halted at Tiělí
for several months,
before advancing to Wùrě Chéng (Wùrě City).
He sought success through plunder and captives.
He requested surrender, but it was refused,
so he ordered an immediate attack.
Those within the city were greatly terrified,
and all fought to the death.
Héshuònú knew they could not conquer it,
so, following the advice of Fù Bùshǔ Xiāo Dé,
he plundered the territory to the southeast,
and returned along the northern border of Gāolì.
Because the region was distant and supplies were exhausted,
and soldiers and horses suffered casualties,
an imperial decree reduced his noble title.
He died.
His son, Wūyě,
was a Lángjūn Bān Xiángwěn (Chief of the Lángjūn Ranks).
Xiāo Tǎliègé,
courtesy name Xióngyǐn,
was a man of the Wǔyuàn Department.
His eighth-generation ancestor, Zhǐlǔ,
once served as Yúrén (Game Warden) during the time of the Yáoniǎn clan.
When Táng’s Ān Lùshān came to attack,
Zhǐlǔ fought them south of Hēishān (Black Mountain),
and defeated them.
Based on this merit, he became Běifǔ Zǎixiàng (Chancellor of the Northern Administration),
and his descendants were selected for this office for generations.
Tǎliègé served during the Kāitài period,
and was repeatedly promoted to Xīnánmiàn Zhāotǎoshǐ (Commissioner for Pacification and Investigation of the Southwest).
In the eleventh year of Chóngxī,
he was sent as an envoy to Xī Xià,
conveying the matter of attacking Sòng,
and arranging for Yuán Hào to advance by a separate route to rendezvous.
In the twelfth year,
he was transferred to Yòu Yílíbì (Right Chancellor) and concurrently served as Tóng Zhī Nánjīng Liúshǒu (Assistant to the Defense Commissioner of Nánjīng).
He was later transferred to Zuǒ Yílíbì (Left Chancellor),
and shortly after, appointed Dōngjīng Liúshǒu (Defense Commissioner of Dōngjīng).
Following the hereditary selection process, he became Běifǔ Zǎixiàng,
and died.
Yēlǜ Sāhé,
courtesy name Shuàilǎn,
was a man of the Yǐshì Department,
and the son of Nánfǔ Zǎixiàng (Chancellor of the Southern Administration) Ōulǐsī.
He began his career during the Tiānlù period.
During the Yìnglì period,
he was appointed Yǐshì Dàwáng (Great King of Yǐshì),
concurrently managing military affairs.
Early in the Qiánhēng period,
Sòng invaded.
By imperial decree, he commanded his departmental troops to defend Nánjīng.
He engaged the invading forces along with Běiyuàn Dàwáng Xīdǐ and Tǒngjūn Xiāo Tǎogǔ, among others.
Xīdǐ and the others were defeated and fled,
but Sāhé alone returned with his entire army intact.
The Emperor admonished him, saying:
"Resistance against the enemy should be like this.
Exert yourself, Sir,
and do not worry about failing to achieve wealth and honor."
He was promoted to Shǒu Tàibǎo (Protector Grand Preceptor).
He died during the Tǒnghé period.
Commentary says: During the Tǒnghé period,
Liáo repeatedly raised troops to attack Sòng.
Generals such as Yēlǜ Xiélǐ, Núguā, and Xiāo Liǔ all achieved merit in capturing cities and seizing generals.
Finally,
Xiāo Tǎlǐn (written as Xiāo Tà●) was appointed Tǒngjūn (Commander),
advancing straight to Chányuān.
As they were about to fight Sòng,
Tǎlǐn was struck by a crossbow bolt.
Our troops lost their leader,
and only then was the peace agreement settled.
Perhaps Heaven was weary of the turmoil,
causing the people of the North and South to gain respite!
Biography Sixteen: Yēlǜ Hézhù, Liú Jǐng, Liú Liùfú, Yēlǜ Niǎolǚ, Niú Wēnshū, Dù Fáng, Xiāo Héshang (Tèmò), Yēlǜ Hélǐzhǐ, Yēlǜ Pōdí.
Yēlǜ Hézhù,
courtesy name Niángǔn,
was the grandson of Tàizǔ’s younger brother, Diélà.
As a child, he disliked frivolous games.
When dealing with affairs, he was insightful and quick-witted,
and skilled in discussion.
He first entered service due to being a close relative,
and achieved merit whenever he accompanied military campaigns.
Early in the Bǎoníng period,
he was granted the title Yòu Lónghǔ Wèi Shàng Jiāngjūn (Superior General of the Right Dragon and Tiger Guard).
Since Sòng forces repeatedly obstructed the southern border,
he was appointed Zhuōzhōu Cìshǐ (Prefect of Zhuōzhōu),
along with the offices of Xīnán Bīngmǎ Dūjiān (Supervisor of Military Forces in the Southwest), Zhāo'ān (Pacification Commissioner), and Xúnjiǎn (Inspector).
He was bestowed the title Tuī Zhōng Fèng Guó Gōngchén (Meritorious Official Serving the State Loyally).
Hézhù served long in border defense.
Although he achieved victories and captures,
he emphasized peace and stability,
and did not recklessly stir up trouble to seek immediate fame.
Neighboring territories respected and feared him,
and the subordinate departments were peaceful and stable.
Sòng repeatedly sent people to establish friendly relations,
hoping to convey their desire for peace.
Hézhù memorialized this matter,
and the Emperor allowed peace negotiations.
In securing the border and appeasing the enemy,
he contributed greatly.
He was appointed Zuǒ Jīnwú Wèi Shàng Jiāngjūn (Superior General of the Left Guards of the Golden Insignia).
When his term of office ended,
he remotely held the title Zhènguó Jūn Jiédùshǐ (Military Governor of the State-Guarding Army),
and died.
Hézhù was intelligent and educated,
and thoroughly familiar with military administration.
While garrisoned at Fànyáng,
he once led a few cavalrymen directly to the North Gate of Xióngzhōu,
standing on horseback with the Prefect to present the advantages and disadvantages for the two nations,
as well as the details of Zhōu's troops invading the border.
His words and manner were impassioned,
and his attendants admired him.
From then on,
the border remained peaceful for several years.
Those who understood the situation believed that one word from Hézhù
was more valuable than several hundred thousand troops.
Liú Jǐng,
styled Kědà,
was a native of Héjiān.
His great-great-grandfather, Pēng,
was the nephew of Zhū Tāo
and served as the Táng Dynasty’s Right Director of the Palace Affairs (Yòu Púshè) and Military Commissioner of Lúlóng Army (Lúlóng Jūn Jiédù Shǐ).
His father, Shǒujìng,
was the Vice-Resident of the Southern Capital (Nánjīng Fù Liúshǒu).
Jǐng possessed upright and sincere qualities
and was fond of learning and skilled in writing.
Zhào Yánshòu, the Prince of Yān, appointed him Literary Scholar of Yōudū Prefecture (Yōudū Fǔ Wénxué).
In the beginning of the Yìnglì era,
he was promoted to Right Reminder (Yòu Shíyí) and Drafting Official (Zhī Zhìgào),
and later served as a Hanlin Academician (Hànlín Xuéshì).
In the ninth year (959),
the Zhōu people invaded Yān.
The Resident, Xiāo Sīwēn, submitted an urgent report on the crisis.
The emperor intended to wait until autumn to dispatch the army,
but Jǐng remonstrated, saying:
“The three passes north of the Yellow River have already fallen to the enemy.
Now they are invading Yān again.
How can we sit and watch?”
The emperor did not listen.
Soon after, he left due to mourning his father.
Not long after,
he was recalled to his former position.
One day,
he was summoned to draft an amnesty decree.
After it was completed,
it was retained for several months without being issued.
Jǐng memorialized, saying:
“Under the Táng system,
an amnesty decree travels five hundred *lǐ* a day.
Now delaying the date and not issuing it
is incorrect.”
The emperor also gave no reply.
After Jǐngzōng ascended the throne,
due to Jǐng’s loyalty and honesty,
he was promoted to Vice Minister of Rites (Lǐbù Shìláng),
and later moved to Academician of the Shū and Xuānzhèng Halls.
The Emperor intended to rely heavily on him,
and inscribed on his tablet (*hù*) the words:
“Liú Jǐng is capable of becoming a chief minister.”
A short time later,
he served as the Vice-Resident of the Southern Capital.
At that time, the Resident Hán Kuāngsì followed the imperial entourage north,
and Jǐng managed the affairs of the capital jointly with Hán’s son, Déràng.
He was soon summoned to be the Commissioner of the Ministry of Revenue (Hùbù Shǐ),
and successively served as Military Commissioner of the Wǔdìng and Kāiyuǎn Armies.
In the sixth year of Tǒnghé (988), he retired
and was additionally granted the concurrent title of Attendant Counselor (Shìzhōng).
He died
at the age of sixty-seven.
He was posthumously granted the title Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Tàishī).
His son was Shènxíng.
His grandsons were Yīdé, Èrxuán, Sānjǐa, Sìduān, Wǔcháng, and Liùfú,
all of whom are covered in the biography of Liùfú.
Liú Liùfú’s
father was Shènxíng.

He rose from Assistant Director of the Bureau of Provisions (Shànbù Yuánwàiláng) to Northern Administration Chief Minister (Běifǔ Zǎixiàng) and Supervisor of the Compilation of State History (Jiān Xiū Guóshǐ).
At that time, the Emperor often conducted executions and bestowed rewards during banquets and drinking sessions.
Shènxíng remonstrated, saying:
“Using happiness and anger to dispense authority and fortune
is perhaps inappropriate.”
The Emperor realized his mistake
and instructed the Privy Council
that, “Henceforth, if there are matters of punishment or reward during banquets,
they shall be reported and enacted the following day.”
He served as Commander-in-Chief (Dūtǒng)
in the campaign against Gāolì.
For missing the designated military schedule, he was handed over to the authorities.
He was spared due to the discussions of high officials,
and was sent out to serve as the Military Commissioner of Zhāngwǔ Army.
He was granted the title Meritorious Official Who Preserves Loyalty (Bǎojié Gōngchén).
He had six sons: Yīdé, Èrxuán, Sānjǐa, Sìduān, Wǔcháng, and Liùfú.
Yīdé died young.
Èrxuán died while serving as the Resident of the Supreme Capital (Shàngjīng Liúshǒu).
Wǔcháng successively held the posts of Commissioner of the Three Agencies (Sānsī Shǐ) and Military Commissioner of Wǔdìng Army.
Sānjǐa, Sìduān, and Liùfú all passed the Presented Scholar (Jìnshì) examination.
Sānjǐa and Sìduān both married princesses
and served as Commandant-Escort (Fùmǎ Dūwèi).
Sānjǐa presented Sèngzōng with a poetic essay (fù) titled "One Arrow Kills Two Deer,"
and the Emperor praised its richness and beauty.
He was not in harmony with the princess
and fled to Sòng.
When he returned,
he was executed.
Sìduān, as Minor Minister of the Imperial Guards (Wèiwèi Shà qīng), was sent as an envoy to Sòng to offer congratulations on the Emperor's birthday.
During the banquet,
when a large female orchestra was deployed,
he did not look at it until the end of the meal,
and people feared his strictness.
Upon his return,
he was appointed Academician of the Bureau of Military Affairs (Shūmì Zhí Xuéshì).
Liùfú possessed integrity and ambition,
and was skilled in writing.
In the beginning of the Chóngxī era,
he was promoted to Drafting Official of the Secretariat (Zhèngshì Shèrén),
and elevated to Hanlin Academician.
In the eleventh year (1042),
he was sent with the Commissioner of the Court of the Imperial Insignia, Xiāo Tèmò, as an envoy to Sòng to demand ten counties of land.
Upon his return,
he served as the Vice Deputy Director of the Han Chinese Traveling Palace (Hànrén Xínggōng Fù Bùshǔ).
When Sòng sent an envoy to increase the annual tribute in exchange for the ten counties,
he was again dispatched as an envoy to Sòng, along with Yēlǜ Rénxiān,
to settle the nomenclature of
“submitting tribute” (Jìn Gòng);
Sòng found this difficult.
Liùfú said:
“That our dynasty’s military is strong and generals are brave
is known throughout the realm,
and everyone desires to engage Sòng.
If we indulge in seizing captives and satisfying our desires,
which is greater, that
or the words 'submitting tribute'?
Moreover, a great army is stationed in Yān;
if by chance it advances south,
how will they defend against it?
To focus on minor details
and forget the great calamity,
what good will regret do?”
Sòng then complied,
and the annual payment was termed
“Tribute” (Gòng).
Upon Liùfú’s return,
he was additionally granted the title of Grand Councillor, Concurrent with Administrative Authority (Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāng Shì).
When the Sòng payment arrived,
Liùfú was ordered to serve as Commissioner of the Three Agencies to receive it.
Liùfú had a falling out with the Auxiliary Administrator of Governmental Affairs, Dù Fáng.
Dù Fáng, alleging that Liùfú had previously accepted bribes from Sòng,
reported the matter.
Liùfú was sent out as Military Commissioner of Chángníng Army,
but was soon recalled to be the Commissioner of the Three Agencies.
When Dàozōng ascended the throne
and was preparing to hold the grand enthronement ceremony,
the Commissioner of the Northern Administration Bureau of Military Affairs, Xiāo Gé, said:
“To hold a grand ceremony with complete rituals and objects,
we must select a broad area.
There is none better than Huángchuān.”
Liùfú said:
“That is not so.
Ritual is the foundation of the state,
and the music of emperors should not be performed in the wilderness.
The Central Capital (Zhōngjīng) is now the ultimate center for all directions,
where all those who attend the court can find their proper place.
The ceremony should be held in the Central Capital.”
The Emperor followed his suggestion.
He soon died of illness.
Yēlǜ Niǎolǚ,
styled Hǎilín,
was a descendant of Púgǔzhī, the Governor-in-Chief of the Six Administrations (Liù Yuàn Yílíjǐn).
His demeanor was refined and outstanding,
and he was skilled in painting.
During the Chóngxī era,
he was successively promoted to Assistant Administrator of the Commission of Inspections (Tóngzhī Diǎnjiǎn Sī Shì).
When the Commandant-Escort, Xiāo Húgǔ, was captured by the Xià people,
Niǎolǚ was commissioned to demand his release.
He returned after three trips,
and was transferred to Palace Commissioner of Yǒngxīng (Yǒngxīng Gōng Shǐ) and Administrator of the Right Vigilance Guard Cadre (Yòu Zhīhòu Lángjūn Bān Xiángwěn).
Niǎolǚ was about to marry the granddaughter of Princess Qínjìn.
His mother had a conflict with the princess’s maidservant
and told Niǎolǚ:
“Only if you can get rid of that maidservant
will I consent to your marriage.”
Niǎolǚ used a plan to kill her,
and the marriage took place.
When the matter was discovered,
the authorities judged it worthy of the death penalty.
Niǎolǚ was good at painting
and presented a portrait of Shèngzōng,
which earned him a reduction in sentence,
and he was exiled to a border post.
He was recalled for painting another portrait
and appointed Assistant Administrator of the Southern Administration Court of the Imperial Insignia (Tóngzhī Nányuàn Xuānhuī Shì).
He was sent as an envoy to Sòng to offer congratulations for the New Year
and returned with a portrait of the Sòng ruler.
During the Qīngníng
period, he was again sent as an envoy to Sòng.
The Sòng ruler bestowed a banquet,
but a vase of flowers separated their faces,
and he did not obtain a true look at him.
When taking leave before the throne,
he only saw him once.
Upon reaching the border,
he showed the likeness (image) to those who saw him off,
and they were astounded by its supernatural skill.
When he heard of Zhòngyuán's rebellion,
he did not immediately rush to serve the throne.
After the rebels were pacified, he entered to offer congratulations,
and the Emperor reprimanded him.
During the height of the banquet,
the Emperor looked at Niǎolǚ and said:
"If the affairs of Zhòngyuán had succeeded,
you certainly would have become the honored guest!"
Niǎolǚ was greatly ashamed.
In the Xiányōng period,
he was promoted to Grand Tutor (Tàishī) of the Crown Prince,
and then died.
Niú Wēnshū
was a native of Fànyáng.
He was firm and upright,
esteemed integrity and righteousness,
and possessed great foresight.
During the Xiányōng period,
he attained the rank of *Jìnshì*,
but remained stuck in minor official posts.
At the beginning of the Dà'ān period,
he was successively promoted to Administrator (Shǐ) of the Ministry of Revenue (Hùbù),
then transferred to Supervising Secretary (Gěishì Zhōng), and concurrently managed the affairs of the Three Bureaus Commission (Sānsī Shǐ).
As the state and the people were both prosperous,
the Emperor considered him capable,
promoted him to Vice Minister (Shìláng) of the Ministry of Revenue,
and then changed his post to Commissioner of the Three Bureaus (Sānsī Shǐ).
During the Shòulóng period,
he was appointed Counselor (Cānzhī Zhèngshì),
concurrently managing the affairs of the Bureau of Military Affairs (Shūmì Yuàn),
and acting as the Defense Commissioner (Liúshǒu) of Zhōngjīng.
The local populace went to the palace gate requesting his true (permanent) appointment,
and this was granted.
He was recalled to serve as Commissioner of the Three Bureaus.
At the beginning of the Qiántǒng period,
he again served as Counselor,
managing the affairs of the Commissioner of the Southern Bureau of Military Affairs.
In the fifth year,
Xià was attacked by Sòng,
and came seeking peace and reconciliation.
Wēnshū and Xiāo Délǐdǐ were sent as envoys to Sòng.
While a grand banquet was in progress,
an entertainer, dressed as a Dàoshì (Daoist priest),
asked for earth and mud for his elixir furnace.
The entertainer said:
"There is too little earth to mix."
Wēnshū immediately stood up
and used his hand to gather the earth and conceal it in his robes.
The Sòng ruler asked the reason.
Wēnshū replied:
"I have received the awesome mandate of the Son of Heaven to come and seek peace.
If you do not consent,
then I must roll up the earth and take it away (i.e., we will take back the land by force)."
The Sòng people were greatly alarmed,
and consequently agreed to peace with Xià.
Upon his return,
he was promoted to Director of the Chancellery (Zhōngshū Lìng),
and then died.
Dù Fáng
was a native of Guīyì County, Zhuō Zhōu.
In the fifth year of Kàitài,
he was elevated through the highest class of the *Jìnshì* examination,
and successively promoted to Attendant-in-ordinary (Qǐjū Láng) and Drafting Official (Zhī Zhìgào).
People believed he had the makings of a Prime Minister (Zǎixiàng).
During the Tàipíng period,
he was transferred to Palace Aide for Administration (Zhèngshì Shèrén),
and appointed Vice Commissioner of Military Affairs (Shūmì Fùshǐ).
In the ninth year of Chóngxī,
the Xià people invaded Sòng.
Sòng sent Guō Zhěn to report the situation,
requesting peace with Xià.
The Emperor ordered Fáng to go as an envoy to Xià to mediate the conflict.
In accordance with the agreement, troops were withdrawn,
and each side returned the encroached territory.
He was appointed Counselor (Cānzhī Zhèngshì).
Hán Shàofāng and Líu Liùfú were jealous of him,
but Fáng treated them with sincerity.
In the twelfth year,
Shàofāng and others were dismissed,
and he was trusted even more.
In the thirteenth year,
he was appointed Prime Minister of the Southern Administration (Nánfǔ Zǎixiàng).
In the fifteenth year,
Fáng had a son,
and the Emperor visited his residence
and bestowed the name Wángménnú upon the child.
Because of an error in presenting a memorial,
he was sent out to serve as Military Governor (Jiédù Shǐ) of Wǔdìng Commandery.
In the seventeenth year,
he was recalled to serve again as Prime Minister of the Southern Administration.
In the autumn of the twenty-first year,
when sacrificing to Empress Réndé,
a decree commanded scholarly officials to compose poems.
Fáng's poem was the best,
and he was granted a golden sash.
During Dàozōng's period of mourning (Liàngyīn),
he served as Commissioner for the Imperial Tomb (Shānlíng Shǐ) of the Deceased Emperor (Dàxíng Huángdì).
In the second year of Qīngníng,
the Emperor instructed Fáng, saying:
"Since you are old and fond of wine,
We do not wish to burden you with demanding duties.
The affairs of the court
shall simply require your general oversight."
Shortly thereafter,
he was appointed Right Chancellor (Yòu Chéngxiàng),
given the honorary title Shàngfǔ,
and then died.
The Emperor sighed and lamented greatly.
His funeral gifts and posthumous honors were raised in rank,
the government provided burial materials,
he was posthumously granted Director of the Chancellery (Zhōngshū Lìng),
and given the posthumous name Yuánsù.
His son, Gōngwèi,
eventually reached the post of Prime Minister of the Southern Administration.
Xiāo Héshang,
courtesy name Hóngníng,
was a descendant of the lineage of the maternal grandfather of the nation.
He was loyal and upright,
and possessed great intelligence and strategies.
At the beginning of Kàitài,
he was appointed Chamberlain for the Imperial Cup (Yùzhǎn Lángjūn),
and soon became Director (Dū Línyá) of the Bureaus for the Inner Secretariat (Nèishǐ) and Imperial Physicians (Tàiyī), etc.
He was sent as an envoy to Sòng to celebrate the New Year (Hèzhèng).
As the banquet was about to begin,
the Master of Ceremonies announced
that his seating rank was below the Military Governors (Jiédù Shǐ).
Héshang said:
"If the seating arrangement is like this,
it means you are not treating the envoy of a great nation with proper ceremony.
Furthermore, presenting us with embroidered robes as a gift
is treating us like vassal tribes (Fānbù).
If this is truly the case,
I will not participate in the banquet."
The Sòng officials could not respond.
They changed the robes to purple,
and his position was equated with that of the high officials (Zhízhèng),
whereupon the diplomatic ceremony was finally settled.
In the autumn of the eighth year,
he was made Military Governor of Tánggǔ Commandery,
and then died.
His younger brother was Tèmò.
Tèmò,
courtesy name Héníng.
He was perceptive, articulate, and strong-willed.
During the Tàipíng period,
he was successively promoted to Military Governor of Āndōng Commandery,
and was reputed to be capable.
In the eleventh year,
he was recalled to serve as Commander (Xiángwěn) of the Bureau of Left Attendant Gentlemen (Zuǒ Zhīhòu Lángjūn Bān).
Before long,
he was transferred to Commissioner of the Left (Zuǒ Yí Lí Bì).
In the tenth year of Chóngxī,
he was successively promoted to Commissioner of Palace Affairs of the Northern Administration (Běiyuàn Xuānhuī Shǐ).
The following year,
he was sent with Líu Liùfú as envoy to Sòng,
demanding the return of the former ten counties.
Sòng requested to exchange them by increasing the payment of silver and silk by 100,000 ounces and bolts.
Returning,
he reported according to the imperial will,
and was promoted to Manager of Affairs with the Status of Grand Councilor (Tóng Zhèngshì Ménxià Píngzhāng Shì).
A decree ordered the construction of a city southwest of Húndǐdiàn.
Upon his return,
he again served as Commissioner of Palace Affairs of the Northern Administration,
and then died.
Yēlǜ Hélǐzhī,
courtesy name Tèmǎn,
was a descendant of Púgǔzhī, the Commandant (Yí Lí Jǐn) of the Six Divisions.
During the Chóngxī period,
he was successively promoted to Vice Commander-in-Chief (Dū Jiān) of the Southwestern Pacification Command.
He was appointed envoy to Sòng for the celebration of the ruler's birthday (Shēngchén Shǐ),
and lodged at the Báigōu Post Station.
Sòng hosted a banquet to honor him,
during which an entertainer mocked Xiāo Huì's defeat at Hexī.
Hélǐzhī said:
"Victory and defeat are common occurrences in military affairs.
Our Sùishèng Emperor captured Shí Zhòngguì,
and to this day there is the Shíjiā Village (Shíjiā Zhài) in Xīngzhōng.
Huì's single defeat—
why is it worth comparing?"
The Sòng people felt ashamed and accepted the rebuke.
When the Emperor heard of this, he said:
"If an actor missespeak,
how can that damage the friendship between the two states!"
(The entertainer) was whipped 200 times
and dismissed from office.
In the early years of Qīngníng,
Hé Lǐzhī was appointed as the Jiédùshǐ of Huáihuà Prefecture.
In the seventh year,
he entered the court as the Great King of the Northern Department,
and was enfeoffed as the Duke of Bīn.
He successively served as the Jiédùshǐ of Liáoxīng Prefecture and the Xiángwěn of the Northeast Route,
and was additionally granted the concurrent title of Shìzhōng.
He retired from office
and passed away.
Hé Lǐzhī was intelligent, diligent, and loyal.
He managed affairs with a gentle and skillful approach.
The establishment of guest houses and agricultural settlements in the western frontier
were all initiated by Hé Lǐzhī.
Yēlǜ Pōde,
courtesy name Sābǎn,
was the grandson of the maternal uncle's slave, Guā.
He was an independent and aloof individual.
In the early years of Chóngxī,
he was appointed as the Páiyìn Lángjūn.
In the early years of Qīngníng,
he gradually rose to become the Zhī Yìzhōu.
When he resigned from office,
the local people requested him to stay,
which was granted.
In the eighth year of Xiányōng,
he was transferred to be the Jiédùshǐ of Zhāngguó Prefecture.
The emperor hunted at Dàláogǔ Mountain,
and Pōde paid his respects at the temporary palace.
The emperor inquired about border affairs,
to which he replied:
“From the southern border of Yìzhōu to Tiānchí,
it is all our land for cultivation and grazing.
During the Qīngníng period,
the border generals were not vigilant,
and it was encroached upon by the Sòng.
The beacon towers were moved inward,
which seems inappropriate.”
Dàozōng approved of this.
He was appointed as the Běimiàn Línyá.
Later, he was dispatched as an envoy to Sòng,
recovered the encroached territory,
and Pōde was ordered to define the boundaries.
Upon his return,
he was appointed as the Nányuàn Xuānhuīshǐ.
In the fourth year of Dàkāng,
he was promoted to Jiédùshǐ of Zhōngshùn Prefecture,
soon after becoming the Great King of the Southern Department,
then reassigned as the Tóngzhī Nánjīng Liúshǒushì,
and summoned to be appointed as the Nánfǔ Zǎixiàng,
bestowed the title of Zhēnliáng Gōngchén,
enfeoffed as the Duke of Wú,
and became the Běiyuàn Shūmìshǐ.
He was incorruptible and diligent in public service,
knowing no bounds in his efforts.
He retired in the Dà'ān period
and passed away.
His son, Xiámò,
was the Běiyuàn Shūmì Fùshǐ.
The commentary states: Yēlǜ Hézhù pacified the borders and established good relations,
maintained troops, and allowed the people to rest,
his foresight was profound.
Was Liùfú's stirring up trouble to claim merit truly beneficial to the state?
No.
Niú, Dù, Pōde, Hé Lǐzhī and others were sent on missions,
and fortunately did not fail their charge.
Niǎolǐ killing a maid to seek marriage,
bearing the guilt of a crime,
and painting his master's likeness
to hope for avoiding death,
is also disgraceful.
Collation Notes
Biographies, Volume 17: Xiāo Xiàomù (Sābā, Xiàoxiān, Xiàoyǒu), Xiāo Púnú, Yēlǜ Púgǔ, Xià Xíngměi
Xiāo Xiàomù,
whose childhood name was Húdújǐn,
was the fifth-generation grandson of Āgǔzhī, younger brother of Empress Chúnqīn.
His father, Táo Guī,
was the Guójìu Xiángwěn.
Xiāo Xiàomù was incorruptible, diligent, and adhered to rituals and laws.
In the twenty-eighth year of Tǒnghé,
he was successively promoted to Zhāotǎo Dūjiān of the Northwest Route.
In the first year of Kāitài,
he was remotely appointed as the Jiédùshǐ of Jiànxióng Prefecture,
and additionally granted the title of Jiǎnjiào Tàibǎo.
In that year, Zhúliè and others rebelled,
and Xiāo Xiàomù attacked and routed them.
In winter,
he advanced his army to Kědūn City.
The Zǔbù allied with the five tribal chiefs Chálà, Ādù, and others,
planning an internal and external uprising.
Xiāo Xiàomù executed them all,
then made strict defensive preparations to await them,
and the remaining rebels then dispersed.
For this merit, he was promoted to Ānfǔshǐ of the Jiǔshuǐ tribes.
Soon after, he was appointed as the Běifǔ Zǎixiàng,
bestowed the title of Zhōngmù Xībà Gōngchén,
Jiǎnjiào Tàishī,
and Tóng Zhèngshì Ménxià Píngzhāngshì.
In the eighth year,
he returned to the capital.
In the second year of Tàipíng,
he served as Zhī Shūmìyuàn Shì,
and concurrently as the Hànrén Xínggōng Dūbùshǔ.
In the third year,
he was enfeoffed as the King of Yān, Liúshǒu of Nánjīng, and Bīngmǎ Dūzǒngguǎn.
In the ninth year,
Dà Yánlín rebelled in Dōngjīng.
Xiāo Xiàomù served as Dū tǒng to suppress him,
and fought at Púshuǐ.
The central army slightly retreated,
but the Vice Dūbùshǔ Xiāo Pǐdí and Dūjiān Xiāo Púnú attacked from both flanks,
the rebels were routed,
and pursued and defeated north of Shǒushān.
Yánlín fled into the city,
digging deep moats for defense.
Xiāo Xiàomù besieged him,
built a double wall,
and erected towers,
making it impossible for internal and external communication.
People within the city dismantled houses for fuel.
His generals, Yáng Xiángshì and others, captured Yánlín and surrendered,
and Liáodōng was completely pacified.
He was reassigned as Dōngjīng Liúshǒu,
and bestowed the title of Zuǒguó Gōngchén.
His administration was lenient and simple,
and he comforted and resettled the displaced,
and the people were at peace.
When Xīngzōng ascended the throne,
he was transferred to be the King of Qín,
and soon after reinstated as Nánjīng Liúshǒu.
In the sixth year of Chóngxī,
he was promoted to be the King of Wú,
and appointed as the Běiyuàn Shūmìshǐ.
In the eighth year,
he submitted a memorial requesting a census of the empire's households to equalize corvée labor,
and also reported on the advantages and disadvantages of various tribes and the Shèlì army.
This was followed.
Consequently, the administration and taxation became somewhat fair,
and the populace rejoiced.
In the ninth year,
he was transferred to be the King of Chǔ.
At that time, there were no troubles in the empire,
the population flourished,
and the emperor, in his prime,
often spoke of Zhōu's taking of ten counties,
and was filled with a desire to launch a southern campaign.
Most of the officials complied with his wishes.
Xiāo Xiàomù remonstrated, saying:
“In the past, Tàizǔ's southern campaign
ultimately achieved nothing.
Emperor Sìshèng overthrew Táng and established Jìn,
later, because of Chóngguì's rebellion, he drove straight into Biàn;
as soon as the imperial carriage returned,
they in turn invaded.
Thereafter, continuous warfare for more than twenty years
barely achieved peace and good relations,
the common people enjoyed their livelihoods,
and North and South communicated.
Today, compared to former times,
though the state is said to be rich and strong,
however, meritorious ministers and veteran generals have often passed away.
Moreover, the Sòng people have committed no offense;
Your Majesty should not abandon the alliances made by the former emperors.”
At this time, the emperor's decision was already made,
and his memorial was not replied to.
He requested retirement due to old age,
but was not permitted.
In the twelfth year,
he was again appointed as the Běiyuàn Shūmìshǐ,
and then made King of Qí,
and then passed away.
He was posthumously granted the title of Great Chancellor and King of Jìn,
with the posthumous name Zhēn.
Although Xiāo Xiàomù was a relative of the imperial family,
he became more cautious as his position grew higher.
Whenever the Empress Dowager bestowed gifts,
he would always decline them.
His wife and children showed no arrogance.
In his interactions with people,
he was consistent from beginning to end.
Those he recommended and promoted were all loyal and upright individuals.
He once said to people:
“If the Shūmì select and employ the worthy,
what matter will not be accomplished?
If one personally handles trivial matters,
then important affairs will be hindered.”
From the time Xiāo Hézhuó advanced due to his administrative talent,
his successors followed suit,
not understanding the bigger picture.
He sighed, saying:
“If one cannot change customs and practices,
and merely enjoys one's position in comfort,
is this the way of a minister and a son?”
At the time, he was called
“National Treasure Minister,”
and his writings were titled The Precious Old Man's Collection.
His two sons, Ālà and Sābā,
and his younger brothers Xiàoxiān, Xiàozhōng, and Xiàoyǒu,
each have their own biographies.
Sā Bā,
courtesy name Zhōu Yǐn.
At age seven,
due to being a relative by marriage, he was promoted to General-in-Chief of the Left and Right Qiānniú Guards (Zuǒyòu Qiānniú Wèi Dà Jiāngjūn).
At the beginning of the Zhòngxī era,
he was appointed as a Gentleman of the Imperial Guards (Zhīhòu Lángjūn).
His character was honest and steadfast,
his demeanor was bright and cheerful,
and he excelled at ball games, riding, and archery.
Whenever the Emperor held banquets and drank,
he enjoyed jesting and humor.
Although Sā Bā received imperial favor and attention,
he always conducted himself with propriety,
and people of the time praised him for this.
Due to the favor granted during the Cháicè Ceremony (Cháicè Lǐ),
he was promoted to Auxiliary Grand Tutor (Jiǎnxiào Tàifù) and Director of the Yǒngxīng Palace (Yǒngxīng Gōngshǐ),
overseeing the Left and Right Guards,
and concurrently managing the affairs of the Diǎnjiǎn Directorate (Diǎnjiǎn Sī).
He married the Princess of Wèiguó (Wèiguó Gōngzhǔ),
was appointed Commandant of the Imperial Son-in-Law (Fùmǎ Dūwèi),
served as the Commissioner of the Northern Administration (Běiyuàn Xuānhuīshǐ),
and simultaneously supervised all court ceremonies and rites.
In the late Zhòngxī era,
he was sent out to serve as the Commander of the Northwest Circuit (Xīběilù Zhāotǎoshǐ) and Prince of Wǔníng Commandery (Wǔníng Jùnwáng).
His tenure in office was known for good governance.
He died early in the Qīngníng era,
at the age of thirty-nine,
and was posthumously enfeoffed as the Prince of Qí (Qí Wáng).
Xiāo Xiān,
courtesy name Yánníng,
childhood name Hǎilǐ.
In the eighteenth year of Tǒnghé,
he was appointed Gentleman of the Imperial Guards.
He married the Princess of Nányáng (Nányáng Gōngzhǔ),
and was appointed Commandant of the Imperial Son-in-Law.
In the fifth year of Kāitài,
he served as the Khagan of the Imperial Relatives (Guójìu Xiángwěn).
He commanded troops stationed on the eastern frontier.
Upon returning,
he served as the Commander-in-Chief of the Southern Capital (Nánjīng Tǒngjūnshǐ).
In the third year of Tàipíng,
he became the Chief Commissioner of the Chinese Traveling Palace (Hànrén Xínggōng Dū Bùshǔ),
and soon thereafter was promoted to Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Tàifù).
In the fifth year,
he was transferred to be the Resident General of the Supreme Capital (Shàngjīng Liúshǒu).
Because his mother was old, he requested permission to wait upon her,
and was reinstated as Khagan of the Imperial Relatives.
He was subsequently transferred to be the Resident General of the Eastern Capital (Dōngjīng Liúshǒu).
When Dà Yánlín rebelled,
he was besieged for several months,
and escaped by digging a tunnel.
After Yánlín was suppressed,
he served as the Resident General of the Supreme Capital.
In the eleventh year,
the Emperor became ill.
Empress Qīn'āi (Qīn'āi) summoned Xiāo Xiān to take overall command of the Imperial Guards.
During Xīngzōng's (Xīngzōng) period of mourning (Liàngyīn),
Qīn'āi murdered Empress Rén'dé (Réndé Huánghòu).
Xiāo Xiān, along with Xiāo Zhuóbǔ (Xiāo Zhuóbǔ) and Xiāo Pǐdí (Xiāo Pǐdí), played a major role in the conspiracy.
When Qīn'āi assumed regency,
he was nominally appointed Military Commissioner of the Tiānpíng Army (Tiānpíng Jūn Jiédùshǐ),
promoted to Acting Minister of Education (Shǒu Sītú),
and concurrently Commissioner of Political Affairs (Zhèngshì Lìng).
Early in the Zhòngxī era,
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Chǔ (Chǔ Wáng),
and served as the Chief Military Commissioner of the Northern Administration (Běiyuàn Shūmìshǐ).
Due to his connection to the imperial in-laws (Jiāofáng qīn),
Xiāo Xiān was highly favored by the Empress Dowager (Tàihòu).
While in the Privy Council (Shūfǔ),
he indulged his preferences and dislikes arbitrarily,
his power overshadowed the sovereign,
and many in court viewed him askance.
In the third year,
the Empress Dowager and Xiāo Xiān plotted to depose the Emperor.
The Emperor learned of this,
ordered the guards out of the palace,
summoned Xiāo Xiān,
and informed him of his intention to remove the Empress Dowager.
Xiāo Xiān was terrified and unable to reply.
The Empress Dowager was relocated to Qìngzhōu.
Xiāo Xiān was constantly depressed and unhappy.
In the fourth year,
his princely title was changed to Prince of Jìn (Jìn Wáng).
Later, he served as the Resident General of the Southern Capital (Nánjīng Liúshǒu),
and died.
His posthumous name was Zhōngsù.
Xiāo Xiàoyǒu,
courtesy name Tàbùyǎn,
childhood name Chénliú.
Early in the Kāitài era,
as a relative by marriage, he was appointed Junior General (Xiǎo Jiāngjūn).
In the first year of Tàipíng,
due to the Grand Ceremony (Dà Cè),
he was promoted to General-in-Chief of the Left Wǔ Wèi (Zuǒ Wǔ Wèi Dà Jiāngjūn) and Auxiliary Grand Guardian (Jiǎnxiào Tàibǎo),
and granted the name Xiàoyǒu.
In the first year of Zhòngxī,
he was repeatedly promoted to Commander of the Northwest Circuit (Xīběilù Zhāotǎoshǐ),
and enfeoffed as the Prince of Lánlíng Commandery (Lánlíng Jùnwáng).
In the eighth year,
he was advanced to Prince of Chén (Chén Wáng).
Previously,
when Xiāo Huì (Xiāo Huì) was the Commander,
he focused solely on using intimidation to control the Western Qiāng,
causing many of the various barbarians (Yí) to rebel.
When Xiāo Xiàoyǒu took office,
he greatly increased pacification and soothing measures.
Whenever they paid tribute,
he always increased the gifts given in return,
and the Qiāng people were thus pacified.
After a long time,
this gradually turned into excessive leniency,
and the fierce and unruly tendencies of the various barbarians became rampant.
Critics mocked him for going too far.
In the tenth year,
he was promoted to Commissioner of Political Affairs,
granted the honorary title of Meritorious Minister Who Served Loyally, Promoted Virtue, and Pacified the Distant (Xiàojié Xuānyōng Dìngyuǎn Gōngchén),
and his princely title was changed to Prince of Wú (Wú Wáng).
Later, for the funerals of his elder brothers Xiāo Mù (Xiāo Mù) and Xiāo Zhōng (Xiāo Zhōng),
he returned to the Capital.
He was appointed Chief Military Commissioner of the Southern Administration (Nányuàn Shūmìshǐ),
granted the added honorary title of Meritorious Minister Who Assisted the Sage, Harmonized the State, and Protected Righteousness (Yìshèng Xiémù Bǎoyì Gōngchén),
advanced to Prince of Zhào (Zhào Wáng),
and appointed Director of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Lìng).
He entered mourning for his mother,
but was recalled to serve as Chancellor of the Northern Administration (Běifǔ Zǎixiàng),
and sent out to govern as the Resident General of the Eastern Capital.
During the campaign against Xià (Dà Xià),
Xiāo Xiàoyǒu and the Military Commissioner Xiāo Huì suffered a defeat south of the river (Hénán).
The Emperor intended to execute them,
but the Empress Dowager intervened to spare them.
He was reinstated as Resident General of the Eastern Capital,
then transferred to Prince of Yān (Yān Wáng),
changed to Resident General of the Supreme Capital,
and finally changed again to Prince of Qín (Qín Wáng).
Early in the Qīngníng era,
he was promoted to Grand Preceptor (Shàngfù).
Soon after,
he resumed his post as Resident General of the Eastern Capital.
The following year,
he was again made Chancellor of the Northern Administration.
The Emperor personally drafted an imperial decree to praise and honor him.
Due to the favor granted during the Cháicè Ceremony,
he was nominally appointed Resident General of Luòjīng (Luòjīng Liúshǒu),
granted the additional title of Meritorious Minister of Pure Virtue (Chúndé Gōngchén),
retired from office (Zhìshì),
and advanced to Prince of Fēngguó (Fēngguó Wáng).
He was implicated because his son Húdǔ (Húdǔ) initiated a rebellion with Zhòngyuán (Zhòngyuán),
and he was executed,
at the age of seventy-three.
Húdǔ is listed in the Biographies of Rebellious Officials (Nìchén Zhuàn).
Xiāo Púnú,
courtesy name Liúyǐn,
a descendant of the Xī King Chǔ Bùníng (Xī Wáng Chǔ Bùníng).
Young, orphaned, and poor,
he worked as a herdsman for a physician.
He damaged people’s crops
and was frequently beaten and humiliated.
The physician once saw Púnú sleeping soundly
with a snake wrapped around his body,
and considered it extraordinary.
He taught him to read,
and Púnú was intelligent and fond of learning.
Within a few years,
he had read widely in the classics and histories,
and practiced riding and archery.
Once he reached adulthood,
his spirit was heroic and unrestrained.
During the Kāitài period,
he was selected to serve in the Imperial Guard (Hùwèi),
and gradually advanced.
Soon after, he was punished for a crime by branding and banishment to the Wūgǔ tribe (Wūgǔ Bù).
After a long time,
he was recalled.
He served successively in demanding posts,
and was promoted to Great King of the Six Xī Tribes (Xī Liù Bù Dà Wáng).
His governance was renowned.
In the ninth year of Tàipíng,
when Dà Yánlín (Dà Yánlín) occupied the Eastern Capital and rebelled,
Púnú served as Dūjiān (Inspecting Commissioner),
leading the right wing army.
He encountered the rebels and fought them at Púshuǐ.
The central army slightly retreated,
but Púnú and the left wing army attacked the rebels from both sides.
He first occupied the strategic crossing point between Gāolì (Gāolì) and Nǚzhí (Nǚzhí),
preventing them from seeking reinforcement.
He then defeated the rebels at Shǒushān.
Yánlín fled into the city.
Púnú rode swiftly without armor,
pursuing and killing the remaining rebels.
Shortly after, the main army besieged the Eastern Capital.
Púnú suppressed the various rebellious settlements,
pacified the bandits of Hǒushān,
and Yánlín firmly defended the city, daring not to sortie.
After Dà Yánlín was captured,
Púnú was promoted for his achievements to concurrent Grand Mentor (Jiān Shìzhōng).
, he was
made Deputy Commander of the Northern Zǔbǔ,
and later reinstated as Great King of the Xī Six Departments.
In the fifteenth year,
he served as the Commander of Pacification for the Southwest Circuit,
leading a western campaign against Xiàguó.
Púnú occupied the river bridge with two thousand soldiers,
gathering several dozen large ships.
He also constructed large grappling hooks,
which no one understood.
On the day of the battle,
the boats were spread across the river,
stretching continuously for over thirty *lǐ*.
He sent men to watch the upper stream,
seizing any floating objects immediately.
After the main army suffered a defeat,
Púnú did not yet know.
Just then, a large log drifted down the river,
threatening to destroy the pontoon bridge
and cut off the retreat route.
The boat operators rushed to hook and secure it,
preventing the bridge from being destroyed.
The following year,
he resumed the western campaign,
