penetrating deep with a small, exposed force.
He plundered extensively and returned,
and was again made Great King of the Xī Six Departments.
He retired from office,
and died.
Yēlǜ Púgǔ,
courtesy name Tíyǐn,
was the fourth-generation descendant of Tàizǔ’s younger brother, Sū.
He was renowned for his martial valor.
Early in Tǒnghé,
he served as the Governor (Cìshǐ) of Zhuōzhōu,
and gained merit by participating in the campaign against Gāolì.
Late in Kāitài,
he became Deputy Administrator of the Imperial Guest Department in Shàngjīng.
In the second year of Tàipíng,
a city was built on the Yālù Jiāng (Yalu River).
Púgǔ guarded it,
and achieved success in administration while stationed there.
In the fifth year,
he was appointed Military Commissioner (Jiédùshǐ) of Guǎngdé Commandery,
and soon transferred to be the Supreme Commander (Tǒngjūnshǐ) of Dōngjīng.
His governance was strict and solemn,
and all the tribes were awed into submission.
In the ninth year,
Dà Yánlín rebelled
and tried to enlist Bǎozhōu through a letter.
Xià Xíngměi captured the messenger and sent him to Púgǔ.
Púgǔ entered and occupied Bǎozhōu,
causing Yánlín’s morale to drop.
Due to this merit, he was appointed Tìyǐn.
In the eleventh year,
he was assassinated by his son, Tiělí.
Xià Xíngměi
was a Bóhǎi man.
In the ninth year of Tàipíng,
Dà Yánlín rebelled.
At that time, Xíngměi was commanding the Bóhǎi forces in Bǎozhōu.
Yánlín sent a messenger attempting to persuade him to join the rebellion.
Xíngměi captured the messenger and sent him to the Supreme Commander Yēlǜ Púgǔ.
He also lured a hundred members of the rebel faction and killed them.
Yánlín’s plans were frustrated,
so he barricaded himself within the city walls to defend himself,
but the city was defeated several months later.
For his merit, he was promoted to Joint Manager of Affairs (Tóng Zhèngshì Ménxià Píngzhāngshì),
and awarded generously.
The following year,
he was elevated to Military Commissioner of Zhōngshùn Commandery.
In the seventeenth year of Zhòngxī,
he was transferred to Deputy Commander (Fù Bùshǔ).
He followed the Inspector General Diǎnjiǎn Yēlǜ Yìxiān to suppress the Púnúlǐ,
capturing their chief, Táodélǐ, and returning.
He retired from office,
and died.
The Emperor, recalling his merits,
sent an envoy to offer sacrifices at his home.
The Treatise says: If there are no superior men (Jūnzǐ),
how can the state govern?
When they captured Yánlín
and stabilized Liáodōng,
the achievements of the generals of that time were magnificent.
It was fitting that they stroked their swords and clapped their hands,
boasting of surplus courage to overawe the world.
Xiāo Xiàomù's remonstrance against invading the South—
how grand and far-reaching was the foresight of his intent!
How could this be understood by those who merely glare and speak aggressively?
Regarding his discourse on reforming customs as the root of governance,
and considering personal involvement in trivial matters as compromising the dignity of a high minister,
how profound, trenchant, and lucid it was.
To be
a "National Treasure Minister"
was appropriate.
Although Xiàoxiān was involved in the plot to assassinate Réndé,
he still relied on the sanctity of the state to avoid retribution (literally: being smoked out and watered down).
As a great blight upon the nation,
what discussion of his merits can there be?
Memoir 18: Xiāo Díliè (Bálà), Yēlǜ Pénnú, Xiāo Páiyā (Dé, Pǐdí), Yēlǜ Zīzhōng, Yēlǜ Yáozhì, Yēlǜ Hónggǔ, Gāo Zhèng, Yēlǜ Dilù, Dà Kāngyì.
Xiāo Díliè,
courtesy name Nièlǔgǔn,
was the fourth-generation descendant of Chancellor Tàliè.
His insight and disposition were grand and far-reaching,
and he was highly esteemed by his community.
He began as the Supervisor (Chǎngshǐ) of the Cattle Herds.
The Emperor heard of his talent,
summoned him to attend court,
and promoted him to Imperial Uncle Commander (Guójiù Xiángwěn).
In the twenty-eighth year of Tǒnghé,
the Emperor said to his officials:
"Kāng Zhào of Gāolì assassinated his ruler Sòng,
and then installed Sòng's paternal cousin Xūn as king and acted as his minister.
This is high treason.
We should dispatch troops to punish this crime."
All the officials said it was permissible.
Díliè remonstrated, saying:
"The state has been campaigning for successive years,
and the soldiers are exhausted.
Moreover, Your Majesty is in the period of mourning (Liàngyīn);
the annual harvest has been poor,
and our wounds have not yet healed.
The island barbarian (Gāolì) is a small state,
but its defenses and fortifications are sound.
Victory will not count as military achievement;
if by chance we suffer defeat,
I fear it will lead to future regret.
It would be better to send a single messenger
to ask for the reason.
If they submit and acknowledge their crime, then so be it;
if not,
it will not be too late to raise an army
after the mourning period is over and the year yields a good harvest."
Although the order had already been issued,
and the advice was not followed,
those with discernment admired it.
The following year,
he was made Joint Administrator of the Affairs of the Left Yílíbì.
He was then transferred to the Right Yílíbì.
Early in Kāitài,
he led troops to patrol the western border.
At that time, Jiāsàxùpūlǐ, Shīshì, and Bógě, subordinates of the Yílíjǐn, led their tribal people to flee.
Díliè pursued and captured them,
ordered them to return to their occupations,
and was promoted to Imperial Uncle Commander (Guójiù Xiángwěn).
He followed the Commissioner of Military Affairs (Shūmìshǐ) Yēlǜ Shìliáng in attacking Gāolì.
Upon return,
he was awarded the title of Joint Manager of Affairs (Tóng Zhèngshì Ménxià Píngzhāngshì),
and appointed Defender-in-Chief (Liúshǒu) of Shàngjīng.
Díliè was a broad-minded and generous person,
who understood the principles of governance.
All the court officials considered him to possess the talent needed to assist a sovereign.
Wáng Jìzhōng, the Commander-in-Chief (Dū Bùshǔ) of the Han people's Traveling Palace, recommended him as suitable for the position of Commissioner of Military Affairs (Shūmìshǐ),
but the Emperor suspected a faction and stopped the appointment.
He served as Defender-in-Chief of Zhōngjīng,
and died.
His clan nephew, Hūgǔ,
has a biography.
His younger brother was Bálà.
Bálà,
courtesy name Biélèyǐn,
was resourceful
and skilled in mounted archery.
During the Kāitài period,
since his elder brother was the Right Yílíbì,
he initially received the post of Gentleman (Lángjūn),
and was repeatedly promoted to Commandant (Tàiwèi) of the Tūlǐ in the Xī Six Departments.
Late in Tàipíng,
Dà Yánlín rebelled.
Bálà led the troops of the Northern and Southern Administrations to suppress the rebellion.
They met at Pú Shuǐ,
where the Southern Administration forces briefly retreated.
Upon reaching Shǒushān,
they encountered the rebels again.
Bálà then switched the flags of the two Administrations,
encouraged his troops, fought vigorously,
and defeated them.
When the Emperor heard of this,
he issued a handwritten decree commending him
and bestowed upon him an imperial horse.
During the Zhòngxī period,
he was promoted to Commander of the Four Victories Army (Sìjiéjūn Xiángwěn).
He resigned his post and returned to his hometown.
After several years,
he was recalled to serve as Military Commissioner of Zhāodé Commandery,
and soon transferred to Imperial Uncle Commander (Guójiù Xiángwěn).
He died.
Yēlǜ Pénnú,
courtesy name Húdújǐn,
was the grandson of Tìyǐn Nièlǔgǔ.
During the reign of Jǐngzōng,
he served as Xiángwěn of the Wūgǔ Department.
His administration emphasized severity and urgency,
and the people suffered from it.
The relevant officials reported this,
and an imperial edict stated:
"Pénnú holds a post of great importance;
to investigate him for trivial matters
might harm his prestige."
Soon after, he was transferred to Grand Preceptor (Tàibǎo) of the Horse Herds.
In the 16th year of Tǒnghé (998 CE),
he secretly ascertained those in the Yàn Army who were unfit for duty
and discharged them.
In the 28th year (1010 CE),
the Emperor personally led the campaign against Gāolì,
with Pénnú acting as the vanguard.
Upon reaching Tóngzhōu,
the Gāolì general Kāng Zhào divided his troops into three groups to resist our army: one camp was west of the prefecture,
occupying the confluence of the Three Rivers,
with Zhào positioned in the center;
one camp was near the mountains of the prefecture;
and one camped adjacent to the city wall.
Pénnú led Yēlǜ Hónggǔ to attack and destroy the Sānshuǐ camp,
capturing Zhào.
The troops of Lǐ Xuányùn and others scattered at the mere sight of them.
When the main army arrived,
they beheaded over 30,000 enemies,
pursued them to Kāijīng,
and defeated the enemy at Xīlǐng.
Shūn, the King of Gāolì, hearing that the border cities could not be defended,
fled.
Pénnú entered Kāijīng,
burned the royal palace,
and then pacified the common people.
The Emperor praised his achievements,
promoted him to Great King (Dàwáng) of the Northern Administration (Běiyuàn),
and he subsequently died.
Xiāo Páiyā,
courtesy name Hányǐn,
was a descendant of the maternal uncle (Guójìu) Shàofù branch.
He possessed many strategies and intelligence,
and was skilled in archery and horsemanship.
Early in the Tǒnghé era (983 CE),
he became the Xiángwěn of the Left Píshì,
achieving merit in suppressing the Zǔbǔ.
In the 4th year (986 CE),
he defeated the Sòng generals Cáo Bīn and Mǐ Xìn at Wàngdū.
Whenever military matters were in doubt,
he invariably participated in the deliberation and decision-making.
Soon after, he commanded the armies of the Yǒngxīng Palace Division Jīu, Shèlì, Zhuāilá, and the Two Píshì,
and worked with the Commissioner of Military Affairs (Shūmìshǐ) Yēlǜ Xiézhěn to recover the cities and towns in Shānxī that had been captured.
That winter,
attacking Sòng,
he was attached to the vanguard,
surrounding Mǎnchéng.
He led his unit to be the first to ascend the walls,
capturing the city,
and was subsequently appointed Commander-in-Chief (Tǒngjūnshǐ) of Nánjīng.
He married Princess Wèiguó,
was appointed Commandant-Escort (Fùmǎ Dūwèi),
and was concurrently given the title Administrator in Attendance (Tóng Zhèngshì Ménxià Píngzhāngshì).
In the 13th year (995 CE),
he served successively as Commissioner of the Northern and Southern Administrations (Běi, Nán Yuàn Xuānhuīshǐ).
He formally submitted a list detailing the gains and losses in contemporary governance
and methods for taxation and corvée.
The Emperor praised and accepted them.
In the 15th year (997 CE),
he was promoted to Administrator (Zhèngshì Lìng),
and transferred to be the Resident General (Liúshǒu) of Dōngjīng.
In the 22nd year (1004 CE),
he again attacked Sòng,
commanding the Bóhǎi army,
and captured Déqīng Commandery.
Later, after Xiāo Tàlǐn died,
he was exclusively entrusted with affairs concerning the Southern Border.
When peace negotiations with Sòng were successfully concluded,
he became the Chancellor (Zǎixiàng) of the Northern Bureau (Běifǔ).
When Shèngzōng campaigned against Gāolì,
he led troops advancing along the northern route,
reached Xīlǐng near Kāijīng,
defeated the enemy troops,
and beheaded several thousand.
Shūn, the King of Gāolì, was afraid
and fled to Píngzhōu.
Páiyā entered Kāijīng,
carried out a major plunder, and returned.
The Emperor praised him
and enfeoffed him as Prince of Lánlíng Commandery (Lánlíng Jùnwáng).
In the 2nd year of Kāitài (1013 CE),
as Chancellor, he was put in charge of the Commissioner for Pacification (Zhāotǎoshǐ) of the Southwestern Front.
In the 5th year (1016 CE),
he was promoted to Prince of Dōngpíng.
Páiyā’s governance was generous and flexible yet decisive;
the various tribes respected and loved him,
and the people grew prosperous.
Contemporary opinion greatly valued this.
In the 7th year (1018 CE),
he again campaigned against Gāolì,
reaching Kāijīng.
The enemy forces scattered and collapsed,
and he released his troops to take captives and loot before returning.
Crossing the Chá and Tuó Rivers,
the enemy shot at them from both sides.
Páiyā abandoned his armor and weapons and fled,
and for this he was dismissed from office.
In the 3rd year of Tàipíng (1023 CE),
he was reinstated as Prince of Bīn,
and subsequently died.
His younger brother was Dé.
Dé,
courtesy name Xùnníng.
He possessed courage and was skilled in strategy.
In the 1st year of Tǒnghé (983 CE),
he married Princess Yuèguó,
was appointed Commandant-Escort (Fùmǎ Dūwèi),
and transferred to become Línyá of the Southern Front (Nánmiàn Línyá).
Following the Commissioner (Xuānhuīshǐ) Yēlǜ Āmèilǐ on the campaign against Gāolì, upon returning,
he was appointed Línyá of the Northern Front (Běimiàn Línyá).
At that time, the Sòng generals Cáo Bīn and Mǐ Xìn invaded Yàn.
Yēlǜ Xiūgē consulted with Dé on military affairs,
and many of his suggestions were trusted and adopted.
He served as Resident General (Liúshǒu) of Dōngjīng.
In the 6th year (988 CE),
the Emperor attacked Sòng,
besieging Shāduī.
Dé independently commanded one section of the army.
Arrows and stones rained down from the city walls,
but Dé remained composed and spirited,
urging his officers and soldiers to capture the parapet.
When the city fell,
he was struck by a stray arrow.
The Empress Dowager personally came to check on him
and bestowed medicine.
Attacking Chángchéngkǒu,
he again was the first to ascend.
The Empress Dowager increasingly praised his achievements.
As Gāolì had not yet submitted,
Dé received an imperial edict
and led troops to capture their border cities.
Wáng Zhì, the King, was afraid
and submitted a memorial petitioning for surrender.
In the 8th month of the 12th year (994 CE),
he was granted the title of Qǐshèng Jiélì Gōngchén (Meritorious Minister Who Exhausted His Strength to Enlighten the Sage).
He followed the Commander-in-Chief (Dū Bùshǔ) Héshuònú in suppressing the Wùrě.
Before the battle commenced,
the Wùrě requested surrender.
Dé, coveting the captives and spoils,
refused permission.
The Wùrě fought desperately,
and the city could not be taken.
Héshuònú debated whether to retreat.
Dé said:
"Because of their stubborn resistance,
we came here under imperial decree to suppress them.
If we return without achieving merit,
what will the various tribes say about us?
If we advance deep and take many captives,
it is still better than returning empty-handed."
Héshuònú had no choice
and advanced to attack the various tribes in the southeast,
reaching the northern border of Gāolì.
By the time they returned,
the journey was long and provisions were exhausted.
Many soldiers and horses died or were wounded.
For this reason, he was stripped of his Meritorious Minister title.
In the 14th year (996 CE),
he was appointed Commander-in-Chief of the Marching Army (Xíngjūn Dū Bùshǔ),
and attacked the Púlú Máochū Department.
Upon returning,
the Princess became ill.
The Empress Dowager sent the palace attendant Xiánshì to wait upon her,
and Dé had private relations with her.
The Princess died in anger,
and the Empress Dowager was furious,
ordering his death.
He was later posthumously enfeoffed as Prince of Lánlíng Commandery (Lánlíng Jùnwáng).
His son was Pǐdí.
Pǐdí,
courtesy name Sūyǐn,
was also named Chāngyì.
When he was not yet a month old,
both his parents died.
He was raised in the Inner Palace (Jìnyè).
When he grew up,
he married a princess of Qín-Jìn Wáng (秦晉王),
and was appointed Fùmǎ Dūwèi (駙馬都尉).
He served as Diànqián Fù Diǎnjiǎn (殿前副點檢).
In the eighth year of Tǒnghé (統和),
he was changed to Běimiàn Línyá (北面林牙).
In the fourth year of Tàipíng (太平),
he was promoted to Diànqián Dū Diǎnjiǎn (殿前都點檢),
then sent out to serve as Guójiù Xiángwěn (國舅詳穩).
In the ninth year,
Dà Yánlín (大延琳) of Bóhǎi (渤海) rebelled,
and his forces plundered neighboring tribes.
[Pǐndí 匹敵] went to suppress him alongside Xiāo Xiàomù (蕭孝穆), the Administrator of Nánjīng (南京).
Xiàomù wished to preserve the city by accepting surrender,
but [Pǐndí] built a second wall to enclose it.
After several months,
people within the city secretly came to offer submission,
so Yánlín was captured.
Dōngjīng (東京) was pacified,
and for his merit, he was enfeoffed as Lánlíng Jùnwáng (蘭陵郡王).
In the eleventh year,
Shèngzōng (聖宗) became ill.
Before this,
Qīn'āi (欽哀) had a rift with Réndé Huánghòu (仁德皇后).
Since Pǐndí had once been favored by the Empress,
Qīn'āi was jealous of him.
At that time, the guard Féng Jiānú (馮家奴) reported treason,
falsely accusing the Empress’s younger brother Zhuóbǔ (浞卜) and Pǐndí of plotting rebellion,
intending to install the Empress as regent,
and then slowly deliberate on who should be installed.
The princess secretly heard of this plot,
and said to Pǐndí:
"You are about to be executed without committing a crime.
Rather than dying,
why not flee to the Nǚzhí (女直) state to save your life!"
Pǐndí replied:
"How could the imperial court harm loyal and good people based merely on groundless rumors?
I would rather die than go to another country."
When Qīn'āi became regent,
she had him killed.
Yēlǜ Zīzhōng (耶律資忠),
courtesy name Wòyǎn (沃衍),
infant name Zhálà (札剌),
was descended from the line of Zhòngfù Fáng (仲父房).
His elder brother Guóliú (國留) excelled at composition,
and Shèngzōng held him in high regard.
At that time, Āgǔ (阿古), the wife of his wife’s younger brother, committed adultery with a slave.
Planning to flee to the Nǚzhí state,
Guóliú pursued and caught the slave,
and killed him.
Āgǔ hanged herself.
Āgǔ's mother was favored by the Empress Dowager (Tàihòu),
and when the matter was reported,
the Empress Dowager was furious,
and intended to kill Guóliú.
The Emperor, judging that he could not save him,
sent someone to bid him farewell,
and asked about posthumous affairs.
Guóliú expressed his thanks, saying:
"Your Majesty pities that your subject is innocent;
your grace penetrates the Nine Springs (the underworld),
thus even in death, I shall not perish!"
After his death,
many people felt he was wronged.
While in prison, he composed the *Fù on the Rabbit* (*Tù Fù* 兔賦) and the *Song of Waking and Sleeping* (*Wù Mèi Gē* 寤寐歌),
which were praised by the world.
Zīzhōng was widely learned,
and skilled in literary composition.
He had not yet entered officialdom by age forty.
Shèngzōng recognized his talent,
and summoned him to serve in the palace guard.
The Emperor frequently asked him about the order and disorder of ancient and modern times,
and Zīzhōng answered without holding anything back.
During the Kāitài (開泰) period,
he was appointed Zhōngchéng (中丞),
and the Emperor's favor grew daily.
Originally,
Gāolì (高麗) had submitted internally,
and had been given land taken from the six Nǚzhí tribes.
By this time,
the tributes were not arriving on time,
so Zīzhōng was ordered by imperial decree to go and ask the reason.
Gāolì had no intention of returning the land.
Consequently, powerful nobles frequently spoke ill of him to the Emperor,
and he was sent out to be the Deputy Administrator of Shàngjīng (上京).
Three years later,
he was sent again as an envoy to Gāolì,
where he was detained and not allowed to return.
Whenever Zīzhōng thought of his sovereign and family,
he would produce writings,
which were known as the *Collection of the Western Pavilion* (*Xītíng Jí* 西亭集).
When the Emperor held feasts with his officials,
he would sometimes remember [Zīzhōng] and say:
"Does Zīzhōng also enjoy such pleasure?"
Nine years later,
Gāolì presented a memorial apologizing for their offense,
and finally sent Zīzhōng back.
The Emperor welcomed him in the suburbs,
rode with him back to the palace,
ordered high officials to host a banquet for him,
and kept him inside the forbidden palace for several days.
He said to him:
"I plan to inconvenience you by making you a Shūmì (樞密).
What do you think?"
Zīzhōng replied:
"Your subject is untalented,
and dares not obey the decree."
So the Emperor made him a Línyá (林牙),
and placed him in charge of Tìyǐn (惕隱) affairs.
Originally,
while Zīzhōng was detained in Gāolì,
his younger brother Zhāo (昭) was a Zhùzhàng Lángjūn (著帳郎君),
and was convicted and had his family property confiscated.
By this time,
the family was restored to the Héngzhàng (橫帳),
and their former property was returned.
An imperial decree also gave him a woman from the Emperor’s maternal relatives as a wife.
At this time,
the Shūmìshǐ (樞密使) Xiāo Hézhuó (蕭合卓) and the Shàoshī (少師) Xiāo Bǎgē (蕭把哥) were favored.
Zīzhōng refused to humble himself and follow them,
and instead criticized them.
The Emperor grew angry,
and stripped him of his office.
After several years,
he was sent out to govern Lái Yuǎn Chéng (來遠城) affairs,
and subsequently served as Jiédùshǐ (節度使) for the two armies of Bǎo'ān (保安) and Zhāodé (昭德).
When Shèngzōng died,
Zīzhōng submitted a memorial requesting permission to attend the funeral.
Upon arriving,
he prostrated himself before the Emperor’s coffin and wept bitterly, saying:
"Your subject was fortunate to meet an enlightened sovereign,
but was falsely and unjustly accused,
and failed to fulfill the duty of a humble servant."
He fainted from grief, but revived.
Xīngzōng (興宗) ordered a physician to treat his illness.
After a long while,
he stated that the Guójiù Shìzhōng (國舅侍中) [Xiao Han and others] did not have the welfare of the state at heart,
and that Your Majesty should not reuse the old Tang (唐) era name of Jǐngfú (景福).
Consequently, those in power disliked him,
and sent him back to his post.
He died there.
His younger brother, Zhāo,
has his own biography.
Yēlǜ Yáozhì (耶律瑤質),
courtesy name Bálǐjǐn (拔里堇),
was a person of the Jìqìng Gōng (積慶宮).
His father, Hóugǔ (侯古),
was the Jiédùshǐ (節度使) of the Shìwéi (室韋) tribe.
Yáozhì was devoted to study, upright, and resolute,
possessing ambitions for governing the world.
In the tenth year of Tǒnghé,
he was repeatedly promoted until he reached the office of Jìqìng Gōngshǐ (積慶宮使).
Shèngzōng once instructed Yáozhì, saying:
"I have heard that you are upright and honest,
which is why I promote you.
If there are benefits or harms to the state,
your statements should conceal nothing."
Consequently, most of the proposals he presented were favorably accepted.
When the Emperor campaigned against Gāolì,
and defeated Kāng Zhào’s (康肇) army at Tóngzhōu (銅州),
Yáozhì’s efforts were significant.
Wáng Xún (王詢) requested surrender,
and all the officials debated and concluded that the surrender should be accepted.
Yáozhì said:
"Wáng Xún was defeated in just one battle,
and immediately sought submission;
this is merely deceit.
If we accept it,
we risk falling into his wicked scheme.
Waiting until his power is exhausted and his strength spent,
it will not be too late to accept him."
Soon after, Xún indeed fled,
clearing the fields so nothing could be gained.
His remaining troops entrenched themselves in treacherous terrain,
and when attacked, they could not be overcome.
Yáozhì used a strategy to make them surrender.
He was promoted and appointed Sì Fān Bù Xiángwěn (四蕃部詳穩).
At that time, the Zhāotǎoshǐ (招討使) Yēlǜ Pōde (耶律頗的) was the General Controller (Zǒngguǎn),
and Yáozhì felt ashamed to serve under him.
He submitted a memorial saying:
"Your subject is an old retainer of the former court.
Now that I am advanced in age,
I request to return the recent commission,
hoping to constantly attend Your Majesty."
The Emperor said:
"I shall not make you occupy this post for long."
He also ordered that [Yáozhì] should not be subordinate to the Zhāotǎo [Shǐ],
but was allowed to report matters directly upon arriving at his division.
He suppressed the violent and cherished the good,
and his political achievements were outstanding.
He died in office.
Yēlǜ Hónggǔ (耶律弘古),
courtesy name Pénnèyǐn (盆訥隱),
was a descendant of Yáolián Xiānzhì Kèhán (遙輦鮮質可汗).
In the early years of Tǒnghè,
he was once appointed as a Zhuàilá Xiángwěn due to his experience in military affairs,
and soon thereafter, he was transferred to be the Commander of Nánjīng.
In the thirteenth year,
he scouted territory on the southern borders,
defeating the enemy at Sìyuè Qiáo,
and decapitating over a hundred ranks.
When attacking the Sòng,
due to his battle merits, he was promoted to Tōnjīng Liúshǒu (Resident Commissioner of the Eastern Capital),
and enfeoffed as the Duke of Chǔguó.
Later, when attacking Gāolì,
he served as Vice Vanguard under Yēlǜ Pénnú,
capturing Kāng Zhào in Tóngzhōu.
In the thirtieth year,
the Northwestern tribes rebelled,
and he followed the Southern Court Chancellor Yēlǜ Núguā to suppress them.
When he took command of the Imperial Guards,
his orders and prohibitions were strict and orderly,
and many tribes surrendered.
Soon after, he was promoted to Shìzhōng (Attendant Counselor),
and died.
Gāo Zhèng,
it is unknown which commandery he hailed from.
In the early years of Tǒnghè,
he passed the Jìnshì examination,
and was successively promoted to Academician of the Bureau of Military Affairs (Shūmì Zhí Xuéshì).
When the Emperor was about to attack Gāolì,
he sent Zhèng ahead to convey his intentions.
When he returned,
he was promoted to Right Grandee Secretary (Yòu Púshè).
At the time, the King of Gāolì, Xún, submitted a memorial requesting permission for an audience,
and the Emperor granted it,
sending Zhèng to lead a thousand cavalrymen to receive him.
While lodging along the road,
they were surrounded by the Gāolì general Zhuō Sīzhèng.
Zhèng, seeing that the situation was indefensible,
broke out of the siege with the brave men under his command,
but many soldiers were killed or wounded.
The Emperor regretted the rash deployment
and pardoned his crime.
The following year,
he was promoted to Vice Minister of Works (Gōngbù Shìláng),
and served as Vice Commissioner of Military Affairs of the Northern Administration (Běi Yuàn Shūmì Fùshǐ).
He died in the fifth year of Kāitài.
Yēlǜ Dìlù,
courtesy name Yēníng,
was a descendant of the Zhòngfǔ Fáng (Second Uncle lineage).
He was versed in military matters,
and served as the Xiángwěn of the Left Píshì (Guards).
In the twenty-eighth year of Tǒnghè,
when Gāolì was attacked,
Dìlù led his tribal troops, along with Pénnú and others, to capture Kāng Zhào and Lǐ Xuányùn in Tóngzhōu.
The Emperor admired him and said:
“With your great talent,
devoting your strength to the state,
you are truly the ‘thousand-li colt’ of our house!”
He was then gifted an imperial horse and fine armor.
The following year,
he became the Great King of the Northern Administration (Běi Yuàn Dàwáng),
and was later dispatched to serve as the Supreme Xiángwěn of the Wūgǔ Díliè Tribe.
He died at the age of seventy-two.
Dà Kāngyì,
was a Bóhǎi person.
During the Kāitài period,
he successively held office as Chancellor of the Southern Administration (Nán Fǔ Zǎixiàng),
and was sent out to govern Huánglóng Fǔ (Yellow Dragon Prefecture).
He was skilled at pacification,
and the eastern tribes submitted willingly.
Bóyīn, the Chief of the Yúlǐdǐnǎi tribe, and Yúlièbǐ came to submit,
and he sent them to the court.
Furthermore, he stated that the area of Púlú Máochū was populated by many Bóhǎi people,
and requested permission to acquire them.
An imperial edict granted his request.
Kāngyì led troops to the Tuózhǔn City on the Dàshí Hé (Great Stone River),
and returned after seizing several hundred households.
Not long after, he died.
Commentary states: Gāojùlí murdered its ruler Sòng and installed Xún.
When Liáo raised an army to demand an accounting for the crime,
it would have been proper for them to welcome the army with baskets of food and pots of drink,
and to clear their houses to await them;
instead, they relied on natural defenses and military resistance,
causing the wise to exhaust their strategy
and the brave to expend their strength.
Although their leaders were captured,
(Gāolì) stubbornly remained self-sufficient, residing alone across the sea.
Is it not true that those who subdue others do so by virtue (dé) and not by force?
Moreover,
when their palaces and houses are destroyed,
is this not what is meant by "Yān attacking Yān?"
Alas!
The abandonment of Zhūyá
was due to the strength of letting go,
and Díliè's counsel played a part in it.
Biography 19: Yēlǜ Shùchéng (Shùzhēn Púlǔ), Yáng, Yēlǜ Hánliú, Yáng Jí, Yēlǜ Héshàng
Yēlǜ Shùchéng,
courtesy name Xǐyǐn,
small name Chénliù,
was a descendant of the Jìfǔ Fáng (Youngest Uncle lineage).
His father, Wú Jiǔ,
was a Grand Preceptor in charge of Inspection (Jiǎnxiào Tàishī).
Shùchéng loved learning in his youth,
and never forgot anything he read.
He was proficient in both Liáo and Hàn scripts,
and especially skilled at poetry.
In the early years of Zhòngxī,
he was appointed as the Páiyìn Lángjūn (Attendant in charge of Seals and Tallies),
and successively promoted to Academician of the Bureau of Military Affairs (Shūmì Zhí Xuéshì).
He and Xiāo Hánjiānú each presented a Rhapsody on the Leisure and Joy of the Four Seasons,
and the Emperor sighed in admiration.
Previously,
few Qìdān doctors knew how to take pulses or examine medicine.
The Emperor ordered Shùchéng to translate medical texts on prescriptions and pulse examination and disseminate them.
From then on, everyone became familiar with them,
and even the various tribes understood medical matters.
He often entered the Forbidden Palace
to participate in resolving contentious debates.
Together with the Línyá (Chancellor) Xiāo Hánjiānú and others, he compiled the Veritable Records (Shílù) and the Ritual Texts (Lǐshū).
He revised and fixed the laws and statutes with the Vice Commissioner of Military Affairs, Xiāo Dé.
The Emperor issued an edict to Shùchéng saying:
“Currently, the severity of the statutes and laws is disproportionate.
Statutes and laws
are the priority in governance,
and relate to human lives;
they must not be handled carelessly.
You must carefully assess their severity
and revise them appropriately.”
Shùchéng consulted ancient and modern precedents,
edited and corrected errors,
and presented the completed work.
The Emperor reviewed it and praised its quality.
Just as Shùchéng was being promoted and utilized,
he was falsely accused by his wife Húdǔ,
stripped of his office due to this crime,
and degraded to
“Commoner Yēlǜ” (Shù Yēlǜ).
He was sent on a mission to Tǔfān for a total of twelve years,
and only returned during the Qīngníng period.
The Emperor recognized the false accusation,
issued an edict restoring him to his original clan status,
reinstated him to the office from which he had been stripped,
and he subsequently died.
When Shùchéng was serving as Línyá,
he dreamed that a skilled diviner named Húlǚgǔ divined for him, saying:
“Your office will stop at Línyá,
and you will incur a crime because of your wife.”
When the matter was brought to justice,
the law required a divorce.
Húdǔ happened to be pregnant,
but died without giving birth when the time came.
When they cut her open and examined her,
the child was found holding its heart with its hand.
Those who recognized the meaning said this was retribution for falsely accusing her husband.
His poems and writings circulated in the world.
His younger brother was Shùzhēn.
Shùzhēn,
courtesy name Chénpǔ,
was skilled at literary composition.
During the Zhòngxī period,
he served as General of his original clan.
In the first year of Xiányōng,
he was appointed Joint Administrator of the Affairs of the Tōnjīng Liúshǒu (Resident Commissioner of the Eastern Capital),
and soon transferred to be the Jìdùshǐ (Military Governor) of the Wūyǎn Tūjué Tribe.
In the ninth year,
he governed the affairs of Jìzhōu.
The following year,
he was promoted to Dū Línyá (Chief Chancellor).
He submitted a memorial petitioning to broaden the surnames used in the state, saying:
“Since the founding of our dynasty,
the laws and regulations have been refined and clear;
only the surnames are limited to two divisions:
Yēlǜ and Xiāo, and nothing else.
When Tàizǔ first established the Qìdān Large Script,
he adopted the names of the various tribes and villages
and created a supplementary section
which was placed at the end of the scroll.
Your servant requests that this be expanded,
allowing all tribes to establish their own surnames,
so that marriages between men and women conform to ritual propriety.”
The Emperor felt that the old system could not be hastily changed
and did not heed him.
In the second year of Dàkāng,
Yēlǜ Yǐxīn was sent out to serve as Resident Commissioner of the Central Capital (Zhōngjīng Liúshǒu),
and Shùzhēn, along with Yēlǜ Mèngjiǎn, submitted a memorial offering congratulations.
Before long,
Yǐxīn was again appointed Commissioner of Military Affairs (Shūmìshǐ),
monopolizing power and acting tyrannically.
Shùzhēn privately met Yǐxīn and wept, saying:
“The previous memorial presented against you
was not Shùzhēn’s genuine wish.”
Yǐxīn believed his words,
and thus he secured his safety.
Those who heard about this held him in contempt.
In the eighth year,
he retired from office,
and died.
His son was Púlǔ.
Púlǔ,
styled Nǎizhǎn.
As a youth, he was intelligent, perceptive, and loved learning.
When he was just seven years old,
he could recite the Khitan Large Script.
He studied Han literature (Chinese script);
before he was ten years old,
he was widely versed in the classics and books.
During the Zhòngxī period (1032–1055),
he passed the metropolitan examination (Jìnshì).
The chief examiner, citing that the national regulations lacked a clause allowing Khitans to sit for the Jìnshì examination,
reported this to the Emperor.
Because [his father] Shùzhēn arbitrarily allowed his son to take the examination,
he was flogged two hundred times.
Soon after, Púlǔ was ordered to become a Páiyìn Lángjūn (Officer of Seals and Tallies).
When commanded to compose a poem,
he completed and presented it immediately.
The Emperor praised and rewarded him,
and looked to his attendants, saying:
“With literary talent such as this,
he certainly cannot manage military affairs.”
Púlǔ memorialized, saying:
“Since receiving moral instruction (yìfāng), your servant
has also practiced riding and archery,
and among my peers, I am also capable.”
The Emperor did not believe him.
It happened that he accompanied [the Emperor] on a hunt.
He hit three rabbits with three arrows.
The Emperor was greatly impressed by him,
and transferred him to the position of Tōngjìn.
At this time,
his father Shùzhēn had previously sent him a poem offering warning and advice (jièyù shī).
Púlǔ replied with a fu (rhapsody),
which the multitude praised for its refined elegance.
His favor and treatment gradually increased.
He died early in the Qīngníng period (1055–1064).
Yáng,
styled Chāngshí,
was a native of Āncì.
As a youth, he grasped the general meaning of the Five Classics.
Emperor Shèngzōng heard of his sharpness and perception,
and commanded him to be tested by writing a poem.
He was appointed Jiàoshū Láng (Collator of Books) in the Mìshū Shěng (Palace Library).
In the eleventh year of the Tàipíng period (1031),
he was promoted after passing the Jìnshì examination (Grade B),
and served as Zhuòzuò Zuǒláng (Assistant in the Imperial Library).
In the twelfth year of Zhòngxī (1043),
he was successively promoted to Shūmì Dū Chéngzhǐ (Chief Administrator of the Bureau of Military Affairs),
and provisionally held the post of Dùzhī Shǐ (Commissioner of Finance).
When received in audience, his replies pleased the Emperor,
and he was advanced to Shūmì Fùshǐ (Vice Commissioner of Military Affairs).
He successively held the posts of Jiédùshǐ (Military Commissioner) of Chángníng Jūn,
Zhuǎnyùn Shǐ (Transport Commissioner) of the Shānxī Circuit,
and Zhī Xīngzhōng Fǔ (Administrator of Xīngzhōng Prefecture).
Early in the Qīngníng period,
he entered the capital and became Zhī Nányuàn Shūmì Shǐ (Administrator of the Southern Bureau of Military Affairs),
managing the state administration jointly with Yáo Jǐngxíng.
He requested the implementation of the Cháicè Lǐ (Firewood and Tablet Rites).
He was enfeoffed as Zhào Guó Gōng (Duke of the State of Zhào).
Due to a foot ailment,
he was again made Administrator of Xīngzhōng Prefecture.
Early in the Xiányōng period (1065–1074),
he was transferred and enfeoffed as Qí.
He was summoned and granted the title Tóngdé Gōngchén (Meritorious Official of Shared Virtue) and Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè (Left Minister of the Department of State Affairs),
concurrently Zhōngshū Lìng (Director of the Secretariat),
appointed Shūmì Shǐ (Commissioner of Military Affairs),
and his enfeoffment was changed to Jìn.
He was provided with the attendants and entourage of both a Chief Minister (Zǎixiàng) and a Commissioner of Military Affairs (Shūmì Shǐ) in two separate establishments,
and enfeoffed as Zhào Wáng (Prince of Zhào).
He repeatedly requested to retire from state administration,
was further granted the title Bǎojié Gōngchén (Meritorious Official for Maintaining Integrity),
and retired from office (zhìshì).
In the fifth year of Dàkāng (1079),
according to regulation, his title was changed to Liáoxī Jùnwáng (Prince of Liáoxī Commandery),
and he died.
Yēlǜ Hánliú,
styled Sùníng,
was a descendant of the Zhongfù Suí Guó Wáng (Paternal Uncle, Prince of Suí).
He possessed clear understanding,
sincerely practiced righteousness,
his demeanor was dignified and serious,
and he was skilled at composing poetry.
During the Tǒnghé period (983–1012),
he was summoned to provisionally hold the post of Yùyuàn Tōngjìn (Communicator in the Imperial Court).
In the third year of Kāitài (1014),
he was gradually promoted to Dūjiān (Supervisor) of the Wūgǔ Díliè Tribe,
and shortly thereafter became Zhī Xiángwěn Shì (Administrator of Xiángwěn Affairs).
When the Díliè tribe rebelled,
he commanded the Palace Division troops,
and followed Shūmì Shǐ Yēlǜ Shìliáng to suppress them.
He was awarded the title Qiānniú Wèi Dà Jiāngjūn (Grand General of the Ox-Guard).
In the first year of Zhòngxī (1032),
he was successively promoted to Tóngzhī Shàngjīng Liúshǒu (Associate Administrator of the Shàngjīng Residence),
and then changed to Tūlǐ Tàiwèi (Grand Commandant Tūlǐ) of the Six Xī Tribes.
His nature was not to conform lightly,
and he was consequently disliked by Shūmì Shǐ Xiāo Jiělǐ.
The Emperor wished to summon and employ Hánliú,
but Jiělǐ claimed that [Hánliú] suffered from an eye disease and could not see.
The discussion was therefore dropped.
In the fourth year (1035),
he was summoned to become Běimiàn Línyá (Northern Chancellor).
The Emperor said:
“We have long wished to employ you,
but heard you had an ailment,
and thus waited until now.”
Hánliú replied:
“Your servant once had an eye ailment,
but it lasted only a few months;
moreover, it did not cause complete blindness.
It is merely that your servant is clumsy and inept,
and unable to serve the powerful and influential.
For this reason, I was unable to see the Celestial Visage earlier.
Had it not been for Your Majesty’s sagacious observation,
how could this foolish servant have reached this day!”
He was commanded to present a poem expressing his feelings,
and the Emperor praised him with sighs of admiration.
Just as he was about to be appointed to a high office,
he died.
Yáng Jí,
styled Zhèngshū,
was a native of Nánjīng.
As a youth, his sharpness and perception were extraordinary.
When reading, he could naturally form phrases [into poetry];
those who recognized this considered him remarkable.
By the time he was twenty (ruòguàn),
his reputation was widely known.
In the twenty-fourth year of Tǒnghé (1006),
he achieved first place in the Jìnshì examination.
He successively served as Jiàoshū Láng (Collator of Books) and Dàlǐ Zhèng (Judicial Administrator).
In the sixth year of Kāitài (1017),
he was transferred to Yícáo Láng (Director of Ceremonial Affairs),
responsible for drafting imperial commands,
and was promoted to Jiànyì Dàfū (Grand Master of Remonstrance).
He was sent out to become Zhī Yì Zhōu (Administrator of Yì Prefecture).
His administration favored purity and simplicity,
and he was absolutely trustworthy regarding the scheduled collection of taxes and levies.
He returned to the capital to serve as Dàlǐ Shǎoqīng (Vice Minister of the Court of Judicial Review).
He was successively promoted to Hànlín Xuéshì (Academician of the Hànlín Academy).
His literary works were renowned for conforming to the proper standard.
In the eighth year (1019),
the Yān region suffered from famine and plague,
and many people became starving refugees.
Yáng Jí was appointed Tóngzhī Nánjīng Liúshǒu Shì (Associate Administrator of the Nánjīng Residence)
He opened the granaries,
relieved those in severe need,
and for poor people who had sold their children, he calculated the debt and released them.
When Sòng (Song Dynasty) dispatched Méi Xún to congratulate [the Emperor] on his Qiānlíng Jié (Thousand-Year Festival),
Jí was commanded to welcome and send him off.
They frequently exchanged poems (chàngchóu),
and Xún always praised him upon meeting him.
He was reappointed Hànlín Xuéshì.
In the first year of Zhòngxī (1032),
he was promoted to Hànlín Xuéshì Chéngzhǐ (Academician-in-Waiting, Chief Drafting Official).
While mourning his mother,
he was recalled to office as Gōngbù Shàngshū (Minister of Works).
He successively held the posts of Jiédùshǐ of Zhōngshùn Jūn,
Guānchá Chǔzhì Shǐ (Investigating and Disposal Commissioner) for Shuò and Wǔ Prefectures,
Jiédùshǐ of Tiāndé Jūn,
granted the ranks Tèjìn (Special Advanced Rank) and Jiǎnxiào Tàishī (Acting Grand Preceptor), concurrently Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāng Shì (Executive Assistant to the Chancellery),
and again appointed Cānzhī Zhèngshì (Councillor of State),
concurrently Zhī Nányuàn Shūmì Shǐ (Administrator of the Southern Bureau of Military Affairs).
In the fifteenth year (1046),
he was sent out to be Jiédùshǐ of Wǔdìng Jūn.
The territory suffered severe drought,
and the crops were about to wither.
On the evening he took office,
rain fell abundantly.
The common people sang:
“By what means are we revived?
Heaven sent down the rain.
Who is it that comforts us?
Master Yáng is our ruler (zhǔ).”
The Yáng River had lost its original course,
causing annual harm to the people.
He therefore used his own salary to build a long bridge,
so that people no longer suffered hardship crossing the water.
When he was summoned back,
the commandery populace held onto his carriage shaft and wept as they saw him off.
The Emperor held a banquet at the Qīngliáng Diàn (Hall of Clear Coolness) to honor and reward him.
On that same day, he was appointed Lìbù Shàngshū (Minister of Personnel),
concurrently Ménxià Shìláng (Vice Director of the Chancellery) and Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāng Shì.
The Emperor said:
“How is your encounter today inferior to that of Lǚ Wàng meeting King Wén!”
Jí replied:
“Lǚ Wàng met his opportunity ten years later than your servant.”
The Emperor was pleased.
When he held the position of Chancellor (xiàngwèi),
he made promoting the virtuous his personal responsibility.
He focused on the main principles of governance,
and held the hundred bureaus responsible for results.
Everyone was happy to be employed by him.
He requested retirement three times,
which was granted.
He was provided monthly with money, grain, and servants,
and envoys were sent four times a year to check on him.
He died.
His collection, the Dēngyíng Jí, circulated in the world.
courtesy name Tèmò,
belonged to the Jìfù Fáng lineage.
He excelled at humor.
Early in the Zhòngxī period,
he was appointed Zhīhòu Lángjūn.
At that time, the Emperor valued kinship greatly;
all descendants of the Three Fathers
were ranked alongside the Emperor's fathers and elder brothers.
The Emperor was especially familiar and affectionate toward Héshàng.
However, whenever he attended banquets,
although witty,
he never once uttered an inappropriate word.
Because of this, the Emperor esteemed him even more.
He successively served as the Jìqìng and Yǒngxīng Palace Commissioner,
and was repeatedly promoted until he reached Assistant Commissioner of the Southern Chancellery of Military Affairs (Tóngzhī Nányuàn Xuānhuī Shǐ Shì) and Southern Advisor (Nánmiàn Línyá).
In the sixteenth year (of Zhòngxī),
he was sent out to be the Military Commissioner of Huáihuà Prefecture (Huáihuà Jūn Jiédù Shǐ),
and soon after was summoned back as Grand Censor (Yùshǐ Dàfū).
In the twenty-third year,
due to a major imperial conferment,
he was given the titles Military Commissioner of Tiānpíng Prefecture (Tiānpíng Jūn Jiédù Shǐ) and Acting Grand Tutor (Jiǎnxiào Tàishī).
He was transferred to be the Investigator of the Central Capital Circuit (Zhōngjīng Lù Ànwèn Shǐ),
where he died.
Héshàng possessed genuinely fine conduct,
frequently using his wealth to aid relatives and friends,
and everyone loved and respected him.
However, he was addicted to wine and neglected his duties,
and consequently, he was not entrusted with high authority.
When someone mentioned this to him,
he replied:
"It is not that I do not know,
but considering that life is like a lamp in the wind or a spark from a flint,
what else is there to do if one does not drink?"
In his later years, his heavy drinking became even more excessive,
and people called him
the "Wine Immortal" (Jiǔxiān).
Commentary states:
Shùchéng established the laws and statutes;
those who govern the people cannot apply them arbitrarily.
Although Shùzhēn once formally requested the expansion of family names
to organize rites and ceremonies;
his accommodation to circumstances
brought shame upon his son Púlǔ.
Yáng received the Emperor’s favor and treatment,
and was successively titled as a Prince (Wáng Jué),
yet his meritorious achievements were barely evident.
However, the one who grasped the essentials of loving the people and governing the state
was surely Yáng Jí.
Biography Twenty: Xiāo Ālà, Yēlǜ Yìxiān (Xìnxiān), Xiāo Táokuí, Xiāo Tǎlágě, Yēyē Dílù
Xiāo Ālà,
courtesy name Ālǐlǎn,
was the son of Xiàomù, Commissioner of the Northern Chancellery of Military Affairs (Běiyuàn Shūmì Shǐ).
Raised in the palace as a child,
Xīngzōng particularly loved him.
In the sixth year of Zhòngxī,
he became Commissioner of Hóngyì Palace (Hóngyì Gōng Shǐ).
He was repeatedly promoted to Assistant Commissioner of the Northern Chancellery of Military Affairs (Tóngzhī Běiyuàn Shūmì Shǐ),
and was given the concurrent title of Acting Grand Councilor (Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāng Shì).
He was then sent out as Resident General of the Eastern Capital (Dōngjīng Liúshǒu).
In the twenty-first year,
he was appointed Pacification Commissioner of the Northwest Circuit (Xīběi Lù Zhāotǎo Shǐ),
and was enfeoffed as Prince of Xīpíng Commandery (Xīpíng Jùnwáng).
Soon after, he married the Princess of Qínjìn State (Qínjìn Guówáng Gōngzhǔ),
and was appointed Grand Commandant (Fùmǎ Dūwèi).
In the first year of Qīngníng,
by imperial testament, he was appointed Grand Councilor of the Northern Administration (Běifǔ Zǎixiàng),
concurrently serving as Commissioner of the Southern Chancellery of Military Affairs (Nányuàn Shūmì Shǐ),
and was advanced to Prince of Hán.
The following year,
he was changed to Commissioner of the Northern Chancellery of Military Affairs (Běiyuàn Shūmì Shǐ),
transferred to Prince of Chén,
and shared the governance of the state with Xiāo Gé.
Gé was obsequious and lawless,
and when Ālà argued against him without success,
he requested leave to retire.
The Emperor consequently disliked him
and relieved him of his post, making him Resident General of the Eastern Capital (Dōngjīng Liúshǒu).
During the time of the Sèsè ceremony,
he entered court and reported on the advantages and disadvantages of current governance.
Gé used this opportunity to slander him,
the Emperor became enraged,
and had him strangled to death.
The Empress Dowager attempted rescue but failed,
and cried mournfully, saying:
"What crime did Ālà commit to be killed so suddenly?"
The Emperor then bestowed generous funeral gifts and posthumous titles,
and he was buried at Chìshān, near Qiánlíng.
Ālà was loyal and resolute by nature,
understood worldly affairs,
and possessed talent for statecraft.
Commentators suggest that if Ālà had remained alive,
there would have been no rebellions by Chóngyuán or Yǐxīn.
Yēlǜ Yìxiān
was the younger brother of Yuyue Rénxiān.
He possessed a handsome appearance,
and his demeanor was grave and serious.
Early in the Zhòngxī period,
he was appointed Xiángwěn of the Zhīhòu Lángjūn Corps.
In the thirteenth year,
when the imperial carriage campaigned westward,
he served as Superintendent of the Twelve Sections (Shí'èr Háng Jiū Dūjiàn).
His military achievements were outstanding,
and he was transferred to Commissioner of the Southern Chancellery of Military Affairs (Nányuàn Xuānhuī Shǐ).
At that time, Xiāo Gé was Assistant Commissioner of the Bureau of Military Affairs (Tóngzhī Shūmì Yuàn Shì).
Relying on imperial favor, he usurped power,
and Yìxiān detested him.
While attending a banquet,
he said to the Emperor:
"Gé is cunning, treacherous, and prone to trouble.
If he is greatly employed,
he will certainly mislead the state!"
His words were extremely passionate and sharp,
but they were not accepted.
Another day, while attending a banquet,
the Emperor ordered the assembled officials to gamble (play *bó*).
The loser was penalized with a huge goblet of wine.
Yìxiān was supposed to be matched against Gé.
He looked displeased and said:
"Even if I cannot promote the worthy or dismiss the incompetent,
how can I gamble with a state traitor!"
The Emperor stopped him, saying:
"You are drunk, Sir!"
Yìxiān continued to vehemently curse without ceasing.
The Emperor was furious,
but thanks to the Empress’s intervention,
he was spared punishment.
The next day,
the Emperor said to Gé:
"Yìxiān behaved disrespectfully,
he ought to be dismissed."
Gé replied:
"Yìxiān is naturally loyal and upright.
If he is dismissed now due to a mistake made while drunk,
who would dare speak of others' faults?"
The Emperor believed Gé to be loyal and upright
and trusted him even more.
Yìxiān felt depressed and unhappy,
yet when discussing affairs of state, he never showed the slightest discouragement.
Later, while gambling before the Emperor again,
Yìxiān offered a prayer, saying:
"Before, I spoke of someone's fault,
offending Imperial Majesty.
May today's throw
demonstrate my foolish sincerity."
Immediately, he drew the Táng Yìn (Hall Seal, a high throw).
The Emperor was astonished.
In the sixteenth year,
he was made Grand Inspector of the Palace Guards (Diànqián Dū Diǎnjiǎn).
He campaigned against Púnǔlǐ,
achieved many surrenders,
and captured their chieftain Táodélǐ, bringing him back.
An imperial handwritten edict praised and rewarded him.
For his merit, he was transferred to Commander-in-Chief of the Southern Capital (Nánjīng Tǒngjūn Shǐ),
and enfeoffed as Prince of Wǔchāng Commandery (Wǔchāng Jùnwáng).
He memorialized requesting that the money profits of the Commander-in-Chief’s office
be used to support the poor.
Before a year had passed,
military supplies were complete,
and the people received rest.
In the twenty-first year,
he was appointed Tìyǐn,
advanced to Prince of Fùchūn,
and died
at the age of forty-two.
Yìxiān often warned his clansmen:
"The Sānfù Fáng (Three Fathers' Lineages) in the state
are all kinsmen of the Emperor;
being unfilial or unjust is especially unacceptable."
When interacting with subordinates, regardless of their high or low status, worthiness or lack thereof,
he treated everyone with equal respect.
His wife, the daughter of the Eldest Princess of Jìn State (Jìn Guó Zhǎng Gōngzhǔ),
whenever meeting cousins (maternal and paternal),
would not see them unless they wore proper ceremonial attire.
Therefore, many inside and outside the family were influenced by their virtuous example.
During the Qīngníng period,
he was posthumously granted the title Prince of Xǔ.
His younger brother was Xìnxiān.
Xìnxiān,
because Xīngzōng had sworn a blood-oath friendship with his father Guī,
was raised in the palace as a child.
He excelled at riding and archery.
, he became the Grand Guardian of the Left Guards (Zuǒ Hùwèi Tàibǎo),
and concurrently managed the affairs of the Palace Inspection Directorate (Diànqián Diǎnjiǎn Sī Shì).
In the eighteenth year,
he concurrently served as the Xiángwěn (Senior General) of the Right Guard Gentlemen's Corps (Yòu Zhīhòu Lángjūn Bān).
The Emperor (Shàng) asked what he desired.
Xìnxiān replied:
"My late father, Guīyǐn, shared a bond with Your Majesty like that of siblings,
but he never received a princely title (Wáng fēng).
If he could receive this favor in the underworld,
my wish as a subject would be fulfilled."
The Emperor (Shàng) said:
"This is the fault of My having forgotten."
Guīyǐn was posthumously granted the title Prince of Yān (Yān Wáng).
That year,
Xìnxiān followed Xiāo Huì in attacking Xià,
was defeated south of the Yellow River (Hénán),
and was, along with others, reprimanded.
In the beginning of Qīngníng,
he served as the Southern Línyá (Minister of Administration),
and died. Xiāo Táowěi
, courtesy name Wūgǔlín
, was the sixth-generation descendant of the Chancellor Xiátè
. He was firm and upright
, and commanded great respect
. In the beginning of Xiányōng
, he was appointed Grand Guardian of the Horse Herds (Mǎqún Tàibǎo)
. He had long known that the government pastures existed only in name
, so he thoroughly reviewed the old registers
, removed the sick and weak animals
, and recorded the true numbers
. The herdsmen feared and obeyed him
. Táowěi submitted a memorial, saying
: "The government herds count the few as many
, and treat nonexistence as existence
. The superiors and subordinates deceive each other
, and accumulated malpractice has become common practice
. It is better to calculate the visible, true number
, and establish them in a fixed register
, so that both the public and private sectors benefit
." This was followed
. Livestock multiplied yearly
During the Dàkāng period,
he was repeatedly promoted to Chief Commissioner of the Khìdān Traveling Palace (Qìdān Xínggōng Dū Bùshǔ).
The Emperor (Shàng) once said to his ministers
: "The important responsibility of military and state affairs in the Northern Chancellery (Běi Shūmìyuàn)
has lacked the right person for a long time.
Who is better suited: Yēlǜ Āsī or Xiāo Wòtèlà?"
The ministers each praised the strengths of their preferred candidate,
but Táowěi alone remained silent.
The Emperor (Shàng) asked
: "Why does Your Lordship not speak?"
Táowěi replied
: "Wòtèlà is cowardly and will ruin affairs;
Āsī is talented but greedy
, and will become the root of disaster.
If one must be used
, ruining affairs is still preferable to rooting disaster."
The Emperor (Shàng) said
: "Táowěi surpasses even Wèi Zhēng,
I only regret that I am not equal to [Tang] Tàizōng!"
Nevertheless, Āsī was eventually made Commissioner of Military Affairs (Shūmì Shǐ).
Because of this, Āsī bore a grudge against him.
In the ninth year,
the western borders were unstable.
Āsī memorialized, saying
: "Affairs on the frontier are crucial
; a high official should be chosen to suppress and pacify them."
The Emperor (Shàng) said
: "What about Táowěi?"
Āsī said
: "It is truly as the Imperial will commands."
Táowěi was then appointed Commissioner of Pacification for the Southwest (Xīnánmiàn Zhāotǎo Shǐ).
Āsī secretly conspired with Xiāo Āhūdài to falsely accuse Táowěi, alleging that when bandits plundered the horses and livestock of the residents south of the desert (Mònán),
Táowěi failed to urgently pursue and capture them.
The crime deserved death,
but an imperial edict stripped him of his office.
After a long time,
he was recalled to serve as Military Governor of Tāmǔchéng (Tāmǔchéng Jiédùshǐ).
Before he could depart,
a carbuncle developed on his back, and he died.
Táowěi was strong-willed;
when angry, his beard and whiskers would flare out.
Whenever there was a major discussion
, he would resolutely decide upon it.
Even if the Emperor (Shàng) showed displeasure
, he never stopped abruptly.
He never yielded slightly to the powerful and noble.
Ultimately, he was framed by Āsī.
People of the time lamented this.
He had two sons
: Túmù and Xiáshì.
After Āsī died
, they were finally promoted. Xiāo Tǎlàgě
, courtesy name Táoxǐn
, was a man of the Six Divisions Tribe (Liù Yuàn Bù)
. He was fundamentally firm and upright
. During the reign of Tàizǔ
, on account of his great-uncle Táixǐn having plotted to murder the Yùyuè Shìlǔ
, he was confiscated and assigned to the Hóngyì Palace (Hóngyì Gōng)
. When Shìzōng ascended the throne
, because Tǎlàgě was related to the emperor through his mother's clan
, he was removed from the status register (released from servitude)
, and appointed Clerk of the Imperial Uncle's Sub-division (Guójìu Biébù Chǎngshǐ)
. Someone suggested that the Prince of Tàiníng, Cháge, harbored treasonous intentions
. Tǎlàgě said
: "Even if he were ruthlessly unjust
, who would willingly follow him!"
On another day, while attending a banquet
, when the wine was flowing freely
, Tǎlàgě grabbed Cháge's ear
, and forced him to drink, saying
: "The Emperor (Shàng) certainly knows you are arrogant and reckless
, but because you belong to the imperial clan
, he has shown you special compassion
, keeping you close to him
, and moreover gauging what you are capable of with your talent
. If you continue in wickedness and do not repent
, you will merely bring the disaster of total family annihilation upon yourself!"
Cháge could not reply
, and forced a smile, saying
: "Why is this joke so harsh!"
Near the end of Tiānlù
, Tǎlàgě served as the Chancellor of the Northern Administration (Běi Fǔ Zǎixiàng)
. When Cháge raised the rebellion
, Tǎlàgě drunkenly cursed, saying
: "I regret that I did not kill this traitor!"
Soon after, he was killed by Cháge
. Yēlǜ Dílù
, courtesy name Yángyǐn
, was a descendant of Mèngfù, Prince of Chǔ (Mèngfù Chǔ Guó Wáng)
. His nature was straightforward
, and he possessed great physical strength
. When Cháge rebelled
, Dílù
heard of it,
and went to see the Prince of Shòu'ān (Shòu'ān Wáng).
He spoke passionately, saying
: "I wish to obtain a few hundred elite soldiers
, to destroy the bandit faction."
The Prince praised his loyalty.
When Mùzōng ascended the throne
, Dílù became the Northern Administration Commissioner of Palace Affairs (Běi Yuàn Xuānhuī Shǐ).
As the Fēihú Pass (Fēihú Dào) was narrow
, the Emperor (Shàng) ordered Dílù to widen it.
The following year
, he led troops to reinforce Hédōng
, arrived at Tàiyuán
, met with the King of Hàn (Hàn Wáng) at Gāopíng
, attacked the Zhōu army
, and defeated them
, also receiving the surrender of their multitude.
When Xīn and Dài prefectures (Xīn, Dài èr Zhōu) rebelled
, he led troops to suppress them.
Yēlǜ Tàliè arrived just in time
, and defeated the Zhōu army at Xīnkǒu.
Upon the army's return
, Dílù died. Commentary states
: A loyal subject only knows of the State's existence
, and does not consider his own existence (life)
. Therefore, when hating evil, they do not avoid the resulting peril.
Ālà rebuked Xiāo Gé for flattery and unlawful behavior;
Táowěi spoke against Āsī, saying that using him would surely root disaster;
Tǎlàgě rebuked Cháge, warning him that his ruthless injustice would only lead to the disaster of total family annihilation
. Their intentions can certainly be called loyal.
Yet, the moment the words were spoken, disaster followed immediately.
Alas!
If the wicked and the upright are not distinguished
, how can the state avoid chaos!
Biographies, Chapter 21: Yēlǜ Hánbā, Yēlǜ Tánggǔ, Xiāo Zhúzhé (Yàoshīnǔ), Yēlǜ Jué, Yēlǜ Púlǐdǔ.
Yēlǜ Hánbā
, courtesy name Cháoyǐn
, was outstanding and possessed great ambition,
being the fifth-generation descendant of Gǔ, the Northern Xiángwěn (Senior General).
the Tàipíng period, he
traveled to the Jīngshī,
residing near the traveling palace,
possessing only a bag of clothes and a single horse.
The Emperor went hunting in disguise,
saw him, and asked:
"Who are you?"
Hán Bā initially did not recognize
him, and casually replied:
"I am Hán Bā, a man of the Běiyuàn department,
who came here to seek office."
The Emperor spoke with him,
knowing he possessed great talent,
and secretly marked him.
It happened that the Běiyuàn reported that a suspicious case in Nánjīng had long remained undecided.
The Emperor summoned Hán Bā to ride a relay post horse to investigate and review the case.
The entire court was astonished.
Hán Bā handled the matter based on the circumstances,
and no one was wronged.
The Emperor praised him.
When registering the herds of state-owned horses,
two were missing.
His colleagues investigated ceaselessly;
Hán Bā barely questioned the matter
and immediately rode ahead to report to the Emperor.
The Emperor trusted him even more.
In the first year of Jǐngfú,
he became the Zuǒ Yílíbì,
then moved to Běimiàn Línyá.
He received outstanding favor and attention.
In the sixth year of Chóngxī,
he was appointed Běiyuàn Dàwáng.
His governance was lenient and humane,
and he subsequently became Zuǒ Yílíbì again.
In the twelfth year,
he once again became Běiyuàn Dàwáng.
When he attended court,
the Emperor calmly said to him:
"Your post guarding the frontier is critical.
You must replenish the treasuries and relieve the poor and needy to repay Us."
Having received the decree,
he became even more loyal and diligent,
reporting everything he knew,
and the benefits were great.
He died
at the age of fifty-five.
When the Emperor heard the news,
he mourned and regretted.
On the day of his death,
his chests held no old savings,
and his clothes racks held no new garments.
An envoy was dispatched to offer condolences and sacrifices,
and burial necessities were provided.
Hán Bā ordinarily disdained trivial duties,
and his joy or anger was not apparent.
Once, he lost the horse he rode;
his servant replaced it with one of the same color,
and he did not notice for several months.
Yēlǜ Tánggǔ,
courtesy name Díyǐn,
was the illegitimate son of Yúyuè Wūzhì.
He was honest and cautious,
and skilled at writing.
In the twenty-fourth year of Tǒnghé,
he presented Wūzhì’s methods for pacifying the people and controlling bandits.
He was appointed Junior General,
promoted to Xīnánmiàn Xúnjiǎn,
and successively served as the Governor of Háozhōu
and Xiángwěn of the Tánggǔ Department.
He strictly established regulations,
prohibiting unscrupulous people from selling horses along the Sòng and Xià borders.
He subsequently presented essential strategies
for stopping illegal private trade and stabilizing the border regions.
The Empress Dowager praised him,
and decreed that border commanderies must adhere to it,
making it a formal statute.
The court debated expanding the southwestern territory—
west of Hēishān,
stretching several thousand *lǐ*.
Tánggǔ said:
"The garrison forts are too distant;
if there is a sudden alarm,
reinforcements will not arrive in time.
This is not a wise policy."
They followed his advice.
When the Xī Fān invaded,
a decree ordered deliberation on defense strategies.
Tánggǔ was commanded to supervise farming to provision the Western Army,
establishing fields along the Lúqú Hé.
That year saw a great harvest.
The following year,
the garrison was moved to Zhènzhōu.
Over a total of fourteen years,
he accumulated hundreds of thousands of *hú* of grain,
and a *dǒu* of rice cost only a few coins.
During the Chóngxī period,
he was appointed Jiédùshǐ of the Kuíyǎn Dǎngxiàng Department.
Previously,
Kědūn Chéng had been built to pacify the Western Regions.
Various tribes allowed their people to herd livestock,
but this invited looting by bandits.
In the fourth year of Chóngxī,
he submitted a memorial saying:
"Since the establishment of Kědūn Chéng,
the Xī Fān have frequently caused trouble on the frontier,
always necessitating burdensome distant garrisons.
As the years pass,
the nation's strength is depleted.
It would be better to return to guarding the old territories
and reduce and abolish garrison duty."
The proposal was not accepted.
That year,
he retired.
He requested that his father Wūzhì's achievements be engraved on stone.
The Emperor ordered Yēlǜ Shùchéng to compose the inscription,
which was carved on a stele at Chóngxiào Sì in Shàngjīng.
He died
at the age of seventy-eight.
Xiāo Zhúzhé,
courtesy name Shílǔyǐn,
was the son of Xiàomù’s younger brother, Gāojiǔ.
Due to his kinship, he was appointed Jiānmén Wèi Shàngjiāngjūn.
In the thirteenth year of Chóngxī,
he led guard soldiers to campaign against Lǐ Yuán● and achieved merit,
and was promoted to Xīngshènggōng Shǐ.
When Táo Délǐ, chief of the Púnúlǐ tribe, rebelled,
Zhúzhé served as Tǒngjūn Dūjiān,
following Commander-in-Chief Yēlǜ Yìxiān to attack them,
and Táo Délǐ was captured.
Zhúzhé and Yēlǜ Yìxiān were not compatible,
so Zhúzhé falsely accused Yìxiān of a crime
and was dismissed from office.
He was later promoted to Xīnánmiàn Zhāotǎo Dūjiān,
but was imprisoned for an offense.
Based on the request of the Empress Dowager,
he was flogged and released.
Early in the Qīngníng period,
he became Guójiù Xiángwěn and Xīběilù Zhāotǎo Shǐ.
He secretly took three hundred *hú* of official grain,
but when his term ended,
he left livestock
and ordered his steward to sell them for repayment.
Later, his maternal cousin Húdǔ arrived at the department and exposed the matter.
The Emperor was furious,
punished him with a severe beating,
and dismissed him from office.
He was soon reinstated as Zhāodé Jūn Jiédùshǐ,
and summoned to serve as Běiyuàn Xuānhuī Shǐ.
In the ninth year,
the Emperor, recognizing that Zhúzhé had previously been Zhāotǎo
and exercised authority over the various tribes,
reinstated him as Xīběilù Zhāotǎo Shǐ.
He trained the soldiers,
increased weaponry,
curtailed unnecessary demands and summonses,
and strictly enforced orders.
People dared not transgress,
and the frontier was peaceful.
In the tenth year,
he came to court
and was enfeoffed as Liǔchéng Jùnwáng.
In the second year of Xiányōng,
he was appointed Chancellor of the Northern Administration,
but was resented by the Běiyuàn Shūmìshǐ, Yēlǜ Yǐxīn,
who falsely accused Zhúzhé and the Imperial Guard Xiāo Húgǔ of plotting to murder Yǐxīn.
The imperial investigation found no evidence,
so he was dismissed as Chancellor
and sent out to govern Shùnyì Jūn.
When he died,
he was posthumously ennobled as the Prince of the three states of Jìn, Sòng, and Liáng.
His nephew was Yàoshīnǔ.
Yàoshīnǔ
was intelligent in his youth,
strict in observing ritual law,
and was appointed Zhīhòu Lángjūn.
During
the Dàkāng period,
he was appointed Xīngshènggōng Shǐ,
and was repeatedly promoted to Tóngzhī Diànqián Diǎnjiǎn Sī Shì.
The Emperor praised the solemnity of his service in the Imperial Guard
and promoted him to Yòu Yílíbì.
When King Lǐ Qiánshùn of Xià was attacked by Sòng,
he sought mediation.
The Emperor ordered Yàoshīnǔ, bearing the imperial staff, to be an envoy to Sòng,
requesting they cease hostilities and restore good relations.
Sòng complied.
He was appointed Nánmiàn Línyá,
then changed to Deputy Administrator of the Hàn Rén Traveling Palace.
Early in the Qiántǒng period,
he was sent out to serve as Āndōng Jūn Jiédùshǐ,
and died there.
Yēlǜ Jué,
courtesy name Wúzhǎn,
was a descendant of Yáoniǎn Xiānzhì Kèhán.
he was summoned to compile the national history,
and appointed Fúbǎoláng (Seal and Treasure Gentleman).
He was successively promoted to Zhī Běiyuàn Fù Bùshǔ Shì (Acting Vice Commissioner of the Northern Administration).
When he entered to have an audience with the Empress Dowager,
the Empress Dowager looked around and said:
"The former Emperor said Jué would certainly become a great man.
Indeed, he has."
He was appointed Shūmì Fùshǐ (Vice Commissioner of Military Affairs).
He was sent out as the Xīnánmiàn Zhāotǎo Dūjiān (Military Superintendent of the Southwest Circuit Pacification Commission),
and successively held the posts of Tóng Qiān Nánjīng Liúshǒu Shì (Associate Prefect of the Southern Capital) and Nánmiàn Línyá (Southern Circuit Secretary).
When the Emperor's younger brother, the King of Qínguó, served as the Liáoxīngjūn Jiédùshǐ (Military Governor of Liaoxing Circuit),
Jué was made Tóng Zhī Shǐ Shì (Associate Administrator) under him,
and provided much guidance and correction.
In the tenth year (Chóngxī 10),
he was reinstated as Shūmì Fùshǐ.
In the early years of Xiányōng,
he concurrently served as Běiyuàn Fù Bùshǔ (Vice Commissioner of the Northern Administration).
When the King of Qínguó became the Xījīng Liúshǒu (Prefect of the Western Capital),
he requested Jué to be his assistant,
and this was granted.
Three times in that year, the prisons were empty.
He was recalled to serve as Mèngfùfáng Chǎngwěn (Chancellor of the Mèngfù Clan).
Jué did not enjoy accumulating wealth;
the Emperor, knowing his poverty,
bestowed ten palace households upon him.
The Emperor once said to the Zǎixiàng (Chancellors):
"Among the Khitan, there is none as loyal and upright as Jué,
and for the Han Chinese, there is only Liú Shēn.
However, after careful observation,
Jué is superior to Shēn."
Previously,
the various tribes in the Northwest had long been unsubdued.
The Emperor dispatched Jué to investigate the situation,
and he severely punished those who were negligent or slow.
He died from an illness related to alcohol.
Yēlǜ Púlǐdǔ,
courtesy name Yànyǐn,
was the fourth-generation descendant of Liùyuàn Línyá (Secretary of the Six Administrations) Tūlǚbùyě.
During the Kāitài period,
he served as Běnbān Lángjūn (Gentleman of the Home Class).
Having achieved merit in capturing bandits,
Shūmìshǐ Xiāo Pǔ recommended him,
and he was promoted to Shuàifǔ Shuài (Commander of the Commandery).
During the Tàipíng period,
he served as Tóng Zhī Nányuàn Xuānhuī Shì (Associate Administrator of the Southern Administration),
and was successively promoted to Zhāngshèngjūn Jiédùshǐ (Military Governor of Zhangsheng Circuit).
In the sixteenth year of Chóngxī (1047),
he governed Xīngzhōngfǔ (Xingzhong Prefecture),
and was famed for the emptiness of its prisons.
In the eighteenth year (1049),
during the campaign against Xià,
he acted as Xīnánmiàn Zhāotǎo Shǐ (Pacification Commissioner of the Southwest Circuit).
In the nineteenth year (1050),
when the Xià people invaded Jīnsùjūn,
he defeated them,
beheading over ten thousand enemy soldiers,
and was granted the title Yòu Wǔwèi Shàng Jiāngjūn (Superior General of the Right Military Guard).
At that time, the herds near the border were frequently raided.
He was transferred to Dǎotālíng Dūjiān (Military Superintendent of Daotao Ridge) to manage the situation,
and the sounds of drums (of warfare) ceased.
In the twentieth year (1051),
he became Zhī Jīnsùjūn Shì (Administrator of Jinsu Circuit Affairs).
When Zǎixiàng Zhào Wéijié was placed in charge of provisioning fodder and grain, bridges, and routes for the border cities,
he requested an assistant.
The Emperor ordered Púlǐdǔ to serve as his deputy,
and he gained renown for his competence.
In the early years of Qīngníng,
he successively served as Jiédùshǐ for the two circuits of Chángníng and Kuāngyì,
and then retired from office.
He died during the Xiányōng period.
His son, Āgùzhì,
died while holding the post of Dǎotālíng Dūjiān.
Discussion: Hán Bā was only brought into service because the Emperor traveled incognito.
When entrusted with tasks,
he was distinguished and understood the greater principles,
and did not disappoint the Emperor who recognized him.
Tánggǔ and Zhúzhé managed the Northwest border,
encouraged farming to accumulate grain,
and trained soldiers.
Enemies dared not offend.
Jué was praised by the Emperor for his loyalty and uprightness;
Púlǐdǔ was competent and quick-witted, serving as an assistant to the Chancellor;
and both, while governing their circuits, were known for having empty prisons.
These several men,
were they merely soldiers in armor?
They were certainly equals of Lǐ Mù and Chéng Bùshí.
Biographies, Chapter 22: Xiāo Duólà, Xiāo Pǔdá, Yēlǜ Hóushěn, Yēlǜ Gǔyù, Yēlǜ Dúhē, Xiāo Hánjiā, Xiāo Wūyě Xiāo Duólà,
courtesy name Ruólǎn,
belonged to the household of the Khān of Yáoliǎnwā.
His grandfather, Nièlǔgǔ,
was Běiyuàn Shūmì Fùshǐ (Vice Commissioner of Military Affairs of the Northern Administration).
His father, Sāmǒ,
courtesy name Húdújǐn,
was appointed Zhīhòu Lángjūn (Gentleman Attendant) in the early years of Chóngxī,
and was successively promoted to Běimiàn Línyá (Northern Circuit Secretary).
In the nineteenth year (1050),
he followed Yēlǜ Yíxīn and Xiāo Púnú in the campaign against Xià.
Upon reaching the site where Xiāo Huì had suffered defeat,
he captured scouts.
Learning that there were human settlements,
and that many of his countrymen who had been captured could not return,
he captured them all and returned.
He was appointed Dàfù Chǎngwěn (Chancellor of the Elder Clan),
and Zhī Shānběidào Biānjìng Shì (Administrator of the Shanbei Circuit Border Affairs).
In the early years of Qīngníng,
he successively served as Xīnánmiàn and Xīběilù Zhāotǎo Shǐ (Pacification Commissioner of the Southwest and Northwest Circuits),
was granted the title Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì (Grand Counselor),
and died.
Duólà was tall and imposing in appearance,
and his equestrian archery was unparalleled.
He rose from Zhīhòu Lángjūn to Hànrén Xínggōng Fù Bùshǔ (Vice Commissioner of the Han People’s Traveling Palace).
Later, he became Wūgǔdíliè Tǒngjūnshǐ (Commander-in-Chief of the Wūgǔdíliè Tribes).
Having achieved merit in defeating the enemy,
he was granted the title Lónghǔwèi Shàng Jiāngjūn (Superior General of the Dragon and Tiger Guard),
and appointed Xīběilù Zhāotǎo Shǐ (Pacification Commissioner of the Northwest Circuit).
He then reported on the advantages and disadvantages of the northern border,
requesting that the various tribes of his circuit link their forces with the Dǎotālíng Tǒngjūnsī (Daotao Ridge Commandery) for garrison duty.
He submitted this petition twice,
but it was not accepted.
He was transferred to Dōngběilù Tǒngjūnshǐ (Commander-in-Chief of the Northeast Circuit).
In the first year of Qiántǒng (1101),
because of his long experience in border affairs,
he was reinstated as Xīběilù Zhāotǎo Shǐ.
Yēdǔguā of the Northern Zǔbǔ led neighboring tribes to invade.
Duólà attacked them,
pursuing the fleeing enemy for several dozens of *lǐ*.
In the second year (1102),
taking advantage of Yēdǔguā's lack of preparedness,
he attacked them with light cavalry,
capturing fifteen thousand horses,
and oxen and sheep matching that number.
Previously,
there was an imperial decree that if the region was peaceful,
one official among the Zhāotǎo, Fù Tǒngjūn (Vice Commander-in-Chief), and Dūjiān should enter the court for an audience.
At this time, all his colleagues were absent.
Duólà entrusted military affairs to his staff officer and attended court.
Due to this, he was dismissed from office.
He was reassigned as Xījīng Liúshǒu (Prefect of the Western Capital),
and later reinstated as Dōngběilù Tǒngjūnshǐ.
He died while in office.
Xiāo Pǔdá,
courtesy name Tányǐn.
In the early years of Tǒnghé,
he was Nányuàn Chéngzhǐ (Southern Administration Executor).
In the sixth year of Kāitài (1017),
he was sent out as Wūgǔbù Jiédùshǐ (Military Governor of the Wūgǔ Tribe).
In the seventh year (1018),
the Díliè tribe rebelled.
He pacified them by conquest,
and was transferred to Wūgǔdílièbù Dūjiān (Military Superintendent of the Wūgǔdíliè Tribes).
He sent Díliè cavalry to obtain and present famous horses from the Northern Zǔbǔ.
He was commended and rewarded by imperial decree.
In the early years of Chóngxī,
he was transferred to Wūgǔdílièbù Dūxiángwěn (Chief Chancellor of the Wūgǔdíliè Tribes),
and achieved merit by campaigning against various foreign tribes.
Pǔdá was deeply experienced in border affairs,
and was capable of leading men cheerfully.
Whatever he captured,
he distributed entirely among his subordinates.
Because of this, he greatly won the hearts of the people.
He successively served as Xīnánmiàn Zhāotǎo Shǐ (Pacification Commissioner of the Southwest Circuit).
When the Dǎngxiàng rebels fled into Xī Xià (Western Xià),
Pǔdá campaigned against them,
was struck by a stray arrow,
and died in battle.
When the Emperor heard of this,
he greatly mourned him,
and his funeral grants were made particularly generous.
Yēlǜ Hóushěn,
courtesy name Tūníng,
was a descendant of Běiyuàn Yílíjǐn (Northern Administration Chancellor) Púgǔzhī.
His grandfather, Cházhǐ,
was Běiyuàn Dàwáng (Great King of the Northern Administration).
His father, Hūgǔ,
was Huángpíshì Xiángwěn (Chancellor of the Yellow Píshì).
Hóushěn first served as the Xīnán Xúnbīnguān (Southwest Border Inspector),
and was praised for his integrity.
He was successively promoted to Nánjīng Tǒngjūnshǐ (Commander-in-Chief of the Southern Capital),
and soon after became Běiyuàn Dàwáng.
In the eleventh year of Chóngxī (1042),
many people of the Dǎngxiàng tribe rebelled and fled into Xī Xià.
Hóushěn received the imperial order
to inspect the strategic river areas along the western border.
He built many forts and walls to stabilize the region,
and was transferred to Dōngjīng Liúshǒu (Prefect of the Eastern Capital).
In the thirteenth year (1044),
he campaigned with Zhīfǔ (Prefect) Xiāo Ōulǐsī against the Púlú Máochóng tribe and achieved merit,
and was granted the concurrent title Shìzhōng (Palace Attendant).
He retired from office,
and died.
Yélǜ Gǔyù,
courtesy name Mó Lǔjǐn,
was the fourth-generation descendant of Běiyuàn Línyá Tūlǚbù.
He possessed great physical strength
and was skilled in riding and archery.
During the Kāitài period,
he served as the Dūjiān of the Wūgǔ Díliè Tribe.
When the tribesmen rebelled,
he followed the Grand Councilor (Shūmìshǐ) Yélǜ Shìliáng to suppress them.
For this merit, he was ordered to pacify and govern the Northwest Region.
He instructed them in planting trees and raising livestock.
Within a few years,
the people became largely prosperous and substantial.
When bandits arose in Zhōngjīng,
Gǔyù was appointed Xúnluóshǐ (Commissioner of Patrols),
and he captured them all.
When the Emperor personally led the campaign against Bóhǎi,
he commanded the Huáng Píshì Army,
and achieved merit in defeating the enemy.
He was successively promoted to Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng (Imperial Censor-in-Chief).
Soon after, he was granted the position of Jiéduǐshǐ of the Kāiyuǎn Army
and transferred to govern Guīdé.
In the twenty-first year of Zhòngxī (1052 CE),
he was reassigned as Jiéduǐshǐ of the Tiānchéng Army.
He died in office
at the age of seventy,
and was posthumously granted the title Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì.
He had two sons: Yíxīn,
and Wūmò.
Yíxīn,
during the Zhòngxī period, followed Xiāo Huì to campaign against the Xī Xià.
When Huì suffered defeat,
Yíxīn's army alone remained intact.
He was appointed Běiyuàn Dàwáng (Grand Prince of the Northern Administration).
Wūmò,
in the third year of Dàkāng (1077 CE), became the Fù Bùshǔ (Vice Commissioner) of the Hàn Rén Xínggōng (Traveling Palace of the Han People).
When Yǐ Xīn falsely accused and harmed the Crown Prince,
Wūmò was implicated in the testimony.
The Emperor released him.
That autumn,
Yǐ Xīn again reported that Wūmò had privately discussed palace affairs with Xiāo Yángjiǔ,
and Wūmò was subsequently killed.
During the Qiántǒng period,
he was posthumously granted the title Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì.
Yélǜ Dú... (the character following Dú is unreadable/obscured),
courtesy name Hú Dújiǔ,
was the son of Grand Tutor (Tàishī) Gǔyù.
At the beginning of the Zhòngxī period,
he served as Zuǒ Hùwèi (Left Palace Guard).
Leading the Forbidden Troops, he achieved merit in the campaign against Xià,
and was granted the position of Shí'èr Hángjiū Sītú.
When the campaign against Xià was launched again,
Dú... requisitioned horses from the various prefectures west of the mountains.
Upon his return,
he was promoted to Zhuāilá Xiángwěn.
As the Southwest had not yet been pacified,
Dú... was ordered to serve concurrently as Tóngzhī Jīnsù Jūnshì (Co-Administrator of Military Affairs for Jīnsù).
When the Xià people invaded,
he defeated them,
and was promoted to Jiéduǐshǐ of the Nièlào Wèibù.
In the first year of Qīngníng (1055 CE),
