he was summoned to serve as Huáng Tàihòu Zuǒ Hùwèi Tàibǎo (Grand Guardian of the Empress Dowager's Left Guard).
In the fourth year,
he was reassigned as Jiéduǐshǐ of the Níngyuǎn Army.
When the Eastern Circuit (Dōnglù) suffered famine,
he submitted a memorial seeking relief for the area.
He successively held the post of Jiéduǐshǐ in three garrisons: Wǔguó, Wūgǔbù, and Liáoxīng Jūn,
and served as Xiángwěn of the Sìjié Army.
He died in the first year of Dàkāng (1075 CE),
and was posthumously granted the title Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì.
His son, Āsī,
has a separate biography.
Xiāo Hánjiā
was a member of the imperial maternal uncle's (Guójiù) clan.
His nature was dignified and simple,
cautious and sincere,
and his actions consistently followed ritual and law.
During the middle of the Qīngníng period,
he served as Hùwèi Tàibǎo (Grand Guardian of the Palace Guard).
In the second year of Dàkāng (1076 CE),
he was promoted to Zhī Běiyuàn Shūmì Fùshǐ (Co-Administrator of the Affairs of the Northern Chancellery).
In the third year,
he planned and surveyed the old trenches at Tiānchí on the southwest border,
established fortifications,
rectified the boundary markers,
and, after carving inscriptions on stone, returned.
He was appointed Dū Bùshǔ (Grand Commissioner) of the Hàn Rén Xínggōng.
During the imperial hunt that autumn,
he fell from his horse and died.
Xiāo Wūyě,
courtesy name Cǎoyǐn,
his ancestors belonged to the Xīngshènggōng Fēn (Branch of the Xīngshèng Palace),
and he was the grandson of the Surveillance Commissioner (Guānchásǐ) Tǎlǐzhí.
His nature was filial and fraternal,
he esteemed ritual and law,
and was highly praised by his local community.
In the middle of the Zhòngxī period,
he was appointed to the Palace Guard (Hùwèi).
Xīngzōng, seeing his diligence and sincerity,
promoted him to Hùwèi Tàibǎo.
In the ninth year of Qīngníng (1063 CE),
he assisted Yélǜ Rénxiān in suppressing the rebellion of Zhòngyuán.
For this merit, he was granted the additional title of Tuánliànshǐ (Militia Commissioner).
At that time, the Díliè Tribe was repeatedly invaded and harassed by neighboring tribes,
and the people were greatly distressed and impoverished.
Wūyě was ordered to serve as Jiéduǐshǐ of the Díliè Tribe.
He provided relief to the poor and needy
and reduced forced labor and taxes.
Within a few months,
the tribesmen became secure.
Soon after, because his mother was elderly,
he returned home to care for her.
When his mother died,
he grieved and wasted away profoundly.
When the mourning period ended,
he successively held the positions of Commissioner (Gōngshǐ) of the Xīngshèng and Yánqìng Palaces,
and then died.
Commentary states: The Wūgǔ Díliè
was a great tribe.
Duócì served as the Commander (Tǒngjūn)
and achieved merit in overcoming the enemy.
Pǔdá served as Xiángwěn
and used the people with satisfaction.
The Northwest (Xīběi)
was an important garrison.
Hóu Shěn patrolled the borders and was known for his integrity.
Gǔyù governed and pacified the region, resulting in wealthy people.
Dú... was stationed at Jīnsù, and the Xià people dared not raid eastward.
Alas!
The tribesmen joined the interior,
and the frontier areas were peaceful.
Although the court's arrangements were appropriate,
the efforts of the various generals certainly could not have been overlooked.
Biographies Chapter 23: Xiāo Huì (Císhìnú), Xiāo Yūlǔ (Duóluó), Xiāo Túyù, Yélǜ Duózhěn.
Xiāo Huì,
courtesy name Bórén,
childhood name Tuōgǔsī,
was the fifth-generation descendant of Āgǔzhī, the younger brother of Empress Chúnqīn.
Initially, due to his relation to the Empress (Zhōnggōng),
he served as Guójiù Xiángwěn (Grand Prince of the Imperial Maternal Uncles).
He followed his uncle Pái Yā in the campaign against Gāolì.
Upon reaching the northern ridge of Núgǔdá,
Gāolì troops relied on the dangerous terrain to resist.
Huì fought fiercely
and defeated them.
When attacking Kāijīng,
he became known for the strictness and order of his military discipline.
He was granted the position of Qìdān Xínggōng Dū Bùshǔ (Grand Commissioner of the Qìdān Traveling Palace).
In the second year of Kāitài (1013 CE),
he was reassigned as Tǒngjūnshǐ of Nánjīng.
Not long after,
he became Yòu Yílíbì (Right Yílíbì),
and was granted the additional title Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì.
The court deliberated that Liáodōng was a vital area,
and that only distinguished imperial relatives could govern and pacify it.
Therefore, Huì was ordered to serve as Zhī Dōngjīng Liúshǒu Shì (Co-Administrator of the Affairs of the Dōngjīng Retainer).
He was reassigned as Zhāotǎoshǐ of the Northwest Circuit (Xīběilù)
and enfeoffed as the Duke of Wèi (Wèiguógōng).
In the sixth year of Tàipíng (1026 CE),
he campaigned against the Āsàlán Tribe of the Huíhú (Uighurs).
He conscripted troops from all circuits,
but Zhǐlá, the chieftain of the Zǔbǔ (Tatar) people, arrived late.
Huì immediately executed him as a warning to others.
He advanced to Gānzhōu,
besieged it for three days,
but failed to take it and returned.
At that time, Zhǐlá's son gathered troops and launched a raid.
Wūbāmì, a Zǔbǔ chieftain, reported this,
but Huì did not believe him.
Soon after, the Western Zǔbǔ rebelled
and attacked the Sānkè Army.
Dūjiān Nièlǔgǔ, Jiéduǐshǐ Xiélǐ of the Tūjǔ Tribe, and Ābùlǚ, leading three thousand troops, came to the rescue.
They encountered the enemy southwest of Kèdūn Chéng.
Xiélǐ and Ābùlǚ died in battle,
and the soldiers scattered and fled.
Huì hurriedly arranged his formation,
but the enemy launched a surprise attack on his camp.
The multitude requested to seize the moment and launch a fierce counterattack,
but Huì, judging that his army was exhausted and weakened,
believed it was not yet usable,
and refused to listen.
Wūbā requested to raid the enemy camp by night,
but Huì again did not permit it.
When the Zǔbǔ forces retreated,
Huì then set up an ambush and attacked them.
As soon as the vanguards engaged,
the enemy was defeated and fled.
Huì served as Zhāotǎo (Pacification Commissioner) for many years,
frequently suffering invasion and plunder,
and his troops and horses were exhausted.
In the seventh year (1027 CE),
he was demoted to Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ (Grand Commissioner-in-Chief) of the Cavalry and Infantry of the Nánjīng Shìwèi Qīnjūn (Imperial Guard),
and soon after was transferred to Nánjīng Tǒngjūnshǐ.
Xīngzōng (興宗) ascended the throne.
He was appointed Zī Zhī Xīngzhōng Fǔ (知興中府).
He successively held the posts of Jiédùshǐ (節度使) of the Shùnyì Jūn (順義軍), Tōnjing Líushǒu (東京留守), and Xīnánmiàn Zhāotǎoshǐ (西南面招討使).
He was granted the titles Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (開府儀同三司) and Jǐanjiào Tàishī (檢校太師),
and additionally served as Shìzhōng (侍中).
He was enfeoffed as the King of Zhèng (鄭王).
He was bestowed the title Tūichéng Xiémóu Jíejí Gōngchén (推誠協謀竭節功臣).
In the sixth year of Chóngxī (重熙),
he was again made Kìdān Xínggōng Dū Bùshǔ (契丹行宮都部署).
He was promoted to Shǒu Tàishī (守太師).
His title was transferred, making him the King of Zhào (趙王).
He was appointed Nányuàn Shūmìshǐ (南院樞密使).
His royal title was changed again, making him the King of Qí (齊王).
At this time, the Emperor desired to unify all under Heaven,
and planned to seize the Three Passes.
He gathered his officials to deliberate.
Hùi (惠) said:
“Your sagely wisdom comprehends [the situation regarding] the strength and weakness of the two states.
The Sòng (宋) people have been campaigning in the west for years;
their troops are weary and their people exhausted.
If Your Majesty personally leads the Six Armies to confront them,
victory is certain.”
Xiāo Xiàomù (蕭孝穆) said:
“Our former court maintained peaceful relations with Sòng.
If we attack them without cause,
the fault lies with us.
Moreover, victory or defeat cannot be predicted beforehand.
I implore Your Majesty to consider this carefully.”
The Emperor followed Hùi’s advice,
and immediately sent an envoy to demand ten Sòng cities,
assembling all armies in Yān (燕).
Hùi and the Imperial Younger Brother led the army to pressure the Sòng border.
The Sòng people, fearing the loss of the ten cities,
increased the annual tribute and requested peace.
Hùi, relying on the merit of having initiated the matter,
was advanced to become the King of Hán (韓王).
In the twelfth year,
he concurrently served as Běifǔ Zǎixiàng (北府宰相),
and Tóngzhī Yuánshùai Fǔshì (同知元帥府事).
He was later appointed Běi Shūmìshǐ (北樞密使).
In the thirteenth year,
Lǐ Yuánhào (李元昊) of the Xià (夏) state lured the various Dǎngxiàng (党項) tribes south of the mountains [into revolt].
The Emperor personally led a campaign.
Yuánhào, fearing this,
requested surrender.
Hùi said:
“Yuánhào forgot the grace extended through generations
and conceived a treacherous plot.
Although the Imperial Carriage personally arrived,
he has not completely returned what he plundered.
Heaven is inducing his true intentions
by making him come to welcome [the Emperor].
If we fail to capitalize on what Heaven grants,
how can we remedy the future regret?”
The Emperor followed him.
The next morning,
the army advanced.
The Xià people arranged chevaux de frise west of the river,
standing shielded behind them.
Hùi attacked and defeated them.
Yuánhào fled.
Hùi ordered the vanguard and the right flank to intercept him.
Over a thousand Xià soldiers broke through the encirclement and fled.
Our army struck them in reverse.
A great wind suddenly arose,
flying sand blinding their eyes.
The army fell into disorder,
and the Xià people seized the opportunity.
Innumerable soldiers were trampled and killed.
An imperial edict ordered the army to return.
In the seventeenth year,
he married the Emperor's elder sister, the Grand Princess of Qínjìn Guó (秦晉國長公主),
and was appointed Fùmǎ Dūwèi (駙馬都尉).
The following year,
the Emperor again campaigned against the Xià state.
Hùi advanced from Hénán (河南);
the warships and grain vessels stretched continuously for several hundred *lǐ*.
Upon entering enemy territory,
his scouts did not venture far.
Armor was loaded onto carriages,
and the soldiers were not allowed to ride horses.
All the generals requested preparations be made for the unforeseen,
but Hùi said:
“Liàngzuò (諒祚) is certain to personally welcome the Imperial Carriage;
how would he have time to attack us?
Making preparations without cause
will only wear ourselves out.”
A few days later,
our army had not yet pitched camp.
The scout reported that the Xià army had arrived.
Hùi was just about to question him for the crime of false reporting
when Liàngzuò’s army descended from the slope.
Hùi and his immediate subordinates fled without putting on their armor.
Pursuers shot at Hùi,
and he narrowly escaped.
The number of soldiers killed and wounded was especially great.
After the army returned,
because Hùi’s son Císhìnú (慈氏奴) had died in the battle,
an edict pardoned his offense.
In the nineteenth year,
he requested retirement due to old age.
An edict permitted him to enter the court in a sedan chair
and ascend the hall with the aid of a walking stick.
After he submitted his resignation documents a second time,
it was finally granted,
and he was enfeoffed as the King of Wèiguó (魏國王).
An edict ordered him to attend the imperial residence in winter and summer,
to participate in settling difficult deliberations.
After he returned home,
the dispatch of medicinal soup and other gifts never ceased.
On every birthday,
the Emperor always bestowed poems to show him honor and favor.
He passed away in the second year of Qīngníng (清寧),
at the age of seventy-four.
His dying instruction to his family was for a frugal burial.
Upon hearing the news of his death,
the court was suspended for three days.
Hùi was generous and tolerant by nature,
and lived a simple and frugal life.
Xīngzōng had once instructed Hùi to take any precious objects he desired,
but Hùi said:
“I hold an important position due to being related to the imperial family.
My salary is sufficient to maintain integrity,
and with over a thousand servants,
I lack nothing.
If Your Majesty still gives gifts to me,
how will you treat those who are poorer than I?”
The Emperor considered this true.
Therefore, although he was often defeated
when acting as a general,
he was not punished for it.
His younger brother was Xūliè (虛列),
Jiédùshǐ of the Wǔdìng Jūn (武定軍).
He had two sons: Císhìnú (慈氏奴)
and Wùgǔnì (兀古匿).
Wùgǔnì eventually became Běifǔ Zǎixiàng.
Císhìnú’s
courtesy name was Níngyǐn (寧隱).
In the beginning of Tàipíng (太平),
he was appointed Zhīhòu Lángjūn (祗候郎君) because of his relation to the imperial family.
The Emperor cherished his diligence and prudence,
promoting him to Zhásà Chùe (閘撒狘)
and granting him the title of Yòu Jiānménwèi Shàng Jiāngjūn (右監門衞上將軍).
When there was an alert on the western border,
he was appointed Xīběilù Zhāotǎo Dūjiān (西北路招討都監),
and concurrently led the Jiédùshǐ of the Bǎodà Jūn (保大軍).
His administration balanced benevolence and severity,
and the various tribes were pleased and submitted to him.
He returned to court to serve as Diànqián Fù Diǎnjiǎn (殿前副點檢),
and successively held the post of Xiángwěn (詳穩) of the Wūgǔ Díliè Bù (烏古敵烈部).
When campaigning against Lǐ Liàngzuò,
he served as Tǒngjūn Dūjiān (統軍都監).
He and Xīběilù Zhāotǎoshǐ (西北路招討使) Dí Lǔgǔ (敵魯古) led the various armies of the Fān (蕃) tribes via the northern route toward Liángzhōu (涼州),
capturing Liàngzuò’s relatives.
The Xià people blocked the strategic passes to resist.
Císhìnú was struck by a stray arrow and died,
at the age of fifty-one.
He was posthumously granted the title Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì (中書門下平章事).
Xiāo Yūrǔ (蕭迂魯),
whose courtesy name was Hútūjǐn (胡突堇),
was a native of the Wǔyuàn Bù (五院部).
His father, Yuēzhì (約質),
successively held official posts as Jiédùshǐ.
During the Chóngxī era, Yūrǔ served as Pái Yìn Lángjūn (牌印郎君).
In the ninth year of Qīngníng,
after the state had pacified the rebellion of Chóngyuán (重元),
his partisans, such as Guō Jiǔ (郭九), fled.
An edict ordered Yūrǔ to pursue and capture them.
He captured them,
and was promoted to Hùwèi Tàibǎo (護衞太保).
In the first year of Xiányǒng (咸雍),
he was sent as an envoy to Sòng to discuss border affairs.
His mission satisfied the Emperor,
and he was appointed Zī Diànqián Fù Diǎnjiǎn Shì (知殿前副點檢事).
In the fifth year,
when the Zǔbù (阻卜) rebelled,
he served as Xíngjūn Dūjiān (行軍都監).
He defeated them,
capturing a great number of prisoners.
When the army first set out,
they were only supplied with five months of provisions.
When the deadline passed and provisions ran out,
soldiers often deserted and returned home.
Yūrǔ was held accountable for miscalculation,
dismissed from office,
and degraded to serve in the Xīběi Bù (西北部) garrison.
Before he departed,
it happened that troops in the Northern Department (Běibù, 北部) rose in rebellion.
Yūrǔ led the Wūgǔ Díliè troops and defeated them.
In every battle, he personally charged ahead,
and consequently, his previous offense was pardoned,
and he was ordered to take overall charge of the Wūgǔ Díliè Bù.
In the ninth year,
the Díliè rebelled.
The Military Commissioner, Yēlǜ Dúdié, due to having few troops, did not fight,
camping at Lúqú Hé.
The Díliè allied with border people and plundered the inhabitants.
Yūlǔ led four hundred elite cavalry and fought vigorously,
defeating them,
and seizing all their baggage train.
Next, he heard that the chieftain Héshù, leading over three thousand cavalry, was raiding nearby tribes.
He unleashed his troops to pursue them closely,
fighting continuously for two days,
beheading several thousand people,
and retrieving all the captured people and livestock before returning.
At that time, a Díliè contingent of over five hundred cavalry was looting and capturing falconers (Yīnghù).
He met and attacked them, driving them away.
The captives and those beheaded were numerous.
Thereafter, the power of the Díliè was diminished.
At this time,
the Díliè were causing border trouble,
and the Zhǔbǔ subsequently plundered as well.
Because of this, the border people were exhausted and impoverished.
The court considered the area remote
and could not constantly reinforce it with relief troops.
That the borders remained secure
was entirely due to Yūlǔ's efforts.
The Emperor commended his accomplishments
and appointed him Xiángwěn of the Left Píshì Division.
When the Sòng requested the land of Tiānchí,
an edict ordered Yūlǔ to concurrently command the troops of both Píshì Divisions, garrisoning Tàiláo Gǔshān to defend against them.
Early in the Dàkāng era,
the Zhǔbǔ rebelled.
He was transferred to be the Commissioner of Pacification of the Northwest Circuit.
He followed the Supreme Commander, Yēlǜ Zhàosān, on the punitive expedition and achieved merit,
and was subsequently changed to be the Nánjīng Commander-in-Chief Commissioner and Xiángwěn of the Yellow Píshì Division.
Not long after,
he was transferred to be the Northeast Circuit Commander-in-Chief Commissioner,
and died.
His younger brother was Duóluówò.
Duóluówò,
courtesy name Sābǎn.
As a child, he was exceptionally intelligent.
At the age of three, he lost his mother and cried with utmost grief;
those who saw him were moved to sorrow.
When he grew up,
he was big, imposing, and profound and resolute.
He loved learning,
was skilled at writing essays,
and possessed talent and capability.
He began his official career at the age of thirty
and was highly esteemed by the court and the populace.
He served as the Administrator of Edicts (Zhī Shèngzhǐ Shì) in the Northern Chancellery (Běi Yuàn).
In the second year of Dàkāng,
Yǐxīn re-entered the Privy Council.
Duóluówò had always been friendly with Xiāo Yánshòu.
He was falsely accused of a crime
and banished to garrison duty in the Northwest Department.
Due to his involvement in the matter of the Crown Prince,
a special clemency commuted his death sentence,
but he was still imprisoned for life.
He spent over ten years in banishment.
When the Crown Prince affair was somewhat rectified,
he was finally allowed to return to his hometown
and lived in seclusion, declining official duties.
One day, standing by a stream,
he heard the call of a pheasant.
He repeatedly recited Confucius's
"What a time!"
utterance,
and composed three stanzas of ancient poetry to express his ambition/will.
The famous scholars of the time praised his noble sentiment and refined demeanor,
saying they were no less than those of the ancients.
He died in the sixth year of Shòulóng,
at the age of sixty-one.
Early in the Qiántǒng era,
he was posthumously granted the title of Military Commissioner of the Zhāngyì Army.
Xiāo Túyù,
courtesy name Wūyǎn,
was the son of the Chancellor of the Northern Chancellery (Běi Fǔ Zǎixiàng), Hǎilí.
Early in the Tǒnghé era,
the Empress Dowager assumed regency (Chēng Zhì).
He entered the palace to serve as a relative by marriage.
He was soon appointed Commissioner of the Wūgǔ Department.
He achieved merit suppressing the Sùmǔlǚ and other departments,
and was promoted to Military Commissioner of the Wūgǔ Department.
In the nineteenth year,
he was put in overall command of the military affairs of the Northwest Circuit.
Later, using the troops of his circuit, he attacked Gānzhōu
and received the surrender of its chieftain, Yǎlǎn.
After some time, Yǎlǎn rebelled again.
He was ordered to suppress him,
capturing Sùzhōu,
and completely relocating its inhabitants to the old city at Tǔwěikǒu.
When the army returned,
an edict ordered him to marry Princess Jīnxiāng,
appointing him Commandant-Escort (Fùmǎ Dūwèi),
and granting him the additional title Tóng Zhèngshì Lìng Ménxià Píngzhāngshì.
He submitted a memorial, saying:
"The Zhǔbǔ are now submissive and assimilated.
They should be divided into various departments
and governed by Military Commissioners (Jiédùshǐ)."
The Emperor followed his advice.
Thereafter,
the Military Commissioners were often incompetent,
and the tribal people resented them and contemplated rebellion.
In the eleventh month of the first year of Kāitài,
the Shíliè Grand Tutor Ālǐdǐ killed his Military Commissioner
and fled west to Wōlǔyán Chéng,
which was the place anciently called the Shànyú City of Lóngtíng.
Soon after,
the Zhǔbǔ rebelled again,
surrounding Túyù at Kědūn Chéng.
Their power greatly increased.
Túyù ordered all his armies to shoot together, repelling them,
and then garrisoned Wōlǔyán Chéng.
The following year,
the Chief Administrator of the Northern Chancellery (Běi Yuàn Shūmìshǐ), Yēlǜ Huàgē, led troops to provide relief.
Túyù sent envoys to entice the various tribes, and they all surrendered.
The Emperor considered that although Túyù had initially miscalculated,
he later won the hearts of the people.
He released him from punishment
and allowed him to continue leading the various departments.
Túyù requested more troops.
An edict rebuked him, saying:
"Since the rebels are already submissive,
why is there need for more troops?
Furthermore, in the previous campaign,
the dead and wounded were numerous.
If we follow your plan,
when will border matters ever cease?"
Thereupon, the matter was dropped.
Coincidentally, the Princess was implicated in killing a household maid
and was demoted in rank to Commandery Princess (Jùnzhǔ).
Túyù was dismissed from his post as Acting Chancellor.
Soon after, he was recalled to serve as Xiángwěn of the Wūgǔ Díliè Department.
He retired due to old age,
returned home, and died.
His son, Shuānggǔ,
was the Commander-in-Chief of Nánjīng.
His grandson, Éduówò,
married Princess Gǔyù, the daughter of the Prince of Sānhán Commandery, Hélǔ.
He ultimately served as the Commander-in-Chief of the Wūgǔ Díliè Department
and was renowned in the world for being skilled in combat.
Yēlǜ Duózhěn,
courtesy name Díniǎn,
was a man of the Jìqìng Palace.
He served during the Tǒnghé period.
His nature was frank and simple,
and he did not pay attention to minor details.
People initially criticized him for this failing.
Later, during the invasion of the Sòng,
he was given command of the weaker detachments to follow the main force.
When battle was joined,
he took crimson silk and covered his armor and helmet to make himself stand out,
galloping and charging in and out of the enemy formation,
slaying a great number of opponents in hand-to-hand combat.
The Empress Dowager saw him from a distance and was pleased.
She summoned him and said:
"Since you exert yourself thus,
what difficulty can prevent success!"
She richly rewarded him.
Consequently, many military affairs were entrusted to him.
Soon after, he was appointed Xiángwěn of the Northeast.
In the second year of Kāitài,
he advanced to suppress the Zhǔbǔ
and defeated them.
During the Chóngxī era,
he successively held the posts of Commander-in-Chief of the Northeast Circuit and Military Commissioner of the Tiāndé Army.
In the seventeenth year,
when constructing fortifications on the western border,
Duózhěn was ordered to survey the land and construct warships.
Consequently, he completed one hundred and thirty tower ships (Lóuchuán).
Troops were placed on the upper decks
and horses were housed below.
The design and structure were sturdy and strong,
meeting the imperial expectation.
When the campaign against the West (Xī Zhēng) began,
an edict commanded Duózhěn to lead troops and advance via a separate route,
meeting at the riverside.
The enemy troops arrayed themselves across the river.
The Emperor personally commanded the warships to cross the river and attack them,
achieving a great victory before returning.
The Emperor personally bestowed a goblet of wine upon him.
He then asked what Duózhěn desired.
Duózhěn replied:
"Your servant is fortunate to receive your sacred grace
and to be able to exert his humble strength.
Even ten thousand deaths would not suffice to repay the state;
what more could I ask for?"
The Emperor valued him even more
and personally wrote on Duózhěn's robes:
"Diligent for the country and loyal to the ruler,
unmatched in the entire world."
He died in office
at the age of seventy.
His son, Dīliè,
successively served as Surveillance Commissioner (Guānchá) and Military Commissioner (Jiédùshǐ).
A commentary states: Initially,
when the Liáo planned to recover the Sānguān,
Xiāo Huì advocated for attacking Sòng,
and the Sòng people increased their tribute and sought peace.
Satisfied with this single victory,
they moved their troops to the Xīxià,
where their courage and wisdom both failed,
and defeat and collapse followed.
Was this not because they coveted a small gain,
and were blind to the greater long-term plan?
Moreover, what they gained did not compensate for what they lost,
so where was the profit indeed?
At the same time, the generals who pacified the borders,
such as Yū Lǔ, who was loyal, diligent, and humble;
Duólǔwò, who possessed noble sentiments and elegant demeanor;
and Duózěn, who, though incorruptible, did not surpass Xiāo Huì,
but was without the fault of seeking glory or instigating conflict –
they too were nearly gentlemen.
Collated Notes
Biographies, Chapter 24: Yēlǜ Huàgē, Yēlǜ Wòlà, Yēlǜ Sùsā, Xiāo Ālǔdài, Yēlǜ Nàyě, Yēlǜ Hélǔsǎogǔ, Yēlǜ Shìliáng
Yēlǜ Huàgē,
courtesy name Hóngyǐn,
was a descendant of Mèngfù, King of Chǔ.
He was skilled in horsemanship and archery.
In the early years of Qiánhēng,
he became the Línyá of the Northern Court.
In the 4th year of Tǒnghé,
during the invasion of Sòng from the south,
Huàgē captured a spy,
learning that the enemy was attacking by sea.
He immediately occupied the strategic location of Píngzhōu first.
After the matter was settled,
he was appointed Liúshǒu of Shàngjīng,
then promoted to Dàwáng of the Northern Court.
In the 16th year,
he again invaded Sòng,
serving as vanguard,
and defeated the enemy at Suìchéng.
For this achievement, he was promoted to Dàwáng of the Southern Court,
and soon after, changed to Shūmìshǐ of the Northern Court.
In the 1st year of Kāitài,
he attacked the Zǔbǔ,
who abandoned their baggage train and fled,
resulting in many captives.
The Emperor praised him,
and enfeoffed him as Bīnwáng.
Later, a border official reported
that since Huàgē had returned to the capital,
provisions were scarce and horses weak,
making defense untenable.
The Emperor again dispatched Huàgē to manage the western border.
Huàgē and the border generals advanced deep into enemy territory.
Hearing that the Fānbù tribes were rebellious and residing at Yìzhǐshuǐ,
Huàgē slowly advanced his troops.
The enemy scattered at the sight of them,
and he captured sheep, horses, and baggage.
On the way through Báliè,
they encountered the Āsàlán Uighurs
and plundered them.
The Dūjiān, Niǎolǐ, arrived soon after,
and said to Huàgē:
"You have erred!
This tribe is truly loyal."
Huàgē returned all the captives.
From this, the various Fān tribes became disaffected.
The Emperor ordered an investigation,
and stripped him of his princely rank.
He was made Shìzhōng and remotely held the title of Dàtóng Jūnjié Dùshǐ,
and then died.
Yēlǜ Wòlà,
courtesy name Sīníng,
was a native of the Xīdiélà tribe.
He was swift, agile, powerful,
and skilled in horsemanship and archery.
In the early years of Bǎoníng,
he was appointed a personal guard.
When the imperial carriage was hunting at Jiéshān,
a wild boar lay hidden in the thicket.
The Emperor shot and hit it,
and the boar charged out.
The charioteer, Tuōmǎn, dropped the reins and fled.
Hègǔ protected the Emperor,
and Wòlà shot the boar again, killing it.
The Emperor greatly praised him.
Later, when hunting at Chìshān,
a charging deer with antlers darted forward.
The path was narrow, leaving no room to avoid it,
and it was about to run into the imperial retinue.
Wòlà intercepted it with his body,
and the deer struck him and fell.
The Emperor said to him:
"Because of hunting,
I twice faced danger,
and thanks to you, I was spared.
Only now do I see your true heart."
He was promoted to Hùwèi Tàibǎo.
He followed the Shūmìshǐ Yēlǜ Xiézhěn and defeated the Sòng general Yáng Jìyè's army in Shānxī.
In the autumn of the 13th year of Tǒnghé,
he was appointed Xíngjūn Dūjiān,
and followed the Dūbùshǔ, Xīwáng Héshuònú, to attack Wùrě Wūzhāodù.
After several months, they reached its city.
Wūzhāodù requested to surrender.
Héshuònú coveted the spoils of war
and ordered a fierce assault from all sides.
Wūzhāodù led his troops in a desperate defense,
repelling attacks from all directions.
They constructed temporary battle platforms on the ramparts,
luring our army to climb the parapets.
Suddenly, they removed the supporting pillars,
and all who had climbed fell.
Héshuònú knew he could not take the city
and wished to retreat.
Xiāo Dé said that if the campaign had lasted long without success,
how could they justify it?
If they advanced deep and plundered extensively,
it would still be better than returning empty-handed.
Wòlà said:
"Going deep
might result in gains that do not offset the losses."
Dé did not listen,
and plundered the southeastern region,
returning along the northern border of Gāolí.
The journey was long, provisions ran out,
and many people and horses died.
An imperial edict stripped all generals of their offices,
but Wòlà was spared due to his earlier advice.
Soon after, he was granted the title Tóng Zhèngshì Ménxià Píngzhāngshì
and made Dōngjīng Liúshǒu.
He died during the Kāitài era.
Yēlǜ Sùsā,
courtesy name Āmǐn,
was loyal, straightforward, resolute,
and skilled in military affairs.
In the early years of Yìnglì,
he served as an attendant,
and was successively promoted to Jiédùshǐ of the Tūlǚbù tribe.
He successively served as Dūzǒngguǎn of the five prefectures: Bà, Jì, Xiáng, Shùn, and Shèng,
and soon after became Tàishī of the Dūnmù Palace.
In the 3rd year of Bǎoníng,
he was made Jiǔbù Dūxiángwěn.
In the 4th year,
he campaigned against the Dǎngxiàng,
achieving many military successes.
The Empress Dowager personally issued an edict to commend him.
In the early years of Tǒnghé,
the Empress Dowager assumed regency.
The western border was newly pacified,
and Sùsā diligently worked to settle the various Fān tribes.
He always reported benefits and harms to the Empress Dowager,
who trusted him even more.
Whenever he commanded troops,
he shared hardships with his soldiers,
and distributed all spoils equally among his generals and officers.
He rewarded loyalty and punished rebellion,
and his prestige and credibility greatly increased.
He died after twenty years on the border.
Xiāo Ālǔdài,
courtesy name Yǐxīnyǐn,
was a native of the Wūkuí tribe.
His father, Nǚgǔ,
served as Jiūxiángwěn.
Ālǔdài learned horsemanship and archery when young,
and understood military strategy.
He began his career during the Qīngníng era,
and was successively promoted to Sītú of his own tribe,
then changed to Tǒngjūn Dūjiān of Wūgǔdíliè.
In the 7th year of Dà'ān,
he was promoted to Shānběi Fùbùshǔ.
In the 9th year,
when the Dálǐdé and Bászìmǔ tribes invaded,
he led troops to repel them.
The Dálǐdé again plundered cattle and sheep and departed.
Ālǔdài led troops in pursuit and caught up,
recovering all that had been plundered,
and beheading several chieftains.
That winter,
the Dálǐdé and others, with over three hundred men, harassed the border.
He again fought and repelled them,
beheading over two hundred.
He was granted the title Jīnwǔwèi Shàngjiāngjūn
and enfeoffed as Lánlíng Xiàngōng.
In the 1st year of Shòulóng,
for his merits,
he was granted the title Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì,
promoted to Jùngōng,
and changed to Xīběilù Zhāotǎoshǐ.
In the 3rd year of Qiántǒng,
he was dismissed from office for keeping Sòng captives who should have been repatriated as slaves.
Later, he was summoned,
but retired due to old age and illness,
and then died.
Yēlǜ Nàyě,
courtesy name Yísīliǎn,
was a descendant of Yílíjǐn Púgǔzhī.
His father Wò
once served as Běikè,
and died in battle while following the campaign against Xià.
His youngest paternal uncle, Zhào Sān,
initially served as a Sùzhíguān (Official of the Night Watch),
gradually rising through promotion to Běimiàn Línyá.
In Xiányōng fourth year (1068),
he was appointed Běiyuàn Dàwáng (Great King of the Northern Chancery),
then changed to Xīnánmiàn Zhāotǎoshǐ (Commander of Pacification for the Southwest Circuit).
During the Dàkāng era,
various tribes in the Northwest harassed the border,
and deliberation was held to launch a punitive expedition.
The Emperor believed that only Zhào Sān could manage it,
so he was appointed Xīběilù Zhāotǎoshǐ (Commander of Pacification for the Northwest Circuit),
concurrently serving as Xíngjūn Dūtǒng (Supreme Commander of the Expeditionary Forces).
He pacified them,
and for his merit, he was reinstated as Běiyuàn Dàwáng.
Nàyě was honest, generous, talented, and quick-witted.
Because his father Wò had died serving the state,
at nine years old, the Emperor conferred upon him the title Zhūwèi Xiǎojiàngjūn (Minor General of the Various Guards),
and made him Tílí Sītú (Supervisor of the Tílí clan).
Soon after, he was summoned to be a Sùzhíguān.
In Dàkāng third year (1077),
he became Yáoliǎn Kè.
In Dà'ān ninth year (1093),
he became Dǎotālíng Jiédùshǐ (Military Governor of Dǎotālíng).
In the winter of the following year,
because Mógǔsī, the chieftain of the Northern Zǔbǔ, rebelled,
he led two thousand elite cavalry with Zhāotǎo Dūjiān (Vice Commander of Pacification) Yēlǜ Húlǚ to suppress them,
and defeated them.
Nàyě recommended Húlǚ to be Hànrén Xínggōng Fùbùshǔ (Vice Commissioner of the Han People's Traveling Palace).
In Shòulóng first year (1095),
he again achieved merit by suppressing Dálǐdé, Básīmǔ, and others.
He was presented with an edict praising his accomplishments,
and transferred to be Wūgǔ Díliè Bù Tǒngjūnshǐ (Commander of the Wūgǔ Díliè Department).
The border region became peaceful as a result.
The people of the department pleaded for him to remain,
and an imperial edict permitted his reappointment.
In Qiántǒng sixth year (1106),
he was appointed Zhōngjīng Liúshǒu (Resident Grandee of the Central Capital),
then changed to Běiyuàn Dàwáng,
and passed away.
Nàyě was honest and upright in character,
and skilled in governing the people.
Whenever there were disputes or lawsuits,
he personally investigated the right and wrong,
and did not rely on strict intimidation.
He often said:
"The purpose of governing people
is fundamentally to distinguish right from wrong.
Why rely on coercion and threats merely to establish a reputation?"
Therefore, wherever he served, he was known for his benevolent governance.
Yēlǜ Hélǔsǎogǔ,
courtesy name Wūgǔlín,
was a descendant of the Mèngfǔ branch.
At the end of the Zhòngxī era,
he was appointed Zhīhòu Lángjūn (Attendant Gentleman).
In the beginning of the Qīngníng era,
he was promoted to Ānzhōu Tuánliànshǐ (Commander of Militia for Ān Prefecture).
During the Dàkāng era,
he successively held the posts of Huáidéjūn Jiédùshǐ (Military Governor of Huáidé Commandery) and Xī Liùbù Tūlǐ Tàiwèi (Grand Marshal Tūlǐ of the Six Xī Departments).
He was ordered by edict to plan border affairs in the Northeast with the Shūmìguān (Officials of the Privy Council),
and was transferred to Zuǒhùwèi Tàibǎo (Grand Guardian of the Left Guard).
When attending the Emperor,
his speech was often straightforward and casual,
but it was observed that he harbored no malice,
and thus the Emperor treated him with exceptional leniency.
In Dà'ān eighth year (1092),
he was made acting Xīběilù Zhāotǎoshǐ.
At that time, the border tribes, led by Yēdǔguā, came to invade.
Hélǔsǎogǔ persuaded Mógǔsī, the chieftain of the Northern Zǔbǔ, to attack them,
capturing many prisoners.
For this merit, he was promoted to Zuǒpúyè (Left Grandee Secretary).
While suppressing Yēdǔguā and others again,
he mistakenly attacked Mógǔsī.
The Northern Zǔbǔ consequently rebelled against the mandate.
He dispatched Dūjiān Zhāng Jiǔ to suppress them,
but he was unsuccessful.
The forces of the Èrshìwěi (Two Shìwěi), Liùyuànbù (Six Departments), Tèmǎn Qúnmù (Tèmǎn Herds), and Gōngfèn (Imperial Divisions) were all defeated by the enemy.
Hélǔsǎogǔ failed to report the truth,
and for this, he was stripped of his office
and punished with heavy caning.
During the Shòulóng era,
he was successively promoted to Tìyǐn,
concurrently serving as Shìzhōng (Chamberlain),
and was granted the title Bǎojié Gōngchén (Meritorious Official for Maintaining Integrity).
When Dàozōng died,
he managed the affairs of the imperial mausoleum alongside Zǎixiàng (Chancellor) Yēlǜ Yǎn.
During the Qiántǒng era,
he retired from office,
and died.
Yēlǜ Shìliáng,
courtesy name Wò,
was a native of the Liùyuànbù (Six Departments).
He was talented, quick-witted, and articulate,
and deeply familiar with the precedents and genealogy of the imperial court.
He submitted a memorial disputing legitimate versus secondary lineage status with his cousin Díliè,
through which the Emperor first recognized him.
At that time, Běiyuàn Shūmìshǐ (Northern Chancery Commissioner) Hán Déràng was ill.
The Emperor asked:
"Who can replace you, Lord?"
Déràng replied:
"Shìliáng can."
Běiyuàn Dàwáng Yēlǜ Shìlǔ again asked about candidates for the Northern Chancery,
and Déràng replied:
"None surpass Shìliáng."
At the end of the Tǒnghé era,
he became Běiyuàn Dàwáng.
In the beginning of the Kāitài era (1012),
during the great imperial enfeoffment ceremony,
he was granted the additional titles Jiǎnxiào Tàiwèi (Acting Grand Commandant) and Tóng Zhèngshì Ménxià Píngzhāngshì (Joint Manager of Affairs with the Secretariat-Chancellery).
At that time, border tribes refused to submit to the mandate.
An edict ordered Běiyuàn Shūmìshǐ Yēlǜ Huàgē to lead troops,
with Shìliáng serving as Dūjiān,
to go and defend against them.
The following year,
Huàgē returned,
intending to disband the army.
Shìliáng submitted a memorial stating:
"Huàgē assumes there is no trouble and returns,
without considering that the troops are weary and supplies are short.
If the enemy has already departed,
how can we hold the position for long?
If we reinforce the troops,
we can overcome them."
The Emperor immediately ordered Huàgē to reinforce the troops
and pursue the enemy with Shìliáng.
Upon reaching the Ānzhēnhé River,
they achieved a great victory and returned.
From this point,
the border region became peaceful.
For his merits, he was enfeoffed as Wáng Qí (Prince of Qí),
and appointed Běiyuàn Shūmìshǐ.
In the third year,
he was ordered to select horses and camels from the Wūgǔ Department.
Coincidentally, Yīlà of the Díliè Department killed their chieftain Shāowǎ and rebelled.
Neighboring departments all responded,
attacking and seizing the city of Jùmǔgǔchéng.
Shìliáng led troops to the border,
sent envoys to persuade them,
and several departments surrendered,
each returning to their former territory.
In the fourth year,
during the campaign against Gāolì (Koryŏ),
he served as Fùbùshǔ (Vice Commissioner).
Dūtǒng Liú Shènxíng delayed and missed the deadline,
and was arrested and returned to the capital.
Shìliáng advanced the troops alone.
The following year,
he reached the Běi Dūhùfǔ (Northern Protectorate),
and defeated the pursuing troops at Guōzhōu.
He died of a sudden illness.
Commentary states: The great nurture the small through Virtue,
and control them through Power.
If Virtue is insufficient to nurture,
and Power is insufficient to control,
then gaining the submission of others is difficult.
Huàgē valued spoils and captives,
and thus the various foreign tribes did not attach themselves to him.
Hélǔsǎogǔ mistakenly attacked Mógǔsī,
leading to the Zǔbǔ rebelling against the mandate.
These men all rejoiced in temporary accomplishments,
but failed to plan against future troubles.
What more needs to be said about them?
If Wòlà warned against deep penetration,
and Sùsà sought only peaceful settlement,
were they not the truly outstanding figures?
Biographies 25: Yēlǜ Hónggǔ, Yēlǜ Mǎliù, Xiāo Dīliè, Yēlǜ Shìlù, Yēlǜ Chénjiānú, Yēlǜ Tèmó, Yēlǜ Xiāntóng, Xiāo Sùsà, Yēlǜ Dàbēinú.
Yēlǜ Hónggǔ,
courtesy name Húdǔjǐn,
was the younger brother of Shūmìshǐ Huàgē.
During the Tǒnghé era,
he was successively promoted to Shùnyìjūn Jiédùshǐ (Military Governor of Shùnyì Commandery),
and entered the court as Běimiàn Línyá.
In Tàipíng first year (1021),
he was granted the additional title Tóng Zhèngshì Ménxià Píngzhāngshì (Joint Manager of Affairs with the Secretariat-Chancellery),
and went out to serve as Zhāngguójūn Jiédùshǐ (Military Governor of Zhāngguó Commandery),
concurrently serving as Shānběidào Bīngmǎ Dū Bùshǔ (Supreme Commander of Military Affairs for the Northern Mountain Circuit).
He was transferred to Wǔdìngjūn Jiédùshǐ.
In the sixth year,
he was appointed Tìyǐn.
He achieved merit in suppressing the Zǔbǔ.
Shèngzōng once drew blood from his arm and swore an oath of friendship with Hónggǔ,
treating him with exceptional deference.
He was appointed Nánfǔ Zǎixiàng (Chancellor of the Southern Chancery),
then transferred to Shàngjīng Liúshǒu (Resident Grandee of the Supreme Capital).
In Zhòngxī sixth year (1037),
he was promoted to Nányuàn Dàwáng (Great King of the Southern Chancery),
and the Emperor personally drafted an imperial decree to honor him.
In the twelfth year (1043),
he was granted the additional title Yúyuè.
The Emperor, pitying his hardship,
reinstated him as Wǔdìngjūn Jiédùshǐ,
where he died.
When the obituary arrived,
the Emperor wept and said:
"Alas, a good man!"
When the coffin arrived,
he personally went to perform the libation ceremony.
Yélǜ Mǎliù,
courtesy name Yángyǐn,
was a descendant of the King of Chǔ of the Mèngfù lineage.
His nature was tolerant and gentle,
and he was skilled at jesting and wit;
when relatives and friends gathered,
the whole assembly was won over.
He was indifferent to fame and profit.
He and Yélǜ Hónggǔ became sworn blood-brothers.
When Hónggǔ became Tìyǐn,
he recommended Mǎliù to be appointed as a Sùzhíguān (Official of the Imperial Guard).
At the beginning of the Chóngxī period (1032),
he was promoted to Qígǔ Zhuāilā Xiángwěn.
He was a man who was cautious, discreet, and tolerant of others;
if anyone publicly insulted or belittled him,
he remained undisturbed, as if he had not heard it,
and he did not criticize or comment on current affairs.
For this reason, the Emperor became increasingly close and familiar with him.
In the third year (1034),
he was promoted to Chóngdégōng Shǐ (Commissioner of the Chóngdé Palace),
and then became Tìyǐn.
The Emperor personally composed an edict praising him.
He was appointed Běiyuàn Xuānhuīshǐ (Commissioner of the Northern Chancery).
The favor and treatment he received surpassed that of the chief ministers;
the Emperor always addressed him as 'Elder Brother.'
He was reassigned as Liáoxīngjūn Jiédùshǐ (Military Commissioner of the Liáoxīng Army).
He died
at the age of seventy.
His son, Núgǔdá,
died serving as Nánjīng Xuānhuīshǐ (Commissioner of the Southern Capital Chancery).
Xiāo Dīliè,
courtesy name Túníng,
was from the palace personnel of the Yáoliǎn Xiānzhì Khān.
At the beginning of the Chóngxī period,
he was remotely appointed as Zhèngguójūn Jiédùshǐ (Military Commissioner of the Zhèngguó Army).
In the sixth year (1037),
he was dispatched by imperial decree as an envoy to Sòng.
He had injured his foot and was limping,
but he did not report this and proceeded with the mission.
The Emperor was angry.
When he returned,
he was punished with a heavy caning
and demoted to be a Co-Signatory of the Nánjīng Liúshǒushì (Superintendent of the Southern Capital).
He was remotely appointed Jìngjiāngjūn Jiédùshǐ (Military Commissioner of the Jìngjiāng Army),
served successively as Qúnmù Dūlínyá (Chief Chancellor of the Herding Administration),
and was successively promoted to Yòu Yílíbì.
He was employed due to his talent and capability.
When the imperial carriage campaigned in the West,
Yuánhào sought surrender.
Because the Emperor was concerned about his previous repeated betrayals,
he sent Dīliè to observe whether the sincerity was genuine.
Dīliè then explained to Yuánhào the consequences of disaster and fortune,
and only returned after Yuánhào obeyed the order.
He was appointed Běiyuàn Shūmì Fùshǐ (Vice Commissioner of Military Affairs of the Northern Chancery),
and then posted outside as Zhōngjīng Liúshǒu (Superintendent of the Central Capital).
In the nineteenth year (1050),
he was transferred to Xījīng Liúshǒu (Superintendent of the Western Capital),
and died there.
Yélǜ Shìlù,
courtesy name Sǎlǎn.
At the beginning of the Qīngníng period (1055),
he was a Běnbān Lángjūn (Gentleman of the Original Class),
and gradually promoted to Sùzhíguān (Official of the Imperial Guard).
During the Qiántǒng period (1101–1110),
he participated in the campaign against the Zǔbǔ and had merits,
and was given the title Fèngchén.
He successively served as Hùwèi Tàibǎo (Grand Guardian of the Imperial Guard),
and was transferred to Hóngyìgōng Fùshǐ (Vice Commissioner of the Hóngyì Palace).
At that time, Zhào Zhōnggē, a villainous bandit in Shàngjīng, was arrogant and unrestrained.
Shìlù captured him,
and was given the additional title Tàizhōu Guāncháshǐ (Surveillance Commissioner of Tàizhōu),
and served as Dá Lǔguó Bù Jiédùshǐ (Military Commissioner of the Dá Lǔguó Department).
During the Tiānqìng period (1111–1120),
he was appointed Zhī Xīngzhōngfǔ (Administrator of Xīngzhōng Prefecture),
and was given the additional title Jīnwǔwèi Shàngjiàngjūn (General-in-Chief of the Jīnwǔ Guard).
He was killed by bandits.
Yélǜ Chénjiānú,
courtesy name Miánxīn,
was an eighth-generation descendant of Gělà, the younger brother of Yìzǔ.
During the Chóngxī period,
he was appointed Pái'yìn Lángjūn (Gentleman of the Tablet Seal).
He was penalized for failing to attend his duty rotation
and demoted to the Běnbān (Original Class).
Coincidentally, when the Emperor was hunting,
Chénjiānú chased a deer inside the enclosure,
and was punished with two hundred lashes.
At that time, Yélǜ Rénxiān recommended Chénjiānú, saying he was as swift and agile as a sea-east falcon (Hǎidōngqīng Hú),
and he was granted the position Yùzhǎn Lángjūn (Gentleman of the Imperial Goblet).
He successively served as Vice Commissioner of the Yīngfāng (Falconry Bureau), Shàng (Court of Sacrifices), and Sìfāngguǎn (Bureau of the Four Directions),
and was transferred to Tú lǔgǔ Pīshì Xiángwěn.
On the occasion of the Empress Dowager's birthday,
he presented a poem and offered a tamed deer.
The Empress Dowager praised and rewarded him,
giving him two strings of pearls
and two hundred rolls of miscellaneous colored silks.
When his elder brother Sābō died,
Chénjiānú heard the訃告,
and left without reporting it.
The Emperor was angry
and had him flogged.
At the beginning of the Qīngníng period (1055),
he was successively promoted to Yòu Yílíbì.
It happened that the Emperor and the King of Yān both shot and hit a deer.
The King was nine years old at the time.
The Emperor was delighted,
and Chénjiānú composed a poem in response to the imperial request.
The Emperor was pleased
and bestowed his robe upon him.
Later, when the Crown Prince was deposed,
the Emperor suspected Chénjiānú of being affiliated with the faction
and dismissed him.
At that time, various northwestern tribes were raiding the border.
Chénjiānú was appointed Wūgǔbù Jiédùshǐ Xíngjūn Dūjiān (Supervisor of Campaigns and Military Commissioner of the Wūgǔ Department),
and was granted one set of armor and two horses,
to subdue the tribes.
He captured their chieftain and sent him to the court.
Scouts spotted horse tracks
and suspected invaders had arrived.
Chénjiānú sent a report to the Marshal.
Yélǜ Àinú looked at the tracks and said,
"These are wild horses!"
As he was about to go hunting,
the bandits arrived,
and Àinú died in battle.
The competent authorities investigated the matter,
but Chénjiānú refused to admit guilt.
An imperial decree released him.
Because of this, he was moved with gratitude
and exerted all his strength in every matter.
Later, the various tribes invaded again.
Chénjiānú led troops there three times,
and was victorious in all of them,
and the border region was consequently pacified.
He requested retirement due to old age,
but this was not granted.
When Dàozōng died,
he served as Shānlíngshǐ (Commissioner for the Imperial Mausoleum),
and then retired from office.
He died at the age of eighty.
Yélǜ Tèmó
was a descendant of the line of his uncle (Jìfù).
During the Chóngxī period,
he served as Běikè (Northern Commander),
and was successively promoted to Liùbù Tūlǐ Tàiwèi (Grand Commandant of the Tūlǐ of the Six Departments).
In the fourth year of Dà'ān (1088),
he became Dàotǎlǐng Jiédùshǐ (Military Commissioner of Dàotǎlǐng).
After a short while,
he was made Jīnjūn Dūjiān (Supervisor of the Imperial Guard).
That winter,
he campaigned against the Mógǔsī,
beheading over two thousand enemies.
In the tenth year (1094),
he campaigned against them again.
After achieving victory,
he was appointed Nányuàn Xuānhuīshǐ (Commissioner of the Southern Chancery).
In the first year of Shòulóng (1095),
he became Běiyuàn Dàwáng (Great King of the Northern Chancery).
In the fourth year (1098),
he was appointed Zhī Huánglóngfǔ Shì (Administrator of Huánglóng Prefecture),
and passed away.
Yélǜ Xiāntóng
was a descendant of the line of his paternal second uncle (Zhòngfù).
At the beginning of the Chóngxī period,
he was a Sùzhíguān (Official of the Imperial Guard),
and was successively promoted to Tìyǐn and Dūjiān (Supervisor).
He was known for his broad-mindedness and generosity.
When Púnúlǐ rebelled,
Xiāntóng was appointed Wǔguó Jiédùshǐ (Military Commissioner of the Five States),
and led troops to suppress them,
capturing their commander Táo Délǐ.
He also attacked the Wūkuí rebels,
and secured the surrender of their multitude.
He was transferred to Zhāngguójūn Jiédùshǐ (Military Commissioner of the Zhāngguó Army),
and appointed Běiyuàn Dàwáng (Great King of the Northern Chancery).
In the second year of Qīngníng (1056),
he was appointed Zhī Huánglóngfǔ Shì (Administrator of Huánglóng Prefecture),
and promoted to Shìwèi Qīnjūn Mǎbùjūn Dūzhīhuī (Commander-in-Chief of the Cavalry and Infantry of the Imperial Bodyguard).
He successively served as Military Commissioner of the Zhōngshùn and Wǔdìng Armies.
He retired from office
and was enfeoffed as the Duke of Jiǎngguó.
At the beginning of the Xiányǒng period (1065),
his enfeoffment was changed to the State of Xǔ,
where he died.
Xiāo Sùsà,
courtesy name Tèmǐn,
was a man of the Wǔyuànbù (Five Courts Department).
He began his official career during the Chóngxī period,
and was successively promoted to Běiyuàn Chéngzhǐ (Secretariat of the Northern Chancery)
and Zhāngmǐngōng Shǐ (Commissioner of the Zhāngmǐn Palace).
Early in Qīngníng,
he successively served as Zuǒ Píshì Xiángwěn and Yòu Yílíbì.
In the fifth year of Xiányōng,
the Pōu'ālǐ tribe rebelled.
Sùsà campaigned against them and forced their surrender,
leading their chiefs to come and pay homage at court.
The Emperor praised his achievement,
transferred him to Běiyuàn Línyá,
then changed him to Nányuàn Fù Bùshǔ,
and he died.
His son, Móu Lǔwò,
courtesy name Huíliǎn,
was initially appointed Yílíbì Lángjūn,
and then promoted to Wénbān Tàibǎo.
During the Dàkāng era,
he was changed to Nánjīng Tǒngjūnshǐ,
and became Yòu Yílíbì.
His discussions with the Grand Councilor (Shūmìshǐ) Yēlǜ Āsī were incompatible,
and he became the object of jealousy.
He was sent out to serve as Mǎqún Tàibǎo.
When the Northern Tribes invaded,
Móu Lǔwò defeated them.
Because of his merit, he was promoted to Tóngzhī Wūgǔ Díliè Tǒngjūn,
and was further permitted to act according to discretion.
Later, due to slander,
he was demoted to take charge of the Xīběilù Garrison Army,
and then returned to being Mǎqún Tàibǎo,
and he died.
Yēlǜ Dàbēinú,
courtesy name Xiūjiān,
was a descendant of Prince Bānnièlǐgǔ.
During the Dàkāng era,
he successively served as Yǒngxīng Yánchāng Gōngshǐ and Yòu Píshì Xiángwěn.
When the Zǔbǔ revolted,
he received an imperial edict to campaign against them and secure their surrender.
In the second year of Shòulóng,
he was appointed Diànqián Dūdiǎnjiǎn.
Early in the Qiántǒng era,
he successively served as Shàngjīng Liúshǒu and Tìyǐn,
then returned to being Dūdiǎnjiǎn,
and was changed to Xīnánmiàn Zhāotǎoshǐ.
He requested retirement due to age,
but it was not permitted.
During the Tiānqìng era,
he served as Liúshǒu in Shàngjīng,
managing affairs for the Superintendency of the Northern and Southern Grand Councils, and various bureaus.
He retired (zhìshì) with the title Zhāngguójūn Jiédùshǐ,
and then died.
Dàbēinú’s demeanor was gentle and refined,
and he loved propriety and ritual;
he was praised by the people of his time.
The commentary states: Since Shéncè,
Liáo occupied a position of wealth and strength.
Internally, it cultivated laws and regulations;
externally, it undertook campaigns and conquests.
At that time, the generals and commanders displayed powerful might,
sweeping across like wind and lightning.
They campaigned against Xīxià,
conquered the Dǎngxiàng,
defeated the Zǔbǔ,
and pacified the Díliè.
All the tribes were struck with dread;
upon hearing the war drums, their courage failed and their legs trembled.
This can truly be called a heroic and martial state.
In its victories in battle and subsequent conquests,
there must have been strange strategies, secret plans, and divine changes that defy prediction.
Is it that what previous historians have recorded
is insufficient to reveal these?
Or was it rather bestowed by Heaven,
so that the multitude could not contend with it, allowing them to succeed?
Be that as it may,
weapons of war are instruments of ill omen;
they should be put away, not played with.
Contention is a trivial matter;
it should be suppressed, not provoked.
This is what Huángshígōng called the ability of the soft to control the hard,
and the weak to control the strong.
How much more so when the benevolent person is truly invincible!
If the rulers and ministers of Liáo had possessed the wisdom to uphold this,
could the Jīn people truly have taken advantage of their decay and followed upon their heels?
Therefore, concerning generals like Yēlǜ Hónggǔ and his peers,
one cannot help but feel a sense of regret.
Biographies Twenty-Six: Yēlǜ Rénxiān (Tàbùyě), Yēlǜ Liáng, Xiāo Hánjiānú, Xiāo Dé, Xiāo Wéixìn, Xiāo Yuèyīnnú, Yēlǜ Díliè, Yáo Jǐngxíng, Yēlǜ Āsī.
Yēlǜ Rénxiān,
courtesy name Jiūlín,
nickname Chálà,
was a descendant of the Mèngfù Branch.
His father, Guīyǐn,
was the Prime Minister (Zǎixiàng) of the Southern Prefecture,
and was enfeoffed as King of Yān (Yānwáng).
Rénxiān was imposing, handsome, and brilliant,
and possessed strategic foresight.
In the third year of Zhòngxī,
he was appointed Imperial Guard (Hùwèi).
When the Emperor discussed governance with him,
he recognized his talent.
Rénxiān, seeing that he had met with a rare opportunity,
spoke without holding anything back.
He was granted the position Sùzhí Jiāngjūn,
and was successively promoted to Diànqián Fùdiǎnjiǎn.
He was changed to Hèlè Tánggǔ Bù Jiédùshǐ,
and soon after was recalled to serve as Běimiàn Línyá.
In the eleventh year,
he was promoted to Běiyuàn Shūmì Fùshǐ.
At that time, Sòng requested an increase in the annual tribute of silver and silk to compensate for the land yield of the ten counties.
Rénxiān, along with Liú Liùfú, went as envoy to Sòng,
and insisted on discussing writing the character
"gòng" (tribute).
Sòng found this difficult.
Rénxiān said:
"In the past, Shí Jìn, in gratitude to our dynasty,
ceded territory and presented it.
The Zhōu people seized and took it.
The right and wrong, the profit and loss,
are clearly evident."
Sòng had no words with which to reply.
Thus, the decision was finalized to increase the silver and silk by 100,000 liǎng/pǐ (taels/bolts),
and the payment was still referred to as
"gòng" (tribute).
After returning,
he served as Tóngzhī Nánjīng Liúshǒu Shì.
In the thirteenth year,
when they campaigned against Xià,
Rénxiān was left to guard the border.
Not long after,
he was recalled to serve as Qìdān Xínggōng Dū Bùshǔ.
He memorialized for the restoration of the service of the Prince Bān Lángjūn and the various palace attendants.
In the sixteenth year,
he was promoted to Běiyuàn Dàwáng.
He memorialized that the households in the two divisions (liǎng yuàn) were now thriving and numerous,
and requested exemption from corvée labor assistance (zhùyì) by other departments.
This was granted.
In the eighteenth year,
when the campaign against Xià was launched again,
Rénxiān served as the vanguard along with the Imperial Younger Brother Chóngyuán.
Xiāo Huì suffered a setback south of the river (Hénán).
The Emperor still wished to advance the troops,
but Rénxiān strongly remonstrated,
and so the campaign was halted.
Later, he was made Administrator of the Běiyuàn Shūmìshǐ,
and then promoted to Tōnjīng Liúshǒu.
The Nǚzhí relied on the difficult terrain
and did not stop their invasions and plunder.
Rénxiān requested that mountains be opened and roads constructed to control them,
and the border people lived peacefully in their occupations.
He was enfeoffed as King of Wú (Wúwáng).
Early in Qīngníng,
he became Nányuàn Shūmìshǐ.
Due to slander by Yēlǜ Huàgē,
he was sent out to serve as Nánjīng Bīngmǎ Fù Yuánshuài,
and Shǒu Tàiwèi,
and his kingly title was changed to Suí.
In the sixth year,
he was reinstated as Běiyuàn Dàwáng.
The people welcomed him for hundreds of *lǐ*,
as if seeing a father or elder brother.
At that time, the officials of the Northern and Southern Grand Councils, Nièlǔgǔ, Xiāo Húdǔ, and others, were jealous of him,
and requested that Rénxiān be made Xīběilù Zhāotǎoshǐ.
Yēlǜ Yǐxīn memorialized, saying:
"Rénxiān is an old official;
his virtue is foremost in this era.
It is inappropriate to appoint him outside the capital."
He was again appointed Nányuàn Shūmìshǐ,
and his kingly title was changed to Xǔ.
In the ninth year, seventh month,
the Emperor hunted at Tàizǐ Shān.
Yēlǜ Liáng reported that Chóngyuán was plotting rebellion.
The Emperor summoned Rénxiān and spoke to him about it.
Rénxiān said:
"This fellow is fierce and cruel.
Your subject has long suspected him."
The Emperor quickly ordered Rénxiān to capture him.
Rénxiān went out,
and also said:
"Your Majesty should prepare carefully!"
Before he could mount his armored horse,
Chóngyuán attacked the imperial tent camp.
The Emperor wished to proceed to the Northern and Southern Courts.
Rénxiān said:
"If Your Majesty leaves the escort and travels,
the bandits will surely follow behind you.
Moreover, the loyalty of the Northern and Southern Grand Princes (Dàwáng) is unknown."
Rénxiān's son, Tàbùyě, said:
"How can the Sacred Will be disobeyed?"
Rénxiān grew angry,
and struck his head.
The Emperor realized the truth,
and completely entrusted Rénxiān with the task of suppressing the bandits.
Thereupon, he formed a camp by circling the chariots,
dismantled the temporary fences (xíngmǎ),
prepared weapons,
and led his officials, subordinates, and close attendants—more than thirty horsemen—to array outside the stockade.
When battle was joined,
many of the bandits surrendered.
Nièlǔgǔ was hit by an arrow and fell from his horse.
He was captured.
Chóngyuán was wounded and retreated.
Rénxiān, noting that Xiāo Tǎlá of the Wǔyuànbù (Five Divisions Department) was camped nearest,
urgently summoned him,
and dispatched men separately to gather the various armies.
At dawn,
Chóngyuán led two thousand Xī people to attack the temporary imperial residence (xínggōng).
Xiāo Tǎlá's troops arrived just then.
Rénxiān judged that the bandits' momentum would not last long.
He waited until their spirit flagged before attacking.
He arrayed his troops with their backs to the camp,
seized the opportunity, and fiercely struck.
The bandit forces broke and scattered.
They were pursued and slaughtered for over twenty *lǐ*.
Chóngyuán fled away with a few horsemen.
The Emperor held Rénxiān's hand and said:
"The suppression of the rebellion is all due to your merit."
He was honored with the title Shàngfǔ (Senior Mentor),
promoted in rank to be the Prince of Sòng (Sòng Wáng),
and made the Commissioner of Military Affairs of the Northern Court (Běiyuàn Shūmìshǐ).
The Emperor personally composed a text praising him,
and commanded that the battle map of the Luánhé be drawn to commemorate his achievement.
In the first year of Xiányōng (1065),
he was additionally honored with the title Yúyuè,
and his title was changed to Prince of Liáo (Liáo Wáng).
He shared control of the affairs of the Northern Court Military Commission with Yēlǜ Yǐxīn.
Yǐxīn relied on imperial favor and acted unlawfully.
Rénxiān restrained him,
and was consequently resented.
He was sent out to serve as the Defense Commissioner of Nánjīng (Nánjīng Liúshǒu),
and his princely title was changed to Prince of Jìn (Wáng Jìn).
He took pity on the orphans and the desolate,
and prohibited deceit and wickedness.
The Sòng (Dynasty) heard of his reputation and were awed and subdued.
Commentators believed that since Yúyuè Xiūgē,
Rénxiān was the only person comparable.
Tǎlǐgān of the Zǔbǔ rebelled against imperial orders.
Rénxiān was made the Commissioner for Pacification of the Northwest Route (Xīběilù Zhāotǎoshǐ),
and was granted a seal with a hawk handle and a sword.
The Emperor decreed:
"You are far from the imperial court.
If you wait for memorials to be submitted and orders issued,
the opportunity may be lost.
You may act at your convenience."
Rénxiān rigorously managed the patrols,
held the enemy's vital points,
and mollified those who submitted.
All affairs were put in order.
Tǎlǐgān again came to raid.
Rénxiān met and attacked him,
pursuing and killing for more than eighty *lǐ*.
When the main army arrived later,
he defeated them again.
Bǎlǐsī, Tūmò, and others from different tribes came to assist,
but seeing their repeated failures,
they did not dare to fight and surrendered.
The northern border was thus pacified.
He died in the eighth year (1072),
aged sixty.
He left instructions for his family to prepare a simple funeral.
His younger brothers, Yìxiān and Xìnxiān,
both have biographies.
His son was Tàbùyě.
Tàbùyě,
courtesy name Húdújǐn.
In the second year of Qīngníng (1056),
he was appointed Palace Guard Gentleman (Zhīhòu Lángjūn).
He was successively promoted to Prefect of Yǒngxīng Gōng.
For suppressing Chóngyuán's rebellion,
he was remotely awarded the title Military Commissioner of Zhōngzhèng Jūn,
granted the title Meritorious Minister for Quelling the Disorder,
and appointed concurrent Administrator of the Directorate for Palace Inspection.
He successively held the posts of Military Commissioner for Gāoyáng and Línhǎi, and Commandant of the Left Píshì.
In the sixth year of Dàkāng (1080),
he was appointed Commissioner for Pacification of the Northwest Route.
He led the chiefs of various tribes to the court,
and was additionally granted the concurrent post of Attendant Counselor (Shìzhōng).
Since Xiāo Dílù served as the Commissioner for Pacification,
the imperial court focused on appeasement,
often choosing those who were gentle and compliant for the post.
Consequently, the various tribes gradually became arrogant and unbridled.
Tàbùyě was especially tolerant and lenient,
and border defense deteriorated further.
Soon thereafter, his title was changed to Commissioner for Pacification of the Southwest Sector.
Móugǔsī, the chieftain of the Zǔbǔ, came to invade.
Hélǔ Sàogǔ, the Commissioner for Pacification of the Northwest Route, suffered a defeat in battle.
An edict ordered Tàbùyě to replace him.
Móugǔsī's rise to chieftain
had been due to Tàbùyě's recommendation.
At this point, Tàbùyě sent a messenger to lure him in.
Móugǔsī feigned surrender.
Tàbùyě met him in the sandy wastes southwest of Zhènzhōu,
forbidding his soldiers from making any rash movements.
When the enemy arrived,
the subordinate generals Yēlǜ Guǎnsī and Xú Liè saw the sharp momentum of the enemy,
failed to fight, and fled.
Tàbùyě was subsequently killed,
aged fifty-eight.
He was posthumously granted the concurrent title of Attendant Counselor (Shìzhōng),
and given the posthumous name Zhēnmǐn.
When Tàbùyě was young, he was prudent and compliant.
Later, he was infatuated by a widowed woman of his clan,
divorced his wife,
and ultimately died without sons.
People criticized him for this.
Yēlǜ Liáng,
courtesy name Xínyǎn,
small name Sū,
was a descendant of the Zhùzhàng Lángjūn.
He was born in Qiánzhōu.
He studied at Yīwūlǘ Shān.
After his learning became extensive,
he intended to enter Nánshān to continue his studies.
His friend stopped him and said:
"You have no servants or drivers,
and traveling a thousand *lǐ*,
even if your knowledge and insight surpass others,
you will also be nearing old age.
If you take office now,
there is already room for success."
Liáng said:
"Poverty or success
is destiny (mìng),
it is not something you would understand."
He did not listen,
and returned after staying several years.
During the Chóngxī era,
he was appointed Palace Attendant (Qǐndiàn Xiǎodǐ).
Soon, he became a close attendant to the Prince of Yān and Zhào (Yān Zhào Guówáng).
Because his family was poor,
an edict permitted him to ride a horse.
He was promoted to Compiler of the Diary of Activity and Repose (Xiū Qǐjūzhù).
During a collective hunt on the Autumn Mountain,
Liáng presented the *Rhapsody on the Autumn Excursion* (Qiūyóu Fù).
The Emperor praised him.
During the Qīngníng era,
the Emperor visited the Yāzǐ Hé (River).
Liáng composed the *Rhapsody on Fishing* (Bǔyú Fù).
From this, his favor and treatment became somewhat elevated.
He was promoted to Drafting Official (Zhī Zhìgào),
concurrently overseeing the Affairs of the Deployment Directorate.
He memorialized requesting to compile the Emperor's personally composed poems and essays.
The collection was titled *Qīngníng Jí*.
The Emperor commanded that Liáng's poems be titled *Qìnghuì Jí*,
and personally wrote the preface for it.
After a while,
he was made Prefect of Dūnmù Gōng,
concurrently serving as Acting Administrator of all directorates under the Empress Dowager's Palace.
heard that Zhòngyuán and his son Nièlǔgǔ were plotting rebellion,
but because the Emperor was devoted to them with parental affection,
he did not dare to report it immediately.
He secretly spoke to the Empress Dowager (Huáng Tàihòu).
The Empress Dowager feigned illness,
summoned the Emperor, and informed him of the matter.
The Emperor said to Liáng:
“Do you wish to alienate me from my own flesh and blood?”
Liáng reported, saying:
“If your subject speaks falsely,
I willingly submit to the executioner’s axe and block.
If Your Majesty does not prepare early,
I fear you will fall into the rebel’s trap.
If you summon Nièlǔgǔ and he does not come,
you may divine the truth of the matter.”
The Emperor followed his advice.
When the envoy arrived at the gate,
Nièlǔgǔ intended to kill him,
and detained him beneath his tent.
The envoy cut the tent curtain with his waist knife and escaped,
galloping to the temporary palace (xínggōng) to report the situation.
The Emperor finally believed.
After the rebellion was pacified,
due to his merit, he was promoted to Hánrén Xínggōng Dū Bùshǔ (Commander-in-Chief of the Han People’s Temporary Palace).
In the beginning of the Xiányǒng era,
he concurrently managed the affairs of the Southern Chancellery Commissioner (Nányuàn Shūmìshǐ Shì),
became Tìyǐn,
and went out to govern the affairs of the Defender of Zhōngjīng (Zhōngjīng Liúshǒu Shì).
He died shortly thereafter.
The Emperor sighed in sorrow,
sent high officials to present funeral gifts and sacrifices,
provided burial supplies,
and posthumously enfeoffed him as Prince of Liáoxī Commandery (Liáoxī Jùnwáng).
His posthumous title was Zhōngchéng.
Xiāo Hánjiānú,
courtesy name Kuòníng,
was a descendant of Xī chieftain Bólǔ'ēn.
His nature was filial and brotherly.
During the Tàipíng era,
he was appointed Zhīhòu Lángjūn (Attendant Gentleman),
and repeatedly promoted to Dūnmùgōng Shǐ (Commissioner of the Dunmu Palace).
When campaigning against Xià,
he served as Zuǒyì Dūjiān (Supervisor of the Left Wing),
and was promoted to Běimiàn Línyá (Northern Chancellery Minister).
Soon after, he became Nányuàn Fù Bùshǔ (Deputy Commander of the Southern Chancellery),
and was granted a jade belt.
He was appointed Great King of the Six Xī Divisions (Xī Liùbù Dàwáng),
and his administration was renowned.
In the beginning of the Qīngníng era,
he was enfeoffed as Duke of Hánguó (Hánguó Gōng),
served successively as Nánjīng Tǒngjūnshǐ (Nanjing Military Commissioner) and Běiyuàn Xuānhuīshǐ (Northern Chancellery Commissioner of Affairs),
and was enfeoffed as Prince of Lánlíng Commandery (Lánlíng Jùnwáng).
In the ninth year,
the Emperor was hunting on Prince Mountain (Tàizǐ Shān).
Upon hearing of Zhòngyuán’s rebellion,
he rushed to the temporary residence (xíngzài).
In his confusion, the Emperor wished to take refuge in the residence of the Northern and Southern Great Kings (Běi, Nán Dàwáng Yuàn).
Hánjiānú, along with Yēlǜ Rénxiān, seized the reins and firmly remonstrated,
whereupon the Emperor stopped.
The following morning,
Zhòngyuán again lured the Xī hunters to join him.
Hánjiānú went out alone and addressed them, saying:
“You are abandoning loyalty and assisting rebellion;
you will merely bring about the destruction of your entire clan.
Why not repent your error,
and turn misfortune into fortune!”
The hunters threw down their weapons and submitted.
For this merit, he was promoted to Diànqián Dū Diǎnjiǎn (Commander of the Imperial Guard),
enfeoffed as Prince of Jīng (Jīng Wáng),

and granted the title of Meritous Subject for Supporting Loyalty, Upholding Righteousness, Serving the State, Exhausting Fidelity, and Pacifying the Rebellion (Zī Zhōng Bǎo Yì Fèng Guó Jié Zhēn Píng Luàn Gōngchén).
In the second year of Xiányǒng,
he was transferred to Xīnánmiàn Zhāotǎoshǐ (Commissioner for Pacification of the Southwest Frontier).
In the beginning of the Dàkāng era,
he was moved and enfeoffed as Prince of Wú (Wú Wáng),
and was granted a white Hǎidōngqīng falcon.
When the Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ) was falsely accused by Yǐxīn,
he was imprisoned in Shàngjīng.
Hánjiānú submitted a memorial strongly arguing for the Crown Prince’s innocence,
but received no reply.
In the fourth year,
he was again made Commissioner for Pacification of the Southwest Frontier.
According to convention, his single-character princely title was reduced,
and he was re-enfeoffed as Prince of Lánlíng (Lánlíng Wáng).
He died.
His son, Yángjiǔ,
ultimately held the rank of Yòuzhīhòu Lángjūn Bān Xiángwěn,
and was posthumously granted the title of Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì (Concurrently Administrator of Affairs in the Department of the Secretariat-Chancellery).
Xiāo Dé,
courtesy name Tèmòyǐn,
was a man of the Chǔtè tribe.
His nature was gentle and amicable,
and he was devoted to scholarship and fond of ritual law.
During the Tàipíng era,
he was in charge of tallies and seals, and served nightly duty.
He was repeatedly promoted to Běiyuàn Shūmì Fùshǐ (Deputy Commissioner of the Northern Chancellery).
His reports and presentations were detailed and clear,
and mostly accorded with the Emperor’s wishes.
An imperial edict ordered him and Línyá Yēlǜ Shùchéng to revise the laws and ordinances.
He was appointed Qìdān Xínggōng Dū Bùshǔ (Commander-in-Chief of the Khitan Temporary Palace),
and was granted fifteen palace households.
In the first year of Qīngníng,
he was promoted to concurrently manage the affairs of the Northern Chancellery Commissioner,
and enfeoffed as Duke of Lǔguó (Lǔguó Gōng).
Because the Emperor regarded Dé as having been favored by the previous court,
he was appointed Nánfǔ Zǎixiàng (Chancellor of the Southern Administration).
In the fifth year,
he was transferred to Nánjīng Tǒngjūnshǐ (Nanjing Military Commissioner).
In the ninth year,
he was again made Chancellor of the Southern Administration.
During Zhòngyuán’s rebellion,
he spearheaded the attack and fought fiercely,
beheading Nièlǔgǔ and presenting the head.
Based on his merit, he was enfeoffed as Prince of Hàn (Hàn Wáng).
In the beginning of the Xiányǒng era,
he requested retirement on account of old age and wished to return home,
but a gracious imperial edict did not permit it.
After a long time,
he was granted the additional title of Shàngfù (Imperial Mentor),
and retired from office.
He died
at the age of seventy-two.
Xiāo Wéixìn,
courtesy name Yēníng,
was a man of the Chǔtè tribe.
His fifth-generation ancestor, Xiálài,
was Chancellor of the Southern Administration.
His great-grandfather, Wūgǔ,
was Zhōngshū Lìng (Director of the Secretariat).
His grandfather, Āgǔzhǐ,
was Governor of Píngzhōu.
His father, Gāobā,
was highly intelligent and resourceful,
and widely read in ancient and modern texts.
In the beginning of the Kāitài era,
he became Běiyuàn Chéngzhǐ (Secretariat of the Northern Chancellery),
and was gradually promoted to Yòu Yílíbì (Right Yilibi).
He was famed for his capability and astuteness,
and was appointed Chancellor of the Southern Administration.
He was repeatedly promoted to Jiédùshǐ (Military Governor) of Dǎotā Lǐng,
served as Governor of Xīngzhōng Fǔ,
and was again made Right Yílíbì.
When Língqīng incited the masses to rebel,
the plot was discovered.
Gāobā investigated the case,
and only executed the ringleaders;
all the others were released.
He returned and reported,
and his actions were praised by the Emperor.
Wéixìn possessed a deep strength of character and decisiveness,
was devoted to learning,
and was skilled in debate.
He first entered official service in the beginning of the Zhòngxī era,
and was repeatedly promoted to Zuǒ Zhōngchéng (Left Vice-Director).
In the fifteenth year,
he was transferred to Tutor (Fù) of the Prince of Yānzhào (Yānzhào Guówáng).
The Emperor instructed him, saying:
“Those surrounding Yānzhào often flatter him to his face,
and he hears no loyal advice.
Gradually, this has become his habit.
You must use the Way to guide and instruct him,
so that he understands the duty owed to ruler and father.
If there are any [attendants] who should not be allowed in the princely residence,
report their names to me.”
Wéixìn assisted and instructed him according to ritual.
In the seventeenth year,
he was promoted to Deputy Commissioner of the Northern Chancellery,
but was dismissed from office due to involvement in an affair.
He soon resumed his post,
and concurrently served as Běimiàn Línyá.
In the ninth year of Qīngníng,
when Zhòngyuán launched his rebellion
and attacked the temporary palace at Luánhé,
Wéixìn followed Yēlǜ Rénxiān and defeated the rebels.
He was granted the title Meritorious Subject for Exhausting Loyalty and Quelling the Rebellion (Jié Zhōng Dìng Luàn Gōngchén).
He successively held the posts of Nánjīng Liúshǒu (Nanjing Defender) and Left and Right Yílíbì,
and was again made Deputy Commissioner of the Northern Chancellery.
During the Dàkāng era,
he requested retirement (lit., begged for his bones) on account of old age,
but was not permitted.
When Shūmìshǐ (Commissioner of the Chancellery) Yēlǜ Yǐxīn slandered and deposed the Crown Prince,
everyone inside and outside the court knew he was wronged,
but none dared to speak up.
Wéixìn repeatedly argued against it at court,
but could not reverse the decision.
He requested retirement,
was granted the additional title of Shǒu Sītú (Superintendent of Works),
and died.
Xiāo Yuèyīnnu,
courtesy name Pódān,
was the sixth-generation descendant of Xī Liùbù Chǎngwěn (Chancellor of the Six Xī Divisions) Tūlǚbù.
Bálà,
lived through the mourning period for his parents starting at age three.
His decline and emaciation were excessively severe,
and he was raised by the family slave Xīliè Ābù.
Early in the Chóngxī era,
Xīngzōng hunted on Xīshān,
and passed by where Bálà lived.
Xīliè Ābù spoke to a close minister,
and Bálà was granted an audience with the Emperor.
He was just ten years old,
but his bearing was like that of an adult.
The Emperor was pleased with him,
and bestowed exceedingly generous gifts upon him.
Once he grew up,
he possessed lofty aspirations,
and did not enjoy official career advancement.
He lived in seclusion in the Chāhé Gǔ valley of Xīwáng Lǐng.
The Emperor, because he came from a famous family,
and also had a contemporary reputation,
immediately appointed him as Shèlì Jūn Xiángwěn.
Yuèyīn nú had an imposing appearance and eloquent speech.
He was conversant with Khitan (Liáo) and Han Chinese scripts,
excelled at riding, archery, and polo (jī jū),
and those he associated with were all famous scholars of the time.
At age forty,
he first became a Protector (Hùwèi).
For suppressing Zhòngyuán's rebellion,
he was promoted based on merit to Hùwèi Tàibǎo,
then changed to the Nánkè of his own tribe,
and shortly thereafter became Qígǔ Yèlà Xiángwěn.
While supervising the capturing of Hǎidōngqīng Hú falcons,
he acquired thirteen white-marked falcons.
He was rewarded with a Gǔduò Xī rhinoceros horn (vessel) and a Yù Tǔhú (jade spitting falcon).
He was appointed Wǔfān Bù Jiédùshǐ,
and died.
His son, Yáng'ā,
has a biography.
Yēlǜ Díliè,
courtesy name Sǎlǎn,
was the fifth-generation descendant of Cǎifǎng Shǐ Hǒu.
He was magnanimous and generous,
fond of studying,
and skilled in literary composition.
At the end of the Chóngxī era,
he was appointed Páiyìn Lángjūn,
concurrently serving as Zhī Qǐjūzhù (Recorder of the Emperor's Daily Life).
In the first year of Qīngníng (1055),
he was gradually promoted to Tóng Zhī Yǒngzhōu Shì,
and gained merit in suppressing banditry.
He was reassigned as Běimiàn Línyá Chéngzhǐ.
In the ninth year (1063),
Zhòngyuán launched a rebellion.
Díliè rushed to the aid,
fought bravely, and suppressed it.
He was appointed Línhǎi Jūn Jiédùshǐ (in absentia).
In the tenth year (1064),
he was transferred to Wǔ'ān Zhōu Guāncháshǐ.
In the fifth year of Xiányōng (1069),
he was repeatedly promoted to Chángníng Gōngshǐ.
He audited the outstanding debts of cash and silk in the Hùbù Sī (Ministry of Revenue) of Qián Zhōu,
established rules for collection, expenditure, and planning,
which benefited both the government and the private sector.
In the fourth year of Dàkāng (1078),
he became Nányuàn Dàwáng.
When his term was complete,
the regional people requested that he stay.
He served as Tóng Zhī Nánjīng Liúshǒu Shì.
When he fell ill,
the Emperor ordered him to travel by relay carriage to the capital,
and dispatched imperial physicians to treat him.
He was promoted to Shàngjīng Liúshǒu.
During the Dà'ān era,
he was reassigned as Tāmǔ Chéng Jiédùshǐ.
He retired due to illness,
was concurrently granted the rank of Shìzhōng,
and given the stipend of the first rank.
He died in the eighth year (1092).
Yáo Jǐngxíng,
was originally named Jǐngxǐ.
His grandfather, Hànyīng,
was originally a general of the Zhōu dynasty (Later Zhōu),
and came as an envoy early in the Yìnglì era (c. 951).
Because he observed the rites of a hostile state,
the Emperor was angered,
and detained him,
placing him under the administration of the Hànrén Gōngfēn (Han Chinese division).
When Jǐngxíng later achieved eminence,
he was finally released from that register,
and registered in Xīngzhōng Xiàn.
Jǐngxíng was widely learned.
In the fifth year of Chóngxī (1036),
he passed the Jìnshì Yǐkē (second class) examination,
and became Jiāngzuò Jiān (Director of the Imperial Works),
then reassigned as Yānzhào Guówáng Jiàoshòu.
Within a few years,
he reached the rank of Hànlín Xuéshì,
Shūmì Fùshǐ,
and Cānzhī Zhèngshì.
His nature was honest, incorruptible, and upright,
and public respect turned toward him.
When Dàozōng ascended the throne,
he was frequently consulted (by the Emperor),
and served as the Běifǔ Zǎixiàng.
In the autumn of the ninth year (1063),
he requested retirement.
En route, he heard of Zhòngyuán's rebellion,
gathered travelers and obtained over three hundred cavalry to support the throne.
By the time he arrived,
the rebels had already been suppressed.
The Emperor praised his loyalty,
and bestowed upon him the property of the traitors.
In the first year of Xiányōng (1065),
he was sent out as Wǔdìng Jūn Jiédùshǐ.
The following year,
he was recalled by dispatch and appointed Nányuàn Shūmìshǐ.
