The Emperor calmly asked him about the methods of governance,
brought him into the inner palace,
showed him the Emperor’s own writings and those of the Crown Prince,
and presented him with various vessels and carriage equipment.
The Emperor intended to attack Sòng,
and summoned Jǐngxíng, asking:
"The Sòng people frequently cause trouble on the border,
what should be done?"
Jǐngxíng replied:
"Since Emperor Shèngzōng used his majesty and virtue to placate distant peoples,
Sòng has maintained official tribute payments.
Nearly sixty years have passed since then.
If we employ military force over minor matters,
I fear it would violate the established covenant of the former Emperor."
The Emperor agreed with his statement and stopped the plan.
He retired from office,
but did not spend a full month before resuming his former post.
When he experienced a period of domestic mourning,
he was recalled immediately,
concurrently holding the title of Zhōngshū Lìng.
The Emperor asked about the relative merits of Confucian scholars past and present.
His answers and replies were satisfactory to the Emperor,
and he was appointed Zhī Xīngzhōng Fǔ,
then reassigned as Shuòfāng Jūn Jiédùshǐ.
Early in the Dàkāng era (c. 1075),
he was transferred to govern Liáoxīng.
As Shàngjīng had many backlog cases in prison,
he was commanded to serve as Liúshǒu there.
In less than a few months,
he reported that the prisons were empty.
He repeatedly requested retirement,
but it was not granted.
He requested again,
and it was permitted.
He was granted the honorary title of Shǒu Tàishī.
When he died,
an envoy was dispatched to offer condolences and sacrifices.
He was posthumously enfeoffed as Liǔchéng Jùnwáng,
and given the posthumous name Wénxiàn.
In the fifth year of Shòulóng (1099),
an imperial decree ordered the establishment of a memorial shrine for him.
Yēlǜ Āsī,
courtesy name Sābān.
Early in the Qīngníng era (c. 1055),
he was appointed Zhīhòu Lángjūn.
Because he excelled at archery,
he was put in charge of hunting affairs,
and advanced to Bóhǎi Jìnshì Xiángwěn.
During Zhòngyuán's rebellion,
he and the Protector Sū shot and killed Nièlǔgǔ.
He was granted the title Jìngluàn Gōngchén (Meritorious Minister for Suppressing the Rebellion),
and transferred to Qìdān Xínggōng Dū Bùshǔ.
Early in the Dà'ān era (c. 1085),
he became Běiyuàn Dàwáng,
and was enfeoffed as Qīshuǐ Jùnwáng.
In the first year of Shòulóng (1095),
he became Běiyuàn Shūmìshǐ,
and supervised the compilation of the national history.
When Dàozōng died,
he received the dying emperor's instructions,
and was elevated to Yúyuè.
When listing members of the Yǐxīn faction,
those whose crimes were severe ought to have their families confiscated (and registered as slaves).
Āsī accepted bribes,
and granted much leniency and release.
Xiāo Hélǔ once suggested strengthening border defenses,
but Āsī vigorously obstructed the effort.
Some critics mocked him, saying he used gold to sell out the nation.
Later, due to a stroke (wind sickness), he lost his voice,
and retired.
He was granted the honorary title of Shàngfù,
and enfeoffed as Zhào Wáng.
He passed away,
at the age of eighty.
He was posthumously enfeoffed as Qí Guówáng.
The discussion states: Regarding the incident at the Luán Hé,
when Zhòngyuán commanded troops at the field headquarters,
if not for Rénxiān and others,
Dàozōng would have been in danger!
When he stopped the imperial progress to the Northern and Southern Administrations,
and summoned Tǎlà soldiers to quell the great rebellion,
his merit should rank first.
Liáng revealed the plot to the Empress Dowager (Tàihòu);
Hán Jiānú convinced the Xī Rén to switch allegiance;
Dé and Āsī killed Nièlǔgǔ;
all had the strength to suppress the rebels.
Rénxiān was equally famous as Xiūgē,
possessing both meritorious service and virtue.
This is perhaps one segment (of his character).
Biographies, Chapter 27: Yēlǜ Wòtèlā, Háilǐ, Dòu Jǐngyōng, Yēlǜ Yǐnjí, Yáng Jì, Zhào Huī, Wáng Guān, Yēlǜ Xǐsūn
Yēlǜ Wòtèlā,
courtesy name Yǐxīnyǐn,
was the sixth-generation descendant of Yǐndǐshí, Prince of Xǔguó.
In his youth, he did not desire official salary or rank.
At the age of forty-one,
he was first appointed to the post of cadet (lángjūn) in his native division.
At that time, the Commissioner of Military Affairs (Shūmì Shǐ), Yēlǜ Yǐxīn, wielded unauthorized power,
slandering and harming loyal and good people.
Wòtèlā, fearing calamity might reach him,
kept himself deeply reserved and cautious.
In the middle of the Dàkāng period,
he served as an official on duty (Sùzhí Guān),
and successively held the posts of Grand Guardian (Tàibǎo) of the Left and Right Guards.
In the first year of Dà'ān,
he was promoted to Tutor (Fù) of the Prince of Yān,
and transferred to be the Left Yílíbì.
In the fourth year,
he was changed to Deputy Commissioner of Military Affairs of the Northern Administration.
The Emperor bestowed a poem upon him in praise,
and promoted him to Administrator of the Affairs of the Commissioner of Military Affairs of the Northern Administration,
and granted him the meritorious title Yìshèng Zuǒyì Gōngchén.
Mógǔsī, the chieftain of the Northern Zǔbǔ, rebelled,
and Wòtèlā led troops to advance and suppress him.
Coincidentally, there was a heavy snowfall,
he defeated four detached sections of Mógǔsī’s army,
beheading over a thousand enemy soldiers,
and was appointed Commissioner of Pacification of the Northwest Circuit,
enfeoffed as Prince of Qīshuǐ Commandery,
and further granted the meritorious title Xuānlì Shǒuzhèng Gōngchén.
Soon after, he was appointed Chancellor of the Southern Administration.
He again suppressed the Zhágǔ Húlíbā tribe,
defeating them.
He was recalled to serve as the Commander-in-Chief of the Khitan Imperial Travelling Palace.
Previously,
when there were lawsuits in the Northern and Southern Administrations,
various prefectures and administrations could investigate them locally;
in recent years,
if they did not receive a dispatch from the Bureau of Military Affairs,
they were not allowed to interrogate cases,
which consequently led to the delay of lawsuits.
Wòtèlā presented a memorial requesting a return to the old system,
and it was granted.
In the fifth year of Shòulóng,
he was again made Commissioner of Pacification of the Northwest Circuit,
and suppressed the Yēdǔguā tribe.
He captured and executed a great many people,
and seized tens of thousands each of horses, camels, cattle, and sheep.
The following year,
he captured Mógǔsī,
was promoted to Acting Grand Guardian,
and granted the meritorious title Fèngguó Kuānghuà Gōngchén.
In the early years of Qiántǒng,
he requested retirement,
but it was not permitted;
only the position of Commissioner of Pacification was removed.
He concurrently resumed the position of Commissioner of Military Affairs of the Southern Administration,
and was enfeoffed as Prince of Hùntóng Commandery.
He was transferred to Commissioner of Military Affairs of the Northern Administration,
promoted to Acting Grand Preceptor,
and granted the meritorious title Tuīchéng Zànzhì Gōngchén.
He retired,
and died.
His posthumous title was Jìngsù.
Háilǐ,
courtesy name Húliǎn,
was a Huíhú (Uygur) person.
His ancestors came to offer tribute during the time of Grand Progenitor,
and wished to remain;
consequently, they were appointed to official posts.
Háilǐ,
served successively as Chief of Imperial Attendants during the Zhòngxī period.
In the ninth year of Qīngníng,
having merit in suppressing the rebellion of Zhòngyuán,
he was promoted to Senior General of the Jīnwú Guard,
and granted the meritorious title Píngluàn Gōngchén.
He was successively promoted to Commander-in-Chief of the Palace Guard,
and was renowned for the strictness and solemnity of his palace guard duties.
In the early years of Dàkāng,
he was promoted to Acting Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent.
In the second year,
he was promoted to Concurrent Administrator of Affairs of the Chancellery.
In the third year,
he was changed to Concurrent Administrator of Affairs of the Commissioner of the Southern Chancery.
When Yēlǜ Yǐxīn was sent out to govern the Central Capital,
Háilǐ entered to offer congratulations;
when discussion arose about recalling him,
he explained why it should not be done.
Later, Yǐxīn re-entered the Bureau of Military Affairs,
and had Háilǐ sent out to be the Regional Commander of Guǎnglì Commandery.
When the Crown Prince was falsely accused,
Háilǐ was supposed to be implicated by association,
but an imperial edict decreed that he should not be questioned.
In the early years of Dà'ān,
he served successively as Regional Commander of the Pǐndálǔ Guó Bù.
In the fifth year of Shòulóng,
he became ill.
He said himself, "My destined time is already complete,"
and refused medicine and treatment.
He passed away,
at the age of seventy-seven.
Háilǐ had always believed in Buddhism.
In the early years of Qīngníng,
he accompanied the Emperor on a hunt,
fell from his horse,
fainted, and then revived.
He said that he first saw two men leading him to a city.
The palaces were grand and spacious.
A man wearing a crimson robe was seated in the hall,
with attendants lined up on the left and right.
They led Háilǐ up the steps.
The person holding the writing tablet showed it to him and said:
"We were originally supposed to fetch Dàfù Gǔyù,
but mistakenly apprehended you."
The tablet read:
"Official rank reaches Minister-Chancellor,
lifespan seventy-seven."
After a moment, he was returned,
pushed into a great ravine, and woke up.
Dàozōng heard of this,
and commanded that the event be recorded.
It was all verified later.
Dòu Jǐngyōng,
was a native of Zhōngjīng,
and the son of Zhèn, the Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
He was intelligent, clever, and fond of learning.
During the Qīngníng period,
he passed the Imperial Examination,
and was appointed Proofreader in the Palace Library.
He was successively promoted to Vice Minister of the Imperial Treasury.
In the sixth year of Xiányōng,
he was appointed Academician of the Bureau of Military Affairs,
and soon administered the affairs of the Deputy Commander-in-Chief of the Han People’s Imperial Travelling Palace.
In the early years of Dà'ān,
he was transferred to Deputy Commissioner of Military Affairs of the Southern Administration,
Supervisor of the Compilation of National History,
Administrator of the Affairs of the Bureau of Military Affairs,
and granted the meritorious title Tóngdé Gōngchén,
and enfeoffed as Duke of Chén State.
He became ill,
and presented a memorial requesting retirement;
it was not granted.
He was promoted to Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent,
and appointed Regional Commander of Wǔdìng Commandery.
He carefully reviewed and settled delayed or wrongful cases,
applying appropriate severity,
and was renowned for having empty prisons.
In the seventh year,
he was appointed Resident General of Zhōngjīng.
He died in the ninth year.
His posthumous title was Sùxiàn.
His son, Yú,
was Deputy Commissioner of the Three Judicial Offices.
Yēlǜ Yǐnjí,
courtesy name Ākuò,
was a man of the Pǐn Bù.
His father, Shuānggǔ,
guarded the western border for more than twenty years.
His governance was highly strict and solemn,
and he did not accumulate wealth.
People of the time frequently praised him.
Yǐnjí was reverent, cautious, and fond of righteousness.
He entered officialdom via hereditary privilege,
and was successively promoted to Deputy Resident General of the Eastern Capital and Imperial Censor of the Northern Bureau of Military Affairs.
At that time, Xiāo Gé, Xiāo Túgǔcí, and others were appointed based on flattery,
selling ranks and accepting bribes.
Yǐnjí lived among them based on the upright path,
showing no bias or compliance.
He was changed to Commissioner of the Guest Bureau.
At that time, the Imperial Court sent envoys to enumerate the hidden households in the three capitals but failed.
Yǐnjí was appointed to replace them,
and he managed to find several thousand hidden households.
At that time, Zhāohuái Tàizǐ (昭懷太子) supervised the Northern and Southern Chanceries.
Yǐn Jí (引吉) was selected to be his instructor/advisor.
The Commissioner of Military Affairs, Yǐ Xīn (乙辛), intended to overthrow the Crown Prince.
He resented Yǐn Jí (引吉) being at his side,
and memorialized to have him dismissed,
making him the Línyá (林牙) of the Directorate of Herds.
In the first year of Dàkāng (大康, 1075),
Yǐ Xīn (乙辛) requested the grant of pasture land.
Yǐn Jí (引吉) memorialized, saying:
“Currently, the pasture land is limited,
and the livestock are not flourishing.
How can it be divided and granted to officials?”
The Emperor then stopped the plan.
Yǐ Xīn (乙辛) consequently resented him even more,
and appointed him Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Huáidé Jūn (懷德軍).
He was transferred to be Tàibǎo (太保) of the Horse Herds at Huá Shuǐ (猾水) north of the desert.
He died.
Yáng Jì (楊績),
was a native of Liángxiāng (良鄉).
In the eleventh year of Tàipíng (太平, 1031), he passed the Jìnshì (進士) examination,
and was successively promoted to Deputy Commissioner of Military Affairs of the Southern Chancery.
Together with Dù Fáng (杜防) and Hán Zhībái (韓知白), he illicitly issued diplomas to Jìnshì (進士).
He was demoted to Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Chángníng Jūn (長寧軍),
then transferred to govern Zhuō Zhōu (涿州).
At the beginning of Qīngníng (清寧, 1055),
he was appointed Cānzhī Zhèngshì (參知政事, Associate Administrator),
and concurrently Director of the Bureau of Military Affairs (Tóngzhī Shūmì Yuàn Shì, 同知樞密院事),
serving as Southern Prefecture Chancellor (Nán Fǔ Zǎixiàng, 南府宰相).
In the ninth year (1063),
hearing of Zhòngyuán’s (重元) rebellion,
he worked with Yáo Jǐngxíng (姚景行) to support the Emperor.
The Emperor commended him.
In the tenth year (1064),
he governed Xīngzhōng Fǔ (興中府).
At the beginning of Xiányōng (咸雍, 1065),
he entered court to direct the Bureau of Military Affairs.
In the second year (1066),
he requested retirement,
but it was denied.
He was appointed Commissioner of Military Affairs of the Southern Chancery.
Because the Emperor regarded Jì (績) as an old official,
he specially summoned him for a private audience,
discussing governance and chaos throughout history,
and the integrity or corruption of ministers.
The Emperor said:
“Currently, among my loyal and upright ministers,
there are only Yēlǜ Jué (耶律玦) and Liú Shēn (劉伸);
however, Shēn (伸) is not as unyielding as Jué (玦).”
Jì (績) bowed and offered congratulations, saying:
“Which era lacks worthy men?
When the world is chaotic, they cultivate virtue in solitude;
when the sovereign is sagely, they benefit the whole realm.
Your Majesty weighs integrity and corruption with precision,
and promotions and demotions are clear.
The realm is extremely fortunate.”
He repeatedly submitted memorials announcing his desire to return home,
but it was not permitted.
He was enfeoffed as Zhào Wáng (趙王).
During the Dàkāng (大康) era,
he was formally changed by precedent to Wáng (王, Prince) of Liáoxī (遼西).
He retired,
was granted the title Grand Tutor (Shǒu Tàibǎo, 守太保),
and passed away.
His son, Guìzhōng (貴忠),
governed Xīngzhōng Fǔ (興中府).
Zhào Huī (趙徽),
was a native of Nánjīng (南京).
In the fifth year of Chóngxī (重熙, 1036),
he was promoted through the Grade A examinations,
and successively promoted to Minister of the Court of Judicial Review (Dàlǐ Zhèng, 大理正).
In the second year of Qīngníng (清寧, 1056),
when the people of Tóng Zhōu (銅州) falsely slandered the Three Teachings,
Huī (徽) investigated and interrogated them,
reporting the facts to the throne,
which pleased the Emperor.
He served in numerous arduous posts,
and gained a reputation for competence.
He was successively promoted to Academician-in-Waiting (Hànlín Xuéshì Chéngzhǐ, 翰林學士承旨).
At the beginning of Xiányōng (咸雍, 1065),
he served as Director of the Court of Finance (Dùzhī Shǐ, 度支使).
In the third year (1067),
he was appointed Cānzhī Zhèngshì (參知政事).
He was posted out as Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Wǔdìng Jūn (武定軍).
When his replacement arrived,
the soldiers and the people requested that he remain.
Later, he became Director of the Bureau of Military Affairs,
concurrently serving as Southern Prefecture Chancellor, Vice Director of the Chancellery, and Executive Administrator.
He retired,
and died.
He was posthumously granted the title Grand Secretary of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Lìng, 中書令),
and given the posthumous name Wénxiàn (文憲).
Wáng Guān (王觀),
was a native of Nánjīng (南京).
He was widely learned and eloquent.
In the seventh year of Chóngxī (重熙, 1038),
he passed the Jìnshì (進士) examination, Grade B.
When Xīngzōng (興宗) died,
he served as the Envoy to Xià Guó (夏國) to announce the death;
upon returning,
he was appointed Supervising Secretary.
At the beginning of Xiányōng (咸雍, 1065),
he was promoted to Hanlin Academician.
In the fifth year (1069),
he concurrently served as Academician of the Qiánwén Gé (乾文閣).
In the seventh year (1071),
he was transferred to Deputy Commissioner of Military Affairs of the Southern Chancery,
granted the Imperial surname,
and made Cānzhī Zhèngshì (參知政事),
concurrently directing the affairs of the Southern Chancery Bureau of Military Affairs.
He was convicted of fraudulently using Imperial authority to renovate his private residence,
stripped of his title, reduced to a commoner,
and died.
Yēlǜ Xǐsūn (耶律喜孫),
courtesy name Yíngyǐn (盈隱),
was from the subdivision of Yǒngxīng Gōng (永興宮).
When Xīngzōng (興宗) was Crown Prince,
Xǐsūn (喜孫) often remained at his side, offering guidance.
When Shèngzōng (聖宗) was critically ill,
Xǐsūn (喜孫) and Féng Jiānú (馮家奴) reported to Réndé Huánghòu (仁德皇后) that the Chancellor Xiāo Zhuōbǔ (蕭浞卜) and others were plotting rebellion.
When Qīn'āi (欽哀) became Empress Dowager and assumed regency,
Xǐsūn (喜孫) was especially favored and trusted.
During the Chóngxī (重熙) era,
his son, Niègē (涅哥), serving as an attendant,
was executed for an offense.
Because the Emperor recognized Xǐsūn’s (喜孫) meritorious service in supporting the throne,
and mourned the criminal death of his son,
he wanted the office to be hereditary.
Xǐsūn (喜孫) did not belong to a specific administrative department;
upon seeing that the horse brand had a section number,
he ordered Xǐsūn (喜孫) to be registered under that section.
He was appointed Southern Prefecture Chancellor.
Soon after, he was posted out as Xiángwěn (詳穩) of the Northeast Circuit.
He died.
The appraisal says: Hái Lǐ (孩里) and Yǐn Jí (引吉), in their roles as ministers,
lived during the days when Yǐ Xīn (乙辛) monopolized power and Xiāo Gé (蕭革) was corrupt and grasping.
Although they served alongside them,
they managed to conduct themselves with integrity,
without the slightest flattery or compliance,
surpassing others greatly!
The tradition states:
“It is only in the cold winter that one realizes the pine and cypress are the last to fade.”
These two men exemplified this.
As for Huòtèlā’s (斡特剌) military achievements,
Dòu Jǐngyōng’s (竇景庸) judicial expertise,
and Yáng Jì’s (楊績) loyal advice,
they were also worthy men.
Biographies, Chapter Twenty-Eight: Xiāo Wùnà (蕭兀納), Yēlǜ Yǎn (耶律儼), Liú Shēn (劉伸), Yēlǜ Húlǚ (耶律胡呂)
Xiāo Wùnà (蕭兀納),
also named Tàbùyě (撻不也),
courtesy name Tèmiǎn (特免),
was a native of the Liù Yuàn Bù (六院部) tribe.
His ancestors had served as Zuàilā (拽剌) of the Southwest Circuit.
Wùnà (兀納) was imposing and dignified,
and skilled in riding and archery.
At the beginning of Qīngníng (清寧, 1055),
his elder brother, Tú Dú (圖獨), came for an audience on official business.
The Emperor asked if there were any capable men among his relatives.
Tú Dú (圖獨) responded by mentioning Wùnà (兀納).
He was appointed Gentleman of the Imperial Guard.
He was promoted to Grand Clerk of the Imperial Attendants,
then Guardian Grand Tutor.
At the beginning of Dàkāng (大kāng, 1075),
he became Commissioner of Court Affairs of the Northern Chancery.
At that time, Yǐ Xīn (乙辛) had already harmed the Crown Prince.
He then suggested that Chún (淳), the son of Héluwò (和魯斡), the Prince of Sòng-Wèi (宋魏國王), could be designated as heir.
No officials dared to speak up.
Only Wùnà (兀納) and Yílìbì (夷離畢) Xiāo Táokuí (蕭陶隗) remonstrated, saying:
“To abandon the rightful heir and not establish him,
is to give the state away to others.”
The Emperor remained indecisive.
In the fifth year (1079),
the Emperor went hunting.
Yǐ Xīn (乙辛) requested to leave the Imperial Grandson behind.
The Emperor intended to agree.
Wùnà (兀納) memorialized, saying:
“I secretly heard that when Your Majesty travels,
you plan to leave the Imperial Grandson behind.
If the protection is inadequate,
I fear there may be other incidents.
If he is indeed left behind,
I request permission to attend to him.”
The Emperor then realized the danger,
and ordered the Imperial Grandson to accompany him.
From this incident,
he began to suspect Yǐ Xīn (乙辛).
A short while later,
he was appointed Associate Administrator (Tóngzhī) of the Southern Division Bureau of Military Affairs (Nányuàn Shūmìshǐ Shì),
and dismissed Yǐxīn, Chún, and others.
The Emperor praised his loyalty,
and enfeoffed him as Prince of Lánlíng Commandery (Lánlíng Jùnwáng).
People said he was close to the ancient ministers of state (shèjì chén).
He was granted the title Grand Inspector of the Palace Guard (Diànqián Dūdiǎnjiǎn).
The Sovereign said to Wáng Shīrú, Yēlǜ Gù, and others:
"Wùnà is loyal and pure.
Even Dí Rénjié assisting Táng,
or Wūzhì establishing Mùzōng,
could not surpass him.
You gentlemen should inform the Prince of Yàn (Yànwáng) of this."
Thereafter,
he ordered Wùnà to assist and guide the Prince of Yàn (Yànwáng),
and he was treated with increasing favor and trust.
In the beginning of the Dà'ān era,
an imperial decree ordered him to marry the Princess of Yuègúo (Yuègúo Gōngzhǔ).
Wùnà firmly declined.
He was reassigned as Administrator of the Southern Division Bureau of Military Affairs (Nányuàn Shūmìshǐ).
He memorialized, requesting that clerks and subordinates should be promoted based on seniority (years and months).
This was adopted.
In the first year of the Shòulóng era,
he was appointed Chancellor of the Northern Administration (Běifǔ Zǎixiàng).
Previously,
when Tiānzuò was still in the royal residence (qiándǐ),
Wùnà frequently opposed the imperial will with straightforward criticism.
When Tiānzuò succeeded to the throne,
Wùnà was sent out as Military Commissioner (Jiédùshǐ) of Liáoxīng Commandery,
holding the title Grand Tutor (Tàifù).
Because Wáng Huá, a minor attendant in the Buddhist temple, falsely accused Wùnà of borrowing rhinoceros horns from the Inner Treasury,
an edict was issued to investigate him.
Wùnà memorialized, saying:
"When your servant was serving the previous court,
an edict permitted me to take 100,000 treasury coins daily for private expenses.
Your servant never improperly took a single coin.
Would I then be willing to borrow rhinoceros horns?"
Tiānzuò grew increasingly angry,
stripped him of the post of Grand Tutor (Tàifù),
demoting him to Prefect (Cìshǐ) of Níngbiān Prefecture,
and soon after changing this to Military Commissioner (Jiédùshǐ) of Línhǎi Commandery.
Wùnà submitted a letter, saying:
"Since Xiāo Hǎilǐ fled and defected to the Nǚzhí,
they have developed a disregard for the imperial court.
Troops should be increased to guard against unexpected events."
No reply was given.
In the first year of the Tiānqìng era,
he was appointed Administrator (Zhī) of Huánglóng Prefecture.
He was later changed to Commander of the Northeast Circuit (Dōngběi Lù Tǒngjūnshǐ).
He again submitted a letter, saying:
"Your servant governs the area bordering the Nǚzhí.
Observing their actions,
their ambitions are considerable.
It is fitting that before they act,
we raise an army and plan against them."
He submitted several memorials,
but none were heeded.
When the Jīn army invaded,
they fought at Níngjiāng Prefecture.
His grandson Yídíjiǎn died there.
Wùnà retreated and entered the city.
He left his officials and subordinates to defend,
and personally crossed the Húntóng River westward with three hundred cavalry.
The city subsequently fell.
Later, he and Xiāo Dílǐ resisted the Jīn forces at Chángluò,
but due to the military defeat, he was dismissed from office.
In the fifth year,
Tiānzuò personally led a campaign.
Wùnà commanded the rear guard,
and was defeated again.
Several days later, he entered the court with the other officials for an audience.
He was appointed Resident Commissioner of Shàngjīng (Shàngjīng Liúshǒu).
In the sixth year,
Yēlǜ Zhāngnú rebelled
and came to attack the capital city.
Wùnà opened the treasury and granaries to reward the soldiers,
enlightened them about righteousness and treason,
repaired the walls and moats,
and fought back fiercely, refusing to surrender.
Zhāngnú gained nothing and departed.
For this achievement, Wùnà was granted the title Deputy Marshal (Fù Yuánshuài).
Soon after, he became Chief Palace Commissioner of the Qìdān (Qìdān Dū Gōngshǐ).
Because Tiānzuò considered Wùnà a senior minister of the previous court,
who had the merit of establishing the succession,
he frequently summoned and questioned him about governance.
Wùnà's replies were very pointed.
Although the Sovereign treated him graciously,
he ultimately did not employ him.
He died of illness
at the age of seventy.
Yēlǜ Yǎn,
courtesy name Ruòsī,
was a native of Xījīn.
His original surname was Lǐ.
His father, Zhòngxī,
began his official career during the Chóngxī era.
In the beginning of the Qīngníng era,
he served as Associate Administrator (Tóngzhī) of the Southern Division Privy Council (Nányuàn Xuānhuīshǐ Shì).
In the fourth year,
he constructed fortifications between the Yāzǐ and Húntóng Rivers.
He was appointed Commissioner of the Northern Division Privy Council (Běiyuàn Xuānhuīshǐ).
In the beginning of the Xiányōng era,
he was implicated for mistakenly reporting an event
and was sent out as Prefect (Cìshǐ) of Yú Prefecture.
Soon after, an imperial decree restored him to his former post,
and he was promoted to Grand Commissioner of the Travelling Palace for Hàn People (Hànrén Xínggōng Dū Bùshǔ).
In the sixth year,
he was granted the imperial surname [Yēlǜ],
enfeoffed as Duke of Hán (Hánguó Gōng),
and reassigned as Administrator of the Southern Division Bureau of Military Affairs (Nányuàn Shūmìshǐ).
At that time, the military official Yǐxīn and others falsely implicated the Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ).
An edict ordered Zhòngxī, along with Yǐxīn, to investigate the case.
Many innocent people were dragged into the case,
and he never managed to clear the wrongly accused.
Yǐxīn recommended that Zhòngxī was fit for appointment.
He was appointed Military Commissioner (Jiédùshǐ) of Guǎngdé Commandery,
and later reinstated as Administrator of the Southern Division Bureau of Military Affairs (Nányuàn Shūmìshǐ).
He died,
and was given the posthumous title Qīnhuì.
Yǎn had a handsome and dignified appearance.
He loved learning,
and was famous for his poetry.
He passed the imperial examination (Jìnshì) during the Xiányōng era.
He served as Assistant Recorder (Zhùzuò Zuǒláng).
He was appointed Clerk (Lìngshǐ) in the Secretariat (Zhōngshūshěng),
where he was known for his diligence and quickness.
In the beginning of the Dàkāng era,
he served successively as Judicial Clerk (Pànguān) to the Grand Commissioner (Dū Bùshǔ) and Vice Minister of the Court of Imperial Manufactories (Jiàngzuò Shàojiān).
Later, when the officials of the Two Administrations (Liǎngfǔ) memorialized,
discussing the merits and faults of the various officials,
they specifically praised Yǎn's talent and ability.
He was reassigned as Vice Minister of the Court of the Treasury (Shàofǔ Shàojiān),
appointed Administrator (Zhī) of the Chief Justice position (Dàlǐ Zhèng),
and granted purple robes.
In the sixth year,
he was promoted to Vice Minister of the Court of Judicial Review (Dàlǐ Shàoqīng).
His case reviews and judgments were thorough and fair.
The following year,
he was promoted to Minister of the Court of Judicial Review (Dàlǐ Qīng).
When his father died, he went into mourning.
He was ordered to abandon mourning [to return to work],
serving as Associate Commissioner of the Office of the Grand Commissioner (Tóng Qiān Bùshǔ Sī Shì).
In the beginning of the Dà'ān era,
he became Prefect (Cìshǐ) of Jǐng Prefecture.
He strictly controlled clerks and yamen runners,
restrained powerful and crooked elements,
comforted the elderly, and aided the poor.
Before many months had passed,
his good governance had spread far and wide.
The people of the commandery carved his virtues onto stone tablets.
In the second year,
he was reassigned as Vice Censor-in-Chief (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng).
An edict ordered him to investigate pending cases in Shàngjīng (the Supreme Capital),
and he reversed many unjust convictions.
He served as Associate Administrator (Tóngzhī) of the Privy Council,
and concurrently Supervised the Court of Judicial Review (Tídiǎn Dàlǐ Sì).
In the winter of the sixth year,
he was reassigned as Grand Commissioner of Fiscal Transport for the Shānxī Circuit (Shānxī Lù Dū Zhuǎnyùnshǐ).
He cleaned out accumulated corruption and abuses,
memorialized to fix tax quotas,
and increased the salaries of prefectural and county officials.
All these matters were implemented.
In the beginning of the Shòulóng era,
he was granted the title Academician of the Bureau of Military Affairs (Shūmì Zhí Xuéshì).
He resigned his post due to mourning for his mother,
but was soon recalled and restored to his former position.
When Sòng attacked Xià,
Lǐ Qiánshùn sent an envoy requesting mediation and peace.
The Emperor ordered Yǎn to go to Sòng to settle the matter.
He was appointed Vice Grand Councilor (Cānzhī Zhèngshì).
In the sixth year,
the imperial carriage went to Yuānyāng Lake (Yuānyāng Luò).
He was summoned to the inner palace
and consulted on affairs of government.
In his later years, the Emperor grew weary of his duties
and could not personally select officials.
He ordered candidates to throw dice,
and whoever achieved the highest score was appointed to office.
Yǎn once obtained the highest score.
The Sovereign said:
"This is an omen of a High Chancellor!"
He was promoted to Administrator of the Bureau of Military Affairs (Zhī Shūmìyuàn Shì),
awarded the title Meritorious Minister Who Managed the State and Assisted the Dynasty (Jīngbāng Zuǒyùn Gōngchén),
and enfeoffed as Duke of Yuègúo (Yuègúo Gōng).
He compiled seventy volumes of the Veritable Records of the Imperial Dynasty (Huángcháo Shílù).
was critically ill.
Yǎn, along with the Northern Chancellery Commissioner (Běiyuàn Shūmìshǐ) Āsī, jointly received the dying command.
In the third year of Qiántǒng,
he was transferred and enfeoffed as the Prince of Qín Guó.
In the sixth year,
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Qīshuǐ Commandery (Qīshuǐ Jùnwáng).
During the Tiānqìng period,
due to illness,
he was commanded to enter the court riding a small carriage.
When his illness became severe,
a Grand Physician was dispatched to examine him.
Upon his demise,
he was posthumously granted the title Shàngfǔ,
with the posthumous name Zhōngyì.
Yǎn was always honest and clean,
taking not a single thing from others.
He could memorize classics and books after a single reading.
Moreover, he was skilled at observing the intentions of the sovereign.
His wife, Xíng Shì, was beautiful
and often entered and exited the palace inner quarters.
Yǎn instructed her, saying:
"Be careful not to displease the Emperor!"
Because of this, his authority and favor became even stronger.
He had three sons: Chǔzhēn,
Assistant Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Tàicháng Shàoqīng);
Chǔlián,
Acting Deputy Defender of the Central Capital (Tóngzhī Zhōngjīng Liúshǒushì);
Chǔnéng,
Assistant Supervisor of the Imperial Treasury (Shǎofǔ Shàojiān).
Liú Shēn,
courtesy name Jìshí,
was a native of Wǎnpíng.
He was clever and insightful in his youth,
and as an adult became known for his literary skill.
In the fifth year of Chóngxī,
he passed the civil service examination (Jìnshì grade),
and successively served as Secretary to the Military Commissioner of the Zhāngwǔ Army (Zhāngwǔ Jūn Jiédùshǐ Zhǎngshūjì) and Chief Justice (Dàlǐ Zhèng).
While reporting a legal case,
the Emperor happened to be speaking with his close ministers
and did not pay attention.
Shēn stepped forward and said:
"Your subject hears that since ancient times, Emperors and Kings must value the lives of the people.
I request Your Majesty review your subject's report."
The Emperor was greatly surprised and impressed,
promoting him to Director of the Chancellery (Shūmì Dūchéngzhǐ),
and temporarily serving as Deputy Defender of the Central Capital (Quán Zhōngjīng Fù Liúshǒu).
An edict commanded the relocation of wealthy citizens to populate Chūn and Tài prefectures.
Shēn believed this was improper
and memorialized to have the order abolished.
He was transferred to Assistant Minister of Justice (Dàlǐ Shàoqīng);
people considered him free of wrongful accusations.
He was promoted to Minister of Justice (Dàlǐ Qīng),
and then appointed Deputy Defender of the Western Capital (Xījīng Fù Liúshǒu).
Due to mourning for his father,
after completing the mourning period,
he was made Vice Commissioner of the Three Bureaus (Sānsī Fùshǐ),
given the additional rank of Grand Master of Remonstrance (Jiànyì Dàfū),
and made Supervisor of the Court of Judicial Review (Tídiǎn Dàlǐ Sì).
As Shēn was clear in the law yet merciful,
the number of people saved from wrongful verdicts in the cases he handled was great.
He was transferred to Deputy Defender of the Southern Capital (Nánjīng Fù Liúshǒu).
Soon after, he was appointed Military Commissioner of the Chóngyì Army (Chóngyì Jūn Jiédùshǐ);
his administration was simple and quiet,
the people were not troubled,
leading to the unusual sight of crows and magpies nesting together.
He was praised in a special edict.
He was appointed Commissioner of Revenue (Hùbù Shǐ);
the annual surplus revenue reached three hundred thousand *mín* in cash.
He was appointed Vice Commissioner of the Southern Chancellery (Nányuàn Shūmì Fùshǐ).
Dàozōng once said to his ministers:
"Those who are loyal and upright today
are none other than Yēlǜ Jué and Liú Shēn!"
The Chancellor Yáng Jì congratulated [the Emperor] on having found such a man,
and Shēn was appointed Administrator of Governmental Affairs (Cānzhī Zhèngshì).
The Emperor admonished him, saying:
"You must not fear the Chancellor!"
At that time, the power and influence of the Northern Chancellery Commissioner Yǐ Xīn was flourishing.
Shēn memorialized, saying:
"I do not even fear Yǐ Xīn,
why should I fear the Chancellor!"
Yǐ Xīn resented this,
and together with others, he attacked and defamed Shēn,
who was sent out to serve as Military Commissioner of the Bǎojìng Army (Bǎojìng Jūn Jiédùshǐ).
The Emperor ultimately wished to employ him greatly,
granting him the title Grand Tutor to the Heir Apparent (Shǒu Tàizǐ Tàibǎo),
and transferring him to Defender of the Supreme Capital (Shàngjīng Liúshǒu).
Yǐ Xīn was later transferred due to an incident to govern Xióngwǔ,
and Shēn subsequently retired holding the title of Military Commissioner of the Chóngyì Army.
Coincidentally, the people of Yān and Jì were starving.
Shēn, along with the retired officials Zhào Huī and Hán Zào, provided gruel daily for relief.
The number of people saved could not be calculated.
He died in the second year of Dà'ān.
The Emperor was deeply distressed and mourned,
and his funeral grants and posthumous gifts were increased.
Yēlǜ Húlǚ,
courtesy name Sūsā,
was from the Hóngyì Palace Division.
His ancestor, Yùwěn,
had performed meritorious service assisting Tàizǔ
and was made the Yílíjǐn of the Diéliè Tribe.
His father, Yáng Wǔ,
was the Grand General of the Left Guard of Palace Gates (Zuǒ Jiānmén Wèi Dàjiàngjūn).
Húlǚ was humble and prudent by nature
and had no favorites or enemies among people.
Late in the Chóngxī era,
he was appointed to the Imperial Bedchamber Retainers.
Due to his excellent service,
he repeatedly held prestigious and important posts,
and was promoted to Grand General of the Ox-Rider Guard (Qiānniú Wèi Dàjiàngjūn).
During the Dà'ān period,
when Mólǔsī, the chieftain of the Northern Zǔpǔ, rebelled,
Húlǚ was made Commandant for Pacification (Zhāotǎo Dūjiān),
and together with Yēlǜ Nàyě, he led two thousand elite cavalry to suppress the revolt.
For his merit, he was made Deputy Commander of the Southern Imperial Residence (Hànrén Xínggōng Fù Bùshǔ),
concurrently overseeing the affairs of the Tàihé Palace.
He retired,
was granted the additional title of Grand Councilor (Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì),
and died.
Commentary states: Wùnà, during Dàozōng's confused and uncertain period,
supported and protected the Imperial Grandson,
preventing Yǐ Xīn's wicked schemes from succeeding again,
thus ensuring the continuation of the Liáo dynasty.
Comparing him to Wūzhì establishing Mùzōng,
this is not excessive praise.
Yǎn governed with outstanding talent,
and everywhere he went he earned a reputation for competence.
In compiling the History of Liáo (Liáo Shǐ),
detailing the order and chaos of a dynasty,
he can be said to have been diligent.
However, in order to secure imperial favor,
he could not regulate his household according to proper rites—
what a pity!
Liú Shēn served three times in the Court of Judicial Review (Dàlǐ),
and the people suffered no injustice.
Once appointed to the Ministry of Revenue (Hùbù),
both the government and the people were prosperous.
To be jointly praised alongside Yēlǜ Jué as loyal and upright,
is this not fitting?
Biographies Twenty-Nine: Xiāo Yánshòu, Yēlǜ Sālā, Xiāo Sùsā, Yēlǜ Tàbùyě, Xiāo Tàbùyě, Xiāo Hūgǔ, Yēlǜ Shíliǔ.
Xiāo Yánshòu
was a member of the Yǐshì Tribe.
His nature was firm and upright,
and he valued spirit and vigor.
He served during the end of the Chóngxī era.
When Dàozōng ascended the throne,
the Empress Dowager (Huáng Tàihòu) frequently praised his worthiness,
and thus he was promoted.
When the Emperor went out for hunting and martial exercises,
Yánshòu oversaw the affairs,
never showing partiality.
The Emperor respected him even more.
He successively held the posts of Grand Tutor of the Civil Staff (Wénbān Tàibǎo) and Acting Commissioner of the Chancellery (Tóngzhī Shūmìyuàn Shì).
In the fourth year of Xiányōng,
he followed Yēlǜ Rénxiān to attack the Zǔpǔ,
and defeated them.
An edict ordered the troops to remain stationed there,
but many soldiers deserted and returned.
Because of this, he was demoted two ranks.
In the tenth year,
he performed meritorious service suppressing the Díliè Tribe,
and was made Military Commissioner (Jiédùshǐ) of that tribe.
In the first year of Dàkāng,
he was appointed Acting Commissioner of the Southern Chancellery (Tóngzhī Nányuàn Xuānhuīshǐ Shì),
and transferred to Northern Minister (Běimiàn Línyá).
He secretly memorialized that Yǐ Xīn, seeing the Crown Prince oversee state affairs,
felt uneasy,
and frequently visited and associated with Zhāng Xiàojié.
He feared they had a conspiracy
to destabilize the Crown Prince.
The Emperor realized the situation
and sent Yǐ Xīn out to be the Defender of the Central Capital (Zhōngjīng Liúshǒu).
Coincidentally, it was Yǐ Xīn's birthday.
The Emperor dispatched his close minister, Yēlǜ Báisīběn, to bestow gifts for the occasion.
Yǐ Xīn then secretly instructed Báisīběn to report to the Emperor:
"Your subject sees treacherous men at court,
and Your Majesty is isolated and in danger.
Although my body is outside the capital,
I secretly worry deeply."
Báisīběn returned
and reported this.
The Emperor sent someone to bestow a carriage upon Yǐ Xīn,
admonishing him, saying:
"Have no fear that you will not be employed;
you shall soon be recalled."
Because of this, the Emperor instead grew suspicious of Yánshòu
and sent him out to serve as Military Commissioner of the Shùnyì Army (Shùnyì Jūn Jiédùshǐ).
Yǐ Xīn returned to court and was again made Chancellery Commissioner (Shūmìshǐ),
banishing Yánshòu to Wūkuí Circuit,
where he was confined and forced to labor for life.
Although Yánshòu was banished,
he constantly worried about the state.
People at the time created a saying about it:
"If wolves herd the sheep,
how can stability endure?"
Three years later,
Yǐ Xīn falsely accused Yánshòu of plotting deposition and establishment,
had him arrested and brought back, and then killed him
at the age of forty-nine.
During the *Gāntǒng* period,
he was posthumously granted the title of *Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì*,
and his portrait was hung in the *Yífú* Hall.
*Xiāo Yánshòu* was upright and honest,
openly debating and remonstrating in court.
He frequently clashed with *Yēlǜ Yǐxīn*,
and therefore met with disaster.
*Yēlǜ Sālā*,
courtesy name *Dǒngyǐn*,
was the grandson of *Nányuàn Dàwáng* (King of the Southern Chancellery) *Mólǔgǔ*.
His nature was loyal, upright, and deep.
Early in the *Qīngníng* era,
he was successively promoted to *Xīnánmiàn Zhāotǎoshǐ* (Commissioner of Pacification for the Southwest Circuit),
where he was known for his governance.
In the ninth year of *Xiányōng* (1073),
he was appointed *Běiyuàn Dàwáng* (King of the Northern Chancellery).
Not long after,
he served as *Qìdān Xínggōng Dūbùshǔ* (Commander-in-Chief of the Khitan Traveling Palace).
In the second year of *Dàkāng* (1076),
when *Yēlǜ Yǐxīn* served as *Zhōngjīng Liúshǒu* (Viceroy of the Central Capital),
an imperial edict commanded the officials to deliberate in court,
whether they should recall him.
None of the officials dared to speak honestly.
*Sālā* alone submitted a memorial, saying:
“*Xiāo Yánshòu* stated that *Yǐxīn* was guilty
and should not be a minister of the Privy Council,
which is why Your Majesty dismissed him;
if he is recalled now,
I fear the realm will harbor suspicion.”
He presented this remonstrance three times,
but it was not accepted.
Those around him were startled and terrified by his boldness.
*Yǐxīn* was again made *Shūmìshǐ* (Commissioner of Military Affairs).
When he met *Sālā*, he reproached him, saying:
“I have no grievance with you,
why were you the only one to voice a differing opinion?”
*Sālā* replied:
“This was a consideration for the state (*Shèjì*);
what grievance could there be!”
*Yǐxīn* falsely accused *Sālā* of conspiring with *Sùsā* to depose and enthrone an emperor.
An imperial investigation found no evidence,
so he was sent out to be *Shǐpíngjūn Jiédùshǐ* (Military Commissioner of Shǐpíng Commandery).
When *Xiāo Éduō* later submitted a false denunciation,
an envoy was eventually dispatched to kill him.
During the *Gāntǒng* period,
he was posthumously enfeoffed as *Qīshuǐ Jùnwáng* (Prince of Qīshuǐ Commandery),
his portrait was hung in the *Yífú* Hall,
and the official ranks and titles of his three sons were also posthumously restored.
*Xiāo Sùsā*,
courtesy name *Tūlǔjǐn*,
was a man of the *Tūlǚbù* tribe.
His nature was deep and resolute.
During the *Chóngxī* era,
he was successively promoted to *Yòu Hùwèi Tàibǎo* (Grand Protector of the Right Guard).
When *Púnúlǐ* rebelled,
he followed *Yēlǜ Yìxiān* to suppress them,
capturing *Táodélǐ*, the leader of the rebels, and returning.
In the middle of the *Qīngníng* era,
he served successively as *Běimiàn Línyá* (Northern Circuit Chancellor) and *Zhāngguójūn Jiédùshǐ*,
and then entered court to become *Běiyuàn Shūmì Fùshǐ* (Vice Commissioner of Military Affairs of the Northern Chancellery).
In the tenth year of *Xiányōng* (1074),
he managed the southwest border,
dismantling the Song fortifications,
and garrisoning them with *Píshì* troops.
The Emperor praised him for this.
In the second year of *Dàkāng* (1076),
he was appointed to supervise the affairs of the *Běiyuàn Shūmìshǐ*.
*Yēlǜ Yǐxīn*'s power and favor were then flourishing,
and many who attached themselves to him attained prominence;
but *Sùsā* never once visited his gate.
*Yǐxīn* resented this,
and falsely accused *Sùsā* of being the primary plotter in the scheme to depose and enthrone.
An investigation found no proof,
so he was sent out to be *Shàngjīng Liúshǒu* (Viceroy of the Supreme Capital).
*Yǐxīn* then ordered *Xiāo Éduō* to submit a false denunciation using the previous charges.
The Emperor became angry
and conducted no further interrogation,
but dispatched an envoy to kill him.
It was high summer at that time,
and his corpse lay in the fields,
but his countenance did not change,
and magpies and crows dared not approach him.
During the *Gāntǒng* period,
he was posthumously enfeoffed as *Lánlíng Jùnwáng* (Prince of Lánlíng Commandery),
and his portrait was hung in the *Yífú* Hall.
*Yēlǜ Tàbùyě*,
courtesy name *Sābān*,
was descended from the lineage of the paternal uncle (*Jìfù Fáng*).
His father was *Gāojiā*.
He served up to the rank of *Línyá* (Chancellor).
During the *Chóngxī* era, he had merit in defeating the Xīa people at *Jīnsù Jūn*,
and was generously rewarded.
*Tàbùyě*,
in the middle of the *Qīngníng* era, was appointed *Páiyìn Lángjūn* (Gentleman of the Seal and Tablet),
and was successively promoted to *Yǒngxīng Gōngshǐ* (Director of Yǒngxīng Palace).
In the ninth year (1063),
he suppressed the rebellion of *Zhòngyuán*.
Due to his merit, he was appointed to supervise the affairs of the *Diǎnjiǎn Sī*,
was granted the title of Meritous Official for Pacifying the Rebellion,
and served as *Huáidéjūn Jiédùshǐ* (Military Commissioner of Huáidé Commandery).
In the fifth year of *Xiányōng* (1069),
he was moved to *Yáoliǎn Kè* (Yáoliǎn Overseer).
In the third year of *Dàkāng* (1077),
he was appointed *Běiyuàn Xuānhuīshǐ* (Commissioner of Ceremonies of the Northern Chancellery).
*Yēlǜ Yǐxīn* plotted to harm the Crown Prince.
*Tàbùyě* knew of his treachery
and wished to kill *Yǐxīn*, along with *Xiāo Tèlǐdé*,
and *Xiāo Shísān*, etc.
*Yǐxīn* learned of this
and ordered his faction to falsely accuse *Tàbùyě* of involvement in the conspiracy to depose and enthrone,
and subsequently had him killed.
During the *Gāntǒng* period,
he was posthumously enfeoffed as *Qīshuǐ Jùnwáng* (Prince of Qīshuǐ Commandery),
and his portrait was hung in the *Yífú* Hall.
*Xiāo Tàbùyě*,
courtesy name *Wòlǐduān*,
was the grandson of *Guójiù Jùnwáng* (Imperial Maternal Uncle and Prince of a Commandery) *Gāo Jiǔ*.
His nature was firm and upright.
In the middle of the *Xiányōng* era,
he was appointed *Zhīhòu Lángjūn* (Gentleman-in-Waiting).
In the first year of *Dàkāng* (1075),
he served as *Zhāngmǐn Gōngshǐ* (Director of Zhāngmǐn Palace),
married the Princess of *Zhàoguó*,
and was granted the title of *Fùmǎ Dūwèi* (Imperial Son-in-Law Commandant).
In the third year (1077),
he was changed to *Tóngzhī Hàngrén Xínggōng Dūbùshǔ* (Joint Supervisor of the Commander-in-Chief of the Han People's Traveling Palace).
He was on good terms with *Běiyuàn Xuānhuīshǐ* *Yēlǜ Tàbùyě*.
*Yǐxīn* was jealous of this
and ordered someone to falsely accuse him of plotting to depose and enthrone.
Unable to endure the severe beating and torture,
he falsely confessed.
When the Emperor brought him in for questioning,
he was confused and unable to articulate his defense,
and was consequently killed.
During the *Gāntǒng* period,
he was posthumously enfeoffed as *Lánlíng Jùnwáng* (Prince of Lánlíng Commandery),
and his portrait was hung in the *Yífú* Hall.
*Xiāo Hūgǔ*,
courtesy name *Āsīlián*,
was loyal and upright by nature,
and quick and powerful.
As soon as he reached manhood,
he was assigned to the Imperial Guards.
Early in the *Xiányōng* era,
he followed *Zhāotǎoshǐ* (Commissioner of Pacification) *Yēlǜ Zhàosān* to attack the tribal groups who disobeyed imperial orders.
When they requested surrender,
an envoy came who was able to leap onto the hump of a camel,
exhibiting his nimbleness and quickness.
*Zhàosān* asked those around him who could do this.
*Hūgǔ* donned heavy armor and stepped forward.
His hands did not touch the hump,
but in one leap, he was atop it.
The envoy was greatly shocked.
*Zhàosān* gave him his daughter in marriage.
The Emperor heard of this
and summoned him to be a Guard.
At that time, *Běiyuàn Shūmìshǐ* *Yēlǜ Yǐxīn* had gained favor through cunning and treachery,
and acted with unrestrained violence.
*Hūgǔ* hid beneath a bridge,
watching for him to pass,
intending to kill him.
Suddenly, heavy rain destroyed the bridge,
and the plan failed.
Later, he again planned to kill him during a hunt,
but was dissuaded by friends and relatives.
In the third year of *Dàkāng* (1077),
he again planned to kill *Yǐxīn* and *Xiāo Délǐtè*, etc.
*Yǐxīn* learned of this and shackled him.
Though subjected to investigation and torture, he did not confess,
and was banished to the border.
When the Crown Prince was deposed and exiled to the Supreme Capital (*Shàngjīng*),
*Hūgǔ* was summoned
and killed.
Early in the *Gāntǒng* era,
he was posthumously granted the title of *Lónghǔwèi Shàng Jiāngjūn* (Superior General of the Dragon Tiger Guard).
*Yēlǜ Shíliǔ*,
courtesy name *Chóuwǎn*,
was a man of the Six Tribes (*Liùyuàn Bù*).
His grandfather, *Dúkè*,
was *Nányuàn Dàwáng*.
His father, *Ānshí*,
was *Tǒngjūn Fùshǐ* (Vice Commissioner of Military Command).
*Shíliǔ*'s nature was firm and upright,
and he possessed ambitions for managing the world.
He began his career as *Páiyìn Lángjūn*.
Early in the *Dàkāng* era,
he became *Yílíbì Lángjūn* (Gentleman of the *Yílíbì*).
At that time, *Shūmìshǐ* *Yēlǜ Yǐxīn* falsely accused and killed the Empress,
plotted to depose the Crown Prince,
dismissed loyal and worthy officials,
and promoted treacherous partisans.
*Shíliǔ* despised his actions,
and *Yǐxīn* became aware of this.
After the Crown Prince was deposed,
*Shíliǔ* was accused of being affiliated with the Crown Prince
and banished to *Zhènzhōu*.
Tiānzuò ascended the throne,
and summoned [Shí Liǔ] to serve as the Censor-in-Chief (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng).
At that time, they were still prosecuting the faction of Yǐxīn (Yēlǜ Yǐxīn),
but the relevant authorities did not treat it seriously.
Shí Liǔ submitted a memorial, saying: "I was previously framed by wicked officials,
and banished to a frontier commandery.
Fortunately, I have been summoned back to service.
I dare not remain silent.
When rewards and favors are clear, worthy men are encouraged.
When punishments are fitting, wicked men disappear.
When these two principles are established,
the world will be governed without undue effort.
I observed Yēlǜ Yǐxīn,
though originating from humble beginnings,
rising to a position of critical importance,
usurping power and committing unchecked evil,
too numerous to describe fully.
He obscured the sagacity of the Former Emperor,
falsely implicated Shùnshèng,
contrived to harm loyal and upright men,
ruined the state
and deceived the sovereign—
a situation unprecedented since antiquity.
Relying on the good fortune of the ancestral temples and the altars of the soil and grain,
Your Majesty has been able to inherit and complete the great enterprise,
and grievances accumulated over many years
were suddenly cleared away.
This is precisely the time for Your Majesty's decisive wisdom
to fulfill the way of filial piety.
For instance, Xiāo Déyòu was truly a member of the Yǐxīn faction,
and Yēlǜ Hélǔ did not clarify this early enough.
Relying on Your Majesty’s sagacity,
the matter
was finally rectified.
I observe that Your Majesty harbors many doubts,
thus the responsible officials hesitate and look around,
and do not press the investigation thoroughly.
Yǐxīn, during the reign of the Former Emperor,
possessed incomparable power and favor.
If the Former Emperor truly believed Shùn
Kǎo was guilty,
then Yǐxīn would be a meritorious minister.
How then could Your Majesty have succeeded to the throne?
The Former Emperor deposed and banished the favored Empress,
and decreed that Your Majesty should remain at his side.
This indicates that he also regretted his former errors.
How can Your Majesty forget his father's vengeance and not seek retribution,
or treat the rebellious faction leniently and not execute them?
Now, the spiritual remains have not yet been recovered,
yet the search for them is not thorough.
The Tradition says,
'Among the virtues of the sage,
none surpasses filial piety.'
Formerly, Emperor Dézōng of Táng lost his mother due to chaos,
and his yearning and grief
further demonstrated his filial path.
The Duke of Zhōu (Zhōu Gōng) executed Fēilián and Èlái,
and the world rejoiced greatly.
Currently, the rebellious faction has not been eliminated,
and the great grievance has not been avenged.
Above, there is no way to console the spirit of Shùn Kǎo;
below, there is no way to release the indignation of the world.
Resentful energy gathers above,
causing floods and droughts
as calamities.
I request that Your Majesty issue a clear decree,
search for the burial place of Shùn Kǎo,
and round up the entire rebellious faction to rectify the laws of the state,
thus gratifying the hearts of loyal and righteous people across the four directions,
and making manifest the state's use of rewards
and punishments.
Only then can the path to achieving good governance be carried out."
"I respectfully append a separate record detailing the ascent to heaven of Shùnshèng and the actions of Yǐxīn and his group,
presenting this, risking death, for your consideration."
The memorial was submitted but received no reply.
Those who heard about it were filled with sorrow and regret.
During the Qiántǒng reign period,
he was remotely appointed Military Commissioner (Jiédùshǐ) of the Jìngjiāng Army,
and he died.
His son, Mǎgē,
served as Acting Chancellor (Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāng Shì).
The Appraisal states: The *Yì* (Book of Changes) says,
"Tread upon the frost,
and hard ice arrives,"
meaning one must be careful at the beginning.
Had Dàozōng been able to heed the remonstrances of Yánshòu and Sālā,
how could the Empress have been falsely accused,
and how could the Crown Prince have been deposed?
Sùsā and Tàbùyě were killed for their loyal words.
If the state desires to avoid chaos,
is that achievable?
Shí Liǔ's memorial
fortunately appeared after Yǐxīn was already defeated,
allowing his proposals to be put forth.
Those who possess the state
must surely know men!
Biographies, Chapter 30: Yēlǜ Tánggǔ, Xiāo Délǐdǐ, Xiāo Chóuwò, Yēlǜ Zhāngnú, Yēlǜ Zhúzhě
Yēlǜ Tánggǔ,
courtesy name Púsùwǎn,
was a descendant of Gélà, a Chief (Lángjūn) of the Six Divisions.
During the Dàkāng reign period,
he was appointed to his native division as a Chief,
and subsequently promoted incrementally to Great General (Dàjiāngjūn).
His nature was straightforward and frank;
he liked to distinguish black from white.
If anyone behaved improperly,
he would speak his mind completely without reservation.
At the time he was nicknamed
"Strong Tánggǔ."
While serving at court, he repeatedly criticized the merits and failings of the Chief Ministers.
Due to this, he was not promoted for a long time.
Later, he was sent out to be the Commandant of the Northwest Garrison.
In the third year of Qiántǒng (1103),
Xiāo Délǐdǐ served as the Commissioner of Pacification of the Northwest Circuit,
and, relying on his kinship with the Empress's family, he treated his subordinates and officials arrogantly and insultingly.
Tánggǔ refused to yield,
and Délǐdǐ dismissed him.
Tánggǔ brought the case before the court,
but it was not investigated.
Early in the Tiānqìng reign period,
the Wūgǔ Díliè rebelled.
He was summoned and appointed Military Commissioner of the Wūgǔ Tribe.
Upon arriving at the tribe,
he persuaded them to surrender.
He then used his private wealth and drew upon the stored provisions of wealthy citizens
to relieve the destitution of the people.
The tribal people were greatly pleased,
and he was promoted to Upper General Who Guards the State.
Subsequently, when Xiāo Délǐdǐ, leading troops as Commander-in-Chief, was defeated in battle against the Jīn people,
Tánggǔ requested that he be judged according to military law.
He also said:
"Although I am old,
I wish to destroy the enemy for the state."
This was not accepted.
In the first year of Bǎodà (1121),
he requested retirement.
The following year,
Tiānzuò fled.
Tánggǔ met with him at Dǎotā Lǐng,
and wept for the emperor.
The emperor comforted him and bade him stop,
and reappointed him Military Commissioner of the Wūgǔ Tribe.
When he arrived at the tribe,
the Díliè came to attack with five thousand men.
Tánggǔ led his household servants and defeated them.
He was promoted to Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince.
He died at the age of seventy-two.
Xiāo Délǐdǐ,
courtesy name Jiūlín,
was the grandson of the Prince of Jìn, Xiào Xiān.
His father, Sābō,
held various high offices.
Délǐdǐ was short and hunchbacked,
outwardly cautious but inwardly arrogant.
During the Dàkāng reign period,
he was appointed Guard Chief,
gradually promoted to Deputy Commissioner of Xīngshèng Palace,
and concurrently Acting Director of the Censorate.
During the Dà'ān reign period,
the consort of the Prince of Yān gave birth to a son.
Because Délǐdǐ was the consort's uncle,
he successively held the posts of Military Commissioner of the Níngyuǎn Army and Commissioner of Chángníng Palace.
In the second year of Shòulóng (1096),
he supervised the punitive expedition against the Dálǐdé and Bāsīmǔ tribes.
He returned with many captives,
and was transferred to Acting Resident Administrator of the Southern Capital.
In the first year of Qiántǒng (1101),
he was appointed Northern Chancellor and Acting Director of the Northern Bureau of Military Affairs.
He received an imperial decree to jointly prosecute the remaining members of the Yǐxīn faction alongside Yēlǜ Āsī, the Commissioner of the Northern Bureau of Military Affairs.
Āsī accepted bribes,
allowing many criminals to escape punishment.
Délǐdǐ could not control him,
and simply went along with him.
In the fourth year (1104),
he became Director of the Northern Bureau of Military Affairs.
When the Prince of Xià, Lǐ Qiánshùn, was attacked by Sòng,
he sent an envoy to request mediation for peace.
An imperial decree ordered Délǐdǐ and Niú Wēnshū, the Commissioner of the Southern Bureau of Military Affairs, to be envoys to Sòng to settle the matter.
Once Sòng agreed,
on the day Délǐdǐ received the document,
he said:
"I was initially ordered to obtain the essential terms and return.
If I do not see the contents of the document,
how dare I return empty-handed?"
He then opened the envelope and read it in the presence of the Sòng ruler.
After returning,
the court consensus considered this proper.
In the third year of Tiānqìng (1113),
he was given the honorary title of Minister of Education,
and enfeoffed as Prince of Lánlíng Commandery.
(女直) first arose,
and many court officials wished to take advantage of their lack of preparation
to raise troops and go on a punitive expedition;
but Déldǐdǐ (得里底) alone discouraged this,
which led ultimately to defeat and rout.
Tiānzuò (天祚) considered that Déldǐdǐ (得里底) did not meet popular expectations,
and sent him out as the Southwest Circuit Pacification Commissioner (Xīnánmiàn Zhāotǎoshǐ).
In the eighth year,
he was recalled to serve as Commissioner of Military Affairs of the Northern Chancellery (Běiyuàn Shūmìshǐ),
and the Emperor’s favor and trust became profound.
At this time,
the various circuits were in great chaos,
and petitions reporting urgent crises arrived one after another,
but Déldǐdǐ (得里底) did not immediately report them to the Emperor,
nor were those who had achieved merit duly recognized.
Because of this, the generals and officers resented and were angry,
and the men lacked the will to fight.
In the second year of Bǎodà (保大) (1122),
Jīn (金) troops reached the east of the ridge (Lǐngdōng).
At the time, the plot by Yēlǜ Sābā (耶律撒八), Xíqí Sābá (習騎撒跋), and others to enthrone Āolúwò (敖盧斡), the Prince of Jìn (Jìn Wáng), was exposed,
and the Emperor summoned Déldǐdǐ (得里底) and discussed it, saying:
"The rebels must use this boy's name,
if he is not eliminated,
how can we achieve safety?"
Déldǐdǐ (得里底) merely assented repeatedly,
but ultimately did not utter a single word in justification [for the Prince].
Once the Prince was dead,
people's hearts became even more alienated.
Jīn troops crossed the ridge,
and Tiānzuò (天祚) led the guard troops and fled west.
The Primary Consort Xiāo Shì (蕭氏),
who was Déldǐdǐ's (得里底) niece,
said to Déldǐdǐ (得里底):
"You held national governance,
bringing the sovereign to this point,
why should you remain alive!"
Déldǐdǐ (得里底) only apologized,
and could not reply.
The next day,
Tiānzuò (天祚) grew angry,
and banished Déldǐdǐ (得里底) and his son Mosā (麼撒).
After Déldǐdǐ (得里底) had left,
he was seized by Yēlǜ Gāoshānnú (耶律高山奴) and sent to the Jīn troops.
Déldǐdǐ (得里底) watched for the guards to become lax,
broke free and fled back,
but was again captured by Yēlǜ Jiǔjīn (耶律九斤),
and sent to Yēlǜ Chún (耶律淳).
At that time, Chún (淳) had already usurped the title [of Emperor],
Déldǐdǐ (得里底), knowing he could not escape,
said deceitfully:
"I cannot serve a usurping ruler!"
He refused food for several days,
and died.
His son Mosā (麼撒)
was killed by Jīn troops.
Xiāo Chóuwò (蕭酬斡),
courtesy name Èlǐběn (訛里本),
was a descendant of the maternal uncle (Guójìu) Junior Father lineage (Shàofǔ Fáng).
His grandfather, Ālà (阿剌),
served until the post of Commissioner of Investigation (Cǎifǎngshǐ).
His father, Biélǐlà (別里剌),
was enfeoffed as the Prince of Zhào (Zhào Wáng) because he was the father of an Empress.
Chóuwò (酬斡) had a majestic appearance,
and his nature was gentle and accommodating.
At age fourteen,
he married the Princess of Yuègúo (Yuègúo Gōngzhǔ),
was appointed Commandant-Escort (Fùmǎ Dūwèi),
and became the Commander (Xiángwěn) of the Attendant Gentleman Division (Zhīhòu Lángjūn Bān).
At age eighteen,
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Lánlíng Commandery (Lánlíng Jùnwáng).
At that time, the Emperor wished to establish the Imperial Grandson as heir,
and fearing that he would have no means to dispel the suspicion of the world,
he sent Chóuwò (酬斡) out as Commander of the Imperial Maternal Uncles (Guójìu Xiángwěn),
demoted the Empress to Consort Huì (Huì Fēi),
and relocated her to Qiánzhōu (乾州).
Previously, when Chóuwò's (酬斡) mother entered the court,
she arbitrarily took postal horses.
When this was discovered,
her enfeoffment title was revoked;
furthermore, she and her younger sister Lǔjiě (魯姐) practiced witchcraft,
and were executed.
An imperial decree ordered Chóuwò (酬斡) to divorce the Princess,
confiscated Xīngshèng Palace (Xīngshèng Gōng),
and exiled him to the Wūgǔdíliè (烏古敵烈) tribe.
During the Tiānqìng (天慶) period,
because his younger sister was reinstated and honored as Grand Consort Dowager (Tàihúang Tàifēi),
Chóuwò (酬斡) was recalled to serve as Commander of the Southern Nǚzhí (Nán Nǚzhí Xiángwěn),
and promoted to Vice Commander-in-Chief for the Eastern Expedition (Zhēngdōng Fùtǒngjūn).
At that time, the Bóhǎi (渤海) people in Guǎngzhōu (廣州) revolted.
[Chóuwò] then, along with Commandant-Escort Xiāo Hánjiānú (蕭韓家奴), attacked them while they were unprepared,
and pacified them.
He further defeated the enemy general Hóu Gài (侯㮣) at Chuānzhōu (川州).
That same year,
Dōngjīng (東京) rebelled.
When they encountered the enemy coming to attack,
the army scattered;
only Chóuwò (酬斡) led a few men under his command in fierce combat,
and died on the battlefield.
He was posthumously granted the title of Superior General of the Dragon and Tiger Guard (Lónghǔ Wèi Shàng Jiāngjūn).
Yēlǜ Zhāngnú (耶律章奴),
courtesy name Tèmòyǎn (特末衍),
was a descendant of the Younger Uncle lineage (Jìfù Fáng).
His father, Chálà (查剌),
maintained a high character and did not serve in office.
Zhāngnú (章奴) was perceptive, quick-witted, and skilled in discussion.
During the Dà'ān (大安) period,
he was appointed to the post of Seal Gentleman (Pái Yìn Lángjūn).
In the first year of Qiántǒng (乾統) (1101),
he was successively promoted to Right Vice Director (Yòu Zhōngchéng),
simultaneously overseeing the duties of the Seal Guard (Pái Yìn Sùzhí).
In the sixth year,
because he was not careful while on night duty,
he was demoted to Deputy Director of the Palace Guest Department (Nèi Kèshěng Shì).
In the fourth year of Tiānqìng (天慶) (1114),
he was appointed Vice Commander-in-Chief of the Northeast Circuit (Dōngběilù Tǒngjūn Fùshǐ).
In the fifth year,
he was transferred to Joint Administrator of Military Affairs of Xiánzhōu Circuit (Xiánzhōu Lù Bīngmǎ Shì).
When Tiānzuò (天祚) personally led the campaign against the Nǚzhí (女直),
Xiāo Húdǔ (蕭胡篤) was the Vanguard Commander-in-Chief (Xiānfēng Dūtǒng),
and Zhāngnú (章奴) was the Area Commander (Dūjiān).
When the main army crossed the Yāzǐ Hé (鴨子河),
Zhāngnú (章奴), together with Xiāo Díli (蕭敵里)—the elder brother of Chún (淳), Prince of Wèigúo (Wèigúo Wáng), and his wife—and his nephew Xiāo Yánliú (蕭延留), plotted to enthrone Chún (淳).
They enticed over three hundred officers and soldiers to defect and return.
Soon after, Tiānzuò (天祚) was defeated by the Nǚzhí (女直).
Zhāngnú (章奴) then dispatched Díli (敵里) and Yánliú (延留) to rush back and report the matter of the deposition and enthronement to Chún (淳).
Chún (淳) hesitated and could not decide.
Just then, Yǐ Xìn (乙信), an envoy from the traveling palace, arrived holding an imperial decree from Tiānzuò (天祚),
fully detailing Zhāngnú's (章奴) rebellion and disobedience.
Chún (淳) wailed and wept before the envoy,
and immediately cut off the heads of Díli (敵里) and Yánliú (延留) and presented them to Tiānzuò (天祚).
Zhāngnú (章奴), seeing that Chún (淳) did not comply,
enticed several hundred bandits to attack and plunder Shàngjīng (上京),
taking treasures from the official treasuries.
Reaching Zǔzhōu (祖州),
he led his subordinates to report to the temple of Tàizǔ (太祖), saying:
"The founding enterprise of our Great Liáo (Dà Liáo)
was completed by Tàizǔ (太祖) through a hundred battles.
Now the realm is crumbling,
and I humbly observe that Chún (淳), Prince of Wèigúo (Wèigúo Wáng), grandson of Emperor Xīngzōng (Xīngzōng Huángdì), possesses exalted and profound virtue,
and is capable of governing the world and bringing peace to the people.
We, your servants, wish to enthrone him to rule the nation.
However, it happened that Chún (淳) merely favored the grasslands [i.e., was cautious],
and the great undertaking was not achieved.
Recently, Tiānzuò (天祚) has pursued nothing but dissipation and pleasure,
neglecting the myriad affairs of state;
powerful enemies commit outrage,
and our armies suffer defeat.
Furthermore, bandits are rising up everywhere,
and the nation is in peril like stacked eggs.
We, your servants, are unworthy members of the Imperial Clan,
having received generations of immense favor.
Above, we desire to comfort the spirits of the Nine Temples,
below, we desire to save the lives of the common people,
hence we have undertaken this action.
This truly originates from utmost sincerity,
and we hope that the successive sages will grant their protection."
Traveling west to Qìngzhōu (慶州),
he again offered sacrifices to the various temples,
and reiterated the reasons for raising troops,
sending circular manifestos to the prefectures and counties, and the officials serving at the imperial tombs.
Soldiers and common folk gradually began to side with him.
At this time, the Bóhǎi (渤海) people of Ráozhōu (饒州) and Hóu Gài (侯㮣), among others, successively came to support him.
The multitude reached tens of thousands,
and they hurried toward Guǎngpíng Diàn (廣平淀).
His followers, Yēlǜ Nǚgǔ (耶律女古) and others, were violent, tyrannical, and lawless,
plundering women, wealth, and livestock.
Zhāngnú (章奴) assessed that he could not control them,
and harbored internal remorse and regret.
Furthermore, he attacked Shàngjīng (上京) but failed to overcome it,
and fled north to the surrendered captives.
Āgǔchǎn (阿鶻產) of the Shuìngúo Nǚzhí (順國女直) led troops in pursuit and defeated him,
killing his general Yēlǜ Mílǐzhí (耶律彌里直),
and capturing over two hundred noble family members.
Their wives and children were assigned to labor in the embroidery bureau,
or dispersed among the court attendants as servants.
The rest who managed to escape all fled.
Zhāngnú (章奴) falsely posed as an envoy,
intending to flee to the Nǚzhí (女直),
but was captured by patrolmen,
bound and sent to the traveling residence,
where he was executed.
Yēlǜ Zhúzhě (耶律朮者),
courtesy name Néngdiǎn (能典),
was a descendant of the Grand King (Yúyuè) Púgǔzhī (蒲古只),
and was imposing, magnificent, and eloquent.
Early in the Qiántǒng (乾統) period,
he was appointed Attendant Gentleman (Zhīhòu Lángjūn).
In the sixth year,
due to the sacrifices (Cháicè),
he was additionally given the post of Commissioner of Investigation (Guāncháshǐ).
In the fifth year of Tiānqìng (天慶) (1115),
he received an edict to supervise Commander-in-Chief Yēlǜ Wòlǐjìn (耶律斡里𩽆) in battle.
When [Wòlǐjìn] was defeated,
he was demoted to the left to Prefect of Yínzhōu (Yínzhōu Cìshǐ),
and then transferred to Commander of Military Discipline at Xiánzhōu (Xiánzhōu Jiū Jiàng).
Once he plotted with Yēlǜ Zhāngnú to install Wèiguó Wáng Chún.
When he heard Zhāngnú had fled from Yāzǐ Hé,
he immediately led several subordinates to meet him.
On the road, he was captured by scouting troops
and sent to the Xíngzài Suǒ.
The Emperor asked:
"In what way have I failed you that you rebelled?"
Shùzhě replied:
"I truly have no personal grievance.
But the world is in great disorder,
no longer held by the Liáo;
petty men fill the court,
and worthy ministers are exiled and banished.
I truly could not bear to see the difficult undertaking of the Tiān Huángdì collapse suddenly.
The reason I took this action, feeling pain to the bone marrow,
was not for my own sake."
Several days later,
he was questioned again.
Shùzhě, with a stern voice, recounted the Emperor’s many faults
and laid out the fundamental reasons for the imminent demise of the state.
Consequently, he was executed.
The judgment states: Among the ministers serving together at the end of the Liáo,
how widely did their good and evil actions diverge!
Tánggǔ was upright and unyielding to influential officials;
in his two postings to Wūgǔ,
his kindness and authority were equally evident.
Chóuwò pacified the rebellion in Bóhǎi
and later died fighting fiercely while suppressing rebels.
His loyalty can be esteemed.
Déldǐdì allowed the Nǚzhí to grow without attacking them,
and suppressed warnings of change, causing them not to be heard.
His actions screened the sagacity of the sovereign
and provided the steps to national chaos;
nothing was more extreme than this.
Zhāngnú and Shùzhě seized a time of great difficulty,
secretly plotted the deposition and installation (of a new emperor),
intending to gain favor and fortune,
thereby committing high treason.
How could they avoid the execution carried out by the empire!
Biography Thirty-One: Xiāo Táosūwò, Yēlǜ Āxībǎo, Xiāo Yǐxuē, Xiāo Húdǔ
Xiāo Táosūwò,
courtesy name Yǐxīnyǐn,
was a man of the Tūlǚbù tribe.
His great-great-grandfather, Yīnjí,
had hair five feet long,
and was
called "Long-Haired Yīnjí" at the time.
His grandfather, Lǐbá,
was the Jiédù Shǐ of the Àowěi tribe.
Táosūwò was cautious and prudent,
and did not form reckless associations.
His uncle, Liúgē, was dismissed from office due to an incident.
Hearing of Chóngyuán’s rebellion,
he took his family to the Xíngzài Suǒ.
Although Táosūwò was young at the time,
he was already like an adult,
and was appointed as a junior scribe.
He was repeatedly promoted to Zhīhòu Lángjūn,
and then transferred to the Shūmì Yuàn as a Shìyù.
In the fifth year of Xiányōng (1069),
he was promoted to Chóngdé Gōng Shǐ.
There were people who complained that the Běi Nán Yuàn were unjust in hearing lawsuits.
When the matter was sent down,
Táosūwò corrected all of them,
which led to Yēlǜ Āsī becoming jealous of him.
Whenever the Emperor wanted to appoint him,
Āsī always thwarted it.
In the eighth year (1072),
he successively served as Tàibǎo of the Horse Herds at Huá Shuǐ, north of Mò Běi.
He was not promoted for several years,
and once said:
"If my talents cannot be fully utilized,
it is better to be idle."
During the Qiántǒng era (1101–1110),
he was promoted to Tàibǎo of the Horse Herds south of Mò Nán.
Because a great wind damaged the grass,
many horses died,
and he was whipped three hundred times
and dismissed from office.
In the ninth year (1109),
he was transferred to guard the Tiānqí Diàn Sùwèi.
The following year,
grain prices soared,
and many of the guards were unable to sustain themselves.
Táosūwò used his private granary to aid them,
and was summoned to serve as Tóngzhī Nányuàn Shūmì Shǐ Shì.
In the fourth year of Tiānqìng (1114),
he became the Hànrén Xínggōng Fùbùshǔ.
At that time, the Jīn army had just risen
and attacked and captured Níngjiāng Zhōu.
Tiānzuò summoned his officials to deliberate.
Táosūwò said:
"Although the Nǚzhí state is small,
its people are brave and skilled archers.
Since they captured our rebel Xiāo Hǎilǐ,
their power has only increased.
Our troops have long been untrained.
If they meet a strong enemy
and suffer the slightest disadvantage,
the various tribes will become disloyal
and ungovernable.
As for the current strategy,
nothing would be better than greatly mobilizing the troops from all circuits
to suppress them with power,
which might make them submit."
Běiyuàn Shūmì Shǐ Xiāo Déldǐdì said:
"A plan like Táosūwò's
merely demonstrates weakness.
Just dispatching the troops north of Huá Shuǐ
will be enough to resist them."
Consequently, his plan was not adopted.
Within a few months,
the border troops were repeatedly defeated,
and the populace became increasingly uneasy.
The Bóhǎi people in Ráozhōu established the Tóuxià city structure and rebelled,
fielding more than thirty thousand infantry and cavalry,
and refused to submit when summoned.
Táosūwò led troops to suppress them,
captured their leader,
executed several thousand people,
recovered the plundered goods,
and returned all of them to their owners.
When Yēlǜ Zhāngnú rebelled,
Táosūwò and the Liúshǒu Yēlǜ Dàbēinú maintained the defense.
After Zhāngnú was pacified,
Táosūwò requested:
"Now the border troops are lax and undisciplined.
If we clear the area west of the Qīngshǔ Lǐng,
the Hàn people will gather and revolt,
and the hearts of the populace will be further unsettled.
I foolishly believe this campaign should be abandoned."
The request was not accepted.
Instead, Táosūwò was ordered to command and control the eastern route
and recruit scattered soldiers.
Later, he retired as Tàizǐ Tàifù
and died.
Yēlǜ Āxībǎo,
courtesy name Tèlǐdiǎn,
was a man of the Wǔyuàn tribe.
His grandfather, Húliè,
moved to the Northwest Department during the reign of Tàizǔ,
and his family served as clerks in the Zhāotǎo Sī Lì for generations.
Āxībǎo was fervent and had great ambitions.
At the age of sixteen,
due to his ability, he was appointed Nèishǐ.
Early in the Tiānqìng era (c. 1111),
he was transferred to Shūmì Yuàn Shìyù.
When the Jīn people mobilized their army near the border city,
Āxībǎo was sent to question them.
The Jīn people said:
"If Āshū returns,
how dare we disobey orders."
Āxībǎo fully reported this.
When the Jīn army captured Níngjiāng Zhōu
and the border forces were repeatedly defeated,
Āxībǎo and Yēlǜ Zhāngnú, among others, were dispatched eastward carrying a letter,
hoping to coerce them into submission.
Āxībǎo said:
"When I was sent on the previous mission,
I explained the imperial decree,
but they did not yield at all.
When I was about to return,
they said to me: 'If your requests are not fulfilled,
do not attempt to see us again.'
I now request to go alone."
This was not permitted.
As he was about to depart,
he bid farewell to Xiāo Déldǐdì and said:
"This unworthy servant is heading to a foreign country
and will certainly not return alive.
I hope you will assist the state well."
Upon arrival,
Āxībǎo was captured.
After a long time, he managed to escape and return.
When Tiānzuò suffered defeat,
Āxībǎo was promoted to Dū Xúnbǔ Shǐ.
In the sixth year (1116),
he followed Āshū to suppress Yēlǜ Zhāngnú,
and was promoted to Lǐngjūn Wèi Dàjiāngjūn.
When Āshū led troops eastward,
Āxībǎo escorted them to the army
and then returned.
Tiānzuò was angry at his arbitrary actions
and had him whipped three hundred times.
Soon after, he became the Tàiwèi of the Tūlǐ tribe of the Six Xī Departments.
Later, when Āshū rebelled,
Āxībǎo advanced and attacked with a contingent force.
He fell from his horse during the battle
and was captured.
Because of his old acquaintance with Āshū, he was spared.
At that time, Āshū was rather fond of killing.
Āxībǎo said to him:
"If you wish to undertake a great enterprise,
why resort to killing?"
Because of this, many lives were saved.
When Āshū was defeated,
he returned.
Because of the loss in battle,
he was imprisoned in Zhōngjīng for several years.
the Jīn troops reached Zhōngjīng,
and he was finally released from prison.
Soon after, he became the Xiángwěn of the Díliè Píshì.
At that time,
Wèiwáng Chún usurped the title,
and repeatedly sent people with letters to recruit him.
Āxībǎo sealed the letters and presented them (to Tiānzuò),
and subsequently advised:
"The troops in the east are extremely fierce,
and should not be treated lightly."
When Shíliǎnduó was defeated,
Tiānzuò fled and hid.
He summoned Āxībǎo,
but he did not arrive promptly,
raising suspicion of disloyalty.
He was also angered by the recruitment attempt by Chún,
and had him executed.
Previously,
Āxībǎo knew the state was nearing collapse,
and his previous counsel had been extremely sharp.
When he died unjustly,
people especially lamented him.
Xiāo Yǐxuē,
courtesy name Tèmiǎn,
was a descendant of the guójìu shàofù fáng (maternal uncle's minor paternal branch).
His nature was cautious and upright.
During the Shòulóng period,
he repeatedly held important official posts.
Early in the Tiānqìng period,
he served as Zhī Guójìu Xiángwěn Shì,
and was promoted to Diànqián Fù Diǎnjiǎn.
When the Jīn troops arose,
he served as Xíngjūn Fù Dūtǒng.
Because he lost a battle,
he was dismissed from office.
In the sixth year (of Tiānqìng),
he was sent out as the Jiédùshǐ of Wǔdìng Jūn,
and later promoted to Xījīng Liúshǒu.
The following year,
he campaigned against the serious bandit Dǒng Máng'ér.
He fought west of Yì Shuǐ,
and utterly defeated them.
For his merit, he was made Běifǔ Zǎixiàng,
given the additional title of Zuǒ Púshè,
and concurrently served as Dūtǒng of the Dōngběi Lù.
In the tenth year (of Tiānqìng),
the Jīn troops captured Shàngjīng.
An edict ordered him to concurrently serve as Shàngjīng Liúshǒu and Tǒngjūnshǐ of the Dōngběi Lù.
His governance balanced leniency and strictness appropriately.
To those among the people who were impoverished,
he consistently provided aid and relief,
and everyone loved him.
In the second year of Bǎodà,
the Jīn troops arrived in great numbers,
and Yǐxuē's army dispersed.
He was demoted to Xīnánmiàn Zhāotǎoshǐ.
Because his subordinate people had scattered,
he did not report to the post.
When Tiānzuò fled and relocated,
he provided attendants and services without fail.
He was appointed Diànqián Dū Diǎnjiǎn.
Wherever the Jīn troops had passed,
the scattered soldiers from various camps regrouped at Shàngjīng.
Yǐxuē was sent as Shàngjīng Liúshǒu to pacify them.
The following year,
Lú Yànlún rebelled using the city (as a base).
Yǐxuē was captured for several months,
but because he had committed no error while holding office,
he was released.
Later, he was killed by Yēlǜ Dàshí.
Xiāo Húdǔ,
courtesy name Héshùyǐn.
His ancestor, Sāgězhǐ,
during Tàizǔ's time, desired to be registered under the Gōngfēn (Palace Division),
and thus became a member of the Tàihé Gōngfēn.
His great-grandfather, Dílǔ,
was a brilliant doctor.
When someone was sick,
he knew where the illness lay simply by observing their appearance and complexion.
During the Tǒnghé period,
Chancellor Hán Délàng was highly favored.
Dílǔ, seeking to please the Emperor,
suggested that Délàng should be granted the Imperial surname,
and be registered among the Héngzhàng (Imperial tribes).
Due to this, his family for generations was selected for Imperial Medical posts.
Many descendants subsequently entered officialdom because of this.
