Húdǔ was obsequious and flattering,
and never offended anyone.
Early in the Qīngníng period,
he was appointed to the position of Imperial Attendant (jìnsì).
In the first year of Dà'ān,
he became Tàishī of the Zhāngmǐn Gōng.
In the second year of Shòulóng,
he transferred to Tàishī of the Yǒngxīng Gōng.
Early in the Tiānqìng period,
he was successively promoted to Diànqián Fù Diǎnjiǎn.
In the fifth year,
he accompanied Tiānzuò on the eastern campaign,
serving as Xiānfēng Dūtǒng.
He hesitated when facing tasks,
and all his units were named after hunting preserves (wéichǎng).
Advancing to Cìlí Shuǐ,
he fought against the Jīn troops,
was defeated,
and the main army also retreated.
When campaigning against Yēlǜ Zhāngnú,
he conscripted private slaves into the army.
He was promoted to Zhī Běiyuàn Shūmìshǐ Shì,
and then died.
Húdǔ was skilled in mounted archery.
Seeing that Tiānzuò enjoyed hunting excursions,
he constantly spoke of the joys of following the prey,
thereby catering to his wishes.
Tiānzuò was pleased and indulged in it.
The collapse of state affairs,
they say, began from this time.
Appraisal: How serious it is
that when peace lasts for a long time,
those above and below become complacent in the face of dreadful, enduring custom!
During the Tiānqìng period,
when the Nǚzhí were rapidly rising,
only Táo Sūwò was insightful in estimating the enemy
and good at offering loyal advice.
Pity that Tiānzuò was willfully blind
and did not trust or use him.
Āxībǎo avoided death during the disaster involving Āshū,
and Yǐxuē passively endured capture by Lú Yànlún.
Their great integrity was already lost.
Even if they possessed other talents,
what use were they?
Húdǔ catered to Tiānzuò through hunting expeditions, thereby bringing down state affairs.
Can his crime ever be fully accounted for?
Biography Section Thirty-Two: Xiāo Fèngxiān, Lǐ Chùwēn, Zhāng Lín, Yēlǜ Yúdǔ.
Xiāo Fèngxiān
was the elder brother of Tiānzuò's primary consort.
He appeared generous but was internally jealous.
Because his sister, the primary consort, was favored and relied upon by the Emperor,
he was repeatedly promoted to Shūmìshǐ,
and enfeoffed as Lánlíng Jùnwáng.
In the second year of Tiānqìng,
the Emperor visited Hùntóng Jiāng to fish.
According to custom,
the chiefs of the Uncivilized Nǚzhí living within a thousand *lǐ* were all required to pay court at the imperial residence (xíngzài).
During the first fish banquet (tóuyú yàn),
the Emperor ordered the chiefs to sing and dance in turn for entertainment.
When it was Āgǔdǎ's turn,
he merely stood upright and stared directly ahead,
declining on the grounds of inability.
Although the Emperor repeatedly commanded him,
he refused to obey.
The Emperor secretly said to Fèngxiān:
"Āgǔdǎ is defiant to this extent!
We can use a pretext concerning border affairs to execute him."
Fèngxiān replied:
"He is a coarse person,
ignorant of propriety and righteousness,
but he has committed no major offense.
Killing him would harm the goodwill of those who wish to submit.
Even if he harbored rebellious intentions,
how much could that tiny, insignificant state
possibly accomplish?"
The Emperor then ceased the matter.
In the fourth year,
Āgǔdǎ raised troops and attacked Níngjiāng Zhōu.
Xiāo Tànbùyě, the Tǒngjūnshǐ of the Dōngběi Lù, lost the battle.
The Emperor ordered Fèngxiān’s younger brother, Sìxiān, to be Dūtǒng,
leading Khitan and Han troops to campaign against them,
and encamp at Chūhé Diàn.
The Nǚzhí secretly crossed the Hùntóng Jiāng,
taking advantage of our unprepared army to attack.
Sìxiān was utterly defeated,
and many military commanders fled.
Fèngxiān feared his younger brother would be executed,
so he memorialized:
"The defeated soldiers from the eastern campaign are escaping punishment,
pillaging wherever they go.
If a general pardon is not issued,
they will gather together and cause trouble."
This was adopted.
Sìxiān went to the court to await punishment,
but was merely dismissed from office.
Consequently, the soldiers lost their will to fight;
whenever they met the enemy, they immediately scattered,
and the prefectures and counties lost grew daily.
Initially,
Xiāo Fèngxiān falsely accused Yēlǜ Yúdǔ of conspiring with the Imperial Son-in-Law Xiāo Yù to establish his nephew, the Prince of Jìn (Jìn Wáng).
When the matter became known,
Yù was killed.
Yúdǔ, hearing this while in the army, was fearful
and fled to the Nǚzhí.
In the second year of Bǎodà,
Yúdǔ acted as the Supervisor of the Army for the Nǚzhí,
leading troops that suddenly arrived.
The Emperor was greatly troubled.
Fèngxiān said:
“Yúdǔ is a descendant of Wángzǐ Bān.
His coming here truly does not aim to destroy Liáo;
he merely wishes to establish the Prince of Jìn.
If we plan for the sake of the State,
we should not begrudge one son;
if we execute him,
they can be made to retreat without a battle.”
Consequently, the Prince of Jìn was granted death.
All within and outside the court wept,
and the people's loyalty further disintegrated.
When the Nǚzhí troops had not yet arrived,
Fèngxiān flattered Tiānzuò,
saying:
“Although the Nǚzhí can attack our Shàngjīng,
they ultimately cannot stray far from their nest.”
But suddenly they crossed three thousand *lǐ* and struck directly at Yúnzhōng.
Having no plan to offer,
he could only request migration to Jiāshān.
Tiānzuò finally realized this,
and looking at Fèngxiān, said:
“You, father and son, have misled me to this point.
What good would killing you do now!
You leave,
do not accompany me on my journey.
I fear the army's resentment and anger
will surely bring disaster upon me.”
Fèngxiān and his son cried bitterly and departed,
but they were seized by those around them and delivered to the Nǚzhí forces.
The Nǚzhí forces executed his eldest son, Āng,
and sent Fèngxiān and his second son, Yù, to their sovereign.
On the way, they encountered our troops,
were captured back,
and Tiānzuò granted them both death.
Lǐ Chùwēn
was a native of Xījīn.
His paternal uncle, Yǎn,
was appointed Vice Director of the Palace Buildings (Jiàngzuò Shàojiān) early in the Dàkāng era.
He accumulated offices, reaching the rank of Policy Adviser (Cānzhī Zhèngshì),
and was enfeoffed as the Prince of Qīshuǐ Commandery (Qīshuǐ Jùnwáng).
He was an intimate and long-time friend of the Northern Commissioner of Military Affairs (Běi Shūmìshǐ), Xiāo Fèngxiān.
He held power for more than ten years,
skilled at flattery and ingratiation,
and Tiānzuò highly favored and trusted him.
When Yǎn died,
Fèngxiān recommended Chùwēn to be Chancellor.
Since Chùwēn relied on Fèngxiān having the power to support him,
he dedicated himself wholeheartedly to flattering and clinging to him,
in order to consolidate his authority and position.
Moreover, his greed and avarice were extreme.
All those whom he recommended and patronized
were mostly petty men.
Early in the Bǎodà era,
the Jīn people captured Zhōngjīng.
None of the generals could hold out.
Tiānzuò was frightened
and fled to Jiāshān.
The military pressure grew daily.
Chùwēn, along with his cousin Chùnéng
and his son Shì,
externally pretended to support the disgruntled army,
and colluded with the Commander-in-Chief (Dūtǒng) Xiāo Gàn to plan the establishment of Chún, the Prince of Wèi (Wèi Guówáng).
They summoned both Qìdān (Fān) and Hàn officials to the residence of the Prince of Wèi to urge him to ascend the throne.
When the Prince of Wèi was about to step out,
Shì then held up a vermilion robe and dressed him in it,
ordering the hundred officials to bow, dance, and offer congratulations.
The Prince of Wèi firmly declined but was unable to refuse,
and subsequently proclaimed himself Emperor Tiānxī.
Chùwēn was made Acting Grand Commandant (Shǒu Tàiwèi),
Chùnéng was made Assistant in the Bureau of Military Affairs (Zhí Shūmì Yuàn),
and Shì was made Vice Minister of the Imperial Treasury (Shàofǔ Shàojiān).
Zǔo Qǐgōng and others, as well as relatives and old friends who participated in the affair,
were granted offices in varying degrees.
It happened that the Prince of Wèi fell ill,
knowing himself that he would not recover.
He secretly conferred upon Chùwēn the title of Grand Marshal of the Qìdān and Hàn Cavalry and Infantry (Fān Hàn Mǎ Bù Jūn Dū Yuánshuài),
intending to entrust him with the affairs that followed.
When his illness became critical,
Xiāo Gàn and others issued a forged imperial edict, summoning the chancellors and administrators of the Southern Face to enter and deliberate.
Only Chùwēn pleaded illness and did not attend,
secretly gathering valiant fighters for preparedness,
deceptively claiming that he had received a secret decree to guard against other changes.
When the Prince of Wèi died,
Xiāo Gàn, commanding Qìdān troops,
declared that they should establish the consort, Lady Xiāo (Xiāo Shì), as Empress Dowager (Tàihòu),
and have her temporarily preside over military and state affairs.
No one in the assembly dared to disagree.
Gàn, acting on the Empress's command,
summoned Chùwēn to appear.
As the time was fraught with difficulties,
they did not wish to execute him immediately,
but only revoked and destroyed the tablet confirming his rank as Grand Marshal.
Chùnéng feared disaster would reach him
and shaved his head to become a monk.
Soon after, Fù Zūnshuō, a native of Yǒngqīng who had followed Guō Yàoshī into Yān,
was captured.
He fully detailed that Chùwēn had previously sent a letter, via the wealthy commoner Zhào Lǚrén of Yìzhōu, to the Sòng general Tóng Guàn,
intending to coerce Empress Xiāo into surrendering the territory to Sòng.
The Empress seized Chùwēn and questioned him.
Chùwēn said:
“My son and I had the merit of establishing Xuānzōng's position.
We should be granted amnesty and tolerance for generations.
How can we be allowed to incur guilt because of slander?”
The Empress said:
“If the Prince of Wèi had been like the Duke of Zhōu (Zhōu Gōng),
he would have enjoyed the reputation of valuing worthy people throughout later generations.
Those who misled the Prince were entirely you, father and son.
What merit do you possess!”
She then enumerated his previous crimes and misdeeds.
Chùwēn had no reply,
and was granted death.
Shì was also executed.
Zhāng Lín
was a native of Shěnzhōu.
As a youth, he had great ambition.
At the end of the Shòulóng era,
he served as Central Palace Clerk (Mìshū Zhōngyǔn).
When Tiānzuò ascended the throne,
he was repeatedly promoted to Prefect of the Ministry of Revenue (Hùbù Shǐ).
After a short time,
he was promoted to Chancellor of the Southern Administration (Nánfǔ Zǎixiàng).
Initially,
when Tiānzuò was defeated by the Nǚzhí,
he thought that Xiāo Fèngxiān did not understand warfare.
Therefore, he summoned Lín and entrusted him with the campaign to the east.
Lín declined,
citing the old rule that
Hàn people were not involved
in major military and state affairs.
The Emperor did not permit it.
Lín memorialized, saying:
“The defeat of the previous day
was due to rash action.
If we use two hundred thousand Hàn soldiers and advance to attack along separate routes,
there is none we cannot conquer.”
The Emperor granted half that number,
and moreover decreed that the four circuits of Zhōngjīng, Shàngjīng, Chángchūn, and Liáoxī should raise troops according to household wealth.
At that time, there were those who had to raise as many as two hundred soldiers;
their livelihoods were ruined and dispersed,
and the people greatly suffered from this.
As soon as the armies from the four circuits were gathered,
they immediately fled again.
When Zhōngjīng fell,
Tiānzuò went to Yúnzhōng,
leaving Lín and Lǐ Chùwēn to assist Chún, the Prince of Wèi, in defending Nánjīng.
Chùwēn and his son summoned Lín,
wishing to establish Chún as emperor.
Lín said:
“Although the Prince is of Imperial lineage,
he has no initial decree from the Emperor.
Acting as regent is permissible,
but ascending the throne in truth is not.”
Chùwēn said:
“The affair of this day
is granted by Heaven and men;
how can it be changed!”
Although Lín showed hesitation,
he reluctantly complied.
After Chún proclaimed himself emperor,
all the generals occupied positions of power and importance.
Lín alone was appointed Acting Grand Tutor (Shǒu Tàishī).
He attended court once every ten days
to oversee military and state affairs.
Ostensibly, they honored him as an elder statesman,
but in reality, they did not allow him to participate in government.
Because of this, Lín became melancholy and died.
Yēlǜ Yúdǔ,
whose other name was Yúdūgū,
was a close relative of the Imperial clan.
He was passionate and valued bravery and righteousness.
Early in the Bǎodà era,
he successively held the office of Deputy Commander-in-Chief (Fù Dūtǒng).
; Wén Fēi bore Jìn Wáng
, who was the most virtuous
, and the people of the state all held high expectations for him
. At that time, Xiāo Fèngxiān's younger sister was also Tiānzuò Yuán Fēi
, and she bore Qín Wáng
. Fèngxiān feared that Qín Wáng would not be established (as heir)
, and deeply envied Yú Dǔ
, planning secretly to scheme against him
. It happened that the wife of Yēlǜ Tàgélǐ met Yú Dǔ's wife within the army
, so Fèngxiān instigated people to falsely accuse Yú Dǔ of collaborating with the imperial son-in-law Xiāo Yù and Tàgélǐ
, plotting to establish Jìn Wáng
, and to honor Tiānzuò as Tàishàng Huáng (Retired Emperor)
. When the affair was discovered
, Yù and Tàgélǐ's wife were executed
, and Wén Fēi was granted death
. Yú Dǔ, upon hearing this while in the army
, feared that he would be unable to clear himself and would be executed
, so he immediately led over a thousand soldiers
, taking his family and military camp (belongings), and defected to the Nǚzhí
. It happened there was a great continuous rain
, obstructing their path

. Tiānzuò urgently dispatched the Manager of the Xī Princely Residence, Xiāo Xiámǎi; the Northern Chancellor, Xiāo Dégōng; the Dàcháng Gǔn, Yēlǜ Dìlǐgū; the Guī Zhōu Surveillance Commissioner, Xiāo Héshàngnú; and the Grand Tutor of the Four Armies, Xiāo Gàn, to pursue and capture him
. Reaching Lǘ Shān
, they caught up to him
. The generals deliberated, saying
: “Xiāo Fèngxiān relies on favor
, and disregards and harms officers and soldiers
. Yú Dǔ is a heroic talent of the imperial clan
, and has always refused to be subordinate to him
. If we capture him
, then someday we will all become Yú Dǔ
. It is better to release him
.” They returned
, falsely reporting that the pursuit had failed to overtake him
. After Yú Dǔ entered the Nǚzhí territory
, he served as the vanguard for their state
, leading Lóushì Bóujǐn’s troops to attack and seize prefectures and commanderies
, arriving unexpectedly
. Tiānzuò was greatly alarmed upon hearing this
, knowing he could not resist
, he led his guards into Jiā Shān
. Yú Dǔ served as Supervisor of the Army for the Nǚzhí
, but for a long time was not promoted
, feeling uneasy
, he therefore pretended to go hunting
, and fled to the Xī Xià
. The Xià people asked
: “How many soldiers do you have with you
?” Yú Dǔ replied, “Two or three hundred”
, The Xià people did not accept him
, and he subsequently died
. Commentary states: The fall of the Liáo
, although perhaps a calamity descended from Heaven
, was also due to the ministers holding the reins of government misleading the state
. From the Tiānqìng era onward
, governance devolved to the empress’s kin
. Fèngxiān thwarted Tiānzuò’s plan to guard against danger
, and entrapped Jìn Wáng into execution for a non-crime
, the disaster at Jiā Shān was already foretold in these actions
. Chǔ Wēn pressured Wèi Wáng into usurping the title
, and allied with Sòng generals to betray the country
; tracing their treachery and deceit
, they seem to follow the same pattern
. Alas
! If those upon whom Tiānzuò relied were like this
, how could the state avoid ruin
? It could not
. Zhāng Lín timidly held his position
, and Yú Dǔ, reaching the point of ruin, endangered himself
; why then are they worth discussing
? Biographies, Chapter 33: Literature, Part One: Xiāo Hánjiānú, Lǐ Hàn
When the Liáo arose in Sōngmò
, Tàizǔ used military force to manage the territories within
, and ritual matters were certainly not yet his priority
. When Tàizōng entered Biàn
, he took Jìn's maps, documents, and ritual vessels back north
, only then did institutions gradually begin to be refined and implemented
. By the time of the Jǐng and Shèng reigns
, the examination systems flourished
, scholars were promoted from low-ranking posts to serve at court
, rapidly achieving the refinement of honoring Confucianism
. However, the overall character (of the state) was vigorous and firm
, neighbors bordered on three sides
, and annual hunts were considered important tasks
, while rituals, statutes, and culture were still incomplete compared to antiquity
. Nevertheless, the endeavor of two hundred years
, if not for several gentlemen managing and organizing it
, how could later generations investigate and recount it
? Therefore, this Biography of Literature is written
. Xiāo Hánjiānú
, courtesy name Xiūjiān
, was a man of the Nièlào Department
, and the grandson of the Central Secretariat Director, Ān Tuán
. As a youth, he loved learning
, and upon coming of age, he entered Nán Shān to study
. He widely read the Classics and Histories
, and was proficient in both Liáo and Hàn script
. He first entered officialdom in the fourteenth year of Tǒnghé (996 CE)
. His household owned an ox
, which was unfit for driving
. His slave sold it for a good price
. Hánjiānú said
: “To profit oneself while misleading others
, is not what I desire
.” He then returned the payment and retrieved the ox
. In the twenty-eighth year (of Tǒnghé)
, he served as Yòu Tōngjìn
, overseeing the Chestnut Orchard in Nánjīng
. In the beginning of the Chóngxī era
, he became Vice-Director of the Three Judicial Offices
. In the fourth year
, he was promoted to Military Commissioner of Tiānchéng Commandery
, and later transferred to be Commissioner of Zhāngmǐn Palace
. The Emperor conversed with him
, appreciating his talent
, and commanded him to be a poetry companion
. On one occasion, the Emperor casually asked
: “When you resided in the provinces, did you hear anything unusual
?” Hánjiānú replied
: “Your servant only understands roasting chestnuts: if the small ones are thoroughly cooked
, then the large ones will definitely be raw
; if the large ones are thoroughly cooked
, then the small ones will definitely be burnt
. Only by making both large and small equally cooked
, can perfection be achieved
. I know nothing else
.” Since he had once managed the Chestnut Orchard
, he used the chestnut analogy for indirect remonstrance
. The Emperor laughed heartily
. He was commanded by imperial decree to compose the *Fù* on the Pleasures of the Four Seasons
, which the Emperor praised
. At that time, an imperial decree was issued instructing all under heaven to speak on the essentials of governance
. The decree posed questions
: “Corvée labor has not increased beyond the old standards
, and military campaigns are not constant
; the harvests are good
, and the treasuries and granaries are full
, yet the people are severely distressed
. Is this because the officials are negligent, or because the people are lazy
? Which of the current corvée labors is the heaviest
? Which is the most bitter
? What should be remitted or reduced for the benefit of the people
? How can the system of compensatory labor be restored
? How can the harm caused by bandits be halted
?” Hánjiānú replied: Your servant observes that in recent years
, since Gāolì has not submitted
, and the Zǔbǔ are still strong
, preparations for battle and defense
, truly cannot be stopped
. Recently
, wealthy commoners were selected to guard the frontier
, providing their own provisions
. The roads are long and treacherous
, often taking months and years
; by the time they reach the garrison
, more than half their resources have already been spent
; few return with their ox or cart intact
. Those families without adult males
, hire substitutes at double the price
. Men dread the labor
, and flee midway
, thus, food for the garrison soldiers is often insufficient
. When they seek loans from others
, the interest is tenfold
, resulting even in selling children and cutting off land
, yet still being unable to repay the debt
. If some evade service and do not return
, or die while on military duty
, they are replaced by young and strong men
. East of the Yālù Jiāng
, garrison
. Furthermore, Bóhǎi, Nǚzhí, and Gāolì join together in alliances
service is generally like this
, causing frequent campaigns
. The rich follow the army
, and the poor serve as scouts
. Added to this are floods
, causing beans and grains to fail
, and the people become increasingly distressed
. This is simply due to the circumstances
. Currently, the heaviest labor
, is none other than the western garrison duty (Xīshù)
. If there were no Xīshù
, even in a year of bad harvests
, the distress and exhaustion would not reach this extent
. If the Xīshù could be moved slightly
closer
, then travel would be less arduous
, and the people would be free from deep suffering
. Those who argue against moving it say it is inconvenient: first, it would diminish our prestige
, second, it would invite encroachment and insult
, and third, it would abandon farming and pasturage
territory.
Your servant believes this is not so.
The various tribes of *Zhǔbǔ*
have existed since time immemorial.
Formerly, extending north to the *Lúqú Hé*
and south to the border,
the people lived widely dispersed,
without
unified control.
They only raided back and forth.
When *Tàizǔ* campaigned in the West
, reaching *Liúshā*
, the *Zhǔbǔ* submitted instantly upon sight of his approach.
All the states of the Western Regions (*Xīyù*) desired to present tribute.
Consequently,
their tribes and settlements
were moved, and three divisions were established internally
to benefit our state.
No walled cities were built,
nor were garrison troops stationed.
For generations, the *Zhǔbǔ* dared not become bandits.
During the *Tǒnghé* period
, the Empress Dowager *Huáng Tàifēi*
launched an expedition to the Western Regions (*Xīyù*).
As the acquired territory was vast,
the number of surrendered and attached peoples was also great.
Since then, if one division occasionally rebelled,
the neighboring divisions would attack it,
allowing them to restrain each other with combined force.
This was precisely the method for managing distant
peoples.
Since the construction of *Kědūn*
, thousands of miles of borders have been opened.
For the people of the Northwest,
corvée duties increase daily,
and their livelihoods are exhausted daily.
Since they cannot be saved in times of alarm or emergency,
their rebellion or submission
is also inconsistent.
We merely have the name of vast territory,
but lack the reality of acquiring the land.
If the greed for land does not cease,
gradually leading to depletion and waste,
the resulting disaster will be inexpressible.
Moreover, the situation on the borders should not be deeply trusted,
nor should it be abruptly severed.
Acquiring [more land] is not beneficial,
abandoning [it] is not harmful.
The nation's great enemy
lies only in the South.
Although we are currently maintaining
peace,
it is difficult to guarantee the future.
If trouble arises in the South,
the garrisons are stationed far away,
making it difficult to send aid quickly.
When we advance, the enemy retreats;
when we return, the enemy comes.
This must be
taken into consideration.
Since peace has reigned for a long time now,
it is exactly the time to bind the various tribes with benevolence,
release them from their faults, and return the territory,
move the garrison troops inwards to strengthen our defenses,
and externally clarify the agreements to rectify
the borders.
For each division, appoint a chieftain,
and let them present annual tribute.
If they rebel, attack them;
if they submit, pacify them.
Once the various divisions are stable,
they will surely not cause trouble.
If this is done,
although your servant cannot guarantee that they will remain stable forever without change,
I know they definitely will not invade deeply and plunder.
Some say
that abandoning territory harms prestige.
They entirely fail to realize that by exhausting expenditures and draining
wealth
in greed for useless territory,
allowing those minor tribes to rival a great nation,
if by chance we suffer a defeat,
how slight will the harm to our prestige be?
Others also say
that fertile land should not be immediately abandoned.
Your servant believes that even if the soil is fertile,
the people cannot reside there permanently.
If the enemy comes suddenly,
they will inevitably have to move inward.
How can we claim it is our territory and cherish it?
Although financial resources are managed by the various divisions,
this is merely a limited benevolence to aid the urgent needs of the local populace,
and cannot provide universal relief to the entire realm.
If you wish to provide universal relief to the realm,
then
you must understand the reasons for the people's distress
and block the source of the trouble.
Restrain pleasure excursions,
reduce postal services,
lighten taxes and levies,
and forbid extravagance.
If this is maintained for several years,
then those in distress can recover,
and the poor can become wealthy.
Indeed, the people are the foundation of the state,
and the military is the defense of the state.
If the troops are not levied, military service is neglected;
if they are levied, the national foundation is harmed.
Furthermore, the various divisions
all have systems for replacement service.
Formerly, when replacement service began,
both those residing at home and those serving on duty were generally wealthy and substantial.
Therefore, when serving in the garrison for generations,
it was easy to rotate the duty.
In recent years, border
troubles have frequently arisen,
and the people are mostly destitute.
Since they are incapable of performing service duties,
replacements are deficient as soon as they are assigned.
If the highest-ranking households are absent,
then the middle-ranking households must bear the burden.
As days and years pass,
their poverty
grows worse,
which is why providing replacements is difficult.
This difficulty is not limited to replacement service;
it is the same for the troops garrisoned on the border.
It is like a handful of earth—
how can it fill a chasm spanning ten feet
or more?
If you desire a long-lasting benefit,
nothing is better than allowing the weary troops garrisoned far away to return to their native places,
lighten their corvée duties,
so that everyone has sufficient resources.
Then the system of replacement service
can be restored to its former condition.
Your servant has also heard that
since antiquity, those who possess a state
cannot be without robbers.
In recent years,
the common people have become worn out and destitute,
resorting to robbery and theft.
Good citizens often turn
into vicious criminals.
The worst indiscriminately commit murder,
even fleeing to mountains and marshes
to form the basis of disorder and lead rebellion.
The saying that the people, due to distress and poverty,
all become robbers and thieves,
is truly in accord with
Your Majesty's wise consideration.
Now, if you wish to eradicate the root cause,
I request Your Majesty to lighten corvée and reduce service,
and encourage the people to focus on agriculture.
Once food and clothing are sufficient,
they will peacefully embrace education and civilization,
and treat violations of the law seriously.
Consequently, the people will incline towards rites and righteousness,
and punishments will rarely be needed.
Your servant heard that *Táng Tàizōng* asked his officials about methods for controlling robbers.
They all replied:
"Severe penalties and strict laws."
*Tàizōng* laughed
and said:
"The reason bandits flourish
is due to excessive taxation and levies,
which makes the people unable to sustain their lives.
Now, I examine my internal desires,
and externally cease pleasure trips and hunting expeditions,
causing the realm within the four seas to become peaceful.
Then banditry will naturally cease."
Viewing it in this light,
the abundance or scarcity of robbers
is entirely determined by the sufficiency or deficiency of food and clothing,
and the weight or lightness of corvée duties.
Currently, it is fitting to move *Kědūn Chéng* to a nearby location,
connecting its strategic support with the southwestern Vice Grand Commissioner *Wūgǔ Díliè* and the *Kuí Wūgǔ* and other divisions.
Dismiss the two armies at *Hēilǐng*
and merge *Kāizhōu* and *Bǎozhōu*.
Let them all belong to *Dōngjīng*.
Increase the garrison troops in the Northeast and the forces under the Commander-in-Chief of *Nánjīng*.
Increase and repair the ramparts and defensive walls,
so that observation posts are visible from one another,
and repair the towers
Watchtowers,
deepening and repairing the city walls and moats,
to serve as border defenses.
This is the urgent task of the present time;
I request Your Majesty deliberate upon it.
He was promoted to Hànlín Dū Línyá,
concurrently overseeing the compilation of the National History.
The Emperor further issued an edict instructing him, saying:
"The duty of literary composition
is the splendor of the state;
those without talent are not employed.
Since your scholarship
makes you the great scholar of the age,
you are hereby granted the post of Hànlín.
My daily activities
must all be recorded factually."
From this time forward, he was increasingly seen as a trusted confidant.
Whenever he entered to serve,
he was granted a seat.
On festive days,
the Emperor drank wine and composed poetry with him,
exchanging verses.
The harmonious relationship between ruler and minister was unmatched.
Hán Jiānú spoke everything he knew,
and although he joked, he never forgot to offer admonishment and critique.
In the spring of the thirteenth year,
he submitted a memorial which stated:
"Your subject has heard that after the former ancestor Yáo Niǎn Kèhán Wā,
the continuity of the state was interrupted.
It was not until Yílíjǐn Yǎlǐ established Zǔwǔ
that the supreme position was first stabilized.
However, the ancient generations were simple and rustic,
and had not yet adopted honored titles.
Your subject believes that just as the ceremonial practices of the Sān Huáng (Three Sovereigns) were incomplete,
so too was the case for the Yáo Niǎn Shì.
Later rulers governed the realm using rites and music,
and consequently, the principle of honoring the origin and remembering the distant past emerged.
Recently, Táng Gāozǔ founded ancestral temples
and honored four generations as Emperors.
Formerly, our Tàizǔ superseded the Yáo Niǎn and ascended the throne,
whereafter he created a script,
revised the rites and laws,
established the title Tiān Huángdì,
built palaces and chambers to display his majesty and command submission,
promoted benefits and eliminated harm,
and unified the entire realm.
Since then, successive sage rulers have inherited the position.
Yet, from Yílíjǐn Húliè downwards,
the great titles have not been conferred;
the father of Tiān Huángdì, Yílíjǐn Dǐlǔ, is still referred to by his personal name.
Your subject believes that we should follow the Táng precedents
and posthumously honor the four ancestors as Emperors.
Then Your Majesty’s grand endeavor will shine brightly,
and the lapsed ceremonial code will be reinstated."
When the memorial was presented,
the Emperor accepted it
and initiated the ceremony of posthumously conferring titles upon the two ancestors, Xuán and Dé.
Whenever Hán Jiānú saw the Emperor hunting,
he never failed to remonstrate.
It happened that officials reported a hunt on Qiūshān,
where bears and tigers injured and killed dozens of people.
Hán Jiānú recorded this in his register.
The Emperor saw it
and ordered it removed.
After Hán Jiānú had left,
he recorded it again.
Another day,
the Emperor saw it and said:
"The historian’s brush ought to be like this."
The Emperor asked Hán Jiānú:
"Since our dynasty was founded,
who has been the most virtuous ruler?"
Hán Jiānú answered with Mùzōng.
The Emperor was surprised and said:
"Mùzōng was addicted to wine,
his joy and anger were erratic,
and he viewed people as mere grass and straw.
Why do you call him virtuous?"
Hán Jiānú replied:
"Although Mùzōng was brutal,
he reduced corvée labor and lightened taxes,
and people enjoyed their lives.
Throughout Mùzōng’s reign,
the number of innocent people executed
did not exceed those injured and killed on Qiūshān today.
Therefore, your subject regards Mùzōng as virtuous."
The Emperor fell silent.
He was ordered by edict to collaborate with Yēlǜ Shùchéng to record the events from Yáo Niǎn Kèhán up to the Chóngxī era,
which were compiled into twenty volumes
and presented.
In the fifteenth year,
a further edict stated:
"Those in antiquity who governed the realm
clarified rites and righteousness
and standardized laws and measures.
Since the rise of our court,
generations have possessed illustrious virtue.
Although territories internal and external have submitted to our influence,
yet ritual codes have not been compiled,
leaving nothing to display to later generations.
You may, alongside Shùchéng, evaluate ancient practice and gauge the present
to formulate a ritual code.
Should any matter be doubtful,
discuss it jointly with the North and South Chanceries."
After Hán Jiānú received the edict,
he extensively researched the classics and texts.
He compiled the sentiment, form, and regulations, applicable from the Son of Heaven down to the common people,
that were suitable for the current age
He completed the compilation in three volumes
and presented them.
He was also ordered by edict to translate various books.
Hán Jiānú, wanting the Emperor to understand the successes and failures of antiquity and the present,
translated the Tōnglì, the Zhēnguān Zhèngyào, and the Wǔ Dài Shǐ.
At that time, the Emperor considered his old age
and his inability to attend court audiences,
and appointed him Guīdé Jūn Jiédùshǐ.
He became known for his excellent governance.
The Emperor sent an envoy to inquire after his welfare and comfort him,
and Hán Jiānú submitted a memorial in thanks.
He was recalled to compile the National History,
and then passed away
at the age of seventy-two.
His collection, the Liù Yì Jí, in twelve volumes, circulated widely.
Lǐ Hǎn,
initially served the Jìn dynasty,
as Zhōngshū Shèrén.
When Jìn fell, he submitted to Liáo.
When Tàizōng passed away and Shìzōng was established,
the situation was unstable and tumultuous.
Hǎn, along with Gāo Xūn and more than ten others, was detained in Nánjīng.
After a long time,
he followed them back to Shàngjīng
and was granted the position of Hànlín Xuéshì.
When Mùzōng ascended the throne,
he was repeatedly promoted, reaching the position of Gōngbù Shìláng.
At that time, Hǎn’s elder brother, Tāo, was in Biàn serving as Hànlín Xuéshì,
and secretly sent someone to summon Hǎn.
Hǎn received the letter,
claimed to be seeking a doctor in Nánjīng,
changed his clothes and left by night,
intending to escape back to Biàn.
When he reached Zhuō,
he was captured by the patrolling guards,
sent to Nánjīng,
and imprisoned.
Hǎn waited until the jailer was soundly asleep
and attempted to hang himself with his sash.
He did not die,
and the guarding became even stricter.
Chained, he was transported to Shàngjīng.
He threw himself into the middle current of the Huáng Hé,
but was pulled back by the iron chain,
and again did not die.
When he arrived at Shàngjīng,
the Emperor wanted to execute him.
At that time, Gāo Xūn was already Shūmìshǐ,
and pleaded for his life.
He repeatedly addressed the Emperor, saying:
"Hǎn was not fundamentally ungrateful.
Because his mother was eighty years old,
his urgency to visit her caused him to commit this crime.
Furthermore, Hǎn possesses great literary skill,
and few today can rival him.
If he is kept to manage literary decrees,
he can enhance the prestige of the state."
The Emperor’s anger gradually subsided,
but he was still ordered to be imprisoned in Fèng Guó Sì.
For a total of six years,
he endured countless hardships.
It happened that the Emperor wished to erect a stele celebrating the merit and virtue of Tàizōng.
Gāo Xūn memorialized, saying:
"No one except Lǐ Hǎn is suitable to hold the writing brush."
An edict granted the request.
The text was completed and presented,
the Emperor was pleased,
and he was released from prison.
Soon after, he was granted the titles Lǐbù Shàngshū
and Xuānzhèng Diàn Xuéshì,
and then passed away.
The commentary states: During the period between Tǒnghé and Chóngxī,
efforts were made to cultivate civil administration.
Hán Jiānú's proposals,
articulated outstandingly in several hundred words,
could largely be applied to practical affairs.
Was he not the Cháo Cuò and Jiǎ Yì of Liáo?
Although Lǐ Hǎn was praised for his literary talent,
his decisions regarding advancement or retreat are not worth discussing.
Biographies, Thirty-Fourth, Literature (Part Two): Wáng Dǐng, Yēlǜ Zhāo, Liú Huī, Yēlǜ Mèngjiǎn, Yēlǜ Gǔyù.
Wáng Dǐng,
courtesy name Xūzhōng,
was a man from Zhuōzhōu.
As a youth, he loved learning.
He lived on Tàiníng Shān for several years,
becoming widely versed in the classics and histories.
At that time, Mǎ Tángjùn had a literary reputation between Yān and Jì.
Coincidentally, on the Shàngsì Festival,
he and his associates performed the purification ritual on the riverbank,
pouring wine and composing poetry.
Dǐng happened to approach the gathering.
Tángjùn saw that Dǐng was simple and rustic,
and placed him in a lower seat.
Wishing to embarrass him with poetry,
Tángjùn first presented his own compositions, demanding that Dǐng match them.
Dǐng picked up the brush and completed his poem instantly.
Tángjùn was astonished by his quick brilliance,
and consequently established a friendship with him.
In the fifth year of Qīngníng (1059 CE),
he was promoted as a *jìnshì*.
He was appointed Investigating Judge of Yìzhōu,
then changed to Magistrate of Láishuǐ Xiàn,
and subsequently rose through the ranks to Hànlín Xuéshì (Academician of the Hànlin Academy).
Many contemporary statutes and regulations came from his hand.
He submitted a memorial discussing ten matters concerning the principles of governance.
The Emperor considered Dǐng knowledgeable in political structures,
and frequently consulted him on various matters.
Dǐng was upright and uncompromising;
if someone made a mistake,
he would certainly rebuke them face-to-face.
At the beginning of Shòulóng's reign,
he was promoted to Guānshū Diàn Xuéshì (Academician of the Hall for Viewing Books).
One day, while feasting in the imperial residence,
he became drunk and offended a guest.
He complained that the Emperor did not understand his worth,
and because of this, he was handed over to the authorities.
When the details were reported,
the Emperor became furious,
sentenced him to caning and tattooing (branding), stripped him of his office,
and exiled him to Zhènzhōu.
He lived there for several years.
When a general amnesty was granted,
Dǐng alone was not included.
Coincidentally, the local governor summoned Dǐng to compose a congratulatory memorial.
Dǐng therefore gave a poem to the envoy,
which contained
the lines: "Who knows that Heaven's rain and dew
alone do not reach the lonely and poor."
The Emperor heard this and pitied him,
immediately summoned him back,
and restored him to office.
He died in the sixth year of Qiántǒng (1106 CE).
When Dǐng was serving as county magistrate,
while in his courtyard,
suddenly a violent wind lifted his couch into the air.
Dǐng showed no sign of fear,
only sensing that both his pillow and couch were high up.
He then said:
"I am a leading scholar of the central court.
Evil cannot interfere with righteousness.
You may slowly put it down."
Shortly thereafter,
the couch returned to its original place,
and the wind then stopped.
Yēlǜ Zhāo,
courtesy name Shùníng,
was widely learned
and skilled in literary composition.
During the Tǒnghé era,
because of the incident involving his brother Guóliú,
he was exiled to the Northwest Department.
Coincidentally, Xiāo Tàlǐn was the Commissioner of Pacification for the Northwest Circuit.
Tàlǐn esteemed him,
memorialized for him to be relieved of hard labor,
and treated him with respect under his supervision.
When Tàlǐn wished to summon him for official service,
Zhāo declined due to illness.
Tàlǐn asked:
"Now that military campaigns have just ceased,
the three borders are peaceful.
Only the Zǔbǔ watch for gaps and make incursions.
If we try to attack them,
the road is distant and difficult to reach;
if we tolerate them,
the border populace will be plundered;
if we increase the garrison troops,
logistics and supplies will be insufficient;
if we try to secure momentary peace,
we cannot ultimately guarantee freedom from change.
What plan should be implemented?"
Zhāo replied in a letter: I humbly heard that if governance obtains its essential principle,
then enemies become one family;
if the method is lost,
then subordinates become strangers.
For the various tribes in the Northwest,
every farming season,
one man is assigned as a scout,
one man cultivates public fields,
and every two years, they provide labor service for the Jiū officials.
Generally speaking, among four able-bodied men, not one remains at home.
The tasks of fodder and grazing
rely on their wives
and children.
Once they suffer banditry and plunder,
poverty immediately arrives.
When relief is distributed in spring and summer,
officials often mix it with chaff and husks,
further aggravated by extortion.
Within only a few months,
they report distress again.
Furthermore, livestock raising
is the foundation of a wealthy state.
The responsible authorities prevent the hiding or dispersal of animals
by gathering them in one location,
preventing them from going to favorable locations with water and grass.
Moreover, fugitive garrison soldiers
are constantly used to supplement the ranks.
Since they are unfamiliar with the local customs and climate,
the animals become thinner day by day and diminish month by month,
gradually leading to depletion.
As for the current plan,
nothing is better than relieving the impoverished and lightening the taxes,
supplying them with cattle for breeding,
and allowing them to engage in plowing and harvesting.
Establish mobile troops to prevent banditry and plunder,
distribute captured livestock to assist with the Fú
and Là sacrifices,
and scatter the herds to utilize suitable ground.
Within a few years,
wealth and strength can be anticipated.
After that, select and train elite troops
to reinforce the ranks.
How could our defenses not be firm,
and how could any action not be victorious?
However, it is necessary to eliminate those (tribes) that are difficult to control;
then the remaining tribes will submit out of fear.
If we abandon the major issues to focus on the minor ones,
or avoid the strong and attack the weak,
we would not only waste
resources and manpower in vain,
but also fail to truly subdue their hearts through authority.
These two points
are the pivots of benefit and harm,
and must be thoroughly examined.
Zhāo has heard that ancient famous generals,
when securing the borders and establishing merit,
relied on virtue, not merely numbers.
Therefore, Xiè Xuán defeated Fú Jiān’s million-man army with eight thousand,
and Xiū Gē defeated Cáo Bīn’s hundred thousand with five contingents.
This was truly because kindness secured the hearts of the soldiers,
obtaining their willingness to fight to the death.
Your Excellency has received extraordinary treatment
and is entrusted with command over a whole region.
You should emulate the ancients
to achieve great meritorious works.
Observe the celestial phenomena above,
exhaust human counsel below;
examine the dangers and advantages of the terrain,
and estimate the enemy's strength and weaknesses.
If your plans leave no stone unturned,
the benefits will extend
to future generations.
Tàlǐn considered this correct.
During the Kāitài era,
while hunting on Báldǔ Shān,
he was gored by a ram
and died.
Liú Huī
loved learning, was skilled in literary composition,
and was straightforward and possessed far-reaching strategies.
In the fifth year of Dàkāng (1079 CE),
he passed the *jìnshì* examination.
At the end of the Dà'ān era,
serving as Grand Master of the Crown Prince's Household,
he submitted a memorial stating:
"The various barbarian tribes on the western border are causing trouble.
Our soldiers are garrisoned far away,
and the people of the central regions are exhausted by rapid transportation (of supplies).
This is not a long-term strategy.
As for the current necessity,
nothing is better than building a city at Yánluò,
filling it with Hàntribes households,
making them cultivate fields and accumulate grain,
and using this to cover the expenses of the Northwest."
Although his words were not adopted,
those who understood the situation praised them.
second year,
he again submitted a memorial, saying:
"Sòng Ōuyáng Xiū compiled the *Wǔdài Shǐ* (History of the Five Dynasties),
and appended our dynasty to the Four Barbarians (Sì Yí),
recklessly adding defamation and criticism.
Moreover, the Sòng people relied on the generosity of our dynasty,
were permitted to communicate and maintain peace,
and were allowed to fully observe the rites of brotherhood.
Now, conversely, they allow their officials to recklessly compile history,
and calmly pay it no heed.
I, your subject, request that the early deeds of the Zhào clan
be fully appended to the National History."
The Emperor praised his words,
and promoted him to Lǐbù Lángzhōng (Director in the Ministry of Rites).
He was summoned by imperial decree to participate in the examination for the "Worthy and Good" (Xiánliáng Duìcè).
Huī's statements often hit upon the ailments of the time.
He was promoted to Shǐguǎn Xiūzhuàn (Compiler in the Historiography Institute),
and then died.
Yēlǜ Mèngjiǎn,
courtesy name Fùyì,
was the fifth-generation descendant of the Yūyuè Wūzhì.
His father, Liú Jiānú,
held the office of Jiédùshǐ (Military Commissioner).
Mèngjiǎn was naturally intelligent and perceptive.
At six years old,
his father went out hunting in the morning.
He was asked to compose a poem about the stars and moon in the dawn sky.
Mèngjiǎn composed it instantly,
and his father was greatly astonished.
When he grew up,
he was skilled at writing compositions.
Early in the Wénkāng era,
the Chief Military Commissioner Yēlǜ Yǐxīn seized power through treachery and deceit.
When Yǐxīn was sent out to serve as the Zhōngjīng Liúshǒu (Residential Administrator of the Central Capital),
Mèngjiǎn and Yēlǜ Shùzhēn submitted a memorial of congratulation.
Not long after,
Yǐxīn returned to his former post.
He resented (Mèngjiǎn and Shùzhēn) for this,
and demoted Mèngjiǎn to inspect the Cíyáo Pass.
Although he was driven out due to slander at the time,
he showed no bitterness in his words or expression.
Whenever he encountered scenic spots with forests and springs,
he would forget to return all day long.
The following year,
he was exiled to Bǎozhōu.
When he heard that the Crown Prince had been murdered,
he was overwhelmed with sorrow and pain.
He expressed his grief through poetry,
writing twenty poems titled *Fànghuái Shī* (Poems of Liberating the Mind).
His own preface says:
"Birds and beasts have sounds of sorrow and joy,
and mole crickets and ants have forms of movement and stillness.
If this is true even for creatures,
how much more so for humans?
However, the sorrow and joy of the worthy and accomplished,
do not lie between poverty and prosperity, or misfortune and fortune.
The *Yì* (Book of Changes) says: 'He who takes pleasure in Heaven and knows fate,
therefore has no worries.'
Therefore, Yán Yuān was contented with his simple basket and gourd (dān piáo).
This is what it means to know fate and be happy.
Although I am in exile,
I rely on the Dao to find comfort in myself.
What further doubt can there be?"
During the Dàkāng era,
he was finally allowed to return to his hometown.
He went to the palace and submitted a memorial, saying:
"Our dynasty has flourished
for nearly two hundred years.
It is proper that there should be a National History to pass down to future generations."
He then compiled the biographies of Yēlǜ Hélǔ, Wūzhì, and Xiūgē, and presented them.
The Emperor ordered the establishment of an office for compilation and revision.
Mèngjiǎn said to the other officials:
"The historical pen is the greatest trust of the world.
Whether a single word is right or wrong,
hundreds of generations follow it.
If there is no clear judgment,
and preferences and dislikes follow personal feelings,
then disaster is unpredictable.
Therefore, Zuǒ Shì, Sīmǎ Qiān, Bān Gù, and Fàn Yè all suffered calamity and misfortune.
How can one not be cautious!"
During the Qiántǒng era,
he was promoted to Liùyuànbù Tàibǎo (Grand Guardian of the Six Divisions).
He handled matters without adhering strictly to legalistic forms,
and people often laughed at his impracticality.
Mèngjiǎn heard this and said:
"In the time of high antiquity,
there were no registers, documents, or statutes,
yet the world was well-governed.
Indeed, registers, documents, and statutes
are only sufficient to breed deceit and favoritism,
and are not the foundation upon which the sage achieves governance."
He was transferred to Gāozhōu Guānchásǐ (Investigating Commissioner of Gāozhōu),
where he restored schools
and recruited students.
He was promoted to Zhāodéjūn Jiédùshǐ (Military Commissioner of Zhāodé Army).
Because the Central Capital (Zhōngjīng) suffered famine,
he was ordered by decree, along with Scholarly Official Liú Sìchāng, to sell grain at reduced prices.
Before the task was finished,
he died.
Yēlǜ Gǔyù,
courtesy name Xiūjiān,
was a man of the Liùyuànbù (Six Divisions).
His father, Āgǔzhī,
held the office of Jiédùshǐ.
Gǔyù was humble, composed, and adhered to ritual law.
He was skilled at writing.
During the Tǒnghé era,
he served as Tàibǎo (Grand Guardian) of his Division.
During the Kāitài era,
he was gradually promoted to Tàmǔchéng Jiédùshǐ.
He interrogated a complex legal case in Bàzhōu.
His findings satisfied the Emperor's intent,
and he was appointed Qǐshèngjūn Jiédùshǐ.
During the Tàipíng era,
he again served as Tàibǎo of his Division.
He resigned, citing illness, and returned home.
Soon after, he was promoted to Nányuàn Dàwáng (Great King of the Southern Chancery).
He lamented the daily decline of customs and morals.
He requested retirement,
but was not permitted.
Xīngzōng appointed him a Poetry Companion (Shī Yǒu),
frequently asking him about important matters of governance,
and he offered much guidance and counsel.

By imperial decree, he was instructed to compile the historical records of the early generations of Liáo, along with the Veritable Records of the various emperors, collaborating with Línyá Yēlǜ Shùchéng and Xiāo Hánjiānú.
He died before completion,
at the age of ninety.
The Commentary says: Kǒngzǐ (Confucius) stated:
"If a man can recite the three hundred poems (of the *Shī Jīng*),
but when entrusted with governance,
he cannot achieve results,
then even if he recites many,
what use are they?"
Wáng Dǐng was loyal and straightforward in achieving governance.
Liú Huī served the Eastern Palace (Qīng Gōng),
offering counsel on national strategies,
and clearly outlining the advantages and disadvantages of border defense.
All were insightful, broad-minded, and perceptive.
Mèngjiǎn disliked Yǐxīn's treachery and wickedness,
and though demoted, bore no resentment.
Who can say that men of literary attainment
are of no benefit to governance?
Biographies, Chapter Thirty-Five: Competent Officials (Néng Lì): Dà Gōngdǐng, Xiāo Wén, Mǎ Rénwàng, Yēlǜ Duóluōwò, Yáng Zūnxù, Wáng Táng.
The Hàn dynasty granted imperial letters to officials ranked two-thousand piculs (Èr Qiān Dàn),
and the Táng dynasty posted the names of Cìshǐ (Prefects) and Xiàn Lìng (County Magistrates) on screens,
to encourage and lead them.
Therefore, the histories of those two dynasties contain biographies of Model Officials (Xún Lì) and Good Officials (Liáng Lì).
Since the establishment of the state by Liáo Tàizǔ (Founding Emperor),
and the acquisition of Yān and Jì by Tàizōng,
the principle of appointing the worthy and employing the capable was also generally realized.
However, only the court appointed officials for the state (Guó Guān).
Those serving as officials in prefectures and counties largely followed the Táng system.
As the generations passed,
selection became increasingly strict.
At the time, high ministers were also dispatched to tour the territory,
to observe the worthy and the unworthy and promote or demote them accordingly.
Thus, for governing the people, managing finances, deciding legal cases, and suppressing banditry,
there were appropriate people for each task.
Examining their virtuous governance,
although they are not fully sufficient to be ranked among the Model or Good Officials,
they may still be called Competent Officials.
Therefore, the Biographies of Competent Officials is written.
Dà Gōngdǐng,
was a native of Bóhǎi.
His ancestors were registered in Shuàibīn County, Liáoyáng.
During the Tǒnghé era,
wealthy and influential families from Liáodōng were relocated to populate the Central Capital (Zhōngjīng).
He subsequently settled in Dàdìng.
His great-grandfather, Zhōng,
was Lǐbīnshǐ (Director of Receptions).
His father, Xìn,
was Xīngzhōng Zhǔbù (Registrar of Xīngzhōng).
Gōngdǐng was solemn and earnest in youth,
and loved learning as he grew up.
In the tenth year of Xiányōng (1074),
he passed the *Jìnshì* examination,
and was assigned as Shěngzhōu Guānchá Pànguān (Observational Judge of Shěn Prefecture).
At that time, rain and floods in Liáodōng damaged the crops.
The Northern Chancellery (Běi Shūmì Yuàn) heavily conscripted able-bodied men along the riverbanks to repair the dikes and defenses.
The supervising officials enforced the order harshly and urgently,
but Gōngdǐng alone said:
"The border defenses have just achieved peace;
to greatly undertake corvée labor
is not a method that benefits the state or aids the farmers."
He therefore submitted a detailed memorial regarding this matter.
The court accepted his advice,
halted the labor,
and the water did not cause disaster.
Along a thousand *lǐ* of riverbanks,
there was no one who was not pleased.
He was transferred to become Liángxiāng Lìng (Magistrate of Liángxiāng),
where he reduced corvée labor,
focused on farming and sericulture,
and established Confucian temples and schools.
The people of the region submitted to his civilizing influence.
He was successively promoted to Xīngguójūn Jiédù Fùshǐ (Deputy Military Commissioner of Xīngguó Army).
At that time, there were those attached to the Falconry Office,
using the name Luóbì
to harass and harm the fields and villages.
As years passed,
the common people could not endure it.
Gōngdǐng spoke to the Emperor,
who immediately ordered them forbidden and suppressed.
When Gōngdǐng had an audience at court,
the high officials informed the Emperor of the intention to praise and accept [his proposal].
Gōngdǐng said:
“One commandery gaining peace
is truly a great fortune;
however, there are many other commanderies similarly afflicted,
I wish for this grace to be equally bestowed upon the entire realm.”
This was agreed to.
He was transferred to become the Controller of Coin and Silk for Chángchūn Zhōu.
When the Imperial Procession traveled like the spring floods,
noble ladies routinely requested loans,
Gōngdǐng said:
“How can official funds be halted
to satisfy personal sentiment?”
He refused them.
He heard many words of resentment and cursing,
and he said:
“This is my duty,
I dare not neglect it.”
Soon after, he was appointed Dàlǐ Qīng (Minister of the Court of Judicial Review),
and he corrected many wrongful judgments.
When Tiānzuò ascended the throne,
he successively served as the Jìedùshǐ of Chángníng Jūn and Deputy Resident General of Nánjīng,
and was later appointed Minister of Revenue in Dōngjīng.
At that time, bandits murdered Xiāo Bǎoxiān, the Resident General,
initially coveting his wealth,
and thereby incited rebellion.
The common people also began to suspect and resent each other,
and households fought among themselves.
Gōngdǐng rode alone through the commandery,
explaining the consequences of disaster and fortune.
The masses all cast down their weapons, bowed, and said:
“He does not deceive us;
how dare we not obey his command.”
He pacified and settled the region as before.
He was appointed Resident General of Zhōngjīng,
bestowed the title Zhēnliàng Gōngchén (Meritorious Official of Loyalty and Integrity),
and traveled by courier station to his post.
At that time, bandits were rampant.
Those who met Gōngdǐng on the road
would immediately kneel before his horse and beg to reform themselves.
Gōngdǐng provided them with tallies and agreements,
allowing them to return to their former occupations.
Those who heard of this arrived one after another.
In less than ten days,
the territory was clear and peaceful.
Tiānzuò heard of this
and further bestowed upon him the title Bǎojié Gōngchén (Meritorious Official for Protecting Integrity).
At that time, people’s loyalty was wavering.
Gōngdǐng, concerned about potential disturbances,
requested that kindness and grace be spread to stabilize them,
and a general amnesty was granted for this purpose.
Gōngdǐng repeatedly submitted memorials requesting retirement,
but was not permitted.
Then, the Nú bandit Zhāng Sābā led scoundrels to gather,
and Gōngdǐng wished to attack but was unable due to lack of resources.
He sighed, saying:
“I have wished to retire from service for a long time.
I have been constrained by worldly circumstances,
and unfortunately, it has come to this.
Is this truly fate?”
He subsequently grew ill from worry and indignation.
He died in the first year of Bǎodà,
at the age of seventy-nine.
His son, Chānglíng,
was Zuǒ Chéngzhì;
Chāngsì
was the Cìshǐ of Míngzhōu;
Chāngcháo
was the Jìedù of Zhènníng Jūn.
Xiāo Wén,
courtesy name Guóhuá,
was the most worthy among the Empress’s relatives.
His father, Zhíshàn,
was the Fángyùshǐ of Ānzhōu.
Wén devoted himself earnestly to study,
and his joy or anger was never outwardly visible.
Early in Dàkāng,
he oversaw the affairs of the Zhōngchéng Division of the King of Qín and Yuè,
and was renowned for his talent and capability.
Soon after, he managed the Běimiàn Tiēhuáng (Northern Administration Imperial Secretary's Office).
The sons of Wáng Bāngyàn disputed an inherited official privilege (yìn),
and for several years it could not be settled.
The responsible authorities reported this.
The Emperor commanded Wén to investigate,
and he settled it immediately.
When the Imperial Procession was about to return to the palace,
he received the edict to review and practice the ritual guards.
Although the officials involved were numerous,
his commands were obeyed seamlessly.
He was promoted to Deputy Jìedùshǐ of Fèngguó Jūn,
and subsequently served as Dūjiān of the Emperor’s Maternal Uncles.
At the end of Shòulóng’s reign,
he was appointed Magistrate of Yìzhōu,
concurrently serving as Pacification Commissioner for the Southwest Region.
Gāoyáng had fertile land and wealthy people,
but officials governing the area
were always corrupted by bribes,
which caused the people great suffering.
When Wén first arrived,
he completely abolished the old abuses,
focused on farming and sericulture,
and promoted rites and education.
The people were all transformed by his influence.
At that time, there was a great drought,
and the hundred clans were extremely worried.
Whenever Wén prayed, rain followed immediately.
A subordinate county also suffered from locusts,
and there was a discussion about capturing and eliminating them.
Wén said:
“Locusts
are a heavenly disaster;
what good is catching them?”
He simply reflected on his own conduct and blamed himself,
and the locusts all flew away;
those remaining did not eat the sprouts,
but scattered in the weeds,
and were eaten by crows and magpies.
Later, when continuous heavy rain would not stop,
Wén again prayed, and the weather cleared immediately.
That year,
there was a great harvest.
The court considered Wén suitable for high office,
and promoted him to Jìedùshǐ of the Tánggǔ Department.
The people of Gāoyáng erected a stone stele to praise him.
Afterward, his final destiny is unknown.
Mǎ Rénwàng,
courtesy name Yǎnshū.
His great-great-grandfather, Yìnqīng,
was the Cìshǐ of Qīngzhōu during the Shí Jìn dynasty.
When the army of Tàizōng arrived,
he held firmly and did not surrender.
When the city fell, he was captured.
Tàizōng admired his righteousness and released him,
moving his clan to Yīwūlǘ Shān,
where they settled.
His great-grandfather, Tíngxù,
was the Resident General of Nánjīng.
His grandfather, Yuān,
was the Deputy Resident General of Zhōngjīng.
His father, Quán,
was the Wénsī Shǐ of Zhōngjīng.
Rénwàng was quick-witted.
He was orphaned young,
and grew up renowned for his talent and scholarship.
During the middle of Xiányōng,
he passed the Jìnshì examination
and became the Magistrate of Sōngshān County.
Annually, official charcoal had to be transported from Zézhōu,
but only Sōngshān County was conscripted for labor.
Rénwàng requested Xiāo Tǔhún, the Resident General of Zhōngjīng, to equalize the labor among other areas.
Tǔhún was enraged,
and handed him over to the officials,
imprisoning him for nearly a hundred days.
He was again summoned for questioning,
but Rénwàng remained unyielding.
Xiāo [Tǔhún] was pleased and said:
“Since you serve the people like this,
you will certainly be used for great things later.”
He reported the matter to the court,
and everything Rénwàng had requested was granted.
He was transferred to become the Magistrate of Xīnchéng County, Zhuōzhōu.
The county bordered Sòng territory,
and the main postal route passed through it.
Rénwàng governed without causing disturbance,
and the officials and people both feared and loved him.
When close officials returned from missions to Sòng,
the Emperor questioned them about external affairs,
and many recommended him.
He was promoted to Revenue Judge overseeing Salt and Iron for the Finance Bureau in Zhōngjīng.
He was transferred to Revenue Judge for the Three Agencies in Nánjīng,
where both public and private finances prospered.
He was promoted to Jǐngxún Shǐ (Inspector and Patrol Commissioner).
Lawsuits and prison cases piled up in the capital city.
Rénwàng decided them,
without a single person being wrongly convicted.
At that time, there was an inspection and count of households.
It was completed in less than twenty days.
Xiāo Bǎoxiān, the Deputy Resident General, found this strange and asked him about it.
Rénwàng replied:
“If the people's property is counted down to the last item,
it will certainly lead to the abuse of heavy taxation in the future.
Generally, counting six or seven out of ten is sufficient.”
Bǎoxiān bowed and said:
“Your consideration is far-reaching;
I could not reach that conclusion.”
Previously,
the Commissioner of Military Affairs (Shūmìshǐ), Yǐxīn, secretly manipulated power,
eventually harming the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ).
When Tiānzuò succeeded to the throne,
intending to avenge his father,
he selected Rénwàng and Xiāo Bàogēn to investigate the matter.
Rénwàng handled the matter impartially,
saving many people.
He was appointed as Vice Resident Commissioner of the Upper Capital (Shàngjīng Fù Liúshǒu).
At that time, the notorious bandit Zhào Zhōnggē invaded the palace grounds,
seizing palace women and imperial belongings.
Rénwàng led troops to capture him.
His right arm was struck by an arrow,
and cauterized with moxa,
but enduring his injury, he rode swiftly in pursuit.
The bandit abandoned what he had plundered and fled.
Rénwàng ordered the border passes and ferries to scrutinize travelers,
capturing all of the robbers.
Soon after, he was promoted to Chief Administrator of the Bureau of Military Affairs (Shūmì Dū Chéngzhǐ).
The Chancellor (Zǎixiàng) Yēlǜ Yǎn disliked Rénwàng
because he differed from himself, and had him transferred to Commissioner overseeing the palaces in the Southern Capital (Nánjīng Zhūgōng Tíxiá Zhìzhì).
Within a year,
he became the Military Governor of Bǎojìng Commandery (Bǎojìng Jūn Jiédùshǐ).
There were two cruel and violent officials,
whom the people feared like tigers.
Rénwàng treated them mildly in speech and appearance,
but secretly ordered their crimes to be exposed,
and had them branded and exiled.
That year, there was famine and scarcity everywhere,
but only in the area governed by Rénwàng
was there no shortage of grain, and no one needed to beat drums on the roads.
He was appointed in absentia as Military Governor of Zhāngyì Commandery (Zhāngyì Jūn Jiédùshǐ).
He was transferred to Commissioner of Finance for the Central Capital (Zhōngjīng Dùzhīshǐ).
When he first arrived,
the government granaries were all empty;
after working for half a year,
he had accumulated 150,000 *hú* of grain,
and 200,000 strings of cash.
He was moved to Palace Counsellor of the Left (Zuǒ Sànqí Chángshì),
and subsequently transferred to Academician Directly Serving in the Bureau of Military Affairs (Shūmì Zhí Xuéshì).
Not long after,
he was appointed Participant in Determining Governmental Affairs (Cānzhī Zhèngshì),
and concurrently acted as Commissioner of the Three Bureaus of the Southern Capital (Nánjīng Sānsīshǐ).
At that time, corruption in the receipt and disbursement of money and grain,
was most severe in Yān.
Rénwàng used silk to create a comprehensive ledger,
recording every item entering and leaving the treasury,
all separately registered.
He named it
"Línkù."
Wicked people and cunning officials could not manipulate the accounts,
so they publicized rumors on the streets that he was old.
The court discussion failed to investigate the truth,
and changed his post to Commissioner of the Southern Chancery (Nányuàn Xuānhuīshǐ),
to show respect for his age.
After a year,
Tiānzuò personally wrote
"Xuān Mǎ Xuānhuī"
(Summons Mǎ, the Xuānhuīshǐ) to summon him.
When he arrived,
the Emperor instructed him, saying:
"The assumption that you are old
was a mistake caused by listening to rumors."
He was then appointed Commissioner of Military Affairs of the Southern Chancery (Nányuàn Shūmìshǐ).
No one dared to approach him with private requests,
and when appointing people, he always used those whom public opinion deemed worthy.
For example, Cáo Yǒngyì and Yú Zhòngwén had previously been driven out by wicked men,
but Rénwàng recommended them,
and both became famous ministers.
What greatly troubled the people at that time
were the corvée duties related to the postal relay stations, horses and oxen, banners and drums, village heads, bureau servants, and granary staff.
These duties were so heavy that people went bankrupt trying to fulfill them.
Rénwàng required the people to contribute money,
while the government itself hired laborers.
This was considered highly convenient at the time.
After a long time, he requested retirement due to age,
and retired with the honorary titles of Honorary Minister of the Masses (Shǒu Sītú) and Concurrently Palace Attendant (Jiān Shìzhōng).
He died,
and was posthumously titled Wénxiàn.
Rénwàng maintained strict moral integrity,
showing no sign of happiness or anger.
He never fawned upon others seeking promotion.
When he was first appointed to the administration,
his family congratulated him.
Rénwàng said sadly:
"Do not rejoice at gaining office,
and do not worry if you lose it.
If one is raised extremely high,
the push down will surely be severe."
Such was his cautious apprehension.
Yēlǜ Duóluówò,
courtesy name Yǐxīnyǐn,
was a descendant of the household of the youngest paternal uncle.
He was honest, frugal, and valued righteousness.
Late in the Zhòngxī era,
he served in the Bureau of Edicts (Gàoyuàn).
During the Xiányōng era,
he was repeatedly transferred until he became Vice Resident Commissioner of the Southern Capital (Tóngzhī Nánjīng Liúshǒu Shì).
When he was summoned (for a new post),
because the people of his district earnestly requested him to stay,
an imperial decree was issued commending him.
Early in the Dàkāng era,
he was appointed Commissioner of Pacification for the Southwest Circuit (Xīnánmiàn Zhāotǎoshǐ),
served as Northern Chancellor of the Secretariat (Běimiàn Línyá),
and was transferred to Chief Justice of the Left (Zuǒ Yílíbì).
In the fifth year of Dà'ān,
he was appointed Chancellor of the Southern Administration (Nánfǔ Zǎixiàng).
Early in the Shòulóng era,
he retired
and died.
Wherever Duóluówò served, he earned fame;
officials and commoners both respected and loved him.
When he retired and lived in his hometown,
his son, Pǔgǔ, was Military Governor of the Wūgǔ Tribe (Wūgǔbù Jiédùshǐ),
and sent someone to welcome him.
After arriving,
he observed that Pǔgǔ's accumulated wealth was enormous.
He said to Pǔgǔ:
"Leaving your family to enter officialdom,
your duty should be to enrich the state and secure the people.
To violate principle and deceive the ruler,
merely to chase after profit and gain,
is not my ambition."
He ordered his carriage and returned home.
Pǔgǔ was later killed by bandits.
Yáng Zūnxù,
courtesy name Yìjiè,
was a native of Fànyáng in Zhuōzhōu.
In the nineteenth year of Zhòngxī, he passed the *jìnshì* examination,
and was assigned as Judicial Assistant (Pànguān) for Rúzhōu Commandery.
He was repeatedly promoted until he became Vice Administrator of the Bureau of Military Affairs (Shūmìyuàn Fù Chéngzhǐ).
In the third year of Xiányōng,
he served as the Envoy to the Sòng State to offer New Year’s greetings;
upon his return,
he was transferred to Chief Administrator (Dū Chéngzhǐ).
Affairs of the empire
accumulated in the Bureau of Military Affairs (Shūfǔ),
where documents piled up like mountains.
Zūnxù could read five lines at a glance,
deciding cases swiftly,
and reporting clearly and ably.
The Emperor praised him.
He received an imperial decree to collect overdue money owed to the Ministry of Revenue,
recovering over 400,000 strings (*mín*),
and was appointed Academician Directly Serving in the Bureau of Military Affairs (Shūmì Zhí Xuéshì),
then changed to Vice Commissioner of Military Affairs (Shūmì Fùshǐ).
Early in the Dàkāng era,
he served as Participant in Determining Governmental Affairs (Cānzhī Zhèngshì),
transferred to Administrator of the Bureau of Military Affairs (Zhī Shūmìyuàn Shì),
concurrently Palace Attendant and Manager of Governmental Affairs (Ménxià Shìláng Píngzhāngshì),
and appointed Chancellor of the Southern Administration (Nánfǔ Zǎixiàng).
When Yēlǜ Yǐxīn falsely accused the Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ),
Zūnxù and Yàngē were commanded to investigate the matter,
but Zūnxù dared not speak truthfully,
and contemporaries criticized him for this failing.
Soon after, he was appointed Chancellor of the Northern Administration (Běifǔ Zǎixiàng).
During the Dà'ān era, he died suddenly,
at the age of fifty-six.
He was posthumously granted the title Honorary Minister of Works (Shǒu Sīkōng),
and given the posthumous name Kāngyì.
His son, Huì,
eventually became Academician Directly Serving in the Zhaowen Hall (Zhāowénguǎn Zhí Xuéshì).
Wáng Táng,
was a native of Xīnchéng in Zhuōzhōu.
He was widely learned in antiquity
and skilled at composition.
In the fifteenth year of Zhòngxī, he was selected as a *jìnshì*.
In the local recommendation, Ministry of Rites, and palace examinations, he ranked first in all answers.
He was repeatedly transferred until he became Salt and Iron Commissioner of the Upper Capital (Shàngjīng Yántiěshǐ).
Some falsely accused him of bribery,
but the accusation was unsubstantiated,
and he was released.
He was transferred to Commissioner of Revenue for the Eastern Capital (Dōngjīng Hùbùshǐ).
In the second year of Dàkāng,
Liáodōng suffered a famine,
and many people died.
He requested famine relief,
and the request was granted.
In the third year,
he entered the central government as Vice Commissioner of Military Affairs (Shūmì Fùshǐ),
and was appointed Chancellor of the Southern Administration (Nánfǔ Zǎixiàng).
Late in the Dà'ān era,
he died.
Táng was experienced and successful in court administration,
and was never remiss when facing a task.
While in government, he reformed and clarified the laws and regulations,
and achieved renown.
Discussion: Mèngzǐ said,
“The people are the most valuable,
the altars of soil and grain (Shèjì) come next.”
How should those who govern expend their efforts completely?
Gōng Dǐng requested the cessation of the dike completion project to give the people rest,
and refused the princess's requests for loans to uphold the law.
He traveled through the commandery alone on horseback,
transforming bandits into good people.
He was almost comparable to the excellence of Zhāo and Dù.
Wén governed Yìzhōu,
and the rain and sun answered his prayers;
locusts caused no disaster.
When the people hoped he would not shirk from imprisonment,
he served as Judge of the Department of Finance (Pàndùzhī);
public and private resources were both abundant.
He was truly outstanding and difficult to surpass.
Duó Lǔ Wò was feared by officials and loved by the people.
Yáng Zūn Xù settled affairs like flowing water.
They were truly capable officials!
Biography 36: Eminent Conduct (Zhuóxíng) Xiāo Zhá Là, Yēlǜ Guānnú, Xiāo Pú Lí Bù
During the establishment of the Liáo state, those entrusted with affairs
were only the two clans, Yēlǜ and Xiāo.
Among these two clans,
there were those who were humble and self-sufficient,
not corrupted by wealth and honor,
not bent by fame or gain,
who could uplift declining customs
and inspire a shallow society.
They are also worthy of commendation.
We have selected three such individuals.
Therefore, we compose the Biography of Eminent Conduct (Zhuóxíng Zhuàn).
Xiāo Zhá Là,
whose *zì* was Xū Liǎn,
was the younger brother of the Northern Chancellery Chancellor (Běi Fǔ Zǎixiàng) Pái Yā.
His nature was forthright and independent;
he did not engage in creating a livelihood (business).
During the Bǎoníng era (969–979),
he advanced through his relations,
and was successively promoted to Military Governor of Níngyuǎn Commandery (Níngyuǎn Jūn Jiédù Shǐ).
When his term was complete, he returned to his home community,
living a life of indifference and contentment.
At the end of the Tǒnghé era (1012),
he was summoned to be Commander-in-Chief of the Cavalry and Infantry of the Southern Capital (Nánjīng Mǎ Bù Jūn Dū Zhǐhuī Shǐ).
Citing illness, he sought retirement,
but was refused.
He was transferred to be Yí Lí Bì.
He again resigned due to illness,
and this time, he was granted permission.
He then entered Xié Shān,
closing his door and not going out.
The Emperor praised his resolve
and did not summon him again.
Thereafter, Zhá Là made his home in Xié Shān.
When relatives and friends occasionally visited him,
they spoke throughout the day without touching upon current affairs.
Whenever banquets or excursions were organized,
he did not refuse to attend.
For more than half the year, he lived in the mountains,
out of sync with common society.
Yēlǜ Zī Zhōng respected him greatly
and named him "The Elder of Xié Shān."
He died.
Yēlǜ Guānnú,
whose *zì* was Xī Yǐn,
was the grandson of the Chief Minister Wò Lǔ (Línyá Wò Lǔ).
He was reserved, scholarly,
and particularly detailed regarding the genealogy of the ruling dynasty.
He loved wine and enjoyed leisure.
Initially,
he was summoned to be a General of the Imperial Guard (Sùzhí Jiāngjūn).
In the ninth year of Zhòngxī (1040),
he left office due to illness.
Because the Emperor considered Guānnú a distinguished relative
and wished to fulfill his ambition,
he permitted him to choose a Military Governorship (Jiédù Shǐ) position in any circuit.
Guānnú declined, saying:
“I am dull and foolish;
I am unfit for official duties.”
He was subsequently appointed Military Governor of Guīyì Commandery (Guīyì Jūn Jiédù Shǐ),
but immediately requested retirement.
Guānnú was close friends with Xiāo Wā of the Ōu Lǐ Bù tribe.
Wā said to Guānnú:
“If an official cannot bring imperial grace to the people
or achieve great merit,
why bother being fussy about it?
If you and I live in the woods,
with only mats and pillows to accompany us,
enjoying ourselves with wine and poetry,
even without official positions,
we would have no regrets.”
Guānnú agreed with him.
At the time, they were called
“The Two Recluses” (Èr Yì).
During the Qiántǒng era (1101–1110),
Guānnú died.
Xiāo Pú Lí Bù,
whose *zì* was Ruǐ Lǎn,
was a fourth-generation descendant of Wèi Guó Wáng Huì.
His parents died early,
and he was raised by his grandfather, Wù Gǔ Nì.
He was naturally filial and fraternal.
At age thirteen,
Wù Gǔ Nì died.
He felt that having already lost his father and mother early,
he now suffered the loss of his grandfather again.
His mourning and grief exceeded propriety,
earning the praise and admiration of his clan and community.
He once said to others:
“I was unable to care for my parents until the end.
Now who will guide me?
If I do not exert myself,
how can I repay the kindness of my nurture and upbringing!”
From then on, he studied diligently,
mastering every literary art.
During the Qiántǒng era,
he was summoned because of his grandfather Wù Gǔ Nì’s service,
but he did not respond.
He often toured mountains and rivers, hunting with relatives and acquaintances.
He served his needs without excessive possessions or servants,
living joyfully.
Someone asked:
“Why do you not consider succeeding to the merits and fame of your ancestors?”
He replied:
“I judge myself inadequate to follow the ancestral industry.
I am past the age of strength (*qiáng shì*—around forty);
how could I benefit the sovereign or protect the people now?”
He was summoned multiple times,
but always declined, citing illness.
In his later years,
he ceased all interaction with society,
settled in Mǒ Gǔ Shān,
shunned meat and vegetables,
and devoted himself to Buddhist scriptures,
inviting virtuous men to converse all day long.
People asked what spiritual gains he had achieved,
he merely said:
“There is profound joy!
I only perceive that the six senses do not interfere with each other;
I know nothing else.”
One day,
he changed his clothes
and passed away without illness.
Discussion: Reclusion (Yǐn),
is indeed not easily achieved,
nor should it be lightly attributed to others.
If Zhá Là resigns office and avoids discussing current affairs,
Guānnú twice declines Military Governorships,
and Pú Lí Bù is summoned but does not attend—
though they are perhaps not sufficiently worthy of being called recluses;
yet in their time, they were able to understand the distinction between public and private life,
and were content with living an abundant withdrawal (fěi dùn).
Is this not superior to those who seek wealth, honor, and success, only to be shamed by their wives and concubines?
Thus, calling them figures of Eminent Conduct (Zhuóxíng) is acceptable.
Biography 37: Notable Women (Liènǚ) Chén Shì, wife of Xíng Jiǎn; Yēlǜ Shì Cháng Gē; Xiāo Shì, wife of Yēlǜ Nú; Xiāo Shì, wife of Yēlǜ Zhú Zhě; Xiāo Shì, wife of Yēlǜ Zhōng
The coupling of male and female to establish a household
is a great human relationship.
Rather than acquiring a notable (martyr) woman (liènǚ),
it is better to acquire a virtuous woman (xiánnǚ).
If the realm must rely on the fame of a liènǚ,
that is not fortunate.
The *Shī Jīng* praises Wèi Gòng Jiāng,
and the *Chūn Qiū* commends Sòng Bó Jī;
this was done out of necessity,
to emphasize the importance of human relationships in times of distress.
Liáo occupied the North,
and its customs and culture were considered looser compared to the Central Plains.
Throughout the Liáo dynasty,
we find two virtuous women (xiánnǚ)
