and three notable (martyr) women (liènǚ),
demonstrating that the innate moral principle of the human heart does not fluctuate with the rise and fall of society.
Chén Shì, wife of Xíng Jiǎn,
was a native of Yíngzhōu.
Her father, Xíng,
served successively as Minister of Works (Sītú) during the Five Dynasties period.
As soon as Chén Shì came of age (*fǔ jī*),
she became proficient in the meaning of the classics.
Whenever she read poetry and rhapsodies,
she could immediately recite them.
She was especially fond of composing verse;
at the time, she was known as the Female Cultivated Talent (Nǚ Xiùcái).
At age twenty,
she married Jiǎn.
She was filial to her parents-in-law,
and her household was harmonious;
her relatives and in-laws greatly respected her.
She had six sons.
Chén Shì personally taught them the classics.
Later, her two sons, Bǎo Pǔ and Bǎo Zhì, were both deemed virtuous
and reached the position of Chancellor (Zǎixiàng).
She died in the twelfth year of Tǒnghé (994).
Empress Ruìzhì heard of this,
sighed in sorrow,
and granted her the posthumous title Lady of Lǔ State (Lǔ Guó Fūrén).
A stone inscription was carved to memorialize her conduct.
When her coffin was moved for joint burial,
an envoy was sent to conduct the sacrifice.
Commentators said that she was chaste, serene, gentle, and compliant,
and her conduct as a wife and example as a mother was faultless from beginning to end.
the younger sister of Tàishī Shìlǔ,
her nickname was Chánggē.
As a child, she was bright and elegant,
possessing the demeanor of an adult.
When she grew up,
her conduct was refined and pure,
and she swore an oath never to marry.
She was capable in poetry and prose,
but did not compose carelessly.
She read the *Tōng Lì* (Comprehensive History),
saw the successes and failures of past generations,
and was skilled at evaluating history.
During the Xiányōng period,
she composed an essay discussing contemporary governance.
A summary of it reads:
"The ruler takes the people as the body;
the people take the ruler as the heart.
The sovereign should employ the loyal and worthy,
and ministers should eliminate partisanship;
then governance will be balanced,
and Yin and Yang will be harmonious.
If you wish to attract those far away,
then promote grace and value virtue;
if you wish to strengthen the nation,
then lighten labor duties and reduce taxes.
The Four Beginnings and the Five Constants are the foundation of rule and teaching,
and the Six Stores and the Three Matters truly concern the life of the people.
Extravagance can serve as a warning,
while diligence and frugality can serve as a model.
When injustice is rectified, people dare not deceive;
when loyalty is made manifest, people dare not cheat.
Do not cling to the Buddhist path (the empty gate),
excessively decorating with earth and wood;
do not needlessly deal with remote borderlands,
rashly wasting gold and silk.
When full, one must consider overflowing;
when safe, one must contemplate danger.
When punishments match the crime,
the people will be encouraged towards goodness.
If exotic goods are not treasured,
then worthy men will arrive.
Establish an enduring foundation of ten thousand generations,
and control the arrogance of the various tribes.
If you wish to lead your subordinates,
first correct yourself;
if you wish to govern the distant,
then begin with the imperial court."
The Emperor praised it.
At that time, the Grand Councilor (Shūmì Shǐ) Yēlǜ Yǐxīn admired her talent
and repeatedly requested poems.
Chánggē sent him a palindrome poem (*huíwén*).
Yǐxīn knew she was satirizing him
and held a grudge.
In the third year of Dàkāng,
the Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ) was implicated in an affair.
Yǐxīn falsely accused him of a crime,
but upon investigation, there was no evidence,
so he was acquitted.
Just then, her elder brother Shìlǔ was banished to Zhènzhōu.
Chánggē went with him,
often wearing coarse clothes and eating simple food.
People asked her,
"Why do you inflict such suffering upon yourself?"
She replied,
"The Crown Heir (Huáng Chǔ) was wrongly deposed;
how can people like us enjoy fine food and peaceful sleep?"
When the Crown Prince was murdered,
her grief was immense.
At the age of seventy,
she died at home.
Xiāo shì, the wife of Yēlǜ Nú,
her nickname was Yìxīn,
the daughter of Guójiù Fùmǎ Dūwèi Táo Sūwò.
Her mother was Princess Húdú.
Yìxīn had beautiful looks,
and at the age of twenty,
she first married Nú.
She served her parents and maintained harmony with her clan,
known for her filial piety and prudence.
She once gathered with her younger sisters-in-law and sisters-in-law,
who argued about using witchcraft to gain their husbands' favor.
Yìxīn said,
"Witchcraft is not as good as ritual principles."
The others asked her why.
Yìxīn replied:
"Cultivating oneself through purity,
serving elders with respect,
attending to one's husband with gentleness,
and treating subordinates with broadness,
without allowing gentlemen to see her behaving frivolously—
this is what ritual principles are,
and naturally one will gain respect from one's husband.
To gain favor through witchcraft,
is one not ashamed in one's heart!"
Those who heard this were greatly embarrassed.
Previously,
Nú had a feud with Grand Councilor Yǐxīn.
When the Crown Prince was deposed,
Nú was falsely accused and stripped of his rank,
confiscated into the Xīngshèng Palace,
and exiled to the Wūgǔ tribe.
The Emperor, considering that Yìxīn was the daughter of a princess,
wished for her to divorce.
Yìxīn refused, saying:
"Your Majesty, by considering my peripheral kinship
and allowing me to avoid exile,
this is truly the grace of Heaven and Earth.
However, the righteousness of husband and wife
persists through life and death.
Since my coming of age, I have followed Nú;
if I suddenly abandon him when facing disaster,
immediately separating,
I would be abandoning the path of the fundamental principles (Gāngcháng).
How would I be different from a beast?
I beg Your Majesty to show pity,
and allow me to go with Nú.
Then even if I die, I will have no regret!"
The Emperor was moved by her words
and granted her request.
Yìxīn remained in the place of banishment for a long time,
personally performing manual labor.
Although weary, she showed no sign of hardship.
She served her husband with courtesy and respect,
even more than before.
During the Shòulóng period,
she submitted a petition requesting that her descendants be made Zhùzhàng Lángjūn (Attendant Gentlemen).
The Emperor praised her integrity
and summoned the entire family back.
Her son, Guóyǐn,
began his official career during the Qiántǒng period.
During the Bǎodà period,
Yìxīn was at Línhuáng.
She said to her sons,
"I estimate that Lú Yànlún will certainly rebel.
You should hurry and escape;
I will remain and die here."
When the bandits arrived,
she was killed.
Xiāo shì, the wife of Yēlǜ Zhúzhě,
her nickname was Élǐběn,
daughter of Guójiù Bó Jǐn.
Her nature was upright and pure;
she had a beautiful appearance,
and from youth, she was different from other girls.
At the age of eighteen,
she married Zhúzhě.
She was prudent, generous, chaste, and gentle;
her sisters-in-law held her in high esteem.
When observing mourning for Zhúzhě,
she was extremely sorrowful and frail.
After the burial,
she said to her close relatives:
"The Way of husband and wife
is like Yin and Yang, or the outer layer and lining of a garment.
Without Yang, Yin cannot stand;
without the outer layer, the lining has nothing to cling to.
I am now unfortunate to have lost my husband (my heaven).
Although life inevitably leads to death,
this is the natural order.
Zhúzhě rose to court early,
but though talented, he lacked longevity.
Heaven has brought misfortune upon me,
suffering this cruel penalty;
what reliance do I have left?
If the deceased could be seen,
I would follow him;
since he cannot be seen,
I ought to be with him."
Her maids tried to encourage and comfort her, but she did not change her mind.
She took her own life with a blade and died.
Xiāo shì, the wife of Yēlǜ Zhōng,
her nickname was Ruólán,
the fourth-generation descendant of Hánguó Wáng Huì.
She was intelligent, prudent, and sincere.
At the age of twenty, she married Zhōng.
She served her husband respectfully and obediently;
all her relatives praised her virtue.
Zhōng once said to her,
"You should acquire a basic understanding of books,
taking the chaste and virtuous women of the past as mirrors."
Thereupon, she determined to recite and study,
encompassing much of antiquity and the present.
Yēlǜ Zhòng's wife, Lady Xiāo
—her childhood name was Ruólán
—was the fourth-generation descendant of Hánguó Wáng Huì.
She was intelligent, wise, and virtuous.
At the age of twenty, she married Zhòng.
She served her husband with reverence and obedience,
and all her relatives praised her virtue.
Zhòng once said to her:
"You should learn to read a little,
taking the virtuous women of the past as your example."
Thereupon, she resolved to recite and study,
delving into many ancient and modern texts.
During the Tiānqìng reign,
she was captured by bandits.
She secretly placed a blade in her shoe,
and swore:
"If anyone tries to defile me,
I will die by it."
By night,
the bandits fled, and she escaped.
After a long time,
the emperor summoned Zhòng to be the Wǔyuàn Dūjiān.
Zhòng said to his wife:
"Originally, I had no desire for officialdom,
but now I cannot avoid it.
I will repay the country with my death.
Can you follow me?"
Ruólán replied:
"I will respectfully obey your instruction."
When the Jīn army swept through the lands west of the mountains,
relocating all its people,
Zhòng upheld his integrity and died.
Ruólán's grief was not outwardly expressed,
which surprised people.
Suddenly, she leaped onto a horse and rode out,
and committed suicide at the place where Zhòng had died.
A commentary states: Lady Chén taught her two sons with scriptures,
and they both became worthy prime ministers.
Lady Yēlǜ kept herself pure and did not remarry.
Though she resided within her boudoir, she did not forget to be loyal to her lord.
Could this be achieved if she were not virtuous?
The integrity of these three Lady Xiāos
surpasses even what some valiant men could accomplish.
Biographies, Volume 38: Fangjì: Zhílǔgǔ, Wáng Bái, Wèi Lín, Yēlǜ Dílǔ, Yēlǜ Yǐbùgē
Kǒngzǐ said,
"Even minor arts must have something worth observing,"
and medicine and divination are precisely that.
Medicine saves from untimely death and plague,
and divination resolves indecision.
Both are beneficial to the state
and provide favor to the people.
Earlier historians recorded them without omission,
hence these biographies.
Zhílǔgǔ,
a Tǔyùhún person.
Initially,
Tàizǔ defeated the Tǔyùhún.
A cavalier abandoned a bag,
shot an arrow back without hitting, and left.
When the pursuing soldiers opened the bag to examine it,
they found a baby inside,
who was Zhílǔgǔ.
They questioned the captured soldiers about the reason,
and learned that the one who shot at the bag
was the baby's father.
His family had been skilled physicians for generations.
Even diagnosing from horseback,
he knew the root and symptoms of illnesses.
He didn't want his son to be captured by others,
and intended to kill him.
Because of this, he was presented to Tàizǔ,
and Chúnqīn Huánghòu adopted him.
When he grew up, he was also skilled in medicine,
specializing in acupuncture and moxibustion.
During Tàizōng's reign,
he served as a grand imperial physician.
He once compiled a book on pulse diagnosis and acupuncture and moxibustion,
which circulated in the world.
He died at the age of ninety.
Wáng Bái,
a native of Jìzhōu.
He understood astronomy
and was skilled in divination.
He was Sītiān Shàojiān of the Jìn.
Tàizōng obtained him when he entered Biàn.
In the nineteenth year of Yìnglì,
Prince Zhǐmò was imprisoned for an incident.
His mother sought divination.
Bái said:
"This person is destined to become king.
He cannot be killed yet.
Do not worry excessively!"
When Jǐngzōng ascended the throne,
he pardoned his crime
and enfeoffed him as Níngwáng,
which indeed happened as he said.
Many of his predictions of fortune and misfortune were like this.
During the Bǎoníng reign,
he successively served as Jìedùshǐ of Zhāngwǔ and Xīngguó military commands.
He compiled the "Bǎizhòng Gē," which circulated in the world.
Wèi Lín,
it is unknown from which prefecture he was.
He was famous for divination.
Tàizōng obtained him in Biàn.
In the first year of Tiānlù,
the emperor ordered a horse race to determine speed,
and thus the winner and loser.
He asked Wáng Bái and Lín who would win.
Bái reported:
"The red one will win."
Lín said:
"As I see it,
the dappled-grey horse should win."
After the race,
it was indeed as Lín had said.
The emperor was surprised and asked him.
Bái said:
"Today, Fire is dominant,
so I knew the red one would win."
Lín said:
"That is not so.
Although Fire is dominant,
there is smoke above it.
Observing by the smoke,
the blue one will surely win."
The emperor praised him.
In the fifth year,
Chágē plotted rebellion
and privately sought divination from Lín.
When Lín first divined,
he said:
"Your Highness's fate
has but one day left.
You should be cautious!"
When the rebellion occurred,
it indeed failed.
During the Yìnglì reign,
Zhōu soldiers invaded Yān.
The emperor asked Lín about the victory or defeat.
Lín said:
"The Zhōu surname is Chái (wood),
and Yān is divided by Huǒ (fire).
When wood enters fire,
it will surely be consumed."
His words indeed came true.
Lín once divined for Tàipíng Wáng Yǎnsāgē regarding an illegal usurpation.
When the emperor heard of it,
he was spared death
and exiled to the Wūgǔ tribe.
One day,
the Jiédùshǐ summoned Lín.
Just then, someone presented a pair of carp.
He jokingly said:
"When do you predict we will eat this fish?"
Lín replied after a long pause:
"You and I will not get through today
without unforeseen disaster.
How will we have time to eat the fish?"
He immediately ordered them to cook it.
Before they could eat,
bandits arrived,
and both were killed.
Yēlǜ Dílǔ,
courtesy name Sābùwǎn.
His ancestors were originally from the Wǔyuàn clan.
When the palace division was first established,
they were subordinate to it.
Dílǔ was skilled in medicine.
He could discern the origin of an illness just by observing a person's appearance.
Even without feeling the pulse,
he had a perfect success rate.
In the early Tǒnghé period,
he was recommended by Grand Chancellor Hán Déràng
and rose to the official position of Jiédùshǐ.
Initially,
the wife of Pímìshǐ Yēlǜ Xiézhěn suffered from a chronic illness.
Several doctors had tried and failed to cure her.
Dílǔ observed her and said:
"Her heart has accumulated heat.
This cannot be reached by medicine alone.
It must be treated with intent.
Because she is deaf,
we should deafen her further and induce madness to expel the toxins. This will work."
Thereupon, he ordered large gongs and drums to be beaten in front of her.
The next day, she indeed went mad,
shouting and cursing furiously,
until her strength was exhausted, and she stopped.
She then recovered.
Many of his treatments were like this,
and people could not fathom them.
He died at the age of eighty.
Yēlǜ Yǐbùgē,
courtesy name Xíniǎn,
was a descendant of the Liùyuàn Lángjūn Niǎogǔzhí.
From a young age, he loved learning,
and was especially skilled in divination. He did not enjoy official careers.
During the Tiānqìng era,
he was captured by bandits.
He secretly placed a blade in his shoe,
and vowed, saying:
"If anyone tries to defile me,
I will immediately kill myself."
When night came,
the bandits fled, and he escaped.
After a long time,
the Emperor summoned Zhōng to be the Administrator-in-Chief of the Five Courts (Wǔ Yuàn Dūjiān).
Zhōng said to his wife:
"I originally had no ambition for official life,
but now I cannot avoid it.
I ought to repay the nation with my death.
Can you follow me?"
Ruólán replied, saying:
"I respectfully follow your instruction."
When the Jīn army scoured the lands west of the ridge (Lǐngxī),
moving all its inhabitants,
Zhōng maintained his integrity and died.
Ruólán’s grief was not outwardly expressed,
and people found this strange.
Suddenly she leapt upon a horse and rushed out,
going to the place where Zhōng had died and killing herself.
The Commentary says: Chén Shì educated her two sons using the Classics,
and both became virtuous prime ministers.
Yēlǜ Shì maintained her purity and did not marry;
residing within the women's quarters, she did not forget loyalty to her lord.
If not virtuous, how could she achieve this?
As for the integrity of the three Xiāo Shì women,
even fierce men might not be able to equal it.
Memoir Thirty-Eight: Practitioners of Arts and Skills: Zhílǔgǔ, Wáng Bái, Wèi Lín, Yēlǜ Dílǔ, Yēlǜ Yǐbùgē
Kǒngzǐ stated,
"In minor arts there must be something worthy of observation,"
and medicine and divination fit this description.
Medicine saves against untimely death and plague,
and divination resolves hesitation.
Both offer aid to the state
and bestow kindness upon the people.
Previous historians recorded them and did not omit them,
thus they are included in this memoir.
Zhílǔgǔ
was a Tǔyùhún person.
Initially,
when Tàizǔ defeated the Tǔyùhún,
a horseman abandoned a pouch,
shot an arrow back, missed, and rode off.
When the pursuing troops opened the pouch and looked,
inside they found an infant,
who was Zhílǔgǔ.
They questioned the captives about the reason,
and learned that the one who had shot at the pouch
was the infant's father.
He was hereditarily skilled in medicine,
and even when diagnosing sickness from horseback,
he knew both the symptoms and the root cause.
His intention was that he did not want his son to be captured by others;
he wished only to kill him.
Because of this, he was presented to Tàizǔ,
and Empress Chúnqīn adopted and raised him.
When he grew up, he was also skilled in medicine,
specializing solely in acupuncture and moxibustion.
During the reign of Tàizōng,
he served as an attendant Palace Physician.
He once compiled *The Secrets of the Pulse* (Mài Jué) and a book on Acupuncture and Moxibustion (Zhēn Jiǔ Shū),
which circulated widely.
He died at the age of ninety.
Wáng Bái,
a person from Jìzhōu,
understood astronomy,
and was skilled at divination.
He was Vice Director of the Bureau of Astronomy (Sī Tiān Shàojiān) under the Jìn Dynasty.
Tàizōng obtained him upon entering Biàn.
In the nineteenth year of Yìnglì,
Prince Zhǐmò was imprisoned for an offense,
and his mother requested a divination.
Bái said:
"This person is destined to become king;
they cannot kill him yet.
Do not worry excessively!"
When Jǐngzōng ascended the throne,
he pardoned his crime,
enfeoffed him as Prince Níng,
and it ultimately happened just as he had predicted.
His predictions concerning misfortune and fortune were mostly of this accurate nature.
During the Bǎoníng era,
he successively served as Military Commissioner (Jiédùshǐ) for the Zhāngwǔ and Xīngguó armies.
He compiled the *Song of A Hundred Hits* (Bǎi Zhōng Gē), which circulated widely.
Wèi Lín.
It is unknown from which prefecture he hailed,
but he was renowned for his divination.
Tàizōng acquired him in Biàn.
In the first year of Tiānlù,
the Emperor ordered a horse race to compare the speeds of the horses,
in order to determine the winner and loser.
He asked Wáng Bái and Lín who would win.
Bái memorialized, saying:
"The red one will win."
Lín said:
"As your servant sees it,
the dappled horse should win."
When they raced,
it was ultimately just as Lín had said.
The Emperor was astonished and questioned them.
Bái said:
"Today the element of Fire is dominant,
thus I knew the red one would win."
Lín said:
"That is incorrect.
Although Fire is dominant,
there is smoke above it.
By observing the smoke,
the dark-colored one must win."
The Emperor praised him.
Five years later,
Chágē plotted treason
and secretly sought divination from Lín.
When Lín finished the divination,
he said:
"Your Majesty’s destiny
has but one day left.
You must be cautious!"
When the rebellion broke out,
he was indeed defeated.
During the Yìnglì era,
Zhōu troops invaded Yān,
and the Emperor asked Lín about the outcome.
Lín said:
"The ruling house of Zhōu has the surname Chái (Firewood),
and Yān is associated with Fire.
When Firewood enters Fire,
it will inevitably be consumed."
His prediction was indeed validated.
Lín once performed divination for Prince Tàipíng, Yǎnsāgě, concerning his plot for usurpation.
The Emperor heard of this,
spared him from death,
and exiled him to the Wūgǔ tribe.
One day,
the Military Commissioner (Jiédùshǐ) summoned Lín.
It happened that someone presented two carp,
and he jokingly said:
"Can you divine when these fish will be eaten?"
Lín remained silent for a long time, then replied:
"Neither you nor I will survive today;
there is unforeseen disaster.
How can we have leisure to eat the fish?"
He immediately ordered them to be cooked.
Before they could eat,
bandits arrived,
and both were killed.
Yēlǜ Dílǔ,
courtesy name Sābùwǎn.
His ancestors were originally of the Five Courts clan.
When the palace divisions were first established,
they were enrolled there.
Dílǔ was highly skilled in medicine;
by observing the patient’s form and complexion, he immediately knew the origin of the disease.
Even without taking the pulse or examining thoroughly,
he achieved perfect efficacy.
In the early Tǒnghé era,
he was recommended by Grand Chancellor Hán Déràng,
and his official position reached that of Military Commissioner (Jiédùshǐ).
Once,
the wife of Privy Council Minister Yēlǜ Xiézhěn had a chronic illness.
Several doctors were changed, but none could cure her.
Dílǔ examined her and said:
"Her heart has stored heat,
which cannot be reached by medicine or surgical instruments.
It must be treated using psychological means.
Taking advantage of her confused state,
distract her until she goes mad,
using this method to vent the toxin, and she will recover."
Thereupon, he ordered gongs and drums to be beaten loudly in front of her.
The next day she indeed went mad,
shouting, yelling, and furiously cursing.
When her strength was exhausted, she stopped,
and subsequently recovered.
His treatment methods were often of this nature,
and people could not fathom them.
He died at the age of eighty.
Yēlǜ Yǐbùgē,
courtesy name Xíniǎn,
was a descendant of Niǎogǔzhí, Gentleman of the Six Courts (Liù Yuàn Lángjūn).
As a youth he loved learning,
was especially skilled at divination,
but did not enjoy entering officialdom.
He once chose a burial site for someone, saying:
"After three days,
when a cow rides a man chasing a cow passes by,
then start digging."
When the time came,
indeed, one man was carrying a sucking calf
and leading a cow past.
That man said:
"The so-called 'cow riding a man'
is this."
Thereupon, they started digging.
After the burial,
the fortunes (auspicious or inauspicious) were entirely as he had predicted.
Furthermore, he divined for a person who had lost a hawk, saying:
"The hawk is thirty *lǐ* northeast of your house, on an elm tree west of the *Luò*."
They went to search for it,
and indeed found it.
At that time, all his divinations and predictions were effective.
The appraisal states: Experts in technical arts (*fāngjì*),
are specialists in skills (*shùzhě*).
If they master their profession and do not deviate from the Way (*Dào*),
the noble person must adopt them.
*Zhílǔgǔ*, *Wáng Bái*, and *Yēlǜ Dílǔ* committed no major faults or achievements;
it is appropriate to record them.
*Wèi Lín* divined for *Chágē* regarding treasonous plotting,
and divined for *Yǎnsāgě* regarding usurpation;
his crimes are unforgivable.
Even if he possessed a minor skill,
how could it be worth adopting?
(We) preserve this without omitting it,
to serve as a warning for those who follow.
Clowns (*Líng*),
are minor officials.
The *History of the Five Dynasties* lists *Jìng Xīnmó* in a biography,
surely there must have been a reason for adopting him.
While there were certainly many such clown-officials in the *Liáo* court at that time,
only *Luó Yīqīng* was able to use humor to offer remonstrance,
thereby dispelling disorder before it materialized.
Confucius (*Kǒngzǐ*) said:
"The noble person does not reject worthy words because of the person speaking."
Thus, he deserves a biography.
*Luó Yīqīng*'s
native place is unknown.
He was humorous and adaptable,
and his jokes and buffoonery during that era
often contained corrective advice.
When *Xīngzōng* was defeated by *Lǐ Yuánhào*,
he broke out alone on horseback,
barely managing to escape.
Previously,
when *Yuánhào* captured *Liáo* people,
he would immediately cut off their noses.
Those who fled north
were only afraid of being overtaken.
Therefore, *Luó Yīqīng* stopped the emperor and said:
"First, check whether your nose is still there!"
The Emperor was enraged,
tied him behind the tent with a wool rope,
and intended to kill him.
The Crown Prince laughed and said:
"The joker is not *Huáng Fanchuò*!"
*Luó Yīqīng* immediately retorted:
"The one commanding the troops is also not *Táng Tàizōng*!"
The Emperor heard this and released him.
The Emperor had always been close to his younger brother, the Imperial Younger Brother *Chóngyuán*.
During a feast,
he promised to pass the throne to him after his death.
*Chóngyuán* was overjoyed,
and became arrogant and lawless.
Furthermore, during games of *shuānglù* (backgammon),
they gambled with cities and their residents.
The Emperor often lost the competition,
and had already forfeited several cities previously.
*Chóngyuán*, relying on the favor shown to *Liáng Xiàowáng*,
also committed many transgressions like *Zhèng Shúduàn*.
Court officials dared not speak out,
and people signaled to each other with their eyes on the roads.
One day they gambled again,
and *Luó Yīqīng* pointed at the board and said:
"Stop being foolish about *shuānglù*!
If you continue, you will lose everything!"
The Emperor finally realized the error,
and stopped gambling.
During the *Qīngníng* era,
he died of illness.
Eunuchs: *Wáng Jì'ēn*, *Zhào Ānrén*
In the *Zhōu Lǐ* (Rites of Zhōu),
eunuchs managed the prohibitions of the inner gates.
Later, the poem *Xiàng Bó* was listed in the *Yǎ* section of the Odes,
and *Bó Diāo*'s merit was renowned in *Jìn*.
Although they were loyal to their duties,
this exceeded their proper function.
During the middle periods of the *Hàn* and *Táng* dynasties,
they usurped power and corrupted governance,
causing things too terrible to mention.
These were all due to excessive favor and treatment.
The two eunuchs of *Liáo*,
both the worthy and the unworthy among them, can serve as a warning to later generations,
therefore they are recorded here.
*Wáng Jì'ēn*,
was a native of *Dìzhōu*.
When Empress *Ruìzhì* campaigned in the south,
*Jì'ēn* was captured.
Initially,
the Empress took nearly a hundred children under the age of ten, captured privately and publicly, who were good-looking,
transported them to *Liángxíng*,
and had them all castrated to become serving boys.
*Jì'ēn* was among them.
(He was) intelligent and quick-witted,
familiar with books and the *Liáo* language.
He was promoted to Palace Usher (*Nèi Yèzhě*) and Left Wing Supervisor of the Inner Servants (*Nèishì Zuǒxiāng Yābān*).
When *Shèngzōng* assumed personal rule,

he was successively promoted to Director of the Imperial Robe Depot (*Shàngyī Kùshǐ*), Left Administrator (*Zuǒ Chéngxūan*), Grand General of the Gate Guard (*Jiānmén Wèi Dàjiàngjūn*), Commissioner of *Língzhōu* (*Língzhōu Guānchásǐ*), and Chief Supervisor of the Inner Treasury (*Nèikù Dū Tídiǎn*).
*Jì'ēn* enjoyed pure discourse (*qīngtán*)
and did not desire power or profit.
Whenever he received gifts or rewards,
he purchased up to ten thousand volumes of books,
carried them with him,
and recited and read them tirelessly.
Whenever envoys from *Sòng* came to visit,
*Jì'ēn* often served as the Commissioner for Imperial Awards (*Xuāncìshǐ*).
His eventual fate is unknown.
*Zhào Ānrén*,
courtesy name *Xiǎoxǐ*,
was a native of *Lèshòu* in *Shēnzhōu*.
He was captured when young.
During the *Tǒnghé* period,
he served as Prefect of the Yellow Gate (*Huángmén Lìng*) and Attendant in the Residence of the Prince of *Qín* and *Jìn* (*Qín Jìn Guówáng Fǔ Zhīhòu*).
When the Prince died,
he was granted the posts of Supervisor of the Inner Servants Bureau (*Nèishì Shěng Yābān*) and Communicator of the Imperial Court (*Yùyuàn Tōngjìn*).
In the eighth year of *Kāitài* (1019 CE),
he plotted with *Lǐ Shènggē* to flee to the Southern Territory,
but was captured by patrolling soldiers.
Initially,
Empress *Réndé* had a rift with Empress *Qīn'āi*.
*Qīn'āi* secretly ordered *Ānrén* to monitor the Empress's movements,
so nothing was unknown (to *Qīn'āi*).
Once the authority and power of Empress *Réndé* became immense,
*Ānrén* feared disaster,
and again planned to escape and return (south).
*Réndé* wanted to execute him,
but *Qīn'āi* used words to save him.
*Shèngzōng* said:
"*Xiǎoxǐ* stated that his parents and brothers are all in the Southern Court,
and every time he thinks of them,
his spirit is overwhelmed.
Now, seeking to see his family,
he risked death to flee.
This is also the intention of a filial son,
and truly deserving of pity."
He pardoned him.
In the early *Chóngxī* period,
*Qīn'āi* acted as regent,
intending to depose the Emperor
and enthrone her younger son, *Chóngyuán*.
The Emperor plotted with *Ānrén* to move the Empress Dowager to guard the tombs in *Qìngzhōu*.
He appointed *Ānrén* Left Administrator (*Zuǒ Chéngxūan*), Grand General of the Gate Guard (*Jiānmén Wèi Dàjiàngjūn*),
and made him Chief Director of Inner Servants for the *Qìdān*, *Hànrén*, and *Bóhǎi* (peoples),
concurrently serving as Chief Supervisor (*Dū Tídiǎn*).
It happened that the Emperor missed the Empress Dowager,
and personally drove the carriage to welcome her back.
The Empress Dowager reproached him, saying:
"You were guilty of ten thousand crimes,
and I previously saved you.
I did not expect you to repay me,
but why did you try to separate me from my son!"
*Ānrén* had no reply.
His eventual fate is unknown.
The appraisal states: Titles and positions are used to encourage excellence in the realm.
Unless someone is worthy and possesses merit, they should not be granted.
How much more so for eunuchs?
*Jì'ēn* serving as Palace Usher (*Nèi Yèzhě*),
and *Ānrén* serving as Prefect of the Yellow Gate (*Huángmén Lìng*),
seemed appropriate.
Why go so far as to be submerged in private affection
and grant them posts like Commissioner and Grand General?
The *Yì* (Classic of Changes) says:
"Carrying burdens and riding,
invites bandits to approach."
Is this why *Ānrén* failed to meet a good end,
while *Jì'ēn* was fortunate enough to escape (misfortune)?
Biographies Forty: Treacherous Ministers, Part One: *Yēlǜ Yǐxīn*, *Zhāng Xiàojié*, *Yēlǜ Yàngē*, *Xiāo Shísān*
The *Chūnqiū* (Spring and Autumn Annals) praises and criticizes,
recording both good and evil,
to demonstrate encouragement and warning.
Therefore, *Qiān* and *Gù* included biographies of sycophants and cruel officials,
and *Ōuyáng Xiū* also recorded treacherous ministers,
intending that those who rule should know what to scrutinize,
and those who serve should know what to guard against.
This is the mind of Heaven, Earth, and the Sages,
the critical point for a nation's safety or danger,
and the origin of order and chaos.
In the *Liáo* Dynasty, starting with *Yēlǜ Yǐxīn*,
there were ten treacherous ministers.
Their ruining of the state is sufficient to serve as a warning,
therefore they are listed in the biographies.
Yélǜ Yǐxīn,
whose courtesy name was Húdǔgǔn,
was a man of the Wǔyuàn tribe.
His father, Diélà,
was poor;
clothing and food were insufficient,
and the tribesmen nicknamed him
"Poor Diélà."
Initially,
when Yǐxīn’s mother was pregnant,
she dreamt at night that her hands wrestled a black ram,
pulling off its horns and tail.
After waking, she consulted a diviner.
The diviner said:
"This is an auspicious sign.
When the ram (羊 yáng) loses its horns and tail, it forms the character for king (王 wáng).
Your future son will surely be a king."
When Yǐxīn was born,
they happened to be on the road,
with no water for bathing.
Turning the carriage and breaking the wheel ruts,
suddenly a spring gushed forth.
Diélà, feeling blessed to have a son,
wanted wine to celebrate.
He smelled the fragrance of wine
and found two flasks among the grass and thorns.
He then performed a sacrifice to the east.
Yǐxīn was clever and cunning in his youth.
Once, he was herding sheep until sunset.
Diélà looked at him
and saw Yǐxīn fast asleep.
Diélà poked him awake.
Yǐxīn angrily said:
"Why startle me so suddenly?
I just dreamt that someone held the sun and moon in their hands to feed me.
I had already eaten the moon,
and was halfway through devouring the sun when I woke up.
It is a pity I didn't finish eating it."
From then on, Diélà did not make him herd sheep.
When he grew up,
he had a fine demeanor,
appearing harmonious outwardly but being treacherous inside.
During the Chóngxī era,
he served as a clerk in the civil department,
managed the seal of the Tàibǎo,
and accompanied the emperor into the palace.
The Empress saw that Yǐxīn was refined and elegant, like a veteran palace official,
and ordered him to be appointed as a clerk for writing utensils (bǐyàn lì);
the Emperor also favored him,
and he was repeatedly promoted to Hùwèi Tàibǎo.
When Dàozōng ascended the throne,
because Yǐxīn had been employed and entrusted during the previous reign,
he was granted forty households of Hàn people,
and served concurrently as Associate Administrator of the Diǎnjiǎn Bureau.
He was frequently summoned to resolve difficult matters,
was promoted to Associate Administrator of the Northern Chancellery,
and successively served as Vice Commissioner of Military Affairs.
In the fifth year of Qīngníng (1059),
he was made Commissioner of Military Affairs of the Southern Chancellery,
then changed to Administrator of the Northern Chancellery,
and enfeoffed as the Prince of Zhào.
In the ninth year (1063),
Yélǜ Rénxiān became Commissioner of Military Affairs of the Southern Chancellery.
At that time, the Imperial Son-in-Law Commandant Xiāo Húdǔ was part of Chóngyuán's faction.
Displeased with Rénxiān being in court,
he memorialized, saying:
"Rénxiān should be appointed Commander of Military Affairs for the Northwest Route."
The Emperor was about to consent.
Yǐxīn memorialized, saying:
"I have recently joined the state administration,
and do not yet understand the principles of governance.
Rénxiān is an old retainer of the former Emperor,
and must not be hastily removed from the court."
The Emperor agreed with him.
After Chóngyuán's rebellion was quelled,
Yǐxīn was appointed Commissioner of Military Affairs of the Northern Chancellery,
advanced to Prince of Wèi,
and granted the title "Meritorious Official for Rescuing the Age, Assisting the Sage, Exhausting Loyalty, and Quelling Disorder."
In the fifth year of Xiányōng (1069),
he was promoted to Grand Preceptor (Shǒu Tàishī).
An imperial edict allowed him,
whenever there were military affairs in the four directions, to handle matters expediently according to his discretion.
His power shook both the court and the outside world,
and gifts and bribes flowed ceaselessly to his gate.
Those who flattered and obeyed were recommended and promoted,
while those who were loyal and upright were denounced and banished.
In the first year of Dàkāng (1075),
the Crown Prince began to participate in court affairs,
and the laws and regulations were reformed and perfected.
Yǐxīn could not have his way,
and plotted to frame the Empress with false charges.
After the Empress died,
Yǐxīn felt uneasy,
and further sought to harm the Crown Prince.
Seizing an opportune moment, he entered the court and memorialized:
"The Emperor and the Empress are like Heaven and Earth placed side by side.
How can the Central Palace be left empty?"
He greatly praised the beauty and virtue of the younger sister of his partisan, Imperial Son-in-Law Commandant Xiāo Xiámǒ.
The Emperor believed him,
admitted her into the palace,
and soon crowned her as Empress.
At that time, the imperial guard Xiāo Hūgǔ knew of Yǐxīn's wickedness.
He hid beneath a bridge,
intending to kill him.
Soon after, a sudden rainstorm destroyed the bridge,
and the plot failed.
The Chief Secretary (Línyá) Xiāo Yánshòu secretly memorialized, saying:
"Since the Crown Prince began participating in governance,
Yǐxīn has harbored suspicion and fear internally.
Furthermore, he has allied himself with the Chancellor Zhāng Xiàojié.
Fearing they may have other designs,
they must not be allowed to occupy crucial positions."
Yǐxīn was sent out to be the Resident of the Central Capital (Zhōngjīng Liúshǒu).
Yǐxīn wept and told people:
"Yǐxīn is innocent,
but has been dismissed due to slander."
His partisans, such as Xiāo Xiámǒ, reported his words to the Emperor.
The Emperor regretted it.
Not long after,
Xiāo Yánshòu was dismissed to become the Regional Commander of Shuìnyì Prefecture.
An imperial edict commanded close officials to deliberate on the matter of recalling Yǐxīn.
None of the Northern Officials dared to speak.
Yélǜ Sālā said:
"Yǐxīn was initially dismissed
based on Xiāo Yánshòu's memorial.
If what he said was inappropriate,
he should be charged with a crime;
if it was appropriate,
then Yǐxīn must not be recalled."
His repeated remonstrances were ignored.
Yǐxīn was then recalled to serve again as Commissioner of Military Affairs of the Northern Chancellery.
At this time, the Crown Prince, mourning his mother the Empress,
showed worry in his appearance.
Yǐxīn's faction rejoiced enthusiastically,
slanders boiled over,
and loyal and good officials were almost entirely purged and banished.
Yǐxīn, utilizing the words of Xiāo Shísān,
secretly summoned Xiāo Déshǔ at night to plot the fabrication of charges against the Crown Prince.
He instructed the Hùwèi Tàibǎo Yélǜ Zhālà to falsely accuse Yélǜ Sālā and others of conspiring to establish the Crown Prince.
An imperial edict ordered an investigation, which found no evidence, and the case was dropped.
Yǐxīn then ordered the Chief of Seal and Tally (Lìngyìn Lángjūn) Xiāo Èduō to approach the Emperor and falsely confess:
"The former accusation by Yélǜ Zhālà against Yélǜ Sālā and others was all true,
and I was also involved in the plot.
We originally intended to kill Yǐxīn and the others and install the Crown Prince.
If we do not confess,
we fear being implicated once the matter is revealed."
The Emperor commanded an envoy to investigate and prosecute.
Yǐxīn coerced them into fully confessing.
The Emperor was furious
and ordered Sālā and Sùsā and others to be executed.
Fearing the Emperor might be suspicious,
Yǐxīn brought several people to the court and interrogated them.
He forced each person to wear heavy cangues,
tied ropes around their necks,
making it impossible to breathe out,
so everyone found the cruelty unbearable
and only begged for a swift death.
Yǐxīn then reported back, saying:
"There were no dissenting statements."
It was summer at the time,
and the bodies could not be buried,
until the ground stank.
He then imprisoned the Crown Prince in the Supreme Capital (Shàngjīng),
and the guards supervising him were all his partisans.
Soon after, he dispatched Xiāo Dálǔgǔ and Sābǎ to murder the Crown Prince.
Yǐxīn’s faction was greatly pleased
and gathered to drink for several days.
The Resident of the Supreme Capital, Xiāo Tàdá, reported the death.
The Emperor mourned and grieved,
and wanted to summon the Crown Prince's wife,
but Yǐxīn secretly sent men to kill her
to silence her.
In the first month of the fifth year (1079),
when the Emperor was about to go hunting,
Yǐxīn memorialized requesting to leave the Imperial Grandson behind.
The Emperor intended to agree.
The Associate Administrator Diǎnjiǎn, Xiāo Wūnà, remonstrated, saying:
"If Your Majesty follows Yǐxīn’s advice and leaves the Imperial Grandson behind,
the Imperial Grandson is still young
and will have no one around him.
I request to stay and protect him,
to prevent any unforeseen circumstances."
Consequently, he traveled together with the Imperial Grandson.
From this, the Emperor began to suspect Yǐxīn
and became somewhat aware of his treachery.
During an excursion to the North,
as they were approaching Píngdiàn at Hēishān,
the Emperor happened to see that many of the attending officials were following closely behind Yǐxīn.
Displeased by this,
he dismissed Yǐxīn to become the Administrator of the Southern Chancellery Grand Princely Affairs (Nányuàn Dàwáng Shì).
In accordance with regulations, his princely title was reduced by one character,
and he was renamed Prince of Húntóng.
He felt somewhat reassured.
When he arrived at the capital to express gratitude for the appointment,
the Emperor immediately sent him back
and changed his post to Administrator of Xīngzhōng Prefecture Affairs.
In the winter of the seventh year,
he was charged with selling prohibited goods to foreign countries.
The case was submitted to the responsible officials for deliberation,
and the law dictated death.
Yēlǜ Yāngē (a member of the Yǐ Xīn faction) alone memorialized, arguing that he ought to be included in the 'Eight Deliberations' (Bā Yì).
He was thereby allowed a commutation of the death penalty.
He was beaten with an iron shackle (tiě gǔ bèi)
and imprisoned in Láizhōu.
Later, when his plan to flee to Sòng and his private storage of weapons were discovered,
he was hanged.
In the second year of Qiántǒng,
his tomb was opened,
and his corpse was subjected to public mutilation (lù).
Zhāng Xiàojié
was a native of Yǒngbà County in Jiànzhōu.
His family was poor,
but he loved learning.
In the twenty-fourth year of Chóngxī,
he was promoted, achieving the first rank in the presented scholar (jìnshì) examination.
During the Qīngníng period,
he was successively promoted to Academician-in-waiting of the Bureau of Military Affairs (Shūmì Zhí Xuéshì).
At the beginning of Xiányǒng,
he was charged with making an erroneous report
and was exiled to serve as Administrator (cìshǐ) of Huìzhōu.
Soon after, he was recalled to his former position
and concurrently managed the affairs of the Ministry of Revenue (Hùbù Sī).
In the third year,
he was appointed Participant in Determining Political Affairs (Cānzhī Zhèngshì),
concurrently holding the position of Associate Administrator of the Bureau of Military Affairs (Tóngzhī Shūmìyuàn Shì),
and was granted the additional title of Vice Minister of Works (Gōngbù Shìláng).
In the eighth year,
he was enfeoffed as the Duke of Chén State (Chén Guó Gōng).
The Emperor, seeing Xiàojié's diligence and industry,
frequently consulted him on matters,
and he served as the Chancellor (zǎixiàng) of the Northern Administration (Běi Fǔ).
No Hàn person was more favored or powerful than him.
In the first year of Dàkāng,
he was granted the imperial surname (guó xìng).
The following year, during the autumn hunt,
the Emperor shot thirty deer in one day.
He hosted a feast for the attending officials.
In the midst of the wine,
he commanded them to compose poems on the theme "Clouds Ascend to Heaven" (Yún Shàng Yú Tiān),
and decreed that Xiàojié sit beside the imperial couch (yù tà).
The Emperor recited the poem Shǔ Lí:
"Those who know me say my heart is anxious;
Those who do not know me ask what I seek."
Xiàojié reported, saying:
"Today the world is peaceful,
why is Your Majesty anxious?
You possess the wealth of the four seas,
what does Your Majesty seek?"
The Emperor was greatly pleased.
In the third year,
when the officials attended a feast,
the Emperor said:
"The previous emperor employed Rénxiān and Huàgě
because of their wisdom and ability.
I have Xiàojié and Yǐ Xīn,
who are no inferior to Rénxiān and Huàgě;
I have truly obtained worthy men."
They drank merrily until night,
and then dispersed.
In the summer of that year,
Yǐ Xīn slandered the Crown Prince,
and Xiàojié provided joint assistance to him.
When Yǐ Xīn received the imperial edict to investigate the Crown Prince's faction,
and falsely accused and harmed loyal and good people,
Xiàojié's schemes accounted for the majority.
Yǐ Xīn recommended Xiàojié as loyal to the state (shèjì).
The Emperor compared Xiàojié to Dí Rénjié
and bestowed upon him the name Rénjié.
He was then permitted to release a peregrine falcon (hǎidōng qīng hú).
In the sixth year,
after Yǐ Xīn had been exiled,
the Emperor also realized Xiàojié's treachery and wickedness.
Soon after, he was exiled to serve as Military Commissioner (Jiédùshǐ) of Wǔdìng Command.
He was charged with privately trading salt from Guǎngjì Lake and unauthorized alteration of imperial edicts.
His titles were revoked,
and he was demoted to Ānsùzhōu.
He returned only after several years.
During the Dà'ān period,
he died in his hometown.
At the beginning of Qiántǒng,
his coffin was opened, his corpse mutilated,
and his clan property was divided and bestowed upon the officials.
Xiàojié held the chancellor position for a long time,
and his greed for wealth was insatiable.
When he met and drank with relatives,
he once said:
"Without a million taels of gold,
one is not qualified to be the head of a chancellor's family."
In the beginning,
when Xiàojié passed the examination,
he visited a Buddhist temple.
Suddenly, a swift wind blew off Xiàojié's head wrap (pū tóu),
which rose as high as the stupa (fútú),
then fell to the ground and shattered.
An old monk said:
"This man will certainly become powerful suddenly,
but he will also not die a natural death."
It turned out exactly as he said.
Yēlǜ Yāngē,
courtesy name Shànníng,
was a descendant of the household of Jìfù.
His great-great-grandfather, Duówěn,
was the half-brother of Tàizǔ.
His father, named Huōlǐsī,
reached the office of Grand Preceptor (Tàishī).
Yāngē was cunning, wicked, and quick-witted.
During the Qīngníng period,
he served as Grand Guardian of the Left Imperial Guard (Zuǒ Hùwèi Tàibǎo).
At the beginning of Dàkāng,
he was transferred to be the Northern Administrator of Imperial Decrees (Běimiàn Línyá).
Initially, when Yēlǜ Yǐ Xīn returned to the Bureau of Military Affairs from his post as Central Capital Grand Warden (Zhōngjīng Liúshǒu),
he used Yāngē as his eyes and ears.
Whatever Yāngē heard or saw, he always reported it.
Yǐ Xīn cherished and recommended him,
and the Emperor also regarded him as worthy,
appointing him Chief Administrator of Judicial Affairs for the Left (Zuǒ Yílíbì).
When the Crown Prince was falsely accused,
the Emperor sent Yāngē to interrogate him.
The Crown Prince said to Yāngē:
"I am the Emperor's only son,
now heir apparent.
What else could I seek,
that I would dare to commit this act!
You and I are of the same generation, like brothers.
You should consider my innocence
and convey my thoughts to the Emperor."
He pleaded very sincerely.
Xiāo Shísān heard of this
and said to Yāngē:
"You should substitute the Crown Prince's words
with a confession (fúzhuàng)."
Yāngē nodded
and reported exactly as instructed.
When the Crown Prince was banished,
Yǐ Xīn murdered loyal and good people,
much of it being Yāngē's schemes.
He served as Commissioner of the Khitan Traveling Palace (Qìdān Xínggōng Dū Bùshǔ).
In the summer of the fifth year,
he was appointed Chancellor of the Southern Administration (Nán Fǔ Zǎixiàng),
and promoted to Commissioner of Palace Affairs (Tì Yǐn).
In the third year of Dà'ān,
he served as Western Capital Grand Warden (Xījīng Liúshǒu)
and retired.
At the beginning of Shòulóng,
he died of illness.
Xiāo Shísān
was a native of the Miègǔnǎi tribe.
His father, Duóluǒwò,
held successive posts as Military Commissioner (Jiédùshǐ).
Shísān was eloquent and astute,
and skilled at figuring out people's intentions.
During the Qīngníng period,
he was promoted to Grand Guardian of the Imperial Guard (Hùwèi Tàibǎo) due to his years of service.
At the beginning of Dàkāng,
when Yēlǜ Yǐ Xīn returned to the Bureau of Military Affairs,
he became increasingly arrogant and reckless.
At that time, Shísān frequented Yǐ Xīn's home,
and any court official who did not align with them was quickly expelled through his efforts.
Shísān was thus promoted from Imperial Guard (sù wèi) to Vice Commissioner of the Palace Gate (Diànqián Fù Diǎnjiǎn).
In the summer of the third year,
the imperial guards Xiāo Hūgǔ (蕭忽古) and others plotted to assassinate Yēlǜ Yǐxīn (耶律乙辛).
The plot was discovered, and they were imprisoned.
Shísān (十三) said to Yǐxīn (乙辛):
“The Crown Prince is still alive now,
and the officials and people look to him.
You, Great King, fundamentally lack support,
and furthermore bear the resentment for falsely accusing the Empress.
If the Crown Prince is enthroned,
where will you place yourself?
You ought to think carefully about this.”
Yǐxīn (乙辛) replied:
“I have been worrying about this for a long time!”
That night,
he summoned Xiāo Dé'ěrtè (蕭得𩹉特) to secretly plan the means to frame the Crown Prince.
Once Shísān's (十三) scheme was enacted,
he was soon promoted to Diànqián Dū Diǎnjiǎn (殿前都點檢, Chief Inspector of the Palace Guards),
concurrently holding the post of Tóngzhī Shūmìyuàn Shì (同知樞密院事, Assistant Administrator of the Bureau of Military Affairs).
He then ordered Xiāo È'dūwò (蕭訛都斡) and others to falsely claim that the previous accusations made by Yēlǜ Zhālà (耶律查剌) against Yēlǜ Sālā (耶律撒剌) and others were all true.
An imperial edict ordered an investigation into the matter,
but the Crown Prince refused to admit guilt.
Another person, the Yílíbì (夷離畢) Yēlǜ Yàngē (耶律燕哥), was dispatched to question the Crown Prince.
The Crown Prince fully explained the circumstances of his being falsely accused.
When Shísān (十三) heard this,
he said to Yàngē (燕哥):
“If you report it this way,
the great matter will be ruined!
You must change the wording to an admission of guilt (fú fà, 伏[⿰⺨發]).”
Yàngē (燕哥) entered,
and reported the matter just as Shísān (十三) had instructed.
The Emperor was greatly angered,
and deposed the Crown Prince.
As the Crown Prince was about to leave,
he said:
“What crime have I committed to deserve this!”
Shísān (十三) shouted at him to get into the carriage,
and ordered the guard soldiers to close the carriage door.
In that same year,
he was promoted to Běiyuàn Shūmì Fùshǐ (北院樞密副使, Vice Commissioner of Military Affairs for the Northern Administration).
He further proposed a scheme to secretly harm the Crown Prince,
and Yǐxīn (乙辛) followed it.
When Yǐxīn (乙辛) was sent out to administer the Nányuàn Dàwáng Shì (南院大王事, Affairs of the Southern Administration Great King),
Shísān (十三) was also sent out as Bǎozhōu Tǒngjūn Shǐ (保州統軍使, Commander-in-Chief of Baozhou).
He died there.
During the Qiántǒng (乾統) period,
his coffin was broken open and his corpse was mutilated.
His two sons, Díli Dé (的里得) and Niànjīng (念經),
were both executed.
Biographies, Chapter 41, Corrupt Ministers (Part 2): Xiāo Yúliyě (蕭余里也), Yēlǜ Hélǔ (耶律合魯), Xiāo Dé'ěrtè (蕭得𩹉特), Xiāo È'dūwò (蕭訛都斡), Xiāo Dálǔgǔ (蕭達魯古), Yēlǜ Tǎbùyě (耶律塔不也), Xiāo Túgǔcí (蕭圖古辭)
Xiāo Yúliyě (蕭余里也),
courtesy name È'dūwǎn (訛都椀),
was the second son of Guójiù Ālà (國舅阿剌, Imperial Uncle Ālà).
He was glib, flattering, and witty,
and skilled in women's crafts.
During the Zhòngxī (重熙) period,
he advanced due to being an imperial relative by marriage (wàiqī).
At the beginning of the Qīngníng (清寧) period,
he was appointed Zhīhòu Lángjūn (祗候郎君, Attendant Gentleman).
He married Princess Zhèngguó (鄭國公主),
was appointed Fùmǎ Dūwèi (駙馬都尉, Commandant of the Imperial Son-in-Law),
and was successively promoted to Nánmiàn Línyá (南面林牙, Southern Chancellor).
Because his father Ālà (阿剌) was slandered by Xiāo Gé (蕭革),
Yúliyě (余里也) was sent out as Jìedùshǐ (節度使, Military Commissioner) of Fèngxian Commandery.
In the winter of the tenth year,
he was recalled to serve as Běimiàn Línyá (北面林牙, Northern Chancellor).
In the middle of the Xiányōng (咸雍) period,
someone reported that Yúliyě (余里也) and his clansman Shùzhé (朮哲) plotted to harm Yēlǜ Yǐxīn (耶律乙辛).
The investigation found no evidence,
and he was sent out to serve as Jìedùshǐ of Níngyuǎn Commandery.
Afterward, Yúliyě (余里也), guessing Yǐxīn's (乙辛) intentions,
devoted himself entirely to serving him,
and was recommended as Guójiù Xiángwěn (國舅詳穩, Imperial Uncle Commandant).
At the beginning of the Dàkāng (大康) period,
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Liáoxī Commandery.
At that time, Yǐxīn (乙辛) wielded arbitrary power,
and dismissed anyone who did not join his faction.
He then brought Yúliyě (余里也) in as Běifǔ Zǎixiàng (北府宰相, Chancellor of the Northern Administration),
concurrently holding the post of Zhī Qìdān Xínggōng Dū Bùshǔ Shì (知契丹行宮都部署事, Administrator of the Affairs of the Khitan Traveling Palace General Headquarters).
When Yǐxīn (乙辛) plotted to frame the Crown Prince,
Yúliyě (余里也) provided much assistance in bringing it to fruition.
Consequently, he was appointed Zhī Běiyuàn Shūmì Shì (知北院樞密事, Administrator of Military Affairs for the Northern Administration),
and was bestowed the title of Tuīchéng Wèizàn Gōngchén (推誠[⿰崙頁]贊功臣, Meritorious Official who Exhibits Sincerity and Supports Achievements).
He married his niece to Yǐxīn's (乙辛) son Suīyě (綏也),
and relying on his influence, behaved wantonly,
even speaking words suggestive of disrespect towards the ruler.
The court and the populace viewed him askance.
When the Emperor sent Yǐxīn (乙辛) out to administer the Nányuàn Dàwáng Shì,
Yúliyě (余里也), being part of Yǐxīn's (乙辛) faction,
was dismissed to his residence as Tiānpíngjūn Jìedùshǐ (天平軍節度使, Military Commissioner of Tianping Commandery).
Soon after, he was appointed Xīběilù Zhāotǎoshǐ (西北路招討使, Commander of the Northwestern Circuit).
He resigned his post due to mourning for his mother,
and died.
Yēlǜ Hélǔ (耶律合魯),
courtesy name Húdūjǐn (胡都菫),
was a descendant of the Liùyuàn Shèlì Niǎogǔzhí (六院舍利褭古直, Commandant Niǎogǔzhí of the Six Ordos).
He was pliant and sycophantic,
and enjoyed being in accord with others indiscriminately.
He began his career at the start of the Qīngníng period.
At that time, Yǐxīn (乙辛) employed a group of small-minded men,
and Hélǔ (合魯) attached himself to him.
He thus gained Yǐxīn's trust and appointment,
and was soon promoted to Nánmiàn Línyá (Southern Chancellor).
When Yǐxīn (乙辛) slandered the Crown Prince
and killed loyal and upright officials,
Hélǔ (合魯) participated in many of his schemes.
His younger brother Wūyě (吾也) was also a follower of Yǐxīn (乙辛).
At the time, they were called
“the two villains.”
Yǐxīn (乙辛) recommended him as Běiyuàn Dàwáng (北院大王, Great King of the Northern Administration),
and he died in office.
Wūyě (吾也) also reached the rank of Nán Dàwáng (南大王, Great King of the Southern Administration).
Xiāo Dé'ěrtè (蕭得𩹉特)
was a man from the Yaolián Wākèhán Gōngfēn (遙輦洼可汗宮分, Household of Khan Wā of the Yaolián Clan).
He was good at anticipating people's wishes and following their preferences.
In the early Qīngníng period,
when Yǐxīn (乙辛) was in power,
Dé'ěrtè (得𩹉特) was greatly employed by him,
and was successively promoted to Běimiàn Línyá (Northern Chancellor) and Tóngzhī Běiyuàn Xuānhuīshǐ Shì (同知北院宣徽使事, Assistant Administrator of the Northern Administration Commission of Court Affairs).
When the Crown Prince was deposed,
Dé'ěrtè (得𩹉特) was sent to supervise his transport to Shàngjīng (上京, the Supreme Capital).
Dé'ěrtè (得𩹉特) hurried his journey,
not allowing him to alight from the carriage.
He frequently insulted the Crown Prince regarding his daily life and meals.
Upon arrival, he built a circular wall to imprison him.
In the Dàkāng period,
he was promoted to Xīnán Zhāotǎoshǐ (西南招討使, Commander of the Southwest),
and successively served as Shùnyìjūn Jìedùshǐ (順義軍節度使, Military Commissioner of Shunyi Commandery),
and transferred to Guójiù Xiángwěn (Imperial Uncle Commandant).
In the fifth year of Shòulóng (壽隆),
he was charged with harboring resentment and ambition.
He was spared the death penalty due to his age,
but his entire household was confiscated and annexed to the Xīngshèng Palace.
He was demoted to the Xīběi Tǒngjūnsī (西北統軍司, Northwestern Command Headquarters),
where he died.
His two sons, Démò (得末) and Èlǐ (訛里),
were executed during the Qiántǒng period
because their father had plotted with Yǐxīn (乙辛).
Xiāo È'dūwò (蕭訛都斡)
was a descendant of the Imperial Uncle Shàofù Branch (國舅少父房).
In the Xiányōng period,
he was appointed Páiyìn Lángjūn (牌印郎君, Gentleman of the Seal and Credentials).
In the third year of Dàkāng,
the Commissioner of Military Affairs Yǐxīn (乙辛) secretly harbored treasonous intentions.
He ordered the Guard Grand Mentor Yēlǜ Zhālà (耶律查剌) to falsely accuse Yēlǜ Sālā (耶律撒剌) and others of plotting deposition and enthronement.
An edict ordered an investigation that found no evidence,
and all were sent to external posts.
Soon after,
È'dūwò (訛都斡), seeking to satisfy Yǐxīn's (乙辛) desires
and to substantiate the accusations,
entered the palace with Yēlǜ Tǎbùyě (耶律塔不也) and others,
and falsely reported:
“Regarding the plot by Yēlǜ Sālā (耶律撒剌) and others to harm Yǐxīn (乙辛)
and enthrone the Crown Prince,
I, your subject, was also involved.
If I do not confess now,
I fear I will be implicated if the matter is exposed.”
The Emperor was indeed angered,
and banished the Crown Prince to Shàngjīng.
È'dūwò (訛都斡) married the Imperial Daughter, Princess Zhàoguó (趙國公主),
and became Fùmǎ Dūwèi.
Later, he disagreed with Yǐxīn's (乙辛) counsel,
and held a grudge against him.
Furthermore, he overstepped his bounds by imitating the ruler's apparel and carriages,
and was executed.
When È'dūwò (訛都斡) faced execution,
he said to people:
“The previous accusation against Yēlǜ Sālā (耶律撒剌)
was all instructed by Yǐxīn (乙辛).
He fears the truth will come out,
and is killing me to silence me!”
Xiāo Dálǔgǔ (蕭達魯古)
was a man from the Yaolián Cháogǔ Kèhán Gōngfēn (遙輦嘲古可汗宮分, Household of Khan Cháogǔ of the Yaolián Clan).
His nature was treacherous and sinister.
During the Qīngníng period,
Yǐxīn (乙辛) served as Commissioner of Military Affairs,
usurping power and authority,
and secretly harboring treasonous plots.
Dálǔgǔ (達魯古) joined his faction,
and was consequently praised and promoted,
gradually rising to Qígǔ Yèlà Xiángwěn (旗鼓拽剌詳穩, Commandant of the Banner and Drum Yèlà Division).
Yǐxīn (乙辛) intended to kill the Crown Prince,
and finding Dálǔgǔ (達魯古) ruthless and capable of being used,
he dispatched him along with the Aide of the Close Attendants, Sābǎ (撒把), to Shàngjīng.
There, they joined the Resident Administrator Xiāo Tàdé (蕭撻得) in secretly leading strongmen to the prison cell at night.
They lied that a pardon had been issued
and summoned the Crown Prince out.
They killed him,
and sealed his head in a box to bring back,
falsely claiming he died of illness.
Dálǔgǔ (達魯古) was made Guójiù Xiángwěn (Imperial Uncle Commandant).
Dálǔgǔ (達魯古), fearing that the murder of the Crown Prince would be revealed,
always wore a knife when going out or entering.
If urgently summoned,
he intended to commit suicide immediately.
During the Qiántǒng period,
an imperial edict ordered the Commissioner of Military Affairs Yēlǜ Āsī (耶律阿思) to thoroughly search for Yǐxīn's (乙辛) partisans.
Dálǔgǔ (達魯古) avoided capture through bribes.
Later, he died of illness.
Yélǜ Tǎbùyě
was a descendant of the Zhòngfǔ Fáng (Second Uncle Branch).
Because he was skilled at playing *jū* (a ball game, often polo),
he was favored by the Emperor.
Whenever he rode,
the ball never left his stick.
At the beginning of the Xiányōng era,
he was appointed Zhīhòu Lángjūn (Attendant Gentleman).
He was friendly with Yélǜ Yǐxīn,
therefore, those inside and outside the court feared him.
When the Crown Prince was slandered,
investigations found no evidence.
Tǎbùyě attached himself to Yǐxīn,
wishing to confirm the accusation.
He and Édūwò submitted a secret memorial, saying:
“The matter of the Crown Prince plotting rebellion is actually true,
if your subject does not report it,
I fear that when the matter is discovered, I will be implicated.”
The Emperor believed him
and deposed the Crown Prince.
He was transferred to be the Vice Envoy of the Yánqìng Palace.
In the first year of Shòulóng,
he became the Commander-in-Chief of the Temporary Palace.
When Tiānzuò succeeded to the throne,
because Tǎbùyě was a partisan of Yǐxīn,
he was sent out to be the Jiédùshǐ (Military Commissioner) of the Tèmiǎn Department.
When the Chief of the Bureau of Military Affairs, Yélǜ Āsī, extensively searched for Yǐxīn’s former partisans,
Tǎbùyě escaped indictment through bribery.
He was relocated to be the Jiédùshǐ of the Díliè Department,
and later served again as the Envoy of the Dūnmù Palace.
In the first year of Tiānqìng,
he was sent out to be the Commander of the Northwest Circuit.
He died of illness.
Xiāo Túgǔcí,
courtesy name Héníng,
was a man from the Chǔtè Department.
He began his official career during the Zhòngxī era,
was known for his ability,
and was successively promoted to Zuǒ Zhōngchéng (Left Palace Assistant).
At the beginning of Qīngníng,
he held the post of Běimiàn Línyá,
and was then transferred to be the Deputy Chief of the Northern Bureau of Military Affairs.
He was discerning and quick-witted,
good at observing facial expressions,
and his responses always pleased the Emperor.
The Empress Dowager once said:
“If there is a great matter,
only Yélǜ Huàgē and Xiāo Túgǔcí can resolve it.”
His favor and treatment grew daily.
He served as Acting Chief of the Northern Bureau of Military Affairs.
In the sixth year,
he was sent out to govern Huánglóng Fǔ (Huanglong Prefecture).
In the eighth year,
he was appointed Prime Minister of the Southern Chancellery.
Shortly thereafter,
he became Chief of the Northern Bureau of Military Affairs,
and an edict permitted him to act expediently.
As a person, he was excessively treacherous and flattering,
loved to accumulate wealth,
was willful,
and frequently altered laws and regulations.
After being Chief of the Bureau of Military Affairs for several months,
many of the people he recommended and promoted were partisans of Zhòngyuán,
due to this, he was dismissed and reduced to commoner status.
Later, he was confiscated and sent to the Xīngshèng Palace,
where he died.
The Commentary states: Shùn exiled Gònggōng,
and Kǒngzǐ executed Shàozhèng Mǎo;
the laws for dealing with villainy were strict indeed.
Later generations failed to perceive this,
but instead considered the wicked loyal and trusted them,
not stopping until their poison infected the imperial house and the state.
The case of Dàozōng and Yǐxīn is an example of this.
When he detained Rénxiān
and suppressed Zhòngyuán,
he seemed truly concerned for the state's welfare;
but who knew he concealed a sinister motive,
waiting only for the right moment to act?
Once he monopolized power,
and furthermore gained Xiàojié, Yāngē, and Shísān as his confidants,
he thus indulged in evil without restraint.
He first slandered the Empress,
and then killed the Crown Prince and his consort.
The severity of this catastrophe
is truly lamentable.
Alas!
Among those closest to the ruler,
none were like the Empress and the Crown Prince.
The wicked minister killed them, yet the Emperor did not know;
his officials spoke out, yet he did not realize.
The loyal and upright officials of that time
were nearly all dismissed or executed.
Although [Yǐxīn] at Hēishān personally saw the vastness of his own retinue and subordinates,
Dàozōng merely stripped him of a one-character princely title.
It was not until he secretly hid armor and weapons
that he was finally executed.
Alas!
Yǐxīn’s crimes
certainly could not be expiated by one death alone to the world,
but also Dàozōng was unenlightened and indecisive,
which allowed [Yǐxīn] to be nurtured and grow.
As for those like Xiāo Yúlǐyě,
who forgot their sovereign and sided with the wicked,
in order to greedily seek wealth and honor,
though they fortunately died before him,
how could they escape the shame of leaving behind a notorious reputation?
Biographies, Chapter 42: Rebellious Ministers I: Yélǜ Xiáǐ (Diélǐtè), Yélǜ Chágē, Yélǜ Lóuguó, Yélǜ Zhòngyuán (Nièlǔgǔ), Yélǜ Huágē.
The *Yì* (Book of Changes) says:
“Heaven is honored and Earth is humble,
thus the positions of *Qián* and *Kūn* are established;
when the humble and the high are set forth,
the positions of the noble and the base are determined.”
Only when the positions of the noble and the base are determined can the distinction between ruler and minister be fixed.
Only when the distinction between ruler and minister is fixed can Heaven and Earth be in harmony.
Only when Heaven and Earth are in harmony can the myriad things be created.
The governance of the Five Emperors and the Three Kings
utilized this principle.
Since the time of the Three Dynasties,
there have been cases of ministers murdering their rulers,
and cases of sons murdering their fathers.
Kǒngzǐ compiled the *Chūnqiū* (Spring and Autumn Annals) to embody the royal statutes,
punishing the dead for the sake of the past
and causing fear in the living for the sake of the future.
His foresight was profound and far-reaching.
Ōuyáng Xiū, when writing the *Táng Shū* (History of Táng),
created the Biographies of Rebellious Ministers,
which also embodied the intent of the *Chūnqiū*.
There are twenty-two rebellious ministers recorded in Liáo,
and tracing their deeds shows there are those worse than others.
However, how could this be due to causes arising only overnight?
By listing them in the biographies,
we make public the condemnation of the world,
and thereby provide a warning.
Xiáǐ,
courtesy name Nièliègǔn,
was the son of Yīlíjǐn Tiēlà, the grandson of Sùzǔ.
As a youth, he was shrewd and eloquent,
and at that time, many dangerous and villainous individuals attached themselves to him.
During the reign of Yáoliǎn Héndéjǐn Kèhán (Khagan),
his half-brother, Yǎngǔzhī, was the Yīlíjǐn of the Diélà Department.
According to custom,
one who became Yīlíjǐn
was permitted to perform the Rebirth Ceremony.
While Yǎngǔzhī was approaching the tent to change his robes,
Xiáǐ immediately took the red robe and the *diāochán* cap (sable and cicada cap),
mounted a white horse, and rode out.
He then commanded his partisans to shout loudly:
“The Yīlíjǐn has come out!”
Everyone bowed down,
and consequently, he performed the Cháicè Ceremony
and established himself as Yīlíjǐn.
He governed the state jointly with the Yúyuè, Yélǜ Shìlǔ.
When Shìlǔ was killed,
Xiáǐ feared that others would plot against him.
He took his two sons, Diélǐtè and Shuòguā, and fled to Bóhǎi,
pretending to be blind.
Later, during a *qiúmǎ* (ball and horse, or polo) gathering,
he and his two sons seized good horses and fled back to the state.
He became increasingly villainous and evil,
but often used clever words to escape punishment.
Tàizǔ was about to ascend the throne.
He yielded the position to Xiádǐ.
Xiádǐ said:
“The Emperor is a Sage,
mandated by Heaven.
How dare your subject presume to take it!”
Tàizǔ appointed him Yúyuè.
When Tàizǔ personally led an army to attack the various southwestern tribes,
Xiádǐ instigated Lāgě and others to rebel.
Those who did not follow were killed.
When the imperial carriage returned to Chǐshuǐchéng,
Xiádǐ was afraid,
and together with Lāgě, he fled north.
When they reached Yúhé, they were captured by the pursuing troops.
Tàizǔ asked:
“When I first ascended the throne,
I offered the state to you,
Uncle, but you declined it.
Now, on the contrary, you wish to install my younger brother.
Why is this?”
Xiádǐ replied:
“Originally, your subject did not know the nobility of the Son of Heaven.
But after Your Majesty ascended the throne,
the security and retinue were extremely strict,
and you were different from common people.
When your subject once reported on affairs, my heart was stirred,
and I began to harbor intentions of usurpation.
I estimated Your Majesty is heroic and martial,
and surely cannot be overthrown;
whereas the various younger brothers are weak,
and if I gained control, they would be easily manipulated.
If the matter had succeeded,
how could I have tolerated the existence of the younger brothers?”
Tàizǔ said to his younger brothers:
“Did you truly listen to this man's words?”
Diélà said:
“Those who plan great affairs
must employ men such as this;
but once the affair is complete,
they must also certainly eliminate them.”
Xiádǐ did not reply again.
He was imprisoned for several months,
and then strangled.
When he was about to be executed,
Tàizǔ said to him:
“Uncle, your crime warrants death,
and I dare not grant pardon.
If there are matters beneficial to the state,
you should tell me everything.”
Xiádǐ said:
“The people of the Diélà Bù are numerous and powerful;
therefore they often cause unrest.
It is advisable to divide them into two,
to weaken their power.”
His son was Diélǐtè.
Diélǐtè,
courtesy name Hǎilín.
He possessed great physical strength,
was skilled at riding and shooting,
and even when his horse stumbled, he would not fall.
He was especially miraculous in medicine.
When looking at a person’s illness,
it was as if he saw objects through gauze,
seeing everything completely.
When Tàizǔ was still obscure,
he had already received his favor and kind treatment.
When Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
he appointed him Yílíjǐn of the Diélà Bù.
Tàizǔ once desired venison relish to relieve his hangover,
and considering what the mountains and forests contained,
he asked who could procure it.
Diélǐtè said:
“Your subject can obtain it.”
He rode a court horse to chase a deer,
and shot one of them.
When he wanted to shoot again,
his horse stumbled and died.
Diélǐtè leaped forward,
his bow still taut,
and captured another one.
The Emperor was extremely delighted and said:
“My brother is a match for ten thousand men!”
It happened that the Emperor suffered from heart pain.
He summoned Diélǐtè to examine him.
Diélǐtè said:
“In your *gāohuāng* there is a blood clot the size of a pellet,
but medicine cannot reach it.
It must be cured with acupuncture.”
The Emperor followed his advice.
He vomited up the clotted blood,
and the pain ceased.
Because the Emperor considered him close kin,
he always gave him generous gifts;
however, knowing his character,
he never entrusted him with high office.
Later, he participated in Lāgě's rebellion,
and together with his father Xiádǐ, he was strangled.
Chágē,
courtesy name Ōuxīn,
was the son of Míngwáng Ānduān.
He was skilled at riding and archery.
He appeared respectful but was cunning in heart;
people thought he was weak.
Tàizǔ said:
“This man is ferocious and stubborn;
he is not weak.”
His father Ānduān once sent him to report on affairs.
Tàizǔ said to his close attendants:
“This boy’s eyes resemble those of a startled camel,
and his face displays the appearance of a rebel.
If I am staying alone,
do not allow him to enter the door.”
When Shìzōng ascended the throne at Zhènyáng,
Ānduān heard of this,
and wished to remain neutral.
Chágē said:
“The Tàidì is jealous and harsh.
If he is truly established,
how could he tolerate us!
Yǒngkāng Wáng is generous and kind,
and moreover, he is on good terms with Liúgē.
We should go and plan with him.”
Ānduān immediately conspired with Liúgē to submit to Shìzōng.
When the peace agreement was concluded,
he was enfeoffed as Tàiníng Wáng for his merits.
It happened that Ānduān was serving as Dà Xiángwěn of the Southwestern Front.
Chágē pretended to hate his father,
and secretly sent someone to inform the Emperor,
who immediately summoned him.
When he reached the presence of the Emperor,
he wept and lamented with unbearable sorrow.
The Emperor pitied him,
and ordered him to command the Nǚshíliè Army.
He moved in and out of the forbidden palace,
and frequently received imperial favor.
Whenever the Emperor went out hunting,
Chágē pretended to have a hand ailment,
and did not handle a bow and arrow,
but only carried a chained hammer while riding.
He repeatedly reported small matters concerning his family to the sovereign,
and the sovereign believed him to be sincere.
Chágē felt that since the various tribal groups were intermingled,
he could not execute his plans successfully.
He gradually moved his tents closer to the temporary palace.
Yòupíshì Xiángwěn Yēlǜ Wūzhì observed his treachery,
and submitted a memorial detailing his condition.
The Emperor did not believe it,
and showed the memorial to Chágē.
Chágē claimed that Wūzhì envied him,
and choked back sobs while shedding tears.
The Emperor said:
“I already knew this was untrue;
why do you weep?”
Chágē sometimes uttered resentful words.
Wūzhì said:
“Although you do not have that intention,
because I wrongly suspected you,
it would be permissible not to do anything unrighteous.”
Another day, Wūzhì made a further request to the Emperor.
The Emperor said:
“Chágē abandoned his father to serve me;
I can guarantee he intends nothing else.”
Wūzhì said:
“Since Chágē is already unfilial toward his father,
how can he be loyal to his sovereign?”
The Emperor did not accept this.
In the seventh month of the fifth year of Tiānlù,
the Emperor visited Tàiyè Gǔ.
He stayed and drank for three days.
Chá Gē plotted rebellion, but it did not succeed.
The Emperor attacked Zhōu.
When they reached Xiánggǔ Shān,
the Empress Dowager and the Emperor offered sacrifices to Emperor Wénxiàn at the temporary palace.
All the officials were drunk.
Chá Gē returned and saw the Prince of Shòu'ān.
He invited him to speak,
but the Prince refused to follow.
Chá Gē informed Yēlǜ Péndū of the plot,
and Péndū agreed to it.
That evening,
together they led troops in to assassinate the Empress Dowager and the Emperor,
and thereupon usurped the title.
For officials who did not follow,
their family members were seized.
That night,
inspecting the objects in the Imperial Treasury,
he saw an agate bowl.
He said:
“This is a treasure rarely seen in the world,
now it belongs to me!”
He boasted to his wife.
His wife said:
“Shòu'ān Wáng and Wū Zhì are still alive.
None of us will survive,
what good is this object?”
Chá Gē said:
“Shòu'ān is young.
Wū Zhì merely commands a few slaves.
When they come to court tomorrow morning,
they are certainly not worth worrying about.”
His partisan, Shěn Sī, reported that Shòu'ān and Wū Zhì had surrounded them outside with troops.
Chá Gē immediately sent someone to assassinate the Empress before the coffin,
and hastily went out to join the battle line.
Shòu'ān sent someone to announce:
“Since you have already committed regicide and treason,
what more do you plan to do?”
A certain Yílí Jǐn Huà abandoned his troops and returned to the Prince of Shòu'ān.
The remaining masses looked on,
and slowly dispersed.
Chá Gē knew that his cause was failing,
so he tied up the families of the various officials,
held his bow and arrows, and threatened:
“You will not stop me from killing these people!”
He shouted orders for them to quickly leave.
At that time, the chancellor Yēlǜ Díliè was also among those tied up.
He stepped forward and said:
“If you do not depose [the Emperor],
how can Shòu'ān Wáng rise to power?
Use this as an excuse,
and you might still be spared.”
Chá Gē said:
“If it truly is as you say,
who should be the envoy?”
Díliè requested to go together with Yănsāgě to persuade him.
Chá Gē followed his plan.
Shòu'ān Wáng later ordered Díliè to lure Chá Gē out,
and he was sliced to death.
All his sons were also executed.
Lóu Guó,
courtesy name Miǎnxīn,
was the son of Emperor Wénxiàn.
In the fifth year of Tiānlù,
he was appointed titular Military Governor of Wǔdìng Jūn.
When Chá Gē instigated rebellion,
Mù Zōng and Wū Zhì followed the plan of chancellor Díliè,
lured him out,
and Lóu Guó personally stabbed Chá Gē to death.
He was later appointed Defender of Nánjīng.
Mù Zōng indulged in drinking,
and paid no heed to government affairs.
Lóu Guó harbored ambitions for the throne,
and induced Díliè and other discontented people to plot treason.
When the matter was discovered,
interrogation did not yield a confession.
The Emperor said:
“When I was Shòu'ān Wáng,
you repeatedly used this matter to advise me.
How can today's situation be false?”
Lóu Guó could not reply.
When the remaining partisans had all confessed,
he was consequently hanged in the western valley of Kèhán Zhōu.
An imperial decree ordered the relevant authorities to select a place where his descendants could not settle for his burial.
Zhòng Yuán,
childhood name Bójízhǐ,
was the second son of Shèng Zōng.
His talent and bravery surpassed others.
His features were refined and handsome,
and he spoke and laughed little.
People looked upon him with awe.
In the third year of Tàipíng,
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Qín Guó.
When Shèng Zōng died,
Empress Qīn'āi administered the government as regent.
She secretly plotted to establish Zhòng Yuán.
Zhòng Yuán revealed this plot to the Emperor.
The Emperor valued him even more,
and enfeoffed him as the Imperial Younger Brother.
He successively held the posts of Commissioner of Military Affairs of the Northern Administration,
Defender of Nánjīng, and Administrator of the Grand Marshal's Office.
Zhòng Yuán occupied military positions,
but never left the vicinity of the imperial carriage.
Previously, when Qìdān people committed crimes,
the general rule was that Hàn people were required to investigate and prosecute them,
resulting in many instances of injustice.
Zhòng Yuán memorialized requesting that each of the Five Capitals establish a Qìdān Surveillance Commissioner.
An imperial decree adopted this measure,
and he was granted a gold warrant and an oath document.
When Dào Zōng ascended the throne,
he was conferred the title of Imperial Elder Uncle,
exempted from the usual courtesies and addressing him by name,
made Grand Marshal of All Military Forces,
and again granted a gold warrant, a four-pointed hat, and a two-colored robe.
The honor and favor he received were unprecedented.
In the ninth year of Qīngníng,
when the imperial carriage was hunting by the Luán Shuǐ River,
following the prior plan made with his son Nièlǔgǔ,
he, along with his partisans including Prince Chén Guó Wáng Chén Liù, Administrator of Military Affairs of the Northern Administration Xiāo Húdǔ, and over four hundred others,
lured and threatened crossbowmen to form a battle line outside the temporary imperial tent.
Just as they were about to fight,
many of his partisans regretted their actions and demonstrated loyalty,
scattering and fleeing individually.
Since Zhòng Yuán knew his plan had failed,
he fled north to the Great Desert,
sighing:
“Nièlǔgǔ brought me to this!”
He then committed suicide.
Previously, when Zhòng Yuán was about to raise troops,
rain, red like blood, fell in front of his tent.
Those who understood omens called it a sign of defeat and ruin.
His son was Nièlǔgǔ.
Nièlǔgǔ,
childhood name Yēlǔwǎn.
His nature was malicious and ruthless.
Xīng Zōng, upon seeing him once,
said:
“This child's eyes show the mark of rebellion.”
In the eleventh year of Zhòngxī,
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Āndìng Jùn.
In the seventeenth year,
he was promoted to Prince of Chǔ,
and served as Tīyǐn.
In the third year of Qīngníng,
he was sent out to serve as Military Governor of Wǔdìng Jūn.
In the seventh year,
he became Administrator of Military Affairs of the Southern Administration.
He persuaded his father Zhòng Yuán to feign illness,
wait for the imperial carriage to visit and inquire,
and then commit regicide and treason.
During the autumn hunt of the ninth year,
the Emperor, using the plan of Yēlǜ Liáng,
sent someone to urgently summon Nièlǔgǔ.
Nièlǔgǔ, believing the plot had been discovered,
hastily led troops to attack the temporary palace.
The Commissioner of Military Affairs of the Southern Administration, Prince Xǔ Rénxiān and others, led the Imperial Guards to suppress him.
Nièlǔgǔ leapt on his horse and broke out,
but was shot and killed
by the close attendant Xiángwěn Bóhǎi Ā Sī
Huá Gē,
courtesy name Sīlǎn,
was the son of Suí Guó Wáng Shì Lǔ.
His nature was insidious and treacherous.
He initially had sexual relations with his father's concubine.
Fearing the matter would be exposed,
