he conspired with Kè Xiāo Tái Shěn and others to harm his father.
He blamed Tái Shěn for the deed,
and Huá Gē was spared.
When Tài Zǔ ascended the throne,
he strove to extend kindness and favor.
Although he knew Huá Gē was cruel and treasonous,
he temporarily displayed tolerance,
and bestowed upon him the post of Tīyǐn.
In the sixth year,
Huá Gē was involved in the rebellion of the various younger brothers.
When the matter was settled,
the assembled officials discussed his crime,
all agreeing that Huá Gē should not be released.
Consequently, he and his son Hén Zhǐ were executed by slow cutting and died.
An imperial command allowed the soldiers to freely take his property.
The Emperor said:
“Huá Gē did not fear Heaven above.
He rebelled against his sovereign and murdered his father.
His wickedness is inexpressible.
The rebellions committed by my younger brothers
were all instigated by this man.”
Biographies, Chapter 43: Traitorous Subjects including Xiāo Hàn, Yēlǜ Diélà, Yēlǜ Lǎng, Yēlǜ Liúgē (Péndū), Yēlǜ Hǎisī, Yēlǜ Díliè, Xiāo Gé.
Xiāo Hàn,
alternative name Díliè,
courtesy name Hánzhēn,
was the son of Chancellor Dílǔ.
In the beginning of Tiānzàn
era, Táng troops besieged Zhènzhōu.
The military governor (jiédùshǐ), Zhāng Wénlǐ, sent an envoy to report the urgency.
Xiāo Hàn received the imperial order and went with Kāng Mòdá to relieve the city.
They conquered it,
killed its general, Lǐ Sìzhāo,
and captured Shíchéng.
In the beginning of Huìtóng era,
he was appointed commander of the Hàn Army Imperial Guards.
In the eighth year
he campaigned against Jìn,
defeated the Jìn general Dù Chóngwēi,
and pursued him to Wàngdū.
Hàn reported:
“We can order the troops to dismount and shoot.”
The Emperor followed his suggestion,
and the soldiers advanced on foot.
The enemy suddenly approached with short weapons,
and our army suffered a defeat.
The Emperor regretted it and said:
“This is the result of my using your suggestion!”
When he followed the imperial carriage into Biàn,
he was made Military Governor of Xuānwǔ Commandery.
When the Emperor died in Luánchéng,
Shìzōng ascended the throne.
When Hàn heard of it,
he entrusted affairs to Lǐ Cóngmǐn
and hastened directly to the temporary seat of government (xíngzài).
In the autumn of that year,
Shìzōng and the Empress Dowager confronted each other at Huánghé Héngdù,
and peace negotiations were unsettled.
The Empress Dowager asked Hàn:
“Why did you rebel out of resentment?”
He replied:
“My mother was innocent,
yet the Empress Dowager killed her.
Because of this, I cannot be without regret.”
Initially, Yēlǜ Wūzhì had been imprisoned for siding with the Empress Dowager.
Hàn heard of it and was pleased.
He immediately imprisoned the one referred to and said:
“You once said that our group was inferior.
Now you are in prison (bì'àn).
Why is that?”
He replied:
“I only wish that you, Sire, do not meet such a fate!”
Hàn remained silent.
In the second year of Tiānlù,
he married the Emperor's younger sister, Ābùlǐ.
Later, he plotted rebellion with Tiāndé
and was put into prison.
He again colluded with the Tìyǐn Liú Gē and his younger brother Péndōu to cause unrest.
Yēlǜ Shílà reported it to Wūzhì.
Wūzhì urgently entered the court to report it,
but Hàn and others did not submit.
The Emperor did not want to expose the matter,
but Wūzhì strongly argued that it was unacceptable.
An edict was then issued ordering Wūzhì to interrogate and investigate.
Hàn pleaded guilty,
but the Emperor ultimately released him.
He again collaborated with the Princess by letter to plot rebellion with the Prince of Brightness, Ānduān.
Wūzhì obtained the letter and presented it to the throne.
Hàn was executed.
Diélà,
courtesy name Shùlán,
was a descendant of Púgǔzhī, the Yílíjǐn of the Six Departments.
During the Tiānxiǎn era,
he served as the Right Chancellor of the Central Terrace Department (Zhōngtái Shěng Yòuxiàng).
In the first year of Huìtóng,
he carried the insignia (chí jié) with Zhào Sīwēn to invest the Jìn Emperor.
When our army campaigned against Jìn,
reaching the Hūtuó River,
the Jìn general Dù Chóngwēi surrendered,
and Diélà’s contribution was the greatest.
In the first year of Dàtóng,
he suppressed the rebellion in Xiāngzhōu,
beheading tens of thousands of people.
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
he dispatched an envoy to rush the report,
and also ordered Diélà to arrest the subordinate general Zhúzhě and bring him.
The envoy mistakenly entered Zhúzhě’s camp.
Zhúzhě received the edict
and instead lured Diélà,
captured him, and sent him to the Empress Dowager.
Diélà escaped and returned to Shìzōng.
Once the peace agreement was concluded,
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Yān
and served as the Commissioner of the Southern Capital (Nánjīng Liúshǒu).
In the fifth year of Tiānlù,
Chágē committed regicide.
Diélà was drunk at the time.
His wife helped him into Chágē’s tent,
and he consequently joined him.
The following morning,
the Prince of Shòu'ān suppressed the rebellion.
All those who had been coerced into joining abandoned their weapons and surrendered.
Diélà did not surrender
and was slowly executed (língchí).
His wife and children were all executed.
Lǎng,
courtesy name Ōuxīn,
was the grandson of Yǎngǔzhī from the family branch of his father’s younger brother.
He was frivolous by nature,
possessed great strength,
and people called him
“Hǔsī” (Tiger-like).
During the Tiānxiǎn era, he advanced due to his talent and bravery.
He was victorious in every battle,
and thus gained renown.
In the ninth year of Huìtóng,
Tàizōng entered Biàn
and ordered him to govern Chányuān,
controlling and guarding the river crossing.
In the first year of Tiānlù,
regions south of Yān and Zhào all responded to Liú Zhīyuǎn.
Lǎng and the defender of Biàn, Xiāo Hàn, abandoned the city and returned to the capital.
Prior to this,
Lǎng's grandfather Yǎngǔzhī had the office of Yílíjǐn fraudulently seized by his younger brother Xiádǐ.
Since then, no one in that clan held a position in the Six Departments.
Shìzōng was unaware of this history
and appointed Lǎng as the Grand Prince (Dàwáng) of the Six Departments.
When Chágē started the unrest,
he sent a messenger to report to Lǎng:
“The deed is accomplished!”
Lǎng sent the Xiángwěn Xiāo Húli with his troops,
ordering him:
“You must hold both sides
and assist whichever side is victorious.”
When Mùzōng ascended the throne,
Lǎng was executed,
and his family property was confiscated.
Liú Gē,
courtesy name Míngyǐn,
was the son of Tàizǔ's younger brother Yǐndǐshí.
As a child, he was arrogant and brutal,
and loved to insult others.
As he grew older, he became more wicked and cunning.
Tàizōng disliked him
and made him guard the borderlands.
He was repeatedly promoted, finally reaching the position of Grand Xiángwěn of the Southwestern Border.
In the tenth year of Huìtóng,
his uncle Ānduān followed the Emperor to campaign against Jìn.
Due to illness, he returned early
and was a neighbor of Liú Gē.
When Shìzōng was established within the army,
Ānduān deliberated on where to go.
Liú Gē was the first to propose the strategy of attaching to Shìzōng
and assisted him with troops from his own department.
At that time, the Empress Dowager ordered the Imperial Younger Brother Lǐ Hú to lead troops south.
Liú Gē and Ānduān met him at Tàidé Quán.
Once the battle engaged,
Ānduān fell from his horse.
The Prince Tiāndé rushed over,
intending to stab him with a spear.
Liú Gē shielded Ānduān with his body
and shot at Tiāndé,
piercing his armor but not his skin.
Ānduān regained his horse and resumed fighting,
and the Imperial Younger Brother's army was defeated.
Liú Gē and Ānduān paid respects at the temporary seat of government.
When the peace agreement was concluded,
the Empress Dowager asked Liú Gē:
“Why did you rebel out of resentment?”
He replied:
“My father was innocent,
yet the Empress Dowager killed him.
This is the cause of my resentment.”
When the matter was settled,
he was made Tìyǐn because of his merit.
During the Tiānlù era,
he plotted rebellion with his younger brother Péndōu, Prince Tiāndé, and Imperial Guard Xiāo Hàn.
Yēlǜ Shílà revealed the matter.
Liú Gē avoided punishment by using fabricated excuses.
Later, he invited the Emperor to a game (bó),
intending to commit regicide by presenting poisoned wine.
The Emperor realized his intention
and the plan failed.
He was imprisoned.
One day,
Liú Gē was summoned
and played the game while chained by the neck.
The Emperor asked:
“Did you truly rebel?”
Liú Gē swore:
“If I had rebellious intentions,
I will surely die from a thousand-pimple carbuncle (qiāndǐng jū)!”
He was then pardoned.
Yēlǜ Wūzhì strongly argued
that his crime was unforgivable.
The Emperor ordered Wūzhì to investigate him,
and he fully confessed.
An edict was issued sparing him from death,
but banishing him to the Wūgǔ tribe.
He indeed died from a thousand-pimple carbuncle.
His younger brother was Péndōu.
Péndū,
was cruel and extremely strong.
His skin was like snakeskin.
In the beginning of Tiānlù’s reign (947 CE),
he was appointed Píshì Xiángwěn based on his clan affiliation.
In the second year (948 CE),
he plotted rebellion with his elder brother, Liúgē.
He was spared death
and sent as an envoy to the Xiágāsī country.
After he returned,
he was again implicated in Chágē’s rebellion,
and he died by slow slicing.
He had two younger half-brothers: Huàgělǐ and Xījiǎn.
At the beginning of Yìnglì’s reign (951 CE),
they held no official positions,
but because they were members of the imperial clan,
they were treated with great courtesy.
In the third year (953 CE),
someone accused Huàgělǐ and Xījiǎn of plotting rebellion with the Prince of Wèi, Wǎn.
They were imprisoned,
but they fabricated excuses and were acquitted.
In the spring of the fourth year (954 CE),
they plotted rebellion again
and were executed.
Hǎisī,
courtesy name Duógun,
was the illegitimate son of the Prince of Suí, Shìlǔ.
He was astute and eloquent.
In the fifth year of Huìtóng’s reign (942 CE),
an imperial edict was issued requesting straightforward advice.
At that time, Hǎisī was eighteen years old.
Wearing a sheepskin coat
and riding an ox, he went to the palace gate.
The official in charge asked:
“Why have you come?”
He replied:
“I am responding to the edict to speak on current affairs.
If I am not rejected for being poor and young,
I might also be suitable for the selection of straightforward speakers.”
The official reported this to the emperor.
The emperor was about to go hunting,
so he sent a message saying:
“Wait until I return, and then I will see him.”
Hǎisī said:
“I came because I thought Your Majesty was urgently seeking worthy people;
that is why I came.
Now you are postponing it for hunting,
so I request to return from here.”
When the emperor heard this,
he immediately summoned him and granted him a seat,
asking him about the principles of governance.
He ordered the Illustrious Prince Ānduān and Yēlǜ Pōdé to test him.
A few days later,
Ānduān and others reported:
“Hǎisī’s talent
surpasses ours.”
The emperor summoned Hǎisī and asked:
“What kind of people are those you spoke with?”
He replied:
“Ānduān speaks without restraint,
like an empty cart running down a steep slope;
Pōdé is like wearing boots and walking across a wilderness to shoot bustards.”
The emperor laughed heartily.
He promoted him to Xuānhuīshǐ
and repeatedly entrusted him with responsibilities.
The emperor knew he was poor
and bestowed gold vessels upon him,
but Hǎisī immediately distributed them to his relatives and friends.
Later, he followed the emperor in the campaign against Jìn and rendered service.
When Shìzōng ascended the throne in the military camp,
the Empress Dowager assembled troops to oppose him at the Héngdù crossing of the Huánghé River.
The Empress Dowager sent Yēlǜ Wūzhì to reproach Shìzōng for his self-proclamation.
When Wūzhì arrived before the emperor,
he conveyed the Empress Dowager’s mandate without yielding.
Shìzōng sent Hǎisī to argue the case,
and Hǎisī was also not subservient,
and the emperor commanded him:
“When you see Wūzhì, do not fear!”
Hǎisī returned from seeing the Empress Dowager
and did not report favorably.
After peace was achieved,
he managed the affairs of the Empress Dowager’s various bureaus.
When Mùzōng ascended the throne,
Hǎisī plotted rebellion with the Prince of Jì, Díliè,
and died in prison.
Díliè,
courtesy name Wūlián,
was the son of the Yílíjǐn of the Six Ordos, Zhútbùlǔ.
He was deceitful in his youth.
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
he became the Qúnmù Dūlínyá.
When Chágē plotted rebellion,
many officials were imprisoned.
When the Prince of Shòu'ān and Yēlǜ Wūzhì led troops to suppress the rebellion,
Chágē’s followers gradually withdrew.
Chágē estimated that the plot would fail,
so he went to the prison
and threatened the captives with a bow and arrows, saying:
“Kill all these people!”
Díliè stepped forward and said:
“What good will killing them do for the situation?
I estimate that Wūzhì intends to install the Prince of Shòu'ān,
and that is why he took this action,
and the Prince of Shòu'ān may not even know of it.
If we send someone to use this as an excuse,
we might be spared.”
Chágē said:
“As you say.
Who can be the envoy?”
Díliè said:
“If Your Highness does not doubt me,
I, Díliè, request to go with Yǎnsāgē to persuade them.”
Chágē sent them.
The Prince of Shòu'ān followed Díliè’s plan,
luring and killing Chágē.
None of the people who had been threatened were harmed;
this was all due to Díliè’s effort.
Once the rebellion was pacified,
the emperor commended and rewarded him,
but he was not prominently employed.
Díliè was disappointed
and often felt resentful.
He gathered a group of malcontents
and secretly harbored rebellious intentions.
In the second year of Yìnglì (952 CE),
he and his associates plotted to install Lóu Guó.
The matter was discovered,
and he died by slow slicing.
Xiāo Gé,
minor name Huágē,
courtesy name Hútūjǐn,
was the son of the Guójìu Fáng Línyá, Héshàng.
He was perceptive and resourceful.
At the beginning of Tàipíng’s reign (1021 CE),
he was repeatedly promoted in office.
He associated closely with those near the emperor,
ingratiating himself with flattery and gaining intimacy,
which earned him praise among his peers.
Because of this, his name reached the emperor.
In the early years of the Chóngxī reign,
he was appointed Běimiàn Línyá.
In the twelfth year,
he became Běiyuàn Shūmì Fùshǐ.
The Emperor once feasted with his close ministers,
and said to Gé:
“I know your talent,
and thus personally promoted you.
You should exert yourself!”
Gé replied:
“I am untalented,
and mistakenly received Your Majesty’s recognition.
I have no way to repay even a ten-thousandth;
I can only exhaust my foolish loyalty,
how dare I be lazy?”
The next year,
he was appointed Běifǔ Zǎixiàng.
In the fifteenth year,
he was reassigned to Tóngzhī Běiyuàn Shūmì Shì.
Gé relied on imperial favor and wielded exclusive power;
his colleagues merely filled their positions.
At that time, Yīlíbì Yēlǜ Yìxiān knew of Gé’s treachery and cunning,
and while attending a banquet,
spoke of Gé’s shortcomings,
saying that using him would lead to failure.
The Emperor did not listen.
One day,
the Emperor ordered Yìxiān to play a game of "patrol and throw" with Gé.
Yìxiān, in a drunken state, said:
“I hold the position of a great minister;
even if I cannot advance the loyal and remove the treacherous,
how can I gamble with a villain!”
Gé bore a grudge,
and feigned a smile, saying:
“Are you not being too playful, Prime Minister?”
Yìxiān continued to insult and revile him.
The Emperor was angry.
The Empress interceded, saying:
“Yìxiān is mad with wine;
he can be dealt with when sober.”
The next day,
the Emperor issued an edict to Gé, saying:
“Yìxiān was disrespectful;
you may severely punish him.”
Gé replied:
“How can Yìxiān’s talent
escape Your Majesty’s sagely discernment!
However, the whole world knows him to be loyal and upright.
To punish him now for a transgression committed while drunk
might displease the people’s hopes.”
The Emperor, seeing Gé endured the offense without retaliating,
treated him with even greater favor.
His feigned feelings and flattery of the emperor were often of this type.
He was appointed Nányuàn Shūmì Shǐ,
and an edict ordered his rank to be above all princes;
he was enfeoffed as King of Wú (Wúwáng).
He was then reassigned to Zhī Běiyuàn,
promoted to King of Zhèng (Zhèngwáng),
and concurrently held the position of Zhōngshū Lìng.
When the Emperor was critically ill,
he issued an edict to Gé, saying:
“The great position cannot be vacant for a day.
If I do not recover,
you should immediately enthrone the King of Yān and Zhào.”
In the first year of Qīngníng,
he was again made Nányuàn Shūmì Shǐ,
and his title was changed to King of Chǔ (Chǔwáng).
He was again transferred to Běiyuàn,
and jointly managed court affairs with the maternal uncle, Xiāo Ālà.
Gé had many private deviations,
which Ālà often corrected.
From this, a rift formed,
and Ālà was sent out as Dōngjīng Liúshǒu.
During the southern suburban sacrifice,
Ālà came to the capital as per custom.
The Emperor consulted his ministers on current affairs.
Ālà presented the advantages and disadvantages,
speaking very intensely.
Gé, observing that the Emperor was displeased,
then slandered him, saying:
“Ālà relies on imperial favor
and has a disrespectful attitude towards Your Majesty,
which is not the courtesy of a minister.”
The Emperor was greatly angered
and had Ālà strangled below the hall.
Later, the Emperor realized Gé’s treacherous plot,
and his imperial favor gradually waned.
In the eighth year,
he retired from office
and was enfeoffed as King of Zhèngguó.
In the ninth year, in autumn,
Gé, because his son was a son-in-law of Chóngyuán,
was involved in Chóngyuán’s plot,
and was subsequently executed by slow strangulation.
Collation Notes
Biographies, Chapter 44, Treacherous Officials, Part 2: Xiāo Húdu, Xiāo Diélǐdé, Gǔdiē, Yēlǜ Sālāzhú, Xī Huílǐbǎo, Xiāo Tèliè
Xiāo Húdu,
courtesy name Yǐxīn.
He stuttered,
had a squint,
and curly hair.
His paternal uncle, Xiàomù, saw him and said:
“This child’s appearance
is unprecedented in our clan.”
When he grew up,
he was burly and arrogant,
and liked to expose people’s faults.
During the Chóngxī reign,
he was Zhīhòu Lángjūn.
Soon after, he was promoted to Xīngshènggōng Shǐ.
He married Princess Qínguó,
and was granted Fùmǎ Dūwèi.
Due to incompatibility, they divorced,
and he remarried Princess Qíguó,
becoming Běimiàn Línyá.
During the Qīngníng reign,
he successively held the positions of Běi and Nányuàn Shūmì Fùshǐ,
and replaced his paternal cousin, Zhúzhé, as Xīběilù Zhāotǎoshǐ.
At that time, Xiāo Gé and Xiāo Ālà were both Shūmì Shǐ,
and they were at odds.
Gé, knowing that Zhúzhé was favored by Ālà,
was jealous of him.
When Zhúzhé was replaced and returned to the capital,
he had previously borrowed official grain,
leaving behind payment before departing.
Húdu, to please Gé,
brought up this matter,
and Zhúzhé was consequently punished.
Húdu also wished to wield power.
Annually, he would present rare treasures, exotic playthings, and livestock to Gé.
The two loved each other more than brothers.
Húdu’s clan-cousin, Díliè, was Běikè.
He recommended the maternal uncle Xiángwěn Xiāo Húdù to Húdu.
Húdu, seeing his eloquence, resourcefulness, and bravery,
devoted himself to befriending him.
Whenever they had a day off,
they would converse all day long,
which everyone found strange.
When Húdu was Tóngzhī Běiyuàn Shūmì Shì,
he memorialized that Húdù and Díliè could be useful.
The Emperor appointed Díliè as Qígǔ Yuēlā Xiángwěn,
and Húdù as Sùzhíguān.
When Gé framed his elder brother Ālà,
Húdù secretly assisted him.
People at the time found this disgraceful.
Yēlǜ Yǐxīn was Zhī Běiyuàn Shūmì Shì,
and Húdu’s rank was below Yǐxīn,
so he felt resentful and discontent.
Initially,
Húdu had conspired with Chóngyuán’s son, Nièlǔgǔ, to rebel,
wanting them to act quickly.
When the imperial carriage was hunting at Tàizǐ Shān,
he and Nièlǔgǔ coerced archers and troops to attack the imperial traveling palace.
During the battle,
Nièlǔgǔ was hit by a stray arrow and died,
and the crowd scattered.
At that time, his accomplice, Yēlǜ Sālāzhú, happened to be in the hunting ground.
Hearing of the chaos,
he led hunters to assist.
His partisans said to Húdu and others:
“Our army is numerous.
Taking advantage of their unpreparedness,
if we fight a decisive battle in the middle of the night,
the matter might succeed;
but if we wait until tomorrow,
who will follow us?”
Húdu said:
“In a rush,
black and white cannot be distinguished.
If the inner and outer armies respond to each other,
then our cause will be lost.
What delay is there in departing at dawn!”
Chóngyuán listened to Húdu’s plan
and ordered patrols on all sides to wait for dawn.
That night,
the accomplices enthroned Chóngyuán with a usurped title,
and Húdu appointed himself Shūmì Shǐ.
The next day, they were defeated in battle.
Húdu was wounded
and fled on a single horse.
Upon reaching Shíqī Luò,
he drowned himself.
His five sons
were executed on the same day.
Xiāo Diélǐdé,
courtesy name Húdujǐn,
was a descendant of the maternal uncle’s young father’s branch.
His father, Shuānggǔ,
married Princess Diànnì
and rose to the position of Guójìu Xiángwěn.
Diélǐdé was perceptive and unrestrained in his youth,
he loved archery and hunting.
During the Tàipíng [era],
he was appointed Zhīhòu Lángjūn based on being a maternal relative,
successively holding the posts of Yánchāng Gōngshǐ and Diànqián Fùdiǎnjiǎn.
In the thirteenth year of Zhòngxī, when they attacked Xià,
Diélǐdé led a detached force and was the first to enter enemy territory,
capturing and looting extensively.
He was promoted to Dūdiǎnjiǎn,
and then changed to Wūgǔ Díliè Bù Dūxiángwěn.
In the eighteenth year,
a second western campaign was launched.
Diélǐdé memorialized:
“Regarding military horses and weapons,
the priority is selecting the generals.
The Xià people are certainly not difficult to control.
If we strictly establish scouts and advance posts,
and do not rely on surprise attack strategies,
why worry about failing to win?”
The Emperor said:
“You should leave quickly,
do not delay the military schedule.”
Soon after, Diélǐdé suffered a defeat and returned,
and was reinstated as Dūdiǎnjiǎn.
In the nineteenth year,
the Xià people came to invade Jīnsù Jūn.
The sovereign ordered Diélǐdé to lead light troops to oversee the battle.
He reached Hénán Sānjiǎochuān,
executed eight lookouts,
and captured the Guānchásǐ.
Due to his merit, he was appointed to manage the affairs of the Hànrén Xínggōng Dū Bùshǔshì,
and was sent out as Xīnánmiàn Zhāotǎoshǐ.
His cousin Huáng Bājiānú reported that his master had privately discussed matters concerning the Imperial Palace,
but Diélǐdé suppressed the matter.
When the incident was discovered,
he was severely beaten with a large staff,
stripped of his rank, and reduced to a commoner.
During the Qīngníng [era],
the sovereign, judging that the crime was not committed by Diélǐdé himself,
raised him up to be the Nánjīng Tǒngjūnshǐ.
At this point,
he joined the rebellion led by Zhòngyuán’s son, Nièlǔgǔ, and others,
was defeated, fled, and was captured,
and executed.
Gǔdié,
was originally a man from the Palace Division,
his surname is unknown.
He enjoyed play and familiarity,
and disliked strict regulations.
His physical strength surpassed ordinary men,
and he was skilled at *jījú*.
In the beginning of the Zhòngxī [era],
he served as a Hùwèi,
and successively held posts as an Official on Duty.
In the thirteenth year,
during the western campaign,
Gǔdié was made the vanguard.
The Xià forces lay in ambush and encircled them.
Gǔdié fought fiercely,
but many soldiers under his command perished.
He then broke out alone on horseback.
He encountered Lǐ Yuánhào, King of Xià, who had come to besiege them,
the situation was extremely urgent.
Gǔdié galloped and shot,
whenever an arrow left the string, someone fell;
he leaped his horse directly to strike the central solid ranks,
the Xià soldiers could not withstand him.
He returned to the camp only in the late afternoon.
He was transferred to Xīngshèng Gōng Tàibǎo.
In the ninth year of Qīngníng,
he joined the rebellion of Zhòngyuán and Nièlǔgǔ.
He fought against the Imperial escort troops,
was defeated and fled.
He was pursued and captured,
and died by slow slicing.
Sālāzhú,
was the grandson of Díliè of the Mèngfù Branch.
His nature was fierce and violent.
During the Qīngníng [era],
he was repeatedly promoted to Xuānhuīshǐ,
and then changed to Diànqián Dūdiǎnjiǎn.
He was the first to conspire with Zhòngyuán in the rebellion.
When the Emperor was hunting at the Luánhé River,
Zhòngyuán, fearing the matter would be exposed,
hastily fought against the escort troops.
After his son Nièlǔgǔ died,
the fellow conspirators dispersed in defeat.
Sālāzhú happened to be at the hunting grounds.
Hearing of the rebellion,
he coerced the hunters to assist him.
When he arrived,
and learned that Nièlǔgǔ was already dead,
he regretted it greatly,
and said:
“We have nothing left but to fight to the death.
Why act like children playing games,
bringing destruction upon yourselves?
Now the temporary palace is unprepared.
If we attack it tonight,
the great endeavor can succeed.
If we wait until dawn,
they will have prepared,
and how do we know our own forces won't waver?
Once the opportunity is lost,
regret will be useless.”
Zhòngyuán, Xiāo Húdǔ, and others said:
“Tonight we should simply surround it on all four sides,
preventing external armies from entering.
How can they prepare!”
He did not follow this advice.
When dawn approached,
they threw down their weapons and fled.
Sālāzhú died in battle.
Xī Huílíbǎo,
also named Hàn,
courtesy name Ruólǎn,
was a descendant of Xī King Tèlín.
He was skilled at horsemanship and archery,
agile, quick, and brave,
and was as famous as his older brother Biēlǐlà.
During the Dà'ān [era],
when the imperial procession visited Zhōngjīng,
he was appointed Hùwèi,
gradually rising to Tiěyào Jūn Xiángwěn.
During the Tiānqìng [era],
he was transferred to Běi Nǚzhí Xiángwěn,
concurrently managing military affairs for Xiánzhōu Lù,
and was changed to Dōngjīng Tǒngjūn.
Subsequently, various tribes invaded.
He defeated them all,
and was promoted to Xī Liù Bù Dàwáng,
concurrently supervising all military affairs for the Eastern Circuit.
In the second year of Bǎodà,
when the Jīn army arrived,
Tiānzuò moved away (fled).
Huílíbǎo led officials and commoners to install Qínjìn Guówáng Chún as Emperor.
Chún falsely appointed Huílíbǎo to manage the affairs of the Northern Chancellery,
and concurrently as Commander-in-Chief of all armies.
He repeatedly defeated the Sòng troops.
After Chún died,
his wife Pǔxiánnǚ managed the affairs as regent.
In that year,
the Jīn army entered via Jūyōng Guān.
Huílíbǎo, who was managing the affairs of the Northern Chancellery,
immediately established himself at Jiàngǎn Shān,
proclaiming himself Emperor of the Xī State,
changing the era name to Tiānfù,
and establishing three Secretariats for the Xī, Hàn, and Bóhǎi peoples,
and changing the Eastern and Western Jiédùshǐ to two Kings,
dividing responsibilities and establishing offices.
At that time, Xī people Bāzhé, Hán Jiānú, and others led troops to attack nearby Qìdān tribes,
looting people and livestock.
The populace was greatly terrified.
Meanwhile, Huílíbǎo was defeated by Guō Yàoshī,
and his entire army became disaffected.
His associates Yēlǜ Āgǔzhé and his nephew Yǐshì Bājīn assassinated him,
and his spurious reign lasted a total of eight months.
Xiāo Tèliè,
courtesy name Éduōwǎn,
was a man from the Palace Division of Yáoliánwā Kèhán.
During the Qiántǒng [era],
he entered the Imperial Guard.
He was posted out as Shùnyì Jūn Jiédùshǐ.
In the fourth year of Tiānqìng,
he concurrently managed military affairs for Xiánzhōu Lù.
In the fifth year,
he was stripped of his Jiédùshǐ title due to military defeat.
In the first year of Bǎodà,
he was promoted to Wěigǔ Bù Jiédùshǐ.
When Tiānzuò gathered the tribal pastoral forces in Shānxī,
Tèliè served as Deputy Commander.
Hearing that the Jīn army was approaching,
Tèliè instructed his soldiers on the principle of loyalty between sovereign and subject,
and fought to the death at Shíliǎn Duó.
The Jīn army did not engage in battle.
Tèliè watched for an opportunity and intended to attack them.
Tiānzuò was extremely pleased,
summoning his concubines, ladies-in-waiting, and sons to climb a high place to watch together,
intending to surprise them.
The Jīn army, sighting the sun and moon banners,
knew Tiānzuò was located beneath them.
They used elite troops to advance directly and attack fiercely.
No one dared to resist,
and Tiānzuò fled.
Wherever Tèliè went,
he recruited and gathered the scattered and missing troops.
He was soon made Zhōngjūn Dūtǒng,
but was again defeated at Tījǐ Shān.
Tiānzuò decided to cross the river and flee to Xià.
His attendant officials strongly remonstrated, but he would not listen.
The hearts of the people were terrified and they did not know what to do.
Tèliè secretly said to Yēlǜ Wùzhí:
"The situation is like this.
The millions are losing faith.
This is precisely the moment for our generation to demonstrate loyalty.
If we do not make plans early,
what will become of the state and the altars of the soil and grain!"
They then together seized the Prince of Liáng, Yǎlǐ,
and fled to the various tribes in the northwest,
falsely establishing him as Emperor.
Tèliè appointed himself Grand Councilor (Shūmìshǐ).
Yǎlǐ died.
They wished to select someone suitable to enthrone.
At that time, Yēlǜ Wùzhí said that Zhúliè possessed complete talent and virtue,
and moreover, was the grandson of Xīngzōng.
Everyone said he was acceptable.
So they presumptuously established him (as Emperor).
Tèliè's false office remained the same.
Before thirty days passed,
he and Zhúliè were both killed by rebel soldiers.
The commentary says: When Liáo held the balance of power in the nation,
and grasped military authority,
controlling and regulating the various departments and tents,
they did not employ anyone who was not a member of the imperial clan (Zōngshì) or an external relative (Wàiqī).
Was this not intended as a strategy for the eternal longevity of the imperial house?
Yet when it came to rampant rebellion,
leading to chaos and downfall,
it was all these very people.
Those who possess a state
must not fail to take this as a profound warning!
Biographies, Chapter 45, Supplementary Record of Two States: Gāolì
Since Gāolì first established its nation,
the succession of reigns, whether long or short,
its people, lands, and fields,
and the policies of its successive generations have all had their own distinct intentions.
However, Gāolì and Liáo maintained relations from beginning to end for more than two hundred years.
Starting from the Shéncè period of Emperor Tàizǔ,
Gāolì sent envoys to present treasured swords.
In Tiānzàn 3rd year,
they came to pay tribute.
In Tiānxiǎn 2nd year of Tàizōng,
they came to pay tribute.
In Huìtóng 2nd year,
they received the imperial patent conferring an honorific title presented by Jìn,
and sent envoys to reply.
In the 7th month of autumn in Tǒnghé 3rd year of Shèngzōng,
an edict commanded all circuits (dào) to complete their military equipment,
in preparation for an eastern campaign against Gāolì.
In the 8th month,
due to the marshy conditions of Liáozé,
the troops were dismissed.
In the 10th year,
Xiāo Dé, the Resident General of Dōngjīng, was appointed to attack Gāolì.
In the 11th year,
Wáng Zhì sent Pǔ Liángróu to present a memorial requesting pardon.
An edict commanded that several hundred *lǐ* of territory east of the Yālù Jiāng belonging to the Nǚzhí state be taken and granted to him.
In the 12th year,
they paid tribute.
In the 3rd month,
Wáng Zhì sent an envoy requesting the return of the captured populace (shēngkǒu).
An edict commanded that they gradually be returned,
and also sent envoys to pacify and instruct them.
In the 12th month,
Wáng Zhì presented singing girls and musicians.
An edict rejected them.
In the 13th year,
Zhì sent Lǐ Zhōuzhēn to offer tribute.
He also presented falcons.
In the 10th month,
(He) sent Lǐ Zhībái to present tribute.
In the 11th month,
an envoy was sent to invest Zhì as King.
He sent ten boys to come and learn the language of our nation.
In the 14th year,
King Zhì memorialized, requesting a marriage alliance.
The daughter of Xiāo Dé, the Resident General of Dōngjīng and Imperial Son-in-Law (Fùmǎ), was given in marriage to him.
In the 6th month,
he sent an envoy to inquire after the Emperor's well-being.
From then on,
those who arrived came frequently.
In the 15th year,
Hán Yànjìng came to present betrothal gifts,
and to mourn the death of the Princess of Yuèguó, the wife of Imperial Son-in-Law Xiāo Dé.
In the 11th month,
Zhì died.
His nephew, Sòng, sent Wáng Tóngyǐng to announce the news.
In the 12th month,
an envoy was sent to offer sacrifices.
An edict commanded his nephew Sòng to provisionally manage state affairs.
In the 16th year,
an envoy was sent to invest Sòng as King.
In the 20th year,
Sòng sent an envoy to congratulate (us) on the victory against Sòng.
In the 7th month,
they came to present a map of their own country's territory.
In the 22nd year,
an edict was issued to inform and instruct them regarding the southern campaign.
In the 23rd year,
Gāolì, upon hearing that (Liáo) had made peace with Sòng,
sent envoys to offer congratulations.
In the 26th year,
they presented mats made of dragon-whiskers grass,
and congratulated (us) on the construction of the Central Capital (Zhōngjīng) city.
In the 27th year,
Chéngtiān Huáng Tàihòu passed away.
Envoys were sent to inform them of the national mourning.
In the 28th year,
Sòng sent Wèi Shǒuyú and others to offer sacrifices.
In the 3rd month,
an envoy came to attend the funeral.
In the 5th month,
Kāng Zhào, the Resident General of Gāolì's Western Capital (Xījīng), assassinated his sovereign Sòng,
and arbitrarily enthroned Xún, Sòng's cousin.
In the 8th month,
Shèngzōng personally led the army to attack Gāolì.
He informed Sòng,
and sent the Director of Diplomacy (Yǐnjìnshǐ), Hán Shí, to interrogate Xún with an imperial declaration.
Xún presented a memorial begging for the withdrawal of the troops,
which was not granted.
In the 11th month,
the great army crossed the Yālù Jiāng.
Kāng Zhào resisted the attack at Tóngzhōu.
(We) defeated him.
Zhào attacked again.
Yēlǜ Dílǔ, the Commandant (Xiángwěn) of the Right Píshì Division, captured Zhào and others.
(We) pursued the fleeing enemy for several tens of *lǐ*,
seizing the abandoned provisions, armor, and weapons.
Tóngzhōu, Huòzhōu, Guìzhōu, and Níngzhōu, and other prefectures, all surrendered.
Xún presented a memorial requesting permission to come to court.
This was granted,
and the soldiers were forbidden from taking captives or looting.
Mǎ Bǎoyòu, a Secretariat Drafter (Zhèngshì Shèrén), was appointed Resident General of Kāijīng.
Wáng Bā, the Commander of the Regiment Militia (Tuánliànshǐ) of Ānzhōu, was appointed Deputy Resident General.
Yǐ Lǐn, the Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Tàishī), led one thousand cavalry
to escort Bǎoyòu and the others to the capital.
The defending general Zhuó Sīzhèng killed our envoy Hán Xǐsūn and ten others,
led troops out to resist,
and Bǎoyòu and the others returned.
Yǐ Lǐn led troops to attack him.
Sīzhèng then fled to the Western Capital.
(We) besieged it for five days,
but could not overcome it.
The Emperor stayed at a Buddhist temple west of the city.
Bóhǎi Tuóshī, the Director (Lángzhōng) of the Board of Rites of Gāolì, came to surrender.
(The Emperor) sent Páiyā and Pénnú to attack Kāijīng.
They met the enemy west of the capital
and defeated them.
Xún abandoned the city and fled.
(The army) then burned Kāijīng,
and returned after reaching Qīngjiāng.
In the 1st month of the 29th year,
the troops were recalled.
The cities that had surrendered rebelled again.
When reaching the valley of Nánlǐng in Guìzhōu,
heavy rain fell for days.
Only when the weather cleared could they cross.
The horses and camels were all exhausted,
and much armor and weaponry was abandoned.
Upon reaching the Yālù Jiāng,
the captured people were divided up and placed at the various imperial tombs and ancestral temples,
and the remainder were granted to the imperial relatives and high ministers.
first year (1012),
Xún sent Cài Zhōngshùn to request the old status of claiming vassalage.
An imperial decree ordered Xún to personally attend court.
In the eighth month,
he sent Tián Gǒngzhī to present a memorial,
claiming illness prevented him from attending court.
An imperial decree ordered the recovery of the six prefectures' territory.
The second year (1013),
Yēlǜ Zīzhōng was sent as an envoy to Gāolì to reclaim territory,
but he returned shortly after.
The third year (1014),
Zīzhōng was again sent as an envoy,
demanding territory as before.
In the fifth month,
an imperial decree ordered the Emperor's Maternal Uncle Xiángwěn Xiāo Díliè, Yēlǜ Tuánshí (Administrator of Dōngjīng), and others to construct a pontoon bridge over the Yālù Jiāng,
and to build walled cities in the prefectures of Bǎo, Xuānyì, and Dìngyuǎn.
The fourth year (1015),
the Emperor appointed the Chancellor of the Northern Administration, Liú Shènxíng, as Supreme Commander (Dūtǒng),
the Commissioner of Military Affairs, Yēlǜ Shìliáng, as Deputy,
and the Commander of the Imperial Guard, Xiāo Xūliè, as Supervisor (Dūjiān).
Shènxíng brought his family to the border,
which caused the campaign timing to be delayed.
He was recalled;
Shìliáng and Xūliè were put in overall command of the troops to attack Gāolì.
The fifth year (1016),
Shìliáng and the others fought Gāolì west of Guōzhōu,
and defeated them.
The sixth year (1017),
the Commissioner of Military Affairs, Xiāo Hézhuó, was appointed Supreme Commander,
Wáng Jìzhōng (Commissioner-General of the Travelling Palace for Hàn people) as Deputy,
and the Commander of the Imperial Guard, Xiāo Xūliè, as Supervisor to advance and attack.
Xiāo Hézhuó attacked Xīnghuàjūn but failed to conquer it,
and the army returned.
The seventh year (1018),
an imperial decree appointed Xiāo Páiyā (Prince of Dōngpíng Commandery) as Supreme Commander,
Xiāo Xūliè as Deputy Commander,
and Yēlǜ Bāgē (Administrator of Dōngjīng) as Supervisor,
to again attack Gāolì.
In the twelfth month,
Xiāo Páiyā fought a battle between the Chá and Tuó rivers.
Our army suffered a setback.
Many soldiers from the Tiānyún and Yòupíshì armies were drowned,
including Xiángwěn Hǎilǐ of the Tiānyún Army, Xiángwěn Āguǒdá of the Yáoliǎn Account, Guest Service Commissioner Zhuógǔ, and Xiángwěn Gāo Qīngmíng of Bóhǎi, all of whom perished in battle.
The eighth year (1019),
an imperial decree enumerated Páiyā’s crimes during the Gāolì campaign,
but he was released.
Those generals and officers who had merit were promoted,
the wives of those generals and officers who died in battle received increased enfeoffments,
and their sons and younger brothers were appointed to office.
Because the officers of the Nánpíshì Army had achieved merit,
they were granted clothing, silver, and silk according to rank,
and gold and silk were issued and granted to the two Xī armies: Yáolǐ and Niègē.
In the eighth month,
the Emperor sent Lángjūn Kōngbùlǚ and others to lead the troops of various tribes,
to join the main army in jointly attacking Gāolì.
Xún sent an envoy to request permission to offer regional tribute.
The ninth year (1020),
Zīzhōng returned,
and presented Xún’s submission memorial.
Xún was pardoned for his crimes.
Tàipíng first year (1021),
Xún died.
An envoy was sent to report the succession,
and immediately an envoy was dispatched to invest Wáng Qīn as King.
The ninth year (1029),
Qīn was granted goods.
The eleventh year (1031),
Shèngzōng collapsed (died).
An envoy was sent to report the mourning.
In the seventh month,
an envoy came to offer condolences and sacrifices.
Xīngzōng, Zhòngxī seventh year (1038),
they came to present tribute.
The twelfth year (1043), third month,
on account of the addition of an honorable title [to the Emperor],
they came to congratulate.
The thirteenth year (1044),
an envoy was sent to present tribute.
The fourteenth year (1045), third month,
they again came to present tribute.
The fifteenth year (1046),
they entered to present tribute.
In the eighth month,
King Qīn died.
An envoy was sent to report this.
The sixteenth year (1047),
they came to present tribute.
The following year (1048),
they again came to present tribute.
The nineteenth year (1050),
they presented tribute again.
In the sixth month,
an envoy was sent to congratulate us on the victory over Xià.
The twenty-second year (1053),
they entered to present tribute.
The twenty-third year (1054), fourth month,
King Huī requested official positions for his sons.
An imperial decree granted his son the title of Examiner-Grand Commandant (Jiǎnxiào Tàiwèi).
Xīngzōng collapsed (died).
Dàozōng ascended the throne.
Qīngníng first year (1055), eighth month,
an envoy was sent to report the national mourning,

In the eleventh month,
an envoy came to attend the funeral.
The second (1056) and third (1057) years,
they all came to present tribute.
The fourth year (1058), spring,
an envoy was sent to report the mourning for the Grand Empress Dowager.
In the fifth month,
an envoy came to attend the funeral.
Xiányǒng seventh (1071) and eighth (1072) years,
they came to present tribute.
In the twelfth month,
a complete collection of Buddhist scriptures was granted to Huī.
The ninth (1073) and tenth (1074) years,
they came to present tribute.
Dàkāng second year (1076), third month,
the Empress Dowager collapsed (died).
An envoy was sent to report the mourning.
In the sixth month,
an envoy came to offer condolences and sacrifices.
The fourth year (1078),
King Huī requested the territory east of the Yālù Jiāng as a gift,
which was not permitted.
The ninth year (1083), eighth month,
King Huī died.
Huī’s son, Xūn (Duke of Sānguó), was temporarily put in charge of state affairs.
In the twelfth month,
Xūn died.
Dà'ān first year (1085),
Xūn’s son, Yùn, was invested as King of the State.
The second year (1086),
an envoy was sent to offer thanks for the enfeoffment and investiture.
The third year (1087),
they came to present tribute.
The fourth year (1088), third month,
they were exempted from the annual tribute.
The fifth (1089) and sixth (1090) years,
they presented tribute consecutively.
The ninth year (1093),
King Yùn was granted sheep.
The tenth year (1094),
Yùn died.
His son, Yù, sent an envoy to report it,
and funeral gifts were immediately sent.
Shòulóng first year (1095),
they came to present tribute.
In the eleventh month,
King Yù fell ill.
The Emperor ordered his son, Yóng, to temporarily take charge of state affairs.
The second year (1096),
they came to present tribute.
The third year (1097), third month,
King Yù died.
The fifth year (1099),
King Yóng requested enfeoffment and investiture.
The sixth year (1100),
Yóng was enfeoffed as Duke of Sānguó.
The seventh year (1101),
Dàozōng collapsed (died).
Tiānzuò ascended the throne.
The era was changed to Qiántǒng first year (1101).
Envoys reported the mourning for Dàozōng,
and envoys came to offer condolences and sacrifices.
In the twelfth month,
an envoy was sent to offer congratulations.
The fifth year (1105),
Yóng (Duke of Sānguó) died.
His son, Yǔ, sent an envoy to report it.
The eighth year (1108),
Yǔ was enfeoffed as Duke of Sānguó,
and his father Yóng was posthumously granted the title of King of the State.
In the twelfth month,
an envoy was sent to express thanks.
The ninth year (1109),
they came to present tribute.
Tiānqìng second year (1112),
King Yǔ’s mother died.
They came to report it.
An envoy was sent to offer sacrifices,
and Yǔ was recalled to office [from mourning].
The third year (1113),
an envoy was sent to express thanks for the offering of sacrifices,
and again came to thank us for recalling him to office.
The tenth year (1120),
they begged troops from Gāolì to defend against Jīn,
and the Jīn people reprimanded them.
At this point, the Liáo State was destroyed.
Xīxià (Western Xià)
originally descended from the Tuòbá clan of Wèi.
Their territory was the state of Hèlián.
Their distant ancestor, Sīgōng,
received the bestowed surname Lǐ during the end of the Táng dynasty.
Spanning the Five Dynasties until the Sòng dynasty,
they held that territory for generations.
It was not until Lǐ Jìqiān that they truly became powerful.
They occupied the five prefectures of Xià, Yín, Suī, Yòu, and Jìng,
along with seven garrisons around the border.
Their territory spanned twenty-five stages east to west,
and more than ten stages north to south.
His son, Démíng,
was knowledgeable in Buddhist scriptures
and understood law.
He once studied the *Tàiyī Jīnjiàn Jué* and the *Yězhàn Gē*.
He created twelve volumes of Fān scripts,
and also created characters resembling tallies or seals.
Their customs:
they wore narrow white robes,
had caps,
and behind the caps hung red knotted ribbons.
They called themselves Wěimíng,
and established officials divided into civil and military ranks.
Their caps were adorned with gold thread appliqué,
sometimes depicting clouds,
and silver foil appliqué.
They wore crimson robes,
silver belts coated in gold,
and carried *diéxiè* (utility belts), awls, short knives, bows, and arrows.
They wore boots,
had shaven hair,
heavy earrings,
and six layers of purple *xuánlán* robes.
When going out, they rode horses,
holding up blue canopies,
preceded by two guiding flags,
followed by over a hundred riders.
The common people wore green and blue.
They reduced the five notes of music to one note,
and reduced the nine bows of rites to three bows.
Whenever they dispatched troops, they first performed divination.
There were four methods: First, burning the shoulder blade (*zhì bó jiāo*):
using moxa to scorch a sheep's shoulder bone.
Second, scattering the counting sticks (*pǐ suàn*):
scattering bamboo pieces on the ground to determine numbers,
similar to casting yarrow stalks.
Third, cursing the sheep (*zhòu yáng*):
leading a sheep that night,
burning incense and praying to it,
and also burning grain fires in the field.
The next morning they slaughtered the sheep;
if the intestines and stomach were clear, it was auspicious;
if there was blood in the sheep's heart, it meant defeat.
Fourth, striking strings with an arrow:
listening to the sound
to know victory or defeat and the date the enemy would arrive.
Sick people did not use medicine;
they summoned shamans to dispel the spirits.
In the Xī Xià language, the shaman is called
*sī*
Sometimes they moved to another room,
calling this
"fleeing the sickness" (*shǎnbìng*).
They enjoyed seeking revenge.
If a family suffered a death, they would not attack others,
marking this by carrying armor plates on their backs.
When a feud was resolved,
they mixed the blood of chickens, pigs, and dogs with wine,
stored it in a skull, and drank it.
Then they swore an oath, saying:
"Should revenge be sought again,
grain and wheat will not be harvested,
men and women will suffer baldness and leprosy,
the six domestic animals will die,
and snakes will enter the tent."
If someone was weak and unable to seek revenge,
they would assemble strong women,
treat them with beef, mutton, wine, and food,
and then rush to the enemy's house to set fires,
burning their dwellings.
The custom was that fighting female soldiers was inauspicious,
so they would usually avoid them and flee.
When appealing to the authorities,
the officials would select eloquent and forthright people to act as arbitrators (*héduànguān*),
listening to the merits and faults of the case.
Those who committed murder
paid a life-price fine of 120,000 cash.

Local products included barley, common vetch, highland barley (*qīngkē*), *mùzi*, *gǔzǐmàn*, berries of the salty field tumbleweed, *rùróng* sprouts, small musk-mallow, seeds of *xī jī cǎo*, foxglove leaves, *dēng xiāng cǎo*, wild onion, wild chives, *jù huī tiáo*, white artemisia, and seeds of the salty field pine.
People at age fifteen were registered as adults (*dīng*).
If a household had two adults,
one was selected as a regular soldier (*zhèngjūn*).
One person responsible for various duties and carrying supplies was called a *chāo*.
Four adults formed two *chāo*.
The remaining men were allowed to shoot other adults (for practice),
and all practiced fighting and combat.
Each regular soldier (*zhèngjūn*) had one horse and one camel,
and each family provided its own tent.
Above the rank of Commander of Training (*Tuánliànshǐ*),
(the required equipment included) one tent, one bow, and one quiver of arrows,
five hundred horses,
one camel,
five flags and drums,
and one of each: spear, sword, club, supply bag, raincoat, felt cloak (*húntuō*), shovel, mattock, arrow shield, and iron ladle;
Below the rank of Prefect (*Cìshǐ*),
each man had one camel,
300 arrows,
and one felt screen/tent.
The remaining soldiers shared one tent among three men.
There were 200 artillerymen,
named
*Pōxǐ*.
The brave and robust were named
*Zhuànglìngláng*.
The rations they carried did not exceed ten days.
During the day, they raised smoke and stirred up dust;
at night, they made fire as a signal.
If they captured people or horses,
they shot them,
calling it "killing the spirits and summoning the souls."
Sometimes they shot at figures bound in straw.
They deployed troops on odd-numbered days,
avoiding the last day of the month.
They often established false camps
and set up ambushes.
They wore heavy armor,
rode excellent horses,
used iron cavalry as the vanguard,
and employed hooks and ropes to link them together,
so that even if they died, they would not fall from the horse.
Their people and customs were brave and fierce.
Regarding their attire, caps, riding customs, local products, and dynastic succession,
this is a brief overview of what is known.
Initially,
Xīxià (Western Xià) had been a vassal of Sòng for many years,
and had been granted the surname Zhào;
However, in the fourth year of Tǒnghé (986) of Liáo Shèngzōng,
Jìqiān rebelled against Sòng,
and first came to submit to Liáo,
He was granted the titles Tèjìn Jiǎnxiào Tàishī (Grand Master) and Dūdū Xiàzhōu Zhū Jūnshì (Military Commander of Xiàzhōu and other prefectures),
and thereupon reverted to the surname Lǐ.
In the tenth month,
he sent an envoy to offer tribute.
In the sixth year (988),
he offered tribute.
In the seventh year (989),
he came to offer tribute,
the daughter of the prince Yēlǜ Xiāng was enfeoffed as Princess Yìchéng,
and married down to Jìqiān.
In the first month of the eighth year (990),
he came to express thanks.
In the third month,
he again came to offer tribute.
In the ninth month,
Jìqiān sent an envoy to present Sòng captives.
In the tenth month,
he came to report his defeat of the Sòng army.
In the twelfth month,
after conquering Sòng's Línzhōu and Fūzhōu, etc.,
he came to report this,
and an envoy was sent to enfeoff Jìqiān as the King of Xià (Xiàguówáng).
In the second month of the ninth year (991),
he sent an envoy to report the victory in the campaign against Sòng.
In the fourth month,
he sent Lǐ Zhībái to express thanks for the enfeoffment and credentials.
In the seventh month,
he recovered Suízhōu and Yínzhōu,
and came to report this.
In the tenth month,
Jìqiān took the imperial edicts previously bestowed by Sòng
and sent an envoy to present them.
In this month,
Lǐ Jìběng, the Military Commissioner (Jiédùshǐ) of Dìngnán Command, came to submit,
He was granted the titles Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, Jiǎnxiào Tàishī,
and concurrently Shìzhōng (Attendant at the Palace Gate),
and was enfeoffed as Prince of Xīpíng (Xīpíng Wáng),
and was further bestowed the title of Meritorious Official (Gōngchén), Tuīzhōng Xiàoshùn Qǐshèng Dìngnán.
In the twelfth month,
Jìqiān secretly submitted to Sòng,
so Hán Déwēi was sent carrying an imperial edict to admonish him.
In the second month of the tenth year (992),
Hán Déwēi returned,
and reported that Jìqiān refused to come out under pretense,
and had returned after capturing and looting in Língzhōu.
Xīxià sent an envoy to report Déwēi's capturing and looting,
and an imperial edict was issued for consolation and admonition.
In the tenth month,
he came to offer tribute.
In the twelfth year (994),
he offered tribute.
In the thirteenth year (995),
he defeated the Sòng army,
and sent an envoy to report this.
In the fourteenth year (996),
he again came to offer tribute.
In the third month of the fifteenth year (997),
he came to report the destruction of the Sòng troops,
and Jìqiān was enfeoffed as Prince of Xīpíng (Xīpíng Wáng).
In the sixth month,
he sent an envoy to express thanks for the enfeoffment and credentials.
In the sixteenth year (998),
he came to offer tribute.
In the eighteenth year (1000),
Jìqiān’s son, Démíng, was granted the title of Military Commissioner of Shuòfāng Command (Shuòfāng Jūn Jiédùshǐ).
In the nineteenth year (1001),
he sent Lǐ Wénjì to offer tribute.
In the sixth month,
he reported the capture of Sòng's Huánzhōu and Qìngzhōu, three prefectures in total,
and an imperial edict was granted in praise.
In the twentieth year (1002),
he sent an envoy to present horses and camels.
In the sixth month,
he sent Liú Rénxù to report the capture of Língzhōu.
In the twenty-first year (1003),
Jìqiān died,
and his son, Dézhāo, sent an envoy to report the death.
In the sixth month,
Jìqiān was posthumously granted the title of Shàngshū Lìng (Director of the Department of State Affairs),
and Dīng Zhèn, the Envoy of the Western Upper Gates (Xī Shàng Gémén Shǐ), was sent to offer condolences.
In the eighth month,
Dézhāo sent an envoy to express thanks for the condolences and posthumous grant.
In the third month of the twenty-second year (1004),
Dézhāo sent an envoy to present the items left behind by Jìqiān.
In the seventh month,
Dézhāo was enfeoffed as Prince of Xīpíng (Xīpíng Wáng).
In the tenth month,
he sent an envoy to express thanks for the enfeoffment and credentials.
In the twenty-third year (1005),
he captured Sòng's Qīngchéng,
and came to report this.
In the twenty-fifth year (1007),
Dézhāo's mother died,
