In the twenty-seventh year (1009),
Empress Dowager Chéngtiān died,
and an envoy was sent to report the mourning to Xià.
In the twenty-eighth year (1010),
an envoy was sent to formally invest Dézhāo as the King of Xià (Xiàguówáng).
In the first year of Kāitài (1012),
Dézhāo sent an envoy to present fine horses.
In the second year (1013),
Lǐ Yánhóng, the Envoy for Receiving Guests (Yǐnjìn Shǐ), was sent to bestow carriages and horses upon Lǐ Dézhāo, King of Xià, and Princess Yìchéng.
In the first year of Tàipíng (1021),
he came to offer tribute.
In the eleventh year (1031),
Shèngzōng died,
and the mourning was reported to Xià;
Dézhāo sent an envoy to present funeral money and silks (fùbì).
When Xīngzōng ascended the throne,
Princess Xīngpíng was married down to Lǐ Yuánhào,
and Yuánhào was made Auxiliary Commandant (Fùmǎ Dūwèi).
In the first year of Chóngxī (1032),
the State of Xià sent an envoy to offer congratulations.
Lǐ Dézhāo died,
and his son, Yuánhào, Duke of Xià (Xiàguógōng), was formally invested as King.
In the second year (1033),
he came to offer tribute.
In the twelfth month,
the envoys of the State of Xià were forbidden from privately trading official iron along the route.
In the seventh year (1038),
he came to offer tribute.
Lǐ Yuánhào did not harmonize with Princess Xīngpíng,
and the princess died.
Yēlǜ Shùchéng, the Grand Secretary of the Northern Chancellery (Běiyuàn Chéngzhǐ), was sent bearing an imperial edict to inquire about this.
In the ninth year (1040),
Sòng sent Guō Zhēn to report their military campaign against Xià.
In the tenth year (1041),
the State of Xià presented the captured Sòng general and common captives.
In the eleventh year (1042),
an envoy was sent to ask Sòng the reason for raising troops to attack Xià.
In the twelfth month,
Tǔhún was forbidden from selling horses to Xià,
and defensive barriers were built along the border to guard against them.
In the first month of the twelfth year (1043),

Yēlǜ Díliè, Deputy Prefect of Xījīnfǔ (Tóngzhī Xījīnfǔ Shì), and Wáng Wéijí, Grand Secretary of the Bureau of Military Affairs (Shūmì Dū Chéngzhǐ), were sent to admonish the State of Xià to seek peace with Sòng.
In the second month,
Yuánhào, having been granted an honored title,
sent an envoy to offer congratulations.
Yēlǜ Díliè and the others returned from their mission to the State of Xià,
reporting that Yuánhào had stopped fighting,
and an envoy was sent to inform Sòng.
In the fourth month,
the State of Xià sent an envoy to present horses and camels.
In the seventh month,
Yuánhào submitted a memorial requesting permission to attack Sòng,
but this was not permitted.
In the tenth month,
the Xià people invaded Dǎngxiàng territory,
so Gāo Jiānú, the Palace Commissioner of Yánchāng (Yánchāng Gōng Shǐ), was sent to reprimand them.
In the fourth month of the thirteenth year (1044),
Qūliè, the Military Commissioner of the Dǎngxiàng and Shānxī tribes, rebelled with five divisions and defected to Xīxià;
an imperial edict ordered the troops of various circuits to subdue him.
In the sixth month,
Wū Bā, the chief of Zǔbǔ, sent his son to bring Wāyìgǎi, the envoy sent by Yuánhào to request aid, who had been captured.
In the eighth month,
the Xià envoy failed to answer truthfully regarding the situation,
and was detained.
Another envoy came,
and when questioned regarding the circumstances, he also failed to answer truthfully,
so he was whipped.
In the tenth month,
Yuánhào submitted a memorial apologizing for his offense,
and offered to gather the rebellious factions to present them,
which was granted;
He presented regional products,
and Xiāo Gé, the Deputy Commissioner of the Bureau of Military Affairs of the Northern Chancellery (Běiyuàn Shūmì Fùshǐ), was ordered to receive him.
Yuánhào personally led three Dǎngxiàng divisions to surrender.
When questioned regarding harboring rebels and breaking the treaty,
Yuánhào admitted his guilt.
Earlier,
the Xià people had captured Xiāo Húdǔ.
At this point,
they requested to return the captive person.
An edict commanded that the detained Xià envoy also be returned to his state.
In the twelfth month,
Húdǔ returned,
and an envoy was again sent to offer tribute.
In the seventeenth year,
Yuán Hào Hōng (died),
and his son, Liàng Zuò, sent an envoy to announce it,
presenting the items left by his father.
Tiě Bù Dé Guó begged to use the troops of his own tribe to assist in attacking Xià Guó,
but this was not granted.
In the eighteenth year,
it was again proposed to campaign against Xià.
The envoy sent by Xià to congratulate the New Year was detained and not sent back,
and Xiāo Wéi Xìn, Vice Commissioner of the Northern Chancellery of Military Affairs (Běi Yuàn Shū Mì Fù Shǐ), was sent to inform Sòng of the campaign against Xià.
In the sixth month,
Xià Guó sent an envoy to present tribute,
and he was detained.
In the seventh month,
the Emperor personally led the campaign.
In the eighth month,
the river was crossed,
and the Xià people fled.
In the ninth month,
Xiāo Huì was defeated by the Xià people.
In the tenth month,
Yēlǜ Dí Gǔ, the Pacification Commissioner (Zhāo Tǎo Shǐ), led Zǔ Bǔ troops to Hè Lán Shān,
capturing Yuán Hào’s wife and her attendant officials.
They encountered three thousand of their troops coming to resist,
and destroyed them;
Xiāo Cí Shì Nú, the Xiáng Wěn, and Yēlǜ Wò Lǐ, the Nán Kè, died in battle.
In the first month of the nineteenth year,
an envoy was sent to chastise Xià for its crimes.
The Xià general Wā Pǔ and others attacked Jīn Sù Chéng,
but Yēlǜ Gāo Jiā Nú and others defeated them.
Wā Pǔ was wounded and fled,
and Wěi Huò Yǐ Líng Jǐ was killed.
In the third month,
Xiāo Dié Lǐ Dé, the Grand Inspector of the Palace Guards (Diàn Qián Dū Diǎn Jiǎn), fought the Xià army at Sān Jiǎo Chuān,
and defeated them.
Xiāo Pó Nú, the Pacification Commissioner (Zhāo Tǎo Shǐ), and Yí Xīn, the Prince of the Northern Division (Běi Yuàn Dà Wáng), led troops to campaign against Xià,
with Bié Gǔ Dé, the Commander-in-Chief (Dū Bù Shǔ), overseeing the battle.
In the fifth month,
Xiāo Pó Nú and others entered Xià territory,
did not encounter the enemy,
and allowed their troops to capture and plunder before returning.
Wā Pǔ of Xià Guó came and surrendered.
In the tenth month,
Lǐ Liàng Zuò's mother sent an envoy petitioning to resume the previous status of being a subject (chēng chén).
In the twelfth month,
Liàng Zuò submitted a memorial according to his mother's instruction.
In the second month of the twentieth year,
an envoy was sent to demand the return of Dǎng Xiàng rebels.
In the fifth month,
Xiāo Yáo Kuò returned from his mission to Xià,
presenting a memorial from Liàng Zuò's mother: petitioning to offer horses, camels, cattle, sheep, and other goods on behalf of the Dǎng Xiàng for the time being;
she also requested Táng Lóng Zhèn,
and further petitioned for the abandonment of the walled cities that had been constructed.
This was answered with an imperial edict.
In the sixth month,
Yuán Hào’s wife was captured,
and the captured Xià people were settled in Sū Zhōu.
In the tenth month of the twenty-first year,
Liàng Zuò sent an envoy petitioning for the relaxation of border defenses.
Yáo Kuò was sent bearing an edict to instruct him.
In the seventh month of the twenty-second year,
Liàng Zuò presented a memorial of submission.
Gāo Jiā Nú, the Lín Yá, was sent bearing an edict to soothe and instruct him.
In the first month of the twenty-third year,
tribute items were presented.
In the fifth month,
a request was made to present horses and camels,
and an edict permitted this as an annual tribute.
In the seventh month,
Liàng Zuò sent an envoy to request a marriage alliance.
In the tenth month,
a memorial containing an oath was presented.
In the twenty-fourth year,
Xīng Zōng Bēng (died).
An envoy was sent to Xià to report the mourning.
Dào Zōng ascended the throne.
In the first year of Qīng Níng,
an envoy came to offer congratulations.
In the ninth month,
the items left by the previous emperor were bestowed upon Xià.
In the fourth month of the fourth year,
an envoy was sent to attend the funeral.
In the first month of the ninth year,
the populace was prohibited from selling copper to Xià.
In the fifth month of the first year of Xián Yǒng,
tribute was presented.
In the eleventh month of the third year,
an envoy was sent to present a Huí Hú (Uyghur) monk, a golden Buddha statue,
and a Fàn Jué scripture.
In the twelfth month,
Liàng Zuò Hōng (died).
In the second month of the fourth year,
Liàng Zuò's son, Bǐng Cháng, sent an envoy to report the mourning,
and an envoy was immediately dispatched to offer condolences and sacrifices.
Bǐng Cháng presented the items left by his father.
In the tenth month,
Bǐng Cháng was formally invested (cè) as the King of Xià Guó.
In the twelfth month,
tribute was presented.
In the seventh month of the fifth year,
an envoy came to express gratitude for the formal investiture.
In the intercalary eleventh month,
Bǐng Cháng petitioned for the bestowal of the official seal and ribbon (yìn shòu).
In the ninth year,
an envoy was sent to present tribute.
In the first month of the second year of Dà Kāng,
Empress Rén Yì Hòu Bēng (died).
An envoy was sent to Xià to report the mourning,
and the items left by the Empress Dowager were bestowed upon them.
An envoy came to offer condolences and sacrifices.
In the fifth year,
tribute was presented.
In the second month of the eighth year,
an envoy was sent to present the captured Sòng general, Zhāng Tiān Yì.
In the tenth month of the first year of Dà Ān,
Bǐng Cháng sent an envoy to report the mourning for his mother.
In the tenth month of the second year,
Bǐng Cháng Hōng (died).
An envoy was sent bearing an edict for his son, Qián Shùn, to manage the affairs of the state.
In the twelfth month,
Lǐ Qián Shùn sent an envoy to present the items left by his father, Bǐng Cháng.
In the seventh month of the fourth year,
Qián Shùn was formally invested (cè) as the King of Xià Guó.
In the sixth month of the fifth year,
an envoy was sent to express gratitude for the formal investiture.
In the sixth month of the eighth year,
Xià was invaded by Sòng,
and an envoy was sent petitioning for aid.
In the sixth month of the third year of Shòu Lóng,
because the Sòng people established fortifications in strategic locations,
an envoy was sent to report this.
In the sixth month of the fourth year,
aid was requested.
In the eleventh month,
Yēlǜ Yǎn, Academician of the Bureau of Military Affairs (Shū Mì Zhí Xué Shì), was sent as an envoy to Sòng,
to subtly urge them to make peace with Xià.
Xià again sent an envoy to request aid.
In the first month of the fifth year,
Qián Shùn was commanded by edict to campaign against the Bó Sī Mǔ and other tribes.
In the eleventh month,
Xià sent an envoy to express gratitude
because the Sòng people had withdrawn their troops.
In the eleventh month of the sixth year,
an envoy was sent to request marriage with a princess.
In the seventh year,
Dào Zōng Bēng (died).
An envoy was sent to Xià to report the mourning.
An envoy came to offer comfort and sacrifices.
Tiān Zuò ascended the throne.
In the first year of Qián Tǒng,
Xià sent an envoy to offer congratulations.
In the second year,
they again requested marriage with a princess.
Furthermore, believing they had been invaded by Sòng,
they sent Lǐ Zào Fú and Tián Ruò Shuǐ to request aid.
In the third year,
an envoy was again sent to request marriage with a princess.
In the tenth month,
an envoy came again to request aid.
In the fourth and fifth years,
Lǐ Zào Fú and others arrived,
petitioning for aid.
Nán Xiān, a female relative of the Imperial clan, was enfeoffed as Princess Chéng Ān Gōng Zhǔ and married to Qián Shùn.
In the first month of the sixth year,
Niú Wēn Shū was sent as an envoy to Sòng,
ordering them to return the Xià territory they had invaded.
In the sixth month,
Lǐ Zào Fú was sent to express gratitude.
In the eighth year,
Qián Shùn, because Princess Chéng Ān Gōng Zhǔ had given birth to a son,
sent an envoy to announce it.
In the ninth year,
they sent an announcement concerning Sòng’s failure to return the territory.
In the tenth year,
Lǐ Zào Fú and others were sent to present tribute.
In the sixth month of the third year of Tiān Qìng,
tribute was presented.
In the second year of Bǎo Dà,
when Tiān Zuò was forced to flee (bō qiān),
Qián Shùn led troops to come to his aid,
but they were defeated by the Jīn forces (Jīn Shī).
Qián Shùn requested to oversee his state.
In the sixth month,
an envoy was sent to formally invest (cè) Qián Shùn as Emperor of Xià Guó,
while Tiān Zuò had already been captured and taken back to Jīn.
A commentary states: Gāolì and Xīxià served the Liáo,
although they sometimes requested marriages and gave daughters in marriage,
how could this be sufficient to secure their fixed allegiance?
The Sānhán bordered them,
their repeated betrayals were easy to anticipate;
Liángzhōu relied on its distance,
accepted defectors and encroached upon the borders,
always acting when opportunities arose;
while tribute envoys were just departing,
conflicts arose immediately.
Raising armies to punish offenses,
frequently necessitated imperial expeditions (qīnzhēng).
Victories were certainly many,
but defeats also caused regret.
Formerly, Zhào Zī of Wú, when speaking to Wèi, said:
"Great states have armies for conquest,
but small states have strong defenses for preparation."
How could this not be true!
The ancient kings pacified distant peoples (róu yuǎn),
using virtue (dé) and not force (lì);
this is lofty tradition.
When the Liáo perished,
they sought assistance from these two states,
and although they were able to mobilize troops,
how could they oppose the Jīn?
*Guóyǔ Jiě* (Explanations of the National Language).
The histories, from Qiān [Sīmǎ Qiān] and Gù [Bān Gù],
up to the Jìn and Táng dynasties,
are magnificent, profound, vast, and extensive works.
Readers could not fully understand them.
Thereupon, scholars like Péi Yīn, Yán Shīgǔ, Lǐ Xián, Hé Chāo, and Dǒng Chōng,
provided textual exegesis, pronunciation, and explanations.
Only then could institutions, names of objects, regional dialects, and rare characters
be widely known after a single reading.
Their aid to subsequent scholars was immense.
When the Liáo first rose,
they were closely neighboring the Xī and Shìwéi;
their local customs and language were generally rustic.
By the time of Tàizǔ and Tàizōng,
they had taken control of the northern regions (Shuòfāng),
and although their governance utilized Hàn laws,
the systems of the early generations, the Qíshǒu and Yáoniǎn, still largely remained.
Their descendants succeeded them,
and also adhered to them without change.
Therefore, what is recorded in the history,
concerning official systems, palace guards, tribes, and geography,
mostly uses the names from the national language.
If there are no commentaries to distinguish them,
how can people of this era know them,
and how can later generations study them?
Now, based on the original history and mutual research,
I have compiled the *Liáo Guóyǔ Jiě* and attached it after the history,
hoping that readers will avoid the difficulty of discordance.
Imperial Annals (Dì Jì)
Annals of Tàizǔ:
Yēlǜ Shì, Xiāo Shì. The beginning of the Annals first records Tàizǔ’s surname as Yēlǜ Shì,
followed by the Empress’s surname, Xiāo Shì.
Thus, at the start of the state's founding,
the two surnames were already distinguished.
Some say that the place where they first arose was called Shìlǐ,
and translators rendered Shìlǐ as Yēlǜ,
thus all members of the imperial clan used Yēlǜ as their surname.
Some say that the Empress Shùlǜ’s nephew was named Xiāo Hàn,
who served as Xuānwǔ Jūn Jiédùshǐ.
His sister later became Empress,
hence all members of the Empress’s clan used Xiāo as their surname.
This explanation does not align with the Annals,
thus Chén Dàrèn did not adopt it.
Furthermore, there is a saying that those written in Hán characters are Yēlǜ and Xiāo,
and those written in Qìdān characters are Yílà and Shímò;
this is also impossible to verify.
Xiálài Yì Shíliè. A village name.
Below every palace there is a Shíliè,
where officials are established to govern it.
Mǐlǐ. A small village.
Tǎmǎ Yuè Shālǐ. Tǎmǎ
means people following (followers).
Shālǐ
means gentleman (lángjūn).
It is an official who controls and commands the multitudes.
Later, some were simply called Tǎmǎ.
Dà Diéliè Fǔ. This is the government office of the Diélà Tribe.
Originally,
Zǔwǔ Kèhán and his younger brother Sālǐběn ruled it.
When Tàizǔ ascended the throne as the tribal Yílíjǐn,
because it was strong and difficult to control,
it was divided into two Courts (yuàn).
The sounds *liè* and *là* are similar.
Yílíjǐn. A high official who commands the army and horses.
At the start of the Huìtóng era,
it was changed to Dàwáng.
Jíhuì Guō (The character Guō has two pronunciations: *wō* and *tuó* below it.
) A place name.
Āzhǔ Shālǐ. Āzhǔ
is a term of address for father or grandfather.
Tìyǐn. An official who oversees the clan members.
This is the office of Zōngzhèng.
Xī, Xí (The character below is pronounced *xí*.
) State names.
They are located in the region of Zhōngjīng.
Hēichēzi. A state.
It got its name because its people were skilled at making chariots and tents.
The ancestors of the Qìdān,
once sent people to learn from them.
Yúyuè. A noble official,
who held no specific duty.
His rank was above the Northern and Southern Great Kings (Dàwáng),
and it was not bestowed upon anyone who lacked great merit or virtue (gōngdé).
Yīngjūn (Eagle Army). Yīng
means raptor;
naming the army after it
signifies speed and swiftness.
The later records of the Lóngjūn (Dragon Army), Hǔjūn (Tiger Army), and Tiěyào Jūn (Iron Hawk Army),
follow this model.
Wǎnniánggǎi (The character above is pronounced *wǎn*.
) A place name.
Xīlóu (Western Tower). Liáo had four Towers: the one in Shàngjīng was called Xīlóu;
Mùyè Shān was called Nánlóu (Southern Tower);
Lónghuà Zhōu was called Dōnglóu (Eastern Tower);
Tángzhōu was called Běilóu (Northern Tower).
Throughout the year, when traveling and hunting,
they were constantly among these four Towers.
Ādiǎn Yílídì. Ādiǎn
is an honorific address.
Yílídì
is the title for the wife of a high official.
Jiūxiá. Jiū
is an army name.
Xiá
means to control and restrain.
Yílíbì. This is equivalent to Cānzhī Zhèngshì (Vice-Administrator of Governmental Affairs).
Later, the Yílíbì Yuàn was established to oversee penal administration.
Diāo Yuē of Sòng, when sent on a mission to Liáo, wrote a poem saying:
"Yālù Yílíbì (The Yílíbì who oversees the banquet),"
showing that he was an executive official.
Shè Guǐjiàn (Shooting the Ghost Arrow). Whenever the Emperor personally campaigned (qīnzhēng),
donned armor and helmet,
and offered sacrifices to the preceding emperors,
upon setting out, he would take one condemned prisoner,
place him in the direction of the advance,
and shoot him with a flurry of arrows.
This was called Shè Guǐjiàn (Shooting the Ghost Arrow),
used to ward off misfortune.
When the army returned,
they would shoot the captives.
Later, this became a type of punishment.
Bàolǐ. The name of a wicked person.
Dà Hú Jūn, Xiǎo Hú Jūn (Great/Small Egret Army). The military titles of the two Shìwéi tribes.
Shéndú (Spirit Banner). Held by the attendants.
It was made from yak tails,
belonging to the feathered spears/pennants.
Lóngméi Gōng (Dragon Eyebrow Palace). Tàizǔ adopted the strategic positioning of the three mountains — Tiāntī, Méngguó, and Biélǔ — at Wěidiàn,
and shot a Jīnchuò arrow to mark the spot.
It was named Lóngméi Gōng.
In the third year of Shéncè (918 CE),
a capital city was constructed on that land.
This is Línhuáng Fǔ.
Chuò,
pronounced *cè jiǎo qiè*,
is the name of an arrow.
Xiáolǐ. The name of a Shìwéi tribe.
Jūnjī Tàiyī Shén. The name of a Fortune God.
In the state where this spirit descends,
if the ruler can establish the Supreme Standard (jiànjí),
and inspire trust among high and low,
then governance will be orderly and peaceful,
and the people will enjoy many blessings.
Tàlín. An official title.
Later, the two Shìwéi tribes changed this title to Púshè,
and it was also called Sīkōng.
Shèlì. Among the influential Qìdān commoners, those who donned turbans,
paid ten head of cattle and camels,
and one hundred horses,
were then given the official title of Shèlì.
Later, they became officials of the various encampments (zhàng),
adding the title Lángjūn (Gentleman) to it.
Ālúwūlǐ (also known as Ālǔdūn).
) A name of nobility and prominence.
Among the Liáo officials holding the Yúyuè title who also held this post,
only Hélǔ did so.
Xuǎndǐ. The official in charge of prisons.
Chánggǔn. An official title.
Responsible for matters like the census registers of the Yáoniǎn tribes;
the Chánggǔn of the Six Xī Tribes managed the Xī clan affairs.
Yīnchuàn. The name of the ruler of the Bóhǎi state.
Kè Shìlǔ. Kè
is an official title.
Shìlǔ
is a personal name.
Later, Kè Lǎng and Kè Táishěn followed this pattern.
Wūlǔgǔ, Ālǐzhǐ. The names of the two horses ridden by Tàizǔ and Empress Shùlǜ when they received Yīnchuàn’s surrender.
Consequently, they gave these names to Yīnchuàn and his wife.
Annals of Tàizōng:
Jiàngǎn Shān (The character *gǎn* is pronounced *gǎn*.
) The place where the Húsǔn Xī resided.
Chái Cè: The name of a ritual.
Piles of firewood are stacked to form an altar,
where the emperor receives jade tablets (*cè*) from his officials.
When the ritual is complete,
the firewood is burned,
sacrificing to Heaven.
Instituted by Zǔwǔ Kèhàn.
Yáolián Shì Jiǔ Zhàng (Nine Tents of the Yáolián Clan): The divisions of the palaces belonging to the nine Yáolián Kèhàn.
Běikè, Nánkè (Northern Kè, Southern Kè): Names of military officials who manage the army,
similar in duty to the Northern and Southern Armies of the Hàn dynasty.
Offering to the God of the Tufted Deer (*Biāo Lù*): It was a custom of the Liáo people to enjoy shooting *biāo lù*.
Whenever they went hunting,
they always sacrificed to its god to pray for a plentiful catch.
Línyá: An official in charge of literary affairs and documents.
At the time, they were called Scholars (*Xuèshì*).
Those established in the various Herding Bureaus (*Qún Mù Suǒ*),
only managed ledgers and records.
Sèsè Lǐ (Sèsè Ritual): A ceremony for praying for rain and shooting the willow branch,
instituted by Yáolián Sū Kèhàn.
Zàishēng Lǐ (Rebirth Ritual): A national custom.
Every twelve years, once,
they perform the ritual of initial birth,
named "Rebirth" (*Zàishēng*).
Only the Emperor, the Empress Dowager, the Crown Prince, and the Yílíjǐn were permitted to perform it.
It was also named Fù Dàn (Returning Birth).
Shénsùgū: The personal name of a member of the imperial clan,
who could understand the speech of snakes.
Púgē
: The name of a Princess (*Gōngzhǔ*).
Sān Kè (Three Kè): A commander of armies,
equivalent to saying the Three Commanders (*Sān Shuài*).
Xiángwěn: The chief official supervising and managing the various government offices.
Tīlǐyǐ: An official subordinate to the various tribes/departments.
Later promoted to Minister of Education (*Sītú*).
Dálàgān: A county official.
Later promoted to Deputy Envoy (*Fùshǐ*).
Mádōubù: An assistant to the county official.
Later promoted to Magistrate (*Lìng*).
Mǎbù: It is not clear what type of official this was;
Dálàgān were promoted to this rank.
Yáshǔ: An official title.
It is suspected to be Yáshū,
an official of the Shíliè rank.
Shìzhú: The official known as the Palace Attendant (*Shìzhōng*) of the Yáolián Tent.
Chǎngshǐ: An assistant clerk in a government office.
Sīnúgǔ: An official rank close to Chǎngshǐ.
Túndǔgǔ: A small state beyond the border frontiers.
Annals of Shìzōng and Mùzōng:
Dàilín
: A place name,
which is the old site of Sōnglín.
Zhásā'è: An official of the Mǒlǐ Division,
who also managed the prohibitions within the palace guards.
Tàmǎ: An official of the retinue.
Nóngwù: A divisional name.
Yè Gè Xì (Leaf Grid Game): At the residence of Qián Xīgōng of the Sòng dynasty, there was a game called *Yèzi Jiē Gé*.
Annals of Jǐngzōng and Shèngzōng:
Fēilóng Shǐ (Flying Dragon Envoy): An official in charge of horses,
who also served as an escort cavalry.
Héng Zhàng (Horizontal Tent): The clan members of Dézǔ were known as the Sān Fù Fáng (Three Fathers' Households).
They were called Héng Zhàng,
being the most esteemed members of the imperial clan.
Zhù Zhàng (Registered Tent): Households of hereditary officials and people of various classes,
who were confiscated due to crimes, became *Zhù Zhàng Hù* (registered households).
There was also an official called *Zhù Zhàng Lángjūn*.
Sháowā Yìn (Sháowā Seal): *Sháowā*,
is the general term for raptors,
used as the knob of the seal,
signifying speed and urgency.
It was used whenever troops and horses were dispatched.
It was somewhat similar to the Gold Fish Tallies (*Jīn Yú Fú*) and Silver Plaques (*Yín Pái*).
Guójiù Zhàng Kè (Imperial Uncle Tent Kè): The official system included the Dà Guójiù Zhàng (Great Imperial Uncle Tent).
This was the official in charge of soldiers under that tent.
Bài Ào Lǐ (Kneeling at the Ào Ritual): Whenever an Empress was inducted,
one respected person from the clan was chosen to sit facing the *ào* (corner/chamber),
to preside over the ritual.
This person was called the Ào Gū (Aunt of the Chamber).
The person delivering the Empress kneels and shows respect,
hence the name Bài Ào Lǐ.
Bài Shān Lǐ (Kneeling at the Mountain Ritual): The ceremony for sacrificing to Mùyè Shān (Wood Leaf Mountain).
Chǎngwěn: Officials subordinate to the various tents.
Also written as Chánggǔn,
because the characters sound similar.
Wànyì Xiànhé Yě
: A place name.
Originally the Tǔyín County of the Hàn dynasty.
It had a silver mine.
Tàizǔ recruited people and established a fortified camp to specialize in mining and smelting,
hence the name Xiànhé Yě (Trap River Smeltery).
Hésūgǔn: The name of a separate Jurchen (*Nǚzhí*) tribe,
also written as Hésūguǎn.
Zhíshǒu Lǐ (Hand Holding Ritual): When a commander achieved merit in defeating the enemy,
the Emperor personally held his hand to comfort and reward him.
If the commander was still with the army,
someone would be dispatched to perform the Zhíshǒu Lǐ on his behalf.
This signifies excellent treatment.
Āzhágēzhǐ: An official title.
The position was below the Commissioner of Military Affairs (*Shūmìshǐ*).
It was a *dūn* (platform) official.
Sìjié Jūn (Four Victories Army): The Liáo divided those who surrendered from Sòng into two divisions: one called the Sìjié Jūn,
and the other called the Guīshèng Jūn (Returning Sagely Army).
Shānjīn Sī (Mountain Gold Bureau): Because the Yīnshān Mountains produced gold,
a smelting operation was established to mine and refine it.
Hence the name of the Bureau.
Later changed to the Tǒngjūn Sī (Army Command Bureau).
Annals of Xīngzōng:
Bié Niǎn Dǒu
: A place name.
Hǔ
: The personal names of the Pólíbābù (Pólí Eight Tribes).
Jiě Xǐ Lǐ (Untie and Wash Ritual): A purification rite before untying the gear,
signifying the meaning of "drinking upon arrival."
Dúlújīn: A place name.
The officials and subordinates of the Liù Yuàn (Six Bureaus) lived there during autumn and winter.
Performing the Shí'èr Shén Dú Lǐ (Ritual of the Twelve Divine Standards): The explanation of *Shéndú* can be found earlier.
During major sacrifices or grand imperial audiences,
the twelve standards were arranged before the Emperor.
Nánsāgěbǎi: A place name.
Hézhǐhūlǐ: A place name.
Tuōgǔliè: A place name.
Hélǐ'è: A place name.
Annals of Dàozōng:
Tǎlǐshě: A place name.
Sālǐnǎi: A place name.
Sānbān Yuàn Zhīhòu (Attendant of the Three Ranks Bureau): The Left Rank, Right Rank, and Temporary Rank combined formed the Three Ranks.
*Zhīhòu*,
is an official title.
Gāodūn (High Platform): In the Liáo court rank diagrams,
there were ranks of Gāodūn, Ăidūn (Low Platform), and Fāngdūn (Square Platform).
Officials ranging from the Grand Chancellor (*Dà Chéngxiàng*) down to the Āzhágēzhǐ,
were all *dūn* (platform) officials.
Annals of Tiānzuò:
Hòulǐjí
: A place name.
Tóuyú Yàn (First Fish Feast): When the Emperor caught the first fish of the season,
having obtained the first fish,
he would immediately set up wine and a great feast,
similar to the Tóu'é Yàn (First Goose Feast).
Ésuōliè: A place name.
Ōulǐjǐn: A place name.
Huāntà Xīnchálà: A place name.
Shè Liáng Jūn (Begging Rations Army): *Shè*,
means "to request."
Nǚgǔdǐ: A place name.
Luòkūnsuǐ: A place name.
Ālǐzhěndǒu: A place name.
Hū'érshān: The name of a great military commander in the Western Regions (*Xīyù*).
Qǐ'érmàn: A place name.
Hǔsī Wòlǔǎn: *Sī* (思) is also written as *Sī* (斯),
meaning "having strength."
*Wòlǔǎn*,
is the name of a palace tent.
Gě'érhǎn: The title for a monarch north of the desert (*Mòběi*).
Treatise
on Rituals (*Lǐ Zhì*):
Jì Dōng (Sacrifice to the East): A national custom.
All sacrifices face east,
hence it is called Jì Dōng.
Díliè Mádū: The official in charge of rituals.
Qígǔ Zhuāilá (Flag and Drum Zhuāilá): *Zhuāilá*,
is an official title.
The military system includes the Zhuāilá Division.
This refers to the one in charge of flags and drums.
Ruò Jié (Burning Ceremony): The name of a miscellaneous ritual performed seasonally.
Jiǔ Xī Shǒu (Nine Xī Chiefs): *Xī Shǒu*,
is the name of a camp/tent.
Shí Gǔ Zhī Cì (Place of Eating the Ram): When the Grand Funeral Procession departs,
the officials sacrifice a ram (*gǔ yáng*) on the road.
It is named the Shí Gǔ Zhī Cì.
Yǎn Jì
(Yǎn Sacrifice): Whenever they went on a campaign,
one female and one male *biāo* (deer) were sacrificed; this was called *Yǎn*.
It was a curse against the enemy.
Kān Jiàn (Verifying the Arrows): When the imperial carriage returned from afar,
the Envoy of the Palace Gate (*Gémén Shǐ*) held the male arrow,
and the Kān Jiàn official held the female arrow.
They compared them to ensure they matched,
and only then entered the palace.
Yán Chuáng (Carrying Bed): If one person carried the burden on the shoulder, it was called *yán*.
If two people lifted it together with their hands, it was called *chuáng*.
Cuán Duì (Clustered Ranks): Soldiers gathered closely together,
forming various ranks and files.
Fāng Yīn, Ān Diàn (Square Mat, Ān Hall): During imperial banquets,
if the official rank was low,
they would sit on the ground upon a square platform (*fāng dūn*) inside the hall.
Those who were not permitted to ascend the hall,
were granted seats in the left and right Ān Diàn.
Dì Pāi: The name of a field mouse.
On New Year's Day (*Zhèng Dàn Rì*),
the Emperor would throw rice balls through the window.
If he obtained an odd number, it was considered unlucky,
so they would burn the *Dì Pāi* mouse to avert misfortune.
Nǎiniē Yī'ér: The morning of the first day of the first lunar month.
●lǐ pō. ● is read as xiá,
pō is read as pō.
It is the first day of the second month.
The eighteenth day of the sixth month, when the maternal uncles' clan (guó jiù zú) is feasted,
is also called ●lǐ pō.
Táo Lǐ Huà. The Shàng Sì Rì (third day of the third lunar month),
name of the festival for shooting rabbits.
Tǎo Sài Yī Ār. It is the Double Fifth Day (Chóng Wǔ Rì).
Sài Yī Ār Shē. The goodness of the day and time.
Niē Hè Nài. The dog head.
Bì Lǐ Chí Lí. It is the Double Ninth Day (Chóng Jiǔ Rì).
Dài Là. Burning the armor.
Chǎo Wǔ Ér Pō. Name of a battle.
Zhuó Zhàng. Zhuó,
means to stand.
Zhàng,
means felt tent.
Treatise on Officials:
Shí Liè Xīn Gǔn. The chief of the Shí Liè officials.
Lìng Wěn. An official title.
Mí Lǐ Mǎ Tè Běn. An official title,
later promoted to Xīn Gǔn.
Má Pǔ. This is Má Dōu Bù,
the deputy of the county official,
initially named Dá Là Gān.
Zhī Shèng Zhǐ Tóu Zi Shì. The official managing imperial mandates and reporting affairs.
Tí Xiá Sī. The officials managing troops in the various palaces.
Pí Shì. A military system.
There were the Nán, Běi, Zuǒ, Yòu Pí Shì, and the Huáng Pí Shì;
all were in charge of elite troops.
Tīng Fáng. This is the Gōng Bù (Ministry of Works).
Méi Lǐ. An official title for noble relatives.
The clan of Empress Shù Lǜ had Shèn Sī Méi Lǐ and Pó Gū Méi Lǐ,
but their duties are not detailed.
Mò Gǔ. An official of the Wǎ Lǐ Sī.
Xiān Lí Tà Lǎn. An official title in the states of Xī and Bó Hǎi, etc.
Suspected to be a corruption of the character Tà Lín.
Treatise on Palaces and Guards:
Xiàng Wěn. When the Huáng Dì governed the palace,
he molded an image of Chī Yóu and placed it on the ridge beam,
naming it Chī Wěn.
Wǎ Lǐ. Name of an official agency,
established in the imperial camps and tribal units.
Whenever members of the imperial clan, maternal relatives, or high ministers committed crimes,
their family members were confiscated and assigned here.
Mò Lǐ. Name of an official agency.
Zhá Sā Yuè is also one of the Mò Lǐ officials.
Suàn Wò Lǔ Shī. Suàn,
means trusted inner aide (fù xīn zhuài là).
Wò Lǔ Shī,
means palace.
From Guó Ā Niǎn down to Jiān Mǔ,
all are names of Wò Lǔ Shī;
their definitions
indicate the meaning of their initial establishment.
Guó Ā Niǎn. Receiving the state.
Duó Lǐ Běn. Subduing and pacifying.
Yé Lǔ Wǎn. Prosperity.
Pú Sù Wǎn. Meaning is the same as Yé Lǔ Wǎn.
Nǚ Gǔ. Gold.
Gū Wěn. Jade.
Wō Dǔ Wǎn. Reproduction and increase.
Ā Sī. Broadness and magnanimity.
Ā Lǔ Wǎn.
Assisting and protecting.
Dé Shī Dé Běn.
Filial piety.
Jiān Mǔ. Remaining.
Treatise on Geography:
Shǔ Shān. Empress Yīng Tiān followed Tài Zǔ on campaigns,
and the captured households who possessed skills were placed under her tent.
They were named Shǔ Shān,
likely comparing them to the treasure of coral (shān hú).
Yǒng Zhōu. Its land is located between the two rivers, Huáng Hé and Tǔ Hé,
thus it is named Yǒng Zhōu,
which is because the character [Yǒng] is derived from the components for ‘two’ (èr) and ‘water’ (shuǐ).
Mò Jié (Upper character pronunciation Mù Gè Qiè,
Lower character pronunciation Hú Jié Qiè).
Name of a Bó Hǎi prefecture.
Qiě Lǜ (Both are level tones).
Name of a county in Xīng Zhōng Fǔ.
Xī Yǎng (The first character is pronounced xī).
Name of a marsh in Yōu Zhōu,
found in the Zhōu Zhí Fāng.
Zī and Shí. Names of flooded areas in Yōu Zhōu,
cited from the same source as above.
Duò Guī. Name of a gate.
The Liáo had the Duò Guī Department.
Yě Lǚ Yín. Yě refers to the celestial field,
Lǚ refers to the orbital sequence;
Yín
is a celestial mansion.
It is the northeast position,
which corresponds to the Yān astrological division Fēn Jīn.
Treatise on Rites and Guards:
Jīn (Lower character pronunciation Zǔ Cóng Qiè).
An ornament for a horse's head.
Guǒ Xià Mǎ. Name of a horse.
Meaning one that can be ridden under fruit trees,
indicating its small size.
Shí Lǐ Xuē Gǔn. A crown used with sacrificial robes,
worn when performing the rite of mountain worship (bài shān lǐ).
●Dié Dài (Upper character pronunciation Tā Xié Qiè,
Lower character pronunciation Tú Xié Qiè).
A belt worn by military officials.
Hàn Yāo. This is Zhǔ Yāo,
made from goose necks and duck heads.
Hú Mù Móu. Name of a helmet.
Dàn Mǎ (Upper character pronounced dàn).
A horse ridden without a saddle or reins is called Dàn.
Bái Èr (Pronounced èr).
A net made of white egret feathers,
and also a rug.
Treatise on Military Affairs and Guards:
Zhuō Mǎ. Catching and grooming horses.
Lán Zi Jūn. Troops stationed twenty or more lǐ ahead of the vanguard,
to scout the enemy’s movements.
Gōng Zi Pù. A Liáo military stable and bivouac.
No camp fortifications or trenches were set up.
They bent the tips of branches into bows
to serve as a place for assembly.
Furthermore, when envoys from various states arrived,
bow-shaped twigs were placed along the road
to serve as fences.
Treatise on Food and Money:
Yún Wéi Hù.
The meaning is managing operations,
a corruption of the characters.
Treatise on Law:
Zhōng Yuàn. Those who had a grievance struck the bell
to reach the authorities above,
similar to the "Drum of Complaint" (Yuàn Gǔ).
Chǔ Gǔ. An official title.
In charge of interrogating prisoners facing north.
Tables:
Table of Imperial Sons:
Wǔ Shí Liè. This is the Wǔ Yuàn (Five Bureaus).
It is not that the bureau was divided into five,
but that the Wǔ Shí Liè constituted one bureau.
Liù Zhǎo. Zhǎo,
means the number hundred.
The Liáo had six hundred Xī families,
which later became the Liù Yuàn (Six Bureaus).
The meaning is the same as the Wǔ Yuàn.
Èr Yuàn (Two Bureaus).
This refers to the Dié Là Department being split into two.
Liè Pí.
Male deer.
The strength required to tear the hide of a male deer.
Genealogical Tables:
Mò Fú Gē. Title used by the chieftains of various tribes,
also said to be Mò Fú Hè.
Rú Ruǎn (Pronunciation Ér Xuān Qiè).
Name of a state.
Qí Jīn. A Tū Jué official title.
Table of Imperial Tours:
Tiǎn Xián Lù (Licking Salt Deer).
Deer naturally crave salt.
Salt is sprinkled on the ground to lure the deer
and shoot them.
Nǚ Guī.
Name of a game warden.
Biographies:
Kě Dūn. The title for the Empress of the Tū Jué.
Tè Lǐ Jiǎn. The title for the Empress of the Liáo.
Nòu Wò Ma. Ma,
is also written Gǎi.
Nòu Wò,
is the title for the Earth Goddess (Hòu Tǔ).
Ma,
is the title for mother.
Yǐ Shì and Bá Lǐ. Names of the two clans of the Imperial Maternal Uncle’s tent (Guó Jiù Zhàng).
Biographies of Meritorious Ministers:
Lóng Xī Jīn Pèi (Dragon-Bestowed Gold Pendant). Tài Zǔ’s cousin, Duó Gǔ Zhá, heard a snake crying under his own tent.
He ordered Shén Sù Gū, who understood snake language, to interpret it.
It was learned that the snake meant there was gold inside the tree next to its hole.
They went and retrieved it,
and indeed obtained gold,
which was made into a belt
named
“Lóng Xī Jīn.”
Sā Là. Name of a wine vessel.
Yáo Niǎn Jiū. The troops under the Yáo Niǎn Tent.
The terms written as Yǒng Xīng Gōng Fēn Jiū, Shí Èr Háng Jiū, and Huáng Pí Shì Jiū
follow this precedent.
Tù Lǐ. An official title.
It is the same as the Tū Lǐ of the Xī Six Departments.
The characters Tù and Tū are corruptions.
Qǐn Diàn Xiǎo Dǐ. An official title.
The Liáo system frequently used Xiǎo Dǐ officials,
the remainder are not annotated.
Miscellaneous *Dīng Huáng* (Adults and Minors)
In the rites, a young male is called *huáng*,
four years old is *xiǎo* (small/junior),
sixteen is *zhōng* (middle/intermediate),
twenty-one is *dīng* (adult/able-bodied).
In the military, the young and weak were mixed in,
in order to confuse the enemy.
*Yáoliǎn Kè*: The officer in charge of military affairs under the *Yáoliǎn* tent.
*Dǐhù*: Temporary barricades (*xíngmǎ*) outside the gates of the palace guard.
*Gǔduò Xī*: The horn of a thousand-year-old serpent/dragon.
It is also called *Dǔnà Xī*.
Two *bèi* of pearls (The character below is pronounced *pú wèi qiē* [a Fanqie spelling]).
Five hundred pearls constitute one *bèi*.
*Tílǐ Sītú*: *Tílǐ*
is the name of the governmental office.
*Zhìzhōng* (The character above is pronounced *zhì lì qiē* [a Fanqie spelling]).
A place name.
*Tángyìn*: The name of a scoring result in the game of *bó* (a kind of dice/board game).
*Línkù*: Using silk as a comprehensive register,
listing all the objects in one treasury,
recording them all,
is called *Línkù*.
*Tángtiě*: Under the *Liáo* system,
when prime ministers were appointed or dismissed,
a preliminary assignment was issued via a *tángtiě* from the *tóuzi* (head official),
and after further imperial approval was sought,
the formal edict (*gàochì*) was issued.
Therefore, the officials had the role of "knowing the affairs of the *tóuzi*."
Seen in *Yīnshān Zá Lù*.
*Yílíjǐn Huàzhě*: *Huàzhě* is a personal name,
serving as the official *Yílíjǐn*.
*Hǔsī*: A term signifying great strength.
Some records write it as
*Hǔsī* (with the thought radical),
the meaning is the same.
Imperial Edict on Compiling the Three Histories
Imperial Decree: On the fourteenth day of the third month of the third year of the *Zhìzhèng* era,
the third day of *Dǔlián Tièmù'ér*'s *qièxuē* (duty rotation),
at the time when the officials were present in the *Xiánníng* Hall,
attending were *Sùgǔ'érchì Jiāngjiānú*, *Yúndūchì Mánzǐ*, *Diànzhōng Andūlàhāmán*, *Jǐshìzhōng Bólúo Tièmù'ér*, and others.

*Tuōtuō* Right Chancellor, *Yěxiān Tièmù'ér* Administrator, *Tiěmù'ěr Dáshì* Administrator, *Tàipíng* Right Assistant, *Chángxiān* Counselor, *Bólǐbùhuā* Director, *Lǎolǎo* Vice Director, *Bólǐbùhuā* Recorder, and others reported: The histories of the three states—*Liáo*, *Jīn*, and *Sòng*—have not yet been compiled,
we have consulted and believe that the historical accounts of these dynasties should be compiled into books.
Now, suitable people should be selected to compile the accounts of these three states into histories,
without delay.
Regarding all matters that should be carried out,
we have prepared a draft proposal.
How should this proposal be submitted?
It was decreed according to the Imperial Will.
On the twenty-eighth day of the third month,
the second day of *Bié'érqièbùhuā*'s *qièxuē*,
at the time when the officials were present in the *Xiánníng* Hall,
attending were *Sùgǔ'érchì Bùyán Tièmù'ér*, *Yúndūchì Mánzǐ*, *Diànzhōng Andūlàhāmán*, *Jǐshìzhōng Bólúo Tièmù'ér*, and others.

*Tuōtuō* Right Chancellor, *Yěxiān Tièmù'ér* Administrator, *Tiěmù'ěr Dáshì* Administrator, *Tàipíng* Right Assistant, *Wú* Administrator, *Mǎizhúdīng* Counselor, *Chángxiān* Counselor, *Hán* Counselor, *Biélǐbùhuā* Director, Director *Wáng*, *Lǎolǎo* Vice Director, *Kǒng* Vice Director, *Guānyīnnú* Recorder, *Bólǐbùhuā* Recorder, *Dù* Recorder, *Zhíshěng Shèrén Cāngchì Yěxiān*, *Měnggǔ Bìshéchì Suǒzhù*, *Dūmǎ*, and others reported: Previously, concerning the historical accounts of the three states—*Liáo*, *Jīn*, and *Sòng*—
we had already submitted a report proposing that suitable people be selected to compile them into histories.
The systems, institutions, governance, disorder, rise, and fall of these three states, which were absorbed by the Holy Dynasty,
we fear might be scattered and lost due to the passage of time.
It is appropriate to select civil officials,
divide the history projects, and establish separate bureaus,
to compile them into books,
so as to demonstrate how our ancestors, by their great virtue, obtained the lands of the three states of *Liáo*, *Jīn*, and *Sòng*,
serving as a model for later generations,
and establishing a great institution for our era.
The compilation shall be carried out by separate bureaus under the *Hànlín Guóshǐ Yuàn* (Hanlin Academy and National History Office),
with dedicated staff for this duty.
From the *Jíxián* Academy, the Secretariat, the *Chóngwén* Institute, and all inner and outer government offices,
those whose learning is broad and refined, whose talent and virtue are excellent and pure,
and who are qualified for the task shall be judiciously selected and assigned.
During the compilation process,
there will be discussions about what to include or exclude;
there might inevitably be public or private biases regarding what is correct.
Therefore, the Chief Supervisors must be appointed to verify right and wrong,
and decide what is permissible or not.
People of high standing, experience, and maturity,
excelling in historical scholarship,
and respected by all, shall be selected as the Chief Supervisors.
The veritable records (*shílù*), unofficial histories (*yěshǐ*), biographies (*zhuànjì*), stele inscriptions (*bēiwén*), and conduct narratives (*xíngshí*) concerning these three states,
are mostly scattered throughout the four directions.
The Provincial Secretariats (*Xíngshěng*) and the chief officials of various localities shall be instructed to oversee
the extensive search and procurement,
allowing all people to present them,
and providing compensation according to their value.
They shall inform the *Shěng* (Secretariat) and the *Bù* (Ministries),
and send the materials to the History Office,
for selection and reference.
Regarding the necessary paper, writing brushes, and ink,
and all other supplies and materials,
the funds and provisions from the academic colleges and the estates of presented scholars under the jurisdiction of *Jiāngxī*, *Húguǎng*, *Jiāngzhè*, and *Hénán* Provinces,
after reserving the amounts required for sacrifices, stipends, civil examinations, and repairs,
shall all be transferred and delivered,
to meet the expenses of the History Office.
Now, Chancellor *Tuōtuō* of the Secretariat, acting as Supervisor of National History Compilation, shall be the Chief General Supervisor.

*Tiěmù'ěr Dáshì* Administrator, *Tàipíng* Right Assistant, *Zhāng* Vice Censor-in-Chief, Grand Academician *Ōuyáng*, Imperial Attendant *Lǚ*, and Academician *Jiē* shall be appointed as Chief Supervisors.
Regarding the Directors-General:
From the Secretariat, *Yěxiān Tièmù'ér* Administrator and *Wú* Administrator;
From the Bureau of Military Affairs, *Tǎshī Tièmù'ér* Second Deputy and Vice Commissioner *Yáo*;

From the Censorate, Imperial Attendant *Gǒu'ér*, *Zhāng Zhìshū*, *Mǎizhúdīng* Counselor, *Chángxiān* Counselor, *Hán* Counselor, Director *Wáng* (Right Division), Director *Wáng* (Left Division), *Lǎolǎo* Vice Director, *Kǒng* Vice Director, *Guānyīnnú* Recorder, and *Dù* Recorder;
The Chief Officials and the Executive Officials of the Six Ministries shall each be commissioned as Directors-General.
The remaining general rules for historical compilation and all matters that should be carried out
shall be jointly discussed and implemented by the Chief Supervisors and the Historical Compilers.
How should this proposal be submitted?
It was decreed according to the Imperial Will.
Memorial Presenting the *Liáo Shǐ* (History of Liáo)

Report by Your Subject *Tuōtuō*, Grand Minister with Administrative Authority, Pillar of the State, Recorder of Important Military and State Affairs, Right Chancellor of the Central Secretariat, Supervisor of National History Compilation, and Director of the Imperial Lectures: I humbly observe that nothing verifies celestial patterns better than the armillary sphere (*jīhéng*),
and nothing authenticates human civilization better than historical records (*jiǎncè*).
When the ruler observes the auspiciousness or misfortune of celestial phenomena,
he must scrutinize the precision of the *jīhéng*;
when he observes the success or failure of human affairs,
he must examine the reliability of the historical records.
Therefore, those in charge of both matters
are all called Grand Historians (*Tàishǐ*).
However, the Way of Heaven is mysterious and difficult to know,
while human nature is manifest and easy to perceive.
Activity and stillness are omens of fortune and misfortune;
diligence and neglect are the mechanisms of rise and fall.
Although historians recount the actions and institutions of previous dynasties,
the great purpose is to assist the ruler by offering warnings and precedents.
The *Liáo* (dynasty), originating from the end of the *Táng* period,
established its foundation in the northern region (*Shuòfāng*).
Their founding relied fundamentally on weapons and warfare;
their achievement of stable governance was supported by civilized adornment (ritual and law).
They revered Heaven and honored their ancestors,
always offering sacrifices upon departing or returning;
they associated with the benevolent and maintained good relations with neighbors,
managing peace and war appropriately.
The Southern Chancellery governed the people;
the Northern Chancellery governed the military.
The spring hunt was used to observe the plowing;
the autumn hunt was used to observe the harvest.
The evaluation of officials was strict regarding fodder and animal husbandry;
in years of famine, they repeatedly bestowed remissions on agricultural taxes.
As for observing the market and granting pardons,
these actions fully matched the regulations of the Six Canons (*Liù Diǎn*);
and holding imperial examinations from the court balcony to select scholars,
strictly followed the triennial system.
They enjoyed the state for two hundred and nineteen years;
their governance and laws were carried out daily,
and their standards and regulations were complete.
Truly, there were matters worthy of high regard.
However, when their descendants lost control of the government,
the loyalty of those above and below was fractured.
Arrogance and excess flourished, and internal fissures appeared;
slander and wickedness arose, and the foundation was threatened.
The transformation from strength to weakness
was easier than turning one's hand over.
Alas!
How dreadful!
*Tiānzuò* (Emperor of Liáo) brought about his own end,
while *Dàshí* barely prolonged existence (referring to the Western *Liáo*).
The state was reduced to ruins,
and the historical records were also overgrown and neglected.
*Yélǜ Yǎn*'s narrative contained many suppressions and evasions;
*Chén Dàrèn*'s account lacked precision and detail.
The *History of the Five Dynasties* attached it to the end of its chapters;
the old *Sòng* history treated it merely as miscellaneous records (*zǎijì*).
What was included or excluded followed the biases of their respective rulers,
and the transmitted hearsay narratives often lost their veracity.
Our Founding Emperor *Shìzǔ Huángdì*, treating all equally,
extended deep sympathy and compassion.
He once decreed that the literary ministers compile and arrange the Three Histories,
starting first with *Liáo*.
More than sixty years passed,
the years procrastinated,
but Creation awaited (this task).
Your subject, Tuòtuō, reverently and sincerely bows his head.
I respectfully consider Your Imperial Majesty,
who like Yáo, investigates antiquity,
and is broad-minded and accommodating of the multitude;
who like Shùn, loves to inquire,
and whose profound wisdom surpasses all others.
You lecture on the classics while also reciting ancestral precepts,
and in seeking good governance, you extensively consult past records.
Now, this project of compiling history
is decided by Your Imperial heart.
As Your sagacious decree descended, invitations were issued,
court officials congratulated, and forgotten talents emerged.
Thereupon, Your subject Tuòtuō was appointed as Chancellor of the Right of the Central Secretariat, leading as Chief Compiler-in-Chief.
Tiěmùěrdáshì, Grand Councilor of the Central Secretariat;

Hè Wéiyī, Chancellor of the Right of the Central Secretariat, now Grand Councilor; Zhāng Qǐyán, Censor-in-Chief, now Academician-in-waiting of the Hanlin Academy; Ōuyáng Xuán, Hanlin Academician; Lǚ Sīchéng, Imperial Censor, now Scholar of the Jíxián Academy and Libationer of the Directorate of Education; Jiē Xīsī, Hanlin Academician-in-waiting, were appointed as Compiling Officials.

From the Central Secretariat, Confucian scholars and respected eunuchs were selected: Liánhuì Shānhǎiyá, now Minister of War; Wáng Yí, Hanlin Academician; Xú Bǐng, Editor of the Secretariat; Chén Yìzēng, Compiler of the National History Institute, were assigned to compile the History of the Liáo Dynasty.
The work began in the fourth month of the third year of Zhìzhèng,
and concluded in the third month of the fourth year.
From the stored archives of the old imperial library,
and from tributes offered by distant regions,
materials were collected and sifted through,
then edited, refined, and polished.
Annals, Treatises, Tables, and Biographies
were fully compiled into a history of an era;
evaluations of good and bad, right and wrong,
ensure that the truths of a thousand years are not obscured.
Your subject Tuòtuō, having been entrusted with this great responsibility,
is fortunate to witness its completion.
May it proclaim the splendor of the sun and moon,
and may this small effort contribute to Your Majesty's glory.
The discussions of our dynasty are now rightly guided,
for when the spirit is upright, the words flourish;
should the rulers and ministers of the Liáo state possess awareness,
the good among them will rejoice, and the wicked will fear.
The work comprises thirty volumes of Annals, thirty-two volumes of Treatises,
eight volumes of Tables, and forty-six volumes of Biographies,
each with critical essays and eulogies,
fully embodying the established style,
and is herewith presented along with the tables.
May it ascend to Your Heavenly gaze.
Your humble servant's feelings are overwhelmed with shame, fear, trembling, and apprehension.
Your subject Tuòtuō reverently, sincerely, and humbly bows his head, bowing again and again, respectfully submitting this.
On this day in the third month of the fourth year of Zhìzhèng,

Your subject Tuòtuō, Kaīfǔ Yítóng Sānsī, Shàng Zhùguó, Lù Jūnguó Zhòngshì, Chancellor of the Right of the Central Secretariat, Supervisor of National History, and concurrently Overseer of the Imperial Lectures,
submits this memorial.
General Principles for the Three Histories
1. Imperial Annals: For the writing style of the annals of the Three Dynasties,
we follow the Shǐjì, Xī Hànshū, and Xīn Tángshū.
For titles and other matters concerning the various states,
we follow the Nánshǐ and Běishǐ.
1. Treatises: From the contents recorded in the various histories,
we select the most important ones to form the treatises.
1. Tables: Tables are similar to treatises.
1. Biographies: Empresses and Consorts,
Imperial Clan,
Imperial Relatives by Marriage,
Ministers,
and Miscellaneous Biographies.
For those subjects who rendered great service,
even if father and son, each receives a separate biography.
Others are grouped by category,
or several individuals share one biography.
Matters recorded in the Three Histories that relate to our present dynasty
should be reported.
Ministers who died for the Jīn and Sòng dynasties
should all have biographies,
without needing to avoid any taboos.
For other matters that cannot be fully included,
the Chief Compilers and Compiling Officials will deliberate in detail when drafting the text.
1. Doubtful matters are recorded as doubtful,
and credible matters are recorded as credible,
following the Chūnqiū.
